In the summer of 1958 an engineer named Jack Kilby, new at Texas Instruments, had the idea that all the parts of a circuit could be made from the same piece of semiconductor. On September 12 he showed a working circuit, built from a sliver of germanium, with fine wires linking the parts. It was crude, but it worked, and it was the first integrated circuit.
Months later, at Fairchild Semiconductor, Robert Noyce thought of a version that did away with the wires, by laying thin metal lines over a layer of oxide on silicon, using a process invented by his colleague Jean Hoerni. That was the version that could be made in large numbers. The courts gave Kilby credit for the idea and Noyce for the process, and the companies shared their licenses in 1966. Kilby won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000. Noyce had died in 1977.
A calculator and the first microprocessor

In 1969 a Japanese company, Busicom, asked the young company Intel to design a set of chips for a line of printing calculators. The first plan needed a dozen chips, each built for one task. Intel's Ted Hoff and Stan Mazor suggested a simpler design, with one general chip that could be programmed to do different jobs. Federico Faggin, who joined Intel in 1970, and Masatoshi Shima of Busicom worked out the details.
The result was the Intel 4004, a chip that handled four bits at a time, with 2,300 transistors and a clock speed of 740 kilohertz. Intel advertised it in November 1971 as a computer on a chip. Intel bought back the rights from Busicom, which was in financial trouble, in return for the money that Busicom had paid. It is widely called the first commercial microprocessor, and its descendants run phones, cars and machines today.
Three dots, from across the ocean

On December 12, 1901, on a cold hill in Newfoundland, the Italian inventor Guglielmo Marconi and his assistant George Kemp sat with a telephone earpiece pressed to the ear. They had flown a kite, to raise a long wire that served as an antenna, after the wind broke a balloon that they had planned to use. At a station in Poldhu, in Cornwall, England, a transmitter was sending the Morse code for the letter S, three short dots, again and again.
Marconi said that he heard them. The distance was about 3,400 kilometers. Many scientists doubted it, since radio waves were thought to travel in straight lines, and so should not curve around the Earth. The claim could not be checked, since only the two men had heard it. Later and better tests showed that the signals can in fact travel far, by reflecting from a layer in the upper atmosphere. In 1909 Marconi shared the Nobel Prize in Physics.
The song that nearly broke the MP3

In the late 1980s the German engineer Karlheinz Brandenburg was working on how to compress music to a small size. His idea was to throw away the parts of a sound that the ear cannot hear anyway, such as a quiet tone right after a loud one. To test it he used many pieces of music. One of them caused a problem. It was Tom's Diner, a song by Suzanne Vega, sung without any instruments.
A single voice, with nothing else to mask the flaws, was very hard to compress, and in his early version the voice was badly distorted. Brandenburg listened to the song hundreds of times, as he refined the method with colleagues, including Jim Johnston of AT&T. The result was the third layer of the MPEG-1 audio standard, which was named MP3. It made music files about a tenth of their size, and it started the age of downloaded and streamed music.

In 1983 an engineer named Chuck Hull, who worked with ultraviolet light to harden coatings on tables, had an idea. If he aimed a beam at the surface of a bath of liquid plastic, it would harden only the spot that the light touched. By hardening one thin layer, lowering it, and hardening the next, he could build up an object. He made a small black cup that way, and called the method stereolithography.
A team in France had filed a patent for the same process a few weeks earlier, in July 1984, but they let it lapse. Hull's patent was issued on March 11, 1986, and he founded 3D Systems, which sold its first machines in the late 1980s for about 100,000 dollars. At first the machines made models for designers. Later the technique, called 3D printing, was extended to metal, to concrete, and to parts for aircraft and medicine.
The shot-down plane and your phone

On September 1, 1983, Korean Air Lines Flight 007 strayed off its route and into Soviet airspace, and was shot down, with 269 people on board, after a navigation error. In the aftermath President Ronald Reagan said that the American satellite navigation system, GPS, then still being built for the military, would be made freely available for civilian use, to prevent such disasters.
The civilian signal, though, was deliberately degraded, in a program called Selective Availability, so that it was less accurate than the military one. On May 1, 2000, President Bill Clinton ordered that the degrading be stopped, and the switch was made just after midnight. Overnight, civilian receivers became much more accurate. Today GPS guides cars, phones, farm machinery and airplanes, and it keeps the clocks of banks and networks in time.
The cloudy liquid that was almost thrown out

In 1965 the chemist Stephanie Kwolek, who worked for DuPont, was looking for a new fiber, one stronger and stiffer than the nylon that her company already made. She mixed a polymer in a solvent, and got a liquid that was thin and cloudy. Solutions like that were usually thrown away, since they were expected to be thick and clear. She asked a technician to spin it into fibers, in a machine with tiny holes called a spinneret.
The technician at first was reluctant, because he thought that it would clog the machine. When he finally did, the fiber was strong, five times stronger than steel for its weight. It was named Kevlar, and it was sold from 1971. It is used in bulletproof vests, tires, ropes and cables, and in the hulls of boats. It is a good example of looking carefully at an odd result, and not just discarding it.
A gray brick that sold a hundred million

In 1989 Nintendo released the Game Boy in Japan, on April 21. It had a small, gray-green screen with no color, and no backlight, and it ran for many hours on four batteries. Its designer was Gunpei Yokoi, an engineer whose rule was to use old, cheap and well-understood technology in new ways, which he called lateral thinking with withered technology. His rivals' machines had color screens and cost more, and ran out of battery in a few hours.
In North America and Europe, the Game Boy was sold with a game called Tetris, a puzzle of falling blocks that had come from Russia. Anyone could play it, and it drew adults as well as children. Together, the Game Boy and its successor the Game Boy Color sold more than 118 million units. It showed that a game machine did not need the best technology to succeed, and that a good game, and a price, and battery life, could matter more.
The picture that taught computers to compress

In 1973 a group of researchers at the University of Southern California needed a picture to test a method of image compression. They were in a hurry. Someone walked in with a copy of a magazine, and they scanned the top part of the centerfold. It was a photo of a model, Lena Forsén, taken by Dwight Hooker, in the November 1972 issue of Playboy, and it was a lucky choice.
It had faces, fine detail, smooth areas and texture, so it showed what a method did well or badly. Others adopted it, and it became the standard test picture in image processing for decades. It was not licensed. In 1991 Playboy raised its objection, though in time it let it pass. Some journals have since asked authors not to use it, because it was taken from a nude photo. It is a reminder that a convenient choice can set a standard.
Thinking about it over and over

When something bad happens, some people go over it again and again in their minds, asking why it happened and what it means. Psychologists call this rumination. On October 17, 1989, a strong earthquake struck near Loma Prieta, in California. Susan Nolen-Hoeksema and Jannay Morrow had, by chance, measured the moods and the ways of coping of 137 college students about two weeks earlier, and they were able to follow them up.
They checked the students again ten days after the earthquake and about seven weeks after. Those who already tended to ruminate had more symptoms of depression and stress at both times. Students who spent more time in the first ten days brooding on the quake were also still more distressed at seven weeks. It was an unplanned natural experiment, and it suggested that how we think about trouble can keep it going.
Why a lower rung means a shorter life

In the late 1960s the epidemiologist Michael Marmot and his colleagues began to follow more than 17,500 male civil servants in London, all of whom had steady jobs, secure pay and access to health care. The men worked in government offices, in a strict ladder of grades. At the top were the administrators, and at the bottom were messengers and doorkeepers. The researchers recorded each man's grade, and then waited to see who died.
The men in the lowest grade had death rates about three times higher than those in the highest grade. It was not a gap between the rich and the poor, since all of them were in work. The gradient ran through every step, with each grade healthier than the one below. The risk factors of smoking, weight and blood pressure explained only a part. Marmot proposed that a low position, with less control over one's work, is itself a source of stress, and a risk to health.
The town that was said to be safe from heart attacks

In the 1960s a doctor in Pennsylvania mentioned to the physician Stewart Wolf that he had hardly seen any of the patients in the town of Roseto with heart disease. The town had been settled by people from one village in Italy. Wolf studied it, and found that the death rates from heart attack were much lower than in the neighboring towns. The people ate fatty food and smoked, but they lived in close families, with several generations in the same house.
The finding was published in 1964 and became known as the Roseto effect. Wolf's explanation was the closeness of the community. In 1992 a team that included Wolf compared the death certificates from 1935 to 1985. The advantage lasted for about thirty years, and then vanished, as the younger people moved away, and the old customs weakened. The result fits the idea that social ties protect health, but it does not prove it.
The places where people live to a hundred

Starting in 2005 the writer Dan Buettner, with demographers, described several regions of the world where people were said to live unusually long. They included Okinawa in Japan, Sardinia in Italy, Nicoya in Costa Rica, and Ikaria in Greece. He called them Blue Zones, and listed the habits of their people, such as eating plants, staying active, and keeping close ties with family and friends.
The demographer Saul Justin Newman has argued that the records of age in these places are unreliable. He points to errors in old documents, to pension claims, and to the loss of birth records, and notes that the regions are often poor, with low national life expectancy. The researchers behind the Blue Zones answered that they checked ages from several sources. The dispute is not settled. It is a good reason to check the records behind a claim of extreme age.

In 1956 the young psychologist K. Warner Schaie, for his doctoral research at the University of Washington, began to measure the mental abilities of adults of different ages, in Seattle. He kept going for the rest of his career. Every seven years he tested the same people again, and brought in new groups, so that he could tell apart the effect of getting older from the effect of the year that one was born.
The results showed that different abilities follow different courses. Skills in vocabulary and verbal meaning went on improving into middle age, and declined only late, in the seventies. Abilities that require working out new problems, or speed, start to fall earlier. Comparing different people of different ages can make the decline look steeper than it is, since later generations tend to score higher. Most people stay mentally able for a long time.

Some employers have asked experts in handwriting analysis, called graphologists, to judge job applicants from a sample of writing. The experts claim to read personality in the slant, size and pressure of the letters. In the 1980s the Israeli psychologists Gershon Ben-Shakhar, Maya Bar-Hillel and their colleagues tested it. They gave graphologists handwriting samples and asked them to predict how the writers would do at work.
The graphologists did no better than chance, and a psychologist who knew nothing of graphology did as well. In 1989 Eyal Neter and Ben-Shakhar pooled seventeen studies. The validity was near zero when the script was neutral, such as copying a text. When the writers told about their lives, the predictions did better, but the content of what they said was the reason, and not the handwriting. People believe in graphology because the readings sound right about anyone.

In 1876 the Italian doctor Cesare Lombroso published a book that claimed that some people are born criminals. He had examined skulls and bodies of prisoners, and believed that they showed signs of an earlier stage of human evolution, such as a sloping forehead, large jaws and long arms. These signs, he said, could be used to spot a criminal. The idea was very influential in Europe and America.
In 1913 the English prison doctor Charles Goring published a large study. With Karl Pearson's statistical laboratory, he measured ninety-six traits of more than three thousand convicts, and compared them with other groups. He found no physical type of criminal. The convicts were on average a little smaller and lighter, and scored lower on mental tests, but he took those differences to be inherited, a view that was itself criticized. Lombroso's idea lost its standing, but it left a lasting habit of judging character from looks.
The students who were photographed nude

From the 1940s to the 1960s, freshmen at many American universities, including Harvard, Yale and Princeton, were asked to pose for photographs without clothes. The reason given was a study of posture. The psychologist William Sheldon used thousands of the pictures for a different purpose. He rated each body on three scales, which he called endomorphy, mesomorphy and ectomorphy, meaning roundness, muscle and thinness, and claimed that body type reveals temperament.
His 1954 Atlas of Men sorted the types on a scale of one to seven. Other scientists rejected the link to character, and a former assistant said that his methods were unsound. In 1995 the writer Ron Rosenbaum reported in the New York Times that the pictures were in the Smithsonian, and that many of the people photographed had never been told what the pictures were really used for. Most of the photographs were later destroyed. It is a case of bad science and bad consent.

In the late 1940s the Canadian sociologist Erving Goffman spent more than a year on Unst, one of the Shetland Islands, watching how the islanders behaved in everyday life. Out of it came his book, The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life. His idea was that social life resembles theater. We play roles, with a front stage, where we manage the impression that we make, and a back stage, where we can relax and drop the act.
A waiter who is smooth in the dining room may swear in the kitchen. A teacher who is calm in class may complain in the staff room. He called it impression management, and argued that it is not fake, because it is how we all keep social life running. His work led to a style of research that looks at the small details of gestures and speech. It makes a person wonder which of their own roles they take for granted.
The one factor behind many tests

At the start of the twentieth century the English psychologist Charles Spearman made an observation about schoolchildren. Those who did well in one subject, say classics, tended to do well in others, such as French, mathematics and music. They also tended to do well on simple tests of discriminating pitch and weight. Every correlation between these tests was positive. Nobody expected that if the mind were a set of unrelated skills.
In 1904 Spearman proposed that there is a general factor, which he called g, that is in play in all mental tasks, along with specific factors for each. The idea became the foundation of intelligence testing. People still argue about what g is and how much it explains. But the finding that mental tests tend to correlate positively, which is sometimes called the positive manifold, has been found over and over, in many countries and in many kinds of tests.
The gap between primes, in the end, is bounded

Prime numbers get rarer as the numbers get larger, so you might expect the gaps between one prime and the next to grow without limit. The twin prime conjecture says that there are infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by just two, such as 11 and 13, or 17 and 19. Nobody has proved it. In April 2013 a little-known mathematician, Yitang Zhang, who was a lecturer at the University of New Hampshire, showed that there are infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by less than 70 million.
Seventy million is a large gap, but it is finite, and that was the point. Within months, a collaborative online project of many mathematicians brought it down to 4,680. Then James Maynard, a young researcher, and Terence Tao, found a simpler method, and the Polymath project reduced the bound to 246. Nobody has got it down to two. But the first step was taken, by someone who had spent years without an academic post.

Draw parallel lines on the floor, a distance t apart, and drop a needle of length l, no longer than t, at random. The French naturalist Buffon showed that the chance that the needle crosses a line is two times l, divided by pi times t. The odds depend on pi. So you can estimate pi by dropping a needle many times and counting how often it crosses. It was published in 1777, and it is one of the first problems solved with geometric probability.
In 1901 an Italian mathematician, Mario Lazzarini, reported that he had done it, with a needle of 25 millimeters and lines 30 millimeters apart. In 3,408 tosses, he got 1,808 crossings, and that gave 355 over 113, or 3.1415929, correct to six places. It is too good. The number of tosses is 213 times 16, which suggests that he stopped when the count gave the answer that he wanted. It is a standard example of confirmation bias in science.

The Julian calendar, which Julius Caesar introduced, had a year that was slightly too long, by about eleven minutes. Over centuries the error built up, and by the sixteenth century the spring equinox, which the Church used to fix Easter, had slipped by ten days. In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII decreed a new calendar, with a better rule for leap years. To catch up, ten days were dropped. In Spain, Portugal and most of Italy, Thursday, October 4, was followed by Friday, October 15.
Protestant countries held out for a long time. Britain and its colonies changed in 1752, when the gap was eleven days, so that September 2 was followed by September 14. There is a popular story that people rioted and shouted, Give us our eleven days. Historians have found little evidence of it, and the main source seems to be a banner in a painting by Hogarth. Some rural people did keep celebrating Christmas on the old date, in January.
The student who was Monsieur Le Blanc

Sophie Germain was born in Paris in 1776. As a girl she taught herself mathematics from books in her father's library, reading at night, in spite of her family's objections. Women could not enroll at the École Polytechnique, but she managed to obtain the lecture notes of the courses. She sent in her solutions to the problems under the name of a former student, Monsieur Le Blanc. The professor Joseph-Louis Lagrange was struck by the quality, and asked to meet the author. When he found out, he became her mentor.
In 1804 she wrote to the great mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, again as Le Blanc, about number theory and Fermat's Last Theorem. She said that she feared the ridicule that attached to a woman who studied science. Her main result, now called Germain's theorem, proved the first case of the Last Theorem for any odd prime p, when two times p plus one is also prime. It was the most significant progress for a long time. Legendre published it, in a footnote.
The first woman professor of mathematics

Sofia Kovalevskaya was born in Russia in 1850. Women could not go to university in her country, so she married, in a marriage of convenience, to be able to travel abroad. In Germany she could not enroll either, and she studied privately with the great mathematician Karl Weierstrass. In 1874 the University of Göttingen gave her a doctorate, summa cum laude, without an oral examination, on the strength of three papers, one on partial differential equations.
She was the first woman to receive a doctorate in mathematics in modern times. Jobs were hard to find, but in 1883 she was invited to lecture at the University of Stockholm, and in 1889 she became a full professor. In 1888 she won the Bordin Prize of the Paris Academy, for her work on how a spinning top moves, and the judges raised the prize because her paper was so good. She died in 1891, at the age of forty-one.

If you tile a bathroom floor, the pattern repeats, and you can shift it and it matches itself. It was long believed that any pattern with the order of a crystal had to repeat in this way, and that five-fold symmetry, like that of a star with five points, was impossible. In 1974 the mathematician Roger Penrose found two shapes of tile that cover a plane with fivefold symmetry, in a pattern that is ordered but never repeats exactly.
In 1982 the chemist Dan Shechtman saw, in an electron microscope, a metal alloy whose atoms formed a pattern of this kind. His colleagues did not believe him, and the famous chemist Linus Pauling said that there were no quasicrystals, only quasi-scientists. More examples were found, and quasicrystals were accepted as a new kind of solid. In 2011 Shechtman won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. A pattern from mathematics had been found in nature.
The salesman who visited forty-eight states

A traveling salesman wants to visit a set of cities, once each, and return home, by the shortest route. With only a few cities it is easy. With more, the number of possible routes grows so fast that even the fastest computers cannot check them all. For 20 cities there are more than a million billion tours. Despite its simple form, the problem has become one of the best known in computer science.
In 1954 George Dantzig, Ray Fulkerson and Selmer Johnson, at the RAND Corporation, found the shortest road route that visits one city in each of the 48 states and Washington, D.C. They did not try the routes. They used linear programming, and added extra conditions that cut away false solutions, and they solved by hand, with a drawing. They worked on 42 cities and extended it to 49. Their method of adding cuts is still at the heart of the programs that solve such problems.
Waves inside a hot iron bar

Joseph Fourier was a French mathematician who went with Napoleon's army to Egypt, and later served as a prefect. In his spare time he studied how heat flows through a solid. In 1807 he claimed that the temperature along a bar, however irregular, could be written as a sum of simple waves, sines and cosines of different frequencies. Some of the leading mathematicians of the day doubted it. His book on the subject appeared in 1822.
The idea turned out to be one of the most useful in science. Any signal, whether a sound, an image, or a radio wave, can be broken into its component frequencies, and put together again. The methods used to store pictures in a file, to compress music, and to clean noise from a recording are descendants of his idea. He also wrote in the 1820s that the atmosphere helps to keep the Earth warm, an early statement of the greenhouse effect.
A number too big to write down

In 1971 Ronald Graham and Bruce Rothschild proved a result in a branch of mathematics called Ramsey theory, about how large a group of points must be before a certain pattern has to appear. They could not say exactly how large, but they could give an upper limit. It was an enormous number, so large that it could not be written in the ordinary way. In 1977 the writer Martin Gardner described a simpler, slightly larger number in his column in Scientific American, and it was called Graham's number.
It is built up in 64 steps, each of which makes the number unimaginably larger than the one before. If you could write a digit on every particle in the observable universe, there would not be room to write the number. It is still a definite number, and mathematicians can work out that its last digits are 2464195387. The best known limit is now far smaller, and the true answer is thought to be small, perhaps six.

In 1924 the Polish mathematicians Stefan Banach and Alfred Tarski proved something that sounds impossible. A solid ball can be cut into a finite number of pieces, which can be moved around and put back together to make two balls, each the same size as the original. It was later shown that five pieces are enough. It is a theorem, which follows from the usual rules of mathematics, and it is called the Banach-Tarski paradox.
It does not mean that you could double a ball of gold. The pieces are not solid chunks. They are so complicated, with infinitely scattered points, that they have no volume, and they depend on the axiom of choice, a rule that lets you pick from infinite collections without saying how. Mathematicians do not call it a contradiction. It shows that our idea of volume breaks down for sets that are strange enough, and that infinity has surprises.

For centuries people used probability, in gambling, in insurance, in science, without agreeing on exactly what it was. In 1933 the Russian mathematician Andrey Kolmogorov, aged thirty, published a short book that put it on a firm footing. He started from three rules. A probability is never less than zero. The probability that something in the whole set of possible outcomes happens is one. And for outcomes that cannot occur together, the probability that one or the other happens is the sum.
Everything else, such as the laws of large numbers, can be derived from those three. His approach used the language of sets and measure, which mathematicians had developed to deal with areas and volumes. It let them treat chance in the same way as they treated any other branch of mathematics. Today it is the standard definition, and it is the foundation of statistics, of machine learning and of finance.
The machine that draws the bell curve

A Galton board is a board with rows of pegs set in a triangle. A ball is dropped at the top. At each peg, it falls to the left or right, with equal chance, and in the end it lands in a slot at the bottom. Drop one ball and its path is unpredictable. Drop a thousand, and the heaps in the slots form a smooth hump, with most balls near the middle and a few at the edges.
Francis Galton, who invented it in the 1800s, used it to show how many small chance events add up to the bell curve, the normal distribution. A ball's final position is the sum of many small steps. The same thing happens with heights, test errors, and many other measurements. The shape is so common because of what is called the central limit theorem. A pattern can come out of a crowd of random events.

A Möbius strip is a band with a half twist, so that it has only one side. In 1882 the German mathematician Felix Klein described a surface that is like it, in one more dimension. It has no edge, and it has no inside and no outside. You can think of it as a tube whose end passes back through the side of the tube, and joins its own beginning. It is called the Klein bottle.
In three dimensions it cannot be built without the surface passing through itself, since it needs a fourth dimension to close up without a crossing. Glassblowers make models that cross themselves. It is a useful object in topology, which studies the properties of shapes that do not change when they are stretched. Two Möbius strips glued together along their edges make one. It is an example of a shape that we can define, but cannot hold.

How much of what you learned in school do you still know? In 1984 Harry Bahrick tested 733 people who had studied Spanish in high school, from just after the course to 50 years later, and who had not used it much since. Some had taken one year of Spanish, and some had taken several. He tested them on vocabulary, grammar and reading.
Knowledge fell off quickly in the first three to six years, as forgetting curves predict. Then it leveled off, and stayed about the same for decades, up to about 35 years, before it declined again in old age. Bahrick called the stable part permastore. What was in it depended on how well the material had been learned, which was measured by the number of courses and by the grades. People who had learned it well, with practice spread out over time, kept the most.
The peak of the memory of a life

Ask people in their sixties to recall events from their lives, and the memories do not come evenly from all periods. More come from the years between about ten and thirty than from before or after. This is called the reminiscence bump. In 1998 David Rubin, Tamara Rahhal and Leonard Poon reviewed the evidence, and tested other kinds of memory, for facts about the world.
They found that older people also remember best the books, films and music of that period, and name them as favorites. They did better on questions about the Academy Awards and the World Series from those years. Explanations include that it is a time of many firsts, and of the formation of identity. A later study suggested that memory is better in general in adolescence and early adulthood. The songs you loved at seventeen have a special hold on you.
The baby who kicked a mobile

Can a baby of three months remember anything? In a series of studies, Carolyn Rovee-Collier and her colleagues tied a ribbon from the ankle of an infant, lying in a crib, to a mobile hanging above. The baby soon learned that kicking made the mobile move, and kicked more. Later, they brought the baby back and tied the ribbon to a fixed bar, instead, and watched how much the baby kicked when it saw the mobile.
If the infant had learned the connection, it kicked more at the sight of the mobile, even a day or more later. Three-month-olds forgot after a while, but a brief reminder, in which the experimenter moved the mobile without the baby's help, brought the memory back. With a reminder, infants showed no forgetting weeks later. The experiments showed that very young babies learn and remember, and that forgetting is not always loss.
The machine that lit up for blickets

How do young children decide what something is? We often assume that they go by looks. In 2000 Alison Gopnik and David Sobel tested this with a machine that lit up and played music when certain objects were put on it. They called the objects that set it off blickets. Children aged two, three and four saw that a particular object made the machine go. Then they were asked which other objects were blickets.
The children did not simply pick the objects that looked like the first one. They paid attention to what the objects did to the machine. An object that made it light up was a blicket, even if it looked quite different. Gopnik has argued that young children behave like scientists, working out how the world works from evidence. Not every researcher agrees that children work in the same way as scientists.
When children learn that others can be wrong

In a classic test, a child sees a doll, Sally, put a marble in a basket and leave. Another doll, Anne, moves the marble to a box. The child is asked where Sally will look for her marble when she returns. To answer correctly, the child must realize that Sally has a false belief, which differs from the real state of things. Most three-year-olds say that she will look in the box. Older children say the basket.
In 2001 Henry Wellman, David Cross and Julanne Watson pooled the results of 178 studies of tasks like this. They found a steady change over the preschool years. Children moved from below chance to above chance, in many countries. A model with age and the features of the task explained more than half of the differences between studies. It is a milestone in understanding that other people have minds of their own.
Easy, difficult and slow to warm up

In 1956 the psychiatrists Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess began to follow more than a hundred children in New York from infancy. They interviewed their parents about how the babies behaved, such as how regular their sleep was, and how they reacted to new things. They found that babies differ from the first weeks, and that the differences could be grouped.
About 40 percent were easy babies, who were regular, cheerful and adapted quickly. About 10 percent were difficult, with irregular habits, strong reactions and slow adjustment. About 15 percent were slow to warm up, who withdrew from the new but then adapted. The rest did not fit one group. Thomas and Chess stressed goodness of fit. A temperament is not good or bad in itself, but depends on whether the parents and the child's surroundings suit it. Parents are not the only cause of how their children turn out.

How much do genes and upbringing contribute to who we are? Identical twins who are separated at birth, and brought up in different families, offer a natural test. In the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart, Thomas Bouchard and his colleagues brought more than a hundred sets of twins or triplets who had been raised apart to Minneapolis, for a week of tests of intelligence, personality, interests and health.
They reported that identical twins raised apart were about as alike in personality and interests as identical twins raised together. They estimated that about 70 percent of the variation in IQ was associated with genes. Critics argue that the twins were often in touch, that families with adopted children are similar, and that the figures depend on the population. A heritability figure describes a group at a certain time. It does not say how much of one person's traits is caused by genes.
What happened to the children of the orphanages

After the fall of the dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, in 1989, Romania had many thousands of children living in large state institutions, with little attention, in cribs. In 2000 a team of American researchers, Charles Nelson, Charles Zeanah and Nathan Fox, began the Bucharest Early Intervention Project. They assessed 136 institutionalized children, with an average age of 22 months. By lottery, half were placed in foster families, which the project had created, and half stayed in care.
By the age of four and a half, the children who had stayed in the institutions scored far lower on tests of intelligence than children who had never been institutionalized, and lower than those placed in foster care. The earlier a child was moved, the better the outcome. Later follow-ups found benefits in mental health and attachment as well. The study is often cited as evidence of a sensitive period in early childhood, and of the importance of a caring family.
The nested worlds of a child

In 1979 the psychologist Urie Bronfenbrenner argued that a child cannot be understood apart from the places in which the child grows up. He pictured them as nested circles. The innermost is the microsystem, the settings where the child is directly, such as the home, the school and the playground. Around it is the mesosystem, the links between those settings, such as how the parents and teachers get along.
Next is the exosystem, which holds settings that the child is not in, but that affect the child, such as a parent's workplace. A change in a parent's hours can change a child's day. The outermost is the macrosystem, which is the culture, the laws, and the economy. His ecological model shifted attention from the child alone to the whole web around the child. It is a reason why a program for children often works best when it also reaches the family and the community.
What you remember from a list

Read a list of words to people, and ask them to write down all that they remember, in any order. They do best on the words at the end of the list, which is called the recency effect, and well on the first few words, which is called the primacy effect. The words in the middle are the worst remembered. The pattern is called the serial position curve, and it has been found over and over.
In 1966 Murray Glanzer and Anita Cunitz did an experiment to see whether the two ends have the same cause. They had people count backward for thirty seconds before they recalled the list. The recency effect vanished, since the last words had faded from the short-term store. The primacy effect stayed, because the first words had been rehearsed enough to enter long-term memory. It was an early piece of evidence for two kinds of memory.
What each side wants, and what each side says

When people negotiate, they usually start by stating positions. I want this price, or I want that border. Roger Fisher and William Ury, of the Harvard Negotiation Project, argued in their 1981 book, Getting to Yes, that positions are a poor place to begin. Behind each position there are interests, which are the reasons that the person wants it, and the same interest can often be met in more than one way.
Their main example was the dispute over the Sinai Peninsula in 1978, at Camp David. Israel held the Sinai, and Egypt demanded it back, so their positions seemed to clash. But Israel's interest was security, since it did not want Egyptian tanks on its border. Egypt's interest was sovereignty, since it wanted its own land back. The answer was that Egypt took sovereignty, while large areas were kept free of troops. Asking why makes it possible to find a deal that was not visible from the positions.
The open window in the next room

In January 1925 the American writer on management Mary Parker Follett gave a talk about how to deal with conflict. She said that there are three ways. One side can dominate, or both can compromise, or they can integrate, which means finding a solution that gives both what they truly want. She gave a small example, from a library, where one man wanted the window open, and another wanted it shut.
She did not suggest opening it halfway, which would please neither. She asked why each wanted what he wanted. One wanted fresh air, and the other did not want a draft blowing on him. So the librarian opened a window in the next room, which was empty. Both got what they wanted. Follett's example later appeared in Getting to Yes. A compromise splits the difference, and the conflict tends to return, but a solution that meets both needs makes the conflict go away.
The negotiator who copied the other

Psychologists have found that people like those who mimic them, in a small, unnoticed way, by copying their posture or gestures. In 2008 William Maddux, Elizabeth Mullen and Adam Galinsky asked whether it helps in negotiation. In one study, they asked some business school students to copy, in a subtle way, the posture and movements of the person across the table. Others were not asked to mimic.
The mimickers did better. In a negotiation over a job offer, they created more value, and took a larger share of it, though not at the expense of the other side. In a second study, about a gas station for sale where the two sides seemed to be at an impasse, pairs in which one person mimicked were more likely to reach a deal at all. The authors found that trust explained the effect. People who feel mirrored feel understood.
Five ways of handling a quarrel

In 1974 the psychologists Kenneth Thomas and Ralph Kilmann devised a questionnaire about how people behave in conflict. They described five modes, on two dimensions. One is how assertive you are, which is how far you pursue your own concerns. The other is how cooperative you are, which is how far you try to satisfy the other person's.
The competing style is high in assertiveness and low in cooperation. Accommodating is the reverse. Avoiding is low in both. Compromising is in the middle on both, and collaborating is high in both. The authors did not say that one is best. Competing is useful in an emergency, avoiding when an issue is trivial, and collaborating when the stakes are high on both sides. The value is in noticing which style you use by habit, and choosing another when the situation calls for it.
Four steps for saying something hard

In the 1960s the psychologist Marshall Rosenberg, who worked with civil rights groups, developed a method of speaking that he called nonviolent communication. It has four parts. State what you observe, without judging, as in, you came home at nine. Say how you feel about it. Say the need behind the feeling, such as that you need to be able to count on a plan. Then make a specific request, such as would you tell me if you will be late.
He argued that judgments and demands cause people to defend themselves, and that facts and feelings do not. The method is widely taught in schools, workplaces and mediation. The research on it is thin, and some find the formula stiff. The core idea is sound, and matches other findings. A complaint about a specific behavior is easier to hear than an attack on the person, and a request is easier to answer than a demand.

On the evening of October 26, 1962, in the worst days of the Cuban Missile Crisis, President Kennedy received a long, private and emotional letter from the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev. It offered to remove the missiles from Cuba, if the United States promised not to invade. The next morning a second, harder letter arrived, which was broadcast on Moscow radio. It demanded that the United States also remove its missiles from Turkey.
Kennedy's advisers argued over what to do. In the end he answered the first letter, and accepted its terms, and ignored the demand in the second. He sent his brother, Robert Kennedy, to tell the Soviet ambassador, in private, that the Jupiter missiles in Turkey would be removed soon, but that this could not be a public part of the deal. On October 28 Khrushchev announced that the Soviet missiles would be removed. The Jupiters left Turkey in April 1963.

In 1954 the psychologist Gordon Allport suggested that contact between members of different groups can reduce prejudice, but only under certain conditions. The groups should have equal status in the situation, a common goal, and a need to cooperate, and the contact should have the support of authorities, such as a school or an employer. Without them, contact could make things worse. This became known as the contact hypothesis.
In 2006 Thomas Pettigrew and Linda Tropp pooled 713 samples from 515 studies. They found that contact generally reduced prejudice, and that Allport's conditions made it stronger, but were not essential. Later reviews found that the effects are smaller than first thought, especially for prejudice based on race or ethnicity, and that they may not last. Still, the finding that knowing people from other groups is linked to less prejudice is among the best supported in social psychology.
Prison, but with the guards left to themselves

In the 1971 Stanford prison experiment, students acted as guards and prisoners, and the guards became abusive. It has often been said that this shows that people given power turn cruel. In 2001 the psychologists Stephen Reicher and Alexander Haslam, with the BBC, tried a different version. They divided men at random into guards and prisoners, in a purpose-built setting, and watched them. The BBC broadcast it in four hours.
They were not told how to behave. The guards did not agree on how to use their authority, and did not act as a group. The study argued that tyranny does not arise simply from having power. It comes when groups fail, when people feel that they cannot make things work, and then accept a strong hand. The study had its critics, too. But it casts doubt on the idea that the roles alone make people cruel.
The courts held under a tree

After the genocide in Rwanda in 1994, in which an estimated half a million to a million people were killed in about a hundred days, the courts had to deal with more than a hundred thousand suspects in jail. At the pace of the regular courts it would have taken generations. In 2002 Rwanda revived a traditional system, called gacaca, which means grass, where the elders of a village used to settle disputes, seated on the lawn. The new courts were run by judges who were elected by their neighbors.
There were about 11,000 of them. They opened in 2005 and closed in June 2012, and they heard nearly two million cases, with most ending in a conviction. The idea was to establish the truth and allow reconciliation, as well as justice. Human Rights Watch and others criticized the lack of legal training and the unfair trials. The results were mixed. It was a bold attempt to deal with a crime too large for any normal system.
The opera house that cost fourteen times the plan

In 1957 a competition was held to design an opera house for Sydney, and it was won by a young Danish architect, Jørn Utzon, with a design of white shells on a harbor point. The government estimated that it would cost about 7 million Australian dollars. Construction began before the design for the shells had been worked out. The engineers had to solve how to build them, and it took years.
Costs climbed. In 1966, with the building not close to finished, the project had cost about 23 million dollars, and Utzon resigned, after a dispute over payments. The Opera House opened in October 1973, about ten years late, and at a cost of 102 million dollars, more than fourteen times the first estimate. The planner Bent Flyvbjerg, who studies large projects, has called it a standard example. Planners tend to underestimate the cost of what has not been done before, and to start before the hard parts are solved.
The highway that cost nearly six times as much

In the 1980s Boston began to bury its elevated highway, and to build a tunnel to the airport. The project was called the Central Artery/Tunnel Project, and most people called it the Big Dig. The first price tag was about 2.6 billion dollars. When it was finished in 2007, after two decades, the cost reported was close to 14.8 billion dollars, nearly six times as much, without counting the interest on the loans, which brought the total to far more.
There were also problems with quality. In July 2006, in a tunnel, a ceiling panel weighing several tons fell onto a car, and a passenger, Milena Del Valle, was killed. The investigators found that the wrong kind of epoxy had been used to hold the ceiling bolts. The state later reached a settlement with the contractors of more than 450 million dollars. The Big Dig now stands for how large public works can grow past their budgets.

Hospital patients in intensive care are often given a central line, a long tube placed in a large vein. It can carry germs into the bloodstream, and cause serious infection. Peter Pronovost, a critical care doctor at Johns Hopkins, wrote down five steps that the experts agreed on. They were washing hands, cleaning the patient's skin with a strong antiseptic, covering the patient completely with sterile drapes, avoiding one risky site, and removing the line when it was no longer needed.
Starting in 2003 he asked 103 intensive care units in Michigan to follow a checklist of those steps, with a nurse empowered to stop a doctor who skipped one. Within three months, the median rate of infection fell from 2.7 per 1,000 line-days to zero, and it stayed low for at least a year and a half. It was estimated to have saved many lives and a great deal of money. The steps were not new. The checklist made sure that they were done every time.
The baseball team with the cheap roster

In 2002 the Oakland Athletics had one of the smallest payrolls in baseball, a fraction of what teams like the New York Yankees spent. Yet the A's won 103 games and the division, and at one point won twenty games in a row, which was the longest streak in the history of the American League. The general manager, Billy Beane, and his assistant, Paul DePodesta, had given up the old ways of judging players.
Scouts had favored young men who looked like athletes. Beane relied on data. He valued a statistic that scouts undervalued, which was on-base percentage, how often a batter reaches base, because it is closely linked to scoring runs. Players with good records on it were cheaper, since other teams paid less attention. Michael Lewis wrote about it in his book Moneyball. Other teams copied the approach, and the advantage shrank. It showed that an overlooked measure can be worth more than a conventional one.
Telling a patient what a positive test means

Suppose that one woman in a hundred has breast cancer. A mammogram detects 90 out of 100 who have it, and gives a false alarm to 9 out of 100 who do not. A woman has a positive test. What is the chance that she has cancer? Many people, including many doctors, say that it is about 90 percent. The correct answer is about nine percent, or about one in eleven.
The numbers are easier to handle in natural frequencies. Of 1,000 women, 10 have cancer, and 9 of them test positive. Of the 990 without, about 89 test positive. So of about 98 positives, 9 have cancer. In 1998 Ulrich Hoffrage and Gerd Gigerenzer showed that doctors do much better with this kind of statement. In one study, 16 of 24 physicians found the right answer when the information was put in natural frequencies. The way that numbers are shown can make us confused, or clear.
The cards that people get wrong

Here are four cards, which show E, K, 4 and 7. Each has a letter on one side and a number on the other. The rule is that if a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other. Which cards must you turn over to check the rule? Most people pick E and 4. The right answer is E and 7, because a 7 with a vowel behind it would break the rule. Fewer than one person in five gets it right.
In 1982 Richard Griggs and James Cox found that when the same logic was dressed as a rule about drinking, most people got it right. The rule was that if a person is drinking beer, he or she must be over a certain age. In 1989 the psychologist Leda Cosmides argued that people are good at detecting cheaters in social agreements. The logic is the same. It is a reminder that reasoning depends on content and context.

A syllogism is an argument with two premises and a conclusion. Whether it is valid depends only on its form. Here is an invalid one. No addictive things are inexpensive. Some cigarettes are inexpensive. Therefore some cigarettes are not addictive. The conclusion is believable, but it does not follow. Many people accept it, since it fits what they know.
In 1983 Jonathan Evans, Julie Barston and Paul Pollard gave people such arguments, some valid and some invalid, some with believable conclusions and some not. People accepted 89 percent of valid arguments with believable conclusions, and 71 percent of invalid ones with believable conclusions. They accepted 56 percent of valid arguments with unbelievable conclusions, and just 10 percent of invalid ones with unbelievable conclusions. Belief is a strong influence, mostly on arguments that are flawed. It shows why we should be most careful with conclusions that we like.
The bat, the ball, and the lily pad

A bat and a ball cost 1.10 dollars in all. The bat costs a dollar more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? Most people think of 10 cents right away, and it is wrong. The ball costs 5 cents, since the bat then costs 1.05, and the two make 1.10. It is the first of three questions that the economist Shane Frederick used in 2005 as a cognitive reflection test.
In a second question, five machines make five widgets in five minutes. How long do 100 machines take to make 100? The answer is five minutes, not 100. In the third, a patch of lily pads doubles every day, and covers a whole lake in 48 days. How long to cover half? The answer is 47, and not 24. Across 35 studies with 3,428 people, the average score was 1.24 out of three. The test measures whether you stop to check a first impulse.
Sentences that sound deep and say nothing

The philosopher Harry Frankfurt wrote an essay in 1986, On Bullshit, which argued that bullshit is not the same as lying. A liar cares about the truth, since he wants to hide it. A bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true. He wants to impress. In 2015 Gordon Pennycook and his colleagues asked how readily people accept it. They made up sentences from fashionable words, such as wholeness quiets infinite phenomena, which are grammatical but have no meaning.
People were asked to rate how profound they were, alongside real quotations. Many rated the empty sentences as at least somewhat profound. Those who did so scored lower on tests of analytic thinking, and higher on belief in the supernatural. People who were good at spotting the empty ones were not just doubters of everything. They could tell the difference. Vagueness can sound wise, and thinking carefully is some protection.
A misreading that became a fabric

Tweed is a rough woolen cloth from Scotland. The usual story is that the name began as a mistake. Weavers around Hawick made a twilled cloth, which in Scots was called tweel. In the early 1830s a clerk for a London merchant, James Locke, read a letter from a Hawick firm about its tweels, and took the word to be tweed. He thought it was a trade name, from the River Tweed, which flows through the region.
The name caught on, and by about 1850 it was firmly established. Historians are not sure that it happened exactly like that. Different accounts give different dates, and name a London tailor instead of a merchant, and some say the river gave the name directly. It is a nice story, and it may be true in outline, but it is a traditional account. Words often get their forms from a slip of the pen.
Did Dr. Seuss invent the nerd?

The word nerd first appears in print, as far as we know, in a children's book. In If I Ran the Zoo, published in 1950, Dr. Seuss describes a boy's imagined zoo, in which he would have a Nerkle, a Nerd and a Seersucker too. The Nerd in the picture is a small, grumpy creature, with a messy tuft of hair. It has no connection with the later meaning.
In 1951 Newsweek reported on the slang of teenagers in Detroit, and said that someone who was once called a drip or a square was now a nerd. It may be that the word was already in speech before Seuss used it, and that he picked it up. The Oxford English Dictionary says that its origin is uncertain and disputed. Other stories, such as one about a ventriloquist's dummy, have been rejected. We know when the word was first written down, but not who said it first.
The hospital that gave us a word for chaos

In 1247 a priory was founded in London, outside the city wall, in the name of St. Mary of Bethlehem. Over time it began to take in people who were mentally ill, and by the fourteenth century it was a hospital. Londoners had trouble with the name, and called it Bedleem, and then Bedlam. The hospital, now called Bethlem Royal Hospital, still exists, and it is still a place for mental health care.
In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the conditions were bad, and visitors came to watch the patients, which was a form of entertainment. The word bedlam came to mean any madhouse, and then, by the early 1600s, any place of uproar and confusion. A word that was once the name of a place has gone through a change of meaning. Its history is a reminder of how mentally ill people were once treated.
The elephant that made everything large

In 1865 an African elephant called Jumbo arrived at the London Zoo. He grew to be one of the largest elephants in captivity, about eleven feet at the shoulder, and children rode on his back. In 1882 the zoo sold him to the American showman P. T. Barnum, for about two thousand pounds. The sale caused a public outcry in Britain, and many people wrote to the Queen to protest. Jumbo crossed the Atlantic, and Barnum's circus made him a star.
Jumbo died on September 15, 1885, in St. Thomas, Ontario, when a freight train struck him as he was being led back to the circus train after a show. The name was already used in English before the elephant, and some people think it came from an African word. But it was Jumbo who made it mean something huge. Today jumbo is used for jets, shrimp, and bags of potato chips.
The shoe that was never thrown

It is often said that sabotage comes from the sabot, the wooden shoe worn by French workers, and that angry workers threw their shoes into machines to break them. It is a good story, and there is no evidence for it. The word comes from the French verb saboter, which meant to walk noisily, clattering in wooden shoes, and then to do a job badly, or to botch it.
By the 1890s French labor movements had begun to use the word for the deliberate slowing of work, as a tactic in labor disputes. It came into English in the early 1900s, notably in reports on a railway strike in France in 1910. Later the word was applied to the destruction of machines and to acts of war, as in sabotage behind enemy lines. The word arrived from a sound, and the shoe story was invented afterward.
Where the word lynch came from

The word lynch refers to a killing by a mob, without a trial. It is almost certainly from the surname Lynch, but there are two candidates, both of them from Virginia in the 1780s. Colonel Charles Lynch, a justice of the peace, held informal trials of Loyalists in his home county, and he wrote in 1782 about Lynch's Law. The earlier documented use is his.
William Lynch, from another county in Virginia, was also named, since in 1811 he claimed that the phrase came from a compact that he had signed in 1780. Scholars doubt that the document is genuine. A third story, about a mayor of Galway who is supposed to have hanged his own son in 1493, has been rejected. The phrase Lynch law appears in print by 1811, and lynching in 1835. The word has a dark history, and the exact origin is uncertain.
Blackmail was once a payment for protection

In the sixteenth century, on the border between Scotland and England, bands of armed men raided farms and stole cattle. Landowners and farmers found that they could avoid raids by paying a local chief, who promised protection from his own men and from others. The payment was called black mail. Mail was an old Scottish word for rent or tribute, probably from Old Norse. Black may have marked it as illegal, as opposed to the lawful rent, but the reason is not certain.
The term was in use by the 1550s. It had nothing to do with the postal mail, and the idea that it meant extortion by letter is false. By the nineteenth century the word was used for any demand for money under threat, such as the threat of exposing a secret. It is among the many words in English which came from the long, violent history of the border.
The word that gave away who you were

In the Book of Judges, in the Hebrew Bible, a war broke out between the people of Gilead, led by Jephthah, and the tribe of Ephraim. After the battle, the Gileadites seized the crossing places of the Jordan River, to catch the Ephraimites who were trying to flee. Anyone who came to the ford and said that he was not an Ephraimite was asked to say the word shibboleth.
The Ephraimites said sibboleth, because their dialect lacked the sh sound, and so they gave themselves away. The story says that forty-two thousand were killed. The word shibboleth meant ear of grain, or a flowing stream, and what mattered was the pronunciation, and not the meaning. In English it came to mean a test word, a custom, or a phrase that identifies who belongs to a group. The story shows how a small difference of speech can mark someone as an outsider.
A victory that was too costly

In 279 BC King Pyrrhus of Epirus, who had come to Italy to help a Greek city against Rome, fought the Romans at Asculum. He had war elephants and many trained men, and he won the field. But he lost a very large number of his best officers and soldiers, and he could not replace them as the Romans could. According to the Greek writer Plutarch, a companion congratulated him, and Pyrrhus answered that one more victory like that would ruin him.
Historians disagree on whether he really won, and some say that the Romans did. The phrase Pyrrhic victory entered English in the early nineteenth century, to mean a win that costs so much that it is almost like a defeat. It applies to wars, to lawsuits and to political fights. The question to ask is not just whether you won, but what you paid.
The man whose name means to censor

In 1807 a book appeared in London called The Family Shakespeare. It offered the plays of Shakespeare with the parts that were thought unsuitable for reading aloud in a family left out. The first edition came out without a name, and it was mostly the work of Henrietta Maria Bowdler, who was known as Harriet, the sister of a physician, Thomas Bowdler. She was a writer on religion, and she had done the cutting.
In 1818 Thomas published a second edition, in ten volumes, with more plays, under his own name. It was a success, and was reprinted many times. In 1836 the verb bowdlerize appeared in print, and it was used in mockery, for the removal of anything improper from a book. The word is now used for any censoring that is excessive. A woman did most of the work, and a man gave the word his name.

In about 621 BC the Athenians asked a man called Draco to write down their laws. Until then they had been remembered and applied by the nobles, who could interpret them as they pleased. Draco's code was the first in Athens to be written down for all to see, which was a step toward fairness. But it was famous for its severity. Even small offenses, such as stealing a cabbage, were said to carry the penalty of death.
An old saying, which Plutarch repeated, was that Draco's laws were written not in ink but in blood. A later lawmaker, Solon, repealed most of them, but kept the law on murder. From Draco we have the word draconian, for a law or measure that is harsh. He was in fact a reformer, in that he put the law in writing, and the word remembers only his severity.

Sparta was in a region of Greece called Laconia, and its people were known for speaking very briefly. We still use the word laconic for a short, blunt way of speaking. A story that has come down from ancient writers, including Plutarch, illustrates it. Philip II of Macedon, who had conquered much of Greece, sent the Spartans a message. If I enter Laconia, he wrote, I will raze Sparta to the ground.
The Spartans sent back a single word, which was If. Whether it really happened is uncertain, since the anecdote has been told for centuries, and some scholars suspect that it grew with the telling. But it has served for a model of how much can be said in a few words. The Spartans trained their children to answer quickly and with wit. The word reminds us that short speech can have force.

Many words for strong drink began as words for water or fire. Whiskey comes from the Gaelic uisce beatha, which means water of life. It was a translation of the Latin aqua vitae, which medieval alchemists and monks used for distilled spirits. Over time uisce beatha was worn down by speakers, to usquebaugh, and then to whisky.
Vodka is from the Russian voda, water, with an ending that makes it little, so it means little water. Brandy comes from the Dutch brandewijn, which means burned wine, because it is made by heating wine, to distill it. Each name tells something of the way that the drink is made, or of the way that people felt about it. They also show how much of our vocabulary for drink came from languages across Europe.

In Latin the word for left was sinister. In English it came to mean evil, or threatening, as in a sinister plot. How the meaning changed is not certain, but in many cultures the left side and the left hand have been thought unlucky. In Latin the word for right was dexter. We get dexterity from it, meaning skill, and a person who is dexterous is good with the hands.
The French word for left is gauche, which English has borrowed to mean clumsy or awkward. English has a long record of bias against the left hand. Left-handed children were made to write with the right hand in some schools until the twentieth century. Our words keep the old prejudice, long after most people have stopped sharing it.

A pedigree is a record of the ancestors of a person or an animal, and it has come to mean a distinguished background. The word began in medieval French as pié de grue, which means the foot of a crane. In old family trees, the lines that branched from one generation to the next were drawn with three short strokes, like the footprint of a crane, and the mark was used to show the line of descent.
The French words were borrowed into English in the fifteenth century, and were worn down in speech to pedegru and then pedigree. The mark was used to show the descent of nobles, and later of horses and dogs. A family tree is still a diagram of branches. It is a word that records, in its shape, a drawing that has been lost.

Jeopardy now means danger. It comes from the Old French jeu parti, which means a divided game, or an even game. It was a term in chess and other games for a position in which the chances were equal, so that the outcome was uncertain. A player in such a position could win or lose.
In English it was first used in the fourteenth century for a risk or a danger, and the sense of a game faded. The word now is used for a legal term, in which a person who has been tried is not in double jeopardy, and for the name of a television quiz. It is a good example of a word that began in a game, and then took on a serious sense. A divided game is a risk, since you do not know who will win.

An arsenal is a place where weapons are made and stored. The word came through Italian from Arabic, where dar al-sina'a means house of manufacture, or workshop. Italian traders, who had dealings with the Muslim world, borrowed it, and Venetians turned it into arzanà. The famous Arsenale of Venice was the great shipyard of the city.
It was founded in the early twelfth century, and at its height it could build and equip a warship in a matter of days, with workers who assembled pieces along a line, in a way that anticipated the factory. The word was borrowed into English in the sixteenth century. In the end it was applied to any large store of arms, and also to a football club. The word carries in it a record of the trade between Venice and the Arab world.

Many fabrics are named for the cities that were known for making or selling them. Muslin, a thin cotton cloth, comes from Mosul, a city in what is now Iraq, where Europeans first saw it. Damask, a woven fabric with a pattern, takes its name from Damascus. Calico, a plain cotton cloth, came from Calicut, a port on the coast of India, which is now called Kozhikode.
Similar names are found in jeans, which are from Genoa, whose sailors wore a strong cotton cloth, and in denim, from the French serge de Nîmes. The place names are a trace of old trade routes, along which cloth moved to Europe. The words survive long after the cities stopped being the main source. In your clothes there may be a map of the medieval world.
The girl who was found without a first language

In November 1970 the authorities in Los Angeles found a girl of thirteen who had been kept in isolation for most of her life, and who had almost no language. She was admitted to Children's Hospital on November 4, and she became known by the pseudonym Genie. A team of UCLA linguists, led by Victoria Fromkin, with her student Susan Curtiss, spent years testing and teaching her, and recording how she learned.
Genie's vocabulary grew a great deal. Her grammar did not. She learned many words, and she understood more than she could say, but her sentences stayed simple, and she did not master the rules for putting them together as children do. Some linguists saw this as support for the idea that there is a critical period for language, which ends around puberty. Others said that her abuse and neglect made the case impossible to interpret. It is a sad case, and also an inconclusive one.

Helen Keller was born in Alabama in 1880. At nineteen months she became ill with a fever, and she lost both her sight and her hearing. For years she lived with no way to share her thoughts, except a few signs, and she had angry outbursts. In March 1887 a young teacher, Anne Sullivan, who had herself been partly blind, came to the Keller home in Tuscumbia, to teach her. She spelled words into the child's hand, but at first Helen only copied them.
On April 5, 1887, when Helen was six, Sullivan took her to the water pump in the yard. As water ran over one of Helen's hands, she spelled w-a-t-e-r into the other. Helen understood, suddenly, that the movements in her palm stood for the cool stuff that was flowing. She wanted to know the names of everything. That day she learned about thirty words. She went on to graduate from college and write books.

In 1969 the neuroscientist Paul Bach-y-Rita and his colleagues published a letter in Nature about a strange device. A television camera sent its picture to a grid of vibrating pins, twenty by twenty, which pressed against the skin of the back of a blind person. A bright spot in the picture became a buzz at the matching spot on the skin. With practice, the blind users could tell shapes, and say where objects and even people stood.
Their reports said that after some hours, users stopped feeling a pattern of buzzing on the back, and began to perceive objects in front of them, as one does with the eyes. Bach-y-Rita argued that we see with the brain, and not just with the eyes. If the brain receives information in an orderly way, it can learn to use it. The idea, called sensory substitution, has led to devices that give blind people information through the tongue or the ear.
One worm, three hundred and two neurons

A connectome is a complete map of the connections between the nerve cells of a brain. The first one was of a tiny roundworm, Caenorhabditis elegans, which has only 302 neurons. In the 1970s and 1980s Sydney Brenner and his colleagues sliced a worm into thousands of ultrathin sections, photographed them with an electron microscope, and traced every cell by hand. The paper appeared in 1986. It showed some thousands of connections between the cells.
The map did not explain everything about how the worm behaves, and some critics said that it told us less than hoped. In 2024 a team from Harvard and Google published a map of a piece of the human brain, a cubic millimeter of cortex, a speck smaller than a grain of rice. It contained about 57,000 cells and 150 million connections. A whole human brain has about 86 billion neurons, so a complete map is still far away.

In 1957 two French doctors in Paris, André Djourno and Charles Eyriès, placed a wire next to the hearing nerve of a deaf man, and sent an electrical signal into it. He heard noises, but not speech, and the device failed after a few weeks. They stopped, but their report reached an American ear surgeon, William House, in Los Angeles. In 1961 House and an engineer, John Doyle, implanted a device in a patient.
Many doubted that it would work, because the ear has thousands of delicate hair cells, and a few wires could not replace them. But in the 1970s and 1980s the devices improved, and in 1984 the American FDA approved the House and 3M single-channel implant for adults. In about 1990 it approved multichannel devices for children. Today cochlear implants let deaf people hear speech. The brain learns to make sense of the electrical signals, which sound strange at first.
A slime mold in a maze

The slime mold Physarum polycephalum is a single cell that can grow to cover a dinner plate, and that has no brain and no nerves. It grows as a network of tubes, looking for food. In 2000 the Japanese researcher Toshiyuki Nakagaki and his colleagues put a piece of it in a small maze, with food at two ends. At first the slime spread through all the paths. After some hours it had withdrawn from the dead ends, and kept the shortest route between the foods.
In 2010 Atsushi Tero and colleagues put pieces of food on a map in the positions of cities around Tokyo, and let the slime mold connect them. Bright light, which the slime mold avoids, stood for mountains and lakes. The network it grew was comparable in efficiency, resilience and cost to the real Tokyo rail system. It is wrong to say that the slime mold thinks. But a simple rule, of strengthening the tubes that carry the most flow, can find good solutions.
The crow that bent a wire

New Caledonian crows are known for making tools from twigs and leaves, which they use to get insects out of holes. In 2002 the researchers Alex Weir, Jackie Chappell and Alex Kacelnik, at Oxford, were testing two crows, a male, Abel, and a female, Betty. They gave them a small bucket of food at the bottom of a tube, and a hooked wire and a straight wire to fish it out. Abel took the hooked wire, and left the straight wire.
Betty, left with the straight wire, wedged one end in some tape, and bent it into a hook, and lifted the bucket. She did it again in nine of ten trials. She had never been given wire before, and had never watched anyone bend it. Later work found that crows in the wild also bend material, so she may have been using a routine that she already knew. But Betty's skill, with a new material, stood out. She died in 2005.
The sound that is hard to bear

For some people, the sound of someone chewing, or breathing, or tapping a pen, provokes an intense reaction, of anger or disgust, which they find hard to control. It is called misophonia, which means hatred of sound. For years it was thought to be a matter of temperament. In 2017 Sukhbinder Kumar and his colleagues at Newcastle University used a brain scanner on people who had misophonia, and on people who did not.
When the people with misophonia heard their trigger sounds, mostly sounds of eating, a part of the brain called the anterior insula responded far more strongly. This is a hub of the network that decides what is important. It was more connected, too, with areas for emotion and memory. Their heart rates and skin responses rose, and the activity of the insula accounted for these effects. The findings suggest that it is a real condition of the brain, and not just a lack of patience.

In the mid-1970s the linguist John Gumperz was called to Heathrow Airport in London to look at a problem. New cafeteria workers from India and Pakistan and the baggage handlers who ate there each said that the other side was rude. Neither group could point to anything that had been said that was actually insulting.
Gumperz recorded their conversations and played the recordings back to both groups. When a customer pointed at the gravy, the British servers said "gravy?" with a rising voice, which sounded like an offer. The South Asian servers said "gravy" with a falling voice, which the baggage handlers heard as a flat statement, as if it meant take it or leave it. The newcomers had meant a polite offer.
By its own habits, each group was behaving well. Gumperz argued that the trouble lay in small signals, such as the rise and fall of the voice, which people use to show what they mean and rarely notice. The case later became part of a training film, called Crosstalk. A great deal of what feels like rudeness may be a difference in habit that no one has ever named.

In the 1960s the sociologist Harold Garfinkel, who taught at UCLA, asked his students to do something odd at home. For anywhere from fifteen minutes to an hour they were to behave like polite lodgers in their own family's house, using the formal manners one shows a stranger. He called such tasks breaching experiments, and he described them in his 1967 book, Studies in Ethnomethodology.
The families reacted with astonishment, bewilderment, shock, embarrassment or anger, and some demanded to know what had come over the student. Many of the students found it hard to keep up the act, because looking at their own family the way a stranger would turned out to be uncomfortable.
Garfinkel was not trying to prove anything with controls and numbers. He wanted to show that everyday life runs on rules that nobody states, and that they become visible only when somebody breaks them. The anger of the families was the evidence that the rules were real, and that everyone had been following them without ever being taught them aloud.
Did the Hopi have no word for time?

Benjamin Lee Whorf spent twenty-two years working as a fire prevention engineer for the Hartford Fire Insurance Company, and he studied languages in his own time. He died in 1941, at the age of 44. In his writings on the Hopi language of Arizona he argued that Hopi speakers think about time differently from English speakers, partly because Hopi does not treat units of time as nouns, in the way that English treats days and hours.
The idea spread, and it turned into the popular claim that the Hopi had no concept of time at all. In 1983 the linguist Ekkehart Malotki published a study of about 600 pages on the grammar of time in Hopi, with hundreds of Hopi sentences taken from his own field notes. It showed that the language has words and forms that refer to time, and many linguists took it as a refutation.
Some scholars say that Malotki attacked a popular myth more than Whorf's actual claim, which was about how time is conceptualized, and Malotki is reported to have agreed. The Hopi case does not settle the wider question of whether the language we speak shapes the way we think. That question is still studied, with other languages and other methods.

Chaser was a border collie whose owner, John Pilley, was a psychology professor at Wofford College in South Carolina. Pilley and a colleague, Alliston Reid, taught her the names of toys one at a time. He repeated a name, and then hid the toy for her to find. After about three years of this she knew 1,022 names, and they published the results in 2011.
The one-at-a-time method was deliberate. Most people who train a dog put many objects on the floor at once, and Pilley's team used successive teaching instead, with a single object and a single name. Play was a large part of the training, and Chaser was asked again and again to pick out a named toy from among many.
The study does not show that a dog has language. Chaser learned names of objects, and there is no sign that she learned grammar. But it does show that a dog can store more than a thousand arbitrary links between a sound and a thing, and fetch the right one from a pile. Pilley died in 2018 at the age of 89, and Chaser died in 2019, at fifteen.
The dog who guessed a new word

Rico was a border collie in Germany who, by his owners' account, knew the names of more than 200 items.
