In 2004 the researchers Juliane Kaminski, Josep Call and Julia Fischer tested him with something new. They put a toy he had never seen among seven toys he knew, and asked him to fetch it by a name he had never heard. Rico fetched the new toy in seven of ten tests, and picked it out again four weeks later.
He seems to have reasoned by exclusion. The word was new, so it probably meant the one toy that had no name yet. Children do much the same, and psychologists call the quick learning of a word after one meeting fast mapping. In the same issue of Science, the psychologist Paul Bloom wrote a commentary called Can a Dog Learn a Word?
Later critics said that the test four weeks afterward did not prove fast mapping, since Rico could have gotten the right toy by exclusion a second time. So the careful conclusion is that a dog can use a rule of exclusion, which is a part of how children learn words, and the question of how closely it matches a child's learning is still argued.

Picture a toddler who knows the word ball. On the floor there is a ball, and a strange kitchen tool. A grown-up says, "Give me the dax." Most toddlers hand over the strange tool, even though dax could in principle be another name for the ball. In 1988 Ellen Markman and Gwyn Wachtel reported six studies of this kind, and they gave the effect the name mutual exclusivity.
Their idea was that children begin by assuming that each thing has only one name. A new word then most likely points to something that has no name yet. This is a useful shortcut, since a child learning a language faces endless possible meanings for each new word. A 2020 review of many studies found that young children do tend to match a new word to a new object.
Researchers still argue about why. Some say children are using what they know about words. Others, such as Gil Diesendruck and Lori Markson in 2001, argued that children are reasoning about what the speaker knows. The rule is not perfect, since things do have more than one name, and children learn that later.

In 1958 Jean Berko, a graduate student at Radcliffe College in Harvard's circle, wanted to know whether children learn the rules of English or simply memorize each word. She made up a set of pictures of imaginary creatures and actions, and gave them nonsense names. She showed a child a picture and said, "This is a wug. Now there is another one. There are two of them. There are two what?"
Children as young as four said "wugs." They could not have heard the word before, so they must have worked out the rule for plurals and applied it to a word that was new. They did the same with other endings, making the past tense, the possessive and the present participle of nonsense words.
The work was part of her dissertation, and her adviser was Roger Brown. It is often credited as the first clear demonstration that young children pull out the rules of grammar and do not merely repeat what they have heard. She later became known as Jean Berko Gleason. The wug has since become a famous creature in the study of language.
Why children say "goed", and how rarely they do

Most parents have heard a child say "goed" or "foots." It is called overregularization, because the child applies the regular rule to a word that is irregular. It is often described as a stage. First the child says "went," by copying. Then the child learns the rule for adding "ed" and says "goed." Finally the child goes back to "went."
In 1992 Gary Marcus, Steven Pinker and their colleagues studied more than 11,000 irregular past tense forms in the speech of many children. They found that the children said the right form most of the time. The median rate of overregularization was only about 2.5 percent of the irregular past tense forms. The errors began only after children had started to mark regular verbs reliably, and they stayed at a low rate for years.
The figures have been challenged. Michael Maratsos argued in 2000 that overall rates look low partly because of how samples are inspected, and that some children, such as one named Abe, went through long periods when the error was common. Later work by Maslen and colleagues in 2004 also questioned how low the rates are. Children's errors are real, but they are not the whole story.
The same sound, heard two ways

Speech sounds can be made ambiguous on a computer. In 1980 William Ganong made a series of sounds that moved in small steps from a d to a t, and put the same ending after each. With the ending "ash," one end of the series was "dash" and the other was "tash." Only one of them is a word.
Listeners labeled the in-between sounds as the one that made a real word. They heard "dash" far more often than "tash." With an ending such as "ask," where a t makes the word, the boundary shifted the other way. The identical sound was heard as a d in one case and as a t in the other. The effect was strongest for the sounds that were the most ambiguous.
Ganong took it as evidence that what we know about words reaches down into the basic perception of speech sounds. Others argue that it arises later, when we decide what label to give a sound, and the debate has continued, with brain scans and recordings of brain waves. Either way, hearing is not simply receiving a signal. It is shaped by what we expect to hear.
The listener who helps tell the story

When someone tells you a story you do not sit silent. You nod, say "mm-hm," wince, or say "no way." In 1970 the linguist Victor Yngve gave these small responses the name back channel. He pointed out that in a conversation both people are speaking and listening at the same time, and that the listener's part is never really empty.
In 2000 Janet Bavelas, Linda Coates and Trudy Johnson tested what these responses do. In two experiments one person told a story and another person listened. Some listeners were given a distracting task, so that they could not follow the story closely. These listeners made fewer responses, especially specific ones that fit the content, such as a wince at a painful moment.
The narrators then told their stories significantly worse, according to the ratings. The authors concluded that listeners are co-narrators. Their responses help illustrate the story, and they change how well the teller performs. A person who is a good listener is part of how a story gets told well.

Ask a friend whether you are a good cook, and the friend is likely to say yes. Ask a stranger, and you may hear the truth. In 1999 Clifford Nass, Youngme Moon and Paul Carney asked whether people use the same politeness toward machines. In the first study 30 people did a task on a text-based computer. Then they rated how well that computer had done, in one of three ways.
Some answered on the same computer, some on paper, and some on a different but identical computer. Those who answered on the same computer gave kinder and more uniform ratings than the others. A second study, with 30 more people and voice-based computers, got the same result. People gave the machine the courtesy they would give to a person, though a computer has no feelings to hurt.
This was part of a bigger idea in the 1996 book The Media Equation, by Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass. They argued that people tend to treat computers, television and other media as if they were real people and real places. Each of these two studies was small, so the finding is a pointer more than a proof. It suggests that politeness is automatic, and not a choice.
The code the enemy could not read

In 1942 Philip Johnston, the son of missionaries who had grown up on the Navajo reservation, suggested that the Marine Corps use the Navajo language to send secret messages. He argued that it should not be a simple translation of Navajo, but a code built out of Navajo words. In May 1942 the first 29 Navajo recruits began training in California, and they created the code themselves.
When the war began, fewer than thirty people who were not Navajo, and none of them Japanese, could understand the language. The code gave Navajo words to military terms that the language did not have, and the full wartime version grew to about 411 terms. The messages could be sent quickly, and by voice, without the slow work of a cipher machine.
At Iwo Jima in 1945, six Navajo radio networks worked around the clock during the first two days, and by one account they sent more than 800 messages without an error. Major Howard Connor, a signal officer of the 5th Marine Division, credited the Navajo with the success of the landing. The code is reported never to have been broken. Between 350 and 420 Navajo men served as code talkers, and the original 29 were awarded the Congressional Gold Medal in a law signed in 2000.

Marie Smith Jones was born on May 14, 1918, in Cordova, Alaska. She grew up speaking Eyak, a language of the southern coast of Alaska. When her older sister Sophie Borodkin died in 1992, she became the last fluent speaker. People called her Chief Marie.
She died at home in Anchorage on January 21, 2008, at the age of 89. With her, the Eyak language lost its last native speaker. A language can vanish in this way, when the last person who learned it as a child is gone, and it takes with it a way of describing the world that nobody else holds.
But a language is not always lost for good if people kept records. The Manx language of the Isle of Man lost the fisherman Ned Maddrell, who is generally reported as its last native speaker, on December 27, 1974. He was 97. A revival had begun in the 1960s, and the number of people who speak Manx has grown since. Whether a language survives depends on people choosing to learn it.

Dyirbal is an Aboriginal language of northeast Queensland, and it has very few speakers now. Its nouns are sorted into four classes, and each noun is marked with a small word that shows its class. In his 1972 grammar the linguist Robert Dixon described one of these classes, marked with the word balan. It includes human females, water, fire and fighting, and also dogs, the platypus and many birds.
In 1987 George Lakoff took the class as the title of his book, Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things. He used it to argue that categories in the human mind need not be defined by features that all members share. Instead they can be linked in chains, or by stories and beliefs, to a central example.
Not everyone agrees. Dixon wrote in 2015 that Lakoff had misrepresented his account. Other linguists, in a paper titled Women are not dangerous things, argued against the idea that the grouping rests on meaning alone. The Dyirbal classes remain a famous example of how differently languages can sort the world, and of how hard it is to be sure why.
A language with more than a hundred consonants

English has about two dozen consonants, and Hawaiian has just eight. In its central dialect, Rotokas, a language of Papua New Guinea, has only six consonants and five vowels, which makes eleven sounds in all. At the other end of the scale is Taa, a language of southern Africa, which has the largest sound inventory that is commonly cited.
How many sounds it has depends on how linguists count. One tally gives 122 consonants, and another gives 160 sounds counting vowels as well. If some combinations are treated as clusters of two sounds and not as single ones, the number of consonants comes down to about 88. Estimates of the number of click sounds range from 20 to 43.
Clicks are central to the language. One count found that 82 percent of its basic vocabulary words begin with a click. The case shows how much room there is in the human voice, and also that counting sounds depends on rules about what is to count as one. Even the smallest and largest inventories belong to languages that are fully capable of saying anything.
How a blind child learns what "look" means

How can a child who has never seen anything learn the meaning of "look" or "see"? In the 1980s Barbara Landau and Lila Gleitman studied blind children as they learned to talk. Their 1985 book, Language and Experience, described a young blind girl named Kelli, and tested what she understood by words about vision.
When Kelli was told to "look" at something, she explored it with her hands. When she was asked to hide an object from her mother, she put it in her pocket. Her meaning for "look" was not a simple copy of what sighted children mean, and it was not an empty word. She used it for a way of finding out about an object, and she used it in sensible ways.
Landau and Gleitman argued that children can learn a great deal about a word from the sentences it appears in, and not only from what they see. A verb that is used with certain kinds of phrases gives clues to its meaning. It suggests that language is a source of knowledge about the world, and not only a way to report what the senses supply.
Babies who babble with their hands

Hearing babies begin to babble in the second half of their first year, repeating syllables such as ba-ba-ba. Is babbling a matter of the mouth, or of language? In 1991 Laura-Ann Petitto and Paula Marentette studied a small group of babies, some who were deaf and were being raised by signing parents, and some who could hear.
The deaf babies produced repetitive hand movements that were like the rhythmic babbling of hearing babies, with simple shapes made over and over. A much larger share of their hand movements were of this kind than was true of the hearing babies. They appeared to be practicing the building blocks of sign, in the same way that the others were practicing the building blocks of speech.
The authors argued that babbling comes from a capacity for language in the brain, and not from the mouth alone. A baby is ready to pick up the patterns of language in whatever form it is offered. Other researchers have debated the interpretation, including a later study that followed deaf and hearing babies over time, so the case is a strong clue and not a final answer.

Nicaraguan Sign Language arose in the 1970s and 1980s, when deaf children were brought together in new schools. Each new group of children changed it, so that older signers had learned an early, simple form, while younger signers learned a richer one. This allowed researchers to ask what a language does for the mind.
In 2009 Jennie Pyers and Ann Senghas tested adult and adolescent signers on a false belief task, which asks where a person will look for something that has been moved without her knowledge. They also counted the signs that people used for mental states, such as think and know. Adults who had learned the early form as children used few of these signs, and failed the task. Signers whose language grew over the two years of the study came to understand false belief as it grew.
The authors concluded that learning a language, over and above social experience, drives the development of an understanding of other minds. A later study of deaf homesigners, who have no shared language, found that watching others was not enough to pass the task, even when it used little language. The work does not show which part of language matters.
A grammar that grew in one village

In a Bedouin village in the Negev desert of Israel, the rate of inherited deafness is high. Within about three generations, around 150 deaf people were born into the community. Deaf villagers are fully part of village life, and a sign language arose there that is not related to the spoken languages or to the sign languages of the region. It is called Al-Sayyid Bedouin Sign Language.
In 2005 Wendy Sandler, Irit Meir, Carol Padden and Mark Aronoff reported on it. They found that the language had a systematic word order, with the subject first, then the object, then the verb. That order differs from the spoken languages around it, and from the sign languages nearby. A consistent order appeared in the signing of the second generation.
The case shows that a language can acquire regular grammar within a few generations, with no teachers and no model to copy. Like Nicaraguan Sign Language, it is one of the few places where researchers have been able to watch grammar being formed. It suggests that some parts of grammar come from the way people communicate, and from the minds that use the language.
A language that started in how adults spoke to children

In Lajamanu, a Warlpiri community in the Northern Territory of Australia, adults often switched between Warlpiri, Kriol and English as they talked. The linguist Carmel O'Shannessy found that the switching had settled into a regular pattern, and that children there now learn it as one of their first languages. She named it Light Warlpiri.
It is a mixed language. Most nouns and noun endings come from Warlpiri, while most verbs and verb endings come from Kriol or English. It appears to have started in the 1980s, in the pattern of speech that adults used when talking to young children.
Her later work suggested two steps. Adults switched languages in a consistent way when speaking to small children. Then the children took the mixed speech as a single system, and added changes of their own. Estimates of the number of speakers are around 300 to 350, mostly under the age of 35 or 40. Warlpiri itself is still spoken too, so children there grow up with both.

In 1966 Allen and Beatrix Gardner, at the University of Nevada in Reno, began to raise a young chimpanzee named Washoe, and to teach her American Sign Language. Earlier attempts to teach chimpanzees to speak aloud had failed. Washoe lived in a trailer in the Gardners' yard, and the people around her were not allowed to speak.
By the Gardners' strict test, which was that a sign had to be used spontaneously and appropriately, she learned at least 130 signs. Other counts give 250 or 350, depending on how learning is defined. The Gardners reported that she put signs together in new ways, such as "water bird" for a swan.
Skeptics said that such a phrase could be just the naming of two things, the water and the bird, one after another, and that trainers may have cued her signs without meaning to. The question of whether an ape can learn language is therefore still open. Washoe later lived at Central Washington University, and she died in 2007.
Can an ape create a sentence?

Herbert Terrace, a psychologist at Columbia University, raised a chimpanzee named Nim Chimpsky, a joke on the name of the linguist Noam Chomsky, who argued that language is a uniquely human ability. The aim of Project Nim was to teach him sign language, and to see whether he could make sentences.
In 1979 Terrace and his colleagues published a paper in Science called Can an Ape Create a Sentence? They had reviewed more than 19,000 utterances in which Nim used more than one sign. They concluded that there was no clear evidence that apes master the structure of language. Terrace later studied the videotapes closely, frame by frame, and found that many of Nim's signs had been prompted by his teachers' signs just before. The teachers were cuing him without knowing it.
The paper had a large effect, and made researchers far more careful about cues and controls. Terrace said later that Chomsky had been right that a chimpanzee cannot create a sentence, but for the wrong reason, since Nim had not even clearly learned words. Other researchers, working with other apes, did not accept that this settled the matter.

The psychologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh was trying to teach a bonobo named Matata to use symbols on a keyboard. Matata made slow progress. Her young son Kanzi, who had seemed uninterested, had been watching all along, and within days of being separated from her he began to use the keyboard himself. He had learned by observation, with no training of his own.
In one test, Kanzi and a two-year-old girl named Alia were given 660 spoken instructions that asked them to do things with objects in new ways. Kanzi responded correctly to 74 percent of the instructions and Alia to 65 percent. Savage-Rumbaugh concluded that Kanzi understood the words in order, and she estimated that he understood more than 3,000 spoken English words.
Both the figure and the interpretation have been questioned. The vocabulary count is her own estimate, and a 1996 review said that the training and testing were not fully described, which matters for the claim that the skills were learned without training. Linguists also pointed out that an instruction could be followed by taking the words one at a time, without any grammar at all. The results are striking, but they are not proof of language.
Which half of the advertising is wasted?

"Half the money I spend on advertising is wasted, and the trouble is I don't know which half." The line is usually credited to the Philadelphia merchant John Wanamaker. The researcher who runs Quote Investigator found that Wanamaker was given credit for it in 1919, but could not find a speech, letter or interview in which he said it.
A similar idea appeared in a trade magazine, Printers' Ink, in 1890. Close variants were credited to others, among them the soap maker Lord Leverhulme and the chewing gum maker William Wrigley Jr. So the saying is an old adage with an unclear author, and Wanamaker is only the best candidate.
The reason it has lasted is that it describes a real difficulty. A customer may have seen a newspaper ad, a window display, a friend's opinion and a coupon before buying, and no one can say which of these did the work. Better measurement has helped, but the problem of knowing what caused a sale has never gone away.
The mall that was meant to be a town

Southdale Center in Edina, Minnesota, opened on October 8, 1956. It is widely described as the first fully enclosed, climate-controlled shopping mall in the United States, and it had two stories. The architect Victor Gruen designed it for the Dayton's department store, in part to bring shoppers out in the Minnesota winter.
Gruen was born in Vienna, and he had a different aim from the one that followed. He saw an enclosed shopping center as a way to give car-dependent suburbs something like a town center, with a place to meet and walk. His firm designed more than fifty malls in the United States before the middle of the 1970s.
But the idea spread in a form he did not like. In a 1978 speech in London he said that developers had bastardized his ideas, and he refused to take responsibility for the results. The number of traditional enclosed malls in America is said to have peaked at about 2,500 in the 1980s, and by 2022 it had fallen to about 700.
The man who promised fifty percent in forty-five days

In 1920 an Italian immigrant in Boston named Charles Ponzi offered investors a profit of fifty percent in forty-five days, or a hundred percent in ninety. His explanation was a form of arbitrage. International reply coupons, which let a person pay for a return postage stamp, cost less in some countries than their face value in the United States, and he said he was buying them cheaply abroad and redeeming them at home.
The scheme did pay early investors, but it paid them out of the money from new ones. In August 1920 the Boston Post began to look into his returns, and there was a run on his company. Postal officials found that the volume of coupons needed to produce such profits did not exist. Ponzi was arrested on August 12 and charged with mail fraud.
Schemes of this kind are now named after him, though he did not invent the method. They tend to fall apart when new money slows down. A promise of high, steady returns that depends on a story no one can check is the warning sign that his case still illustrates.
The investor whose returns never fell

Bernard Madoff ran an investment firm in New York that was known for dependable returns. His clients included charities and well-known people, and he had been a respected figure on Wall Street. On December 11, 2008, he was arrested after his two sons reported him to the authorities.
The statements that his clients had received showed holdings of about $60 billion, and they were fictitious. The scheme was a Ponzi scheme, in which earlier clients were paid with money from later ones. Estimates of its size vary by source, from about $50 billion to about $65 billion in claimed balances, and the real losses to clients were lower.
Madoff pleaded guilty to eleven felony counts in March 2009. On June 29, 2009, Judge Denny Chin sentenced him to 150 years, the most that the law allowed, though his lawyers had asked for twelve. He died in prison in 2021. The case is often cited for a simple lesson. Returns that are too smooth for the market around them deserve a question.
The blood tests that were not what they seemed

Theranos was a California company, founded by Elizabeth Holmes, that said it could run many blood tests on a few drops from a finger. The idea was attractive, since it would spare people the needle. The company raised large sums from investors, and had famous people on its board.
In 2015 the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was in fact using commercially available blood analysis machines, adapted for small samples, for most of its tests. In January 2022 a jury convicted Holmes on four of eleven counts. One count was conspiracy to commit wire fraud against investors, and three were wire fraud counts, including transfers of more than $140 million. She was not convicted on the counts that dealt with patients.
On November 18, 2022, she was sentenced to eleven years and three months, less than the fifteen that prosecutors had asked for. The story is often told as one about a charming founder. It is also a case of a claim that was hard for outsiders to test, in a field where testing is exactly what matters.
What was in the snake oil

In the 1890s a man named Clark Stanley sold a liniment called Snake Oil, and billed himself as the Rattlesnake King. It was meant to ease aches and pains. Many remedies of the time promised wonders and gave no details of what they contained.
In 1906 the United States passed the Pure Food and Drug Act, which required honest labeling. The government's chemists, in the Bureau of Chemistry, which became the Food and Drug Administration, tested Stanley's liniment. They found mineral oil, a small amount of fatty oil thought to be tallow, capsaicin from red peppers, and turpentine, along with camphor.
Stanley was fined twenty dollars for misbranding in 1917, and pleaded no contest. The phrase snake oil has since come to mean a worthless remedy sold with big claims. The fine was small, but the case helped to establish that what a label says must match what is in the bottle.
The cigarette that was a lady's, until it wasn't

Marlboro was introduced in 1924 as a cigarette for women, and its slogan was "Mild as May." In the early 1950s filters came into fashion, and filter cigarettes were seen as feminine and tasteless.
In 1954 Philip Morris repackaged Marlboro, and hired the Chicago advertising man Leo Burnett to change its image. Burnett chose the cowboy as a masculine symbol. The ads avoided health claims about the filter and showed rugged men in the outdoors. The campaign became one of the best known in advertising.
Sources disagree on the sales figures for the first years, so they are best treated with caution. What is not in doubt is the method. The cigarette itself was not changed very much. Its meaning was changed, by giving a product a new place in the mind of a different buyer. It is often used as the standard example of repositioning.

On January 22, 1984, during the third quarter of Super Bowl XVIII, a commercial for the new Apple Macintosh was shown. It was directed by Ridley Scott. It showed rows of gray workers listening to a giant face on a screen, and a woman in bright clothes running in to throw a hammer at it. It drew on the novel 1984, by George Orwell, and the gray world stood for the computer company IBM.
The commercial said that the Macintosh would be introduced two days later. Apple's board is reported to have disliked the ad, and to have wanted the time slot sold back. How that decision was reversed is not clear in the accounts. It was shown only once nationally, and also in a few local markets on December 31, 1983, which qualified it for advertising awards.
It is credited with starting the modern era of Super Bowl advertising, where big new campaigns are launched for a national audience at once. The commercial did not show the computer well. It sold an attitude, and the fact that people talked about it afterward did much of the work.

Buying online once meant typing an address and card number again for every order. Amazon's chief executive, Jeff Bezos, is said in a court filing to have conceived of letting customers buy with a single click, and the feature went into use in September 1997. Amazon filed for a patent on it that same month, and U.S. Patent No. 5,960,411 was issued on September 28, 1999.
About three weeks later Amazon sued its rival Barnesandnoble.com in Seattle, over a similar feature called Express Lane. On December 1, 1999, Judge Marsha Pechman granted a preliminary injunction that made the bookseller stop using it until the case was decided. The Federal Circuit vacated that injunction in early 2001, and the case was settled in 2002, on terms that were not made public.
The dispute was about whether such a simple idea could be patented. It also showed how much value a company placed on removing small steps in buying. Each field to fill in is a chance for a customer to stop, and one click is the shortest form of a purchase.

A story often told is that Black Friday got its name because stores go from red ink to black ink, from losses to profits, on the day after Thanksgiving. It is not the real origin. Snopes and others report that the earliest known version of that explanation dates from 1981.
The term came earlier, from Philadelphia. By 1961 the city's police were using it, in a sour way, for the day when huge crowds of shoppers and cars filled the downtown streets. The weekend of the Army and Navy football game added to the crowds. Accounts differ on exact dates, from the late 1950s to 1966, but all agree on the police.
Merchants disliked the dark meaning, and in the early 1960s tried to replace it with the idea of a good day. One account credits a retailer, Peter Strawbridge, with inventing the red and black story. It worked, and by the 1980s the name had spread nationwide. A word can start as a complaint and end as a sales event.
The coupon that put a drink in a million hands

Coca-Cola began as a drink sold at one pharmacy in Atlanta in 1886. When the businessman Asa Candler took over, he used a method that was new then. He handed out tickets, which could be exchanged at soda fountains for a free glass. Sources differ about the first ticket, giving a date between 1886 and 1888.
The fountain owners were reimbursed by the company, so they lost nothing, and the free drink was a way of getting people to try the taste. The company's own history says that between 1894 and 1913 about one in nine Americans had been given a free Coca-Cola, a total of some 8.5 million free drinks. It is a cumulative estimate and not a count, and it is widely repeated.
The method has been called the first coupon, though others may have used something like it. It rests on a simple idea. A product that few people have tasted is hard to sell, but one that has been tried for free can be bought out of habit. The cost of the free glass was a cost of advertising.
The phone call that lasted ten hours

On December 8, 2012, a customer service representative at the online shoe store Zappos, named Shaea Labus, spent 10 hours and 29 minutes on a single phone call. The customer wanted help choosing a pair of Ugg boots, and the call ended with a sale. It broke the company's own record for the longest call, which accounts give as a little under nine hours.
Records have been broken since. A call handled by Steven Weinstein in 2016 was reported to have lasted 10 hours and 43 minutes. Most call centers measure how short a call is, as a sign of efficiency. Zappos treated a long call as something to be proud of, since the first of its core values was to wow the customer through service.
The company's idea was that a customer treated well would come back, and tell others. Whether that pays for itself in each case is a fair question, and a ten hour call is an extreme example. But it shows that what is measured shapes what workers do, and that a business can choose to measure something else.
The chicken that is sold at a loss

For years Costco has sold a cooked rotisserie chicken for $4.99, even as other food prices rose. In a 2015 earnings call, the chief financial officer, Richard Galanti, described the company as willing to give up $30 million to $40 million a year in gross margin to keep the price there. By 2019 a senior vice president would not say whether the chicken still lost money.
It is a loss leader, a product sold at or below cost to bring people into the store. A food marketing professor, Ernest Baskin, explained that the aim is to draw shoppers who then buy other things. Costco's hot dog and soda combination, at $1.50 since the mid-1980s, works the same way. A story says that the former chief executive, Jim Sinegal, told a colleague that raising the price would be a firing offense, though accounts differ on who said it.
The idea is that shoppers remember the price of a few items, and judge the whole store by them. A famous low price on one thing can make everything else look fair. Snopes noted that the true cost to Costco is hard to know from outside the company.
How shoppers move through a store

Paco Underhill founded a research company, Envirosell, whose workers watched shoppers. His book Why We Buy, published in 1999, drew on thousands of hours of video, store maps and interviews. He wanted to see what people did in a store, and not what they said they did.
He described the entrance as a decompression zone, or landing strip. People who come in from the street need a few steps to slow down and adjust to the light, and to look around. A sign or display placed right at the door gets little notice, since the shopper's mind is still outside. He also described what is called the butt-brush effect. Shoppers dislike standing where other people may brush against them from behind, and in a narrow aisle some will leave a product and move on.
The findings were practical, on where to place a display and how wide to make an aisle. Some of the numbers repeated about his work cannot be traced to the book, so they are best taken as rules of thumb. The central point is that the behavior of people in a space can be seen, and that design can change it.
The first store where you got your own groceries

Before 1916 a customer in a grocery store usually asked a clerk, who fetched each item from behind a counter. On September 11, 1916, Clarence Saunders opened a new kind of store in Memphis, Tennessee, at 79 Jefferson Avenue. He called it Piggly Wiggly. The company counts its founding from September 6.
Customers took a basket, walked through aisles, and picked up goods that were priced and branded. They paid at checkouts at the front. It is generally described as the first true self-service grocery store. The shop needed fewer clerks, and shoppers could see everything on offer, and take their time.
Saunders filed a patent on a self-serving store on October 21, 1916, and it was granted on October 9, 1917, as U.S. Patent 1,242,872. A later one covered the design of the store. Stores of this kind spread quickly. The change put the package in charge of the sale, since the shopper now met the product with no one to explain it.
Houses that came in the mail

From 1908 to 1940 the retailer Sears, Roebuck and Company sold houses by mail. A buyer picked a design from a catalog, and the materials, already measured and cut, came by railroad, with instructions for putting them together. The company offered hundreds of designs, and some sources count 447 styles over the years.
Estimates of the number of houses sold vary. One source says between 70,000 and 75,000 from 1908 to 1940, while the Hagley Library reports more than 100,000 units, not counting cabins, garages and farm buildings. Sears also gave financing to some buyers who could not get a loan elsewhere, which opened the market to more families.
The program ended in the years around 1940, and sales through local offices lasted into 1942. Its success shows how far a trusted catalog could stretch. If people were willing to buy a house from a page of pictures, then a promise of quality, a guarantee and good financing mattered more than seeing the thing first.
When the sales target became the product

In September 2016 federal regulators fined Wells Fargo a combined $185 million. Of it, $100 million went to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, which was the largest fine the bureau had imposed up to then. They said that bank employees had opened more than two million accounts that customers may not have authorized, about 565,000 credit cards and 1.5 million deposit accounts.
The cause, according to the regulators, was pressure to meet sales targets and win pay incentives. Employees moved money into new accounts without asking, issued debit cards and made up PINs, and in some cases created false email addresses. The bank fired about 5,300 employees over the sales practices between 2011 and 2016, and dropped branch sales quotas after the fine. It paid $110 million to affected customers in 2017.
Later estimates put the number of fake accounts nearer to 3.5 million. The case is taught as a warning about incentives. When a measure is made the goal, people find ways of meeting the measure, whether or not the customer is served, and the people at the bottom of the chain can end up carrying the blame.
The company that laughed at Netflix

In early 2000 the founders of Netflix, Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph, are said to have offered to sell their company to the video rental chain Blockbuster for $50 million. Blockbuster's chief executive, John Antioco, declined. The founders have said that he appeared to be holding back laughter. Antioco has said that serious talks never took place.
Netflix then sent DVDs by mail, and made its name partly by having no late fees. Blockbuster is estimated to have collected about $800 million a year in late fees, which made them hard to give up. It dropped them in 2005, but the effort is reported to have backfired, in part because the terms were confusing.
Hastings has said that he is glad the deal did not happen. The story is often told as a case of a leader missing the future. A fairer way to read it is that a company living on a certain kind of revenue is slow to threaten that revenue, even when its customers dislike it. A rival with nothing to lose has an easier time.
How a company hid its losses

Enron was an energy company in Houston that was ranked among the largest in the United States. On December 2, 2001, it filed for bankruptcy. Its collapse followed the discovery that it had hidden debts and exaggerated its profits.
Two methods were at the center. Its trading business used mark-to-market accounting, which let it record the estimated future gains of a contract as income right away. And it moved debts and troubled assets into partnerships that were kept off its books, some run by its own finance chief, Andrew Fastow. When the value of those partnerships fell, the guarantees that Enron had given came due.
Its auditor, Arthur Andersen, was convicted of obstruction in 2002 for destroying documents, and lost its license to audit public companies. The Supreme Court reversed that conviction in 2005 because of a flawed instruction to the jury, but by then the firm had collapsed. Jeffrey Skilling and Kenneth Lay were convicted in 2006, Lay died before he was sentenced, and Fastow pleaded guilty and received six years.
A luxury brand with no history

By the 1980s Japanese cars had won a place in America as economical and reliable. But people who wanted a luxury car looked to Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Cadillac. Toyota decided to try for that market, and in 1983 began a secret project, called F1, to build a car that would equal them.
It took six years and more than a billion dollars. One account says that about 1,400 engineers worked on it, and some 450 prototypes were built. The LS 400 was shown at the Detroit auto show in January 1989, and production began on May 15, 1989. Sales began in September. Toyota did not use its own name for the car. It created a new brand, Lexus, with its own dealerships.
The first-year target was 16,000 cars, and it was reported to have been met. The lesson that is often drawn is that a company with a reputation for one kind of product may have to build a separate name to be believed in another. People judge a brand by what it has meant before, and Lexus had no past to overcome.

When a food company brings out a new product, it often has to pay the supermarket before the product gets onto the shelf. The payment is called a slotting allowance. The Federal Trade Commission studied it, and in November 2003 it released a staff report with case studies in five product categories.
Retailers say that the money offsets the costs of new products that fail, and the work of making room for them. Manufacturers say that it is a charge for access to a limited resource. The report also looked at pay-to-stay fees, which are charged to keep an established product in place. The FTC warned that the study was based on a small number of anonymous cases, and might not represent the whole industry.
Critics argue that the fees favor large companies that can afford them, and make it harder for small makers to compete. Supporters say that they allocate scarce shelf space to those who value it most. Either way, the arrangement is a reminder that what is on a shelf is partly the result of who paid to put it there.

In 1967 the language teacher Paul Pimsleur published a short paper called A Memory Schedule. He argued that a fact is best kept in memory by recalling it at gaps that grow longer each time, and he named the idea graduated interval recall. His example started with a gap of five seconds, then 25 seconds, then 125 seconds, so that each gap was about five times the last.
Sources list the full schedule as eleven steps: 5 seconds, 25 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes, 1 hour, 5 hours, 1 day, 5 days, 25 days, 4 months and 2 years. His company still builds its audio courses on the same idea, so that a new word comes back just as it is about to be forgotten.
The principle of spacing is well supported. The exact schedule is less certain. A later study at the University of Victoria found that, for long-term retention, a uniform delay did better than a graduated one. The safe lesson is that reviewing at widening gaps works, and that the precise gaps matter less than doing it.

In 1956 the educator Benjamin Bloom and a group of colleagues published a classification of the thinking that schools ask for. It had six levels, from simple to complex: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation. The idea was to help teachers write goals and tests that asked for more than recall.
In 2001 Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl, who had been one of Bloom's collaborators, published a revision. It changed the names from nouns to verbs: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate and create. It also moved creating to the top, above evaluating. The revision added a second scale for the kind of knowledge involved, which can be factual, conceptual, procedural or about thinking itself.
The taxonomy is used in schools around the world. Not everyone agrees that the levels form a strict ladder, and some argue that a person may need to create before fully understanding. As a practical tool, it asks a good question of any lesson. Are the students only remembering, or are they using what they know?

Intuition says that the best way to learn algebra is to solve many problems. In 1985 John Sweller and Graham Cooper found that this is not always so. They compared students who solved problems with students who studied worked examples, which show each step of a solution. The students who studied examples did better on later problems.
In their design, the examples were alternated with similar problems, so that a student would study a solution and then try one. Sweller explained the result by the limits of working memory. A beginner who tries to solve a problem has to search for a method, and that search uses up the mental space that would be needed to learn the pattern.
The finding became a starting point for cognitive load theory. Later work found that it fades as learners become more expert, an effect called expertise reversal, and for them it may be better to solve problems. For a beginner the lesson is plain. Study how a solution works before trying to make your own.
The poet who named the dead

According to the Roman writer Cicero, the first memory trick was found by accident. The poet Simonides of Ceos was paid to recite a poem at a banquet given by a nobleman, Scopas, in Crannon in Thessaly. The poem praised the twin gods Castor and Pollux, and Scopas, annoyed, said that he would pay only half, and that the twins could pay the rest.
A message came that two young men were waiting outside for Simonides. He went out, and no one was there. Behind him the roof fell in and killed Scopas and his guests, and the bodies were crushed past recognition. Simonides could tell the families who had been who, because he remembered where each guest had been lying at the table.
Cicero drew the lesson that order is the key to memory. One should choose places, picture the things to be remembered, and set the pictures in the places. This is the method of loci, or memory palace, and it was written up in a Latin handbook, the Ad Herennium, about 86 BC. The story is a legend, and nothing outside Cicero's telling confirms it. The method itself still works.

People who practice a skill often do better the next morning than they did when they stopped. In 1994 Avi Karni, Dorit Tanne and their colleagues asked whether sleep is the reason. They used a visual task in which people had to pick out a small pattern against a textured background, and they tested people before and after a night.
After a normal night of sleep, performance improved. When the researchers woke people each time they entered REM sleep, the stage with vivid dreams, the improvement did not appear. Waking people from deep slow-wave sleep did not have this effect. Losing REM sleep did not harm a similar task that had been learned earlier. The authors concluded that this kind of memory consolidation depends strongly on REM sleep.
Later work has made the picture more complicated. A study of naps found that a nap of 60 to 90 minutes can produce the same kind of learning, when it contains both slow-wave and REM sleep. The exact role of each stage is still argued. The finding that sleep is part of learning, and not just rest from it, has held up well.

Does exercise help children think? In 2009 Charles Hillman and his colleagues tested children of about nine and ten years old on two days. On one day they walked on a treadmill for 20 minutes at a moderate pace, at 60 percent of an estimate of their maximum heart rate. On the other they sat quietly for 20 minutes. After each, they did tests of attention and of school subjects.
After the walk, the children were more accurate on a task that required them to ignore distracting information, especially on the harder trials. They also did better on a test of academic achievement. The authors saw this as a link between physical activity, attention and school performance, after only a single session.
Hillman himself noted a limit. Children do not normally walk on treadmills, so the design is not like real life, and one session says little about long-term effects. But the finding fits with other work suggesting that a short bout of exercise can make it easier to concentrate for a while afterward. It is a reason to take a walk before an hour of study.
A cousin, a notepad and a million lessons

In August 2004 Salman Khan was working at a hedge fund in Boston when his young cousin Nadia, in New Orleans, was struggling with converting units in math. He began tutoring her over the phone, using Yahoo Doodle, a shared drawing page, to show his work. Within a couple of years he had added more than a dozen relatives and family friends to his lessons.
A friend suggested that he put the sessions on YouTube so that the cousins could watch them when they pleased. In 2006 he began to upload videos. They were simple, a voice and a hand writing on a screen, and strangers began to watch them. Khan Academy was set up as a not-for-profit organization in 2008, and in 2009, he left his job to work on it full time.
The reasons for its success are debated, and so is its effect on learning. Part of the appeal was that a student could pause, replay and go at his or her own pace, which a classroom lecture does not allow. It started with a single tutor who wanted to help one child.
Why most people never finish the online course

Around 2012 free online university courses, called massive open online courses or MOOCs, drew enormous crowds. Many predicted that they would remake higher education. Katy Jordan, a researcher, collected the figures that were available on how many people who enrolled finished.
Her analysis, reported in 2013, found that the average completion rate across 29 courses was 6.8 percent. In a later paper, in 2015, with a dataset of 221 courses, completion rates ranged from 0.7 percent to 52.1 percent, and the median was 12.6 percent. Completion was defined as the share of enrolled students who completed the course.
The numbers need careful reading. Since signing up is free, many who enroll never meant to finish, and some just wanted to watch a few lectures. But the pattern shows how hard it is to keep an adult learner going without deadlines, a teacher or a cost. A course that is easy to start is also easy to leave.

The One Laptop per Child program aimed to give every child in a poor country a cheap, sturdy laptop. Peru bought them in large numbers. In 2012 a team led by Julian Cristia, working for the Inter-American Development Bank, studied what happened in a randomized trial. Of about 320 rural primary schools, 210 were picked by lot to receive the laptops, and the rest did not.
After 15 months the researchers found no effect on test scores in math or language, and no evidence of an effect on enrollment. There were some small gains in general thinking skills, measured by a test of reasoning, a test of verbal fluency and a coding test. A separate experiment with about a thousand children in Lima also found no significant difference between children with laptops and those without.
The bank's own comment on the work was titled One Laptop per Child is not enough. A device brings the chance for learning, but it does not make the lessons. The missing parts may be the training of teachers and suitable software, though the trial did not test that.

How should children be taught to read? In synthetic phonics, they learn the sounds of letters first and then blend them to make words. In the late 1990s the schools of Clackmannanshire, in Scotland, took part in a study of this. Rhona Johnston and Joyce Watson compared three groups of about 300 pupils in all. One group learned synthetic phonics, one an analytic form of phonics, and one practiced sounds without print.
At the end of primary school, seven years later, the synthetic phonics group was about three and a half years ahead of its age in word reading. It was about one year and eight months ahead in spelling, but only a few months ahead in reading comprehension. Boys were nearly a year ahead of girls in word reading, which the researchers had not expected. The synthetic group did better than the analytic one.
There are cautions. The children were not assigned by lot, so other differences may have played a part. How much the study should have shaped policy has also been debated. Still, it was influential, and it is often cited. Its results are strongest for decoding words, and weakest for understanding what they say.
Voting and arguing in a lecture

Eric Mazur taught introductory physics at Harvard. He found that many students could solve the equations in an exam, but could not answer simple questions about the ideas. He changed his lectures. After a short talk, he would put a conceptual question to the room, and students would vote on an answer. Then they would turn to a neighbor, argue for their choice, and vote again.
He called it peer instruction, and the questions ConcepTests. In 2001 Catherine Crouch and Mazur reported on ten years of its use in Harvard's courses for nonmajors. They measured understanding with the Force Concept Inventory and the Mechanics Baseline Test, two standard tests of the ideas of mechanics. They found larger gains than those found with traditional lecturing.
A later paper by Fagen, Crouch and Mazur, in 2002, reported that courses at many other schools that used interactive methods also showed gains above those of traditional teaching. Students who explain an idea to a classmate have to put it in words, and find where their thinking fails. It is a way of making a large room into a place where people talk.
The classroom where everyone held a piece

In 1971 the public schools of Austin, Texas, had recently been desegregated. White, Black and Hispanic children, who had always been in separate schools, were now in the same classrooms, and there were fights and tension. A former student of the psychologist Elliot Aronson, who worked in the school district, asked him for help.
Aronson and his team decided that the competitive classroom was making things worse. Children raced to answer the teacher, and put down others who were slow. He designed the jigsaw method. Students were placed in groups of about six, and each was given one part of the lesson. Each student also met with others who had the same part, and learned it, then went back to teach the group. No one could succeed without the others.
A 1977 study of ten fifth-grade classes in seven schools reported that children in jigsaw classes were absent less often than others, and showed greater improvement in their schoolwork. The method rests on an idea that Gordon Allport suggested earlier: groups get along better when they share a goal and need each other. It is still used in classrooms today.
Teaching a student to ask the questions

Some children can read every word of a passage and still not understand it. In 1984 Annemarie Palincsar and Ann Brown worked with seventh graders who were good at decoding but poor at understanding. They taught them four activities that good readers use without thinking: summarizing, asking questions, clarifying what is confusing, and predicting what comes next.
The method was called reciprocal teaching. An adult first led a discussion of a short text, using the four activities. Then the students took turns being the teacher, with the adult helping. In the first study, the experimenters ran it. It produced larger gains than a comparison method that was like normal classroom practice, and the gains lasted longer. They carried over to new tasks too.
In the second study, volunteer teachers used it with their own reading groups, and many of the results were repeated. The quality of the students' summaries and questions improved. The approach shows that comprehension can be taught, by making the hidden habits of a good reader into things that can be said and practiced aloud.
The test that was meant to find who needed help

In 1904 the French government set up a commission to look at how to teach children who were failing in school. It needed a way to find the children who would do better in special classes, before teachers' guesses and prejudices decided it. The psychologist Alfred Binet, with a doctor, Theodore Simon, was asked to find one.
Their scale of 1905 had 30 tasks, arranged from easy to hard, for children from infancy to about eleven. A revision in 1908 had 58 items, for ages three to thirteen. Binet described a child's result as a level of development, and he wrote that it classified children, and did not measure a fixed quantity. His main goal was to separate children who needed extra help from the rest of the school population.
Binet warned against taking the scores as a permanent label, and he believed that teaching could raise them. When the test was taken up in other countries, and revised, it came to be used in ways he had not intended, including the ranking of people by a single number. The origin was a practical question about how to help children who were struggling.
The man whose memory had no limit

In the 1920s a Moscow newspaper reporter named Solomon Shereshevsky was sent by his editor to see the psychologist Alexander Luria, because he never took notes. Luria tested him, and found that he could remember long lists of numbers and words, apparently without any limit. Luria studied him for about thirty years and described him as S. in a 1968 book, The Mind of a Mnemonist.
Luria linked the memory to synesthesia, the mixing of senses. Sounds, words and numbers produced colors, tastes and images for S. The pictures were the basis of his recall, and he could place them along streets, as in the method of loci. Luria wrote that the capacity of his memory had no distinct limits.
The account has been questioned. Luria did not clearly separate S.'s natural gifts from the memory techniques he used, and a diary that was found later suggests that he did not in fact have perfect recall. The case is among the most famous in psychology, and perhaps shows how far both talent and method can go.
The reporter who won a memory contest

In 2005 the science writer Joshua Foer covered the USA Memory Championship for Slate, and was struck that the contestants said they had ordinary memories. A man there offered to train him. Foer spent about a year learning the methods under a British memory grandmaster, Ed Cooke, and entered the 2006 championship himself. To the surprise of many, including himself, he won.
The core of the method was the old memory palace. He would picture a familiar place, and put vivid, odd images of the things to be remembered in different spots. He set a United States record in the speed cards event that year, memorizing a deck of 52 cards in 1 minute and 40 seconds. In his 2011 book, Moonwalking with Einstein, he described what he had learned.
His story is evidence that a lot of what looks like a gift is trained. Contest memorizers practice for hours, and the skill applies to lists and cards and not to everything. It does not turn a person into someone who remembers everything. But it shows what a well-practiced technique can do for a person who thought that he was average.
The seven ways memory goes wrong

In 2001 the Harvard psychologist Daniel Schacter published a book that sorted the everyday failures of memory into seven kinds, which he called sins. Three are errors of omission, in which something is not remembered. Transience is the fading of memories over time. Absent-mindedness is a lapse in attention, such as putting down keys while thinking about something else. Blocking is failing to bring up something that you know, as with a name on the tip of the tongue.
Four are errors of commission, in which memory is present but wrong or unwanted. Misattribution is remembering something correctly but linking it to the wrong source. Suggestibility is taking in a false detail from a question or a comment. Bias is the way that present beliefs color what we recall. Persistence is the return of memories we would rather forget, as with a painful event.
Schacter argued that these errors are the cost of a system that works well most of the time. Forgetting what is no longer useful, for example, helps us deal with the present. A memory that kept everything would be a different kind of problem. He updated the framework in 2021.
Why the same words feel different as a loss

In 1981 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman put a problem to people. An unusual disease is expected to kill 600 people. In one version, the choice is between a program that will save 200 for certain, and one that has a one third chance of saving all 600 and a two thirds chance of saving none. Of 152 people who were asked, 72 percent chose the sure thing.
In the second version, the choice is the same in fact but is worded in lives lost. One program means that 400 people will die. The other has a one third chance that nobody dies and a two thirds chance that 600 die. Of 155 other people, only 22 percent chose the sure program, and most chose the gamble.
The outcomes are identical, and the only change is the wording, saved or lost. People are cautious when the choice is about gains, and take risks when it is about losses. The finding has been used to explain how the framing of a message can change a decision. Later studies show that the effect is not as general as first thought. It depends on the context, and a pandemic-era attempt to repeat it did not find the original result.
The urn with a hidden mix

In 1961 a young economist, Daniel Ellsberg, described a puzzle. An urn holds 30 balls. Ten are red, and the other twenty are black or white in an unknown mix. You win a prize if you draw a ball of a color you choose. Most people would rather bet on red, where the odds are known to be one in three, than on black, where the odds could be anything.
Then the choice is changed. You can bet on red or white, or on black or white. Now the odds for black or white are known to be exactly two in three, while red or white could be anywhere. Most people choose black or white. The two choices together do not make sense. Choosing red in the first means that you think red is more likely than black, and so red or white should be more likely than black or white.
The effect is called ambiguity aversion. People will give up a better bet to avoid one whose odds they cannot see. Ellsberg later became better known for something else. In 1971 he gave the Pentagon Papers, a secret government study of the Vietnam War, to newspapers.
The pattern that was only chance

During the Second World War, German flying bombs fell on London. Londoners noticed that some districts seemed to be hit again and again, and others never. Some suspected that the bombs were aimed, or that certain places were spared on purpose. Many people had their own theories about it.
After the war a statistician, R. D. Clarke, who worked for an insurance company, tested the idea. He divided an area of south London into 576 squares, each a quarter of a square kilometer, and counted the bombs in each. There were 537 bombs in all. He compared the counts to what a random scatter would give. About 229 squares had none, 211 had one, 93 had two, and a few had more.
The fit to a random pattern was close. His test gave a probability of 0.88, so there was no support for the idea that the bombs clustered. The belief in a pattern is called the clustering illusion. In small samples chance produces streaks and clumps, and we are not good at expecting them. Kahneman and Tversky explained it by the representativeness heuristic, the habit of expecting random things to look evenly spread.
The shapes that seemed to have motives

In 1944 two psychologists at Smith College, Fritz Heider and Marianne Simmel, made a short film. It showed a large triangle, a small triangle, a circle, and a box with a door, all moving around a screen. Nothing in it was alive. They asked 34 people to say what they saw.
Nearly everyone told a story. The big triangle was a bully, and the small shapes were being chased and fighting. The circle was frightened and hid in the box. Only one person described the film in terms of geometry, as moving shapes. Almost all of them said that the shapes wanted things, and that they were being kind or cruel.
The study is a classic on how automatically people see intention and character. From very little, such as the speed and path of a movement, we infer goals and feelings. It helps to explain why people give names to cars and talk to computers, and why a short cartoon can move us. The urge to find minds is built into how we see.
The bridge that made her seem attractive

In 1974 Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron did a field experiment near Vancouver, Canada. A woman interviewer approached young men who had just crossed one of two bridges over the Capilano River. One was a narrow footbridge of wooden boards on wire cables, high above a gorge, and it swayed. The other was a low, solid bridge nearby.
She asked them to write a short story for her survey, and gave each man her phone number in case he wanted to know more. The men from the high bridge wrote stories with significantly more sexual imagery. By one account, nine of eighteen men who took her number from the high bridge later called, while only two of sixteen did from the low one.
The authors' explanation was misattribution of arousal. The men's pounding hearts from fear were taken, in part, as attraction to her. The finding has been repeated in various forms, but the exact numbers differ among accounts, and the study was small. It remains a striking case of how the body's signals can be misread.
Does a small gift of luck make us kind?

In the early 1970s the psychologist Alice Isen asked whether a good mood makes people helpful. She and Paul Levin arranged for some people to find a dime in the coin return of a pay phone, and others not to. Then a stranger walked past and dropped a folder full of papers.
According to a later summary, 88 percent of those who found the dime stopped to help, while only 4 percent of those who had not found one did. It was a small study, and the figures come from a secondhand description. Isen also gave people cookies, or good news about their performance, and found similar effects on helping.
Her work helped found the study of how mood affects thinking. She also showed that people in a good mood tended to be better at solving some creative problems. Not every finding has held up in later tries. But the idea that a small piece of luck can change what we do for a stranger has been influential, and has been repeated in many forms.
When a favor makes a friend

Most of us think that we do favors for people we like. Benjamin Franklin noticed that it may work the other way. In his autobiography he tells of a rival in the Pennsylvania Assembly, who had never been friendly to him. Franklin heard that the man owned a rare book, and wrote asking to borrow it for a few days.
The man sent it at once. Franklin returned it a week later with a note of thanks. The next time they met in the Assembly, the man spoke to him civilly, for the first time, and became a friend for life. Franklin quoted an old maxim: he that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another than he whom you yourself have obliged.
In 1969 Jon Jecker and David Landy tested it. Students who had won money in a contest were asked to give it back, some by the researcher himself, some by a secretary, and some were not asked. Those the researcher had asked personally liked him the most, and those the secretary had asked liked him the least. The usual explanation is cognitive dissonance. Having helped, we decide that he must be worth helping.
Why pretty tools seem easier to use

Suppose you are shown two designs for a machine, and one looks better than the other. Does that change how easy you think it will be to use? In 1995 Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura, researchers at the company Hitachi in Tokyo, tested it with different layouts for the screen of a cash machine.
They found that how usable people thought a layout was had a stronger link to how beautiful it looked than to how well it actually worked. People seemed to be influenced by looks even when they were asked to judge function. Later work by Noam Tractinsky and others found similar results, with other ATM layouts and with a home control system.
The result is now called the aesthetic-usability effect. People tend to see a good-looking design as easier to use, and to forgive its faults. For designers it suggests that appearance is not decoration. But it has a risk, which is that a pretty design can hide real problems that a plain one would have shown. Careful testing must look at what people do, and not only at what they say.
Why friends look better in a group photo

In a television comedy in November 2008, a character called Barney points out a group of women who seem attractive, but who look plain when he considers them one at a time. He named it the cheerleader effect. It sounded like a joke, but psychologists took it up.
In a paper that appeared in 2014, Drew Walker and Edward Vul tested it. They found that faces were rated as about 1.5 to 2 percent more attractive when seen in a group than when seen alone. The effect did not depend on how long the faces were shown, how many people were in the group, or how they were arranged.
The explanation they offered is that the brain sums up a group, forming an average, and our judgment of each face is pulled toward that average. Averages of faces tend to be smooth and symmetrical, and attractive. The effect is small, and not all studies agree on its causes. It is a reminder that we do not judge each thing on its own, but in the setting around it.

If you have a twenty dollar bill, and you break it, the money seems to go faster. In 2009 Priya Raghubir and Joydeep Srivastava tested this idea in three studies, and called it the denomination effect.
In the first, 89 undergraduate students were thanked for taking part, and each was given either four quarters or a one dollar bill. They were told that they could keep the money or spend it on candy. About 63 percent of the students with four quarters bought candy. Only about 26 percent of those with the dollar bill did.
The authors suggested that a large note feels less exchangeable than the same value in small coins, so it is harder to part with. This also means that people who want to control their spending may like to carry large bills. The researchers noted that during the Great Recession, a businessman saw employees using coins more than banknotes at an office vending machine. It is a small effect, but it shows that the form of money changes how we spend it.
Did hunger change the judges' decisions?

In 2011 Shai Danziger, Jonathan Levav and Liora Avnaim-Pesso reported a study of Israeli parole boards. They looked at about a thousand rulings by judges during their day, which had two meal breaks. The share of requests granted was about 65 percent at the start of a session, but fell nearly to zero before a break. After the break it jumped back up.
The authors suggested that mental fatigue pushed the judges toward the safe choice, which was to refuse. Rest and food restored their willingness to take chances. The paper was cited some 2,500 times, and it became a favorite example of how small things can bias serious decisions.
But the findings have been questioned. A few months later a letter in the same journal argued that the order of cases is not random. Prisoners without lawyers tend to go last, for one, and lawyers may arrange the order for their clients. A later analysis suggested that part of the effect could come from scheduling, since cases that were likely to be granted took more time. The psychologist Daniël Lakens argued that the effect was far too large to be plausible. The lesson is to be careful with a striking result.
The feeling of being a fraud

In 1978 two psychologists at Georgia State University, Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, wrote about an experience they had met in their work with clients. Some highly successful women felt that they were not really intelligent, and that their success was luck or a mistake that would soon be found out. The authors called it the impostor phenomenon.
Their paper drew on their therapy work with more than 150 high-achieving women, and was a clinical description and not a test. They linked it to family messages and to stereotypes about women. They took care not to call it a syndrome or a disorder. It is not a diagnosis in the standard manuals of psychiatry.
Later research found that the experience is common among men as well as women, and across ages. It has become one of the best known ideas in popular psychology, and appears in discussions of work and school. Studies suggest that people who feel like impostors are not less able. Their doubt does not follow their performance, and talking about it can help.
Why you suddenly see a word everywhere

Many people have learned a new word, and then seen it three times in a week. In 1994 a reader in St. Paul, Minnesota, Terry Mullen, wrote to his newspaper, the Pioneer Press, about it. He had heard the name of the German militant group Baader-Meinhof once, and then kept coming across it.
Other readers wrote in with their own stories, and the effect became known as the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon, though it has nothing to do with the group. In 2005 a Stanford linguist, Arnold Zwicky, wrote about it on his blog and gave it a better name, the frequency illusion.
Zwicky explained it as the work of two processes. One is selective attention. Once something has caught our notice, we are on the lookout for it. The other is confirmation bias, in which we register each new sighting as proof that it is everywhere. The word was always as common. What changed was that you began to notice it, and your mind counted the hits and ignored the misses.
Why a calm person cannot imagine being angry

When you are angry, it is hard to remember what it felt like to be calm. When you are calm, it is hard to understand how you could have been so angry. Psychologists call this a hot-cold empathy gap. A hot state is one driven by emotion or by bodily urges such as hunger, pain or desire. A cold state is the absence of these.
The point is that what we understand is tied to the state we are in. People in a cold state underestimate how much a hot one will drive them, and people in a hot state have trouble believing they will feel differently later. The economist George Loewenstein has been prominent in studying it. It helps to explain why people make plans they do not keep, and why they give in to temptation.
The idea has practical uses. A doctor who has never had severe pain may underestimate a patient's suffering. A person who makes a rule for a time of temptation, when calm, may find the rule easy to make and hard to follow. A sensible response is to set up the situation ahead of time, so that the hot self has fewer chances to take over.
Why you cannot tell how long you will feel bad

In 1759 the economist and philosopher Adam Smith observed that people who chase wealth think it will bring them lasting peace, and often find that it does not. Two centuries later the idea became a field of research. The term affective forecasting, meaning the prediction of one's own future feelings, was coined by the psychologists Timothy Wilson and Daniel Gilbert.
They found that people are poor at it. People imagine that winning a lottery would make them happy for a long time, and they overlook the many other things in their lives that will go on affecting their mood. In 1998 Gilbert and his colleagues argued that people overestimate how long bad feelings will last, because they are unaware of what they called the psychological immune system, the mental processes that soften pain.
The practical result is that we often choose badly, working hard for things that give less lasting pleasure than we predicted, and dreading things that will bother us less than we fear. One way to improve a forecast is to ask someone who has been through the same experience. It is a better guide than our own imagination.

Many people say that members of another race look alike to them. The first study of the effect was published in 1914. In 2001 Christian Meissner and John Brigham reviewed thirty years of research in a meta-analysis called Thirty Years of Investigating the Own-Race Bias in Memory for Faces.
They found a mirror effect. When people were shown faces and later asked to pick them out, they were more often right about faces of their own race, and also made fewer false alarms, which are wrong claims to have seen a face. With faces of another race they did worse on both. The effect has been found in many groups, and it matters in court, where witnesses are asked to identify strangers.
There are several explanations, including a lack of experience with the faces and the way attention is directed. Contact with people of the other race helps a little, but no one theory explains all the findings. Brain scans show that parts of the brain that handle faces respond differently to faces of one's own group. The effect is not a sign of prejudice, though it can lead to serious mistakes.
The Rorschach test and the problem of validity

In 1921 a Swiss psychiatrist, Hermann Rorschach, published a book describing a test with ten inkblots. He showed them to patients and asked what they saw. He was interested not so much in what the person saw as in how, such as whether he used the whole blot, the details, or the white spaces, and whether he noticed color or movement. He died the next year, in 1922, at the age of 37.
The test became one of the best known in the world, and its blots are a symbol of psychology in popular culture. But its scientific standing has been disputed for decades. Critics argued that psychologists using it did not agree on how to score responses, and that it did not predict behavior well. Later scoring systems were developed to address this.
Today many psychologists regard it as a weak tool for diagnosing most conditions, though some find it useful as a way of starting a conversation and of seeing how a person organizes experience. It is a good example of a test that is popular, and that people trust, without having been shown to measure what it is supposed to.
Why one child moves us more than a thousand

The psychologist Paul Slovic noticed that people who will give to help one named child often feel little when told of thousands in need. He called the effect compassion fade, and he and Deborah Small wrote of a collapse of compassion. The usual explanation is that feeling depends on being able to picture a victim, and that a crowd is hard to picture.
In 2007 Small, George Loewenstein and Slovic ran four field experiments with ordinary citizens. In one, people were shown an appeal about Rokia, a seven-year-old girl in Mali. When her story was given with statistics about the many others in need, donations went down and not up.
Then they tried teaching people about the bias. When people were prompted to think carefully, they gave less to the single identified child, but they did not give more to the statistical group. Information drove down the feeling and did nothing to replace it. The authors found one small gain. People who were told about the effect became more consistent in how they treated the two kinds of victims.

Ask each member of a couple what share of the housework he or she does, and add up the answers. Often the total is more than 100 percent. In 1979 the psychologists Michael Ross and Fiore Sicoly studied this, and called it an egocentric bias.
They asked 37 married couples to estimate their own responsibility for a list of household activities, such as preparing breakfast, shopping and making important decisions. They also studied discussion groups of students, intercollegiate basketball players and groups in the laboratory.
