In each case people remembered their own contributions to a joint product more easily than those of others, and they claimed more responsibility for it.
The reason they gave is not vanity. It is availability. Your own efforts are vivid to you, since you were there for each one, while those of a partner happen out of your view. You remember what you did, and you do not remember what you did not see. A popular account of the study notes that couples even overclaimed responsibility for causing arguments. The sensible response is to expect that everyone feels they do more than their share.
The vaccine that frightens parents more than the disease

Imagine a flu that is expected to kill 10 children in every 10,000. A vaccine prevents the flu, but it can itself kill some children. Would you vaccinate your child? In 1990 Ilana Ritov and Jonathan Baron put questions of this kind to people, and many chose not to vaccinate even when the vaccine's risk was lower than the risk of the disease.
In their later work, many people preferred not to vaccinate when the disease killed 10 in 10,000 and the vaccine killed 5 in 10,000 or fewer. A child who dies of the vaccine would be a result of something the parent did. A child who dies of the flu is a result of something the parent did not do. People judge harm from action as worse than harm from inaction. The pattern is called omission bias.
It is not universal. The authors noted that the effect can reverse when the person making the choice is seen as responsible for those affected, such as a doctor, who may feel pushed to act. The lesson is that doing nothing is also a choice with consequences. If the numbers say that acting reduces harm, the feeling that inaction is safer is a bias.
How a TV show changed how men rated a photo

A contrast effect is a change in how we judge something because of what we saw just before. A gray square looks lighter after a dark one. The oldest known description is by the eleventh-century scholar Ibn al-Haytham, who noticed that spots of paint look darker against a white background and paler on a black one.
In 1980 Douglas Kenrick and Sara Gutierres studied it with people. Male students who were watching the television show Charlie's Angels, whose three main characters were very attractive, were asked to rate a photograph of a woman. They rated her as less attractive than did men who had been watching another program.
Nothing about the woman had changed. The standard in the men's heads had. The finding is used to explain why people may feel less satisfied with their own appearance, or their partner's, after looking at the pictures in magazines and on screens. It applies to many things. A moderate price looks cheap after a very high one, and a good grade looks poor if the last paper was great.
The same proposal, three different senders

A proposal can be judged on its merits, or on who made it. In the late 1980s Lee Ross and Constance Stillinger called the second habit reactive devaluation, in which a proposal is thought worse when it seems to come from an opponent.
In an experiment, pedestrians in the United States were asked about a plan to reduce nuclear arms on both sides. When told that the plan came from President Ronald Reagan, 90 percent said it would be favorable or even-handed for the United States. When told that it came from a group of unspecified policy analysts, 80 percent said so. When told that it came from the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, only 44 percent did.
The plan was the same in each case. Other studies found the same thing. Israeli participants rated a peace proposal lower when told that it came from the Palestinian side than when told that it was an Israeli proposal. It is a problem for negotiation, since a good offer from a rival may be rejected only because of its source. One remedy is to have a neutral party present it.
The fire that was not caused by the closet

When a news report is corrected, people do not always correct their thinking. In 1994 Hollyn Johnson and Colleen Seifert tested this with a story about a warehouse fire. Participants read a series of messages. Early on, it was said that the fire had probably been started by volatile materials, such as paint and gas cylinders, that were carelessly stored in a closet.
Later in the story, they were told that the closet had in fact been empty. Afterward the participants were asked questions about the fire. Even people who clearly remembered the correction still gave answers that used the false cause, such as saying that the fire was so intense because of the stored materials.
This is called the continued influence effect. A false explanation fills a gap in our understanding, and when it is taken away, the gap remains. Later research has found that the effect is robust across stories, and it suggests that a correction works better when it gives a replacement explanation. People would rather have a wrong account than no account.
The child who sees an insult in a smile

Suppose that two children are laughing as you walk by. One child thinks that they are enjoying a joke. Another thinks they are laughing at him. Psychologists call the second kind of thinking hostile attribution bias, a tendency to read hostile intent into behavior that is ambiguous or harmless.
The term was coined in 1980 by Nasby, Hayden and DePaulo. They, and others such as Kenneth Dodge, had noticed that a group of children more often took ambiguous social situations to be hostile. In young children this is common and normal. But those who keep a high level of it through childhood are much more likely to be aggressive, with hitting, verbal attacks or damaging a friendship.
Researchers think that the bias is one path by which other troubles lead to aggression. Children who are teased by peers or treated harshly at home may come to expect the worst from others, and then react in kind. Programs have been designed to help children consider other explanations for what a peer did, on the idea that the problem begins in the interpretation.
Why we blame them and excuse us

Suppose a member of your own group does something kind, and a member of another group does the same. Do you explain the two acts in the same way? In 1979 the psychologist Thomas Pettigrew said that people do not. He named the pattern the ultimate attribution error.
When someone from an outgroup does something bad, we tend to explain it by their character, as in that is the kind of people they are. When they do something good, we explain it away by the situation, luck, or special effort. For our own group the reverse holds. Good acts show good character, and bad acts are blamed on circumstances.
The pattern strengthens prejudice, since each act that is seen seems to confirm what was already believed. The research suggests that it shows up more strongly in Western cultures than in Eastern ones, and that strong emotions such as fear and anger can make it worse. Pettigrew built on the earlier work of Gordon Allport, and his point was that stereotypes persist partly because of the way we interpret what we see.
More candy from a bigger scoop

How do we decide how much to eat? In 2006 Andrew Geier, Paul Rozin and Gheorghe Doros proposed that part of the answer is unit bias. People tend to treat one unit of something as the right amount, whatever size the unit is.
In one study, people were offered Tootsie Rolls in a large or a small size, and could take as many as they wished. Those offered the large ones took and presumably ate much more by weight. With pretzels, the people given whole pretzels ate about twice as much as those given a half pretzel as the unit. In another study, people helped themselves to M&M's with either a large spoon or a small one, and took substantially more with the large spoon, still usually taking one scoop.
The authors thought that a cultural norm, to finish what is served and to take one portion, was behind the effect. It suggests why smaller packages and plates can help people eat less, as they would not make up the difference by taking more. Later researchers have compared unit bias with other effects, and have found that the picture is more complicated.
Why the night sky is dark

If the universe were infinite and full of stars, then in whatever direction you looked, your line of sight would eventually end on a star. The sky should be as bright as the surface of a star. The night sky is dark. This puzzle is called Olbers' paradox, after the German astronomer Heinrich Olbers, who wrote about it in 1823, though he was far from the first to raise it. Halley and Cheseaux had thought about it earlier.
Several people have been credited with the answer. Edgar Allan Poe, in his 1848 prose poem Eureka, suggested that the universe is only so old, so light from the most distant stars has not reached us yet. Some scientists say this was the first correct answer. Others credit Lord Kelvin, in 1901, with the first satisfactory treatment.
The modern view is that the finite age of the stars is the main reason. In 1964 Edward Harrison showed that this was what limits the brightness of the sky. The expansion of the universe also stretches the light of the most distant objects to redder wavelengths, and cuts its energy. A dark night sky is a clue that the universe has a finite history.
The demon that could break the rules of heat

The second law of thermodynamics says that heat flows from hot to cold, and that disorder tends to increase. In his 1871 textbook on heat, James Clerk Maxwell described a thought experiment. A tiny being, later called a demon, guards a door between two chambers of gas. It lets fast molecules go one way, and slow ones the other, so that one side grows hot and the other cold, without any work. That would break the law.
In 1929 the physicist Leo Szilard simplified the problem to an engine with a single molecule. In 1961 Rolf Landauer showed that erasing one bit of information must give off at least a minimum amount of heat, equal to k times T times the natural log of 2. In 1982 Charles Bennett argued that this resolves the puzzle. The demon must record what it sees, and to keep working it must erase its memory, and the erasing pays the entropy cost.
This view has been tested in experiments with small systems, and it is widely accepted. Some physicists argue that it does not cover every version of the puzzle. Whatever the final word, the demon led to the idea that information is a physical thing, with a cost in energy.
Two losing games that win together

Suppose that you are offered two games of chance, and each one loses money on average. Playing either one over and over would ruin you. Is there any way to win by alternating them? In 1999 the physicists Gregory Harmer and Derek Abbott showed that there is, in a result known as Parrondo's paradox, after Juan Parrondo, who discovered it in 1996.
Game A is a coin toss with a coin that is slightly biased against you. Game B uses two coins. If your money is a multiple of 3, you toss a coin with a very poor chance of winning, about one in ten, less a small bias. Otherwise you toss a coin with a good chance, about three in four, less the same bias. Played alone, each game loses. If you switch between them in a random or fixed order, you can win steadily.
The effect resembles a ratchet, where random motion in one direction is blocked and the other allowed. The result was published in Nature as Losing strategies can win by Parrondo's paradox. It has been debated whether it is truly a paradox. It is also of little use for investing in stocks, since the games are very special. It shows how combining two bad things can produce a good one.
The architect who read the oldest Greek

In 1900 the English archaeologist Arthur Evans dug up thousands of clay tablets at Knossos, on Crete, covered in a script nobody could read. It was called Linear B. The signs were of two kinds, about 87 that stood for syllables and over 100 that stood for things such as grain and sheep. The earliest tablets date from about 1450 BC.
The script was cracked in 1952 by Michael Ventris, an English architect who had been interested in the puzzle since he was a boy. He worked from the research of an American classicist, Alice Kober, who had found patterns in the endings of words, and had died in 1950. Ventris had expected the language to be something other than Greek. When the sounds fell into place, the tablets turned out to be Greek, the oldest form we know, now called Mycenaean.
Most of the tablets are dull lists kept by palace officials, counting goods and workers. The handwriting of only a few dozen scribes has been identified, 45 at Pylos and 66 at Knossos. Linear B is the only Bronze Age script of the Aegean that has been deciphered. Its sister script Linear A is still unread, and the language it wrote is unknown.

In 1912 a Polish book dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought an old manuscript of about 240 pages, filled with writing in a script that no one could read. It had drawings of strange plants, charts of stars, and small human figures bathing in green pools. The manuscript is named for him. Since 1969 it has been held by Yale University's Beinecke Library, and in 2020 Yale put the whole book online.
Carbon dating suggests that the vellum was made between 1404 and 1438, somewhere in central Europe. The first owner who can be traced was Georg Baresch, an alchemist in Prague in the 1600s, who wrote that he could make no sense of it. Professional codebreakers from both world wars, and many amateurs, have tried to read it.
No one has succeeded. The suggestions include an unknown language, a cipher, an invented tongue, a hoax and a work of fiction. The text has patterns, such as repeated words, that make it look like language, which is part of what keeps people trying. The honest answer after more than a century is that nobody knows what it says, or whether it says anything.
The dog and the cave of bulls

On September 12, 1940, an 18-year-old named Marcel Ravidat was out in the woods near the village of Montignac, in southwestern France. His dog, Robot, was said to have investigated a hole left where a tree had been pulled up. Ravidat came back with three friends and they climbed down a shaft of about fifteen meters.
They found a cave whose walls were covered with paintings of animals. There are more than 600 painted figures, mostly large animals that lived in the region in the Upper Paleolithic, such as horses, deer, aurochs and ibex. Parts of the cave have names, such as the Hall of the Bulls. The paintings are thought to be 17,000 to 22,000 years old, the work of many generations.
After the war the cave was opened to visitors, and the breath and warmth of crowds began to harm the paintings. It was closed to the public in 1963, and there are now replicas for people to visit. In 1979 UNESCO placed it on the World Heritage List. The story of the dog has been changed in the telling. Ravidat later said that the dog had fallen into the hole, and that is probably not what happened.
The day the forest fell down in Siberia

At about seven in the morning on June 30, 1908, a huge explosion took place over a remote region of Siberia, near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River. Witnesses were knocked to the ground, and at least three people died. Windows shattered in places 200 kilometers away. Seismic stations in Russia and Germany picked up the blast, and for several nights afterward the skies over Europe were bright enough to read by.
No scientific team went there until 1921, when Leonid Kulik led an expedition, and he found the center of the blast only in 1927. About 2,150 square kilometers of forest had been flattened, and the trees lay in a radial pattern, pointing away from a center. Many trees still stood at the center with their branches stripped. That pointed to an explosion in the air.
The consensus now is that a stony object, perhaps 50 to 60 meters across, entered the atmosphere at high speed and exploded between five and ten kilometers up, with the energy of 10 to 15 megatons of TNT. No crater was found, and no fragment has been formally identified. The event is the largest known impact of its kind in recorded history.
The pollution that made the world breathable

For the first half of the Earth's history, the air had almost no free oxygen. Then, about 2.46 billion years ago, oxygen began to build up in the atmosphere and the shallow seas. It is called the Great Oxidation Event. The cause was life itself. Microbes that carried out photosynthesis, using sunlight to make food, gave off oxygen as a waste product.
Oxygen is a reactive gas, and to the organisms that lived then, mostly microbes that did not use it, it was poisonous. The event may have wiped out many of them, though it is not counted among the great mass extinctions, partly because the evidence from microscopic life so long ago is hard to read. It also changed the chemistry of the planet, as iron in the oceans rusted and settled out.
The event is usually dated from about 2.46 billion to about 2.06 billion years ago. Oxygen then stayed at a low level, from under one percent to perhaps ten percent of today's, for a very long time. It rose to modern levels much later. The oxygen that animals now breathe began as the waste of bacteria, and was once a disaster for the life that existed.

For a long time, there was a gap in the fossil record between fish and the four-legged animals that walk on land. In 2004 a team looked for it on Ellesmere Island, in the Canadian Arctic. The team was Edward Daeschler, Neil Shubin and Farish Jenkins. They chose the place because its rocks were of the right age, about 375 million years, and had been laid down by streams, in the late Devonian period.
They found the remains of an animal that was part fish and part land animal. It had scales and gills, but also a flat head, a neck, and sturdy bones inside its fins. The bones would have let it prop itself up in shallow water. They named it Tiktaalik, a word from the Inuit language of the region, and published the find in the journal Nature on April 6, 2006.
It was between 1.25 and 2.75 meters long. Tiktaalik is now one of the best known transitional fossils. It does not mean that fish came ashore in a single step. Related animals such as Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, from Greenland, give other pieces of the story. But it showed that the places and rocks where scientists expected to find such a creature really contained it.
The relatives we found in a finger bone

In 2008 archaeologists digging in Denisova Cave, in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, found a small piece of a finger bone from a young girl. In 2010 researchers who extracted DNA from it announced something unexpected. It was neither modern human nor Neanderthal. They had found a new kind of ancient human, and they called it Denisovan, after the cave.
For years little more was known, because there were few remains. Studies of nuclear DNA showed that the Denisovans were closer to Neanderthals than to us. Other fossils have since been identified as Denisovan, from a cave on the Tibetan Plateau, from Laos, from the sea floor off Taiwan, and from a skull found in Harbin in China, which was shown to be Denisovan from its proteins.
They lived across Asia from about 200,000 to 32,000 years ago. DNA suggests that they had dark skin, eyes and hair. No formal species name has been given, since the first remains were so small. The discovery is a reminder that a species can be found first in DNA, and that a bone the size of a fingertip can change the story of human origins.

On September 2, 2003, a team of Australian and Indonesian archaeologists digging in a cave called Liang Bua, on the island of Flores in Indonesia, found the remains of a very small adult. Stooped over a skeleton, they found a person who would have stood about 1.1 meters, or 3 feet 7 inches, tall, with a skull about the size of a grapefruit. They called her LB1.
Partial skeletons of 15 individuals have since been recovered. The species was named Homo floresiensis, and nicknamed the hobbit. At first it was thought that they may have lived as recently as 12,000 years ago. More careful dating has put the skeletons at 60,000 to 100,000 years old, and the latest evidence for the species at about 50,000 years ago.
Some scientists argued that LB1 was a modern human with a disease. Most now accept that it was a distinct species, whose small size is an example of island dwarfism, which is seen in many animals isolated on islands. What its ancestors were is still debated. The finding showed that other kinds of humans lived on Earth until fairly recently, and not all of them looked as we expected.
The eruption that may have nearly ended us

About 74,000 years ago a volcano on the island of Sumatra, in what is now Lake Toba, erupted on a scale far beyond any in recorded history. It is rated the largest explosive eruption of the last 2.5 million years, at the top of the volcanic explosivity scale. It probably lasted from nine days to two weeks, and happened in the northern summer.
In the 1990s an idea took hold that its ash and sulfur cooled the Earth for years, and that humanity dropped to a few thousand survivors. This is the Toba catastrophe theory, which was supported by the low genetic variation found in people today. It was an appealing story, and it was widely reported.
Later work has made it far less certain. Studies of ash layers and of tools at excavation sites suggest that the eruption did not cause a global disaster, and that people lived through it. Genetic evidence of a bottleneck has other explanations. The case is a warning about neat stories. A major event and a pattern in the evidence can be linked in a way that later turns out to be incomplete.
The jar of lightning and early Earth

In 1952 a graduate student at the University of Chicago, Stanley Miller, set up an experiment to test a question about the origin of life. He was supervised by the Nobel laureate Harold Urey. Miller built a closed set of glass flasks, with water that was boiled, and a mixture of gases that were thought to resemble the early Earth's air, namely methane, ammonia and hydrogen.
He passed electric sparks through the gases, like lightning, and let them cool and run through the water. After a few days the water had turned brown, and it contained amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. He published it in 1953. It showed that molecules of life could form from simple chemicals under plausible conditions, and it supported an idea of Alexander Oparin and J. B. S. Haldane.
After Miller died in 2007, scientists found sealed vials from his old experiments and tested them with modern methods. They found that more amino acids had formed than he had been able to detect. Many researchers now think that the early atmosphere was different from his mixture. But similar experiments under other conditions also produce amino acids, and the work opened the field of experimental origin-of-life research.
The most beautiful experiment in biology

When Watson and Crick described DNA in 1953, they suggested a way it might copy itself. The two strands would come apart, and each would act as a template for a new partner. That would mean that each new molecule has one old strand and one new strand. It is called semiconservative replication. But other ideas were possible. In one, the whole molecule would stay intact as a template, and produce an all-new copy.
In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl found a way to test it. They grew bacteria for many generations in a food that contained a heavy form of nitrogen, so that the bacteria's DNA was heavy. Then they switched them to ordinary light nitrogen, and spun samples of the DNA in a tube to separate heavy from light.
After one generation, all the DNA was of one intermediate weight, which was neither all heavy nor all light. After two generations, there were two bands, one intermediate and one light. That ruled out the other ideas, and fit the Watson and Crick model. The experiment has been called the most beautiful experiment in biology, because the result was so clean.
The mice that carried a message

In 1928 a British doctor, Frederick Griffith, was trying to make a vaccine against pneumonia. He used two strains of the pneumococcus bacterium. One had a smooth coat and killed mice. The other, rough, was harmless. When he killed the smooth ones with heat and injected the remains, the mice lived. When he injected the dead smooth bacteria with living rough ones, the mice died.
He found live smooth bacteria in the dead mice. Something in the dead bacteria had changed the harmless ones into killers. He called it transformation. Until then, people thought that bacterial types were fixed. The experiment was the first sign that bacteria can pass on genetic information.
What the substance was remained a puzzle. In 1944 Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty, at the Rockefeller Institute, reported that it was DNA. Most scientists had believed that proteins carried heredity, since they seemed more complex, and many doubted the result. It took further work, including a famous 1952 experiment with viruses by Hershey and Chase, to settle it. The mice carried the first clue to what genes are made of.
The man who won two Nobel Prizes for reading

Frederick Sanger was born in 1918 in a village in Gloucestershire, England, the son of a doctor, and was brought up as a Quaker. He became a biochemist. In 1958 he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for working out the order of the amino acids in insulin, the first protein to be completely sequenced. It showed that a protein has a definite and exact structure.
He did not stop. At the new Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, he went on to invent a way to read the order of the letters in DNA, which was published in the 1970s. It was the first DNA sequencing method, and a version of it remained in wide use for decades. It made the Human Genome Project possible. In 1980 he shared a second Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Walter Gilbert and Paul Berg.
Only five people have won two Nobel Prizes, and Sanger is one of only three to win twice in the same field. He turned down a knighthood, and preferred to be called plain Mr. Sanger. He died in 2013 at the age of 95. His career shows how much a science can change when someone invents a way to read what is written in it.
The sheep that was not the first clone

Dolly was born on July 5, 1996, at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, Scotland. She was a Finn-Dorset sheep, and the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. Ian Wilmut, Keith Campbell and their colleagues took a cell from the udder of a six-year-old sheep, put its nucleus into an egg cell from which the nucleus had been removed, and gave a pulse of electricity to start development.
It was said that she was named after the singer Dolly Parton, since the cell came from a mammary gland. The importance was that it proved that a cell from an adult body, once specialized, can be made to start again and produce a whole animal. Contrary to what many believe, she was not the first animal to be cloned. John Gurdon had cloned frogs in 1958 from the cells of tadpoles.
Dolly lived at Roslin, and gave birth to lambs. She was put down in 2003 at the age of six because of a progressive lung disease, and no link to her cloning was found. Her body is displayed at the National Museum of Scotland. Her work led to research on stem cells, including the discovery that adult cells can be turned back into a flexible state.
The study that taught medicine to ask permission

In 1932 the United States Public Health Service began a study in Macon County, Alabama, of how syphilis develops when it is not treated. It enrolled 600 poor Black sharecroppers, 399 with syphilis and 201 without. The men were told that they were being treated for bad blood. They were offered free medical care, meals and burial insurance.
They were not told that they had syphilis, and they were not given effective treatment. By 1945 penicillin was widely used to cure the disease, but the study went on without giving it to the men. More than 100 of them died as a result of the disease, and wives and children were also infected. The study went on for forty years.
In 1972 a news report exposed it, and it was ended. The government set up new rules. In 1979 the Belmont Report laid out the principles of respect for persons, doing good and avoiding harm, and fairness, which became the basis of rules for informed consent in research on people in the United States. In 1997 President Bill Clinton formally apologized to the survivors. The study is often named as one reason that many Black Americans have distrusted medical research.
The doctor who made polio a disease of the past

Albert Sabin was born Abram Saperstejn, in 1906, in Białystok, in the Russian Empire, now in Poland. His family emigrated to the United States in 1921 and settled in Paterson, New Jersey. He began a dentistry course at New York University, but wanted to do medical research instead, and he received a medical degree in 1931.
In the 1950s the world had a vaccine against polio, the injected one of Jonas Salk. Sabin believed that a vaccine made of a weakened live virus, taken by mouth, would give longer protection and be easier to give. He worked on it for years at a research center in Cincinnati. Large trials were carried out in the Soviet Union on millions of children, and the oral vaccine was licensed in the United States in 1961.
It was cheap and could be given on a sugar cube, and it played a key role in almost eradicating polio. Sabin never took out a patent, and gave up any profit. He died in 1993. Cases of polio around the world have fallen by more than 99 percent since 1988, and the disease remains in only a few places.
The cook who gave typhoid to dozens

Mary Mallon was an Irish-born cook who worked in the homes of wealthy families in New York in the early 1900s. Between 1897 and 1907, members of four of the families she worked for fell ill with typhoid fever. In 1907 an investigator, George Soper, traced the cases to her. She was a healthy carrier, who gave off the bacteria without being sick herself.
She was the first person in the United States found to be an asymptomatic carrier of typhoid. She is believed to have infected up to 57 people, and three deaths were confirmed. She did not believe that she could be spreading the disease, and she resisted. In 1907 she was held by force at a hospital on North Brother Island, in New York's East River, and released in 1910 after promising not to work as a cook.
She took a job under a false name, and in 1915 there was an outbreak at a maternity hospital with 25 cases. She was returned to the island and lived there until her death in 1938. About 400 other carriers were found while she was confined, and most were not treated as she was. Her nickname has become a phrase for anyone who spreads disease. The case raises the question of when public health can limit a person's freedom.
The merchant who brought printing to England

William Caxton was an English merchant who lived much of his life in Bruges, in Flanders. On his business trips he saw the new printing trade in Cologne, and with a partner, Colard Mansion, he set up a press in Bruges. In 1471 he finished his own translation of a book of tales about Troy, which became one of the first books printed in English.
In 1476 he came back to England and set up a press at Westminster, near London. The first book that he is known to have printed there was Chaucer's Canterbury Tales. He went on to publish romances, histories, and the first English translation of Aesop's Fables, in 1484. Caxton was not a skilled translator, and he worked in a hurry.
His business also forced him to make choices about English. The language varied from one region to another, and he wrote that a book that pleased one county might not please another. In a preface he told of merchants on a ship waiting for good weather on the Thames, and one asked a woman for eggs, and she said she spoke no French, until another said "eyren." Printers began to fix spellings, and a standard form of English started to take shape.
The printer who invented the paperback

Aldus Manutius was an Italian scholar who became a printer in Venice. His press, the Aldine Press, was known for its carefully made editions. He wanted to give readers the works of ancient Greece and Rome in their original languages, and he was the first to print many of the Greek classics, such as Aristotle and Aristophanes.
Until then large books were the rule, meant to sit on a desk. Aldus brought out small books, in a size that could fit in a pocket or saddlebag, called enchiridia. They were the ancestors of the paperback. He also had a new typeface cut, based on the slanting handwriting of scholars of his day. It was the first known ancestor of italic type, and he used it to fit more words on a small page.
He also helped to set the use of punctuation marks, such as the comma and the semicolon. His reputation for accuracy was such that Erasmus came to Venice to have his work printed by him. Other printers copied his innovations, and pirated his editions, in spite of his efforts to stop them. Much of what a modern book looks like was set in his workshop.
One man and a dictionary of everything

In June 1746 a group of London booksellers hired Samuel Johnson to write a dictionary of English. They were unhappy with the ones on the market, and they agreed to pay him 1,500 guineas. Johnson said that he could finish in three years. It took him seven, and the book was published on April 15, 1755.
He did the work almost alone. With only a few clerks to copy out passages, he read widely, marked sentences in books that showed how words were used, and wrote the definitions himself. Instead of just listing words, he supported them with quotations from writers such as Shakespeare, Milton and Dryden. Many of his definitions are still quoted. Oats, he wrote, was a grain which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people.
The dictionary was considered the best in English until the Oxford English Dictionary was finished, 173 years later. The biographer Walter Jackson Bate called it one of the greatest feats of scholarship ever performed by one person working under such disadvantages. Johnson also described his own trade. A lexicographer, he wrote, was a writer of dictionaries, a harmless drudge.
The surgeon who wrote dictionary entries in an asylum

When the editor James Murray began work on the Oxford English Dictionary, he asked the public to help. Volunteers read books and sent in slips of paper, each with a word and a quotation showing how it was used. One of the best contributors was Dr. William Chester Minor, who sent in thousands. By the popular account, Murray knew him at first only by an address in Berkshire, England.
Minor was born in 1834 in Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, to missionary parents from New England. He studied medicine at Yale, and served as an army surgeon in the American Civil War. He later moved to England. In 1872, suffering from delusions, he shot and killed a man whom he believed had broken into his room. He was committed to a secure hospital for the insane, and he stayed there until 1910.
In the hospital he had a large library of old books, and used it to read systematically and send in quotations. After protests about his treatment, Winston Churchill, then the home secretary, ordered him sent back to the United States in 1910. He died in a hospital in Connecticut in 1920. The story was told in a book by Simon Winchester, The Professor and the Madman.
The poet who helped make English respectable

Geoffrey Chaucer was born in London, probably in the early 1340s, the son of a wine merchant. He was a man of public life, who served as a courtier, a diplomat, an official in the customs, and a member of Parliament for Kent. He is best known for The Canterbury Tales, a collection of stories told by pilgrims on the way to a shrine.
He wrote in English at a time when French was the language of the court, and Latin the language of learning. By showing that English could carry poetry, he helped make it a language fit for literature. A younger poet, Thomas Hoccleve, called him the first finder of our fair language. Almost two thousand English words are first recorded in manuscripts of his works.
He also wrote a scientific work, A Treatise on the Astrolabe, for his ten-year-old son Lewis, explaining how to use the instrument. When he died in 1400 he was buried in Westminster Abbey, in a place that later became known as Poets' Corner. He was the first writer to be buried there, and many have been laid there since.
The emperor who turned away from war

Ashoka was the third ruler of the Maurya Empire, and became emperor of Magadha in India in about 268 BC. His realm grew to cover most of the Indian subcontinent, from what is now Afghanistan to what is now Bangladesh, with its capital at Pataliputra. In about 260 BC, in the eighth year of his rule, he conquered the region of Kalinga after a brutal war.
According to his own edicts, which were carved on rocks and pillars, he was moved by the suffering of the war. He turned to a policy of dhamma, which means right conduct, and which includes kindness to others and tolerance of different beliefs. He is believed to have drawn gradually to Buddhism, and Buddhist legends say that he built many stupas and supported missionaries.
Ashoka was nearly forgotten as a historical figure, until scholars in the nineteenth century deciphered the Brahmi script of his inscriptions. Today he is regarded as one of the greatest of Indian rulers. India's national emblem is based on the lion capital that stood on one of his pillars, and the wheel on the national flag is the wheel of Ashoka.
Twenty-eight men and a ship in the ice

In 1914 the explorer Ernest Shackleton set out on a plan to be the first to cross the continent of Antarctica on foot. After Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole in 1911, it was the one great goal that was left. Shackleton's ship Endurance sailed into the Weddell Sea, but before it could land the men, it became trapped in the pack ice.
The ship drifted north with the ice through the Antarctic winter of 1915. In the end the ice crushed it, and it sank, leaving the crew of 28 men stranded on the ice. They camped on the floes, and later took to three small boats and reached remote Elephant Island. Shackleton and five others then sailed a lifeboat, the James Caird, about 800 miles across the stormy ocean to South Georgia, and crossed the island's mountains to reach a whaling station.
He then led the rescue of the men on Elephant Island, and they were taken off in August 1916. Every man of the Endurance crew survived. The expedition did not achieve its goal, but it is remembered as one of the great stories of leadership and endurance. The wreck of the Endurance was found in 2022 on the sea floor.
The man who got to the Pole first

Roald Amundsen was born in Norway in 1872, into a family of shipowners and captains. As a young man he served on a Belgian Antarctic expedition in 1897 to 1899, and from 1903 to 1906 he led the first expedition to sail through the Northwest Passage, in a small sloop called the Gjøa.
In 1910 he left Norway on the ship Fram, and landed in Antarctica in January 1911. His party set up a base at the Bay of Whales, and laid out depots of food along the route. He left for the Pole in October, with five men, skis and sledges pulled by dogs. They reached the South Pole on December 14, 1911. The British party led by Robert Falcon Scott arrived about a month later, found the Norwegian tent, and died on the way back.
Amundsen next turned to the Arctic. On May 12, 1926, he and fifteen others in the airship Norge became the first explorers confirmed to have reached the North Pole. In June 1928 he disappeared while flying to look for the crew of another airship, the Italia. His body was never found. He is often described as the first person to have reached both poles.
The flyer who vanished over the Pacific

Amelia Earhart was born in Atchison, Kansas, on July 24, 1897. She learned to fly in the early 1920s, when few women did. In 1928 she was the first woman to cross the Atlantic by airplane, though as a passenger, and the fame brought her publicity. In 1932 she flew the Atlantic alone and without stopping, the first woman to do so, and received the Distinguished Flying Cross.
She wrote best-selling books about flying, promoted commercial air travel, and helped to found the Ninety-Nines, an organization of women pilots. In 1937 she set out to be the first woman to fly around the world. On July 2, 1937, she and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared over the Pacific Ocean in a twin-engine Lockheed Electra, on a long leg to tiny Howland Island.
The U.S. Navy and Coast Guard searched for them, but no trace of them was found. She was declared dead on January 5, 1939. Many theories have been put forward and searches have gone on for decades, but what happened is still not known. Her disappearance has made her a cultural symbol, and has overshadowed her real achievements as a pilot and as an advocate for women in aviation.
The man who weighed the Earth

How much does the Earth weigh? In 1797 and 1798 the English scientist Henry Cavendish found a way to answer, using a machine designed by a clergyman and geologist, John Michell, who died in 1793 before he could use it. The machine was a torsion balance, a six-foot wooden rod hung from a wire, with a small lead ball of about 1.6 pounds on each end.
Cavendish placed two very large lead balls, of about 348 pounds, close to the small ones. The gravitational pull between them was extremely faint, and it twisted the wire by only about 0.16 of a degree. He measured the twist with a telescope, from outside the room, so that his own body and the heat from it would not disturb the apparatus.
From the force he could calculate the density of the Earth, and from that its mass. He found that the Earth is about five and a half times as dense as water. It was the first time that the force of gravity between objects had been measured in a laboratory. The experiment is often said to have weighed the Earth. It also gave the first accurate value for the gravitational constant, though Cavendish did not state it that way.
The astronomer who noticed the sky was slipping

Hipparchus was a Greek astronomer born in Nicaea, in what is now Turkey, about 190 BC. He worked as an observer between about 162 and 127 BC, partly on the island of Rhodes. He is often called the greatest astronomical observer of antiquity.
He made the first tables of trigonometry, which let one work out the lengths of the sides of a triangle from its angles. He produced the first known star catalog in the Western world, and he built models for the motion of the Sun and Moon that were accurate enough to predict eclipses. To do it, he used records kept by the Babylonians over centuries.
His most famous discovery was precession. By comparing his own measurements of the position of stars to those of astronomers of the generation before, such as Timocharis, he found that the points on the sky where the seasons begin were slowly shifting. The Earth's axis wobbles like a spinning top, in a cycle of about 26,000 years. Hipparchus found it two thousand years before anyone could explain it. A French astronomer, Delambre, called him the father of astronomy in 1817.
The man who fell in a well, and made money

Thales of Miletus lived on the coast of what is now Turkey, about 600 BC. He was one of the Seven Sages of ancient Greece, and is often named as the first philosopher. His claim was that everything in the world is made from one basic substance, and that it is water. The point was less the answer than that he looked for a natural explanation, and not a story about the gods.
He was said to have measured the height of the pyramids, and to have predicted a solar eclipse. A theorem about triangles in a circle is named for him. According to Herodotus, he helped the army of the king of Lydia to cross a river by digging a channel to divide it. Very little of what is told of him can be checked, since our main source, Diogenes Laertius, wrote some eight hundred years later.
Two stories show the two sides of the thinker. Plato told that Thales fell into a well while he was looking up at the stars, and a servant girl laughed that he was so eager to know the sky that he could not see what lay at his feet. Aristotle told another. Thales foresaw a good olive harvest, rented all the olive presses, and made a fortune, to show that a philosopher could be rich if he wanted.

The ancient Greek philosopher Socrates is said to have taught by asking questions and not by giving answers. His way of talking with people is now called the Socratic method. He would start with something that a person believed, such as what courage is, and ask for a definition. Then he would test it with more questions until the person saw a contradiction, or had to admit that he did not know.
In Plato's dialogue Theaetetus, Socrates compares what he does to the work of a midwife. His mother was one. He says that he cannot himself give birth to wisdom, but he can help others deliver their own ideas, and he can tell whether the offspring is healthy or not. The Greek word for it, maieutic, comes from the word for midwifery.
The method begins with common beliefs and checks whether they agree with one another. It has been changed over the centuries, and versions are used today in law schools and in many classes. Its lesson for conversation is plain. A good question can do more than a statement. When people reach a conclusion through their own reasoning, it tends to stay with them.
The rule that sarcasm needs a label

In 2005 a user of an online forum named Nathan Poe made a remark in a debate about creationism that has become known as Poe's law. Without a winking smiley or some other plain sign of humor, he said, it is impossible to parody an extreme view in a way that no one will mistake for the real thing.
The idea is older than his post. As early as 1983 a user of Usenet, Jerry Schwarz, advised people to avoid sarcasm online, since without the tone of voice and body language of a face to face talk, it was easily misunderstood. He noted that a sideways smile, a colon, a hyphen and a closing parenthesis, was becoming widely used to mark a joke.
The law has a double edge. Satire can be taken as sincere. People who do mean extreme things can also claim afterward that they were only joking, if they get too much criticism. The practical lesson is that in writing, where we lose the voice, the face and the timing, it is more likely than we think that our meaning will be lost, and a sign of our intent may be needed.
The smiley that was proposed in a message

On September 19, 1982, a computer scientist at Carnegie Mellon University, Scott Fahlman, wrote a message to the university's online bulletin board. People there had been confused by jokes that others took seriously. He proposed that the characters colon, hyphen and closing parenthesis be used, if read sideways, to mark a joke, and colon, hyphen and opening parenthesis to mark a remark that was serious.
The suggestion spread across the early networks. The pictures made from characters came to be called emoticons, from emotion and icon. People had made faces from typed characters before, in one-off uses going back hundreds of years, but Fahlman is credited with the plan of using them as a code for the mood of a message.
In Japan, a different style grew, called kaomoji, which can be read without turning the head. It arose on a network called ASCII NET in 1986. Later the faces were replaced by little pictures, and then by emoji. The need behind them has not changed. Writing leaves out the tone of voice and the expression on a face, and people look for ways to put them back.
The headline that ends in a question mark

Betteridge's law of headlines says that any headline that ends in a question mark can be answered by the word no. It is named for Ian Betteridge, a British technology writer, who wrote about it in February 2009. He was commenting on a headline on the website TechCrunch, which asked whether the music service Last.fm had just handed over the listening data of its users to the recording industry.
His reasoning was that journalists use the question form because they suspect the story is not solid, and do not have the sources to say it outright, but they want to run it. If they were confident that the answer was yes, they would say so. By asking, they make no claim for which they can be held to account.
The idea is older than his name for it. A 1991 collection of Murphy's law variants called it Davis's law, and the British editor Andrew Marr made a similar remark in a 2004 book. It is not a law of nature, and some headlines with question marks do have an answer of yes. But as a rule of thumb it is useful. When a headline asks a question, ask why it is not a statement.
Why a lie costs ten times more to answer

In January 2013 an Italian programmer, Alberto Brandolini, was reading Daniel Kahneman's book Thinking, Fast and Slow, and then he watched an Italian television talk show with the former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi and a journalist. He wrote down an observation that has since been called Brandolini's law, or the bullshit asymmetry principle. The amount of energy needed to refute nonsense is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it.
The point is about the difference in work. A false claim can be made in a sentence. To answer it, one has to find the facts, explain them, and then deal with the fact that many people have already heard the claim and trusted it. The effort is made harder because it can mean challenging one's own community.
The standard example is the false claim that vaccines cause autism. A fraudulent paper in 1998 by Andrew Wakefield said that there was a link with the MMR vaccine. It was retracted and his medical license was revoked. Many studies since have found no link, yet the false idea has had a lasting effect on public health. The law does not say to give up. It says that prevention, such as teaching people to question claims before they spread, is worth more than cure.
The language made to stop thought

In George Orwell's 1949 novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, the ruling Party of Oceania has a language called Newspeak. It is designed to have a smaller vocabulary every year. The aim is to make certain thoughts impossible to express, such as thoughts about personal freedom, and so impossible to think. If a language has no words for an idea, the idea is harder to hold.
In an appendix, The Principles of Newspeak, Orwell explains that it follows most rules of English grammar, but reduces ideas to simple terms. Many of its words are contractions. The Ministry of Truth is Minitrue and the Ministry of Plenty is Miniplenty. Orwell saw the same kind of contractions in the twentieth century, in words such as Gestapo, politburo and Comintern.
From it and from the idea of doublethink came the word doublespeak, though it is not used in the novel. It means language that deliberately hides or reverses the meaning, as in calling layoffs downsizing or bombing servicing the target. Orwell's essay of 1946, Politics and the English Language, made a similar charge. Political speech, he argued, is often designed to make lies sound truthful, and to give an appearance of solidity to pure wind.
The score that measures how hard a page is

How hard is it to read a passage of English? The Austrian-born writer Rudolf Flesch, who campaigned for plain English, devised a formula in 1948 called the Reading Ease score. It uses two things only, the average length of the sentences and the average length of the words. The longer the sentences and the longer the words, the harder the text is said to be.
In 1975 a psychologist, J. Peter Kincaid, and his team did a project for the United States Navy, and turned the formula into a grade level. The Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level gives a number that matches a school year in the United States. A score of 8 means that the text should be understood by someone at about the eighth grade. It was first used by the Army to check the difficulty of manuals.
The tests are crude. They count the length of words, but cannot tell whether the words are familiar or whether the ideas are hard. A short sentence full of technical terms may score as easy. Even so, such formulas are built into word processors, and are used for legal documents, insurance policies and health information. They show a simple truth. Short words and short sentences are easier to take in.
The language that had a million speakers for a moment

In 1879 and 1880 a Roman Catholic priest in Baden, Germany, Johann Martin Schleyer, created a language that he called Volapük, which means the language of the world. It was the first major constructed language meant for international use. Its grammar was based mostly on German, and its words mostly on English, with changes. Schleyer shortened and altered many of them until they were hard to recognize.
It spread fast. Conventions were held in 1884 in Friedrichshafen, in 1887 in Munich, and in 1889 in Paris, where the proceedings were held only in Volapük. By 1889 there were an estimated 283 clubs, 25 periodicals and 316 textbooks in 25 languages, and the language claimed nearly a million followers.
Then it collapsed. There were quarrels in the movement, and Schleyer wanted to keep control over changes to the language. In 1887 a Polish doctor, Ludwik Zamenhof, published a language that he called Esperanto, and many members of the Volapük clubs moved to it. A small revival of Volapük came in the 1930s, after reforms by Arie de Jong. It still has a few users. A new language needs not only a good design but a community that can agree.
The English of eight hundred and fifty words

In 1930 the Cambridge linguist and philosopher Charles Kay Ogden published a book describing Basic English. It was a smaller form of the language with a vocabulary of only 850 words, and a much simplified grammar. His claim was that almost anything could be said with it. A person could learn it in weeks, and use it as a second language for the whole world.
It was based on ideas in a book that he wrote with I. A. Richards in 1923, The Meaning of Meaning. Richards later promoted it in schools in China. After the Allied victory in the Second World War, it gained great publicity as a tool for peace. Ogden was convinced that the world needed a single language, and he thought that it should be English, in either a simple or a full form.
Basic English itself did not take off. But the idea survives. The Voice of America built a simplified broadcast form, called Special English, for news for learners. A form of controlled language, called Simplified Technical English, is used to write aircraft manuals. The belief behind it was that clarity comes from a small, well-chosen set of words.
The alphabet that a playwright left money for

George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright, was a lifelong critic of English spelling. He argued that it wasted time and money, since the same sound could be spelled in many ways, and one spelling could have many sounds. When he died in 1950, his will left money for a new alphabet for English.
A competition was held, and the winning design was the work of Ronald Kingsley Read, a professional sign-writer. It is now called the Shavian alphabet. Shaw had asked for three things. There had to be at least 40 letters, and in the end there were 48. The letters should match the sounds, one to one. And it should not look like the Latin alphabet, so that the new spellings would not seem to be only mistakes.
The letters come in three kinds. Tall ones, with a stroke going up, stand for sounds made without voice, such as p and t. Deep ones, with a stroke going down, are the same letters turned upside down, standing for the voiced sounds such as b and d. Short ones stand for vowels and for sounds such as m and n. The alphabet never caught on, but people still use it. It remains a serious attempt to fix a real problem.
The man who put America in the dictionary

Noah Webster was born in West Hartford, Connecticut, in 1758, and graduated from Yale in 1778. He studied law and passed the bar, but could not find work as a lawyer, so he opened a private school. To teach his pupils he wrote books, and his Blue-Backed Speller became the main book from which American children learned to read and spell.
He believed that the new nation should have its own culture and its own language, free of English models. In 1828 he published An American Dictionary of the English Language, which is the origin of the modern Merriam-Webster dictionaries. It recorded the words that Americans used, and many of the spellings he preferred, such as color without the u and center with the r before the e. Some of his other proposals, such as tung for tongue, did not catch on.
In 1793 Alexander Hamilton had recruited him to come to New York and edit a newspaper for the Federalist Party. He was a writer of political essays as well as books for schools. His work helped to make a standard American English, and to fix the differences in spelling from British English that persist.
The towers that sent news faster than a horse

Before the electric telegraph, there was a telegraph made of towers. In 1792 a Frenchman, Claude Chappe, invented a system of signals that could be seen from far away. Each station had a tall mast with movable arms on top, which could be set in many positions. A position stood for a letter, a number or a code word. It was called a semaphore telegraph.
Towers were built within sight of each other, five to twenty miles apart. An operator at each tower looked at the neighboring one through a telescope. When the arms began to move, spelling out a message, he copied the positions on his own tower, which passed the message on to the next. Chappe used the word télégraphe for the machine, and so gave the English language the word telegraph.
It was much faster than a rider on a horse, and in the long run it cost less. France built a network of lines. But it could be used only in daylight and fair weather, since the stations had to be within sight of each other. About fifty years later, the electric telegraph replaced it, because it was cheaper, faster and more private. The towers show how a simple code and a chain of watchers can carry a message across a country.
A language of one hundred and twenty words

Toki Pona is a language created by a Canadian translator, Sonja Lang. She first published drafts online in 2001, and the complete form in a 2014 book, Toki Pona: The Language of Good. The name means good language. It was designed to be as small and simple as possible, with a purpose of simplifying her own thoughts.
The language has only 14 sounds, and its first book presented about 120 words. A dictionary in 2021 lists 137 essential words, and a few more that are less used. Words are combined to express more. A friend may be a good person, and a teacher a person who gives knowledge. It is partly inspired by Taoist philosophy, and by the idea, from the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, that a language shapes thought. A small vocabulary is meant to make the speaker concentrate on the simple and positive things.
It was not intended as a world language. But it has a community of speakers, and it has been used for art and for translation. In 2024 a third book appeared, a translation of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz. Toki Pona is an experiment in whether a language can be changed to change how a person thinks, and it tests how much can be said with almost nothing.
The language made for a television series

In the novels by George R. R. Martin on which the television series Game of Thrones is based, the nomadic horse lords called the Dothraki speak their own language. But the books gave only a few words and phrases. When the series was made, the producers at HBO wanted a real language. They turned to the Language Creation Society, and more than 30 people who invented languages applied.
The job went to David J. Peterson, who got the part by building from Martin's words. He delivered over 1,700 words before filming began. He took ideas from several languages, including Estonian, Inuktitut, Turkish, Russian and Swahili. By September 2011 the language had 3,163 words, though not all were public. He went on to create the Valyrian languages, and many others for film.
The result was well received. The magazine The Economist called the Dothraki and Valyrian languages the most convincing fictional tongues since Elvish. The effect went beyond the screen. In 2012, 146 newborn girls in the United States were given the name Khaleesi, the Dothraki word for the wife of a ruler. A made-up language can give a world a feel of being real, and sometimes become real for its fans.
The sound law that showed words obey rules

Why does the Latin word pater look like the English word father, and the Latin pes like our foot? The Latin p became an f in the Germanic languages, and the same thing happens again and again. Latin tres goes with English three, and Latin cornu with English horn. Such regular matches are called Grimm's law, after the German scholar Jacob Grimm.
The first to note the pattern was Friedrich von Schlegel in 1806, who saw that Latin p matches Germanic f. In 1818 a Danish scholar, Rasmus Rask, extended it to Sanskrit and Greek and the whole range of consonants involved. In 1822 Grimm laid it out in his book Deutsche Grammatik, and extended it to German. His name stuck.
It was the first time that scholars saw that sound change is systematic and not random. That gave historical linguistics a method. Grimm himself saw many exceptions, and they puzzled scholars for decades. Then in 1877 another Dane, Karl Verner, showed that they too followed a rule, which depended on where the stress fell in the word. The law is why a person who knows how sounds shift can trace words back to a shared ancestor.
The judge who saw that Sanskrit was a cousin of Greek

William Jones was born in London in 1746, and was a gifted student of languages from an early age. His father, also William Jones, was a Welsh mathematician who introduced the use of the symbol pi. The younger man learned Greek, Latin, Persian, Arabic, Hebrew and the basics of Chinese writing, and by the end of his life he knew eight languages with great thoroughness.
He became a judge in Calcutta, then the center of British rule in India, and in 1784 he founded the Asiatic Society there to study the culture of Asia. He studied Sanskrit, the ancient language of India. In a talk in 1786 he said that Sanskrit was more perfect than Greek and more copious than Latin, and that it had a strong likeness to both, in roots and in grammar, which could not be by chance.
He argued that the three had come from a common source, which perhaps no longer existed. He was not the first to see the link. But his clear statement helped to start the study of the Indo-European family of languages. He died in Calcutta in 1794, aged 47. His idea changed how people think about the languages of Europe and of India, and their shared history.
The fable written in a language no one has heard

In 1868 the German linguist August Schleicher did something no one had done. He wrote a story in Proto-Indo-European, the ancestor of English, Latin, Greek, Sanskrit and many other languages, which was spoken thousands of years ago and never written down. He built it from what the descendant languages have in common. He called it The Sheep and the Horses.
In the fable a sheep with no wool sees horses, one pulling a heavy wagon, one carrying a big load, and one carrying a man swiftly. The sheep says that its heart pains it to see a man driving horses. The horses reply that their hearts pain them too, when they see that a man, the master, makes the wool of the sheep into a warm garment, and the sheep have none. On hearing this the sheep ran off into the plain.
Scholars have rewritten the fable several times, as ideas about how the language sounded have changed. There are versions by Hermann Hirt in 1939, by Winfred Lehmann and Ladislav Zgusta in 1979, by Douglas Q. Adams in 1997, and by Frederik Kortlandt in 2007. Placing them side by side shows how much the reconstruction has changed in 150 years, and how much is a matter of careful guesswork.

These are three ways of saying "typical," and they can give very different answers. The mean is the usual average, found by adding everything up and dividing. The median is the middle value when you line them all up, and the mode is the most common one.
If Bill Gates walks into a bar, the average wealth of the people in it shoots up, but the median hardly moves. For things like income or house prices, where a few huge values pull the mean, the median is usually the more honest summary. When you read that the "average" family earns some amount, it's worth asking which average is meant. A different choice can paint a very different picture of how people are doing.

The average on its own doesn't tell you how spread out the numbers are. The standard deviation does. Karl Pearson gave it its name in 1893, and it's one of the most widely used numbers in all of statistics.
Imagine two classes that both average 70 on a test. In one, the standard deviation is 5, so almost everyone scored between 60 and 80. In the other it's 20, so you have students at 30 and others at 100. The averages match, but the classes are very different places to teach. Whenever you see an average, it's worth wondering about the spread around it, since a number with a wide spread tells you much less about any one case.

Studies often report a "95% confidence interval." It sounds like there's a 95 percent chance the true value is inside the range, but that's not quite what it means. It means that the method used would capture the true value in 95 percent of repeated studies.
The difference is subtle, and surveys have found that many researchers get it wrong, including trained scientists. A practical reading is that the interval shows the range of values the data can't rule out. A narrow interval means a precise estimate, and a wide one means a lot of uncertainty. When a result is reported as a single number with no interval, it's fair to ask how much it could vary.

News stories about polls often mention a margin of error, usually about plus or minus 3 percentage points for a poll of around 1,000 people. It reflects only random chance in picking the sample.
It doesn't cover badly worded questions, or people who didn't respond, which can matter more. If a poll shows 52 percent to 48 percent with that margin, the two sides are statistically tied, even if the headline says someone's ahead. Note that the margin applies to each number separately, so the gap between two candidates has an even larger margin. The next time you see a close poll, it's good to remember that it can't tell you who is leading.

In 1936 the magazine Literary Digest mailed out ten million ballots and got back more than 2.4 million, and predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt in a landslide. Roosevelt won in one of the biggest landslides in history, carrying all but two states.
The magazine had drawn its sample from its own readers and from telephone and car-owner lists, which in the Depression skewed richer. George Gallup, polling a much smaller but representative sample, got it right. The lesson is that how a sample is chosen matters far more than how big it is. A huge sample that's biased is worse than a small one that's fair, and no amount of data can fix a lopsided way of collecting it.

A study can find that something "works" and still tell you nothing about how much. Effect size measures how large the difference is. Jacob Cohen suggested rough benchmarks for a standardized difference: 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium and 0.8 is large.
A "statistically significant" result with a tiny effect may be of no practical use, particularly in large studies where even trivial differences can be detected. For example, a diet that makes people lose a few ounces over a year might be "significant" with enough participants, but nobody would care. So when you read about a finding, it's good to ask two questions. Is it real? And how big is it? The second question is the one that tells you whether it matters.

A study with too few participants may fail to detect a real effect. That's low statistical power. A 2013 review of neuroscience studies estimated that the typical study had a power of only about 21 percent, which means it would miss most real effects.
Worse, low power also means that the results that do cross the threshold of significance tend to exaggerate the true effect. A small study that finds a big result is more likely to be a fluke or an overstatement than a large study. It's one reason why many findings from small studies don't hold up when they're repeated. If a surprising result comes from a few dozen people, it's wise to wait for a bigger one.
How to make music make you younger

In 2011 Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn published a paper claiming that listening to the Beatles song "When I'm Sixty-Four" made people nearly a year and a half younger. It was absurd, and it was done on purpose.
It was a deliberate demonstration of how researchers, by making flexible choices about which data to include and which tests to run, can find "significant" results in nonsense. They then proposed rules to stop that kind of p-hacking, such as stating in advance how many participants you will use. The paper was a landmark in the movement to make research more reliable. It showed that a result can be statistically significant and still be completely meaningless.

In 2009 the neuroscientist Craig Bennett put a dead Atlantic salmon in an fMRI brain scanner, showed it photographs of people in social situations, and asked it to determine their emotions. Without correcting for the thousands of statistical tests involved, the analysis found brain activity in the dead fish.
It was a joke with a serious point. If you run enough tests, some will come out "significant" by chance alone, and you have to correct for multiple comparisons. The study won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012, an award for research that makes you laugh and then makes you think. Since then, brain-imaging researchers have taken the issue much more seriously. It's a good story to remember whenever someone says they found a link after testing many things.

In pre-registration, researchers publicly record their hypotheses and methods before collecting data. That stops them from quietly changing the question after they see which results turn out well. It's like calling your shot before taking it.
A 2021 comparison of studies found that 44 percent of those published in a "registered report" format found a positive result, compared with 96 percent of standard published papers. It suggests that the usual literature is skewed toward positive findings, since negative results rarely get published. It's an important change, and one that makes it easier to trust the results. A finding that was predicted in advance is much more convincing than one that was noticed afterward.

A meta-analysis pools the results of many studies on a question to give a clearer overall picture. The psychologist Gene Glass coined the term in 1976, when he combined hundreds of studies of psychotherapy to see whether it worked.
A larger body of evidence gives more precise answers than any single study. But it can only be as good as the studies it includes, and if negative results were never published, even the pooled answer can be biased. Good meta-analyses look for this problem, and they judge the quality of the studies they include. When you hear that "one study found" something, it's worth asking whether there's a meta-analysis, since a single study can mislead.

A headline says a drug "doubles your risk," which sounds alarming. But if the risk was tiny to begin with, doubling it may mean very little. A very small number doubled is still a very small number.
In 1995 the UK government warned that a new type of contraceptive pill doubled the risk of blood clots. The actual risk went from about 1 in 7,000 women to about 2 in 7,000. Many women stopped taking the pill, and there was a rise in unwanted pregnancies and abortions. The harm from the scare was larger than the harm from the pill. It's a good reason to ask, whenever you see a percentage change in risk, "From what to what?"

One helpful way to express how well a treatment works is the number of people who need to take it for one person to benefit. If a drug cuts a risk from 2 percent to 1 percent, you could call that a 50 percent reduction. It sounds impressive.
But 100 people have to take it for one to be helped, and the others get the costs and side effects. The number makes the trade-offs clearer. A treatment with a number needed to treat of 5 is much more valuable than one with 500. It doesn't tell you whether to take a drug, but it gives you a fair way to weigh the benefit against the downsides. It's a question worth asking your doctor.

Any medical test can make two kinds of error. Sensitivity is how good it is at finding people who do have the condition, and specificity is how good it is at correctly clearing people who don't. A test can do very well on one and badly on the other.
A very sensitive test catches nearly everyone who's sick but may also flag many healthy people, which is why a positive result often needs a follow-up. When a condition is rare, most positive results can even be false alarms, even with an accurate test. That's an important reason why doctors don't screen everyone for everything. A positive result isn't the end of the story, and it's often worth asking, "How sure is this test?"

Screening tests find diseases earlier, and the apparent survival time after diagnosis gets longer. But that can be an illusion. Suppose a cancer is found at age 63 without screening and the patient dies at 70, which is 7 years of survival.
With screening, it's found at 60, and the patient still dies at 70, so survival after diagnosis is 10 years, but the person didn't live any longer. All that has happened is that the clock started sooner. The fairer test of screening is whether fewer people die of the disease. That's why researchers look at deaths in the whole population, and not only at survival after diagnosis, when they judge whether a screening program helps.
Always plot your data: Anscombe and the Datasaurus

In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe made up four small sets of numbers that have almost identical averages, spreads and correlations. Yet when you plot them, they look completely different: one is a neat line, one is a curve, one has a single outlier pulling the line, and one is a vertical stack of points. His point was that you should always graph your data, because summary numbers can hide what's really going on.
Decades later, the idea got a modern twist. In 2016 the data visualizer Alberto Cairo made up a data set that, when plotted, looks like a dinosaur, yet has the same averages, spread and correlation as a random scatter of dots. In 2017 researchers Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice built on it, showing a dozen other shapes, including a star and a bullseye, that all share the same summary statistics.

A bar chart is supposed to show quantities in proportion to the height of the bars. If the vertical axis starts at 95 percent instead of zero, a difference between 97 and 99 can look like the second bar is several times as tall.
It's a common way to make small differences look dramatic, sometimes by accident. Always check where the axis starts. Edward Tufte called misleading graphs a violation of graphical integrity. For line charts, it's often acceptable not to start at zero, since the trend matters more than the size, but for bars it's a distortion. A quick glance at the numbers on the side of a chart can save you from being misled.
The law of truly large numbers

When there are enough chances, even extremely unlikely things are bound to happen. The statisticians Persi Diaconis and Frederick Mosteller pointed out that if an event has a one-in-a-million chance on a given day, then with hundreds of millions of people in America, it should happen to hundreds of people every day.
So coincidences aren't strange. They're expected, when you consider how many opportunities there are. A person who dreams of a friend and gets a call the next morning feels something uncanny, but among millions of dreamers, it will happen to many. That doesn't make it any less memorable for the person it happens to. It just means that you can't take a rare event as proof of anything, if it could have happened to any of a million people.

In 1898 the Russian-Polish statistician Ladislaus Bortkiewicz looked at records of how many Prussian cavalry soldiers were killed by horse kicks each year, in 14 army corps over 20 years. The numbers were small, and each death seemed like a random accident.
He showed that the numbers fit a mathematical pattern known as the Poisson distribution, which describes rare events that occur independently at a steady average rate. It's a classic example of how even odd accidents follow statistical laws. The same pattern describes the number of calls arriving at a switchboard, the number of typos on a page and the number of meteorites that land in a field. Randomness, it turns out, has a shape.

In the 1920s, at an English country research station, a woman claimed that she could tell whether the tea or the milk had been poured into a cup first. The statistician Ronald Fisher turned this into a famous experiment: eight cups, four of each kind, presented in random order.
If she's just guessing, the chance of getting all eight right is 1 in 70. The example became a model for randomization and significance testing. It shows the logic of a good experiment. Decide in advance what would count as evidence, take away every chance of bias by randomizing, and then ask how likely the result would be by luck alone. According to the story, she got all of them right.

When a website wants to know which version of a page works better, it can show version A to some visitors and version B to others, chosen at random, and compare the results. It's the same logic as a medical trial.
It lets companies settle arguments with data instead of opinions. In 2009 Google reportedly tested 41 shades of blue for a link bar, and a designer left the company partly because he felt that such testing was replacing design judgment. The case shows both sides. Testing can find what works, and it can also push toward small, safe changes. It's a powerful tool, but it only answers the questions you ask, and some of the best ideas are the ones nobody thinks of testing.

The chance of winning the Powerball jackpot is about 1 in 292 million. With three drawings a week, if you bought a ticket for every single drawing, you'd expect to wait nearly two million years to win once.
On average, a ticket is worth less than what you pay for it. People still play, and most of the pleasure is in the daydream. That's fair enough, as long as you think of it as the price of an entertainment and not as an investment. It helps to remember that you're far more likely to be struck by lightning than to win.
