If you do play, small amounts you can afford to lose are the sensible way.

If you're offered a bet that's in your favor, how much of your money should you put on it? John Kelly, a physicist at Bell Labs, published a formula in 1956 for the answer. It tells you the fraction of your money to wager, based on your edge and the odds.
Bet too much, and a bad run can wipe you out, even though you have an edge. Bet too little, and you waste the edge. Many professional gamblers and investors use half the Kelly amount, to be safer, since the formula assumes you know your odds exactly, and in real life you don't. The idea is a good reminder that, in a favorable game, the most important thing is to stay in the game long enough for the edge to work.

When something is scarce, its price tends to rise. When it's plentiful, it falls. The English economist Alfred Marshall drew the now-famous crossing curves of supply and demand in his 1890 textbook. One curve shows how much buyers want at each price, and the other shows how much sellers will provide.
The point where they cross is the price at which the amount that sellers want to sell equals the amount that buyers want to buy. It's a simple picture, but it explains a lot about how markets work. It's why umbrellas cost more in a downpour, why concert tickets rise when a show is popular, and why a bumper crop of apples brings down the price. Prices are signals that tell everybody what's scarce.

Water is essential for life but cheap, and diamonds are useless for survival but expensive. Economists puzzled over this paradox until the 1870s, when Carl Menger, William Stanley Jevons and Léon Walras each realized that value depends on the next unit, not the total.
Because you already have plenty of water, one more glass is worth little, while one more diamond is scarce. Decisions are made at the margin. It's a way of thinking that helps in everyday choices. Instead of asking whether something is good, you ask whether a little more of it is worth the cost. Is one more hour of work worth more than one more hour of sleep? The answer depends on how much of each you've already had.

In 1817 the economist David Ricardo showed something surprising: two parties can both gain from trade even if one is better at everything. Imagine a lawyer who also types faster than her assistant. She still comes out ahead by letting the assistant type, because her time is worth more spent on legal work.
The same logic applies to countries, and it's the main reason that economists generally favor trade. Each country does best by focusing on what it does relatively well, and trading for the rest. It doesn't mean that everyone benefits equally, or that nobody loses a job. The theory is about the total, and the losers can be real. But it explains why trade, on the whole, makes people richer and not poorer.
Adam Smith: the pin factory and the invisible hand

In The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, Adam Smith described a pin factory where the work was divided into about eighteen distinct steps. He said ten workers, each specializing in a few tasks, could produce about 48,000 pins a day, while a single worker doing everything might make one pin a day, or at most twenty. The division of labor makes everyone far more productive.
The phrase "invisible hand" is one of the best-known in economics, and Smith used it only once in the book. He argued that people pursuing their own interests may, without intending it, end up helping society. Yet he was no simple cheerleader for business. In the same book, he warned that merchants rarely meet together without it ending in a conspiracy against the public. Smith held both ideas, that markets work well and that they need watching.

Inflation means that prices in general are rising, so each dollar buys less. Many central banks aim for about 2 percent a year, which they consider a healthy level. A little inflation encourages people to spend and invest, and makes it easier for wages to adjust.
Even 2 percent adds up. At that rate, prices double in about 35 years. At 7 percent, they double in about 10. That's why money sitting in a drawer slowly loses what it can buy, and why a savings account that pays less than inflation is losing value in real terms. When you compare what something cost in the past with what it costs now, it's worth adjusting for inflation, since a dollar in 1980 bought far more than a dollar does today.

When a government prints too much money, prices can spiral out of control. In Germany in 1923, prices at one point doubled every few days, and people were paid twice a day and rushed to spend the money before it lost value. Wheelbarrows of banknotes were needed to buy a loaf of bread.
In Zimbabwe, in November 2008, monthly inflation reached an estimated 80 billion percent. When money stops working, people turn to barter or foreign currencies. Savings are wiped out, and the social order can be badly shaken. Hyperinflation is rare, and it usually follows war, collapse or reckless government finance. It's a stark example of how much we rely on money keeping its value, something we usually take for granted.

A central bank sets short-term interest rates to influence the economy: lowering them to encourage borrowing and spending, and raising them to cool down inflation. The US Federal Reserve was created in 1913, after a series of bank panics, especially one in 1907. It has what's called a dual mandate from Congress, to keep prices stable and to promote maximum employment.
The dollar bill in your wallet has no gold behind it, and it isn't worth much as paper. It's money because the government says it is and because everyone accepts it. That's called fiat money, from the Latin for "let it be done." Until 1971, the US dollar could be exchanged for gold at a fixed rate, and when President Nixon ended that, the world moved fully to fiat currencies. Most money today is just numbers in bank accounts.

"Don't put all your eggs in one basket" has a mathematical backing. In 1952 Harry Markowitz showed that if you combine investments that don't all move in the same direction at the same time, you can reduce your overall risk without lowering your expected return.
He won a Nobel Prize for it in 1990. It's often called the only free lunch in finance. A portfolio of many different stocks is much less risky than any one of them, because when one falls, another may rise. The benefit has limits, since in a severe crash nearly everything falls together. But over time, spreading your money across many kinds of assets is one of the most reliable ways to protect it, and it needs no special skill.

An index fund simply buys all the stocks in a market, rather than trying to pick winners. John Bogle founded the first one available to ordinary investors in 1976, at Vanguard, and he was ridiculed for it at the time. People called it "Bogle's folly," because settling for average seemed un-American.
Reports that compare funds, such as the S&P SPIVA scorecards, regularly find that over a 15-year period, around nine in ten professional stock funds do worse than the index they're trying to beat. Part of the reason is the fees they charge. An index fund is cheap, because it doesn't need anyone to do research. It's a sobering lesson that, for most people, the simplest strategy beats most of the experts.

Eugene Fama proposed in 1970 that stock prices already reflect all publicly available information, so it's very hard to consistently beat the market. If a stock were obviously a bargain, so many buyers would rush in that the price would rise until the bargain disappeared.
Other economists, like Robert Shiller, argued that markets can be driven by emotion and bubbles. In 2013 Fama and Shiller, with another economist, shared the Nobel Prize in economics, an indication of how both views have supporters. It's still debated. A reasonable position is that markets are hard to beat but not perfectly rational, and that anyone who claims to be able to predict them should be treated with caution.

In the 1630s tulip bulbs in the Netherlands sold at extraordinary prices, and the craze is retold as the classic example of a speculative bubble that ruined thousands. The story says that a single bulb could cost as much as a house.
Modern historians, like Anne Goldgar, who looked through the records, say it was much smaller than the legend. Few people seem to have been ruined, and the evidence is thin. The story has been told so many times that the myth became the lesson. It's a nice irony that a story about people being carried away by a craze has itself been repeated, for centuries, with little checking. Whatever happened, bubbles in other times were certainly real.

If you have a pile of money to invest, is it better to invest it all at once, or to spread it out over several months? A 2012 Vanguard study found that investing all at once did better about two-thirds of the time, simply because markets tend to rise more often than they fall.
Spreading it out makes you less likely to regret putting everything in just before a drop, so it's a trade-off. Averaging in is a way of buying peace of mind, and a modest price for it. The best choice depends on how much a sudden fall would hurt you. What matters most is not the method, but that you don't wait on the sidelines for the "perfect" moment, which no one can identify in advance.
The time value of money and Franklin's bequest

Would you rather have $100 today or $100 in a year? Most people say today, and they're right. You could invest the money and have more later, and prices will likely have risen. Economists "discount" future money to reflect this. It's the principle behind interest on loans and savings, and it's how the value of any investment or business is worked out.
When Benjamin Franklin died in 1790, he left 1,000 pounds each to the cities of Boston and Philadelphia, to be loaned out at interest and not fully used for 200 years. By 1990 the funds had grown to millions of dollars: about $5 million in Boston's fund and $2 million in Philadelphia's. It's a vivid example of the power of compound interest over a long time.

In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin described a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains by adding another cow, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, so the pasture gets destroyed. It's an image for many shared resources, such as fisheries and the atmosphere.
Elinor Ostrom, who won the 2009 Nobel Prize in economics, showed that many communities have managed shared resources well by creating their own rules. Swiss villages have shared alpine pastures for centuries, and Maine lobster fishermen have set their own limits. So the tragedy isn't inevitable. It tends to happen when there are no rules, no trust and no way to enforce an agreement, and it can often be avoided when people can talk and set limits.

Two suspects are held separately. Each is offered a deal to betray the other. Whatever the other does, betraying seems best for you. But if both betray, they do worse than if both had stayed quiet.
Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the game in 1950, and Albert Tucker told the prison story. In Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments around 1980, the winning strategy was "tit for tat": cooperate first, then copy the other player's last move. It was simple and forgiving, and it did better than much more complicated strategies. It's a powerful lesson. In repeated dealings, being nice, but not a pushover, tends to pay.

A Nash equilibrium is a situation in which no player can do better by changing only their own choice, given what the others are doing. John Nash proved in 1950 that every game with a finite number of players and choices has at least one.
It describes stable outcomes, not necessarily good ones, as the prisoner's dilemma shows, where both players betraying is a stable result that's bad for both. Nash won the Nobel Prize in 1994, after decades of struggling with mental illness, a story told in the book and movie A Beautiful Mind. The idea is used to understand everything from auctions to arms races to traffic. It tells us where a situation might settle, and not where it ought to.

Some things become more valuable as more people use them. A telephone is useless if you're the only one who has one, and valuable if everyone you know does. That's a network effect. Social networks, payment systems and messaging apps all depend on it.
Metcalfe's law says that the value of a network grows with the square of the number of users, but studies of real networks suggest it grows more slowly. It helps explain why one social network or payment system can come to dominate. Once most people are on one, nobody wants to leave, even if a better one is available. It also explains why new services often give away a lot at first, in order to reach the point where the network takes off.

In 1970 the economist George Akerlof wrote a paper about the used-car market. Sellers know whether their car is good or a "lemon," but buyers can't tell, so buyers are only willing to pay an average price. At that price, owners of good cars won't sell, and the market fills up with lemons.
The paper showed how a lack of information can make markets fail. He shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for it. Akerlof's paper was rejected by several journals before it was published, because reviewers thought it was trivial or wrong. The idea has been applied to insurance, jobs and loans. It's the reason why warranties, inspections and reputations are valuable. They help the buyer trust something they can't check for themselves.

When someone else bears the cost of a risk, people tend to take more of it. A driver with full insurance may be a little less careful. A bank that expects the government to bail it out if it fails may place bigger bets.
Insurers try to limit it with deductibles and co-payments, so that the person still has something to lose. The term comes from the insurance business, where it was first used to describe policyholders who were careless because they were covered. The concept helps explain a lot of modern financial history, including the crisis of 2008. It's not that insured people are bad. It's that everyone, if they are shielded from the consequences, tends to behave a little differently.

An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on someone who didn't choose to take part. A factory's pollution harms people downwind, a negative externality. A neighbor's beautiful garden pleases passers-by, a positive one.
In 1920 the economist Arthur Pigou argued that a tax on the polluter can make the price of a product reflect its true cost to society. Many modern carbon taxes follow the idea. Without such a tax, the price of a product leaves out the harm done to others, so people buy too much of it. Externalities help explain why markets, left alone, don't always give the best result, and why some things, like clean air, need rules or prices to be protected.

Some things, like street lighting, clean air or national defense, benefit everyone, whether or not they pay. That creates a free-rider problem: if you can use it either way, why pay? Voluntary contributions tend to fall short.
That's the reason economists give for why governments usually pay for such goods with taxes, to make sure that everyone chips in. Street lighting is a classic case, since you can't easily stop a passer-by from using the light. Public radio and open-source software face the same problem and rely on donations from the people who care. It's a useful way to see why a few things, which markets can't easily provide, are paid for in common.

Ronald Coase argued in a 1960 paper that if people can bargain easily with each other, they'll reach an efficient arrangement no matter who starts out holding the legal rights. For example, a factory and its neighbors could settle the problem of smoke by negotiation, without a government rule.
In real life, the costs of getting everyone together and agreeing are often too high, so the theorem works best for small groups. Coase himself stressed that, and he thought the real lesson was that we should look at how costly it is to make deals. The idea has been influential in law as well as economics. It suggests that a good first step to a dispute is to ask whether the people involved could simply talk and make a deal.

Price elasticity is how much demand changes when the price changes. For things people need and can't easily replace, like gasoline in the short run, demand barely drops when the price goes up. That's low elasticity.
For things with lots of substitutes, like one brand of soda, a small price rise sends buyers elsewhere. That's high elasticity. Businesses and governments use it to predict how changes in price will play out. A tax on cigarettes, for example, raises more revenue if smokers don't cut back much, and reduces smoking more if they do. It's a handy idea for understanding why some price increases cause an uproar and others pass unnoticed.

Gross domestic product measures the total value of goods and services a country produces. Simon Kuznets, who developed the measure in the 1930s, warned in a 1934 report to Congress that the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income.
GDP counts cleaning up after a disaster as growth, but it doesn't count unpaid housework, leisure or the health of the environment. A country can grow richer while its people become sicker or lonelier. That doesn't make GDP useless. It's a good measure of the size of an economy. But it's a poor measure of how well people are living, which is why researchers also look at health, education and happiness.

The Gini coefficient is a single number that measures how unequal an income distribution is, from 0, where everyone has the same, to 1, where one person has everything. The Italian statistician Corrado Gini introduced it in 1912.
It's handy for comparing countries. Scandinavian countries are around 0.25 to 0.28, and some other countries are above 0.6. It doesn't show where in the distribution the inequality lies, so two countries with the same number can look quite different. And it says nothing about how rich a country is overall. It's a rough but useful summary, and it's best used alongside other facts about how people live.
The minimum wage debate and natural experiments

Does raising the minimum wage cost jobs? In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger compared fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which had raised its minimum wage, with neighboring Pennsylvania, which hadn't. They found no loss of jobs in New Jersey. Other studies have found different results, so the debate continues.
Economists can't usually run controlled experiments on whole economies. But sometimes events create something close: a lottery for the military draft, a state border where laws differ or a sudden change in a rule. These are called natural experiments. In 2021 David Card, Joshua Angrist and Guido Imbens shared the Nobel Prize in economics for developing ways to learn about cause and effect from them.

A nudge is a small change in how choices are presented that steers people toward a better decision, without forbidding anything, such as making organ donation or saving for retirement the default. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularized the idea in their 2008 book.
A 2022 review found that, once publication bias is accounted for, the average effect shrinks to nearly zero, though some well-designed nudges clearly work. The lesson is that it's not enough to find a clever idea. It needs to be tested, again and again. Defaults seem to be among the strongest and most dependable, since doing nothing is easy. Other kinds of nudges, such as reminders and slogans, are less certain.

Normally, when a price goes up, people buy less. But for some luxury goods, demand can rise as the price rises, because the high price is part of the appeal. In 1899 the economist Thorstein Veblen wrote about "conspicuous consumption," buying things to show status.
Designer handbags, luxury watches and certain sports cars fit. Ordinary goods don't work that way. If a luxury brand cut its prices sharply, its customers might stop buying, because the thing they were buying was exclusivity. It's one of the rare exceptions to the rule that demand falls as price rises. Veblen was a sharp critic of the wealthy of his time, and his phrase "conspicuous consumption" is still in everyday use.

A company can show a profit on paper and still run out of cash. Profit counts sales when they're made, even if customers haven't paid yet. Cash flow is the money that's actually in the bank.
Many businesses that look healthy fail because customers pay slowly while suppliers and employees need to be paid right away. It's why experienced owners say "cash is king." A growing company can be especially vulnerable, since it has to buy materials and hire people before the money from new sales arrives. If you run a small business, or are thinking of starting one, tracking cash each week is one of the most useful habits you can build.

Margin and markup are easy to mix up. Markup is profit as a percentage of what the item cost you. Margin is profit as a percentage of the price you charge.
If you buy something for $60 and sell it for $100, the profit is $40, so the markup is about 67 percent and the margin is 40 percent. Confusing the two is a common cause of pricing too low. A shop owner who wants a 40 percent margin but adds a 40 percent markup ends up with a margin of only about 29 percent. The same dollars give two different percentages, so it's worth being clear about which one you mean.
Unit economics and the break-even point

Unit economics asks whether you make money on each individual sale, after counting everything it costs to make the product and to win the customer. Suppose it costs $50 in advertising to get a customer who brings in $30 of profit. Every sale loses $20, and growing faster just loses money faster. It's worth working out before you try to scale a business.
The break-even point is how much you need to sell to cover all your costs. You work it out by dividing your fixed costs, such as rent and salaries, by the profit you make on each unit. Below that number, you lose money, and above it, every additional sale adds to your profit. These are among the first numbers to know before starting a business or launching a product.

In 1997 the Harvard professor Clayton Christensen argued that successful companies can be overtaken by cheaper, simpler products that start at the bottom of the market, and improve until they threaten the leaders. Steel mini-mills and small disk drives were among his examples. It became enormously influential.
Critics, including the historian Jill Lepore in a 2014 article, said that his examples were chosen after the fact, and that many companies he called disrupted did fine. So it's better as a way of describing the past than predicting the future. The idea holds something true, that leaders can be blind to threats from below, but it isn't a law. It's a story that sometimes fits and sometimes doesn't.

A minimum viable product is the simplest version of a product that you can put in front of real customers to learn whether they want it. Eric Ries made the term popular in his 2011 book The Lean Startup.
The idea is to learn early, with little cost, before spending months building something nobody wants. It's about testing assumptions, not about shipping something poor. A founder might start with a simple page that describes a product and see if anyone signs up, before building any of it. The same approach works outside business. Before you commit a lot of time to a project, it's wise to find the smallest test that would tell you whether it's worth doing.

Money can be saved for later, but time can't. Every hour is spent on something, and spending it on one thing means not spending it on another. You can't earn more of it, and you can't put it in the bank.
That's why the question "Is this worth doing?" is a weak test, because nearly anything has some value. A better question is "What else could I do with this hour?" That brings the real cost into view. It's a way of seeing that saying yes to one thing is always saying no to something else, so protecting your time is the same as protecting what matters most to you.
The woman who cannot feel fear, except in one way

Urbach-Wiethe disease is a very rare inherited disorder, with about 400 reported cases. It was first reported in 1929 by Erich Urbach and Camillo Wiethe. It mainly affects the skin and the voice, which becomes hoarse. In some patients, the disease also hardens tissue deep in both temporal lobes of the brain, where it destroys the amygdala, a small structure that is important in processing fear.
A patient known as S.M. has this damage on both sides. Reports say that she shows little fear in everyday life. She will pick up a snake, or watch a frightening scene in a film like The Shining, without being affected. For years, she became a prime case for the idea that the amygdala is the brain's fear center.
In 2013 Justin Feinstein and his colleagues tested her with a different threat. She and two other patients with the same condition breathed air with 35 percent carbon dioxide, which gives a sense of suffocation. They felt significantly more fear and panic than 12 healthy people, of whom only three panicked. The authors suggested that the amygdala may normally hold panic back, and that fear from inside the body runs through other regions, such as the brainstem and the insula.
The four colors that most of us cannot see

Most people have three kinds of cone cells in their eyes, which respond to red, green and blue light, and the brain mixes the three signals into all of the colors that we see. A tetrachromat has four kinds. That would give a color space with four dimensions, and such a person might tell apart colors that look identical to the rest of us.
Many animals are tetrachromats, among them birds, fish and reptiles. The common ancestor of all backboned animals was one. Early mammals, which are thought to have lived mostly at night, lost two of the four types and were left with two. Later, some primates, including our ancestors, gained a third type again by a change in a gene.
Researchers have looked for people who see in four dimensions, mostly women who carry gene variants for an extra kind of cone. The idea is attractive, but a fourth cone type does not by itself mean that the brain can use it, and proof is difficult. Tests that show real extra color discrimination have been reported in only a few people. Birds, then, may see a world in colors that humans can only imagine.
Why you never see your eyes move

Try this at a mirror. Look at your left eye, and then at your right. You will never see your eyes move. Yet a person watching can see them move clearly.
The reason is that the brain cuts off vision during fast eye movements. These jumps are called saccades, and you make several each second as you read or look around. A fast movement would blur the image on the retina. So the brain suppresses the signal while the eye moves, and the blur and the gap are never noticed. The effect is called saccadic masking, and it was first described by Erdmann and Dodge in 1898, when they found that an observer could never see the motion of his own eyes.
The brain also fills the gap. After a saccade you may think that the second you looked at a clock lasted longer than usual, with the second hand seeming to hang for a moment. That is chronostasis, or the stopped clock illusion, and the saccadic gap is often used to explain it. What we think is a smooth view of the world is built out of a series of snapshots, with the dark gaps edited out.
The man who lived in a cave to find time

On July 16, 1962, a young French geologist, Michel Siffre, climbed down 130 meters into an icy cave, called Scarasson, in the Alps on the border of France and Italy. His plan was to live there with no clock, no sun and no calendar, to see how a person keeps time. He stayed 63 days.
When the team on the surface called him to say that his time was up, he thought it was only about the 20th of August, and that he had nearly a month to go. In fact it was mid-September, and he had lost track of about 25 days. His sleeping and waking continued in a regular cycle, of about 24 and a half hours, close to the length of a day. In 1972 he went back, and spent 205 days in Midnight Cave in Texas. The American space agency, NASA, studied his work.
His experiments helped to start the study of body clocks. Later work done by Charles Czeisler and colleagues in 1999, in controlled light, found that the average human clock runs at about 24.18 hours, a little closer to a day than the cave studies had suggested. Siffre was a single volunteer, and not a physiologist. He died in 2024 at the age of 85.
The disease that takes away sleep

Fatal familial insomnia is a very rare brain disease. It is caused by a mutation in a gene called PRNP, which makes a protein that can fold into a harmful shape, called a prion. Mad cow disease belongs to the same family of prion diseases. In this disease the damage begins in the thalamus, a part of the brain that helps to regulate sleep. It was first described in an Italian family in the 1980s.
The disease runs in four stages. In the first, lasting about four months, the sleep gets worse and the person has panic attacks, paranoia and phobias. In the second, for about five months, hallucinations and panic grow. In the third, over about three months, sleep is lost altogether, and the person loses weight quickly. In the last, for about six months, there is dementia, and then death.
Death usually comes within a few months to a few years from the start. There is no known treatment that changes the course of the disease. There is also a sporadic form, which occurs with no family history. The disease is a stark case of how much the brain depends on sleep, and it has been the subject of much research on prions.
The syndrome that makes the world grow and shrink

In 1955 a psychiatrist, John Todd, described a condition in which people see objects as the wrong size or distance. Things may look smaller than they are, which is called micropsia, or larger, called macropsia. They may seem too close or too far. Some people also feel that their own body has become larger or smaller. It is now called Alice in Wonderland syndrome, or Todd's syndrome, after Lewis Carroll's story, in which Alice grows and shrinks.
The cause is not known. It is often linked to migraines, head injuries, or an infection with the Epstein-Barr virus, and it may involve abnormal electrical activity in parts of the brain that handle vision. It can also be caused temporarily by certain drugs. It is more common in children, and it usually passes with time.
Some people have wondered whether Carroll himself, who had migraines, drew on such experiences, but that is a guess. Doctors do not agree on exactly which symptoms count. Some use the name only for changes in the body image, and use Alice in Wonderland-like syndrome for the other changes. The condition shows how much the sense of size is something that the brain constructs.
The stroke patient who woke up with an accent

Foreign accent syndrome is an extremely rare condition in which a person begins to speak in a way that sounds like a foreign accent, without having learned one. A speaker of British English may seem to have an Italian accent, or an American may seem to be French. Most often it follows a stroke, though head injuries and migraines can cause it.
The first case was reported in 1907. Between 1941 and 2009 only 62 cases were recorded. The cause seems to be damage to the parts of the brain that plan and coordinate the movements of speech. The changes in rhythm, stress and vowels are what listeners hear as foreign. The patient does not take on any particular accent, and does not become better at any foreign language. No verified case of improved language skill after brain injury has been found.
News stories often name the accent that listeners think they hear. In truth the accents are not accurate, and the listeners are doing the matching. Patients do not say it is effortless. They feel that they have a speech disorder, and many find it upsetting. The condition shows that an accent is a pattern of timing and movement, which the brain can alter.
The man who inspired Rain Man

Kim Peek was born in Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1951. He was called a megasavant, because he had an exceptional memory and a remarkable intelligence, but he also had great difficulty with many everyday tasks and with social life. He was the inspiration for the character Raymond Babbitt, played by Dustin Hoffman, in the 1988 film Rain Man.
He was born with an enlarged head, damage to the cerebellum, and no corpus callosum, the bundle of nerves that joins the two halves of the brain. Doctors thought that he should be institutionalized, but his parents refused and raised him at home. By his father's account, he began to memorize books at 16 to 20 months. He was reported to have memorized about 12,000 books. He had once been called autistic, but is now thought to have had a condition called FG syndrome.
Some scientists speculated that his unusual brain wiring, with extra connections between areas that are normally separate, explained his memory. This is a guess, and the evidence is limited, since he was only one person. Peek died in 2009 at 58. He showed that the range of what a human brain can do is wider than we assume, and that great ability and great difficulty can exist together.
Do rats laugh when they are tickled?

The neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp noticed that young rats make high-pitched sounds, at about 50 kilohertz, far above the range of human hearing, when they play. In 2003 he and Jeff Burgdorf reported that tickling raises the rate of these chirps. The rats also seemed to like it. They sought out the hand that had tickled them, and the ones that were most ticklish were also the most playful.
The chirping dropped when the rats were hungry, or when they were exposed to the smell of a cat, or to bright light, even when the tickling was kept the same. Panksepp called it social joy, and he argued that the sounds may be an evolutionary relative of human laughter. He hoped that mapping the brain systems behind it would help to find medicines for depression.
He was careful to say that it does not mean that rats have a sense of humor. Other scientists have questioned the idea. In 2022 a review by Burke, Pellis and Achterberg argued that the kinds of calls rats make while being tickled differ from those they make while playing with each other, so the calls may not be a simple form of laughter. The work remains a good example of how emotions in animals can be studied.
The nasal spray that raised trust

Oxytocin is a hormone that plays a role in childbirth and in bonding between mother and baby. In 2005 a team led by Michael Kosfeld asked whether it affects trust between adults. They used a game with real money. An investor could hand over some money to a trustee, the amount would be tripled, and the trustee could send back as much as he or she chose.
Of 29 investors who had a nasal spray of oxytocin, 13, or 45 percent, handed over the most money allowed. Of 29 who had a placebo, only 6, or 21 percent, did so. The average amount given was about 17 percent higher in the oxytocin group. The study was double blind, so that neither the volunteers nor the staff knew who had the real hormone.
A control experiment used a game that was like the trust game, but had no human partner. Oxytocin did not make people more willing to take risks in it, so the effect seemed to be about trust and not about taking chances. The paper was widely noted, and it gave oxytocin the nickname of the trust hormone. Later studies have given mixed results, so it is best regarded as an important finding that has not been settled.
The man who recited twenty-two thousand digits of pi

On March 14, 2004, Pi Day, Daniel Tammet sat in front of an audience at the Museum of the History of Science in Oxford and recited the digits of pi. He went on for five hours and nine minutes, and reached 22,514 digits, setting a European record. He did it to raise money for an epilepsy charity.
Tammet has said that he sees numbers as shapes, with colors and textures. Every number up to 10,000, he says, has its own look. He recalled the digits by moving through a landscape of these shapes, in a sense walking along them. His abilities are said to have appeared after epileptic seizures in his childhood. He is a savant who is also a synesthete, a person whose senses are linked.
The record has been disputed. Some record-keeping groups count a lower figure, because of a mistake that was not corrected without help, and the count has also been given as 22,511. A later reciter is said to have surpassed his total. It is still a striking feat of memory, and it gives a rare view into how a different mind can handle numbers.

In 1953 two researchers, Morris Heller and Moe Bergman, asked a simple question. Do people with normal hearing hear anything when it is completely quiet? They put volunteers in a special room built to remove all sound, called an anechoic chamber, and asked them what they heard. Their paper was titled Tinnitus Aurium in Normally Hearing Persons.
Most of the volunteers reported hearing something, such as a buzzing, ringing, humming or pulsing. It was the first time that tinnitus-like sounds had been seen to occur in healthy people in absolute silence. One later account says that 95 percent of the participants reported such sounds. Later studies, which repeated the experiment, found lower figures of around 64 to 68 percent.
The sounds are produced inside the hearing system and the brain, and not by the air. In ordinary life they are covered by background noise. One idea is that in silence the brain turns up its sensitivity, and may even invent a signal. For most people the sound is faint and goes away. For those who have tinnitus all the time, it can be hard to live with. The finding is a reminder that complete silence is rare, and that the brain fills it.
The cliff that was staged for the camera

Many people believe that lemmings, small rodents of the Arctic, throw themselves off cliffs in a mass suicide. The idea was spread by a 1958 Disney nature film, White Wilderness. It showed a crowd of lemmings plunging into the sea. In fact the animals in the scene were pushed off the cliff by the filmmakers, to create the illusion.
The belief is older than the film. It goes back at least to the late nineteenth century, though where it started is uncertain. Lemmings do move around in large numbers when their population is high, and some drown when they try to cross water. But they are looking for food and space, and they are not trying to die.
The phrase has entered everyday speech, and people say that a crowd rushing to a bad decision is like lemmings going over a cliff. It is a good example of a myth that a single powerful film can fix in the public mind. The scene that taught millions of people about animal behavior was made up.
The pen that did not cost millions

A well-known story says that NASA spent millions of dollars to develop a pen that would write in space, while the Soviets simply used pencils. It is a good joke about waste, but it is not true. The pen was developed on his own by Paul C. Fisher, who ran the Fisher Pen Company, and he spent about a million dollars of his own money on it.
Pencils were not a good choice in a spacecraft. Their shavings and bits of graphite can float about, and are a hazard around instruments and in the air that the crew breathes. NASA tested the Fisher pen, which uses pressurized ink and writes upside down and in extreme heat and cold, and approved it. It bought 400 pens at about six dollars each.
The Soviet Union later bought the same pens for its Soyuz flights. A related myth says that NASA invented Tang, Velcro and Teflon. It did not, though many other products, such as memory foam and space blankets, did come from space research. The story survives because it is about a simple answer to an expensive problem, but the reality was that the engineers were right.
Why the far side of the Moon is not dark

The Moon always shows the same face to the Earth, because it turns once on its axis in exactly the time that it takes to go around us once. It is called tidal locking. Because of it, people long thought of the other side as hidden and mysterious, and called it the dark side of the Moon.
But it is not dark. As the Moon travels around the Earth, the sun shines on every part of it. The far side gets about as much sunlight as the near side, and has a day and a night just as the near side does. At new moon, when we see nothing, the far side is fully lit.
Nobody on Earth had seen it until 1959, when the Soviet probe Luna 3 took the first photographs. The word dark refers to the fact that it was unknown, in the sense of the old phrase dark continent, and not to a lack of light. That is why the better name is far side. Astronomers also found it looks different from the near side, with far fewer of the dark plains.
The frog that jumps out, and the one that says ribbit

A famous story says that if you put a frog in a pot of cold water and heat it slowly, the frog will not notice, and will be boiled to death. It is used as a warning about change that creeps up on people. It is not true of frogs. If a frog is dropped into boiling water, it dies at once. If it is in water that is slowly heated, it tries to escape long before it reaches the temperature at which it would be harmed.
The saying is a metaphor, and it can still be used as one. But the frog is not as foolish as it suggests. Frogs, like other animals, react to discomfort, and they get out.
Another mistaken idea about frogs comes from the movies. The classic ribbit sound is made by only a few species, mainly the Pacific tree frog and the Baja California chorus frog. It spread because of its heavy use in films shot in Hollywood, where those frogs live, and soon many viewers thought that all frogs sound like that. Frogs around the world call in very different ways.

The memory of a goldfish is said to last three seconds. It does not. A goldfish can remember for up to a few months. That is why people can train them to expect food at certain times and to respond to signals.
Piranhas are famous as killers. In fact they eat many things, plants as well as meat. They swim in schools mainly to protect themselves from predators and not to attack. Attacks on humans are very rare, and happen when they are under stress and feel threatened, and then the bites are usually on hands and feet.
A relative, the pacu, was falsely said to bite off men's testicles. The story began in 2013, when a report about a pacu found in the strait between Sweden and Denmark was changed by a joke into a claim that it ate nuts. The candiru, a parasitic catfish of the Amazon, is said to swim up a person's urethra. The only documented case, written up in 1997, was heavily criticized by other scientists, and the story is now largely regarded as a myth.
The pink sweat of the hippopotamus

Hippos are said to sweat blood and to give pink milk. They do neither. The skin of a hippo gives off a reddish fluid, and it can look alarming. It is not sweat and it is not blood. The color comes from a red pigment called hipposudoric acid.
The pigment seems to act as a natural sunscreen, protecting the hippo's skin in the strong sun. Hippos spend much of the day in water, but their skin is thin and can crack and burn when it dries. The secretion forms a film over the skin, which helps to protect it.
The milk is not pink, either. It is white or a pale beige. The idea that a hippo's milk could be pink seems to come from the mistaken view of the red secretion as blood. The animal is a good example of the kind of misunderstanding that takes hold, when a very odd-looking natural thing is given a dramatic explanation.
Porcupines and skunks do not do what the stories say

A porcupine cannot shoot its quills. The quills are loose, and they come out easily when they touch an attacker. A porcupine defends itself by turning its back and reversing into the enemy, so that the quills stick in. They do not fly through the air, though the stories say so.
Another idea concerns skunks. Many people think that a bath in tomato juice cures a dog that has been sprayed. It does not. After a time, a person who has been sprayed stops noticing the smell, because of olfactory fatigue, the nose's tendency to tune out a smell that continues. Tomato juice seems to work because the smell has faded, and not because the juice has changed it.
Treatments that really work are chemical, and break down the compounds in the spray. People should not rely on a household remedy because it seems to work. Both myths are about the same mistake, which is believing that an animal weapon does something more dramatic than it does, or that a remedy works because its use was followed by relief.
Three more animal tales that are not true

Rabbits do not live on carrots. In the wild they eat grasses, clovers and dark green plants. Carrots are rich in sugar, and a rabbit that eats a great many of them is likely to be unhealthy. They are a treat, and not a main meal.
Catnip does not affect every cat. Only about two thirds of cats respond to it. Whether a cat does so is inherited. Other plants, such as valerian root, can have a similar effect on cats that are not interested in catnip.
Old elephants do not leave the herd and go to a special graveyard to die. The tale has been told for a long time, and has appeared in adventure stories, but there is no evidence for it. What is true is that elephants show strong interest in the bones of dead elephants, touching and turning them, and this behavior may have helped to feed the legend. They are social animals, and they mourn in their own way.
The eagle that sounds like a hawk

When a bald eagle appears in a film or a television advertisement, it is often accompanied by a loud and fierce scream. The sound is real, but it does not belong to the eagle. It is the cry of a red-tailed hawk, which is used in the sound track because it fits our idea of what an eagle should sound like.
The real call of the bald eagle is much softer and higher. It is a series of weak, chirping notes, and it resembles the calls of gulls more than anything else. To many people it is a surprise, and even a disappointment, for a bird that is the national symbol of the United States.
The mix-up shows how much of what we think we know about animals comes from how they are shown in the media, and how little from the animals. A sound that is used often enough becomes the right one in people's minds. Even those who have seen real eagles are often startled by the sound that they make.
The sixty starlings and the Shakespeare myth

In 1890 a New York drug manufacturer named Eugene Schieffelin released about sixty European starlings in Central Park. The birds thrived and spread. Starlings are now one of the most numerous birds in North America, and they are considered a pest by many farmers.
A popular story says that Schieffelin wanted to bring to America every kind of bird that is mentioned in the works of William Shakespeare, because he was a fan of the playwright, and that the starling, mentioned once in the play Henry IV, was one. It is a good story, but there is no evidence that it is true.
The claim has been traced to an essay in 1948 by the naturalist Edwin Way Teale. His notes appear to show that it was a speculation of his own, and not a fact. Acclimatization societies of the time did bring many species from Europe, for reasons of sentiment and also of use. The Shakespeare tale is an example of an attractive explanation that outlived its source. Starlings did come from the Old World, and they did come in 1890.
Why a meteor glows, and why an egg stands up

When a meteor or a spacecraft hits the upper air, it glows and gets very hot. Many people say that this is caused by friction with the air. It is not the main cause. The air in front of an object moving at several kilometers a second cannot get out of the way, and is squeezed, so that it is compressed very fast. When air is compressed in this way, it gets very hot, and it is that heat that glows and warms the object.
This is called adiabatic compression, and it is the same thing that heats the air in a bicycle pump. At high speed it is so intense that spacecraft returning from orbit need heat shields to survive.
A similar idea is that you can only balance an egg on its end at the time of the spring equinox, when day and night are equal. It is false. With patience, an egg can be balanced on any day of the year, because the tiny bumps on the shell give it several points of contact. The belief is a reminder that when a feat is said to depend on the stars, it is a good idea to try it on a different date.
Two things most people believe about sharks

In 1992 a book called Sharks Don't Get Cancer was published. It claimed that sharks are free from the disease, and that eating the cartilage that makes their skeletons could prevent cancer in people. It sold widely, and extracts of shark cartilage were sold as a supplement. The first claim is wrong. Cancers have been found in sharks, and the data do not support any conclusions about how often they get tumors.
Another belief is that great white sharks attack surfers and divers because they mistake them for seals. The pattern of attacks suggests otherwise. When a great white attacks a seal, it rises fast and strikes with great violence. When it attacks a human, it usually approaches at a normal speed, bites, and swims away. Great whites have good eyesight and color vision.
The researchers who study this think that the bite on a human is a test, a way of finding out what an unfamiliar object is. A human is not food that a shark wants, and a bite is often enough to injure badly, though many people survive. The sharks of the movies are not what the evidence shows.
Snakes that do not unhinge, and do not dance

Snakes can swallow things much larger than their heads. Many people say that this is because they can unhinge their jaws. They cannot. The jaw bones are connected to the skull by a movable bone, called the quadrate, which lets the mouth open very wide. At the front, the two halves of the lower jaw are joined by a flexible ligament, so that they can spread apart.
Snakes are not deaf, as is often said. They can hear sounds carried in the air, though they do not hear high pitches as well as we do. They can also feel vibrations through the ground.
Snake charmers play a flute, and a cobra seems to sway to the music. It is not responding to the tune. Snakes cannot hear music in the way that humans do. The snake follows the movement of the charmer's swaying instrument, which it sees as a threat that it must watch. The music is for the audience. The snake is following the motion, and it is ready to strike.
The bumblebee that was said to be unable to fly

There is a story that scientists have proved that a bumblebee cannot fly. The physics, it says, shows that its wings are too small for its body. It is told as a lesson about believing in yourself. The truth is that no such proof exists. The physics of insect flight is quite well understood. The story seems to come from a calculation that treated the bee as a fixed-wing aircraft, mentioned in a 1934 book. It was repeated in a film, Bee Movie, in 2007.
Another claim is that if bees died out, humanity would starve within four years. Honey bees are important for the pollination of many plants. But the main staple crops of the world, wheat, maize, rice, soybeans and sorghum, are pollinated by the wind or by themselves. Only a little over ten percent of the human plant diet depends on insect pollination.
A third idea is that a bee dies after stinging. That happens in only a small minority of species, including the honey bee when it stings a mammal. Most bees survive a sting, and a honey bee that stings another insect does too. It would be a mistake to ignore the decline of bees, but not for these reasons.

It is said that after a nuclear war, only cockroaches would survive. Cockroaches are more resistant to radiation than humans, but they are not immune to radiation sickness. They are also not unusually tough compared with other insects. Parasitic wasps, tardigrades, and some bacteria, such as Deinococcus radiodurans, can survive much more.
Earwigs are said to creep into the ears of sleeping people and lay eggs. There are a few stories of earwigs found in ears, but the insects are not known to do it on purpose. Their name may come from the shape of their hind wings, which look like a human ear when unfolded.
Houseflies live for about 20 to 30 days, and not 24 hours as people say. The insect with a very short adult life is a different one. Females of an American mayfly, Dolania americana, live as adults for as little as five minutes. These are not true flies, and their adult stage exists only for mating and laying eggs. The myths show how an interesting figure can spread beyond what the facts support.
What the spiders and other crawlers are not

Some people say that you swallow eight spiders a year in your sleep. It is not true. A sleeping person makes breathing and heartbeat sounds that warn off spiders, and most people wake up if a spider crawls on their face.
The daddy longlegs spider is said to be the most venomous spider in the world, but with fangs too short to bite. In truth its fangs can pierce human skin, and the venom is so slight that it causes only a mild burning for a few seconds. The name is also given to harvestmen and crane flies, which are not spiders at all.
Female praying mantises do not always eat the male while mating. It happens sometimes, and it is more often seen in captivity. Termites, often called white ants, are not ants. They are highly specialized cockroaches. Ticks do not jump or fall from trees onto people. They wait on grass and bushes, holding on, until a host passes, and they find it by smell, heat or the carbon dioxide in a breath. Not all earthworms become two worms when cut in half. Only a few species can regrow a head.
What to do about a jellyfish sting

A common piece of advice is to urinate on a jellyfish sting. It is an old tale, and it does not help. Urine may make the pain worse. It can cause the stinging cells that have not yet fired to release more of their venom. The best immediate treatment is to rinse the area with salt water. For some kinds of jellyfish, vinegar helps too.
Another myth about the sea is that the giant clam is a man-eater. According to stories, a diver who puts a foot between its shells will be caught and drowned. The giant clam is not aggressive toward people, and cannot snap a limb. Its shells close very slowly, and some specimens cannot close all the way.
Both stories are about a creature that is thought to be a trap for the unwary. The facts are less dramatic. The sting of a jellyfish is a real hazard, and some, like the box jellyfish, can be deadly, so correct first aid matters. The giant clam is harmless to people. What these cases show is that a good story can last longer than any evidence for it.
Mushrooms are not plants, and other things about plants

Mushrooms, molds and other fungi are not plants. For a long time they were classed with plants, since they stand in one place and have some features in common. But modern genetic evidence shows that fungi are more closely related to animals than they are to plants. They are still often covered in botany classes.
Poinsettias, the red Christmas plants, are said to be deadly poison to children and cats. They are not. They can irritate the skin or the stomach, and if eaten they may cause diarrhea and vomiting, but they rarely cause serious illness.
Sunflowers are said to follow the Sun across the sky. Young plants do this, a movement called heliotropism. Once the plant has flowered, the head stays fixed in one direction, often east, and does not track the sun. A grown sunflower greets the morning sun, which warms it faster, and that may help attract bees. It does not turn through the day, as so many people believe.
What the word theory means in science

When people say, it's only a theory, they mean that it is a guess. In science the word has a different meaning. A scientific theory is a set of principles that explains something in the natural world, and has been tested many times. Evolution is a theory in the same sense as the germ theory of disease or the theory of gravity. A hypothesis is closer to what we mean by a guess.
A second confusion is about what the theory covers. The theory of evolution deals with how living things change over generations after life has begun. It does not try to explain how life itself began. That is the subject of a different field, called abiogenesis. It also does not explain the origin of the universe, which is the business of cosmology and the Big Bang model.
The confusion arises because a word has two meanings, and because the theories are often discussed together. A fact and a theory are not opposites. Facts are observations, and a theory is the explanation that fits them. The theory of evolution would be a better-known idea if the words were used with care.
Survival of the fittest does not mean the strongest

The phrase survival of the fittest suggests a contest of strength, with the biggest and most powerful animal winning. But in biology, fitness has a different meaning. It means reproductive success, how many offspring an individual leaves that themselves survive and reproduce. A small, quiet animal that raises many young can be fitter than a strong one that has few.
Evolution also has no goal. It does not plan to improve an animal. Biologists often speak as if it does, and say that dinosaurs evolved feathers for courtship. That is shorthand. The fuller version is that feathers spread when they gave an advantage to the animals that had them. Students who read the shorthand literally often think that evolution has a purpose.
Nor is evolution a ladder from lower to higher forms, and it does not always lead to more complexity. A population may become simpler. A parasite may lose genes that it no longer needs. Natural selection only makes later generations better suited to their environment than earlier ones. Fitness is always measured against the place and the time where an animal lives.

People often say that humans evolved from chimpanzees. We did not. Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor, which lived about five to eight million years ago. The two lines then went their separate ways, and both have changed since. Chimpanzees are our cousins, and not our ancestors.
A similar mistake is the idea that mammals evolved from the reptiles of today. They did not. The first animals that were fully adapted to land split into two lines, about 320 million years ago, in the Carboniferous period. One line, the synapsids, led to mammals, and the other, the diapsids, led to the lizards, snakes, crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds. The mammals are the only survivors of the synapsid line.
It is also true that humans are animals, though in daily speech we use the word animal as the opposite of human. Biologically we are a kind of ape. The family tree is a branching one, and every living species is at the tip of its own branch.
Are mutations the same everywhere in a genome?

A standard teaching is that mutations are random. It is true that they are random with respect to what the organism needs, since they do not arise because they would help. But they are not equally likely everywhere in the genome. Some regions are more likely to change than others, depending on how well the cell's repair machinery works there, and on other biases in the process.
In a 2022 study of a small plant, Arabidopsis thaliana, researchers found that genes in important regions of the genome were protected from mutation better than other parts. They reported that mutations were biased in a way that benefits the plant, and that beneficial changes were more likely than expected in some places.
The result was a surprise, and it has been debated. Other scientists argued that the pattern might have other explanations, and the claim that mutation is directed to benefit is not accepted by most biologists. What is certain is that mutation rates vary across the genome. The original idea of random change has been refined, and it is still a matter of active research.
The dinosaurs that never went away

The dinosaurs are often given as an example of a species that was too big and too slow to survive. It is not what the evidence shows. The non-bird dinosaurs were widespread and successful for well over a hundred million years, and they were wiped out by a sudden catastrophe, the asteroid impact and its aftermath, about 66 million years ago, and not by being poorly adapted.
Moreover, not all the dinosaurs died. Birds are classified within a group of dinosaurs, the theropods. The question of where birds came from was open for over a century, but there is now a clear consensus that they evolved from small feathered theropods in the Jurassic period. Many lines of dinosaurs ended at the close of the Cretaceous, but one did not.
More than 11,000 species of birds are alive today. When we say that dinosaurs are extinct, we usually mean the non-avian ones. A sparrow at a bird feeder is a dinosaur, in the sense that biologists use. The old textbook picture of a failed group is a good example of how a story can persist after the science has moved on.
Five famous prehistoric animals that were not dinosaurs

Many of the best-known prehistoric animals are not dinosaurs. The mosasaurs, the great sea reptiles, were actually giant lizards. The ichthyosaurs, which looked like dolphins, and the plesiosaurs, with their long necks and flippers, were reptiles that were even more distantly related to the dinosaurs. None of the animals that are known to have been fully marine was a dinosaur, though a few dinosaurs, such as Spinosaurus and the penguins, spent much of their time in water.
The pterosaurs, called pterodactyls in popular speech, were flying reptiles. They were close relatives of the dinosaurs, but a dinosaur is defined as a descendant of the last common ancestor of two groups, and pterosaurs fall outside it.
And Dimetrodon, the animal with the great sail on its back, is often shown with dinosaurs. It died out some 40 million years before the first dinosaurs appeared. It was a synapsid, a member of the line that led to mammals, and it was more closely related to us than to any dinosaur. When you see a toy dinosaur in a set, it is worth asking which of the animals really are.

Humans and the non-bird dinosaurs never lived at the same time. The last of the large dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago in the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous period. The earliest members of our genus, Homo, appeared only about 2.3 to 2.4 million years ago, and our own species much later. Cartoons showing cave people with dinosaurs are fiction.
Many people also believe that oil and gas are made from the bodies of dinosaurs. They are not. Petroleum comes mostly from tiny algae and animals called zooplankton that died and sank to the sea floor, where there was no oxygen to break them down, and were buried. Over millions of years, heat and pressure turned them into oil. Coal comes from plants that were buried and fossilized, mostly in great swamps.
Only a very small part of the world's coal contains fossils of dinosaurs. The idea is so widespread that one oil company once had a dinosaur as its logo. The reality is both less dramatic and more interesting. Most of the fuel that powers the modern world is the remains of microscopic sea life and ancient plants.

The old picture of the dinosaurs was of slow, sluggish reptiles that warmed up in the sun like a modern lizard. That view has changed. How dinosaurs controlled their body temperature is still an active topic of study, but the evidence makes a simple cold-blooded picture hard to accept.
Dinosaurs grew very fast, as shown by the structure of their bones, and growth at that rate needs a lot of energy. Their fossils have been found in polar regions, where winters were cold and dark, and cold-blooded animals would struggle. The pterosaurs had a hair-like covering on their bodies, and it is inferred that they were warm-blooded, since no modern cold-blooded animal has one. Estimates of the body temperature of ichthyosaurs are similar to those of marine mammals in all climates.
The truth is probably more complex than either warm or cold. Different dinosaurs may have had different ways of regulating their temperature, and some may have been in between. Birds, the living dinosaurs, are fully warm-blooded. The question reminds us that a fossil can tell us a lot about how an animal lived, but never the whole story.
The fan that was said to kill sleepers

In South Korea there has long been a belief in fan death, the idea that if you sleep in a closed room with an electric fan running, you will die. The belief has been strongest among older people, and it has been reported in the Korean news for decades, when someone is found dead in a room with a fan on. Explanations given include that the fan uses up the oxygen, cools the body too much, or blows away the air that a sleeper needs.
None of these is true. A fan does not use up oxygen, and it does not make a room airless. Deaths of people found with a fan are explained by other causes, such as heat, a heart problem or another illness, with the fan simply being in the room.
The belief has been fading. By 2019 it was in decline. It is a good example of a folk idea that has an air of plausibility and is passed from one generation to the next. The lesson is to look for the evidence, and to ask how many people have slept happily with fans running without any harm.

Many people think that it is dangerous to wake a sleepwalker. It is not. A sleepwalker who is woken may be confused or disoriented for a short while, but waking does no harm. The risks of sleepwalking come from injury, such as falling down stairs, and from lost sleep. The advice is to guide a sleepwalker gently back to bed.
Another belief is that a person having a seizure can swallow their tongue. That cannot happen, and it is dangerous to try to put anything into the mouth of a person who is convulsing. The recommended action is to lay the person gently on one side, so that the risk of choking is lessened, and to wait until it passes.
The third concerns drowning. Films show a drowning person waving and yelling. In real life drowning is often quiet, and onlookers do not notice. The instinctive drowning response keeps the person from calling out or waving. The arms press on the water to keep the head up, and there is no spare breath for a shout. Most victims show no sign of distress that an onlooker would recognize, so the lesson is to watch children near water closely.
What the movies get wrong about emergencies

In films, a doctor shocks a patient whose heart monitor shows a flat line. It does not work. A flat line, known as asystole, is not a rhythm that responds to a defibrillator. The treatment is high-quality chest compressions and, in a hospital, a drug, epinephrine. Defibrillation is for certain disorders of the heartbeat, but not for a flat line.
Another scene is a person exposed to the vacuum of space, whose body explodes or whose blood boils. It does not happen. In all but the most extreme cases of sudden loss of pressure, the person loses consciousness after the oxygen in the blood is used up, and dies of oxygen starvation within minutes. At altitudes above a level called the Armstrong limit, fluids in the mouth and lungs do boil, but not the body as a whole.
A third is falling into icy water. People think that the cold kills by hypothermia, but it usually takes much longer. The danger in the first minutes is the cold shock response, which can cause a gasp, rapid breathing and a heart attack. The advice that follows is to stay calm and float until the first reaction passes.

Blood in the veins is often said to be blue until it meets the air. It is not. Human blood is always red. The red comes from hemoglobin, a protein that carries oxygen. Blood that has given up its oxygen, in the veins, is a deep dark red. Blood that is rich in oxygen, in the arteries, is a bright cherry red.
The veins under your skin look blue or greenish because of the way light passes through skin. Red light is absorbed more deeply, and blue light is scattered back to the eye, and the brain's way of judging color adds to the effect. Skin changes what you see.
Another reason for the belief is the way that medical diagrams are drawn. By custom, veins are colored blue and arteries red, so that they can be told apart. The picture then comes to seem like the truth. When blood is drawn, the sample in the tube is red. If a person is cut, the blood is red. The idea of blue blood is an illusion of light and of our drawings.
Three numbers about the body that were wrong

The normal body temperature is 37 degrees Celsius, or 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit. That figure comes from a study in 1860. Modern research finds that the average is lower, about 36.4 degrees, or 97.5 degrees Fahrenheit, with small variations through the day and between people.
Another number is that your body has ten times more bacterial cells than human cells. The ratio was an estimate made in 1972. More recent estimates put the ratio at about three to one, and others at about 1.3 to one, so the two are close to equal. The microbes are very small, and they weigh only a small fraction of the body's weight.
A third is that if the capillaries of the body were laid out, they would be 100,000 kilometers long. This comes from a 1929 book by the Danish physiologist August Krogh. He used a model of a person who was larger than real, and a density of capillaries that was too high. The best estimate now is between 9,000 and 19,000 kilometers. Each of the three figures was repeated for decades, because they were in textbooks and nobody checked them.

The advice to wear a hat because you lose half your body heat through your head is not true. Heat is lost in proportion to the amount of skin that is exposed. The head is about seven to nine percent of the body's surface, so it loses about that proportion. Studies of people with the head in cold water showed that they lost only about ten percent more heat overall.
Another belief is that women have one more rib than men, or one fewer. Men and women both have 24 ribs, or 12 pairs. The idea probably comes from the story of Adam and Eve, in which Eve is made from a rib of Adam.
A third is about cleaning the ears. Cotton swabs, the kind sold as Q-tips, are widely used for it. But there is no medical benefit in putting them into the ear canal, and there are risks, such as pushing wax further in, scratching the canal and damaging the eardrum. The ear is self-cleaning, in that wax slowly moves outward. The three ideas are all easy to believe, and none stands up.
The remains that are not ashes

When a person is cremated, the family receives what is called ashes. They are not ashes in the sense of what is left after wood burns. After the body has been through the fire, what remains are dry fragments of bone. They are swept out of the chamber where the cremation takes place, which is called a retort.
The fragments are then put into a machine, called a cremulator, which grinds them into a fine, pale powder. It is, in essence, a high-capacity, high-speed blender. The result is what is given back as cremated remains. The remains of an adult usually weigh several pounds.
The word ashes is used out of habit, and out of a wish to avoid harder words. What we call ashes is really the mineral part of the skeleton, which fire does not destroy, and which has been ground fine. The softer parts of the body are burned away. The fact is not secret, but few people hear it until they have to arrange a cremation, and they are often surprised.
The made-up drug that shares a real chemical's name

Adrenochrome is a real chemical. It is made when adrenaline, the hormone of the fight or flight response, oxidizes, and it has been known to chemists for a long time. It has no use as a recreational drug, and it is not harvested from living people.
The rumors have a literary source. In his 1971 book, Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, the writer Hunter S. Thompson described a fictional drug that he called adrenochrome, which was taken from the adrenal glands of a living person and gave an extreme high. He seemed not to know that a real substance had that name. The substance in the book was made up, and it has nothing to do with the real chemical.
In recent years the invented drug became a part of conspiracy theories that claim that powerful people harvest it from trafficked children. There is no evidence for such claims. It is a clear example of how a work of fiction can become a rumor, as people forget where an idea came from. What circulates is a novelist's invention, mixed up with a real compound.
What does and does not help a cold

The common cold is caused by viruses, and not by being cold. Low temperatures do not make you ill by themselves. But cold may weaken the body's defenses a little, and a person who is infected but without symptoms may start to feel ill after being chilled. Colds are more common in winter, and the reasons include dry air, less ventilation in homes, more time spent indoors, and lower vitamin D levels.
Antibiotics do not cure a cold, because they work on bacteria and not on viruses. The color of what you blow from your nose, which may be clear, yellow or green, does not show whether the cause is a virus or a bacterium. It depends on immune cells fighting the infection.
Vitamin C does not prevent colds or treat them, although taken daily it may shorten them slightly. It has no effect if it is taken after the cold has started. A 2014 review of 24 randomized trials found that echinacea supplements do not prevent colds, and most trials showed no benefit over a placebo. Even the temperature of the water makes no difference when washing your hands. With soap, cold and warm water remove the same amount of germs.
Warts, knuckles and a dry skin

Many children are told that touching a toad gives you warts. It does not. The bumps on a toad are not warts, and warts on human skin are caused by a virus, the human papillomavirus, which infects only humans. A person can catch it from another person, or from a surface, but not from an animal.
Another warning is that cracking your knuckles gives you arthritis. Studies have not found that it causes osteoarthritis. The popping sound comes from gas bubbles in the fluid of the joint. It may annoy others, but it does not seem to harm the joints.
A third idea is about people with eczema. It is thought that bathing dries out the skin and should be avoided. But bathing does not dry out the skin if a moisturizer is applied soon afterward. If it is not, the water that evaporates from the skin can leave it dry. The three examples show how old advice can be reversed by a closer look, and how it can be wrong in a way that is both harmless and widely repeated.
Rumors about tabs, horns and warning labels

Since at least the 1970s a rumor has gone around that collecting the pull tabs from cans of drink will help to pay for dialysis machines for people with kidney disease. It is not true. There has never been such a program in the United States. The National Kidney Foundation, which is usually named in the rumor, has denied it. Dialysis is mainly paid for through Medicare.
Another belief is that powdered rhinoceros horn is used in traditional Chinese medicine as an aphrodisiac. It is not. It has been prescribed for fevers and convulsions, a use that evidence-based medicine does not support. The trade in horn has driven the killing of rhinos, so the myth about its use has real consequences.
A third is about the lists of side effects on the papers in a medicine's box. The frequency stated is how often the effect occurs after taking the drug, and it is not a claim that the drug caused it. What is reported is a correlation, which may or may not be a cause. Some people who take a sugar pill also report headaches. Reading them correctly takes care.
What leprosy is, and is not

Leprosy, now often called Hansen's disease, has a fearful reputation. It is widely thought to make fingers and toes rot and fall off on their own. That is not so. The disease causes rashes and may damage cartilage and nerves. Because nerves are damaged, a person may not feel pain, and so injuries and infections that go untreated can destroy tissue. The disease itself does not cause body parts to drop off.
It is also only mildly contagious. Of the people who are infected with the bacteria that cause it, about 95 percent never develop the disease. It is curable today with antibiotics.
Much of the terror of the word comes from the Bible. A disease of the skin called tzaraath, which makes a person unclean and sends him out of the community, is often identified with leprosy, and may be the source of many myths about it. The Hebrew term may have covered several conditions. For centuries people with leprosy were made outcasts. The reality of the illness is less terrible than the story, and the greater harm was often the stigma.
Three medical legends: rust, rabies and the bubble boy

Rust does not cause tetanus. The bacterium that causes it lives in soil, and it thrives where there is little oxygen. A rusty nail has become a symbol, because rust is a place where oxygen has combined with iron. But any puncture wound can bring in the spores of the bacterium, and it is why a tetanus shot is advised after a deep wound from any object.
Another legend is about rabies shots. People dread a long needle in the stomach. Before the 1980s, the vaccine for rabies did have to be given in the abdomen, but modern vaccines are injected into the muscle of the upper arm, as with other shots.
The third is the bubble boy. People with severe combined immunodeficiency, in which the immune system fails, have been shown in films as living in a sterile bubble. Quarantine was never the standard treatment. The standard is a bone marrow transplant in the first months of life. The case that inspired the idea was David Vetter, who spent most of his life in a sterile enclosure, and did not receive a transplant until the age of 12. He had been born at a time when treatment was less advanced.
Eyes, light and the colors we miss

Reading in dim light does not harm the eyes permanently. It is tiring, and it can cause eye strain, with sore eyes and headaches. But it does not damage the eye, and the strain goes away when you rest. Children who read under the covers with a flashlight need not worry about going blind.
A second belief is that glasses can cure color blindness. They cannot. Color blindness, which is most often inherited, results from a difference in the cone cells of the retina, and it cannot be significantly relieved by glasses or lenses. Some lenses are marketed to the colorblind, but professionals doubt that they work, and they do not give a person the colors they cannot see.
