A third concerns food. There is a broad scientific consensus that the foods from genetically modified crops now on sale pose no greater risk to human health than ordinary foods. This is a matter on which many bodies have given their opinion. Whether other issues about such crops, such as their effects on farming and the environment, are of concern is a separate question, and still discussed.
Natural is not the same as safe

Many people think that something natural must be harmless. Wood smoke, for example, is not a benign sort of pollution because it comes from trees. It is as harmful as other common forms of air pollution, such as diesel fumes. The fine particles in it can get deep into the lungs, and a wood stove in a neighborhood can add to the risk.
The same is true of herbal medicines. They are not necessarily safe or free of side effects. Plants contain powerful chemicals, and some can cause serious harm or react with other medicines. Because they are often sold as supplements, they may not have been tested as carefully as drugs.
And not only heavy metals are toxic. Others, such as beryllium and lithium, can be too. Lithium is used as a medicine, but at a high dose it is dangerous, and doctors check the blood levels of those who take it. Natural origin says nothing about safety. A chemical is what it is, whether it is made by a plant or in a factory, and the dose often makes the difference.
Tin foil is not made of tin

Many people call the thin silver sheets used in kitchens tin foil. It is not made of tin. Aluminum foil replaced tin foil in almost all uses during the twentieth century, though the old name stuck. Tin was expensive, and aluminum is lighter, cheaper and does not impart a taste to food.
The word tin can is also a leftover. Tin cans are not mainly tin now. They are made mostly of steel, with a thin coating, or of aluminum. Tin was used as a protective coat on steel, because it resists rust and is safe with food, and that gave them the name. The tin is now a small fraction.
The same thing happened to the word lead in a pencil. Pencils have never contained the element lead. The core is graphite, which in the past was called black lead. Words keep old meanings after the things have changed. When we talk about tin foil, tin cans and pencil lead, we use names that record how things used to be made.
The deep web is not the dark web

People sometimes use the terms deep web and dark web as if they mean the same thing. They do not. The deep web is simply everything on the internet that ordinary search engines do not index. It includes your private email, your messages, your bank account pages, online databases, and academic libraries. Most of it is quite ordinary.
The dark web is a small part of the deep web. It is made up of sites that can only be reached with special software, and that are built to hide the identity of users and operators. Some of those sites do host illegal markets, but others serve people who want privacy, such as journalists and people living under repressive governments.
So the idea that the deep web is mainly pornography, illegal drugs and stolen bank details is not true. That kind of material is found in a small portion of it. The common picture of an iceberg, with the web above the water and the dark depths below, gives the wrong idea of proportion. Most of what lies beneath the surface is no more sinister than a locked filing cabinet.
Three things in the sky that are not what they seem

The large clouds that rise from the tall, curved towers of power stations are often thought to be smoke or poison. Those towers are cooling towers, and the clouds are water vapor. They give off no smoke or harmful fumes, and no radiation. The vapor does not add to climate change. The tall towers that stand beside nuclear plants are the same.
On a warm summer night, you may see flashes in the sky with no thunder. People call this heat lightning, as if the heat made it. There is no such thing as a separate kind of lightning. What people are seeing is ordinary lightning from storms that are too far away for the thunder to be heard. The flash can be seen across a much greater distance than the rumble can be heard.
The white lines that stay behind airplanes are called contrails. They are made of water vapor and engine exhaust that has frozen into ice crystals in the cold upper air. They are not chemtrails, a name that is given by those who believe they are part of a plot to control the weather or the people below. They are plain condensed water, and whether they last depends on the humidity of the air.
Two things in the atlas that people get wrong

Ask people where the southern tip of Africa is, and many will say the Cape of Good Hope. It is not. The most southerly point of the continent is Cape Agulhas, which lies about 150 kilometers to the east-southeast. The Cape of Good Hope is more famous because of the history of sailing, when ships on the way to Asia had to go around it. The two capes are often mixed up.
Another idea is that rivers flow from north to south, because maps have north at the top and water goes down. Water flows downhill, and the direction depends on the land. Many of the great rivers flow to the north. They include the Nile, the Yenisey, the Ob, the Rhine, the Lena and the Orinoco.
The feeling that north is up and that up means uphill is an effect of how maps are drawn. In fact a map could just as well have south at the top, and some have been made like that. The world has no natural up. It is a reminder that a convention can shape our sense of what is true, when it is a choice made by the mapmaker.
Is there a fixed amount of work to be done?

One idea about jobs is that there is a fixed amount of work to be done in the economy. If a machine does some of it, there is less left for people, and unemployment goes up. Another version is that if some people work shorter hours, there will be work for others. Economists call this the lump of labor fallacy.
The idea has a long history. It was behind the Luddites, English workers who in the early 1800s smashed the machines that they feared would take their jobs. It is still heard in debates about automation and about rules that limit working time. The error is in the assumption that the quantity of work is fixed. In fact the amount of labor needed to produce a given output can change, because of new uses of capital, better efficiency and learning.
When production gets cheaper, people may buy more, or buy new things, and that makes new work. This does not mean that technology never causes hardship. Particular workers and places can lose out, and the change can be painful. What it means is that the total is not a fixed lump, and that the effects of change cannot be read from a simple count of jobs that disappear.

Marie Sklodowska was born in Warsaw and moved to Paris to study, and she went on to a career that nobody has matched. She worked in poverty at first, and in a cold, cramped lab. In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel for their work on radioactivity, a word she coined.
In 1911 she won the Chemistry prize for discovering polonium and radium, which made her the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. In the First World War she helped equip vehicles with X-ray machines, which soldiers called "little Curies," and she drove some of them to the front herself. She died in 1934 of an illness that was almost certainly caused by her years of work with radiation. Her notebooks are still radioactive today.

In 1609 Galileo heard of a Dutch invention and built a better telescope himself, then turned it to the sky. What he saw was astonishing. There were mountains and craters on the Moon, four small moons circling Jupiter and the phases of Venus. All of this was evidence that not everything in the heavens circled the Earth.
He published his findings in 1610 in a short book, and he became famous. But he also became a target. In 1633 the Inquisition forced him to renounce the Sun-centered view, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest. Even then, he kept working, and he wrote one of his best books while confined. Galileo's lasting legacy is the habit of looking and measuring, instead of simply trusting an authority.

For more than a thousand years most people believed that the Sun and planets circled the Earth. It matched what anyone could see, and it was supported by the authority of ancient writers. Copernicus, a Polish astronomer and church official, worked out in detail a system with the Sun at the center.
His book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was printed in 1543, and according to tradition he was handed a copy on his deathbed. The idea wasn't entirely new, since an ancient Greek, Aristarchus, had suggested it, but Copernicus supplied the mathematics. He had waited decades to publish, perhaps from worry about how it would be received. The book started what we now call the Copernican revolution, a change in how we see our place in the universe.

Kepler, a German astronomer, had access to the careful naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe, and spent years trying to fit Mars's orbit to a circle. It wouldn't fit. The error was small, only about eight minutes of arc, but Kepler trusted the data and refused to ignore it.
Eventually he realized the orbit was an ellipse. He published three laws of planetary motion between 1609 and 1619, which Isaac Newton later used to arrive at his theory of gravity. Kepler also wrote an early work of science fiction about a trip to the Moon, called Somnium. It's a nice example of how a scientist can be both rigorous and imaginative, and of how a small discrepancy, honestly respected, can overturn a belief that had stood for two thousand years.

Darwin returned from his five-year voyage on HMS Beagle in 1836 with the beginnings of an idea. For more than twenty years, he gathered evidence and told only a few friends. He was a careful man, and he knew that his theory would be controversial.
In 1858 he received a letter from the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, who had independently come to the same idea. A joint paper was read to the Linnean Society, and Darwin's book On the Origin of Species came out in 1859. The first printing sold out in a day. He spent the rest of his life writing more, including books on orchids, earthworms and human emotion. He is buried in Westminster Abbey, near Isaac Newton.

Wallace was a self-taught naturalist who made a living collecting specimens in the Amazon and in Southeast Asia. He wasn't wealthy or well connected, and he sold beetles and birds to museums and collectors in order to pay for his travels.
In 1858, lying sick with a fever on an island in Indonesia, he thought of natural selection, wrote it up in a few days and sent it to Darwin. Darwin was alarmed to see his own theory, and the two agreed to publish together. Wallace also found that animals on either side of a line through Indonesia are strikingly different, now called Wallace's Line. He was generous about credit all his life, and he even titled one of his books Darwinism. Many consider him the unsung co-discoverer of evolution.

In the 1860s the French chemist Louis Pasteur showed that microbes, not "spontaneous generation," were responsible for fermentation and spoilage. He boiled broth in flasks with long swan-shaped necks, which let in air but trapped dust and germs, and the broth stayed clear.
That supported germ theory, the idea that germs cause disease. He went on to develop vaccines for animals, including chicken cholera and anthrax. In 1885 he gave a boy named Joseph Meister, who'd been bitten by a rabid dog, the first rabies vaccine, and the boy lived. Pasteur also invented a way of heating milk and wine to kill germs, which we still call pasteurization. He's a good reminder that the most useful science often starts with a practical problem.

In the 1860s surgeons in hospitals operated in street clothes and wiped their instruments on their aprons, and many patients died of infection afterward. Many surgeons took pride in their blood-stained coats. Nobody understood why wounds became infected.
The British surgeon Joseph Lister read about Pasteur's work on germs and began to clean wounds and tools with carbolic acid. In 1867 he reported that deaths among his amputation patients fell from about 45 percent to about 15 percent. He also sprayed the operating room with the acid, which later proved unnecessary, but the principle was right. The mouthwash Listerine was named after him, though he had nothing to do with it. Modern surgery depends on the cleanliness that he insisted on.

In 1847 the Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women giving birth in the hospital ward where doctors worked were dying of fever at a much higher rate than in the ward staffed by midwives. He puzzled over the difference, and when a colleague died after being cut during an autopsy, he saw a link.
He realized that doctors were coming straight from autopsies, and he told them to wash their hands in chlorine solution. Deaths fell from about 18 percent to about 2 percent. His colleagues rejected the idea, partly because it implied that doctors were killing their patients, and he ended his life in an asylum. Only after his death did germ theory vindicate him. His story is a lesson in how hard it can be to accept a truth that's uncomfortable.

In the 1790s the English country doctor Edward Jenner heard that milkmaids who'd caught cowpox seemed not to get smallpox. Smallpox killed and disfigured millions, and a way to prevent it would be a great gift. In 1796 he took matter from a cowpox sore and scratched it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps.
Later he exposed the boy to smallpox, and the boy didn't catch it. Jenner would not pass modern standards of research ethics, but his method worked. The word "vaccine" comes from the Latin word for cow, vacca. Smallpox was eventually wiped out worldwide, and the last natural case was in 1977. It is the only human disease so far to have been completely eradicated, and Jenner's experiment started the road to that victory.

Florence Nightingale is remembered as the "Lady with the Lamp," a nurse in the Crimean War, but she was also a brilliant statistician. She gathered data and drew striking charts, including a polar-area diagram, to show that far more soldiers died of disease than of battle wounds.
After sanitary reforms at the hospital at Scutari, the death rate dropped from over 40 percent to about 2 percent. She used her charts to persuade officials and the public, since a picture could succeed where a table of numbers could not. In 1858 she became the first woman elected to the Royal Statistical Society. She spent the rest of her long life as a reformer of nursing and public health, largely working from her bed.

Ada Lovelace was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, and she studied mathematics. Her mother, worried that she would inherit her father's wildness, made sure she had a thorough training in science and numbers.
She translated an article about Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer that was never completed, and added her own notes in 1843. They included a step-by-step method for the machine to calculate Bernoulli numbers, which is regarded as the first computer program. She also saw that such a machine could work with symbols and even music, not just numbers. That vision, of a computer as something more than a calculator, was a century ahead of its time.

In 1936 the young British mathematician Alan Turing described an imaginary machine that could carry out any calculation, a model of what we now call a computer. He was 24, and he made it up to solve a problem in pure logic.
In the Second World War, he worked at Bletchley Park and helped break the German naval Enigma code, work that is thought to have shortened the war. In 1950 he asked whether machines can think, and proposed a test. He was convicted in 1952 for being gay, and the British government pardoned him in 2013. He died in 1954, at the age of 41. The most important prize in computer science, the Turing Award, is named for him.

Grace Hopper was a mathematician who became a rear admiral in the US Navy. In 1952 she created one of the first compilers, a program that translates instructions into machine code, and she argued that programming should be done in words close to English, which led to the language COBOL.
In 1947, when a moth was found stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer, she taped it into the logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found." The term "bug" was already used in engineering, but the story helped make it famous in computing. She was known for handing out short lengths of wire, a nanosecond long, to show how far light travels in a billionth of a second. She was still on active duty in her late seventies.

Katherine Johnson was a mathematician at NASA who worked as a human "computer" at a time when Black women were segregated at the agency. She had been a gifted student, starting college at 15, and she brought exceptional skill to the job.
She calculated the flight path for Alan Shepard's 1961 mission. In 1962, before John Glenn's orbital flight, the astronaut asked for "the girl" to check the computer's numbers by hand, and he wouldn't fly until she had. President Obama gave her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015. She lived to the age of 101. Her story was told in the book and film Hidden Figures, which brought attention to the many women whose work helped put people into space.

The British chemist Rosalind Franklin was an expert in X-ray crystallography. In 1952 she and her student Raymond Gosling produced "Photo 51," a sharp X-ray image of DNA that showed a helical pattern.
Without her knowledge, a colleague showed it to James Watson, and it gave him and Francis Crick crucial information for their 1953 model. She was close to solving the structure herself. She died of ovarian cancer in 1958, at 37, and the Nobel Prize isn't awarded posthumously. Her work before DNA, on coal and viruses, was also important. Today she is widely recognized as one of the key figures in the discovery of the double helix.

Barbara McClintock studied corn, and from the 1940s she noticed that certain genes could move from one place on a chromosome to another, changing the color patterns of the kernels. It was a radical idea, since genes were thought to be fixed in place like beads on a string.
Most scientists didn't believe her, and she stopped publishing about it for years. Decades later, other researchers found similar "jumping genes" in many organisms, including humans. She won the 1983 Nobel Prize in Medicine, alone, at the age of 81. Her story shows the value of patient observation, and the courage to keep believing in what the evidence shows.

In the early 1900s, Henrietta Leavitt worked at Harvard College Observatory as one of the women hired to measure photographs of stars, for low pay. They were called "computers," and they did careful, tedious work that the male astronomers did not want to do.
Studying pulsing stars in the Magellanic Clouds, she noticed that the brighter ones took longer to pulse. That gave astronomers a way of measuring distances to faraway stars and galaxies. Edwin Hubble later used it to show that the Andromeda nebula is a separate galaxy. Leavitt died of cancer in 1921, and a Swedish mathematician who wanted to nominate her for a Nobel Prize learned that she had already died. She is a fine example of an overlooked person whose work changed the way we see the universe.

In 1925 Cecilia Payne, then a graduate student at Harvard, concluded in her PhD thesis that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, not of the same mix as the Earth, as scientists had assumed. It was a startling result, and it went against what everyone thought.
A prominent astronomer, Henry Norris Russell, persuaded her to describe the result as probably not real. Four years later, he reached the same conclusion by other means and published it, giving her credit. The astronomer Otto Struve called her thesis the most brilliant ever in astronomy. She went on to become the first woman to be a full professor at Harvard, and later the head of a department there.

Physicists believed that nature doesn't distinguish left from right. If you looked at an experiment in a mirror, the laws would look the same. In 1956 Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang suggested that it might not hold for the weak nuclear force and needed someone to test it.
Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese-American experimentalist at Columbia, ran a delicate experiment on cobalt-60 at very low temperatures and found that it did break the symmetry. Lee and Yang won the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics, but she did not. Many physicists have said that she should have shared it. She was nicknamed the "First Lady of Physics," and she also worked on the Manhattan Project. Her careful experiment overturned an idea that had seemed beyond question.

In 1905, while working as a patent clerk in Bern, Switzerland, the 26-year-old Albert Einstein published four papers in a single year, now called his miracle year. He had a day job and did his physics in his spare time, with no university position.
The papers explained the photoelectric effect, which showed that light comes in packets. They proved the existence of atoms by explaining Brownian motion, and presented the special theory of relativity. And a short follow-up gave the equation E equals mc squared. Any one of them would have made a career. Ten years later, he completed the general theory of relativity. He became a household name in 1919, after an eclipse expedition confirmed one of its predictions.

In 1900 Max Planck was trying to explain the glow of hot objects, and found that the numbers worked only if energy came in tiny packets, which he called quanta. The old theory predicted that a hot object would give off an infinite amount of energy at short wavelengths, which was plainly wrong.
He thought of the packets as a mathematical trick and was uneasy about it. It took years for physicists, including Einstein, to realize that it described something real, and Planck's constant became a foundation of quantum theory. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics. He was a conservative and modest man, and he said later that he'd been forced into the idea as an act of desperation. It shows that great discoveries can come from people who didn't set out to overturn anything.

In 1913 the Danish physicist Niels Bohr proposed that electrons in atoms can only occupy certain fixed energy levels and give off light when they jump between them. It explained why hydrogen glows in specific colors, something that no earlier model had managed.
He later led the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, and his institute in Copenhagen became a gathering place for the world's best young physicists. During the Second World War, he helped Jewish scientists escape from Nazi-occupied Europe, and he escaped to Sweden himself in 1943, by boat, and then flew to Britain. After the war, he campaigned for open sharing of nuclear knowledge. He is remembered as both a great scientist and a man of principle.

In 1928 the British physicist Paul Dirac wrote down an equation that combined quantum mechanics and special relativity to describe the electron. To his surprise, it had solutions that implied a particle with the electron's mass but opposite charge, which he first thought was the proton.
In 1932 Carl Anderson found just such a particle, the positron, in cosmic rays. It was the first evidence of antimatter, and Dirac shared the 1933 Nobel Prize. Dirac was famously quiet, so much so that his colleagues joked about a unit of speech, a "dirac," meaning one word per hour. His equation was so elegant that he said that it was more important to have beauty in your equations than to have them fit the experiments. It's an unusual view, but in his case, it worked.

In the 1860s the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell wrote down a set of equations that described how electric and magnetic fields behave. He found that they predicted waves that travel at the speed of light, and he concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.
Later, Heinrich Hertz generated such waves, which led to radio. Einstein said that Maxwell's work was the most profound change in physics since Newton. Maxwell also demonstrated the first color photograph, in 1861, and he contributed to the theory of gases and to understanding Saturn's rings. He died at 48, of cancer. Every time you use a phone, a radio or a microwave oven, you are using a prediction he made on paper, 150 years ago.

Michael Faraday left school at 13 to work as a bookbinder's apprentice, and he read the books he bound. One of them, on chemistry, caught his interest, and he attended public lectures by the chemist Humphry Davy and wrote up careful notes.
He became assistant to Davy, and in 1831 he discovered electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field creates an electric current. That's how generators work. He also began the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people in 1825, which are still held every year. He turned down a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society, preferring to stay a plain Mr. Faraday. He had almost no mathematics, but he saw the invisible fields so clearly that Maxwell was able to put them into equations.

Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor who worked briefly for Thomas Edison. He had come to the United States in 1884 with almost no money, and a head full of ideas about electric motors.
He designed a practical alternating-current induction motor, which he patented in 1888, and the American industrialist George Westinghouse bought his patents. In the "war of the currents," Westinghouse and Tesla's alternating current beat Edison's direct current, because AC can be sent over long distances at high voltage. It's how electricity is still distributed today. Tesla had many more ideas, some brilliant and some impractical, and he died in a New York hotel room in 1943, in debt. Today, the unit of magnetic flux density bears his name.

Richard Feynman was a physicist who won the 1965 Nobel Prize for his work on quantum electrodynamics. He was also a gifted teacher, and his lectures on physics, given at Caltech in the early 1960s, are still in print and still admired.
After the Challenger disaster in 1986, he served on the investigating commission. At a televised hearing, he dropped a piece of a rubber O-ring into a glass of ice water and showed that it lost its springiness in the cold, which explained why the seals had failed on the cold launch morning. It took a few seconds and a cup of ice water to make clear what weeks of testimony hadn't. It was typical of his approach, which was to look for the simplest way of seeing the truth.

In 1937, as a master's student, Claude Shannon realized that electrical circuits could carry out logic, laying the foundations for digital computers. Some have called it the most important master's thesis of the century.
In 1948 he published "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," which founded information theory. It showed that any information can be measured in bits and sent through a noisy channel without error, if coded properly. It's behind everything from phone calls to the internet. Shannon was also playful. He rode a unicycle through the halls of Bell Labs while juggling, and built a mechanical mouse that could solve a maze. A man whose work underlies the digital world was, apparently, having a very good time.

John von Neumann was a Hungarian-American mathematician who made major contributions to quantum mechanics, game theory and the design of computers. As a child, he could divide eight-digit numbers in his head, and he'd tell jokes in ancient Greek.
The stored-program architecture used by most computers today, in which instructions and data live in the same memory, is still called the von Neumann architecture. His colleagues, many of them brilliant themselves, often said that he was the fastest mind they ever met. He worked on the Manhattan Project and later on the first hydrogen bomb. He died in 1957, aged 53, of cancer. Many believe that he did more to shape the world of computing than almost anyone else.

In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist at CERN in Switzerland, proposed a system for sharing documents through links over the internet. His boss wrote "vague but exciting" on the proposal. At that time, the internet existed, but it was used mainly by specialists and was hard to navigate.
In 1990 he built the first web browser and server. In 1993 CERN announced that the technology would be free for everyone to use, with no royalties, which is a big reason the web took off. Berners-Lee could have become very rich, but chose not to patent it. The web and the internet are not the same thing. The internet is the network of cables, and the web is one of the things that runs on it.

The Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus created the system that scientists still use to name living things. In his Systema Naturae of 1735 and in Species Plantarum of 1753, he organized plants and animals into groups, and gave each species a two-part Latin name, a genus and a species.
Our own species name, Homo sapiens, means "wise human." Before this, names were long, descriptive phrases, and they differed from one country to another. Linnaeus's tidy system gave naturalists around the world a common language. He also sent his students on voyages to collect specimens, and a number of them died in the process. Today, every newly discovered species is still given a name in the form that he established.

The German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt traveled through Latin America from 1799 to 1804, measuring and collecting at every opportunity. He climbed volcanoes, measured the temperature of ocean currents and collected thousands of plants.
He saw nature as an interconnected web, in which climate, altitude and plants were all linked, long before the word ecology existed. He influenced Charles Darwin, who carried his books on the Beagle, and many others, including the writer Henry David Thoreau. In 1802 he climbed higher on Chimborazo, in Ecuador, than anyone had climbed before. He was probably the most famous scientist in the world in his time, and many places and species carry his name.

Mary Anning grew up poor in the English seaside town of Lyme Regis, where she and her family collected fossils from the cliffs and sold them. Her father died when she was young, and the family depended on what they could find.
Around 1811, when she was about twelve, she and her brother found the skeleton of a giant marine reptile, an ichthyosaur. Later she found the first complete plesiosaur. She was largely uncredited by the scientific community, and as a woman she couldn't join the Geological Society. Even so, scientists traveled to buy her fossils and to ask her advice, and she knew more about the anatomy than many of them. In 2010 the Royal Society included her in a list of the ten British women who most influenced science.

In 1960 Jane Goodall, then 26, went to Gombe in Tanzania to study wild chimpanzees. She had no university degree, and she was accompanied by her mother for the first few months, because the authorities wouldn't allow a young woman to go alone.
She watched one, whom she called David Greybeard, strip leaves from a twig and use it to fish termites out of a mound. It was the first observation of tool-making in animals other than humans. Her mentor Louis Leakey wrote that we must now redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as human. She gave her chimps names and described their personalities, which was unconventional at the time. Her research at Gombe is now the longest-running study of wild chimpanzees.

The American marine biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring in 1962, a book that described how pesticides such as DDT were poisoning birds and the food chain. The title imagines a spring without birdsong.
It was attacked by the chemical industry, but it changed public opinion. It helped lead to the US ban on DDT for agricultural use in 1972 and the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency. She wrote it while being treated for breast cancer, and died in 1964. Carson was also a gifted writer, and her earlier book on the sea, The Sea Around Us, was a best seller. She is a model of how clear writing can move a whole society.

The American agronomist Norman Borlaug spent years in Mexico breeding wheat that was high-yielding and resistant to rust disease. He worked in the field himself, in hard conditions, and crossed thousands of varieties.
In the 1960s his varieties were introduced in India and Pakistan, and yields nearly doubled in a few years, helping to prevent widespread famine. This was a key part of what became known as the Green Revolution. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. Some experts have estimated that his work saved hundreds of millions of lives, though that number is hard to pin down. He kept working into his nineties, and he argued that hunger was a problem that science could solve.

The German chemist Fritz Haber invented a way to make ammonia from nitrogen in the air, which made artificial fertilizer possible and now feeds billions. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it, and it is one of the most consequential inventions of the twentieth century.
But he also led the German chemical weapons program in the First World War, and personally oversaw the first major chlorine gas attack in 1915. His wife Clara, a chemist who opposed his work, took her own life that year. Haber was Jewish by birth, and he was forced to leave Germany in 1933 after the Nazis came to power. His life shows how science can be a source of both great good and great harm, sometimes in the same person.

In 1955 the American physician Jonas Salk announced that his polio vaccine was safe and effective, following a huge trial with 1.8 million children. At the time polio paralyzed and killed thousands every year, and people were jubilant. Church bells rang and factories fell silent.
When the journalist Edward R. Murrow asked who owned the patent, Salk reportedly replied, "Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?" He never earned money from the vaccine. In the US, polio cases dropped from tens of thousands a year to a few thousand by 1957, and to a few hundred in the early 1960s. Salk went on to found the Salk Institute in California, where research continues today.

Hedy Lamarr was a famous film actress in the 1930s and 40s who was also an inventor. She'd fled Austria and her first husband, an arms dealer, and she had picked up some technical knowledge from listening to his conversations.
In 1941 she and the composer George Antheil filed a patent for a system of "frequency hopping," in which a radio signal rapidly changes frequencies in a pattern known to sender and receiver, to prevent enemy jamming of torpedo guidance. It was granted in 1942. The Navy didn't use it at the time. The principle is related to technologies later used in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and GPS, though they were developed independently. She was belatedly honored for her invention in 1997.

In 1977 the Kenyan environmentalist Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement, which paid poor rural women a small amount to plant trees, to restore forests, prevent erosion and provide firewood. She was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate.
Over the decades, the movement planted tens of millions of trees. She was jailed and beaten for her activism, since she also campaigned against corruption and land seizures. In 2004 she won the Nobel Peace Prize, the first African woman to receive it. She said that when she planted a tree, she was planting hope. Her story shows how a simple, practical idea can grow into a movement that changes lives.

In the late 1960s the Chinese government set up a secret project to find a malaria cure, and Tu Youyou led a team that searched ancient Chinese medical texts. Malaria was killing soldiers on both sides in the Vietnam War, and the existing drugs had stopped working.
A recipe for sweet wormwood gave her an idea. The instructions said to soak the plant in cold water, not boil it, and she realized that heat might destroy the active ingredient. The compound she extracted, artemisinin, has saved millions of lives. She won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Medicine. She had no doctorate and no foreign experience, and she was the first Chinese woman to win a Nobel Prize in science. She tested the extract on herself first, to make sure that it was safe.

Ramanujan was a clerk in Madras, India, who taught himself advanced mathematics from a single textbook. In 1913 he sent a letter with pages of formulas to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy, who recognized his genius and brought him to England.
Once when Hardy visited him in the hospital, he mentioned that his taxi had a boring number, 1729. Ramanujan replied that it's the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two different ways. Ramanujan worked out thousands of results, many of them without proofs, and mathematicians are still proving them today. He died in 1920 at age 32. Hardy said that his greatest discovery in mathematics was Ramanujan.

Archimedes of Syracuse was the greatest scientist of the ancient world. He worked out the principle of the lever, found the rule for floating bodies and calculated the area of a circle. He is said to have claimed that, given a place to stand, he could move the Earth.
In the famous story, he stepped into a bath, realized how to measure the volume of a king's crown by the water it displaced, and ran through the streets shouting "Eureka." He was killed in 212 BC when the Romans captured his city. According to one account, he was absorbed in a diagram drawn in the sand when a soldier came upon him. His tomb was marked with a sphere and a cylinder, the result of which he was proudest.

Eratosthenes was the head of the great Library of Alexandria in the 3rd century BC. He'd heard that at noon on midsummer day, the Sun shone straight down a well at Syene in southern Egypt, while in Alexandria, a stick cast a shadow.
From the angle of that shadow and the distance between the two cities, he calculated Earth's circumference. His result was within a few percent of the true value, depending on which unit of length he used. He did it more than two thousand years ago, with a stick, a well and some arithmetic. It's a lasting reminder that educated people knew the Earth was round long before Columbus, and that measuring what's in front of you can reveal what you cannot see.

Hypatia was a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher in Alexandria, Egypt, in the late 4th and early 5th centuries. She taught students from various religions and was widely respected. She was the daughter of a mathematician, Theon, and she edited some of his works.
In 415 she was killed by a mob during a period of political and religious conflict in the city, and her death has been remembered as a symbol of the loss of ancient learning. Very little of her own writing survives, so most of what we know comes from letters by her students and from later accounts. Her story is a reminder of how fragile a tradition of learning can be.

Ibn al-Haytham, known in Europe as Alhazen, worked in Cairo around the year 1000. In his Book of Optics, he proved that we see because light enters the eye, and not because rays leave the eye, as many ancient thinkers believed.
He tested ideas with experiments, used the camera obscura to study light and insisted that claims should be tested. Some historians call him a founder of the scientific method. According to one story, he pretended to be mad in order to escape a promise to control the flooding of the Nile, which he had realized was impossible, and spent years under house arrest. During that time he wrote his greatest book. He's a good example of how much early science came from the Islamic world.

Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi worked in the House of Wisdom in Baghdad in the early 9th century. His book on solving equations, whose title included the word al-jabr, gave us the word algebra.
Another of his books introduced the Hindu-Arabic numerals to the Arab world and, through Latin translations, to Europe. His name, in Latin form, gave us the word algorithm. So two of the most important words in mathematics and computing trace back to one man, who lived more than 1,200 years ago. He also made world maps and helped to calculate the positions of the stars. The House of Wisdom, where he worked, was one of the great centers of learning of its time.

Ibn Sina, known as Avicenna in Europe, was a Persian physician and philosopher. By his early twenties, he had become a well-known doctor, and he is said to have treated a prince of Bukhara.
His Canon of Medicine, completed around 1025, was a huge encyclopedia that described how infectious diseases can spread, recommended quarantine and set out rules for testing drugs. It was translated into Latin and used as a textbook in European universities for about six centuries, into the 1600s. He also wrote on philosophy, and his writings were studied in many countries. His influence on medicine lasted longer than that of nearly any other doctor in history.

The Indian mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata wrote a short, dense book in the year 499. In it he stated that the Earth rotates on its axis, and that this causes the apparent daily motion of the stars, a thousand years before Copernicus.
He also gave a value for pi, 3.1416, which is very accurate, and he explained eclipses as shadows, not as acts of demons. India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after him. He wrote the book when he was only 23, according to his own account. Like many ancient works, it was compressed into short verses to make it easy to memorize. A single, thin volume that held so much was a remarkable achievement.

Leonardo is famous as the painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, but he filled thousands of pages of notebooks with studies of anatomy, water, flight and machines. About 7,000 pages survive, and many were written in mirror image, from right to left.
He drew the valves of the heart and flying machines centuries before others. But he never published his notes, which were scattered after his death, so they had little influence on science at the time. They were rediscovered only much later. If he had published, the history of anatomy and engineering might have been different. His curiosity was endless, and that is perhaps his greatest gift to us.
Vesalius and Harvey: opening the body

For about 1,400 years, doctors relied on the writings of the Roman physician Galen, who'd mostly dissected animals. In 1543 the young Flemish anatomist Andreas Vesalius published De humani corporis fabrica, based on his own dissections of human bodies, and showed that Galen was wrong in many details. The book had magnificent illustrations, and it transformed the teaching of medicine.
In 1628 the English physician William Harvey published a book arguing that blood circulates around the body, pumped by the heart. He had made a simple calculation: the heart pumps out far more blood in an hour than the body could possibly manufacture, so it must be going around in a circle. It contradicted ancient teaching, and many doctors rejected it for years, but he was right.
Hooke and Leeuwenhoek: the first microscopists

In 1665 the English scientist Robert Hooke published Micrographia, a book with spectacular drawings of what he'd seen under his microscope, including a flea and a louse. Looking at a slice of cork, he saw little box-like compartments, which reminded him of monks' cells, and he called them "cells." He was also involved in famous disputes with Isaac Newton over credit for discoveries in optics and gravity.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a cloth merchant in Delft in the Netherlands who ground his own tiny lenses, some magnifying nearly 270 times, better than any microscope of his time. In the 1670s he looked at pond water, and the plaque on his own teeth, and saw swarms of tiny living things, which he called "animalcules." The Royal Society in London doubted him until Robert Hooke confirmed the observations.

Benjamin Franklin was a printer, writer and diplomat, and a serious scientist. He proposed in 1749 that a pointed iron rod could protect buildings from lightning, and the lightning rod was in use by 1752. It was one of the first practical results of the study of electricity.
He also invented bifocal glasses, made one of the first maps of the Gulf Stream and introduced the terms positive and negative for electric charge. His famous kite experiment is probably a mix of fact and legend, since it's not clear that he ever did it as the story is told. He refused to patent his inventions, writing that as we benefit from the inventions of others, we should be glad to serve others by any invention of ours.
Counting in Latin and Greek: uni-, mono-, bi-, tri-

English borrowed its number prefixes from two languages, and once you notice them, you start to see them everywhere. Uni- is Latin for "one." A unicorn has one horn, a uniform is made of one form so that everyone looks alike, and unity is the state of being one. Even "universe" comes from words meaning "turned into one," and "unique" has the same root.
Mono- is the Greek word for "one" or "alone." A monologue is a speech by one person, a monotone stays on one note, and a monopoly is a market with a single seller. Bi- means "two," so a bicycle has two wheels and a bilingual person speaks two languages. Tri- means "three," from both Latin and Greek, which is why we have triangles, tricycles and trilogies. When a word begins with one of these, a number is probably hiding inside it.
Many and all: poly-, multi-, omni-, pan-

Two prefixes mean "many," one from each language. Poly- is Greek, and it gives us polygon, a shape with many angles, and polyglot, someone who speaks many languages. Polytheism is belief in many gods, and a polymath is a person who has learned many things, like Leonardo da Vinci. Multi- is the Latin version, more common in modern words. To multiply is to make many, multimedia mixes text, sound and video, and a multitude is a great crowd.
Two more mean "all." Omni- is Latin, and an omnivore eats all kinds of food. Omnipotent means all-powerful, and the word "omnibus," which means "for all," is where we get "bus." Pan- is the Greek partner. A panorama is a view of everything, a pandemic affects people over a wide area, and the Pantheon in Rome was a temple to all the gods. The pairs work in just the same way, and each language has its own.
Big and small: macro-, micro-, mega-

These three prefixes are all about size, and they're all Greek. Macro- means "large" or "long," and it's used when you look at the big picture. Macroeconomics studies a whole economy, such as national employment and prices. Something macroscopic is big enough to see with the naked eye, and a macrocosm is the large world, in contrast to the small one inside it.
Micro- is its opposite, and it means "small." A microscope lets you see small things, a microbe is a small living thing, and a microchip is a tiny piece of electronics. Microeconomics looks at the choices of individual people and firms. In measurement, micro- stands for a millionth. Mega- comes from the Greek for "great." A megaphone makes your voice great, or loud, and a megabyte is a million bytes. A megalith is a great stone, like the ones at Stonehenge, and megalomania is an obsession with power.
Over and under: hyper-, hypo-, super-, sub-

Two pairs of prefixes mean "over" and "under." In Greek, hyper- means "over" or "too much," and hypo- means "under" or "below." Someone hyperactive is too active. Hypertension is high blood pressure, and something hypersensitive reacts too strongly. Hypothermia is when the body temperature drops below normal, and a hypodermic needle goes under the skin. A hypothesis is something placed under an argument as its foundation.
Latin has its own pair. Super- means "above." To supervise is to look over someone's work, something superior is higher in quality, and the supernatural is above nature. Sub- means "under." A submarine travels under the sea, a subway runs under the street, and to subtract is to draw away from underneath. Sub- often changes its spelling before certain letters, as in "suppose" and "suffer." With these four, you can read the direction of many words.
Between and beyond: inter-, intra-, extra-, ultra-

Four Latin prefixes tell you where something is happening. Inter- means "between" or "among." To interact is to act between each other, international means between nations, and an intermission is a break between two parts of a show. Even the word "internet" is a network between networks. Intra- means "within," and it's the one that's easiest to mix up with inter-. An intravenous drip goes into a vein, and an intranet is a network used only within an organization.
Extra- means "outside" or "beyond." Something extraordinary goes beyond the ordinary, an extraterrestrial comes from beyond Earth, and an extrovert is someone turned outward. Ultra- means "beyond" too. Ultraviolet light lies beyond violet in the spectrum, ultrasound is sound beyond human hearing, and ultramarine was a blue pigment from "beyond the sea." These days, ultra- has become a general word for "extremely." A good way to keep inter- and intra- apart is that "inter" is between, as in "international," and "intra" is inside.
Across and around: trans-, circum-, peri-, para-

Trans- is Latin for "across" or "through." To transport is to carry across, to translate is to carry a meaning across from one language to another, and to transform is to change shape. Something transparent lets light shine through. The prefix is all about crossing from one side to the other, or from one state to another.
Circum- is Latin for "around." The circumference is the distance around a circle, and to circumnavigate is to sail around something, such as the whole world. A circumstance is something that stands around you, and to be circumspect is to look around carefully before acting. Peri- is its Greek partner, with the same meaning. A perimeter is a measure around an area, and a periscope lets you look around obstacles. Para- is Greek for "beside." Parallel lines run alongside each other, and a paramedic works beside the doctor.
Before, after and again: pre-, ante-, post-, re-, retro-

Time has its own prefixes. Pre- means "before," and it's one of the most useful. To predict is to say something before it happens, to prevent is to come before an event and stop it, and prehistoric describes the time before written records. Ante- also means "before," in time or place. An anteroom is a small room before the main room, and antebellum means "before the war." Don't confuse ante- with anti-. Post- means "after." To postpone is to put something off until later, and a postscript, or P.S., is written after the main letter.
Re- means "again" or "back," and you can add it to almost any verb. To return is to turn back, to review is to see again, and to rebuild is to build again. Retro- is Latin for "backward." Retrospect is looking back, and a retroactive law applies to things that happened before it was passed. To retrofit is to add new equipment to something old, and "retro" on its own now means in the style of the past.
For and against: anti-, contra-, pro-

Prefixes can take sides. Anti- is Greek for "against" or "opposite." An antibody is a protein your body makes to fight an invader, an antidote works against a poison, and an antonym is a word that means the opposite of another. Contra- is the Latin version of "against." To contradict is to speak against what someone says, and to contrast is to stand things against each other to show the difference. Contraband is goods brought in against the ban, in other words smuggled.
Pro- has several meanings, from both Latin and Greek: "forward," "in front of" and "in favor of." Progress is a step forward, to promote is to move something forward, and to be proactive is to act ahead of events. A proponent speaks in favor of something. The "in favor of" sense is the opposite of con, as in the old phrase "pros and cons." So the next time you see a word beginning with one of these, ask which side it's on.
Together and both: con-, syn-, ambi-

A few prefixes are about togetherness. Con-, or com- before some letters, is Latin for "with" or "together." To connect is to join together, a community is a group of people together, and a conference brings people together. Its Greek counterpart is syn-, which becomes sym- before certain letters. Synonyms are words that have the same meaning, from "same name." To synchronize is to make things happen at the same time, a symphony is a sounding together, and sympathy is feeling together with another person.
Ambi- is Latin for "both." An ambidextrous person is equally skilled with both hands, though the word literally means "right-handed on both sides." To be ambivalent is to have both feelings at once. Something ambiguous leads in both directions, and so it has more than one meaning. Ambient means "going around," which is why we speak of ambient light or sound, the kind that surrounds you.
Apart, out and toward: dis-, ex-, de-, ab-, ad-

Some Latin prefixes describe the direction of movement. Dis- means "apart," "away" or "not." To disagree is to not agree, to disconnect is to unjoin, and to disperse is to scatter. Ex- means "out" or "from." To exit is to go out, to extract is to draw out, and to exclude is to shut out. With a hyphen, ex- also means "former," as in "ex-president." De- means "down," "away" or "reversal." To descend is to climb down, and to decode is to undo a code.
Ab- means "away from." Something abnormal is away from the norm, to be absent is to be away from a place, and to abduct is to lead someone away by force. Its opposite is ad-, which means "to" or "toward." To adhere is to stick to something, to advance is to move toward, and adjacent means lying next to. Ad- changes to match the next letter, as in "attract," "assist" and "arrive." Together they describe the paths of coming and going.
Good, bad and not: bene-, mal-, dys-, a-, an-

A handful of prefixes carry a verdict. Bene- is Latin for "well" or "good." A benefit is a good result, someone benevolent wishes others well, and a benediction is a good word, a blessing. Its opposite is mal-, which means "bad" or "badly." A malfunction is a bad function, malnutrition is bad nutrition, and malaria comes from Italian words meaning "bad air," from the old belief that the disease came from foul air in swamps, before it was found to be spread by mosquitoes.
Dys- is the Greek counterpart of mal-. It means "bad," "difficult" or "disordered." Dyslexia is difficulty with reading, and a dystopia is a bad place, the opposite of a utopia, a word invented by Thomas More. The Greek prefix a-, or an- before a vowel, means "without" or "not." An atheist is without belief in a god, anonymous means without a name, and anemia literally means "without blood."
Self, half and new: auto-, semi-, neo-

Three small prefixes are easy to use. Auto- comes from the Greek for "self," and it shows up whenever something acts by itself. An automatic machine works on its own, an autobiography is a life written by the person who lived it, and autonomy means governing yourself. An automobile is a vehicle that moves by itself, without a horse. Semi- comes from Latin and means "half." A semicircle is half a circle, a semifinal is the round before the final, and a semiconductor conducts electricity only partly, which is the basis of computer chips.
Neo- comes from the Greek for "new." Neonatal relates to newborn babies, and a neologism is a new word. Even the gas neon takes its name from the same root, since its discoverers called it "the new one" in 1898. If a prefix means "half," "new" or "self," you can usually guess the rest of the word. It's a good habit to try, since the guess is nearly always right.

Doctors use word endings the way mechanics use tools, and four of them are especially useful. The Greek ending -ectomy means "cutting out." An appendectomy is the surgical removal of the appendix, and a tonsillectomy takes out the tonsils. When you see -ectomy, a surgeon is taking something out. The ending -itis means "inflammation." Arthritis is inflammation of the joints, tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils, and bronchitis is inflammation of the airways. It has also become a joke ending, as in "senioritis," a student's lack of motivation near graduation.
The ending -scope comes from a Greek word for "to look at." A microscope is for seeing small things, a telescope for seeing far, and a stethoscope for looking at the chest. A kaleidoscope and even a horoscope, "a look at the hour," follow the pattern. The ending -phobia means "fear." Claustrophobia is the fear of closed spaces, xenophobia is the fear of strangers, and acrophobia is the fear of heights. Phobos was the Greek god of fear.

Some endings build words for you. The Greek ending -ology means "the study of," from "logos," meaning "word" or "reason." Biology is the study of life, geology is the study of the earth, and psychology is the study of the mind. The ending -cracy comes from the Greek "kratos," meaning "rule" or "power." Democracy is rule by the people, aristocracy is rule by the nobles, and bureaucracy is rule by desks, from the French word for a desk.
The English ending -less means "without." To be careless is to be without care, and something endless goes on without end. The Latin ending -ous means "full of": famous, dangerous and glorious are full of fame, danger and glory. Finally, -ify and -ize both turn words into verbs. To purify is to make pure, to simplify is to make simple, to modernize is to make modern, and to realize is to make real. In the US, -ize is the standard spelling, while some other countries use -ise.
Water, earth and sea: aqua, hydr, mar, terr, geo

Many English words about the natural world come from Latin and Greek roots, and the elements are a good place to begin. Aqua is the Latin word for "water." An aquarium is a place for water animals, something aquatic lives in or near water, and an aqueduct is a channel for carrying water, like the great stone ones the Romans built. An aquifer is a layer of rock that holds underground water. The Greek root hydr also means "water." To hydrate is to add water to the body, a hydrant is an outlet where water comes out, and the element hydrogen is named for the water that it makes when it burns.
Mar is Latin for "sea." Something marine belongs to the sea, a submarine travels under it, and a mariner is a sailor. Terr is Latin for "earth" or "land." Terrain is the shape of the ground, a territory is a piece of land, and something terrestrial belongs to the earth. A terrier is a dog that goes into the earth after burrowing animals. Geo is the Greek word for "earth," and geography is earth writing, geology is the study of the earth, and geometry was originally earth measure, from the surveying of land.
Stars, light and heat: astro, luc, photo, therm

Four roots are enough to read much of the vocabulary of light and heat. Astro is Greek for "star." Astronomy is the study of the stars, an asterisk is a little star, the symbol *, and an astronaut is a star sailor. Luc, or lum, is Latin for "light." Something lucid is clear and bright, to illuminate is to throw light on something, and something luminous gives off light. Translucent means letting light through, but not clearly. The word "Lucifer" means light-bringer, and "lunar," relating to the moon, comes from the same family.
Photo is Greek for "light." A photograph is a drawing with light, photosynthesis is how plants put together sugar using light, and a photon is a particle of light. Therm is Greek for "heat." A thermometer measures heat, a thermostat keeps it steady, and hypothermia is a dangerous drop in body heat. A thermos bottle keeps drinks hot or cold. Whenever a word concerns light, or temperature, one of these roots is likely hiding in it.

English has a great many roots for "see," because Latin and Greek each supplied several. Vid, or vis, comes from the Latin videre, and video means "I see." Vision is the power of sight, something evident is clearly seen, and to supervise is to see over, or to oversee. Spect comes from specere, "to look." To inspect is to look into, a spectator looks on, and perspective is a way of looking through. To respect is to look back at someone, to regard them with honor, and to suspect is to look at from below, with doubt.
The Greek roots appear in the sciences. Opt, from the Greek for "eye" or "sight," gives us optic, optician and myopia, which means short sight. The ending -scope, from "to look at," gives us microscope, telescope and periscope. Even the word "television" is a hybrid, built from the Greek tele, "far," and the Latin visio, "sight." It's a pleasing mix, and an example of how English borrows from both languages at once.
Hearing and distance: aud, phon, tele

Three roots can help you with words about sound. Aud comes from the Latin verb audire, "to hear." An audience is a group who listen, audio is sound, and an auditorium is a hall for hearing. Audible means able to be heard, and an audition is a hearing of a performer. Even "audit" comes from it, since early auditors listened as people read out the accounts.
Phon is from the Greek for "sound" or "voice." A telephone carries sound far, a symphony is sounds together, and a microphone makes small sounds bigger. Phonics teaches reading by the sounds of the letters, and the saxophone is named for its inventor, Adolphe Sax, and its sound. Tele, the Greek word for "far," completes the family. The telescope looks far, television sees far, and the telephone sounds far. The prefix keeps coming back in modern words, such as "teleconference" and "telecommute."
Saying and writing: dict, voc, log, graph, scrib

English is full of words about speaking and writing, and they come from five roots. Dict is from the Latin dicere, "to say." To dictate is to say aloud for someone else to write, to predict is to say before, and a verdict is a true saying, the decision of a jury. A dictionary is a book of sayings. Voc comes from vocare, "to call," and vox, "voice." Vocal means of the voice, to invoke is to call upon, and a vocation is a calling. A vocabulary is the collection of words that you can call on.
Log, from the Greek logos, means "word," "reason" or "study." A dialogue is words exchanged between two people, and a prologue is words that come before a story. Graph is Greek for "to write" or "to draw." An autograph is your own writing of your name, a telegram is writing that goes far, and a photograph is light writing. Scrib, or script, is the Latin version. To describe is to write down what something is like, to prescribe is to write before, and a manuscript is handwritten. Between them, these roots cover most of what we do with words.
Knowing and feeling: cogn, psych, sens, path, mem, phil

A good number of roots deal with the inner life. Cogn comes from the Latin cognoscere, "to know." To recognize is to know again, cognitive describes thinking, and incognito means unknown, hiding who you are. It's even related to the English word "know," through an ancestor older than Latin. Psych is Greek for "mind," "soul" or "breath." Psychology is the study of the mind, and a psychiatrist is a healer of the mind. In Greek myth, Psyche was a mortal woman who became the goddess of the soul.
Sens, from the Latin "to feel," gives us sense, sentiment and consent, which is feeling together, or agreeing. Path, from the Greek for "feeling" or "suffering," gives us sympathy, empathy and apathy, a lack of feeling. Mem, from the Latin for "mindful," gives us memory, memorial and memento, a keepsake. Phil is Greek for "to love," and philosophy is the love of wisdom. A bibliophile is a lover of books. These roots remind us that thinking and feeling have always shared the same vocabulary.
Going and coming: ced, gress, ven, migr, mov

A family of roots expresses movement from place to place. Ced, ceed and cess come from the Latin for "to go" or "to yield." To proceed is to go forward, to recede is to go back, and access is a way of going to a place. Only three common English words end in "-ceed": exceed, proceed and succeed. Gress, or grad, means "step." To progress is to step forward, to regress is to step back, and to graduate is to step up a grade. Something gradual happens step by step.
Ven, from "to come," gives us event, which is a coming out, prevent, which is to come before, and convention, a coming together. Migr is "to move from place to place," which gives us migrate, immigrant, who moves into a country, and emigrant, who moves out. Mov, or mot, is "to move." To remove is to move away, emotion is a moving out, since feelings stir us from calm, and a movie is a moving picture. Each root adds its own shade to the idea of travel.
Carrying and leading: port, fer, mit, duc, tract

Five Latin roots describe how things get from one place to another. Port means "to carry." To transport is to carry across, to import is to carry in, to export is to carry out, and something portable can be carried easily. Fer means the same thing. To transfer is to carry across, to refer is to carry back, and a ferry carries people over water. A conifer bears cones, and fertile means able to bear fruit.
Mit, or miss, means "to send." To transmit is to send across, a mission is a task someone is sent to do, and to dismiss is to send away. Duc, or duct, means "to lead." To produce is to lead forth, to reduce is to lead back, and to conduct is to lead with. Education comes from "leading out," drawing out what's in a person. Tract means "to pull." To attract is to pull toward, a tractor pulls, and to distract is to pull your attention apart.
Turning and bending: vert, volv, cycl, flect, plic

Many words about shape and movement come from roots that mean "turn," "roll," "bend" or "fold." Vert, or vers, is Latin for "to turn." To convert is to turn around, to reverse is to turn back, and an introvert is someone turned inward. Volv means "to roll." To revolve is to roll around and back, to evolve is to roll out, to unfold gradually, and a volume was originally a scroll, rolled up. Cycl is the Greek root for "circle" or "wheel." A bicycle has two wheels, a cyclone is a circling storm, and an encyclopedia was once a "circle of learning."
Flect, or flex, means "to bend." To reflect is to bend back, as a mirror does with light, something flexible can bend without breaking, and to deflect is to bend something away. Plic, or ply, is "to fold." To apply is to fold something onto something else, something complicated is folded together, and to reply is to fold back an answer. "Simple" comes from "one fold," and "duplicate" from "two folds." Think of these roots as the moves of a dance.
Taking and touching: cap, tend, pend, tact

Four roots are about the way hands and bodies deal with things. Cap, capt and cept come from the Latin capere, "to take" or "seize." To capture is to take hold of, to accept is to take something to yourself, and a concept is a thing taken together in the mind, an idea. Tend, or tens, means "to stretch." To extend is to stretch out, tension is a pulling tight, and to pretend is to stretch something forward, like a cover. A tent is stretched cloth.
Pend, or pens, means "to hang" or "to weigh." To suspend is to hang something under, a pendulum is a hanging weight, and to depend is to hang from something else. Expensive means weighed out, because money used to be weighed. Tact, or tang, is from the Latin for "to touch." Contact is touching together, something tangible can be touched, and something intact has not been touched, and so is whole. Tact, the skill of handling delicate situations, means a delicate touch.
Breaking and cutting: frag, rupt, cide, sect

Four roots deal with what happens when something is split. Frag, or fract, from the Latin frangere, means "to break." Something fragile is easily broken, a fracture is a break, especially in a bone, and a fraction is a broken piece of a whole number. To refract is to break back, which is what happens to light when it bends as it passes from air into water. Rupt, from rumpere, is also "to break." To erupt is to break out, to interrupt is to break between, and to be bankrupt is to be broken financially.
Cide, or cis, from the Latin for "to kill" or "to cut," gives us homicide, suicide and pesticide, and also incision, a cut, and concise, cut down to the essentials. Even "decide" belongs here, since to decide is to cut off other options. Sect comes from secare, "to cut." A section is a cut part, to dissect is to cut apart, and an insect is a cut-up creature, named for its body, which looks as if it's divided into segments.
Making and building: fac, struct, form, lab, techn

Five roots are about the work of making things. Fac, fact and fect come from the Latin facere, "to make" or "to do." A factory is a place of making, to manufacture was originally to make by hand, and an effect is something made by a cause. A fact was originally a thing done. Struct, from struere, means "to build." A structure is a built thing, to construct is to build together, and to destroy is to unbuild. An instrument is a tool for building.
Form is from the Latin forma, "shape." To transform is to change shape, a uniform has one shape, and a formula was originally a little form, a small pattern or rule. Lab comes from labor, "work." A laboratory is a place of work, to collaborate is to work together, and to elaborate is to work something out in detail. Techn is the Greek root for "art" or "skill." Technique is a way of doing a skill, and technology is the study of crafts and now of machines. To the Greeks, the same word meant both art and craft.
Strength, greatness and balance: fort, magn, equi

Some roots describe qualities. Fort comes from the Latin fortis, "strong." To fortify is to make strong, as with a castle wall, effort is strength put out, and fortitude is inner strength, the courage to endure. To comfort someone is to strengthen them with your presence. Magn comes from magnus, "great." To magnify is to make something appear greater, something magnificent is great in deed or appearance, and magnitude is size, as in the magnitude of an earthquake. Someone magnanimous has a great soul, and is generous.
Equi comes from aequus, "equal" or "even." An equation says that two things are equal, and equilibrium means equal balance, when forces cancel out. An equinox, in spring and fall, is the time when day and night are equal in length, from "equal night." Equity, meaning fairness, is also related. It's pleasing that three roots so basic should give us words for strength, size and fairness, which are things we care about in life as well as in language.
Law, people and rule: jud, dem, arch, liber, cracy

A set of roots from Greek and Latin describes how people govern themselves. Jud, or jus, from the Latin for "law" or "right," gives us judge, a person who speaks the law, and justice. Prejudice is a judgment made before knowing the facts, and a jury is a group sworn to give a lawful verdict. Dem comes from the Greek demos, "the people." Democracy is rule by the people, demographics are statistics about a population, and an epidemic is a disease that comes upon the people. A demagogue is a leader who appeals to the crowd's emotions.
Arch is Greek for "ruler" or "first." A monarchy is rule by one, anarchy is without rule, and archaic means from the first, very old. An architect is a chief builder. Liber is the Latin root for "free." Liberty is the state of being free, to liberate is to set free, and "liberal" first meant generous, free-giving, before the word took on political meanings. The ending -cracy, from the Greek for "power," completes the set, as in democracy and aristocracy.
Family and birth: pater, mater, nat, gen, nov

A few roots describe family and origins. Pater is the Latin word for "father." Paternal means fatherly, and a patriot loves the fatherland, from the Latin for the "country of one's fathers." A patron was a protector, like a father, who looked after his dependents. Mater is "mother." Maternal means motherly, matrimony is the state of marriage, from a word that meant the condition of being a mother, and a matriarch is a woman who rules a family. The words "matter" and "material" are closely related, as if everything were made by a mother.
Nat comes from the Latin "to be born." Something native is born in a place, a nation is people born together in the same land, and prenatal means before birth. Gen means "birth," "kind" or "origin," as in generate, genesis and genre. A gene is a unit of heredity passed from parent to child. Nov is Latin for "new." A novel was once simply something new, which is why the book form got that name. To renovate is to make it new again, and a novice is a beginner.
Belief, trust and thanks: cred, fid, grat

Three roots describe the way that we depend on one another. Cred comes from the Latin credere, "to believe" or "to trust." Credit is trust that you'll pay later, something credible is believable, and a creed is a statement of belief, from the Latin for "I believe." A credential is something that makes people trust you. Fid comes from fides, "faith" or "trust." Fidelity is faithfulness, which is why the motto of the US Marine Corps is "Semper Fidelis." To confide is to trust someone with a secret, and to be confident is to have trust, especially in yourself. The common dog name "Fido" is Latin for "I trust."
Grat comes from gratus, "pleasing" or "thankful." To be grateful is to be full of thanks, gratis means free of charge, given as a favor, and to congratulate is to rejoice together with someone. A gratuity is a tip, a pleasing extra. The Spanish "gracias" and the French "grâce" come from the same root. When you thank someone, you are using a word that began as "pleasing."
Life and death: bio, vit, mort, zoo, anthrop

The biggest subjects have the oldest roots. Bio comes from the Greek word for "life." Biology is the study of life, a biography is the writing of a life, and a biome is a large community of living things, such as a desert or a rainforest. An antibiotic is a medicine "against life," though it is against only the harmful kind. Vit, or viv, is the Latin counterpart. Something vital is of life, something vivid is full of life, and to survive is to live beyond danger. A vitamin was named "vitamine" in 1912, a life amine.
Mort is Latin for "death." Something mortal is subject to death, and immortal is not. A mortgage is a "dead pledge," and a mortuary is a place for the dead. Zoo comes from the Greek for "animal," so zoology is the study of animals, and a zoo is short for "zoological garden." Anthrop is Greek for "human," so anthropology is the study of humans, and a misanthrope is a hater of humankind. Between them, they cover being alive, being human and dying.
Hands, feet and teeth: man, ped, dent, carn, vor

Some roots simply name parts of the body. Man comes from the Latin manus, "hand." A manual is done by hand, a manuscript is handwritten, and to manufacture was to make by hand. To emancipate is to release from the hand, to set free. Ped is from the Latin pes, "foot," and the Greek cousin is pod. A pedal is pushed with the foot, a pedestrian goes on foot, a centipede seems to have a hundred feet, and a podium is a place to stand. A podiatrist is a foot doctor.
Dent comes from the Latin dens, "tooth." A dentist treats the teeth, and a trident is a three-toothed spear. The dandelion is named from the French for "lion's tooth," because of its jagged leaves. Carn is Latin for "flesh." A carnivore is a flesh eater, and carnage is the slaughter of many people. Vor means "to eat," so a herbivore eats plants and voracious means eating greedily. They are everyday roots for everyday words.
Inside the body: cardi, derm, gastr, hem, neuro

Doctors have borrowed most of their words from Greek, and a short list of roots can take you a long way. Cardi means "heart." Cardiac means of the heart, and cardiology is its study. Derm means "skin." Dermatology is the study of the skin, and hypodermic means under the skin. A pachyderm is a thick-skinned animal, like an elephant. Gastr means "stomach," as in gastric juice, and a gastropod is a stomach-foot, such as a snail. Hem, from the Greek for "blood," gives us hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen, and anemia, a shortage of red blood cells.
Neuro means "nerve." A neuron is a nerve cell, and a neurotransmitter carries messages between them. Oste means "bone," so osteoporosis is a condition of weakened bones. Somn is Latin for "sleep." Insomnia is no sleep, and a somnambulist is a sleepwalker. The Roman god of sleep was Somnus, and his Greek counterpart was Hypnos, who gave us "hypnosis." If you meet a word you don't know at the doctor's office, look for one of these.
Breath, god and city: spir, theo, urb

Three roots take us to some larger ideas. Spir, from the Latin for "to breathe," links breath with spirit. To inspire is to breathe into, to fill with an idea. Respiration is breathing again and again, to expire is to breathe out or to breathe one's last, and to conspire is to breathe together, to whisper a plot. The word "spirit" itself is "the breath of life." Theo is the Greek root for "god." Theology is the study of the divine, monotheism is belief in one god, and a theocracy is a state ruled in the name of god.
The word "enthusiasm" began here too, from the Greek for "having the god within." Urb is the Latin root for "city." Something urban is of the city, a suburb is under, or near, the city, and urbane means polished and refined, as city people were once thought to be. A conurbation is a group of cities that have grown together. Urban and rural are opposites, and one of them has been growing for centuries.
Asking, emptiness and truth: quer, vac, ver

Three roots that look unrelated each describe something we all do. Quer, or quis, comes from the Latin for "to ask" or "to seek." A query is a question, to inquire is to ask into something, and a quest is a search. An inquisition is an investigation, and "exquisite" comes from it too, meaning sought out, and so choice. Vac comes from vacare, "empty." Something vacant is empty, a vacuum is an empty space with no air, and to evacuate is to empty out a place. A vacation is a time emptied of work.
Ver is Latin for "true." To verify is to make true, by checking, and veracity is truthfulness. To aver is to declare something to be true. Even the word "very," as in "the very truth," comes from it, by way of an Old French word for true. The three roots make a small story. We ask a question, we find an empty answer, and we look for what's true.
Time and the body: chron, corp

Two roots are about the most basic things we have, time and a body. Chron is from the Greek word for "time." Chronology is the order of events in time, and a chronic illness is one that lasts a long time. To synchronize is to make things happen at the same time.
