The eighth still had old code, which started buying and selling stocks wildly. In 45 minutes the firm lost about $440 million, nearly all of its capital, and it nearly went out of business. In both cases, a small, ordinary mistake did enormous damage.

Many old computer programs stored years as two digits, so that 2000 would look like 1900. It set off a worldwide effort to repair them, which cost hundreds of billions of dollars, and when the new year arrived in 2000, most systems worked. Some people have since said that the problem was exaggerated, but the smooth outcome was the result of a great deal of hard work.
A similar problem looms for systems that count seconds from 1970 in a 32-bit number. It will run out on January 19, 2038, and older systems will need to be fixed. Most modern computers use larger numbers and won't be affected, but there may be old equipment, in factories and other places, that has to be found and updated. The lesson in both cases is that a shortcut taken to save space can come back to cost much more later.

The Therac-25 was a radiation therapy machine used in hospitals in the 1980s. Between 1985 and 1987 it delivered massive overdoses to at least six patients, and at least three of them died. The patients were being treated for cancer, and they were hurt by the very machine that was meant to help them.
The software had a flaw called a race condition, which occurred when an operator typed quickly, and the older hardware safety locks, which would have stopped it, had been removed. The error message was cryptic, and the operators learned to ignore such messages. It's a classic case study in software safety, which engineers study to this day. It teaches that a safety system should not depend on software alone, and that when something goes wrong, it's vital to listen to reports of problems.

On July 17, 1981, two suspended walkways in the lobby of the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City collapsed during a dance, killing 114 people. It was one of the deadliest structural failures in US history, and the hotel was full of people.
The cause was a change to the design that was made during construction, in how the walkway rods were attached, which doubled the load on a critical connection. No one rechecked the calculations. The engineers involved lost their licenses. It's a standard example in engineering ethics classes, because the change looked small and sensible. It shows how important it is to verify every change, and for people who are responsible for a design to take that responsibility seriously.

Traditionally, programmers write rules telling a computer what to do. In machine learning, you show the program many examples and let it find the patterns itself. To make a spam filter, for instance, you show it thousands of spam and non-spam emails. Arthur Samuel used the term in 1959 for a checkers program that got better by playing against itself.
An artificial neural network is made up of layers of simple units, loosely inspired by brain cells, whose connections are adjusted during training. Frank Rosenblatt built an early one, the perceptron, in 1958. A 1986 paper by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams showed how to train deeper networks. In 2012 a network called AlexNet cut the error rate in an image-recognition contest from 26 percent to 15 percent, and launched the modern deep-learning boom.

An overfitted model has memorized its training examples, including their quirks and errors, and so it does badly on new data. It's like a student who memorizes the answers to past exams without understanding the subject, and then fails when the questions change.
The remedy is to test the model on data it has never seen, and to keep the model from being more complicated than it needs to be. The same trap catches people too. If you explain a coincidence by inventing a detailed theory, you may be fitting the noise and not the pattern. The measure of an idea, whether in machine learning or in everyday thinking, is how well it works on cases that you haven't looked at yet.

There are two phases in an AI model's life. Training is the long, expensive process in which it learns from data, which for a large model can take weeks on thousands of specialized chips. Inference is using the finished model, such as when you ask it a question. That takes a fraction of a second.
Most of the cost of running a popular system comes from many people using it, rather than from the one-time training. A useful way to picture it is a person who goes to school for many years, and then uses what they've learned for the rest of their lives. The learning is slow and costly, and the using is quick. A model doesn't normally learn from your conversations once it's been trained, unless its builders choose to train it again.

An AI system learns from its training data, and if that data doesn't represent everyone, it can work much worse for some groups. In 2018 the researchers Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial face-analysis programs in the Gender Shades study.
The error rate was as high as 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women, compared with 0.8 percent for lighter-skinned men. The study led several companies to improve their systems. The problem wasn't malice. The programs had simply been trained on photographs that were mostly of lighter-skinned men. It's a reminder that a computer isn't automatically fair, and that those who build such systems have to test them on the people they'll serve.

A large language model is a program trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next word, again and again, which lets it produce fluent writing, answer questions and carry on a conversation. Most are built on the transformer design introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need." They can be astonishingly capable, but fluent writing isn't the same as accurate writing.
A language model doesn't read letters or whole words. It reads chunks called tokens, and a token is roughly three-quarters of an English word. The model can only consider a certain amount of text at once, known as its context window. It's like the model's working memory. If something falls outside the window, the model can't see it, however important it was earlier in the conversation.

When an AI language model states something false with complete confidence, such as a made-up quotation or a nonexistent book, it's called a hallucination. The reason is that these models produce text that's likely, given their training, rather than text that's been checked against facts.
It's wise to verify any names, numbers, quotes and citations that an AI gives you, particularly when it matters. The false answers often sound as sure and well written as the true ones, which is what makes them hard to catch. A model is a bit like a very well-read person who's always willing to answer, and who sometimes fills in a gap rather than say "I don't know." Builders are working to reduce this, but it hasn't been removed.

In 1950 Alan Turing proposed an "imitation game": if a person chatting by text can't tell whether they're talking to a machine or a human, the machine could be said to think. He thought that this was a more useful question than asking whether a machine really thinks, which he found hard to define.
In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum wrote ELIZA, a very simple program that rephrased what people typed, like a therapist. Some users became convinced that it understood them, an effect now known as the ELIZA effect. Weizenbaum was troubled by it, and spent much of his life warning about the way people project minds onto machines. The lesson still matters. A program that talks like a person need not understand like one.

In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match, the first time a computer beat a reigning champion under tournament conditions. The ancient game of Go was thought to be much harder for computers, because there are so many possible moves. But in 2016 Google DeepMind's AlphaGo beat the top player Lee Sedol four games to one.
A protein's function depends on its three-dimensional shape, which comes from how a chain of amino acids folds, and working it out by experiment can take months or years. Biologists had tried to predict it from the sequence for 50 years. In 2020 DeepMind's AlphaFold matched experimental accuracy for many proteins. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, with David Baker, for this work.

A blockchain is a shared record, kept by many computers, in which new entries are linked to the earlier ones so that no one can quietly change history. It works a bit like a ledger that everybody holds a copy of, so that any attempt to alter one copy would be noticed.
It was invented for Bitcoin, which was described in 2008 by a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto. Nobody knows who that is. Beyond digital currencies, few uses have proved better than an ordinary database, so its broader value is still debated. Supporters point to its resistance to tampering, and critics point to its cost in energy and complexity. It's an interesting idea, and a good example of the need to ask whether a new technology really solves a problem.

A quantum computer uses the strange effects of quantum physics, such as superposition, to tackle certain problems far faster than ordinary computers. It does not simply run all programs faster. It's only useful for particular kinds of problems, such as simulating molecules or breaking certain codes.
In 1994 Peter Shor showed that a large enough quantum computer could break the public-key encryption that protects much of the internet. Today's machines are small and error-prone, and such a computer doesn't exist yet. Researchers are already developing encryption that would resist it, and the US government has chosen standards for it. Whether and when a useful quantum computer arrives is still uncertain, and it's wise to be skeptical of dramatic claims.

The Global Positioning System works by satellites that broadcast signals with the exact time. Your phone listens to several of them and, from the tiny differences in arrival times, works out how far it is from each. To fix its position in three dimensions and to correct its own clock error, it needs signals from at least four satellites.
The system is run by the US Space Force and is free for anyone to use. It depends on very precise atomic clocks on the satellites, and on corrections for the effects of Einstein's relativity, which would otherwise make the clocks drift by kilometers a day. It was first built for the military, and opened for civilian use, and now it helps people to find their way, and times banking systems and power grids.
QR codes and the first barcode

The QR code was invented in 1994 by Masahiro Hara at the Japanese company Denso Wave, to track car parts in factories. It can hold much more than a traditional barcode, and it can be read from any angle. Built-in error correction means that a code can still be read even if up to about 30 percent of it is damaged or covered, which is why a code with a logo in the middle still works.
At 8:01 a.m. on June 26, 1974, at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a cashier scanned the first product with a barcode: a ten-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit chewing gum. The pack is now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Barcodes were slow to catch on, but they went on to change how stores and warehouses track goods. Both inventions were made to solve plain, everyday business problems.

The wireless technology Bluetooth is named for Harald Bluetooth Gormsson, a Danish king who ruled around 960 and is said to have united Denmark and Norway. Engineers who were working on a standard to connect different devices chose the name, first as a code name, because the technology was meant to unite devices. The Bluetooth logo is a combination of the runic letters for H and B, his initials.
You might assume that Wi-Fi stands for "wireless fidelity," but it doesn't. In 1999 the industry group that certifies the technology hired a branding agency, Interbrand, to come up with a catchy name for what was technically called IEEE 802.11. Wi-Fi was chosen because it sounded like "hi-fi." The invented tagline "wireless fidelity" was used for a while, but it was never what the name meant. One name is old and historic, and the other is pure marketing.

The more options you offer, the longer it takes a person to decide. In 1952 William Hick showed that decision time rises with the logarithm of the number of choices. It's a reason to keep menus short, and to group options into categories. A screen with twenty buttons will slow down most users compared with one that shows a few and tucks the rest behind a clear label.
The time it takes to reach a target depends on how far away it is and how big it is. Paul Fitts described the rule in 1954, while studying pilots' movements. It explains why buttons should be large, and why items at the edge or corner of a screen are easy to hit: the cursor can't go past the edge, so you can just fling it there. Good design uses both of these two old findings, and most people never notice.

A dark pattern is a design trick that pushes people into doing something they didn't intend. The designer Harry Brignull coined the term in 2010. Examples include an unsubscribe link hidden in tiny gray type, boxes that are already ticked to add extras to your order, and countdown timers that reset when they reach zero.
Some regulators have begun to treat them as illegal. They work because most of us are busy and don't read everything, and so a company can count on a click that is made out of haste. Once you know the patterns, you can spot them. Look for pre-ticked boxes, for a cancel button that is harder to find than the buy button, and for messages that try to make you feel guilty if you say no.

In 1968 the computer scientist Melvin Conway observed that organizations tend to produce systems that mirror their own communication structure. His example: if four groups work on a compiler, you'll get a compiler with four passes. If departments in a company don't talk to each other, the software they build won't work smoothly together either. To fix the software, you may have to fix the organization.
In 1992 the programmer Ward Cunningham used a financial metaphor to describe the cost of shortcuts in software. Writing a quick fix now is like taking out a loan: you get speed today, but you pay interest later, in the form of code that's harder to change. That can be a smart trade-off if you pay it back soon. If you never do, the interest builds up until it's hard to make any progress.

Donald Knuth wrote in 1974 that "premature optimization is the root of all evil," and it's become a famous warning to programmers. Making code fast before you know where the bottleneck is wastes time and often makes the code harder to read.
But the full quote is more balanced. He said that we should forget about small efficiencies 97 percent of the time, yet not pass up our opportunities in the critical 3 percent. The advice applies well beyond programming. Before you spend a lot of effort improving something, measure first, to find out which part is actually slow, or costly, or in the way. Often the real problem is somewhere other than where you thought.

Programmers have a trick for finding bugs: explain your code, line by line, to a rubber duck on your desk. Saying the problem out loud forces you to state your assumptions, and often you notice the mistake in the middle of the explanation.
The practice was described in the 1999 book The Pragmatic Programmer, and a duck isn't required. A patient colleague or a pet also works. It's a small example of a larger truth. Explaining something to someone else, even a toy, makes you slow down and think clearly, and it shows you the gaps in your understanding. The same trick can help with writing, with decisions and with any puzzle that has you stuck.
The Swiss cheese model and normal accidents

In 1990 the psychologist James Reason proposed picturing the defenses against accidents as slices of Swiss cheese, each with holes. A single hole doesn't lead to disaster, because the next slice blocks it. But sometimes the holes in several layers line up, and a hazard passes straight through. The lesson is to add more layers of defense, and to keep fixing the holes. It's used in aviation, medicine and many other fields.
After the Three Mile Island nuclear accident in 1979, the sociologist Charles Perrow argued in his 1984 book that in systems that are both very complex and tightly coupled, with no slack, some accidents are inevitable. Parts interact in ways that no one expected, and failures spread faster than anyone can respond. Not everyone agrees that this means accidents can't be reduced, but the idea has been very influential.

When something goes wrong, the natural reaction is to ask who was at fault. Engineering teams at companies such as Google and Etsy found that punishing people for mistakes made them hide problems, which made failures worse. Many now hold blameless postmortems, asking "how did our system allow this to happen?" instead of "whose fault was it?"
People report problems earlier, and the system gets safer. The idea is borrowed from aviation and medicine, where safety experts found that the people closest to a mistake are the best source of knowledge about how to prevent the next one. A blameless review doesn't mean that nobody is responsible. It means that the aim is to learn, and to fix the conditions that made the error easy to make.

The rechargeable batteries in phones, laptops and electric cars were developed over several decades. Stanley Whittingham made the first working lithium battery in the 1970s, John Goodenough doubled its voltage in 1980, and Akira Yoshino made a safe, practical version in 1985. Sony began selling them in 1991.
The three shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Goodenough was 97 years old when he received it, the oldest person ever to win a Nobel Prize. Each of the three men solved a different part of the problem, and the result changed the way we live. Without light, powerful batteries, there would be no smartphones, and electric cars would be much less practical.

According to the International Renewable Energy Agency, the average cost of electricity from new utility-scale solar power fell by about 85 percent between 2010 and 2020. A mix of larger production, learning by doing and better manufacturing brought the cost down.
In many places, solar is now among the cheapest sources of new electricity, cheaper than building new coal or gas plants. A famous pattern, called a learning curve, shows that each time that the total amount of solar panels made doubles, the price falls by a fairly steady fraction. It's one of the most encouraging trends in the modern world, since cheap clean power helps both the planet and people's budgets.

The guidance computer that helped land astronauts on the Moon in 1969 had 2,048 words of erasable memory and 36,864 words of fixed memory, about 4 kilobytes of working memory in modern terms. It weighed about 32 kilograms. A modern phone has millions of times more memory.
It was reliable, and it famously handled a series of alarms during the Apollo 11 landing without crashing. The alarms were caused by extra data from a radar, which overloaded the computer, and its software was designed to drop less important tasks and keep the vital ones going. Margaret Hamilton led the team that wrote the software. It's an example of how careful design can do a great deal with very little.

Stuxnet was a computer worm discovered in 2010 and designed to attack industrial equipment. It targeted centrifuges used to enrich uranium at an Iranian nuclear plant, making them spin out of control while showing normal readings to the operators.
It's widely believed to have been created by the United States and Israel, though neither has officially confirmed it. It was the first known digital weapon to cause physical damage. Its discovery showed that software can be used to break machines in the real world, and not only to steal data. Since then, protecting factories, power stations and other critical systems from such attacks has become a serious concern for governments and companies.

The World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines say that adults should aim for 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate activity, such as brisk walking, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening work on two days. But the guidelines also stress that any activity is better than none. If you can't hit the target, doing even a little less still brings most of the benefit, so don't treat it as all or nothing.
The payoff is real. In 2012 researchers pooled data from six large studies covering about 650,000 people. They found that people who got about 150 minutes a week of brisk walking, the recommended minimum, had a life expectancy 3.4 years longer than those who got none. That's an association, not proof of cause, since healthier people may exercise more. But the pattern is strong and consistent across many studies.

The round number didn't come from research. It seems to have started with a Japanese pedometer sold in the mid-1960s, called Manpo-kei, which means "10,000 steps meter." It's often said that the number was chosen partly because the character for 10,000 looks like a person walking.
When researchers looked at actual health data in 2022, they found that the risk of early death fell until about 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day for adults over 60, and 8,000 to 10,000 for younger adults. More is fine, but the gains level off. So if 10,000 feels out of reach, there's no need to feel that you've failed. A smaller number is still very valuable, and the biggest gains come from moving from very little to a moderate amount.

After about age 30, we gradually lose muscle mass, at a rate of roughly 3 to 8 percent per decade, unless we do something about it. The loss is called sarcopenia, and it speeds up in later life, which affects balance, strength and independence. Strength training, such as lifting weights or using resistance bands twice a week, can slow or even reverse it, at any age, and it's linked with a lower risk of early death.
The ache that peaks a day or two after an unfamiliar workout is called delayed-onset muscle soreness. It used to be blamed on lactic acid building up, but lactate clears from muscles within an hour or so of exercise. The soreness is thought to come from tiny tears in muscle fibers and the inflammation that follows. It fades as your body adapts, which is why the same workout hurts less the next time.

Long stretches of unbroken sitting have been linked to health risks. In one 2012 experiment, people who got up for just a couple of minutes of light walking every 20 minutes had lower blood sugar and insulin levels after meals than those who sat the whole time.
How much of sitting's harm is separate from simply not exercising is still debated, and the experiments so far have been small. Either way, getting up often does no harm. A few easy habits can help: stand while on the phone, take a short walk after a meal, or set a timer to remind you to move. You don't need a gym for any of it. The aim is to break up the long, still stretches of the day.
Better sleep: what the evidence supports

For chronic insomnia, the best-supported first treatment isn't a sleeping pill. It's a form of talking therapy called CBT for insomnia, which the American College of Physicians recommended as first-line treatment in 2016. It includes keeping a fixed wake-up time, limiting the time you spend awake in bed, and changing anxious thoughts about sleep. It helps most people, and its benefits last longer than those of sleeping pills.
If you could change just one thing about your sleep habits, a good choice might be to wake at the same time every day, including weekends. It anchors your body clock, which makes it easier to feel sleepy at the right time in the evening. Most sleep experts also recommend a cool bedroom, about 60 to 67 degrees Fahrenheit, since your core body temperature naturally falls as you go to sleep. Comfort varies from person to person, so it's a guide and not a rule.

A drink or two may make it easier to fall asleep, which is why many people use it. But as your body breaks down the alcohol during the night, it disrupts sleep. It reduces REM sleep, the stage when most dreaming occurs, and it fragments the second half of the night.
You may not remember waking, but the sleep is lighter and less restful, and you often feel tired the next day. The effect is larger with more alcohol, and it's stronger in people who aren't used to drinking. If you do have a drink in the evening, it helps to have it a few hours before bed, to give your body time to process it. A "nightcap" is a poor sleep aid, however relaxing it may feel at first.

It's a common worry that the glow from phones and tablets is ruining our sleep. Bright light late in the evening does delay the body clock, and blue-rich light does so a bit more. A 2014 study found that reading on a light-emitting e-reader before bed delayed the release of melatonin.
But the effect of typical screens in real life seems small, and what you're doing on the screen, whether it's exciting or stressful, may matter as much. Doomscrolling is probably worse for sleep than the color of the light. A sensible approach is to dim your screens in the evening, put them away for the last half hour before bed, and keep the bedroom dark. Those habits help, whatever the exact role of blue light turns out to be.

Melatonin is a hormone your brain releases at night to signal that it's dark, and the pills are often taken as sleep aids. But it isn't really a sedative. It works best for shifting the body clock, as with jet lag or for people who go to sleep very late.
Small doses, around 0.5 to 3 milligrams, work as well as large ones, and tests have found that the amounts in supplements vary widely from what's on the label. A 2023 study of gummies found that some contained several times the amount listed. It's sensible to talk with a doctor before giving it to children, since little is known about long-term use. It's a signal for timing, not a knockout drug.

You've probably heard that you should drink eight glasses of water a day. There's no scientific basis for it. It may trace to a 1945 recommendation of about 2.5 liters a day, which also noted that most of that is already in prepared foods.
Needs vary with your size, the weather and how active you are. For most healthy people, thirst is a good guide, and tea, coffee and fruit all count. A simple check is the color of your urine, which should be a pale yellow. Older people feel thirst less, and so may need to drink more deliberately. But for most of us, there's no need to carry a gallon jug around.

Many parents are sure that sugar makes children hyper. But when scientists tested it in controlled trials, giving some children sugar and others a sugar-free placebo without anyone knowing which, there was no effect on behavior. A 1995 review of 23 such studies found nothing, even in children who were said to be sensitive.
In another experiment, parents who were told that their child had had sugar rated the child as more hyperactive, though they hadn't. Expectation shaped what they saw. This doesn't mean that sugar is good for children. It has other well-known downsides, such as tooth decay. But the idea that it makes them wild at a birthday party is more likely to be the effect of the party.

The official recommended minimum for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day, which works out to about 56 grams for a person of 70 kilograms, or 154 pounds. Some experts argue for more, especially for older adults, who absorb protein less efficiently, and for people who lift weights. It's easy to meet from foods like beans, eggs, fish, dairy and meat.
Fiber is the part of plants that your body can't digest, and it's good for your gut and your heart. Experts recommend about 25 grams a day for women and 38 for men, but the average American eats only about 16. Beans, oats, vegetables, fruit and whole grains are good sources. Diets high in fiber are linked with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers. Most people get plenty of protein, but not enough fiber.

In a 2019 study at the US National Institutes of Health, 20 volunteers lived in a research center for a month. For two weeks they ate meals made mostly of ultra-processed foods, and for two weeks, mostly unprocessed foods, with the menus matched for calories, sugar, fat and fiber on offer.
On the ultra-processed diet, they ate about 500 more calories a day, and gained about a kilogram in two weeks. On the unprocessed diet, they lost about a kilogram. They also ate faster on the ultra-processed diet. It was a small study, but a carefully controlled one. It suggests that the way food is made may affect how much we eat, and so it's a reason to eat more food that's close to its natural form.

A pattern of eating rich in vegetables, olive oil, fish, nuts and legumes, with little red meat, has among the best evidence for protecting the heart. The 2013 PREDIMED trial in Spain found that it cut major heart events by about 30 percent.
The paper was retracted in 2018 because of problems with how some participants had been randomized, then reanalyzed and republished with similar results. That kind of correction is how science is supposed to work, and the conclusion held up. The diet isn't exotic or expensive. It's mainly about eating more plants, using olive oil as the main fat, and eating fish more than red meat. The pleasures of sharing meals are part of the tradition.
Breakfast and fasting: what the trials show

"Breakfast is the most important meal of the day" was popularized, in part, by cereal marketing. When researchers reviewed the trials in 2019, they found that eating breakfast didn't help people lose weight, and that those who ate it tended to consume slightly more calories overall. Whether you eat breakfast matters less than what you eat during the day. If you're hungry in the morning, eat. If not, there's no need to force it.
Eating only during a limited window, say eight hours a day, has also become very popular. In a 2022 trial of 139 people with obesity, one group ate within an eight-hour window and another simply counted calories. After a year, there was no difference in weight loss. Time-restricted eating works for people who find it easier, but the best plan is the one that you can stick with.

Vitamin D is essential, and many people take supplements hoping to prevent disease. But in the large VITAL trial, 25,871 healthy adults took 2,000 units a day or a placebo for about five years. There was no reduction in cancer or heart disease. People who are actually deficient do need vitamin D, which a blood test can show, but for everyone else, extra pills don't seem to add protection.
Vitamin C has a long reputation as a cold preventer, popularized by the chemist Linus Pauling. A Cochrane review of dozens of trials found that taking it regularly doesn't prevent colds in most people. It does shorten them slightly, by about 8 percent in adults. The one exception is people under heavy physical stress, such as marathon runners and skiers, among whom it halved the risk.

A multivitamin is a popular daily habit. In 2022 the US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence and concluded that there isn't enough to say whether most vitamin and mineral supplements prevent cancer or heart disease in healthy adults. They haven't been shown to do harm at normal doses, but a balanced diet comes first. Some people, such as pregnant women, do need particular supplements.
Eating fish twice a week is linked with better health, so fish oil capsules seem like a natural idea. But in large trials of healthy people, including VITAL and ASCEND, omega-3 supplements didn't reduce heart attacks or strokes. It may be that the benefit comes from eating fish in place of other foods, or from other nutrients in it. For people with very high triglycerides, a prescription form can help.
Handwashing and colds that aren't from cold

The CDC recommends washing your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, which is about as long as humming "Happy Birthday" twice. Scrub the backs of your hands, between your fingers and under your nails. Soap and friction lift germs from the skin, so they're rinsed away. If you can't wash, an alcohol-based sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol is a good second choice.
Your grandmother may have told you to dry your hair or you'd catch a cold. Colds are caused by viruses, not by chill. But there may be a grain of truth. Cooling of the nose can weaken its defenses against viruses such as rhinovirus, and in winter, people gather indoors, where germs spread. Going out with wet hair doesn't cause an infection by itself, but it may make you more vulnerable if a virus is present.

When enough people in a community are immune, a disease can't spread easily, and even those who can't be vaccinated are protected. This is called herd immunity. For measles, which is extremely contagious, about 95 percent of people need to be immune.
One infected person can pass it on to 12 to 18 unprotected people. That's why even a small fall in vaccination rates can lead to outbreaks. It also explains why babies who are too young for the vaccine, and people with weakened immune systems, depend on the people around them. Vaccination protects the person who gets it, and it also protects the people around them, which is part of what makes it a community effort.

A sunscreen of SPF 30 blocks about 97 percent of the burning UVB rays, and SPF 50 blocks about 98 percent, so the gain beyond 30 is small. In an Australian trial in the 1990s, people told to use sunscreen daily had about half as many new melanomas, the most dangerous skin cancer, as the others, after about ten years of follow-up.
Reapply every two hours and after swimming, as no sunscreen blocks everything. A broad-brimmed hat, a shirt and shade work as well, and they don't wash off. Most of the damage to the skin comes from sun exposure over many years, so it's worth building good habits early. The sun is also the main way our skin makes vitamin D, so the aim is to avoid burns, and not to avoid the sun entirely.

In a large study published in 2013, researchers followed more than 200,000 American adults. Smokers who quit between the ages of 25 and 34 gained about ten years of life compared with those who kept smoking, essentially reaching the life expectancy of those who'd never smoked. Quitting between 35 and 44 gained about nine years, and between 45 and 54, about six.
Even those who quit at 65 gained some years. It's never too late to get something out of quitting. It often takes several tries, and that's normal. Nicotine replacement, medicines and counseling can each improve the chances of success, and a doctor can help to find the right combination. Each attempt teaches you something that can be used next time.

In 2023 the World Health Organization stated that no level of alcohol consumption is entirely safe for health. For years, studies suggested that moderate drinking might protect the heart. But a 2016 analysis found that the apparent benefit mostly disappeared when it was taken into account that the "non-drinkers" in many studies included former drinkers who'd quit because of illness, which made abstainers look unhealthy.
The risks rise with the amount, and they include several cancers, liver disease and accidents. It doesn't mean that one glass of wine is a disaster. It means that no one should take up drinking for their health, and that drinking less is generally better than drinking more. Science on this is still moving, and the best advice is to know the numbers and make your own informed choice.

The "normal" body temperature of 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit came from a huge study of about 25,000 people by the German doctor Carl Wunderlich in the 1850s. Modern measurements find the average is lower, about 97.5 to 97.9, and a 2020 study found that the average in the US has been drifting downward, by about 0.03 degrees Celsius for each decade of birth.
It also varies by time of day and between people. It tends to be lowest in the early morning and highest in the late afternoon. Possible reasons for the drift include less infection and inflammation in modern life. The lesson is that "normal" is a range and not a single number. What matters is how your own temperature compares with your usual, and how you feel.

Blood pressure is written as two numbers, such as 120 over 80. The top number is the pressure in your arteries as the heart beats, and the bottom is the pressure between beats. Normal is below 120 over 80.
High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so the only way to know is to have it measured. It's a major risk factor for heart disease and stroke, and it's treatable. A single reading can be misleading, since pressure rises when you are stressed or have just been hurrying, so doctors look at several. Less salt, more exercise, a healthy weight and, where needed, medicine can bring it down. It's among the most useful numbers to know about your own body.
Three body myths: knuckles, gum and nails

The idea that cracking your knuckles causes arthritis is a persistent myth. The popping sound comes from gas bubbles in the joint fluid. A doctor named Donald Unger cracked the knuckles of his left hand, but not his right, at least twice a day for more than 60 years, to test it. He found no arthritis in either hand, and he received an Ig Nobel Prize in 2009.
You may have heard that swallowed gum stays in your stomach for seven years. That's false. Gum base isn't digested like other food, but the gut moves it along like other indigestible things, such as seeds or fiber, and it passes out within a few days. And it's a classic scary story that hair and nails keep growing after death. They don't. Growth requires the energy supply of living cells. What happens is that skin dries out and pulls back, which exposes more of the nails and the stubble on a face, and makes them look longer.

In cardiopulmonary resuscitation, you push hard and fast on the center of the chest, about 100 to 120 times a minute, to keep blood flowing to the brain. If someone's heart stops, the first few minutes are critical, and what a bystander does can decide whether they live.
The Bee Gees song "Stayin' Alive" has about 103 beats per minute, and in one study, people who practiced to it kept good pace. If you see someone collapse, call emergency services first, and use an automated external defibrillator if there's one nearby. These machines give spoken instructions, and they won't shock someone who doesn't need it. Many communities offer short courses, and learning takes only an afternoon.

A stroke happens when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a vessel bursts. The acronym FAST helps you recognize it: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, and Time to call emergency services. Treatment works best within a few hours.
On average, the brain loses about 1.9 million neurons for each minute that a stroke goes untreated, which is why doctors say "time is brain." If you see any of the signs, don't wait to see if they go away. Note the time that the symptoms began, because it affects which treatments can be used. A call made quickly can mean the difference between full recovery and lasting disability.

The classic picture of a heart attack, crushing chest pain and pain down the left arm, is more typical of men. Women, while they often do have chest discomfort too, are more likely to have other symptoms: unusual tiredness, nausea, shortness of breath, or pain in the jaw, neck or back.
Because the signs can be less obvious, women sometimes delay getting help, and doctors sometimes miss it. Any of these symptoms deserves a call for help. Don't drive yourself if you suspect a heart attack. An ambulance crew can begin treatment on the way. It's one of those areas of medicine where research has long focused on men, and where awareness has been slowly catching up.

In films, drowning looks like a person thrashing and shouting. In reality, it's usually silent. A person in trouble can't call out because they need all their breath just to breathe. Their arms tend to press down on the water, they stay upright, and it can take as little as 20 to 60 seconds.
It's why parents are advised to watch children near water constantly, and not to rely on hearing a splash or a cry. A child who has gone quiet in the water is a reason for alarm. For adults, the signs to look for include a head low in the water, eyes that look glassy, and no kicking. Lifeguards are trained to recognize it, and it's worth knowing for anyone who spends time near water.
Pain is not the same as damage

How much something hurts depends on much more than how badly the body is hurt. The brain decides how to interpret signals from the body, and mood, attention, past experience and the situation all change the result. Soldiers with serious wounds sometimes report little pain, and people with no visible damage can have severe pain.
Both are real. Understanding this can be a helpful part of managing chronic pain. It doesn't mean that the pain is "all in your head," since the pain is produced by the brain and body together, and it feels exactly as bad as it feels. It means that the nervous system can become oversensitive, and that things like gentle movement, good sleep and reassurance can help to turn the volume down.
Time in nature and bright light

In a 2019 survey of nearly 20,000 people in England, those who spent at least 120 minutes a week in green spaces, such as parks and woods, were significantly more likely to report good health and high well-being than people who spent none. There was no benefit with less than that. It didn't matter if the time was in one long visit or several short ones. It's a measure of association, but it fits other research.
Some people become depressed each winter, when the days are short. In 1984 the psychiatrist Norman Rosenthal and his colleagues described the condition, which they called seasonal affective disorder. A common treatment is to sit in front of a special lamp that gives off 10,000 lux of bright light for about 30 minutes in the morning. It has helped many people, and is considered a first-line treatment for the condition.

Probiotics are live bacteria in foods like yogurt or in supplements, and they're marketed for all kinds of health benefits. The evidence is good for a few things, such as preventing diarrhea that's caused by antibiotics.
For general gut health in healthy people, though, results are mixed and depend on the specific strain. Claims on labels often run ahead of what research can support. A strain that helps with one condition may do nothing for another, and the bacteria in a capsule may not survive the stomach. Fermented foods like yogurt, kefir and sauerkraut are inexpensive and can be a pleasant part of a varied diet, though the evidence for their benefits is still being collected.
Small habits: posture, eye breaks and stretching

We're often told to sit up straight to avoid back pain. But reviews of the research haven't found a strong link between slouching and pain. A more useful rule may be that the best posture is the next one: changing position regularly, instead of staying in any one posture for a long time. And for back pain that you already have, staying active generally helps more than resting in bed.
To reduce eye strain from long stretches at a screen, eye doctors suggest the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something at least 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Remembering to blink fully also helps. And holding a stretch for a long time before lifting weights or sprinting has been found in some studies to briefly reduce muscle power. A dynamic warm-up, with light movements like leg swings, is a better way to prepare. The research behind each of these is limited, but all three are sensible.

In the 1970s the developmental psychologist John Flavell noticed that young children are poor at something older children do without effort. A five-year-old who is asked to memorize a list of toys will stare at it for a moment and announce that she is done. An older child studies the list, tests herself and goes back to the items that she keeps missing. In 1979 Flavell gave the skill a name, metacognition, which means knowing about your own knowing.
It has two halves. One is knowledge about how minds work, such as the fact that a long list is harder than a short one, and that you forget things you don't rehearse. The other is control, which means checking how a task is going and changing your approach when it isn't working. Most of us do the first reasonably well and the second badly, and that gap explains a surprising amount of wasted study time.

Two psychologists, Thomas Nelson and Louis Narens, described metacognition as a loop with two parts. Monitoring is the part that watches your own mind and reports back: this passage makes sense, that one doesn't, I know this name, I'm about to lose it. Control is the part that acts on the report, by rereading, slowing down, asking for help or moving on.
The loop works only as well as its monitor. If your sense of what you know is wrong, your control will be wrong too, however hard you work. A student who feels that a chapter is familiar will stop studying it, even though familiarity and knowledge are different things. That's why much of the research on learning is really about how to get a more honest report from the monitor, so that effort goes where it's needed.

Everyone has had the experience of being sure that they know something, like the name of an actor, without being able to produce it. In 1965 Joseph Hart turned this into an experiment. He asked people general-knowledge questions, and when they couldn't answer, he asked them how sure they were that they'd recognize the answer later on a multiple-choice test. Their hunches turned out to be better than chance. People who felt that they knew it were more likely to recognize it.
So the feeling isn't just noise. It's a rough signal that a memory is stored and that it's worth continuing to search, which is why the advice to give up on a tip-of-the-tongue word is half right. The signal can also be fooled, though, since a feeling of knowing can come from the mere familiarity of the question's words. It's a useful hint and a poor guarantee.

Students often decide that they've learned something right after reading it, and that is when the judgment is least accurate. In 1991 Thomas Nelson and John Dunlosky had people study word pairs and then rate how likely they were to remember each one. When the rating was made right after studying, it predicted the later test only weakly. When it was made a few minutes later, it was far more accurate. The gap was large, and it's now known as the delayed-JOL effect, one of the most robust findings in the study of memory monitoring.
The reason is that right after studying, the answer is still sitting in short-term memory, so everything feels known. After a delay, you have to pull it from long-term memory, and you find out what you really have. The practical lesson is simple. Don't judge your learning right away. Wait, then try to recall, and let that attempt tell you what to study next.

In 1982 Arthur Glenberg and his colleagues gave students short passages that contained an obvious contradiction, such as a statement in the middle of a paragraph that said the opposite of an earlier one. Many readers rated the passage as easy to understand and never noticed the problem. They'd been reading the words smoothly and taking the smoothness as a sign of comprehension.
Psychologists call this the illusion of knowing. Fluent reading feels like understanding, and rereading makes the text more fluent, so rereading feels productive even when it adds little. One way out is to put the text away and explain it in your own words, or to ask yourself a question about it that you can't answer without thinking. If you can't do that, you haven't understood it yet, however clear it felt.

In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested students on logic, grammar and humor, and asked them to estimate how they'd done. Those in the bottom quarter scored around the 12th percentile, but on average they thought they'd scored around the 62nd. The top performers were a little modest. The authors argued that skill and the ability to judge skill go together, so the least skilled people can't see their own mistakes.
The idea became famous, and it's often misused as a way to call people stupid. The evidence is more mixed than the legend. Some critics argue that much of the pattern comes from statistics, since anyone who scores very low has more room to overestimate, and that nearly everyone overestimates somewhat. The safe lesson is more modest and more useful. We are all poor judges of our own competence in areas that we know little about, and feedback from outside is the cure.
Calibration: how sure should you be?

A person is well calibrated when their confidence matches their results. If you say that you're 80 percent sure of a hundred different things, you should be right about eighty times. Researchers who tested this in the 1970s and 1980s found that most people are overconfident. When people said that they were 90 percent sure, they were right about 75 percent of the time or less.
The pattern is easy to test on yourself. Write down a prediction with a percentage, such as "I'll finish this by Friday, 70 percent." After a few weeks, look at how often your 70s came true. Weather forecasters are among the few professionals who are well calibrated, because they get daily feedback on exactly this. Most of us never get it, so we never learn that our certainty is a bit too high.

In 2011 Jeffrey Karpicke and Janell Blunt compared two ways of studying a science text. One group read it and then drew detailed concept maps, which is a popular and effortful method. The other group read it and then wrote down everything that they could remember, over and over. A week later, the second group answered more questions correctly, including questions that needed inference, and not only facts.
The students had predicted the opposite. Most thought that concept mapping would work better, because it felt more organized and thorough. Retrieval felt messy and frustrating, so they underrated it. It's a good example of a larger rule in learning: how easy a method feels is a poor guide to how well it works. The struggle of pulling something out of memory is part of what makes it stick.

Robert Bjork, a psychologist at UCLA, coined the term "desirable difficulties" for conditions that make learning feel slower but make it last longer. Spacing out your practice, mixing different kinds of problems, and testing yourself instead of rereading all slow you down at first and cost you some accuracy during practice. They pay back later, in what you can still do weeks afterward.
The catch is that a difficulty is only desirable if you can overcome it. If a task is so hard that you can't make progress, it's just frustrating. Bjork's point is that learners and teachers tend to judge by performance during practice, which rewards the easy conditions. A smooth lesson can produce a lot of quick progress and not much memory, and a bumpy one can do the reverse.

Most students practice one kind of problem at a time: ten of one type, then ten of the next. In 2007 Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor tested a different way. Some students practiced four kinds of geometry problems in blocks, and others practiced the same problems mixed together. During practice, the blocked group did better. A week later, on a test, the mixed group scored 63 percent, and the blocked group scored 20 percent.
Mixing forces you to work out which method a problem needs, which is the skill that the test and real life demand. When problems come in blocks, you can just repeat the last move without thinking. Interleaving feels worse while you're doing it, and the effect has been found in sports, art and math. It's an easy change. Shuffle your flashcards, and mix topics in a study session.

The spacing effect is one of the oldest and most reliable findings in psychology: the same amount of study works better when it's spread over time. In 2008 Nicholas Cepeda and his colleagues tested more than a thousand people, with gaps between study sessions ranging from minutes to months, and with tests at different delays afterward. They found that the best gap depends on how long you need to remember. For a test in a week, a gap of about a day was best. For a test in a year, a gap of three or four weeks was best.
Too short a gap wastes the second session, because the material is still fresh. Too long a gap means you've forgotten it all. A decent rule is to review something when you've begun to forget it but can still dredge it up, which is just what a spaced-repetition schedule does.
Learning styles do not hold up

Many teachers believe that people have a learning style, such as visual, auditory or hands-on, and learn best when teaching matches it. In 2008 four psychologists, led by Harold Pashler, reviewed the research. They looked for experiments that taught people in their preferred style and in another one and compared the results. They found almost none that were well designed, and the few that were didn't support the idea.
People do have preferences, and most enjoy variety. And some content suits a particular form, since you can't learn to read a map without a map or to play a note without hearing it. But the claim that an individual learns better when taught in their favorite style has not been shown. A better approach is to match the method to the material, and to give everyone the benefit of practice, feedback and good examples.

In 1989 Michelene Chi and her colleagues asked students to study worked examples from a physics textbook, and recorded them as they spoke aloud. The students who did best on later problems weren't the ones who read more. They were the ones who stopped to explain each step to themselves: why this formula, what that number means, how this connects to the last page.
Poor students read the same lines and moved on. Researchers call it self-explanation, and its effect has been found in many subjects, from science to math to reading. It works because it forces you to notice gaps. When you can't say why a step follows, you've found something that you'd have missed by reading. A simple habit is to pause after each paragraph and say, in your own words, what it means and why it's true.

In 1978 Norman Slamecka and Peter Graf gave people pairs of words in two ways. In one condition, they were simply told to read the pair, such as "hot, cold." In the other, they were given the first word and the first letter of the second, such as "hot, c," and had to produce the answer themselves. Later, the people who had generated the word remembered it better than the ones who had only read it.
It's now called the generation effect. Working out an answer, even a trivial one, leaves a stronger trace than being handed it. That's why it helps to try a problem before you look at the solution, to predict the ending before reading it, and to write a summary from memory instead of highlighting a page. The effort is the point, and a little struggle is worth more than a smooth read.

If you've ever tutored someone, you may have noticed that you learned a lot yourself. In 2009 Catherine Chase and her colleagues tested the idea with schoolchildren, who were asked to teach a computer character, a virtual student named Betty, about a science topic. The students worked harder for Betty than they did for themselves. They prepared more, they were more careful, and they learned more than students who studied the same material for their own use.
Researchers call it the protégé effect. Teaching makes you organize what you know, find the holes in it and think about how the other person might misunderstand. You don't need a classroom for this. Explaining an idea to a friend, to a rubber duck or to an imaginary audience gives much of the benefit, and a failed explanation is a useful signal about what to study next.

In 1993 Anders Ericsson and two colleagues studied violin students at a music academy in Berlin. They found that the best students didn't just practice more. They spent more of their time on what Ericsson called deliberate practice: working alone, on specific weaknesses, at the edge of their ability, with clear goals and quick feedback. It wasn't much fun, and they could do it for only a few hours a day.
The idea has been very influential, and it's a good picture of what effective practice looks like. Playing through the pieces you already know is pleasant and teaches you little. The useful work is picking out the hardest bars, slowing them down, and repeating them until they work. The same applies to a speech, a sport or a language. A little time spent on what you can't yet do beats a lot of time on what you can.
What the ten thousand hours really said

The "ten thousand hour rule" came from a bestselling book by Malcolm Gladwell in 2008, which took it from the violin study by Ericsson. In that study, the best violinists had accumulated about 10,000 hours of practice by age 20, the good ones about 8,000, and the future music teachers about 4,000. Ericsson later objected that the number was an average and not a magic threshold, and that quality of practice mattered more than the count.
In 2014 Brooke Macnamara and her colleagues combined many studies and found that practice explained about a quarter of the differences in skill in games, around a fifth in music and in sports, and far less in education and in professional fields. So practice matters, but not everything does. Talent, starting age, teaching and luck all play a part, and nobody is guaranteed mastery after 10,000 hours.

In 1981 Michelene Chi and her colleagues gave physics problems to graduate students and to beginners and asked them to sort the problems into groups. The beginners sorted by what the problems looked like: these all have an inclined plane, those all have a spring. The experts sorted by the underlying principle: these are all conservation of energy, those are all about forces.
The experts weren't just faster. They saw different things. What they noticed in a problem was its deep structure, and that told them which tools to use. It's one reason that experience can't simply be replaced by a list of rules. If you want to learn like an expert, practice asking what a problem is really about and not what it looks like, and try grouping examples by the idea behind them.
Comparing cases to learn the principle

In 2003 Dedre Gentner and her colleagues taught business students about negotiation using two short case studies. Some students read the cases separately and wrote about each one. Others were asked to compare the two and write down what they had in common. Later, in a real negotiation exercise, the students who had compared the cases were nearly three times as likely to use the strategy from the cases.
Reading one example teaches you about that example. Comparing two forces you to ask what's the same, which pulls out the principle and makes it portable. The method works for almost anything you want to learn. When you meet a new example of an idea, place it next to the last one, and ask what they share. That's how knowledge moves from one situation to another.

Manu Kapur, a researcher who began his work in Singapore, tested a counterintuitive idea in 2008. Instead of teaching students a concept and then giving them problems, he gave them the problem first, before any instruction, so that they struggled with it and mostly failed. Then he taught the concept. The students who failed first did better on later tests of understanding than those who were taught first.
He called it productive failure. Struggling with a problem seems to prepare you to notice what matters when the explanation comes, because you've felt the problem that the concept solves. The results aren't universal, and it works best when the struggle is guided and the explanation follows. But it's a good reminder that confusion is not always a sign of poor teaching. Sometimes it's the start of understanding.

When you study for a test, the simplest and best-supported technique is to close the book and try to recall what you've read. Henry Roediger and Andrew Butler reviewed the research in 2011 and found that retrieval practice improves long-term memory more than additional study, in laboratory studies and in real classrooms. It works with children and adults, with facts and with ideas.
It works best when you get feedback, so that you can correct what you got wrong. It works even when you fail, as we saw with pretesting. And it works better when the questions need some effort, such as writing a short answer, than when they're simple recognition. The one catch is that it feels harder than rereading, so many people avoid it. A good rule is to spend at least half of your study time on trying to remember, and not on looking again.

In 2014 David Yeager and his colleagues studied what happens when students receive critical feedback on an essay. Seventh graders wrote essays, and their teachers wrote comments in the margins. Some students also received a note that said, "I'm giving you these comments because I have very high expectations and I know that you can reach them." The note was the only difference.
Among Black students, who had often had reason to doubt that critical feedback was fair, about 72 percent revised their essays when they got the note, compared with 17 percent of those who got a bland note. The words didn't make the comments any nicer. They made it clear that the comments were a sign of respect and belief. It's a lesson for anyone who gives feedback. People respond to criticism when they trust that it comes with high expectations and with confidence in them.
Mindset: a good idea with modest effects

Carol Dweck's research on mindset, which she described in her 2006 book, argued that people who believe that ability can grow tend to take on challenges and recover from setbacks better than people who think that ability is fixed. Her early studies with schoolchildren were striking, and the idea spread through schools and companies around the world.
Later work has been more sober. A 2018 analysis by Victoria Sisk and her colleagues combined hundreds of studies and found that the link between mindset and achievement is weak, and that short mindset programs have small effects on average, though they may help students who are struggling. The idea isn't wrong, and it's fine to believe that effort improves ability. But it's not a cure-all, and praising effort doesn't help much if the strategies that you teach don't work.
Making a plan with if and then

Most people who set a goal fail to act on it, not because they've changed their minds, but because they never decide when and where to start. The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer found that a simple change closes much of the gap. Instead of "I'll exercise more," you write, "If it's 7 a.m. on a weekday, then I'll put on my running shoes and go out the door." He called them implementation intentions.
In 2006 Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran combined 94 studies, covering thousands of people, and found that if-then plans had a medium to large effect on reaching goals. The plan works because it hands the decision to the situation. When the cue appears, you don't have to decide or summon willpower. It's easy to try. Pick one goal, choose a clear cue, and write the sentence down.

It feels motivating to picture yourself succeeding, but the psychologist Gabriele Oettingen found that positive fantasies about the future can lower effort. In studies of people trying to lose weight, find jobs or recover from surgery, those who dreamed most vividly of success did worse than those who were more sober about the road ahead.
What worked better was mental contrasting. You imagine the wish, such as passing an exam, and then you picture the main obstacle in your way, such as the temptation to scroll your phone, and then you plan how you'll deal with it. The sequence is sometimes called WOOP, for wish, outcome, obstacle and plan. It gives you the benefit of hope without letting hope stand in for work.
Talking to yourself like a coach

When we're upset, most of us talk to ourselves in the first person: "Why do I keep making this mistake?" In 2014 Ethan Kross and his colleagues found that it helped to change the pronoun. People who prepared for a stressful speech by talking to themselves using their own name or "you," such as "Jacob, you can do this," were less anxious, performed better and looked back on it more calmly.
The explanation is distance. Talking about yourself as another person lets you see your situation more as you would see a friend's, with more calm and less drama. It's a simple, free technique. Next time you're stuck in a loop of worry, try describing the problem in the third person, and ask what advice you'd give someone else who was in the same position.

Thinking about yourself can help or hurt. In 1999 Paul Trapnell and Jennifer Campbell described two kinds of self-focus. Reflection is curiosity about yourself, such as wondering why you react as you do, and what you can learn from it. Rumination is going round the same worries and past mistakes, and it comes with a sense of being stuck and hurt. People who ruminate tend to be more anxious and more depressed, and those who reflect tend to be more open.
The difference lies in the questions. "Why am I such a failure?" invites rumination. "What happened, and what can I do differently next time?" invites reflection. When you notice a loop starting, try changing the question to one that points to action or to a lesson. It doesn't stop the feelings, but it points them somewhere useful.

Does thinking about what you've learned help you to learn it? In 2014 Giada Di Stefano and her colleagues tested the idea in a training program for employees at a tech-support call center run by Wipro in Bangalore, India. Everyone did the same training. One group was asked to spend the last 15 minutes of each day writing down and reflecting on what they'd learned. The others kept practicing instead.
On a final test, the reflection group scored about 23 percent higher than the practice group. The extra practice would have felt more productive, but pausing to put the lessons into words did more. Reflecting makes you consolidate what you did, notice what worked and decide what to do next time. It's a cheap habit, a few minutes at the end of a day, and one of the few that has been shown to pay off in a real workplace. The result comes from a working paper that hasn't yet been repeated independently, so it's best seen as a promising finding.
The mistake of choosing not to notice

In 2005 Petter Johansson and Lars Hall ran an experiment that has been called choice blindness. People were shown pairs of photographs of faces and asked to choose which one was more attractive. After each choice, the experimenter handed over the chosen photograph and asked them to explain why they'd picked it. On a few trials, a magician's trick swapped the photographs, so that people were holding the face that they'd rejected.
Most people didn't notice. And many of them went on to give detailed reasons for a choice that they hadn't made, such as "I like her smile." The result suggests that we often don't know why we do what we do, and that we build the reasons afterward. It's a humbling thing to know about your own explanations. A person's story about their motives can be sincere and still wrong.
We know less about our reasons than we think

In 1977 Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson published a paper whose title gave the game away: "Telling more than we can know." They reviewed experiments in which people were influenced by things they didn't notice, such as the position of an item on a table, and then gave reasons for their choice that had nothing to do with it. Shoppers who picked the pair of stockings on the right side of the display, which most people did, said that they'd chosen on quality.
When people were asked why they'd done something, they didn't look inside and report. They did what an outside observer might do, and offered a plausible theory about themselves. Sometimes it was right and sometimes it wasn't. It's a warning about trusting a first answer when you ask yourself "why did I do that?" You are working out a likely story, and it's worth considering a few other explanations.

Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson have spent decades studying a mistake that nearly everyone makes: we're poor at predicting how we'll feel about future events. They call it the impact bias. We overestimate how happy a win will make us and how miserable a loss will, and we overestimate how long the feeling will last.
In one classic study from 1998, they asked junior professors how they'd feel if they were denied tenure, and checked on those who were. Some time later, the people who had been turned down were about as happy as those who had been promoted. We forget how skillful the mind is at making sense of bad news, and at getting used to good news. It's worth remembering when you're dreading a decision, or when you're sure that something will change your life.

In 1972 the psychologist Daryl Bem proposed an idea that turned common sense upside down. We don't always know our attitudes by looking inside, he said. Often we learn them the way that we learn about other people, by watching what we do and drawing a conclusion. If you notice that you keep going to the gym, you decide you must like exercise. If you see yourself giving money to a charity, you decide you're a generous person.
The theory helps explain why small actions can shift how we see ourselves. A person who volunteers once may start to think of themselves as a volunteer. It's also a nice partner to cognitive dissonance, which explains some of the same findings in a different way. The practical side is that, if you want to see yourself differently, one of the best ways is to act differently first, and let your view catch up.

Metacognition includes a skill that's easy to overlook: noticing that your mind has wandered. Psychologists call it meta-awareness. When you're reading and your eyes keep moving across the page while your mind is on dinner, there's a moment when you realize it. Researchers study this by stopping people at random moments and asking whether they were on task, or by having them press a button whenever they catch themselves drifting.
People vary a lot in how often they catch themselves, and a good deal of reading goes by without anyone noticing that the words aren't going in. Mindfulness training has been found to reduce mind wandering in some studies, and so has the simple habit of asking yourself from time to time, "Where is my mind right now?" That small act of noticing is itself metacognition. You can't steer your attention until you know where it has gone.

Writers know that it's hard to find the mistakes in your own work. In 1993 Meredyth Daneman and Murray Stainton found that people spot fewer errors in a text they wrote themselves than in the same errors planted in somebody else's text. You can read a paragraph five times and still miss a repeated word. One reason is that you know what you meant to say, so your mind fills in the sense even when the page says something else. Your expectation is stronger than the evidence in front of you.
You can fight it with tricks that break the pattern. Read it aloud, since your mouth is less forgiving than your eyes. Read it backward, one sentence at a time. Change the font, print it out, or leave it for a day and come back with fresh eyes. These work because they make the text strange again. The same idea applies to checking math, code and plans. Review them in a different way from the one that you used to create them.
Tired people can't tell how tired they are

Sleep loss has a sneaky effect. It makes us worse at many tasks, and it also seems to make us worse at noticing that we are worse. In a 2003 study led by Hans Van Dongen, healthy adults were limited to four or six hours of sleep a night for two weeks. Their scores on tests of attention kept falling day after day, but their own ratings of how sleepy they felt rose only a little and then leveled off. They had gotten used to being tired and stopped seeing how much it was costing them.
A 1996 review by June Pilcher and Allen Huffcutt found that sleep loss has a large effect on mood and thinking. The lesson for metacognition is humbling. When you've been short of sleep, you can't trust your sense of how well you are doing, and it's better to rely on checklists, double checks and other people's opinions.
Using the outside world as part of your mind

In 2011 Betsy Sparrow and her colleagues reported that when people expected to be able to look something up later, they remembered less of it, but remembered better where to find it. The paper was called "Google effects on memory," and it was widely taken to show that the internet is making us forgetful.
The result has been hard to repeat. When a large team tried to replicate the study in 2018, it didn't get the same effect. Still, the broad idea holds some truth, and it's an old one. Humans have always used notebooks, calendars and other people to store what they don't need to carry in their heads. The metacognitive skill is knowing what you can safely offload, such as a phone number, and what you need to understand yourself.

How can we study what goes on in a person's head? In 1980 Anders Ericsson and Herbert Simon described a method called the think-aloud protocol. You ask a person to say whatever's going through their mind as they solve a problem, without explaining or justifying it. The recordings show where people get stuck, what they notice and which strategies they try.
The method has been used to study chess players, doctors, readers and programmers. It also works as a learning tool. When you talk through a problem out loud, you slow down, you notice your assumptions and you catch mistakes that silent thinking skips over. It's why a friend's question, "What are you thinking?" is often useful. Putting thought into words makes it visible, and what's visible can be checked.

One of the quiet skills in studying is knowing when to stop. Students who stop too soon fail the test, and students who study far past the point of mastery waste time that they could spend on something else. Research by John Dunlosky and others shows that most learners don't stop at the right time, because they use poor signals, such as how familiar the material feels.
A better signal is a test. Try to recall everything without looking, and check the answers. Items that you get right on a delayed test can be set aside for a while, and the ones that you miss go back in the pile. The approach turns a vague feeling of readiness into a simple fact. It also makes studying shorter and more satisfying, since you spend your time on what you don't yet know.

When you press a wrong key, your brain knows before you do. In 1993 William Gehring and his colleagues recorded brain activity from people doing a quick test, and found a distinctive electrical signal that appeared within a tenth of a second after an error, even when the person was not yet aware of making one. It was called the error-related negativity.
The signal seems to come from the brain's performance-monitoring system, which helps you slow down and correct course. People who respond to errors with curiosity, and not with shame, seem to learn more from them. In some studies, a stronger error signal goes with better learning from the mistake. The idea fits nicely with what teachers say. A mistake isn't just a failure. It's a message from your own brain about what to fix.
Thinking about how you think about others

One of the first forms of metacognition is realizing that other people have minds that differ from yours. In 1978 David Premack and Guy Woodruff called this theory of mind, and later researchers found that children develop it around the age of four. In a classic test, a child sees a character hide a toy in one box and leave, then watches the toy be moved to another box. Four-year-olds can say that the character will look in the first box. Three-year-olds say the second.
The same skill underlies every conversation, since you can't explain something well or sense when you've offended someone without a model of what they know and feel. Adults still make errors, such as assuming that others know what we know. That's the curse of knowledge, and it's a reminder that thinking about other minds is a skill that can be practiced all through life.

In 1996 Barak Rosenshine and his colleagues reviewed 26 studies in which students were taught to ask themselves questions as they read. The students might be told to ask, "Who is the main character?" or "Why did this happen?" or "How does this connect to what I already know?" They found that learners who generated their own questions understood and remembered more than those who simply read.
The questions work as a monitor. If you can't answer one, you've found a gap, and if you can, you've practiced retrieval. The most helpful questions begin with why and how, and not with what, because they push you to connect ideas. A simple routine is to turn each heading of a chapter into a question, read to find the answer, and then say it aloud without looking.
Keeping a record of your own learning

Barry Zimmerman, a psychologist who studied self-regulated learning for decades, described good learners as running a cycle. Before a task, they set a goal and make a plan. During it, they watch their own progress. Afterward, they judge how it went and decide what to change. This cycle of forethought, performance and reflection runs through everything from homework to athletic training.
The learners who do this tend to do better, and the cycle can be taught. A simple version is a notebook. Before you study, write down what you plan to do and how you'll know you've succeeded. After, note what worked and what didn't. Looking back over a few weeks, you can see patterns that you'd never notice day by day, such as which times of day you concentrate, and which methods actually help you.

When one person finishes a sentence and another begins, the pause between them is astonishingly short. In 2009 Tanya Stivers and a large international team recorded everyday conversations in ten languages, from Danish to Japanese to one spoken in Papua New Guinea, and measured the gaps. In every language, the typical gap was around 200 milliseconds, about the time it takes to blink. Japanese speakers were the quickest, with only a few milliseconds between turns, and the slower languages were still only a few hundred.
That's faster than the brain can produce a sentence from scratch, which takes about half a second or more. So we must be planning our reply while the other person is still speaking, predicting where they'll finish and getting ready to jump in.
