The study suggests that praise for talent can make children fear failure. Praise for effort and strategy helps them to keep trying.

For more than thirty years, Edwin Locke and Gary Latham studied what kinds of goals lead to better performance, in hundreds of experiments in labs and workplaces. Their finding was simple. Specific and difficult goals lead to better performance than easy goals or vague ones such as "do your best."
The reasons are that a clear goal directs attention, increases effort and persistence, and makes you think of strategies. There are conditions. People need to accept the goal, and receive feedback on their progress, and have the ability and resources to reach it. Overly hard goals set for a complex new task may backfire, because people focus on the outcome and don't learn. A good goal is specific, challenging and within reach.

In the early 1970s, researchers in Dunedin, New Zealand, began to follow more than 1,000 children born in a single year. In 2011 Terrie Moffitt and her colleagues reported on what had happened to them by age 32. They'd measured the children's self-control in childhood using tests and reports from parents, teachers and the children themselves.
Children with lower self-control were more likely, as adults, to have poor health, to have money problems and to have a criminal record. The link held after the researchers took account of intelligence and family background. And among siblings in the same family, the one with better self-control did better. Self-control is a skill that can be taught and strengthened. It's one of the most useful things a child can learn.
The willpower battery that did not charge

In 1998 Roy Baumeister and his colleagues brought hungry students into a room that smelled of fresh-baked cookies. Some were allowed to eat the cookies, and others had to eat radishes instead. Then they were given a puzzle that was impossible to solve. The radish eaters gave up sooner. The researchers proposed that self-control is like a muscle that tires, and called it ego depletion.
The idea became hugely influential, with hundreds of studies. But when 23 laboratories ran the same experiment in 2016, led by Martin Hagger, with more than 2,000 participants, the overall effect was close to zero. The theory is now widely doubted, at least in its simple form. Feeling tired of effort is real, but it may be more about motivation and attention than about a store of willpower that runs out.

In the 1920s Bluma Zeigarnik, a student in Berlin, noticed that waiters could remember complicated orders while they were unpaid, and forgot them after paying. She proposed that unfinished tasks stay active in memory. Her results have been mixed in later studies, but the experience of unfinished business nagging at us is familiar.
In 2011 E. J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister had people think about a goal that they hadn't finished, such as an important exam. Their minds kept returning to it during another task, and it hurt their performance. But when they made a specific plan, writing down what they'd do and when, the nagging stopped, though the task was still unfinished. It suggests that the mind needs a plan more than completion. Write down the next step, and you can put the task out of your head.

In 2007 Piers Steel combined the results of hundreds of studies of procrastination. He found that people put things off when the task is unpleasant, when they're impulsive and easily distracted, when they doubt their ability, and when the reward is far away. He summed it up in an equation: motivation rises with confidence and the value of the reward, and falls with delay and with how easily you are distracted.
Later work, including by Timothy Pychyl and Fuschia Sirois, suggests that procrastination is really about managing mood. We avoid the task because it brings up unpleasant feelings, and delay offers short-term relief. This suggests making the task less aversive by starting with the easiest part, setting a short timer, and forgiving yourself when you slip, since self-blame tends to make it worse.

In 2002 Dan Ariely and Klaus Wertenbroch asked three classes of students at MIT to turn in three papers. One class could choose their own deadlines, and the second had deadlines set for them at evenly spaced dates. The third could turn the work in at any time before the end of the term.
Students who set deadlines for themselves spread them out, which showed that they knew they'd put things off. They did better than the class that had only a final deadline. But the class with deadlines set by the teacher did best of all, with the highest grades. The study shows that precommitment helps, and it also shows that we're not very good at setting deadlines strict enough for ourselves. An outside deadline is a gift.
Choosing for now and for later

In 1999 Daniel Read, George Loewenstein and Shobana Kalyanaraman asked people to choose movies to rent. Some chose three movies to watch over the next few days, one at a time, and others picked all three at once, for three different times. When the choices were made all together, people chose more highbrow films, such as foreign films and historical dramas. When they chose one at a time for tonight, they went for light comedies and action films.
The result shows our tendency to make plans for our future selves that our present selves don't follow. We choose healthy and cultured for next week, and easy and fun for tonight. A good approach is to plan ahead, when you're thinking about the long term, and make it easy to follow through. Prepare meals on Sunday so that on Wednesday night, the right choice is the convenient one.

In 2011 Shai Danziger and his colleagues analyzed more than 1,000 decisions by Israeli parole judges. They found that the proportion of rulings in favor of prisoners started high, at about 65 percent, at the start of each session, and fell to nearly zero just before a break. After the break for food, it jumped back up. The paper became a famous example of how tired and hungry decision makers become harsher.
The study has been criticized. Other researchers pointed out that the order of cases wasn't random, since prisoners without lawyers were scheduled at the end of each session, and that these cases are less likely to succeed. Later analyses suggest that the effect is much smaller than reported, if it exists. The finding is a good reminder that vivid results need to be checked. It's still a sound idea to schedule hard decisions when you're fresh and fed.

In 2014 Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz at Stanford tested whether walking affects creative thinking. People did a test in which they had to think of as many unusual uses as possible for common objects, such as a button. They did it while sitting, and while walking on a treadmill, or while being pushed in a wheelchair around campus, and indoors and outside.
Walking, either on the treadmill or outside, boosted creative output compared with sitting, by an average of about 60 percent in the test. The effect was on the flow of new ideas, and it lingered a little after the walk. It was less helpful for tasks needing a single correct answer. Many writers and thinkers have said that they do their best thinking while walking, and now there's some evidence for it.
The benefit of letting it rest

When you're stuck on a problem, is it better to keep working or take a break? In 2009 Ut Na Sio and Thomas Ormerod combined the results of 117 experiments on what's called incubation, in which people put a problem aside for a time. They found a clear benefit: those who took a break did better, mostly on creative, open-ended problems.
The effect was larger when people had spent longer working on the problem before the break, and when the mind was occupied with an undemanding activity during it, such as a simple task, and smaller when people did nothing or did something hard. The explanation may be that the mind goes on working in the background, or that a break lets you drop a wrong approach. Taking a walk, or washing dishes, may be a good way to solve a stubborn problem.

In 2014 Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman at the University of Central Lancashire asked people to do something very dull: copy numbers from a phone book. Others skipped the dull task. Then everyone did a creative test, in which they had to come up with as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups.
The people who'd done the boring task came up with more, and more creative, ideas. The researchers suggested that boredom makes the mind wander and search for stimulation, which leads to daydreaming and new associations. It's a small study, but it fits other work. It suggests that constant entertainment from a phone, filling every gap, may crowd out the quiet that creative thoughts come from.

In studies of office workers, Gloria Mark found that people are interrupted or switch tasks about every three minutes. In one analysis, it took on average about 23 minutes to return to the original task after an interruption, though people often did other work in between. The figure is quoted widely, though it comes from observation of specific workplaces.
Even a small interruption has a cost. In 2015 Cary Stothart and his colleagues found that when people's phones simply buzzed with a notification during a task, without being picked up, they made more mistakes than people who weren't notified. Hearing the alert was enough to scatter attention. If you need to concentrate, silence your phone, and let it wait.
Easy to remember, so it must be common

Are there more English words that start with the letter K, or words that have K as their third letter? In 1973 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman asked people that question, and most said that more words start with K. In fact, there are about twice as many words with K in third place, such as "ask," "make" and "like."
We find words that start with a letter easier to recall than words with the letter in the middle, and so we judge them to be more common. The researchers called it the availability heuristic: we estimate how frequent something is by how easily examples come to mind. It's usually a good shortcut, but it's thrown off by whatever is vivid, recent or dramatic. A plane crash on the news makes flying seem riskier than the many quiet days of safe flights.
After September 11, the roads were deadlier

After the attacks of September 11, 2001, many Americans were afraid to fly, and drove instead. The psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer wondered what that did to the death toll. He compared the number of people who died in road accidents in the year after the attacks with what would have been expected from previous years, and estimated that there were about 1,500 more deaths than usual.
The people who drove had avoided a vivid risk, and had taken on a more dangerous but less visible one. Gigerenzer called it dread risk: we fear events that are sudden and catastrophic and kill many people at once, and underrate the same number of deaths when spread out over time and place. It's a sobering example of how a bias in how we judge risk can cost lives. Driving is, mile for mile, far more dangerous than flying.
The cab that was seen at night

In a famous problem, a cab was involved in a hit-and-run at night. In the city, 85 percent of the cabs are green and 15 percent are blue. A witness says that the cab was blue. Tests show that the witness is right 80 percent of the time in identifying the colors. What's the probability that the cab was blue?
Most people say 80 percent. The correct answer is about 41 percent. Because green cabs are so much more common, many of the witness's "blue" reports will be mistakes about green cabs. The error is called base rate neglect: we pay attention to the specific evidence and ignore how common the thing was to begin with. It's an important mistake to avoid in medicine and in law, since a good test for a rare condition can still give mostly false alarms.

Problems about probabilities can be hard, even for experts. In 1995 Gerd Gigerenzer and Ulrich Hoffrage showed that the way that the information is presented makes a big difference. Imagine that you're told that 1 percent of women have a certain disease, that a test finds it in 90 percent of those who have it, and that it falsely flags 9 percent of those who don't. What are the chances that a woman who tests positive has the disease? Most people, doctors included, overestimate it badly.
Now say it with counts. Out of 1,000 women, 10 have the disease and 9 of them test positive. Of the 990 who don't, about 89 test positive. So about 98 women test positive, and only 9 of them have the disease, which is about 9 percent. Put in this form, most people get it right. If a statistic confuses you, ask for it in numbers of people.

In 1990 Marilyn vos Savant, a columnist in Parade magazine, answered a reader's question about a TV game show. There are three doors. Behind one is a car, and behind the others are goats. You pick a door, say number one. The host, who knows where the car is, opens another door, say number three, to show a goat. Then he asks if you want to switch to door two. Should you?
She said yes, and that switching wins two thirds of the time. Thousands of readers, including mathematicians, wrote in to say that she was wrong, and that the odds were even. She was right. When you first choose, you have a one-third chance of being right. The host's reveal doesn't change that, so the other door has the remaining two-thirds. If you doubt it, try it with three playing cards, and you'll see.
Red has come up twenty-six times

On August 18, 1913, at a casino in Monte Carlo, the roulette ball landed on black 26 times in a row. Gamblers lost huge sums betting on red, convinced that it was due. But the wheel has no memory, and every spin had the same chance. The belief that a streak must end is called the gambler's fallacy.
In 2016 Daniel Chen, Tobias Moskowitz and Kelly Shue found the same bias outside the casino. They analyzed decisions by asylum judges, loan officers and baseball umpires, and found that each was slightly less likely to make the same decision as the one before, even though there was no reason to do so. A judge who had just granted several cases was more likely to deny the next. It's a quiet bias that we all share, the sense that things have to even out.

Try this: a bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs a dollar more than the ball. How much is the ball? Most people think of 10 cents immediately, and it feels right. But it's wrong. If the ball cost 10 cents, the bat would cost $1.10, and the total would be $1.20. The ball costs 5 cents.
In 2005 Shane Frederick included this question in a three-question test of what he called cognitive reflection, the tendency to stop and check an intuitive answer. About half of the students at top universities gave the wrong answer to this problem. It shows that a smooth, confident answer isn't always right, and that even clever people can be tricked by a quick intuition. A habit of pausing for a second and checking can catch many errors.

In his 2011 book, Daniel Kahneman used the terms System 1 and System 2 for two ways of thinking, which had been described by Keith Stanovich and Richard West. System 1 is fast, automatic and effortless, like knowing that 2 plus 2 is 4, or reading anger on a face. System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful, like multiplying 17 by 24, and it's easily tired.
Many of our mistakes, in his account, come from System 1 being quick and System 2 being lazy. The framework is a useful metaphor, though many psychologists point out that the mind isn't really divided into two neat systems, and intuition can be both good and bad. A more careful way to put it is that some thinking is quick and effortless, and some needs effort and attention, and that it's wise to know when a decision is worth slowing down for.

In 1994 Veronika Denes-Raj and Seymour Epstein offered people a chance to win a dollar by drawing a red jelly bean from one of two bowls. One bowl held 1 red bean among 10, a 10 percent chance. The other held 9 red beans among 100, a 9 percent chance. Many chose the bowl with 9 red beans, though they knew that the odds were slightly worse.
They said that they knew it, but that it felt better to have more red beans to choose from. This is called denominator neglect: we focus on the number of winning chances and ignore the total. It's why a rate such as "1,286 out of 10,000" sounds more frightening than "12.86 percent," and why health risks stated in big numbers can be misleading. When comparing odds, bring both numbers to the same base.

In 1993 William Desvousges and his colleagues asked people how much they'd be willing to pay to save migrating birds from drowning in oil ponds. Some people were told that the number of birds was 2,000, others 20,000 and others 200,000. The average amounts that they said that they'd pay were about $80, $78 and $88.
The number of lives saved had almost no effect on the willingness to pay. It's called scope insensitivity. We react to the feeling that a problem evokes, a bird in oil, and not to the size of the problem. The finding has been repeated for many topics, from saving lives to cleaning lakes. It suggests that when deciding how to give or spend, we should force ourselves to think about numbers, because our feelings won't do the arithmetic.

In logic, the risks and benefits of something, such as nuclear power or pesticides, are separate. Yet in 2000 Melissa Finucane, Paul Slovic and their colleagues found that people's judgments about them are strongly linked. If they like something, they say that it has high benefits and low risks. If they dislike it, they say that it has low benefits and high risks.
The researchers called it the affect heuristic: we let our gut feelings guide our judgment. When people were rushed, the link grew stronger, and when they were given information that something had high benefits, they changed their view of its risks, without being given any new information about the risks. It's an important thing to notice in yourself. When a decision feels easy because you like or dislike something, ask whether you've assessed the facts or only the feeling.

In 1961 the economist Daniel Ellsberg, who later became famous for leaking the Pentagon Papers, described a puzzle. An urn holds 90 balls. 30 of them are red. The other 60 are black or yellow, in an unknown mix. You can bet on red, or on black, and you win if your color is drawn. Most people prefer to bet on red, where the odds are known, to black, where they aren't.
But then, in a second version, most people prefer a bet on black or yellow together, whose odds are known, to red or yellow, whose odds aren't. The two choices contradict each other if we think about probability consistently. The pattern is called ambiguity aversion: we dislike not knowing the odds, even when it makes no logical difference. It shapes how we invest, how we choose doctors, and what we're willing to try.

In 1953 the French economist Maurice Allais proposed a problem that troubled the theory of rational choice. In one choice, people prefer a sure gain of a million dollars to a gamble with a high chance of getting five million and a small chance of getting nothing. In a second choice, between two gambles with small chances of winning, they prefer the one with the larger prize, though it's the same gamble with the chances scaled down.
These preferences are inconsistent with expected utility theory. Going from a 100 percent chance to 99 percent feels like a much bigger drop than from 11 percent to 10 percent. Kahneman and Tversky called this the certainty effect. It helps to explain why people pay a premium for insurance and warranties that remove the last bit of risk, and why a guarantee can be so attractive.
Why a loss and a gain are not mirror images

In 1979 Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published a paper that changed economics, called prospect theory. They found that people don't judge outcomes by final wealth, as classical theory assumed, but as gains and losses relative to a reference point, often the status quo. Losses weigh more than gains. And we're risk-averse when choosing between gains, but risk-seeking between losses.
For example, most people take a sure gain of $500 over a coin flip for $1,000, but they prefer a coin flip to lose $1,000 over a sure loss of $500. The same amounts, framed differently, lead to opposite choices. Kahneman was awarded the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics for this work, and Tversky would have shared it had he not died in 1996. It gave a realistic picture of how people decide.
When confidence is a poor guide

Kahneman told a story from his time in the Israeli army in the 1950s, when he was asked to design a way to select officer candidates. He and his colleagues watched soldiers in a group task and rated their leadership, and felt confident about their predictions. But when they checked how the soldiers did later, their predictions were barely better than guesses.
Yet, to his astonishment, he and his colleagues continued to feel just as confident about the next group. He called it the illusion of validity. A story that seems coherent makes us confident, whether or not it's true. The feeling of certainty comes from how well the evidence fits together, and not from how good the evidence is. It's a reason to keep track of your predictions, and to measure how often they are right.

Daniel Kahneman, who studied the errors of intuition, and Gary Klein, who studied the successes of expert intuition, such as firefighters who sense that a floor is about to collapse, seemed to be on opposite sides. In 2009 they wrote a paper together to find out where they agreed. They concluded that intuition can be trusted when two conditions are met.
First, the environment must be regular enough to be predictable, as in chess, firefighting or nursing. Second, the person must have had long practice and quick feedback, so that they've learned the patterns. In unpredictable fields, such as predicting political events or stocks, confident intuition isn't reliable, however experienced the person. A good test is to ask whether you've had many chances to learn, and whether the world gives clear feedback.

In 1984 Philip Tetlock began asking experts, such as academics, diplomats and journalists, to make predictions about world events, and he kept going for 20 years. He collected about 28,000 forecasts from 284 experts. When he checked the results, the experts did only a little better than random guesses, and not much better than a simple rule such as predicting that things would stay the same.
There was a pattern in who did better. Those he called hedgehogs, who knew one big thing and applied it to everything, did worse. The foxes, who knew many small things, drew from many sources and were willing to change their minds, did better. Fame and confidence went with poorer predictions. It's a call for humility about forecasts, and for keeping score.

In 1954 the psychologist Paul Meehl published a short book that caused an uproar. He compared predictions by clinicians, using their judgment, with predictions from simple statistical formulas based on the same information, such as predicting who would succeed in school or recover from illness. In nearly every case, the formulas did as well or better.
In 2000 William Grove and his colleagues combined 136 studies and confirmed it: mechanical predictions were as good as or better than expert judgment in almost all of them, and clearly better in many. Experts add value by knowing what to look at. But they tend to be inconsistent, swayed by moods and by irrelevant details. A good use of the finding is to let a checklist or a formula do the final combining, and keep human judgment for gathering the information.
Smart people reason with their politics

In 2013 Dan Kahan and his colleagues asked people to look at a small table of data and say what it showed. In one version, the table was about whether a skin cream worked. In another, the same numbers were labeled as showing the effect of a ban on handguns on crime. People who were good at math did well on the skin cream version. On the gun version, they did much worse when the correct answer contradicted their politics.
The people with the best number skills, in other words, weren't more objective. They used their skills to find a way to the conclusion they wanted. The study is often used to argue that facts alone don't settle political arguments. The size of the effect is debated and there are replications of it with different results. But it's consistent with other work on motivated reasoning, and a reminder to ask whether you'd interpret the evidence the same way if it supported the other side.

In 1975 Lee Ross and his colleagues gave students a task: to tell the difference between real suicide notes and fake ones. They gave the students feedback on how well they were doing, which was made up. Some were told that they were very good, and some that they were very bad. Then the researchers explained that the feedback had been completely random, and had nothing to do with their ability.
Even after they'd been told, the students who had been told they were good still believed that they were good at the task, and those who had been told that they were bad believed that they were bad. The beliefs had taken on a life of their own. It's called belief perseverance. Once we've built an explanation for something, it doesn't disappear when the evidence is withdrawn. That's a reason to be careful about the first story you tell about anything.

In 1960 Peter Wason showed people three numbers, 2, 4, 6, and said that they followed a rule. The task was to discover the rule by proposing other sets of three numbers, and being told whether each fit. Most people quickly guessed that the rule was "numbers increasing by two," and tested it with 8, 10, 12 and 20, 22, 24. Each time they were told yes.
They were confident and wrong. The real rule was just "any increasing numbers." They'd never tried a set that would break their idea, such as 1, 2, 3, or 5, 3, 1. We tend to test a hypothesis by looking for confirming examples, which can never prove it, and avoid looking for ones that could prove it false. The remedy is to ask, "What would show me I'm wrong?" and then go and look for that.

Does it matter if a company has a name that's easy to say? In 2006 Adam Alter and Daniel Oppenheimer looked at companies that had recently gone public on the stock exchange. In the first day of trading, those with names that were easy to pronounce did better than those with hard names. The effect was modest and faded with time.
The researchers think that easy-to-process names feel familiar and trustworthy. It's part of a pattern called processing fluency: things that are easy for the mind to handle seem to be better, truer and safer. It affects how we judge claims, products and people. It's a good idea to ask yourself whether you like something because it's good, or because it's easy to grasp.

In 1988 Irwin Levin and Gary Gaeth asked people to taste ground beef and rate it. Some were told that it was "75 percent lean," and others that it was "25 percent fat." It's the same beef. The people who were given the lean label rated it as better tasting and less greasy.
Positive and negative framings of the same facts lead to different reactions, which is known as attribute framing. It's used by food companies, and also by doctors, when they talk about surgery as having a 90 percent survival rate or a 10 percent death rate. It's good to recognize that the way a fact is presented may change your reaction. A useful trick is to restate it in the opposite terms and see if it feels different.

In 2010 Yaacov Trope and Nira Liberman summarized a theory about how we think about things that are close or far away, in time, space or in terms of how likely they are, or how well we know the people involved. It's called construal level theory. Things that are far away are thought about abstractly, in terms of why and what for, while those that are close are seen concretely, in terms of how and the details.
For example, a trip next year is a dream of adventure and relaxation, while a trip next week is a list of tasks and tickets. We often make plans while our minds are in a far state and then are surprised by the details. It helps to think about the same decision in both ways, and to ask both why you're doing something and how you'll go about it.
The wisdom of the crowd in your own head

The wisdom of crowds says that the average of many people's guesses is often better than most individual guesses. In 2008 Edward Vul and Harold Pashler asked whether you could get a similar benefit from a single mind. They asked people questions, such as the year of a historical event, and then asked them to guess a second time, without telling them the first answer. The average of the two guesses was more accurate than either one alone.
The effect was larger if the second guess was made three weeks later, and not right away. The explanation is that each guess is a sample from what you know, with its own random error, and averaging cancels some of it. If you have to make an estimate, and you can, make it twice, with a break between, and use the average.

Feedback is supposed to help people improve, but does it? In 1996 Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi combined the results of 607 experiments with feedback, covering tens of thousands of people. On average, feedback did help. But in more than one third of the cases, it made performance worse.
The pattern depended on what the feedback focused on. When it pointed to the person, as in "you're not good at this," it often backfired, because attention moved from the task to the self. When it focused on the task, and on how to do it better, it was far more likely to help. The researchers also found that feedback worked best when it was specific and gave a clear way forward. The lesson is to talk about the work and not the worker.
Why the best teams reported more mistakes

In the 1990s Amy Edmondson studied hospital teams to find out which ones made the fewest medication errors. She expected the best teams to report the fewest. It turned out to be the opposite: the teams that were rated best by their staff had reported more errors. At first she was baffled.
Her explanation was that they didn't make more mistakes. They were more willing to talk about them. In those teams, people felt safe to speak up, which she called psychological safety. In others, people hid mistakes for fear of blame, so they stayed unreported and uncorrected. Google's own research, called Project Aristotle, found years later that psychological safety was the most important factor in effective teams. A group learns when people can say "I made a mistake" without being punished.
What gestures do for the speaker

We gesture when we talk, even on the phone, where nobody can see. Susan Goldin-Meadow has spent decades studying why. In 2007 she and her colleagues taught children in a math lesson, and asked some of them to move their hands as they explained how to solve the problems, and others not to gesture. The children who gestured went on to learn more from the lesson.
In some cases, children's gestures showed ideas that they couldn't yet put into words, a sign that they were ready to learn. It seems that gesture is part of thinking, and not just a decoration for speech. It helps us find words and organize ideas. If you're trying to understand something, try explaining it with your hands. It may help you think.
Hearing an accent changes what we believe

In 2010 Shiri Lev-Ari and Boaz Keysar had people listen to trivia statements, such as "A giraffe can go without water longer than a camel can," read by native English speakers and by non-native speakers with a mild accent. The listeners were told that the speakers were only reading statements that had been written for them. Even so, they rated statements spoken with an accent as less true.
The accent was easy to understand, so it wasn't a problem of comprehension. The researchers suggested that it's about processing fluency. Speech that's a bit harder to process feels less trustworthy, and we confuse the difficulty with the content. When the listeners were told about the effect beforehand, the bias shrank. It's worth knowing, since it means that we may discount good ideas because of the way they're pronounced.
Do some voices sound less competent?

Vocal fry is a low, creaky quality that's sometimes heard at the end of sentences, and it's often associated with young American women. In 2014 Rindy Anderson and her colleagues played recordings of the same speakers saying the same words, with and without vocal fry, and asked listeners to rate them. The listeners judged the voices with vocal fry as less competent, less trustworthy and less hirable, and the effect was larger for women than for men.
It was a study of young adults in the US, and later work has found that the effect varies. It raises the question of whether the bias is about the voice or about expectations of the speaker. Many experts, including linguists, consider it a normal feature of speech, found in all kinds of voices. It's a reminder that we sometimes judge how people sound without noticing.
The words that show who is on top

In his research on language, James Pennebaker noticed something odd about small words such as pronouns. In 2014 Ewa Kacewicz and her colleagues analyzed the language that people used in emails, and in tasks in which people of different status worked together. They found that people with lower status used the word "I" more. People of higher status used it less, and used more "we."
You might think that the powerful would talk about themselves more. But the pattern was consistent. Using "I" shows that attention is turned inward, a bit like being self-conscious, while higher-status people tend to look outward at others and at the task. The words are used without thought, and it suggests a different way of reading a conversation. The small words can reveal more than the big ones.

Until the late 1970s, deaf children in Nicaragua had no schools, and most lived at home with their families, using improvised gestures. When schools for the deaf opened in Managua in the late 1970s, hundreds of children were brought together for the first time. They didn't have a shared language, and they began to invent one on the playground.
Over the next few years, the signs became more systematic, and each new cohort of children took them further. Ann Senghas and her colleagues, studying the language as it developed, found that younger children added grammar, such as ways of showing the direction of movement, that the first group hadn't used. Nicaraguan Sign Language is one of the few cases of a new language being born in front of scientists. It suggests that children are built to create language.
The window for learning a language

Is it easier to learn a language when you're young? In 1989 Jacqueline Johnson and Elissa Newport tested 46 native speakers of Chinese and Korean who'd come to the US at various ages, and who'd been living there for at least five years. They gave them a test of English grammar. People who arrived before about age 7 did as well as native speakers. For those who'd arrived later, the older they were when they arrived, the worse they did.
The decline continued steadily through the teenage years. It was one of the best-known tests of a critical period for language. Later research suggests that the picture is more complicated, since adults learn more quickly at first, and the age effects are gradual. But it's clear that, for mastering accent and grammar, there's an advantage in starting early, and still it's possible to learn at any age.

Spoken language doesn't have gaps between words. When you listen to a language you don't know, it sounds like a continuous stream. So how do babies find the words? In 1996 Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin and Elissa Newport played eight-month-old infants a stream of nonsense syllables for just two minutes. Certain syllables always went together, such as "bi-da-ku," and others didn't.
Afterward, the babies paid more attention to new combinations that broke the pattern than to those that kept it, which showed that they'd learned which syllables belonged together. They did it after only two minutes, with nothing to look at. It's called statistical learning, and it shows that even babies detect patterns in sounds. It's part of how an infant, in the first year, begins to carve speech into words.
Learning a word in one try

How quickly can a child learn a word? In 1978 Susan Carey and Elsa Bartlett did a simple experiment with three-year-olds at a nursery school. They said to a child, "Bring me the chromium tray, not the blue one, the chromium one." The children had never heard the word chromium, and the tray was olive green. Many of them brought the olive-colored tray.
A week later, many of the children still remembered that chromium has something to do with the color olive, after just one exposure. It was called fast mapping, and it shows that children make a quick hypothesis about a new word from context, and keep it. Children learn about ten words a day through preschool years, and this speed is part of the way they do it.

Richard Mayer has run dozens of experiments on how people learn from words and pictures, and he's drawn some practical rules. People learn better from words and pictures together than from words alone. They learn better when the words are spoken than when they're written on the same screen as the animation, because the eyes have too much to do while the ears are free. And they learn worse when a narrator reads exactly what's on the slide.
It's called the redundancy principle. If you're giving a presentation, use images and a few words, and say the rest. Don't fill your slides with text and read it aloud, since your audience will read faster than you speak, and will stop listening. A slide should support what you say, and not repeat it.
You can ask more people than you think

Most people dislike asking others for help, partly because they think that others will say no. In 2008 Francis Flynn and Vanessa Lake asked people to approach strangers and ask for favors, such as borrowing a cell phone or filling out a questionnaire. Before they went, they'd asked the participants to guess how many strangers they'd have to approach to get a set number of yeses. They underestimated how many people would agree, and by a lot.
The reason is that the person who is asking thinks about the risk of rejection, and the person being asked feels social pressure to say yes, since saying no is awkward. Vanessa Bohns later called it underestimating compliance. It's a good thing to remember when you hesitate to ask. People are generally more willing to help than we expect, and saying no feels harder to them than it looks to us.
Copying the other person at the table

In 2008 William Maddux, Elizabeth Mullen and Adam Galinsky tested whether mimicking the other person helps in a negotiation. In one experiment, business students were asked to negotiate a sale. Some were told to subtly copy the other person's posture and gestures, about 10 to 15 seconds after the other person did, and the others were told not to. The people who mimicked were much more likely to reach a deal.
The mimickers also got more for themselves, and the other person was not aware of the mimicry. The researchers suggest that mimicry builds trust and rapport, so that the other person is more open to finding mutually good solutions. It works best when it's subtle and natural. If it's obvious, it looks mocking, so it's more a matter of staying attuned to the other person than of copying them.

In 2017 Guy Itzchakov, Avraham Kluger and Dotan Castro asked people to talk about a topic on which they had a strong opinion, such as an issue about which they felt passionate, while a listener either paid good attention or acted distracted. The people who were listened to well afterward had a less extreme view, and were more aware of the ambiguity in their own opinions.
Being listened to made them feel safe enough to look at their own thinking. It's the opposite of what many of us expect, that if you let people say their piece without arguing, they'll dig in. In fact, a good listener, who seems interested and doesn't interrupt, can help a person to think more clearly. The most persuasive thing you can do with someone who disagrees may be to listen.
Why video calls tire us out

During the pandemic, many people reported that video calls were exhausting. In 2021 Jeremy Bailenson at Stanford wrote an influential analysis suggesting four reasons. First, there is excessive close-up eye contact, since in a grid of faces everyone seems to be staring at you, and faces appear larger than in life. Second, seeing yourself constantly is tiring, like having a mirror in front of you all day.
Third, video calls reduce movement, since you have to stay in view of the camera. And fourth, they raise the mental load, as we have to work harder to send and receive the nonverbal cues that come naturally in person. Some of his claims have been tested and some haven't, but studies of users find that the experience is real. Turning off your own view, shrinking the window and taking audio-only calls can help.

In 2003 Frances Milliken, Elizabeth Morrison and Patricia Hewlin interviewed 40 full-time employees in a range of organizations about whether there'd been a time when they hadn't spoken up about something important at work. Remarkably, 85 percent said they had. The top reasons were fear of being seen as negative, of damaging a relationship, and a sense that it wouldn't make a difference.
The employees had concerns that they thought would be useful, about pay, a boss's behavior or a safety issue, and still stayed silent. They called it organizational silence. It costs teams a great deal, since the information never reaches those who could act on it. A leader can help by inviting dissent, by thanking people who bring bad news, and by acting on what they hear.
The tone of the voice in a quarrel

John Gottman has said that he can often tell, after listening to just a few minutes of a couple talking, whether they're likely to stay together. In studies, the pattern of the first few minutes of a hard conversation did predict the later outcome, though the accuracy that has been claimed for these predictions has been criticized.
The most important signals were in the tone. Contempt, with a sneer or a sarcastic voice, was the worst. Warmth, humor and appreciation were good signs. The words may be the same, "You forgot to call," but the tone decides whether it's a complaint or an attack. It suggests that, in a close relationship, it matters how you say things as much as what you say. A kind tone can carry a hard message.
Why a call beats a text

The research on voice and text suggests that, for personal messages, a voice often does better than writing. In 2021 Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley asked people to reconnect with an old friend with whom they'd lost touch, some by phone or video, and some by writing. Before they started, people predicted that a call would be more awkward than a text. In fact, those who made the call felt more connected afterward, and found it no more awkward than expected.
A voice carries tone, warmth and emotion in a way that text can't. In the earlier study by Juliana Schroeder and Epley, people who heard a job pitch spoken, instead of reading the same words, judged the speaker as more thoughtful and intelligent. We often choose to write because it feels safer, and we underrate how much a voice conveys. The next time that you want to reach out to someone, consider calling.
The first thing people notice in a story

Linguists William Labov and Joshua Waletzky analyzed the structure of personal stories told in everyday conversations in 1967, and found a common pattern: an abstract that says what the story is about, an orientation of who, when and where, a complicating action, an evaluation, a resolution and a coda. The evaluation, they noted, is the part that tells us why the story is worth hearing.
Storytellers who left out the point were boring even if the events were interesting. It's a lesson for any talk or conversation. Tell people why you're telling it, and make it clear what's at stake. Claims that stories work by releasing oxytocin have been popular but are not well supported by the research. It's enough to know that a story with a clear point, and a person at its center, is how people have always passed on what matters.

In 2004 Samuel McClure and his colleagues ran a version of the Pepsi Challenge inside a brain scanner. When people sipped Coke and Pepsi without knowing which was which, their preferences split about evenly. Then they were told what they were drinking, and the result changed. When a cup was labeled Coke, about three quarters of them said they preferred it, though the contents were the same.
The scans showed more than a change in what people said. Knowing the brand changed activity in the hippocampus and the prefrontal cortex, areas tied to memory and to using emotion to shape a choice. The label seemed to change the experience, and not just the report of it. Oddly, a Pepsi label didn't have the same pull. A brand is a bundle of memories and feelings that you taste along with the product.
The music that sold the wine

In 1997 Adrian North and his colleagues ran a neat experiment in the wine aisle of a supermarket in England. On some days, they played French accordion music, and on others, German beer-hall music. French and German wines of similar price and style stood side by side. When French music played, shoppers bought mostly French wine. When German music played, German wine outsold French.
Afterward, when shoppers were asked whether the music had influenced them, most said no. It's a striking demonstration of how background cues steer us without our awareness. The music didn't make anyone like wine more. It brought one country to mind, and that tilted the choice. It's worth asking what you're hearing, and what it's making you think of, when you decide to buy.
Why we love what we built

In 2012 Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely asked people to assemble IKEA boxes, to fold origami, and to build Lego sets. Afterward they asked how much the people would pay for what they had made. The builders valued their own plain, amateur work about as highly as they valued the same thing made by an expert. People who hadn't built it valued the amateur version much less.
The effect depended on finishing. When people built something and failed, or when their creations were taken apart in front of them, the extra value disappeared. The researchers called it the IKEA effect. It helps to explain why meal kits and do-it-yourself products can be popular, and why you may overvalue your own work. When a project is yours, you aren't the best judge of its worth.

Restaurant tipping has been studied for years, and the results make a good lesson in persuasion. In 1996 Bruce Rind and Prashant Bordia had servers draw a smiley face on the back of some checks. The female server's tips went up with the smiley face. The male server's tips went down. The same gesture could land very differently depending on who made it.
In 1999 Rind and David Strohmetz found that when a server wrote a note on the check about an upcoming dinner special, the tips were higher than on the checks with no note. Other researchers found gains from a server giving her name, crouching down to the table, and touching a diner's shoulder lightly. What these share is a sense of personal attention. The customer feels looked after, and gives a little more.

In 2003 Dan Ariely, George Loewenstein and Drazen Prelec asked MBA students to write the last two digits of their Social Security number, and then to bid on things like wine, chocolate and computer equipment. Students whose numbers were high bid far more than the others. Those in the top fifth bid, on average, more than twice as much as those in the bottom fifth.
The irrelevant number had worked as an anchor, shaping what people were willing to pay though they knew it was arbitrary. This became one of the best known demonstrations of anchoring. Replications of this exact design have been mixed, and some found weaker effects. But anchoring itself has held up well in many other studies. The first number you see, even a random one, tends to color the numbers that follow it.

Most of us trust our own judgment in an interview. In 2013 Jason Dana, Robyn Dawes and Nathanial Peterson tested this. Students were asked to predict other students' grades for the coming semester. They had background information, such as prior grades, and for one of the students they also held a short interview. In one version, the person being interviewed was answering at random, and the interviewer didn't know it.
The interviewers felt just as sure of their impressions after random answers as after real ones. Worse, the interviews made the predictions less accurate than the grades alone. The authors concluded that a conversation gives us a coherent story that feels convincing, even when it is noise. Their advice was to avoid unstructured interviews when screening people, or at least to keep their weight small.
The résumé with the other name

In 2004 Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan sent nearly 5,000 fictitious résumés in response to job ads in Boston and Chicago. The résumés were similar in quality, but some had names more common among white Americans, such as Emily and Greg, and others had names more common among Black Americans, such as Lakisha and Jamal.
The résumés with white-sounding names got about 50 percent more callbacks. A better résumé helped the white-named applicants a great deal, but made much less difference for the others. The study was widely discussed, and similar tests in other places and with other groups have found related results. It shows that discrimination can operate even at the first step of hiring, and that it can do so without anyone saying a word.

In the 1970s and 80s, major American orchestras began to hold auditions behind a screen, so that the judges couldn't see the musician. In 2000 the economists Claudia Goldin and Cecilia Rouse studied records of orchestra auditions and concluded that the screen helped women advance, and that it helped to explain the rise in the number of women in orchestras.
Later researchers have questioned how strong the evidence is, pointing to the small numbers and the way the data was analyzed, and the true effect may have been smaller. But the idea has spread well beyond music. Taking away information that shouldn't matter, such as a name or a photo, lets the decision rest on what does. It's a sensible practice whatever the size of the original effect.

Do bigger rewards make people try harder? In 2009 Dan Ariely and his colleagues tested this with games that needed attention, memory or creativity. They ran them in the United States and in rural India, where the largest reward was many times a typical day's earnings. In general, very large rewards led to worse performance than moderate ones, though there were exceptions.
The authors suggested that when the stakes are very high, the pressure gets in the way of tasks that need thinking. For simple tasks that depend only on effort, bigger rewards do help. The experiments were small, and the result has been debated. But it fits with other research on choking under pressure. A bonus may help when the work is mostly effort, and it can backfire when the work is skilled or creative.

Research by Linda Babcock and others has found that women are less likely than men to start a negotiation over pay, which can add up over a career. In 2007 Deborah Small, Michele Gelfand, Babcock and Hilary Gettman tested whether the words used to describe the opportunity make a difference. The same situation was described to some people as a chance to negotiate and to others as a chance to ask.
When it was framed as negotiating, men were more likely than women to start. When it was framed as asking, the gap disappeared. The authors suggested that negotiation sounds like a contest, which clashes with norms of politeness for people with less power, while asking doesn't. The study can't settle the whole question of pay gaps, but it shows how much a single word can change who speaks up.
Giving when the overhead is covered

Many donors say they don't want their money going to administrative costs. In 2014 Uri Gneezy, Elizabeth Keenan and Ayelet Gneezy tested how much that matters. In a lab study, people were less likely to give to a charity as its overhead went up. But when they were told that someone else had already covered the overhead, many gave even when overhead was high.
They then ran a field experiment with an education foundation. An appeal that said every dollar would go to the cause, because the costs were already paid, brought a much higher rate of giving than the standard appeal. Donors, it seems, don't mind that charities have costs. They mind the thought of their own money paying for them. A charity can use this by finding a few donors to cover overhead.

In 2007 Dean Karlan and John List mailed solicitations to more than 50,000 past donors of a nonprofit, and varied the offer. Some letters made a plain request. Others said that a generous donor would match the gift, one for one, two for one or three for one. A match offer raised both the money collected per letter and the share of people who gave.
But the size of the match made no difference. A three-for-one match did no better than one-for-one. The idea of a match mattered more than its real value. People like to feel that their gift is being multiplied, but the multiple isn't what moves them. It's useful for fundraisers, and for any of us who has wondered whether a bigger promise would have worked better.

In 1998 Frank Schmidt and John Hunter reviewed 85 years of research on how well different hiring methods predict job performance. Among the best predictors were work samples, which test people on the real tasks, tests of general mental ability, and structured interviews, in which each candidate gets the same questions and is scored against a set standard. Unstructured interviews were less useful, and years of experience did poorly.
Combining methods did better still. A test of mental ability together with a structured interview predicted performance better than either alone. The review has been updated since, and some of its estimates have been revised, but the broad lesson has held up. If you're hiring, ask everyone the same questions, score them the same way, and have them do a piece of real work.
What students do that doesn't work

In 2013 John Dunlosky and his colleagues reviewed the research on ten popular study techniques and rated how useful each one is. Several of the habits that students rely on most came out near the bottom. Highlighting and underlining, rereading, summarizing, and drawing mental pictures of a text were all rated as having low or only modest usefulness for learning.
None of these is harmful, and some can help in particular settings. The problem is that they feel productive. A page marked in yellow looks like work. A chapter read twice feels familiar. But familiarity is not the same as being able to recall something next week. The review's message was not to stop studying, but to swap in methods that make your memory work harder.
The two methods that rated highest

Of the ten techniques in the Dunlosky review, only two earned the top rating of high utility. One was practice testing, which means trying to recall what you've learned without looking, using flashcards, practice questions or a blank page. The other was distributed practice, which means spreading your study over several sessions instead of putting it all into one.
Both methods work across a wide range of ages, subjects and kinds of material. They also share a feature. They feel harder than the alternatives, and they often make you feel less sure of yourself in the moment. That feeling is the sign that they are working. If studying feels smooth, it's worth asking whether you're really learning or just recognizing what you've seen before.

You read a chapter, you read it again, and the second time it all seems clear. That clarity is the problem. In 2009 Aimee Callender and Mark McDaniel tested whether rereading a textbook passage helps students learn it. Across several experiments with real textbook material, reading the passage a second time did not reliably improve later test performance over reading it once.
Rereading works on your sense of fluency. The words go by easily, because you've just seen them, and you take the ease as a sign that you know the material. But recognizing a sentence as familiar is a far lower bar than producing the idea on your own. Closing the book and trying to say what you remember is less pleasant, and it teaches you much more.

In 2011 Jeffrey Karpicke and Janell Blunt compared several ways of studying a science text. Students could read it once, read it several times, make a concept map while looking at the text, or read it and then write down everything they could remember. A week later the students who had practiced retrieving the text did best, including on questions that asked them to draw inferences.
Concept mapping is a well respected technique, and it asks you to think hard about how ideas connect. Even so, it did not beat the plain act of recalling. The students themselves guessed that repeated reading would work best, which fits a pattern in this research. We tend to prefer the study methods that feel good and to undervalue the ones that actually build memory.
Restudying wins today and loses next week

In 2006 Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students read short prose passages and then either read them again or take a recall test on them. When the final test came five minutes later, the students who had reread did better. When the final test came two days or a week later, the students who had been tested did better.
This crossover explains why cramming feels so effective. If your goal is to do well in the next few minutes, rereading is a fine tool. If your goal is to remember something next month, it fades quickly, while retrieval practice slows the forgetting. The method you choose should match the time you need the knowledge to last. For most things we care about, it is much longer than a day.

Imagine you are studying vocabulary with flashcards. When you get a card right, you set it aside to save time. In 2008 Jeffrey Karpicke and Henry Roediger tested this habit with students learning Swahili and English word pairs. In one condition, words were dropped from testing after being recalled once. In another, they stayed in, and students kept trying to recall them.
Students who kept being tested remembered about twice as many words a week later. Extra study time, with the words dropped from testing, did little. A later study argued that part of this result came from the way the practice was spaced, and that the picture is more complicated. Still, the common advice holds up. One correct answer doesn't mean a memory is secure. Coming back to it a few more times is where the learning happens.
A test that teaches wrong answers

Multiple-choice questions show the right answer along with several wrong ones, and that has a cost. In 2005 Henry Roediger and Elizabeth Marsh had students read short passages, then take a multiple-choice test on them, and later answer the same questions without any choices. The more wrong options students had seen, the more often they later gave one of those wrong options as an answer.
Later work found that the effect shrinks when students get the correct answers soon afterward. That points to a simple rule for using practice tests. Check your answers, and do it soon. A wrong answer that you've seen but never corrected can feel familiar, and familiarity can feel like truth. It also explains why a question with wrong choices can plant an idea you didn't have before.
The best gap between study sessions

Spacing your study helps, but how far apart should the sessions be? In 2008 Nicholas Cepeda and his colleagues tried to answer this with more than a thousand people who learned facts and were tested after different delays. They varied both the gap between study sessions and the time until the final test, and mapped what worked best.
The best gap depended on how long you needed to remember. If the test was a week away, a gap of a day or so was best. If it was months away, a gap of weeks was better. As a rough guide, the ideal gap was about a tenth to a fifth of the time that you want to remember the material. Too short a gap is wasteful, but a gap that is too long is less costly than one that is too short.

In 2006 Nicholas Cepeda and his colleagues gathered hundreds of experiments on distributed practice and analyzed them together. The pattern was clear. When the same amount of study was spread over several sessions, people remembered more later than when the study was crammed into one. This held for many ages and kinds of material, and it is one of the sturdiest findings in the psychology of learning.
Cramming isn't useless. It can get you through an exam the next morning, and sometimes that is all you need. But what you learn that way tends to disappear quickly, and it leaves little to build on. If the material matters to you beyond a test, it's far better to break it into short sessions and let a few days pass in between, even if each session is only a few minutes.

In 1982 Pierre Salamé and Alan Baddeley found that background speech makes it harder to remember lists of items you've just read, even when you can't understand the language. Speech seems to intrude on the part of working memory that holds words in order. Steady noise without speech, and instrumental music, had much weaker effects.
Later work looked at music with lyrics. In 2014 Nick Perham and Alice Currie tested whether listening to favorite songs helps reading comprehension. It didn't, and songs with lyrics made comprehension worse than silence. Plenty of people feel that music helps them concentrate. It may help your mood or block out something worse, but when the task is understanding sentences, words in the background compete with the words on the page.

Do you understand more when you read on paper or on a screen? In 2018 Pablo Delgado and his colleagues combined the results of dozens of studies, covering well over a hundred thousand readers. They found that reading on paper led to better comprehension than reading on screens, and the gap was largest for informational texts and when readers were under time pressure.
The reasons are still debated. Screens may encourage skimming. People may also be more overconfident about what they understood on a screen. And paper gives a stable sense of where something is on the page and how far along you are. None of this says that screens can't be used well. It does suggest that for long or difficult material, slowing down on a screen, or printing it, can be worth it.

In 2013 Faria Sana, Tina Weston and Nicholas Cepeda ran a lecture experiment. Students listened to a talk with a laptop and were asked to do unrelated tasks on it, such as searching the web for other things, during the lecture. Those who multitasked scored lower on a test about the talk than students who hadn't used a laptop for anything else.
The surprise came from the students sitting nearby. Some were placed where they could see a multitasking classmate's screen, and these students scored lower too, though they hadn't been asked to do anything but listen. Distraction spreads. Moving, flickering content is hard to ignore, and the person next to you may be costing you more than they cost themselves. It's a reason to think about where you sit.

In 2017 Adrian Ward and his colleagues reported that people who had their phone on the desk, even silenced and untouched, did worse on tests of working memory and problem solving than people whose phone was in another room. The idea was that part of your attention is used up on not looking at the phone. The paper was widely covered under the name brain drain.
Later researchers tried to repeat the finding, and several did not find the same effect. The question is still open, and the effect may be smaller, or may depend on how attached to the phone a person is. It remains a sensible, low cost experiment to run on yourself. If you have something hard to do, put the phone out of sight, and notice whether it makes any difference to you.

In 2004 Ullrich Wagner and his colleagues gave people a number task with a hidden shortcut. People who worked through it could solve it the long way, but a rule that was never mentioned could make it far quicker. After training, some people slept for the night, and others stayed awake for the same length of time. Then everyone tried again.
More than half of those who had slept found the hidden rule, compared with under a quarter of those who had stayed awake. Sleep didn't help people who hadn't done the training first. It seems that during sleep, the brain reorganizes recent experience in a way that can reveal a pattern. The old advice to sleep on a problem has some support, as long as you've worked on the problem before you go to bed.

In 1995 Alvaro Pascual-Leone and his colleagues taught people a short five-finger piano exercise. One group practiced at the keyboard for a couple of hours a day for five days. Another group only imagined playing, in the same schedule, without moving their fingers. The researchers mapped the motor cortex with magnetic stimulation each day.
Both groups showed changes in the part of the cortex that controlled the fingers. The group that practiced physically improved more in actual playing. But once the mental-practice group had a single session at the keyboard, they caught up quickly. Later studies and reviews agree that mental rehearsal helps, though it works best as an addition to real practice and not as a replacement for it.

Have you ever watched a how-to video and felt that you could do it? In 2018 Michael Kardas and Ed O'Brien tested this across six experiments. People watched videos of tasks such as throwing darts, doing the moonwalk and juggling. The more times they watched, the more confident they became that they could do it themselves.
But performance did not improve with more viewing. People who watched a dart video twenty times were no better at throwing darts than people who watched it once, though they predicted they would be. Watching lets you see the steps, but it doesn't teach you how they feel. The effect shrank when people picked up the props themselves. The lesson for learning any skill is to move from watching to trying as soon as you can.

In 2019 Louis Deslauriers and his colleagues ran a crossover experiment in a large physics course at Harvard. For one class, half the students got a polished lecture from an expert, and half took part in an active session where they worked on problems in groups. For the next class, the groups switched. All of them took a short test afterward and rated how much they felt they had learned.
The active students scored higher on the test, but they felt they had learned less. The lecture students rated the teaching more highly and said they'd like all their classes taught that way. The effort of working things out felt like a sign of poor learning, and smooth explanation felt like a sign of good learning. It's a reminder not to trust the feeling of ease when you judge your own learning.

Suppose that you were asked to remember a list such as "break the match" and "lift the cup." Half the time you only hear the phrase, and half the time you actually do the action. Researchers found, beginning in the early 1980s, that people recall the phrases they acted out better than the phrases they only heard or read.
This is called the enactment effect, or the subject-performed task effect. It seems to work because movement adds another trace to memory, made of how it felt to do it, as well as how it sounded. It has been seen in many studies, including with older adults. For learning, it suggests that when the material allows it, such as a procedure or the names of objects in another language, doing something physically can give a boost over just reading about it.

In 2016 Jeffrey Wammes, Melissa Meade and Myra Fernandes asked people to learn a list of common words, such as "apple" or "kite." For each word, they either wrote it out several times or drew a picture of it. When they were later asked to recall the words, they remembered the drawn words much better than the written ones.
The authors called it the drawing effect. Drawing seems to combine several kinds of memory at once, including the meaning of the word, the movement of the hand and the look of the picture. The drawings did not have to be good, and the benefit didn't depend on artistic skill. If you're trying to learn vocabulary or labeled parts, a quick sketch in the margin may help.
Choking: when thinking gets in the way

Why do skilled people sometimes fail when it matters most? In 2001 Sian Beilock and Thomas Carr studied golfers putting under pressure. When experienced golfers were told to pay attention to the steps of their swing, they did worse. Beginners, who haven't yet made the skill automatic, seem to need that kind of attention.
The researchers' explanation is that expert skills become automatic. When pressure makes you monitor each step, you break up a well-practiced routine. The remedy tested in later studies was to give attention something else to do, such as a rhythm or a single simple cue. It has a lesson for any performance, from speaking to playing music. After practice, trust the automatic part, and don't give it a running commentary.
Writing your worries before an exam

In 2011 Gerardo Ramirez and Sian Beilock asked students to spend ten minutes writing about their feelings about an upcoming exam just before they took it. In several experiments, students who wrote about their worries did better than those who didn't, and the benefit was greatest among students who tended to feel anxious about tests.
The explanation was that worries use up working memory, and writing them down offloads some of the load. Other labs have had mixed results when they tried to repeat it, so the effect may be smaller or work only in some conditions. It costs ten minutes and carries little risk. If you get nervous before tests or big talks, it's reasonable to try it and see if it helps you.
Babies know when they don't know

Metacognition, knowing what you know, seems like an adult skill. In 2016 Louise Goupil, Margaux Romand-Monnier and Sid Kouider tested toddlers of twenty months. They hid a toy in one of two boxes and let the children try to find it, sometimes after a delay that made them unsure where it was. The children could also ask a parent for help.
When the children had been less sure, they asked for help more often, and when they were sure they searched on their own. They also tended to be right more often when they had been confident. So even very young children seem to track how reliable their own memory is. The ability grows and sharpens over the school years, and it is a skill that can be trained.

In 2001 Robert Hampton tested whether rhesus monkeys can tell when they remember something. Monkeys saw an image, then waited through a delay. On some trials, they could choose to take a memory test or decline it for a smaller reward. On other trials, they were forced to take the test.
The monkeys were more accurate when they chose the test than when they were forced to take it. They tended to decline when the delay was long or the memory was weaker. This suggests that they were monitoring something about their own memory, and not only reacting to the cues in the room. Similar work with rats has been more disputed. The finding supports the idea that a basic form of metacognition is older than humans.
Teaching how to think about thinking

Schools have tried teaching metacognition directly. That means showing students how to plan a task, check their progress and reflect on what worked afterward. The Education Endowment Foundation, a British charity that reviews the evidence, has long rated this among the most promising approaches in schools, adding several months of progress on average, and at very low cost.
The same review stresses a catch. It's hard to get that benefit in practice. The approaches that work are taught inside a particular subject and not as a general course on study skills, and students need practice with real tasks. Telling people to reflect doesn't work as well as modeling how an expert plans and checks their own work out loud. It's a good guide for teaching yourself.

In 2010 Adrian Owen and his colleagues recruited more than 11,000 people to follow online brain-training programs for several weeks. People improved at the tasks they practiced, as you'd expect. But the improvement did not carry over to other mental tasks, even ones that were closely related.
In 2016 Daniel Simons and his colleagues reviewed the evidence behind the claims of the brain-training industry. They concluded that there was good evidence that practice improves performance on the trained tasks, but little evidence that it improves everyday abilities. This doesn't mean that your brain can't change. It means that getting better at a puzzle mostly makes you better at that puzzle. To improve at something real, practice the real thing.
The Dunning-Kruger effect, as usually told

In 1999 Justin Kruger and David Dunning found that people who scored lowest on tests of humor, grammar and logic tended to estimate that they had done much better than they had. The popular summary is that unskilled people are too ignorant to know they are ignorant, and that experts are the humble ones.
The truth is more mixed. Some researchers have argued that a lot of the pattern comes from statistics. Everyone's self-ratings are noisy, and when you sort people by score, the lowest group will tend to guess too high and the highest group too low, even if people had no bias at all. Other work finds that the lowest scorers really do overestimate more than can be explained by chance. So it's not a law that fools are confident. Everyone should check their own judgments against real feedback.
The rules we follow without knowing

The philosopher Paul Grice noticed that conversation runs on an unspoken agreement to cooperate. In his 1975 lecture, he described four habits that speakers assume of each other. Say as much as is needed and no more. Say what you believe is true. Stay on topic. Be clear and orderly. We rarely notice these habits, but we rely on them all the time.
Because we assume them, we can get meaning from what is left out. If someone says that some of the students passed, you hear that not all of them did, since otherwise they would have said all. Grice called such unstated messages implicatures. A great deal of what people mean sits there, and many misunderstandings happen when two people assume different rules.

Most sentences describe the world, but some do something. When a judge says "I sentence you," or a person says "I promise" or "I do," saying the words is the act. The philosopher J. L. Austin, in lectures that were published after his death in 1962, called these performative utterances, and he argued that they can't be called true or false. They can only succeed or fail.
For one to work, the circumstances have to be right. A promise needs someone who means to keep it, and a wedding vow needs a person who is allowed to marry. Austin's insight was that speaking is a kind of action. It's a good thing to remember when you say sorry, thank someone or make a promise. You aren't reporting a feeling, you are doing something that changes the relationship.

Why do we say "Would you like to come up and see my etchings?" instead of just saying what we want? In 2008 Steven Pinker, Martin Nowak and James Lee argued that indirect speech gives the speaker plausible deniability. If the listener is willing, both of them get what they want. If not, the speaker can say that no offer was made, and nobody has to lose face.
The authors used a driver trying to bribe a police officer as an example. "Is there some way we could take care of the ticket here?" can't easily be used as proof of bribery, though both people understand it. The same logic applies in social situations with no legal risk, and in relationships where being too direct might change what two people are to each other. Hints let us test the waters.
Hearing your name across the room

In a crowded room, you can follow one voice and screen out the others. In 1953 Colin Cherry named this the cocktail party problem and studied it by playing different messages to each ear and asking people to repeat one. People could follow the chosen message well and noticed little about the other, beyond whether it was a man's or a woman's voice.
But not everything gets filtered out. In 1959 Neville Moray found that about a third of people noticed their own name when it was played in the ear they were supposed to be ignoring. Your name, and other highly meaningful words, can break through. Attention seems to be a filter that is leaky for what matters to you most. It's why you can suddenly tune in to a conversation across the room when someone mentions you.

In 1976 Harry McGurk and John MacDonald made a discovery by accident while working with infants. They showed adults a video of a person saying "ga" while the soundtrack played "ba." Most people heard neither. They heard "da," a sound in between, as though the brain were blending what they saw with what they heard.
The effect is strong, and it works even when you know about it. If you close your eyes, you hear "ba" again, and when you open them, it shifts back. It shows that speech perception isn't just hearing. Your brain combines sound with the movements of the speaker's lips, which is one reason why it's easier to understand someone in a noisy room when you can see their face.

Adults all over the world change their voices when they talk to babies. They go higher, slower and more musical, with an exaggerated rise and fall. In 1985 Anne Fernald found that young infants prefer to listen to this kind of speech over normal adult speech. It seems to hold their attention and to signal that the message is for them.
In 2022 Courtney Hilton and his colleagues looked at recordings from dozens of societies in different parts of the world. Speech and song directed at infants shared acoustic features that set them apart from adult-directed speech and song. And thousands of listeners from many countries could tell, most of the time, whether a recording was meant for a baby. It suggests a shared human way of soothing and engaging the very young.

Gossip has a poor reputation, but in 2014 Matthew Feinberg, Robb Willer and Michael Schultz found that it can help a group cooperate. They had people play a game in which each player could contribute to a shared pot or keep money for themselves. When players could pass notes about each other's behavior, and could exclude those who didn't contribute, cooperation went up.
