Selfish players changed their behavior when they knew that their reputations would travel. The study doesn't show that all gossip is good, since gossip can be cruel and false. But it helps to explain why people talk about others' conduct so much. In small groups with no police, a reputation is a way of enforcing fairness. Our wish to talk about who did what may have grown out of that need.

If it seems that people love talking about themselves, there may be a reason. In 2012 Diana Tamir and Jason Mitchell scanned people's brains while they were answering questions about their own opinions, or about someone else's. Thinking and talking about themselves lit up areas of the brain's reward system more than thinking about another person did.
In another experiment, people were offered a choice. They could answer a question about themselves, or about others, and get paid slightly more for the second option. Many took less money in order to talk about themselves. It suggests that self-disclosure is rewarding in itself. The practical lesson for conversation is a kind one. Asking someone about themselves gives them something they enjoy, and you can offer it for free.

In 1996 Bella DePaulo and her colleagues asked people to keep a diary of their lies for a week. On average, people reported telling about one or two lies a day. Most were small, told to smooth things over, to avoid hurting someone, or to make themselves look a little better. Few were serious, and most people felt little regret.
But an average can mislead. In 2010 Kim Serota, Timothy Levine and Franklin Boster surveyed a large sample of Americans. Most people reported telling no lies in the past day, and a small group of prolific liars accounted for a large share of all the lies. Later studies in other countries found a similar skew. The picture is that most people are honest most of the time, and a few people tell a great many lies.
Why a name is harder than a job

You meet someone at a party, and a week later you remember that they are a baker, but not that their name is Baker. In 1987 Kate McWeeny and her colleagues tested this. People learned faces paired with surnames and occupations. Some labels were both, like Baker, Cook and Potter. Those labels were remembered better when they were presented as an occupation than when they were presented as a name.
The researchers concluded that names are hard because they usually don't mean anything. A job is attached to a rich set of ideas, such as bread, ovens and early mornings, while a surname often has no meaning to hook onto. This is why a trick to remember names is to give them a meaning, such as a picture. It also explains why forgetting names is normal, and not a sign of a poor memory.
Easy to read, easy to believe

In 1999 Rolf Reber and Norbert Schwarz showed people statements such as "Osorno is in Chile," printed in colors on a white background. Some colors were easy to read and some were faint. People were more likely to judge a statement true when it was easy to read than when it was hard to read, though the statements were the same.
The authors proposed that people use the feeling of ease, which they called processing fluency, as a clue to truth. If something is easy to take in, it feels more familiar, and familiar feels right. The effect is modest, but it appears in many settings. It's a reason to make your own writing easy to read, and a reason to be wary when something seems right because it was presented well.
Long words make you sound less smart

Many people think that using long words makes them look intelligent. In 2006 Daniel Oppenheimer tested this by giving people texts and asking them to rate the intelligence of the writer. In one version, he took a plain essay and replaced words with longer synonyms from a thesaurus. In others, he made texts harder to read in other ways, with a fancier font or poorer printing.
The result was the opposite of what people expect. Texts that were harder to read, or that used complicated words that weren't needed, led readers to rate the author as less intelligent. The reason may be the same as for the last lesson. Hard writing feels like effort, and readers blame the writer. The title of his paper has a joke in it, and it's good advice. Use the simplest word that says what you mean.

In 2011 Paul Thibodeau and Lera Boroditsky gave people a short report on rising crime in a city. In one version, crime was described as a virus infecting the city, and in the other as a beast preying on it. The facts were the same. Then they asked what the city should do about it.
People who read about a virus were more likely to suggest reforms such as fixing the causes, and people who read about a beast were more likely to suggest punishment and enforcement. Few said that the metaphor had influenced them. Some later studies found smaller or less consistent effects, so the size of the effect is uncertain. But the idea matters. The pictures we use to describe a problem can quietly shape which solutions seem natural.
Describing a face can make you forget it

In 1990 Jonathan Schooler and Tonya Engstler-Schooler had people watch a short film of a bank robbery. Some of them then wrote a description of the robber's face, and others did something unrelated. Later, everyone tried to pick the robber out of a lineup. The ones who had described the face were less accurate.
The researchers called this verbal overshadowing. Putting a visual memory into words seems to replace some of it with a description, and the description is a poorer guide than the picture. A large multi-lab replication in 2014 found the effect again, though it was smaller than the original. It suggests that for things like faces, tastes and wines, you may recognize things better than you can describe them, and trying to describe them may get in the way.

In 2009 Cameron Anderson and Gavin Kilduff studied groups of students who had never met before, and had them solve problems together. They measured who in each group was dominant, meaning who liked to take charge, and then asked group members, observers and the researchers to rate everyone's competence.
The dominant people were rated as more competent, even after the researchers accounted for how good they actually were at the task. The way they behaved gave the impression, because they spoke up first, spoke more often, and sounded sure. Being right wasn't what earned the status. The finding is a warning in groups. A confident voice is not the same as a correct one, so it's worth asking for the reasoning.

Written conversation has lost the tone of voice, so punctuation takes on a job. In 2016 Danielle Gunraj and her colleagues showed people text messages that either ended with a period or didn't. For example, a friend replies "Sure" or "Sure." when invited to dinner. The messages that ended with a period were rated as less sincere than those that didn't.
The same effect did not show up on handwritten notes, so it seems to be a feature of texting, where people usually drop the period. Norms like this keep changing, and they differ with age and from group to group, so the effect may be different where you are. But the lesson is useful. In text, small signals carry more meaning than you may intend, and a short reply can read as cold.
Strangers can feel emotion in a touch

In 2006 Matthew Hertenstein and his colleagues ran an experiment in which a person was asked to communicate an emotion to a stranger using touch alone. They sat on opposite sides of a screen, so neither could see or speak to the other. The sender could touch the receiver's forearm in any way they liked.
The receivers, who were guessing from a list of emotions, were able to identify several of them at better than chance levels. They included anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude and sympathy. Touch can carry a message without any words. It's one reason why a hand on the shoulder can comfort someone in a way that a sentence can't, and why being touched in the wrong way can feel so wrong.

In a series of lab experiments, Guy Itzchakov and his colleagues asked people to talk about their views on a topic to a listener who behaved in different ways. A high-quality listener paid close attention, didn't interrupt, and showed that they understood. A poor listener seemed distracted and impatient.
Speakers who were well listened to felt less anxious, thought more carefully about their own views, and became more aware of the contradictions in them. Later studies by the same group suggested that good listening can reduce how extreme a person's attitudes are during a disagreement. Most of this evidence comes from one research group and from lab settings, so it needs more testing. But it suggests that listening is more than a courtesy. It can change the way the other person thinks.
The story that changed in the retelling

In the 1920s Frederic Bartlett gave students at Cambridge a Native American folktale called The War of the Ghosts, and later asked them to retell it. Then he asked them to tell it again, and again, over weeks and months. The stories grew shorter, and details that didn't fit English expectations dropped out or changed.
Bartlett argued that memory isn't a recording. It's a reconstruction in which we fit what we heard to what we already know. Later researchers who tried to repeat his work found that his results were less dramatic than he reported, and that people sometimes do very well on retelling when they are asked to be accurate. Even so, the point stands that stories change as they pass from person to person.

In 1995 Betty Hart and Todd Risley published a study that followed forty-two American families and recorded how much parents talked to their young children. They found that children in professional families heard far more words than those in families receiving welfare. Extended over the early years, the gap was said to be thirty million words.
The idea changed policy and led to campaigns encouraging parents to talk more to their children. But the original sample was small and not typical. In 2019 Douglas Sperry, Linda Sperry and Peggy Miller studied families in several communities and found much more variety, and did not find the large differences. Talking with a child is surely good for them, though recent work suggests that the back and forth of real conversation matters more than a count of words.

In 2013 Andrew Przybylski and Netta Weinstein asked pairs of strangers to have a ten minute conversation. In some pairs, a mobile phone sat on the table, and in others a notebook did. The pairs with the phone nearby later reported less closeness and trust, and less sense that the other person understood them, especially when they were talking about something meaningful.
The idea is that a phone is a reminder of everything else that could be happening, so people hold back. Later studies have had mixed results, and some did not find the same effect. The study is a reminder that attention is a gift in conversation, and that a phone in view may affect it. If someone is telling you something that matters, it costs little to put it away.

Why do so many speeches use lists of three? "Government of the people, by the people, for the people." "Education, education, education." In the 1980s the sociologist Max Atkinson, and then John Heritage and David Greatbatch, studied recordings of political speeches and the moments when audiences applauded. They wanted to know what triggered it.
They found that a small number of rhetorical formats were behind a large share of the applause. Two stood out. One was the three-part list, and the other was a contrast, such as "not this, but that." These patterns let the audience know in advance when the point is about to be completed, so they could start clapping together. A pattern helps listeners follow a speech, and makes it easy for them to join in.

As a child, the writer Sylvia Wright loved a ballad that her mother read aloud. She heard the line "They hae slain the Earl o' Moray, and laid him on the green" as "and Lady Mondegreen." She imagined the lady dying beside him. In 1954 she wrote about it in Harper's Magazine, and gave the name mondegreen to the mishearing of words that creates a new meaning.
The classic examples are lyrics, such as hearing "excuse me while I kiss this guy." They happen because we don't hear speech word by word. The sounds run together, and the brain fills in gaps using what it expects. When the expectation is wrong, we hear something else, and it can feel completely real. It's a small demonstration that what we hear is partly built by the mind.

Read this sentence and see what happens: "The horse raced past the barn fell." Most people stumble at the last word and feel that it is a mistake. But it is a correct English sentence. It means that the horse that was raced past the barn is the one that fell. Thomas Bever described such sentences in 1970 and called them garden path sentences.
They are called garden path sentences because they lead you down one path and then leave you stranded. When we read, we don't wait for the end of a sentence to decide what it means. We guess as we go, and commit to the most likely reading. When the guess is wrong, we have to go back. It shows how quickly we build meaning, and how often that quick guess is the right one.

In 1957 the linguist Noam Chomsky offered a sentence that is nonsense but still sounds like English: "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously." He compared it with "Furiously sleep ideas green colorless," which sounds wrong. His point was that grammar and meaning are separate. We can feel that one string is a sentence even when it makes no sense.
The sentence was meant to show that a language isn't just a matter of what is likely to be said. We seem to hold a system of rules in our heads that tells us what is well formed, and that system works on its own. Later researchers have argued about how much of language is rules and how much is experience. But the example is still a good way to feel that you know a structure that no one ever taught you.

Look at two shapes. One is rounded and soft, and the other is jagged and spiky. Which is called bouba, and which is kiki? Nearly everyone says that bouba is the round one and kiki is the spiky one. The psychologist Wolfgang Köhler found this pattern in the 1920s with other made-up words, and Vilayanur Ramachandran and Edward Hubbard tested it again in 2001.
It isn't just a matter of English speakers. In 2013 Gavin Bremner and his colleagues tested the Himba, a people in Namibia who have no written language, and they matched the words and shapes in the same way. The sounds of a word seem to have a link to its shape. Most words are arbitrary, but this shows a small, shared pull in how people connect sounds and meanings.

In 1978 Robert Cialdini and his colleagues asked students to join a psychology experiment. For some of them, the researcher first got a yes, and only then mentioned that the session started at seven in the morning. For others, the early start was stated in the first request. Roughly half of the students who were asked the first way agreed, compared with about a quarter to a third who were told up front.
Most of the people who had said yes before they knew the cost showed up, even though they were free to back out. The first yes created a commitment, and the later cost didn't undo it. Sellers sometimes advertise a very low price, then add fees. A later meta-analysis found that the technique works across many studies. A good defense is to ask for the full cost before you say yes.

Imagine two used cars. One has 79,999 miles on the odometer, and the other has 80,001. They are nearly the same car. In 2012 Nicola Lacetera, Devin Pope and Justin Sydnor looked at more than twenty million wholesale used-car sales and found that prices drop sharply at each ten thousand mile mark. The drop was around one or two hundred dollars, just from crossing the line.
The reason seems to be that people focus on the leftmost digit of a number and pay less attention to the rest. A mileage of 79,999 reads as seventy something, and 80,001 as eighty. Sellers seemed to know it, because many more cars were brought to auction just before crossing a threshold. It's a case of a sensible-looking market being moved by a quirk in how we read numbers.

Suppose a seller asks five thousand dollars for a car. Another asks $4,985. Which is more likely to be negotiable? In 2008 Chris Janiszewski and Dan Uy found that the precision of an opening number changes how far people move from it. When the anchor was precise, people adjusted their own estimate less than when it was round.
A round number seems like a rough estimate that can be bargained down. A precise number seems to come from careful calculation, so it feels firmer. Later studies of negotiation found that a precise first offer made people think that the other side knew more, and they made smaller counteroffers. If you want to hold your price, a precise number can help. If you're on the other side of the table, it helps to know that the number is not necessarily more reliable.

In 2006 Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier studied the records of several health clubs. Many members chose a monthly contract of over seventy dollars. These members went to the club about four times a month, on average. When the researchers worked out what they paid for each visit, it came to about seventeen dollars, though a ten dollar pay-per-visit option was available.
Members seemed to be too optimistic about how often they would go. The monthly plan felt like a commitment to exercise, but the plan paid off for the club and not for them. Many also stayed on the plan for months after they had stopped going. The study applies to any subscription. We tend to buy for the person we hope to be, and not for the person we are.

In 2006 Anja Lambrecht and Bernd Skiera analyzed the choices of customers of internet access providers. Many customers chose a flat rate, though they would have paid less on a plan that charged for what they used. The researchers called this the flat-rate bias. They found that it is common in many kinds of services.
They suggested several reasons. People like to know their bills in advance. They are afraid of running up charges, and they overestimate how much they'll use. A flat rate also takes away the feeling of paying each time, which can spoil the enjoyment of a service. It's a sensible choice for some people, since the peace of mind can be worth a few extra dollars. It helps to know what you are paying for, though.

When you search for a flight, would you rather get results instantly or wait a bit? In 2011 Ryan Buell and Michael Norton tested this with simulated travel sites. Some showed only a progress bar. Others showed the site working, with a running list of the airlines it was checking. Results were the same in each case.
People valued the search more, and rated the site higher, when it showed its work, even when it made them wait longer. The researchers called it the labor illusion. We tend to value a service more when we can see the effort behind it. This is why a plumber who explains what they're doing can seem more valuable, and why a restaurant with an open kitchen can feel special. Showing the work can be worth the wait.
The complaint that wins a customer

Imagine that a company makes a mistake, and then fixes it very well. Could you end up liking them more than if nothing had gone wrong? In the 1990s researchers who study customer service called this the service recovery paradox, and early studies suggested that it could happen. Customers who were treated generously after a failure sometimes gave higher ratings than those who had no problem at all.
Later reviews found that the effect is smaller and less reliable than it first seemed. It tends to show up only when the failure is small, when it's the first one, and when the fix is fast and goes beyond what was needed. A big failure or a repeated one can wipe it out. The safe conclusion is that a good fix is worth making, but it's no reason to plan for failures.

Suppose that you're choosing a camera, and you see two models, one cheap and basic and one expensive and excellent. Now a third, in the middle, is added. In 1989 Itamar Simonson showed that adding a middle option can change what people pick, with more people choosing the one in the middle than before. He called it the compromise effect.
People are often unsure how to compare features, so they use a simple rule. The extreme options feel risky, and the middle option feels safe and defensible. It's a reason why menus and price lists often have a high-priced item that few people buy. Its job is to make the next one down look moderate. When you notice yourself picking the middle, ask whether it is the best for you, or just the one that is easiest to justify.

Which is better, a two percent raise when prices are rising by four percent, or a two percent pay cut when prices are not rising at all? In real terms, the raise leaves you worse off. In 1997 Eldar Shafir, Peter Diamond and Amos Tversky found that many people said that the raise was better, and they felt better about it.
We tend to think about money in the numbers on the paper, and not in what it can buy. The researchers called it the money illusion. It has real effects. Employers find it easier to hold wages steady in real terms by giving small raises than to cut pay, and people feel richer when their wages go up in a time of high inflation. It's a reminder to ask what a number will buy.

In 1985 Richard Thaler asked people to imagine lying on a beach on a hot day, wishing for a cold bottle of beer. A friend offers to bring one from either a fancy resort hotel or a run-down grocery store. They were asked how much they would pay. The bottle was the same, and they would drink it on the beach either way.
People said that they would pay more when the beer came from the resort. The median answers were about two dollars sixty-five for the hotel and one dollar fifty for the store. Thaler argued that we get a second kind of pleasure from a deal. It's the sense that the price was fair compared with what we expected to pay. It explains why a price that seems unreasonable in one place can feel fine in another.

In 1986 Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler asked people in Canada a question. A hardware store has been selling snow shovels for fifteen dollars. The morning after a large snowstorm, the store raises the price to twenty. Is that fair? Most people, over eight in ten, said that it was unfair.
By the usual logic of supply and demand, the price should rise when demand rises. But people judge a price against a reference point, which is the price they were used to, and they see a rise as taking advantage of someone's need. This explains why companies avoid raising prices after disasters, and why surge pricing can anger customers. Fairness is a force in markets, and it is hard to explain by logic alone.

When you have money to spend, should you buy something to have, or something to do? In 2003 Leaf Van Boven and Thomas Gilovich asked people about recent purchases of each kind. Purchases made to gain an experience, such as a trip or a concert, tended to make people happier than purchases made to own something, such as a gadget or a piece of clothing.
They suggested several reasons. Experiences are more a part of who we are, they're often shared with other people, and they are harder to compare unfavorably with other options. Things lose their novelty as we get used to them. The finding comes with caveats, since the line between the two kinds is blurry, and a thing you use to do something can be an experience. But it's a handy guide when you're deciding where to spend.

In 2013 Anandi Mani and her colleagues studied sugarcane farmers in India. The farmers get most of their income at harvest, so before the harvest they are short of money, and after it they are better off. The same farmers did worse on tests of reasoning and attention before the harvest than after it.
In another experiment, shoppers at a New Jersey mall were asked what they would do if they faced a car repair bill. Lower income people did worse on a reasoning test after thinking about a large bill than after a small bill, while higher income people were not affected. The idea is that worry about money takes up mental space. Some later studies have found weaker effects, so the size of the effect is still under debate. But it suggests that being short of money can affect thinking, and not just the other way round.
You are free to say no

In 2000 Nicolas Guéguen and Alexandre Pascual asked people on the street for a small amount of money. Some were asked in the usual way. Others were asked, and then told "but you are free to accept or to refuse." People who heard the extra sentence were more likely to give. Reminding them that the choice was theirs seemed to take away the feeling of being pushed.
A 2013 review by Christopher Carpenter found that the technique tended to work across studies. But a later and more careful review found that when it limited itself to the best designed studies, the effect shrank a lot, and it may be weaker than it looked. The idea is plausible. People resist pressure, and when they are left free to choose, they are often more willing. Whatever the size of the effect, it's a kind and honest way to ask.

In 1999 Barbara Davis and Eric Knowles went door to door selling packs of note cards for a charity. They varied how they stated the price. The usual pitch was "the cards are three dollars." In another version the seller said the price in an odd way, "three hundred pennies," and then added "that's a bargain."
More people bought when the price was said in the odd way and then reframed as a bargain. The researchers called it disrupt-then-reframe. The strange phrase interrupted the usual script that people use to say no, and the reframing pointed them to a reason to say yes. Later researchers found that the effect is not always reliable, and it works best in some conditions. It's an example of how a small surprise can briefly stop an automatic refusal.

What would happen if you let customers set their own price? In 2010 Ayelet Gneezy and her colleagues tested this at an amusement park, where a photo of visitors on a ride was normally sold at a fixed price. They tried letting customers pay whatever they wanted. Far more people bought, but the average price was under a dollar, which was less than the photo cost to make.
When the researchers added a promise that half of the price would go to charity, the results changed. People paid much more than under plain pay what you want, and the park's total revenue ended up greater than under the fixed price. Offering charity at a fixed price did not help. The idea was that the charity link gave people a reason to pay a fair amount, when they were free to choose. Later studies of pay what you want have been mixed. It seems to work best with small shared goals, and where customers feel a connection to the seller.

When you try to persuade someone, is it better to present only your side or to mention the other? In 1999 Daniel O'Keefe combined the results of many experiments. The answer was that it depends on how you do it. A message that mentions the opposing view and then answers it was more persuasive than a one-sided message.
Mentioning the other side without answering it was the least persuasive of all. It seems to make people think of reasons against you, and leave them with nothing to put against them. The refutation is what counts. It shows that you've thought about the objections, and it makes you seem fair and honest. If you want to make a case, bring up the strongest objection yourself, and say why you still think you're right.
Don't tell me what to do

In 1966 the psychologist Jack Brehm proposed that when people feel that their freedom to choose is threatened, they push back. He called it reactance. A pushy sales pitch, a strict order or a ban can make the forbidden thing more attractive. Parents of teenagers know the effect well.
In 1996 Brad Bushman and Angela Stack tested it with warning labels. People were shown descriptions of television programs, with or without a label saying that the show was violent. The labeled programs were more attractive to many of the viewers. The effect isn't universal, but it explains why a heavy-handed approach can backfire. Giving people reasons and choices tends to work better than giving them orders.
Why a quiet message can stick

In 1951 Carl Hovland and Walter Weiss gave people messages from sources that were trustworthy or not. At first, people were persuaded more by the trustworthy sources. But several weeks later, the difference had shrunk, because people had forgotten where the message came from while still remembering the message. They called it the sleeper effect.
It has been hard to reproduce. A review in 2004 by Tarcan Kumkale and Dolores Albarracín concluded that it happens under certain conditions. It is most likely if people only learn about the weakness of the source after they've heard the message, and if they have a chance to forget it. The finding is a reminder that a claim from a poor source can lose its label in your memory, and what is left is the claim.
A small dose of the trick

In the 1960s William McGuire proposed that people could be protected against persuasion in the same way as against disease. If you give a weak version of an argument, with a refutation, people build defenses. He called it inoculation. The idea sat for years, and in recent times it has been applied to misinformation.
In 2022 Jon Roozenbeek and his colleagues tested short videos that explained common manipulation tricks, such as scapegoating and false dilemmas, without being about any single topic. After the videos, people were better at spotting these techniques in new examples. The effects were modest, and they fade over time without a reminder. It's a promising idea for defending against persuasion. Learning how a trick works makes it harder to fool you.
The story that made trash worth more

In 2009 the writers Rob Walker and Joshua Glenn ran a project to test the power of a story. They bought about a hundred cheap objects, mostly at thrift shops, such as a plastic horse head or a toy mouse. They asked writers to invent a short story about each one, and then sold them online with the story in the listing.
The objects had cost about 129 dollars in total, and they sold for about 3,600 dollars, nearly thirty times as much. It wasn't a controlled experiment, and some buyers were motivated by the project as well as by the objects. But it fits with other studies about stories and value. We don't buy only what a thing is. We buy what it means, and a good story can supply the meaning.
The note that was written by hand

In 2005 Randy Garner mailed surveys to a large number of people. Some got just a cover letter and some a letter with a signature. Others got a small sticky note, written by hand, asking for help. The people with the handwritten note were much more likely to fill in and send back the survey.
Garner suggested that a personal note shows that someone has taken the time to ask. Since it's hard to fake, it triggers a feeling of wanting to return the favor. The effect has been seen in other studies of requests. It's a reminder that in an age of automated messages, a small sign of real effort can stand out. If you need something from someone, take a minute to write them a few personal words.

Avoiding what frightens us feels safe, but the fear tends to stay. Exposure therapy goes the other way. A person faces the feared thing, such as a crowded place, a memory or a physical sensation, in small steps and with support, until the fear falls on its own. In 1986 Edna Foa and Michael Kozak described this as a process of getting new information that doesn't fit the fear.
Exposure is among the best supported treatments for phobias, panic, obsessive compulsive disorder and PTSD. More recent work by Michelle Craske and her colleagues has changed the way it's understood. The old fear isn't erased. A new memory is learned beside it, that the feared thing did not lead to disaster. That helps explain why practice in different places and at different times makes the benefits last.

A panic attack can feel like a heart attack, and the first one is often terrifying. In 1986 the psychologist David Clark proposed an explanation for why some people go on to have more of them. They notice a bodily sensation, such as a racing heart or dizziness, and read it as a sign of immediate danger. The fear makes the sensation stronger, and that seems to confirm the danger.
The result is a loop, with the person afraid of the very sensations that fear produces. This helps explain why panic can seem to come from nowhere. Treatments built on this idea teach people that the sensations are harmless, and let them experience those sensations on purpose until they lose their power. The sensations are unpleasant but not dangerous in themselves, and an attack usually peaks within minutes. New chest pain is still worth having checked by a doctor.

Many anxious people have rituals that make them feel safe. They sit near the exit, carry a bottle of water, avoid eye contact, or rehearse every sentence before they speak. In 1991 Paul Salkovskis called these safety behaviors, and pointed out that they have a hidden cost. When nothing bad happens, the person credits the safety behavior and not the fact that the situation was safe.
So the belief that danger is near is never tested. Treatment often involves dropping the safety behavior and seeing what happens. A person with social anxiety might speak without rehearsing, or stay in the room without checking the exit. They find that the feared outcome mostly doesn't happen, or that they can cope with it. The crutch helps in the moment and keeps the fear in place.
Why avoidance feels like a solution

In the 1940s the psychologist O. Hobart Mowrer offered a two part explanation for why fears last. The first part is that a fear is learned, when something frightening becomes linked to a place or a sign. The second is that avoiding the feared thing brings immediate relief, and relief rewards the avoidance. So the person learns to avoid it again.
This is why a fear can last for decades. Each time you steer around it, you feel better and you lose a chance to find out that the thing was not so dangerous. The relief is real, but it comes at a cost, because your world shrinks. It's also why gradual approach is the usual way out. Each small step that you take without disaster teaches you something that avoidance never can.

People who worry a lot often feel that their worrying protects them, as though thinking about a bad thing might stop it from happening. In 2020 Lauren LaFreniere and Michelle Newman tested what happens to worries over time. In a small study of people with generalized anxiety disorder, participants wrote down what they were worried about, and then checked later what had really happened.
About nine in ten of the worries did not come true. And for many of those that did, people said that they had coped better than they had feared. Seeing this in black and white seemed to help some people worry less. The study was small, and it was about people in treatment, so it doesn't prove that worrying is always pointless. But keeping a record of your worries and checking them later is a simple test that anyone can try.

In the 1960s the psychiatrist Aaron Beck noticed a pattern in what his depressed patients said. They saw themselves as worthless, they saw the world as unfair or empty, and they saw the future as hopeless. He called these three views the cognitive triad. They didn't seem like symptoms of a low mood alone. They seemed to be part of what kept the mood low.
Beck's idea was that these views could be examined, like any other belief. If you think that you are a failure, you can ask what the evidence is, and what you'd say to a friend. This was the beginning of cognitive therapy, which has since been tested in hundreds of trials. It doesn't work by pushing out negative thoughts. It works by treating them as ideas to check, and not as facts.

Do antidepressants work? In 2018 Andrea Cipriani and his colleagues combined the results of more than five hundred trials with over a hundred thousand people. They compared twenty-one drugs with placebo and with each other. Every one of the drugs was more effective than placebo for adults with major depression, though the advantage was modest on average.
The drugs differed a little in how well they worked and in how well people tolerated them. The authors stressed that the best choice depends on the person. Some people respond a lot, and others hardly at all, and an average can hide that. In trials of these drugs, many people also improve on a placebo, which is one reason the measured advantage looks small. The sensible message is that antidepressants help many people, and that treatment is best decided with a doctor.

For decades, many people were told that depression is caused by a chemical imbalance, a shortage of serotonin in the brain. In 2022 Joanna Moncrieff and her colleagues reviewed the research on this idea. They concluded that there was no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin levels or activity.
The review was widely discussed, and critics said that it was too narrow, and that the field has long since moved beyond a simple serotonin story. Other scientists think that serotonin may play a role in some people, or in the way that drugs work. What nobody has shown is that a person's depression comes from a single known shortfall. If you take medicine for depression, this debate is not a reason to stop. Talk to your prescriber before making any change.

Does exercise help with low mood and anxiety? In 2023 Ben Singh and his colleagues gathered the results of nearly a hundred reviews of studies on physical activity and mental health. They found that physical activity helped to reduce symptoms of depression, anxiety and distress, with a moderate effect on average, across many groups of people.
The effect was seen for walking, jogging, strength training and yoga. Shorter programs, of up to twelve weeks, tended to show larger benefits than longer ones, and higher intensity showed more benefit in some analyses. The researchers noted that the quality of many of the studies was limited. But the result agrees with other work. Exercise is not a replacement for therapy or medicine when you need them. It is a useful addition that costs little and has few downsides.

If you often lie awake in bed, your brain may learn to link the bed with being awake. In 1972 Richard Bootzin proposed a treatment based on this idea, called stimulus control. The rules are simple. Go to bed only when you feel sleepy. Use the bed only for sleep, and not for work, scrolling or watching television. If you can't fall asleep after about twenty minutes, get up and do something quiet until you feel sleepy again.
It sounds strange to leave your bed when you want to sleep, but the goal is to break the connection between bed and frustration. Stimulus control is one part of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, and it has been tested in many trials. It works best when it's kept up for a few weeks. It also asks you to keep a regular time for getting up, even after a poor night.
The first treatment for insomnia isn't a pill

In 2016 the American College of Physicians published guidelines for treating long-term insomnia in adults. After reviewing the evidence, it recommended that all adults with chronic insomnia first try cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, often called CBT-I. Medicines were to be considered only if that didn't work, and after a discussion of benefits and risks.
CBT-I is a short course, usually a few weeks, that combines a regular sleep schedule, stimulus control, limits on time in bed, and a way of dealing with worried thoughts about sleep. Studies find that it often works as well as sleeping pills in the short term and better in the long term, because the benefits last after the treatment stops. It can be done with a therapist, or with a well made program or book.

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is sometimes described as the result of poor parenting or too much screen time. The evidence points in a different direction. In 2019 Stephen Faraone and Henrik Larsson reviewed studies of twins and families and concluded that ADHD is highly heritable, with about three quarters of the differences between people explained by genes.
That puts it among the more heritable conditions in psychiatry. It doesn't mean that the environment doesn't matter, or that a gene alone causes it. Many genes, each with a small effect, are involved, along with other influences, such as prematurity and early exposures. The finding matters because it changes how a family and a person can think about it. ADHD is a difference in how the brain manages attention and impulses. It is not a failure of character.
No link between vaccines and autism

In 1998 a British doctor, Andrew Wakefield, published a paper in The Lancet that suggested a link between the MMR vaccine and autism. It was based on twelve children, and it set off a long scare. The paper was found to have serious problems, including undisclosed conflicts of interest and unethical methods, and The Lancet retracted it in 2010.
Since then the question has been studied many times. In 2014 Luke Taylor and his colleagues combined the results of studies that included more than a million children. They found no relationship between vaccination and autism, and none between the ingredients in vaccines and autism. The scare did real damage, since falling vaccination rates were followed by outbreaks of measles. Autism has strong genetic roots, and its signs often become visible at about the age when children receive certain vaccines, which is why the timing fooled people.

After a disaster or an accident, it seems natural to gather the survivors and have them go through what happened in detail, in one session. This was once standard practice, and it was called psychological debriefing. The idea was that talking early would prevent later problems such as PTSD.
In 2002 Suzanna Rose and her colleagues reviewed the trials. They found no evidence that a single debriefing session reduced the risk of PTSD, and in some of the trials, people who took part did worse. This doesn't mean that people shouldn't talk. It means that pressing people to relive an event right away may not help. The guidance now is to offer practical support, to keep people safe, and to be available, and to let each person choose when to talk.

In 2019 Thomas Curran and Andrew Hill combined 164 samples of college students in the United States, Canada and Britain. The students had filled out the same questionnaire about perfectionism between 1989 and 2016. Scores went up in a steady line for three kinds of perfectionism, the kind you demand of yourself, the kind you demand of others, and the kind you feel others demand of you.
The largest increase was in socially prescribed perfectionism, the belief that other people expect you to be perfect. The authors linked this to more competitive schools and workplaces, and to social media. Perfectionism isn't just high standards. It is tied to anxiety, depression and burnout. The rise is a reason to think about the standards that you set for yourself, and who you imagine is judging them.

In 2008 Jean Twenge and her colleagues reported that scores on a widely used narcissism questionnaire had risen among American college students since the 1980s. They suggested that a culture of self-esteem and social media was making young people more self-centered. The idea was taken up by the press, and it became a familiar claim about younger generations.
The same year, Kali Trzesniewski, Brent Donnellan and Richard Robins analyzed other, larger sets of data, and they found no increase. Other researchers have since looked at the question with different methods and have found small changes or none. It's a case where experts looked at much the same numbers and drew different conclusions. It's a good reminder to be cautious about stories that every new generation is worse than the one before.
Don't think of a white bear

In 1987 Daniel Wegner and his colleagues asked people to say whatever came to mind for five minutes, and told them not to think of a white bear. They rang a bell every time they did. People thought of the bear more than once a minute, on average. Then they were told to think of a white bear if they wanted, and those who had tried to suppress it thought of it more than the people who had been free to think of it all along.
This was called the rebound effect, and it has been used to explain why trying to push away an unwanted thought can make it more frequent. Later studies found that the rebound is not always seen, and that the size of the effect varies. But the idea that suppression can backfire has influenced therapies that teach people to notice thoughts and let them pass, and not fight them.

Have you ever had a sudden thought about hurting someone you love, or jumping from a high place, or doing something awful in public? Most people have. In 2014 Adam Radomsky and his colleagues asked hundreds of people in thirteen countries about unwanted intrusive thoughts. Almost everyone, over nine in ten, said that they had them.
For most people, these thoughts pass without any trouble. The difference in people with obsessive compulsive disorder is not that they have the thoughts. It's what they make of them. If you believe that a thought means something about who you are, you may try to control it, and that can make it worse. Knowing that intrusive thoughts are common can take away a good deal of their power.
A placebo you know is a placebo

Placebos are thought to work only if people believe they are real medicine. In 2010 Ted Kaptchuk and his colleagues tried something different. They gave eighty people with irritable bowel syndrome either no treatment or pills that were clearly labeled as placebos, made of an inert substance, and told them that placebos can produce changes through mind-body effects.
After three weeks, the people taking the placebo pills were more likely to say that they had adequate relief, 59 percent compared with 35 percent of the others. The study was small and not blinded, so it can't tell us how much of the change was the pills and how much the hope and attention. Later trials of open label placebos have been mixed, with some benefit for pain and fatigue. It's an intriguing sign of how much expectation matters.
Side effects that come from expecting them

Some people stop taking statins, which lower cholesterol, because of aches and other symptoms. In 2020 Fiona Wood and her colleagues tested whether the pills themselves were responsible. They recruited sixty people who had stopped taking statins, and had them go through months of a statin, a placebo and no tablet, in random order, without knowing which was which.
The symptoms were just as bad during the months on a placebo as during the months on a statin, and both were worse than the months with no tablet. The effect of expecting side effects is called the nocebo effect. The symptoms were real, but they didn't come from the drug. When the results were explained, about half of the people went back on their statin. Don't stop a medicine on your own, but if side effects trouble you, talk to your doctor about it.

Stress has a bad reputation, but is it the stress that harms us, or what we believe about it? In 2013 Alia Crum, Peter Salovey and Shawn Achor measured how much people thought that stress is helpful, as against harmful. In studies of employees at a financial firm, those who saw stress as enhancing reported fewer health problems and better work performance, even at high stress.
In a second part of the study, a short video that presented stress as useful changed people's views, and that changed some of their responses. The research is correlational in part, and later studies of mindset interventions have found modest and varied effects. But the idea is a hopeful one. If your pounding heart and tense body are your body preparing for a challenge, you may be able to use that energy, instead of fearing it.

Many people are afraid to ask a friend directly whether they are thinking about suicide. They worry that it could put the idea in their head. In 2014 Tarquinio Dazzi and his colleagues reviewed thirteen studies that had looked at this question. None of them found that asking about suicide increased suicidal thoughts, and some suggested that talking about it could bring relief.
Later reviews have reached a similar conclusion, though the studies were mostly about thoughts rather than actions. The practical lesson is that if you are worried about someone, ask them plainly and kindly, listen without judging, and help them connect with support. In the United States, anyone in crisis can call or text 988 at any hour. Asking shows that you care, and it opens a door that may be hard for them to open.
The coffee that feels like panic

If you have felt a racing heart, trembling hands and a knot of worry after too much coffee, you were not imagining it. Caffeine is a stimulant. In large amounts, it can cause jitteriness, a fast heartbeat, nervousness and trouble sleeping. These are the same sensations that people feel in anxiety. The standard psychiatric manual lists a caffeine-induced anxiety disorder for severe cases.
People who are prone to anxiety or panic can be especially sensitive. For them the sensation can set off the fear of the fear, which makes it feel like an attack. It is worth checking how much caffeine you take, including tea, energy drinks and pills, when you are feeling anxious. Cutting back gradually, and not all at once, can avoid headaches, and for some people it makes a clear difference.
The brain at rest is busy

When researchers first used brain scans, they looked at which regions turned on during a task. They compared that with a resting baseline, as if the resting brain were switched off. In 2001 Marcus Raichle and his colleagues pointed out something odd. A group of regions was more active when people were doing nothing in particular than when they were focused on a task.
They called this a default mode of brain function, and the regions became known as the default mode network. It is active when we daydream, remember the past, imagine the future or think about other people. A task adds only a small amount to the brain's total energy use, because the brain is always working. The mind at rest isn't blank. It's busy with the story of who you are and what's going on.

To get a license, London taxi drivers must learn the Knowledge, a map of some twenty-five thousand streets, and it takes years. In 2000 Eleanor Maguire and her colleagues scanned the brains of licensed drivers. The back part of their hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, was larger than in other people, and it was larger in those who had been driving the longest.
That left a question. Were people with large hippocampi more likely to become taxi drivers, or did the training change the brain? In 2011 Katherine Woollett and Maguire scanned trainees before and after. Those who went on to qualify showed an increase in gray matter in the posterior hippocampus, and those who did not qualify did not. It's among the clearest demonstrations that adult brains can change with learning.

In the early 1990s a team in Parma, Italy, led by Giacomo Rizzolatti, was recording from single cells in the premotor cortex of macaque monkeys. They found cells that fired both when a monkey grasped a piece of food and when it watched someone else do the same thing. The cells were named mirror neurons, and the discovery was widely celebrated.
Some people went further and said mirror neurons explain empathy, language and autism. Those claims are much shakier. Evidence for such cells in people is mostly indirect, and the link to understanding other people's minds has not been shown. Many neuroscientists think that mirror cells are real and interesting, and that they help to link seeing an action with doing it. They do not think that they explain the whole of social understanding.
Where feelings live in the body

Where do you feel love, or shame, or anger? In 2014 Lauri Nummenmaa and his colleagues asked more than seven hundred people to color in outlines of a human body to show where they felt their sensations when they experienced different emotions. The maps for each emotion were distinct, and they were similar for people in Finland, Sweden and Taiwan.
Anger and fear showed up in the chest and head, and love and happiness spread through the whole body. Depression seemed to reduce sensations in the limbs. The results are based on what people said, not on measurements of the body, so they show what people believe and feel and not necessarily what the body does. But they suggest that emotions are tied to the body in ways that are shared across cultures, and that we may read our own feelings partly through our physical states.

In 1978 Jon Levine and his colleagues studied people who had had a wisdom tooth removed. Some were given a placebo, a harmless inactive injection. Many reported less pain after it. Then the researchers gave some of them naloxone, a drug that blocks opioid receptors, the sites where the body's own painkillers and morphine act.
People who got naloxone lost the relief that the placebo had given them. This suggested that the placebo had worked by releasing the body's own endorphins, and was not just a matter of people being polite or imagining it. It was one of the first findings to show that expectations can turn on real chemistry in the brain. Placebos can't shrink a tumor or cure an infection, but they can change how pain is felt.

In 2020 Marietta Papadatou-Pastou and her colleagues combined the results of a very large body of studies, covering more than two million people, to estimate how many people are left-handed. The answer was about ten percent. The number varies a little with how handedness is measured, and it differs slightly by sex, with more left-handed men than women.
Handedness appears early, before birth, since a fetus tends to suck one thumb more than the other. It runs in families, but not simply. Two right-handed parents can have a left-handed child, and genes explain only a part of the variation. The idea that left-handers are more creative or die younger has been tested, and it is not supported. Left-handedness is a normal variation that has been around for a long time.

Imagine seeing your own friends and family and not being able to tell who they are by their faces. Prosopagnosia, or face blindness, can happen after a brain injury. But it also exists in people who have had it all their lives, and don't have any other problem with vision or memory. In 2009 Donna Bowles and her colleagues estimated that about two or three percent of the population had it.
Many people with the condition work out ways to cope. They use hair, voice, clothing or the way someone walks. They may not realize that other people see faces differently, until they are adults. It runs in families, which suggests a genetic part. The condition is a reminder that face recognition is a specialized skill, and that most of us do it so easily that we don't realize it is a skill.

A few people can name a note the moment they hear it, without a reference, like naming a color. This is absolute pitch, and it is rare in the West. For a long time, the explanation was that it needs early musical training in a critical window in childhood, and perhaps a gene for it.
In 2006 Diana Deutsch and her colleagues compared students at music conservatories in Beijing and in the United States. Among those who began training at a young age, absolute pitch was several times more common in the Chinese students than in the American ones. The authors suggested that growing up speaking a tonal language, where the pitch of a syllable changes its meaning, makes it easier to attach labels to pitches. Early exposure seems to matter along with whatever genes are involved.

Look at the word RED printed in blue ink, and try to say the color of the ink, not the word. It is harder than it sounds. In 1935 John Ridley Stroop showed that people are slower and make more errors when the word and the color disagree than when they agree or when the word is simply a patch of color.
The reason is that reading is so automatic that it happens whether we want it to or not. The word interferes with the task of naming the ink. The Stroop task has been used for decades as a test of attention and cognitive control, since it shows how much effort it takes to override an automatic response. It's a good example of how much of what the mind does is not under our control.

In 2020 an international commission led by Gill Livingston reviewed the evidence on dementia. It listed twelve risk factors that people can do something about. They include less education early in life, hearing loss, high blood pressure, obesity, smoking, depression, social isolation, physical inactivity, diabetes, heavy drinking, head injury and air pollution.
In 2024 an update added two more, high LDL cholesterol and untreated vision loss. The commission estimated that nearly half of the dementia cases in the world might be prevented or delayed if all fourteen could be removed. That is a theoretical ceiling and it assumes that the links are causal, but the direction is encouraging. Many of the steps, such as treating hearing loss, keeping active and staying connected to others, are also good for you in other ways.

For years there was a popular claim that speaking two languages makes the brain sharper, because a bilingual person has to switch and hold back one language while using the other. In 2007 Ellen Bialystok and her colleagues reported that bilingual people in Toronto showed the first signs of dementia about four years later than people who spoke one language.
The claim has been challenged. Later studies found that bilingual children and adults often did not do better on tests of attention and control, and some of the early positive results may have been due to publication bias and differences between the groups. A large review in 2018 found little evidence for an advantage in adults. The dementia finding is also disputed. Learning a language is still worth it for many reasons. Whether it improves your brain in general is unclear.
Do music lessons make you smarter?

In 2004 Glenn Schellenberg assigned six year olds to a year of keyboard or voice lessons, drama lessons or no lessons. At the end, children in all groups had gained in IQ, but those with music lessons gained a little more. The finding was widely taken to mean that music lessons make children smarter.
Later studies have found it hard to repeat. A large analysis in 2020 by Giovanni Sala and Fernand Gobet found that when studies were well controlled, music training had little effect on general thinking skills or school results. Children who take lessons often come from families that value education, and who may have higher scores to begin with. Music has its own value, in enjoyment and skill, and doesn't have to raise IQ to be worth learning.

In 2003 Shawn Green and Daphne Bavelier reported that people who played action video games had better visual attention. They were quicker to find a target among distractors and could keep track of more objects at once. In another part of the study, non-players who were trained for ten days on an action game improved, and those trained on a slow puzzle game did not.
The findings drew a lot of interest, and the idea that games could train attention was taken up by educators. Later work has been more mixed. Some studies found that gamers' advantage is partly due to who chooses to play, and not all training studies could repeat the benefit. Effects on everyday life are less clear than effects on the tasks that were used. It remains a topic where the results are suggestive and not settled.

You may have heard that the brain isn't fully developed until age twenty-five. The idea comes from imaging studies, such as one in 2004 by Nitin Gogtay and his colleagues. They scanned the same young people over years, and found that gray matter in the brain's frontal regions thinned out later than in other regions, continuing into the early twenties.
But the number twenty-five is not a cutoff. Different parts and different abilities mature at different rates, and the brain keeps changing throughout life. Some researchers have argued that the claim is used too freely, for example to argue about when someone is an adult. A 2018 paper by Susan Sawyer and her colleagues proposed that adolescence be seen as lasting from ten to twenty-four. The fair summary is that young adults are still developing, without a sudden finish line.
A mosaic, not a male or female brain

Are there male brains and female brains? Many studies have found average differences between the sexes in some brain regions. In 2015 Daphna Joel and her colleagues asked a different question. They looked at MRI scans of more than 1,400 brains and asked whether an individual brain was consistently at the male end or the female end of every feature that differs on average.
They found that most brains were a mosaic. A person could be at the typical female end for some features, the typical male end for others, and in between for the rest. Brains with consistently one set of features were rare. Other researchers criticized the way the team defined consistency. The study is a useful reminder that a difference between averages does not tell you what any one person's brain is like.

Some pieces of music make the hairs on the back of your neck rise, or send a shiver down your spine. In 2001 Anne Blood and Robert Zatorre asked people to bring in music that gave them chills, and scanned their brains as they listened. The chills went along with changes in the same brain regions that respond to food, sex and drugs.
In 2011 Valorie Salimpoor and her colleagues went further. They found that the brain released dopamine, a chemical linked to reward, both during the peak moments and in the seconds before, as people anticipated a favorite passage. The pleasure of music seems to come from prediction as well as from the notes. A piece builds an expectation and then meets it, delays it or surprises us, and the brain's reward system follows along.

In 2015 a photograph of a dress went around the internet. Some people saw it as blue and black. Others saw it as white and gold. Each group was sure that the other was wrong. Scientists took notice, because the photo was an ordinary picture, and yet people couldn't agree about its color.
The explanation that most researchers favor is about assumptions. Our brains automatically discount the color of the light, so we can see an object's color as constant under different lighting. In this photograph, the lighting is unclear. If your brain assumes that the dress is in shadow, it takes away blue and you see white and gold. If it assumes warm light, it takes away yellow and you see blue and black. The difference is in how the brain solves an ambiguous problem.

In 2014 Timothy Wilson and his colleagues asked people to sit alone in a plain room for between six and fifteen minutes, with nothing to do but think. Most said that they didn't enjoy it, and found it hard to concentrate. In one study, people could choose to give themselves a mild electric shock, something that they had already said they would pay to avoid.
About two thirds of the men, and a quarter of the women, did so at least once. The authors concluded that many people find it unpleasant to be alone with their thoughts. Critics have said that the setting was strange, and that people reported mixed feelings, and not just boredom. It would be wrong to take it as proof that we can't tolerate quiet. But it suggests that when a phone is easy to reach, we may be giving up more stillness than we know.

Have you yawned while reading about yawning? In 1986 Robert Provine showed that seeing, hearing or reading about a yawn can make people yawn. In his work, about half of the people who watched a video of someone yawning yawned themselves within minutes. Contagious yawning isn't unique to people. It has been seen in chimpanzees and dogs.
A popular explanation is that it reflects empathy, since people who score lower on empathy tests seem to yawn less in response. Not all the studies agree, and some researchers think that it may be more a matter of attention and arousal, or of copying behavior without feeling anything. Young children don't catch yawns until about the age of four or five. The reason for yawning itself is also still debated.
The tickle you can't give yourself

Why can't you tickle yourself? In 1998 Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert and Chris Frith studied this with a brain scanner. They compared the brain's response when a person touched their own palm with a soft object, and when a machine did it with the same movement. The self-touch caused less activity in the region that processes touch and pain, and it felt less ticklish.
The brain predicts the sensory results of its own movements, and it turns down the signal when the result is as expected. The cerebellum seems to be involved in making that prediction. This is useful, because it lets us ignore the constant feeling of our own movements and notice things that come from outside. If a delay was added between the movement and the touch, the sensation grew ticklish again.

In 1998 Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen did a simple experiment. A person sat with one hand hidden behind a screen, and a rubber hand placed in front of them in a natural position. The experimenter stroked the hidden real hand and the visible rubber hand at the same time with a brush. After a minute or so, many people felt as if the rubber hand were their own.
When the strokes were out of sync, the illusion didn't happen. Some people even flinched when the rubber hand was threatened. The experiment shows that the sense of owning a body part is built by the brain from signals that match, such as sight and touch. It isn't fixed. The brain keeps working out what belongs to you, and with the right cues, it can be fooled.
Why your recorded voice sounds strange

When you hear a recording of yourself, the voice sounds higher, thinner and not quite yours. Many people dislike it. It isn't that the recording is wrong. When you talk, you hear your voice in two ways. One is through the air, which is how other people hear it. The other is through the bones of your skull, which carry vibrations from your vocal cords straight to the inner ear.
Bone conduction adds low frequencies and makes your voice sound deeper and fuller to you. A recording can't capture that, and so it sounds different from what you're used to. What you hear on the recording is closer to what everyone else hears. It's also why familiarity helps. People who hear their own recorded voice more often tend to get used to it.

In 1985 Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer ran a field experiment at a university theater. People buying season tickets were randomly given the full price, a discount, or a bigger discount, without knowing that the price had been varied. Then the researchers counted how many plays each group attended.
In the first half of the season, the people who had paid the full price went to more plays than those who had paid less. Their money was spent, and they didn't want to waste it. Later in the season, the difference faded. This is the sunk cost effect. What you've already spent, and can't get back, should not affect what you do next, but it does. The sensible question is not what have I put in. It is, from here, what is the best use of my time and money?
The bullet holes that weren't there

During the Second World War, military analysts studied the bombers that came back from missions. They plotted where the planes had been hit by bullets, and the obvious plan was to add armor to the places with the most holes. The statistician Abraham Wald saw the flaw. These were the planes that had survived.
The places without holes were where a hit was fatal, because the planes that were hit there never made it home. So the armor belonged on those parts, such as the engines. This is survivorship bias, which means looking only at the cases that made it through and forgetting those that didn't. It's behind many misleading lessons, like studying successful companies for what makes them successful when the failed ones did the same things.

Daniel Kahneman once taught flight instructors in the Israeli air force. They told him that when they praised a cadet after a very good landing, the next landing was usually worse, and when they scolded one after a bad landing, the next was usually better. They concluded that scolding works and praise doesn't.
Kahneman saw that the pattern could be explained by chance. Any performance has some luck in it. A very good landing is likely to be followed by an average one, and a very poor landing is likely to be followed by an average one, whatever anyone says. Francis Galton had named this effect in the 1880s, regression to the mean. It's easy to miss. We invent causes for what is just a return to normal, and it leads us to credit a cure for an illness that was about to improve anyway.

In 1973 the University of California at Berkeley looked at its graduate admissions for signs of bias against women. The overall numbers looked damning. Around 44 percent of the men who applied were admitted, against about 35 percent of the women. A group of statisticians, led by Peter Bickel, looked at the numbers department by department.
Within most departments, women were admitted at about the same rate as men or at higher rates. The reason was that women had applied in greater numbers to departments that were hard to get into, such as English, and men had applied more to departments with high acceptance rates. This is called Simpson's paradox, where a trend in the whole disappears or reverses when the data is split into groups. It's a warning that a single average can hide what's really happening.

In 1983 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described a woman named Linda. She was thirty-one, single, outspoken and bright, and she had studied philosophy and had taken part in protests as a student. People were asked which was more likely. Was Linda a bank teller, or was Linda a bank teller who is active in the feminist movement?
Most people, including many with training in statistics, said that the second was more likely. But that can't be right. Every feminist bank teller is a bank teller, so the second group can't be larger than the first. This is the conjunction fallacy. A detailed story seems more believable than a plain one, though each added detail makes it less likely to be true. It's one reason why vivid scenarios can lead us astray.

In 1975 Baruch Fischhoff gave people a passage about a little known historical event, the war between the British and the Gurkhas in the early 1800s. Some of them were told how it ended, and the others weren't. Then they were asked how likely they would have thought each possible outcome was, if they hadn't known the answer.
The people who knew the result thought that it had been much more likely than the people who didn't. And they didn't realize that knowing the outcome had changed their view. This is hindsight bias. After something happens, it seems obvious. It makes us overconfident in our ability to predict, and it makes us too hard on people who made decisions before the result was known. Writing down your predictions beforehand is a good defense.

Why do projects take longer than we expect? In 1994 Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin and Michael Ross asked students writing their final theses to predict when they would finish. On average they predicted about 34 days. They actually took about 55 days. Only around a third finished by the date that they predicted.
The problem wasn't a lack of experience. Even when they were asked for their worst case, students' estimates were too optimistic. We tend to picture how a plan will go if all goes well, and we underweight the interruptions and delays that always arise. The authors called it the planning fallacy. A good fix is to look at how long similar projects have taken in the past, and to start from that, and not from your own picture of the plan.

How do you find the weak spots in a plan that you're excited about? In 1989 Deborah Mitchell, J. Edward Russo and Nancy Pennington found that people came up with more reasons for an outcome if they imagined that it had already happened. Asked to explain a future event as if it were a fact, they generated about thirty percent more reasons than when they were asked to consider what might happen.
Gary Klein turned this into a business practice in 2007, called the pre-mortem. Before a project begins, the team imagines that it has failed badly, and each person writes down why. It gives people permission to raise worries without seeming negative, and it surfaces risks that the group has been quietly sensing. It costs about ten minutes and may save months of trouble.

Suppose that a surgeon recommends an operation with a small risk, and the patient dies. Was it a bad decision? In 1988 Jonathan Baron and John Hershey gave people stories about decisions with the same information but different outcomes. They found that people rated the decision as worse when the outcome was bad, though the decision-maker had known no more or less in either case.
This is outcome bias. A good result can come from a poor decision, and a bad result can come from a good one. Chance plays a big part. If we judge only by results, we may reward people for luck and punish them for bad breaks, and we learn the wrong lessons. A better question is whether the choice was reasonable given what was known at the time.

In October 1995 British health authorities warned that a type of contraceptive pill, called third generation, doubled the risk of blood clots compared with older pills. The news was widely reported. Many women stopped taking it. In the following year, the numbers of conceptions and abortions rose, and so did births.
The warning was about relative risk. Doubling a very small risk gives a still small risk, and the extra clots were a handful of cases per ten thousand women, while an unplanned pregnancy is a much more common event. Later studies suggested that the increase in risk was smaller than first thought. Gerd Gigerenzer and others argue that health information should be given in absolute terms, such as how many people out of a thousand, and not as percentages of change.

Here is a question that was put to 160 gynecologists. About one percent of women who are screened have breast cancer. A mammogram will find about nine in ten of those who do. It also gives a false alarm in about nine percent of those who don't. A woman has a positive result. What's the chance that she has cancer?
The correct answer is about one in ten. The most common answer from the doctors was ninety percent. When the same information was given as natural frequencies, such as ten women out of a thousand have cancer, nine of them test positive, and about eighty-nine out of the rest also test positive, most could see that the answer is about nine out of ninety-eight. The way that numbers are presented changes how well even experts reason about them.

In 2015 a large group of researchers, called the Open Science Collaboration, tried to repeat one hundred published psychology studies. They followed the original methods as closely as they could, and used larger samples. Of the original studies, ninety-seven percent had reported statistically significant results. Of the repeats, only about thirty-six percent did.
The size of the effects also dropped, to about half of what was first reported. The result set off a period of reform in psychology, with changes such as preregistering plans, sharing data and publishing replications. It doesn't mean that psychology is worthless, and many findings held up well. It does mean that a single exciting study is not enough, and that it's wise to wait for the result to be repeated.
The song that made people younger

In 2011 Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn reported an experiment in which people who listened to the Beatles song "When I'm Sixty-Four" became nearly a year and a half younger than those who listened to a control song. The finding was statistically significant, and it was also impossible.
The authors had done it on purpose. They wanted to show how researchers can get a false result from ordinary choices, such as stopping data collection when the result looks good, trying a few different ways of analyzing the data, or dropping a condition. Each choice seems reasonable, but together they can make a false finding more likely than not. The paper helped lead to the practice of stating your analysis in advance, so that the same data can't be made to say anything.

Imagine twenty teams test a treatment that doesn't work. By chance, one of them gets a positive result, and publishes it. The other nineteen put their results in a drawer. Anyone reading the published literature sees one study and one success. In 1979 Robert Rosenthal called this the file drawer problem.
In 2014 Annie Franco and her colleagues tracked a group of studies from the start, using records of experiments that had been funded. They found that studies with strong results were much more likely to be written up and published than studies with null results, and that many null results were never even written up. It's a reason why published findings can overstate the truth, and it's why registered trials are valuable.
When a measure becomes a target

In the 1970s the economist Charles Goodhart observed that a statistical measure tends to lose its usefulness once it is used for control. The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later put it in a form that is now well known. When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
The reason is that people adapt. If schools are judged by test scores, they may teach to the test. If hospitals are judged by waiting times, they may find ways to make the clocks look better. If a company rewards the number of calls handled, calls will get shorter. The measure and the real goal drift apart. It's why it helps to use several measures, and to ask whether a number is still telling you what you care about.

Who is happier, an Olympic silver medalist or a bronze medalist? Logically it should be silver. In 1995 Victoria Medvec, Scott Madey and Thomas Gilovich analyzed video of athletes at the 1992 Summer Olympics, and had people rate their expressions as they received their medals.
Bronze medalists looked happier than silver medalists. The researchers suggested that the reason is who each athlete compares with. The silver medalist thinks about the gold that they just missed. The bronze medalist thinks about how close they came to finishing with nothing. What we feel often depends less on what we got than on what we imagine could have happened.
