If a child sees the spot and touches their own nose, it suggests that they know it is a reflection of them.
Babies under about a year looked at the mirror image as if it were another child. The first signs of self-recognition came at around fifteen to eighteen months, and by about two years, most children touched the mark on their own nose. It's the same mirror test that has been used with chimpanzees. It marks an important step in the sense of self, and it comes with other changes, such as the first use of "me" and "mine."

Can newborns recognize their mother's voice? In 1980 Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer let newborns suck on a nipple connected to a recorder. By sucking in one pattern, a baby could turn on a recording of their mother's voice, and in another pattern, a stranger's voice. Within a few minutes, the babies sucked in the pattern that brought their mothers' voices.
The babies had been exposed to their mothers' voices only in the womb, in muffled form. In 1986 DeCasper and Melanie Spence asked pregnant women to read a children's story aloud every day for the last six weeks of pregnancy. After birth, the babies preferred to hear that story over a new one. Learning begins before birth. Babies are born attuned to the voice and the rhythm of the language that they will speak.

In 1977 Andrew Meltzoff and Keith Moore reported something remarkable. Newborns only a few days old, and some just a few hours, seemed to copy an adult who stuck out his tongue or opened his mouth. It appeared to show an inborn ability to match what we see with what we do. It became a staple of psychology textbooks, and it was cited as evidence that babies are born with a link between their own bodies and others'.
In 2016 Janine Oostenbroek and her colleagues ran a large study that followed babies from one week to nine weeks of age and tested eleven different gestures. They found no evidence that babies imitated at any age. The babies stuck out their tongues when they were interested in something, no matter what the adult did. The older finding is now widely doubted. Imitation develops, but probably later than was claimed.

In 1992 Karen Wynn showed five-month-old babies a doll on a stage. A screen came up and hid the doll. Then a hand placed a second doll behind the screen, in sight of the baby. When the screen dropped, the baby saw either two dolls, which is the right answer, or one doll, which is impossible.
The babies looked longer at the impossible result of one doll. Wynn concluded that babies can do simple arithmetic, adding one and one. The result was widely cited, and also criticized, since the babies might have been responding to changes in the amount of stuff on the stage, and not to numbers. Some later attempts to repeat it failed. It's agreed that infants have a rough sense of quantity. How much further it goes remains a matter of debate.

In the 1950s Lawrence Kohlberg asked children and adults how they would solve moral dilemmas. The most famous is the story of Heinz, whose wife is dying. A druggist is charging a price that Heinz can't pay for a medicine that might save her. Should Heinz steal it? What mattered to Kohlberg was the reasoning, and not the answer.
He described three levels. At the first, people think about punishment and reward. At the second, they think about rules, duty and what others expect. At the third, they think about principles, such as justice and rights, that may go beyond the law. Carol Gilligan argued that his scheme favored an ethic of justice over an ethic of care. Studies in other cultures also found that the stages fit less well. It's a valuable idea about moral growth, but not a universal ladder.

In 1950 the psychoanalyst Erik Erikson proposed that life is made up of eight stages, each with a central struggle. An infant faces trust versus mistrust. A toddler, autonomy versus shame. A child of school age, industry versus inferiority. A teenager, identity versus confusion. Then come intimacy versus isolation, generativity versus stagnation, and, in old age, integrity versus despair.
The stages are not tested in the way experiments would test them, and they are better seen as a way of thinking than as a scientific finding. But they have been influential. They gave us the term identity crisis, and they suggested that development continues throughout life, and not just in childhood. They also remind us that people at different times in life can have different tasks. It's useful to ask what the current one might be.

How do young people form an identity? In 1966 James Marcia interviewed college students about their choices of career and beliefs. He saw that two questions mattered. Had they explored different possibilities, and had they made a commitment? Combining the two gave four statuses.
Someone who has explored and committed has achieved an identity. Someone who is exploring and has not yet committed is in moratorium. Someone who has committed without exploring, often following parents' expectations, is in foreclosure. And someone who has neither explored nor committed is diffuse. People move among the statuses, and the order isn't fixed. The scheme is a handy way of seeing that not choosing yet may be part of growing up, and that a choice made without exploring may not hold.

In earlier generations, many people finished school, took a job, married and had children in their early twenties. In industrialized countries today, many do these things later. In 2000 Jeffrey Arnett proposed that there is now a stage between adolescence and adulthood, from about eighteen to twenty-five, which he called emerging adulthood.
He found that people in this stage describe it as a time of exploring identity, instability, a focus on themselves, feeling in between, and a sense of possibility. They don't feel that they are quite adults, but they are no longer teenagers. The idea was influential, though critics say it applies mostly to people with the money and the freedom to delay commitments. It suggests that adulthood doesn't arrive on a fixed date, and that it takes some people longer to find a footing.

The midlife crisis is a staple of popular culture, the idea that people in their forties and fifties go through a period of turmoil, and make dramatic changes. In 2000 Elaine Wethington surveyed a national sample of American adults. Only about one in four said that they'd had a midlife crisis, and most of those said that it was triggered by a specific event, such as a death or a divorce, and not by turning forty.
Other researchers have found a similar pattern. Midlife is often a busy and stressful time, with the care of children and parents and the peak of careers, but turmoil isn't universal. Many people report feeling more in control. The crisis seems to be a story that is more common than the experience. It's a reminder that how we think a stage of life will feel can differ from how it does.

In 1963 Raymond Cattell described two kinds of intelligence. Fluid intelligence is the ability to solve new problems and to reason without relying on what you've learned. Crystallized intelligence is the knowledge and skills that you have built up over time, such as vocabulary and facts. They develop differently.
In 2015 Joshua Hartshorne and Laura Germine tested tens of thousands of people on a range of tasks, and found that different abilities peak at different ages. Speed of processing peaks in the late teens, and memory for names in the early thirties. Vocabulary keeps rising until the sixties or even later. There is no single peak for the mind. We lose some things as we age, and gain others. The skills that grow tend to be those that depend on knowledge.
Why time left changes what we want

Why do older people often seem calmer and more content? In the 1990s Laura Carstensen proposed socioemotional selectivity theory. When people see their time as long, they pursue goals for the future, such as learning, meeting new people and building a career. When they see time as limited, they shift to goals that bring meaning and emotional satisfaction now.
It's about the sense of time, and not about age as such. Young people who are told to imagine that they are about to move far away choose, like older people, to spend time with close friends and family. Older people have smaller social circles, but they are often closer and more satisfying. The theory suggests that the sense of what matters most shifts when we think that time is short, and that this can be a source of wisdom.

Does wisdom increase with age? In 2010 Igor Grossmann and his colleagues asked people of different ages to think about conflicts, such as problems between groups or in relationships, that they read about in newspaper stories. They looked at how people reasoned. Did they consider other points of view, recognize uncertainty and look for compromise?
Older people did better. They were more likely to take different perspectives and to look for a middle path. Wise reasoning was not related to intelligence, but increased with age, up to the oldest group in the study, and people in their sixties and seventies did best. The results suggest that experience builds a particular kind of social reasoning. It also shows that some of what we gain with age is not something that tests of speed and memory measure.

In the Gospel of Matthew, it says that to those who have, more will be given. In 1986 Keith Stanovich applied the phrase to reading. Children who start out as good readers read more, learn more words and gain more knowledge, and so get better still. Children who start out slowly read less, and fall further behind.
The gap isn't just in reading skill. Reading builds vocabulary and background knowledge, which in turn make everything else in school easier. The differences can grow over the years. This is why help in the early years is so valuable, since a small gap can become a large one. It also gives a reason for adults to read, as a way to keep growing.

What happens to what children learn during the long summer break? In 1996 Harris Cooper and his colleagues combined the results of thirty-nine studies that had tested students at the end of one school year and the start of the next. On average, students lost about a month of learning over the summer.
Math skills dropped more than reading skills, on average. For reading, the loss was larger for children from low-income families, who had fewer books and activities in the summer. Middle-class children sometimes held steady or improved. The idea of a summer slide has become an argument for summer reading and programs. Some later studies find that the loss is smaller than first thought, but the pattern of unequal summers has been seen again.

Does class size matter? Many studies had tried to answer this, with mixed results, because schools with smaller classes differ in other ways. In the 1980s the state of Tennessee ran an experiment, called Project STAR. Thousands of children in kindergarten were randomly assigned to small classes of thirteen to seventeen, or regular classes of twenty-two to twenty-five.
The students in the smaller classes did better on tests, and the gains were largest for children from low-income families and for minority students. Follow-ups found some benefits lasting into later years, such as higher rates of college entry. In 1999 Alan Krueger reanalyzed the data and confirmed the effect. Because the assignment was random, it's some of the best evidence that we have. It's expensive, though, so the question is whether the same money could do more elsewhere.
What a great teacher is worth

In 2014 Raj Chetty, John Friedman and Jonah Rockoff used records of millions of students in a large American city, and tracked them from elementary school into adulthood. They asked whether teachers who raised their students' test scores more than others did something that mattered later in life.
They found that students of high value-added teachers were more likely to go to college and earned more as adults. By their estimates, replacing a teacher in the bottom five percent with an average one would raise the lifetime income of a class by hundreds of thousands of dollars. The work has been debated, in particular the use of test scores to judge individual teachers. But it suggests that a good teacher has an effect that lasts long after the school year ends.

Do mobile phones harm learning in schools? In 2016 Louis-Philippe Beland and Richard Murphy studied schools in four English cities. Some of the schools had introduced a ban on phones, and others had not. The researchers looked at students' test results before and after the bans.
After a ban, test scores rose a little, a modest but real amount. The students who gained the most were the ones with the lowest results, while the highest achievers were not affected. This suggests that phones are a distraction, most for those who find it hardest to stay focused. The effect was modest, but the cost was low, and it fits the other studies of the way that distraction harms learning.

Does homework make students learn more? In 2006 Harris Cooper and his colleagues reviewed the research from the previous twenty years. They found that students who did more homework tended to do better in school. But the link was much stronger in middle and high school than in elementary school.
For young children, the link was weak or absent. For older students, a modest amount helped, and the benefits seemed to level off after about one to two hours a night in high school. Most of the studies were correlations, so the cause is unclear. Students who do well may also do more homework. The evidence suggests that the amount matters less than whether it is purposeful, and that long hours for young children probably help little.
Words that make people walk slowly

In 1996 John Bargh and his colleagues asked students to make sentences from scrambled words. For some students, the words were related to old age, such as Florida, wrinkle and gray. Others got neutral words. Then the students walked down a hallway, and a researcher timed them. The ones who had seen the old-age words walked more slowly.
It was a famous finding, and it was taken as proof that words can influence behavior without our knowing it. In 2012 Stéphane Doyen and his colleagues tried to repeat it, using automatic timing instead of an experimenter. They could not find the effect, unless the experimenters had been told to expect it. It suggests that the original result may have come from the experimenters' expectations. It's a major case in the debate about replication in psychology.
Does disgust make us moral judges?

In 2008 Simone Schnall and her colleagues tested whether feelings of disgust change moral judgments. In one experiment, people filled out questionnaires about moral dilemmas, such as whether it is wrong to lie on a résumé. Some people did it in a room that had been sprayed with a foul smell, and others in a clean room. The people in the smelly room judged the acts to be more wrong.
The result fit a theory that moral judgment is rooted in emotion. In 2016 a group led by David Johnson tried to repeat one of the studies with a larger sample, and found no effect. Others have found effects that are small, or only in certain groups. The theory isn't dead, but the specific claim that a bad smell makes us harsher judges is on shaky ground.
Does thinking about money make us selfish?

In 2006 Kathleen Vohs and her colleagues reported that even faint reminders of money change behavior. People who did tasks that mentioned money, such as unscrambling phrases about cash, or sitting near a pile of Monopoly money, later worked longer on a hard puzzle before asking for help. They also helped others less, and preferred to play and work alone.
The study was widely cited as evidence that money makes people self-reliant and less social. Later, other labs tried to repeat the finding, and many of them failed, though a few found small effects. It's another example of an appealing result that didn't hold up. It's a reminder to treat a single study as a hint and not as a fact.

For decades the textbook story was that people don't help in an emergency when others are around. The finding was based on lab experiments, and on an account of the murder of Kitty Genovese in 1964 that turned out to be exaggerated. In 2020 Richard Philpot and his colleagues did something new. They studied security camera footage of 219 real public conflicts, such as fights and threats, in Amsterdam, Cape Town and Lancaster.
In ninety-one percent of the incidents, at least one person stepped in to help. The more people there were around, the more likely it was that someone would help. The researchers suggested that in real, dangerous situations, people are more likely to see that help is needed than they are in a lab. The old effect is real in some settings, but it's weaker than the textbooks say.

In 1989 Abram Rosenblatt and his colleagues asked municipal court judges to set bail for a woman accused of prostitution. Half of the judges were first asked to fill out a questionnaire that reminded them of their own death. The others answered neutral questions. The judges who had thought about their own death set a much higher bail.
The finding was an early result for terror management theory. The idea is that awareness of death makes people cling to their worldviews and to those who share them, and be harsher on those who violate them. There were hundreds of studies. But large replication efforts have not always found the effect, and the theory is debated. It's an intriguing idea about how fear shapes values, with an uncertain base.
Why your fingers prune in water

After a long bath, the skin on your fingers and toes wrinkles. It used to be explained as water soaking into the skin, but that turned out to be wrong. The wrinkling is an active response. The nervous system narrows the blood vessels under the skin, which makes the surface pucker. People whose nerves to the fingers are damaged don't get wrinkles.
In 2013 Kyriacos Kareklas and his colleagues tested what the wrinkles are for. People picked up wet objects, such as marbles, and moved them from one container to another. They were quicker with wrinkled fingers than with smooth ones. With dry objects, there was no difference. The wrinkles seem to work like the tread on a tire, channeling water away, which gives a better grip on wet things.
The baby with three hundred bones

A newborn baby has about three hundred bones. An adult has two hundred and six. The difference isn't that bones are lost. Many of the baby's bones are made partly of cartilage, and they fuse as the child grows. The skull is the clearest example. A newborn's skull is made of several plates, with gaps between them called fontanelles, the soft spots on a baby's head.
The gaps have a purpose. They let the skull squeeze a little during birth, and they give the brain room to grow quickly in the first years. They close over time, most within the first one or two years. Bone is also living tissue. It is constantly broken down and rebuilt, so that most of the adult skeleton is replaced over about ten years.
A new stomach lining every few days

The stomach produces acid strong enough to dissolve metal, yet the stomach doesn't digest itself. It's protected by a thick layer of mucus and by a lining of cells that is constantly renewed. The cells on the surface of the lining live only a few days, and they are replaced by new ones from stem cells below.
If the protection fails, the acid can damage the lining, and cause an ulcer. For many years, doctors thought that ulcers were caused by stress and spicy food. In the early 1980s Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that most are caused by a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori. Marshall famously drank a culture of it to prove his point. They shared the Nobel Prize in 2005. Ulcers can now be cured with antibiotics.
The most common kind of color blindness

Color blindness is often misunderstood. It rarely means seeing in black and white. Most people with it have trouble telling red from green, because one of the three kinds of color-sensitive cone cells in the eye is missing or works differently. About one in twelve men of European descent has this, and about one in two hundred women.
The reason for the difference is that the genes for the red and green cones are on the X chromosome. A man has one X, so a single faulty copy means color blindness. A woman has two, and would need both to be faulty. Many people don't know they have it until they're tested. Designers can help by not depending on color alone, using patterns, labels or shapes as well.
Do some women see more colors?

Most people have three kinds of cones in their eyes. Some women may have four. The genes for two of the cone types lie on the X chromosome. A woman has two X chromosomes, and if the two copies differ slightly, she may carry two different versions of a cone, in addition to the other two. In theory, this could give her four types of color receptor, and the ability to tell apart colors that look the same to others.
In 1993 Gabriele Jordan and John Mollon found a woman who seemed to have four cone types. Later work, especially by Kimberly Jameson, found that some carriers can do slightly better on special color tests. But most carriers, perhaps nearly all, don't show an obvious benefit. The idea of a superhuman color sense is intriguing, but the evidence for it is thin.

A hummingbird's heart can beat more than a thousand times a minute when the bird is flying. The bird's wings beat dozens of times a second, and it hovers in the air, which is very costly in energy. It needs to eat a large part of its body weight in nectar every day, and it can drop into a deep rest called torpor at night, when its heart rate falls to a small fraction of its daytime rate.
By contrast, a blue whale's heart can beat only a few times a minute when the whale dives. In general, smaller animals have faster hearts and shorter lives. Across many kinds of mammals, the number of heartbeats in a lifetime comes out close to the same, with a few exceptions, humans among them. It's a rough rule, and it shows how closely body size and the pace of life are linked.

The Arctic tern breeds in the far north in summer and spends the other half of the year around Antarctica. In 2010 Carsten Egevang and his colleagues attached tiny light recorders to terns in Greenland. The devices kept track of the birds' positions as they flew south and north again.
The terns didn't fly in a straight line. They followed a winding route down the Atlantic and back, riding the winds. The round trip was about seventy thousand kilometers a year, the longest known migration of any animal. Because of the long days at both ends of the journey, the terns are thought to see more daylight than any other creature on the planet. A tern lives for about thirty years, so it may fly a distance equal to two or three round trips to the Moon.

The bar-tailed godwit is a plump shorebird that breeds in Alaska. In the fall, it flies to New Zealand and Australia. In 2007 researchers tracked godwits with small satellite tags, and followed one female for a flight of more than eleven thousand kilometers, across the Pacific Ocean, without stopping to eat, drink or rest. It took her about eight days.
Before the flight, godwits greatly increase their weight by eating, and they shrink some of their digestive organs to make room for fat. During the flight, they burn that fat. It's the longest known nonstop flight of any bird. It shows how migrants can push the limits of physiology.

A salmon is born in a stream, swims to the ocean, and years later returns to spawn in the same stream where it hatched. How does it find the way? In the 1950s the biologist Arthur Hasler suspected that it was smell. Fish that were taken from a stream and had their noses plugged could not find their way home.
In experiments in the 1960s and 1970s, Hasler and his student Allan Scholz treated young salmon with a chemical, morpholine. Years later, when the adult fish swam back, they were drawn to streams into which the researchers had put the same chemical. Salmon imprint on the smell of their home stream when they are young, and follow it back as adults. They use other cues, such as the Earth's magnetic field, on the open sea, but the final steps are guided by scent.
The butterfly that takes four generations

Each fall, millions of monarch butterflies in eastern North America fly up to four thousand kilometers south to overwinter in the mountains of central Mexico. They have never been there. The butterflies that make the journey are not the ones that left the previous spring. The migration takes about four generations. Three generations live for a few weeks in the north, and the fourth is a special generation that lives for months.
The final generation flies south, spends the winter in the forest, and in spring flies north to lay eggs, and then dies. The butterflies navigate using the position of the Sun, and a clock in their antennae that compensates for its movement across the sky. They may also sense the Earth's magnetic field. How a butterfly knows where to go without having been there is still not fully understood.

Humans have farmed for about ten thousand years. Leafcutter ants have been farming for about fifty million. They carry pieces of leaves back to their underground nests, but they don't eat the leaves. They chew them into a paste on which they grow a fungus, and the fungus is their food. The ants tend the garden, weeding out other molds and feeding the fungus fresh leaf material.
In 2008 Ted Schultz and Seán Brady studied the family tree of fungus-growing ants and their fungi. They concluded that agriculture arose once, about fifty million years ago, and has since spread into hundreds of species. The ants even use bacteria on their bodies that make antibiotics to protect the garden from disease. A single nest can have millions of ants, with a division of labor between those who forage, those who farm and those who defend.
The ant that counts its steps

A desert ant in the Sahara goes out looking for food, moving in a winding path, sometimes for hundreds of meters. When it finds a dead insect, it runs straight home, in a nearly straight line. There are no landmarks on the sand. How does it do it? Part of the answer is a kind of dead reckoning. The ant keeps track of the direction it has gone, using the Sun, and of the distance.
In 2006 Matthias Wittlinger and his colleagues tested how the ant measures distance. They attached tiny stilts to some ants, and clipped the legs of others. The ants with stilts overshot their nest on the way home, and the ants with shortened legs stopped short. The ants seem to count their steps, in effect, like a pedometer. It's a remarkable feat for a brain the size of a grain of sand.
The shrimp that punches like a bullet

The mantis shrimp is a small, colorful animal that lives on the seafloor, and it has one of the fastest strikes in the animal kingdom. Some species have clubs that accelerate as fast as a bullet leaving a small gun. The strike is so fast that it creates a bubble in the water, which collapses with a snap and a flash of light, adding a second blow. It can break the shell of a crab or crack the glass of an aquarium.
The mantis shrimp's eyes are also extraordinary. They have up to sixteen kinds of photoreceptors, compared with our three. It was thought that this gave them an amazing range of color vision. In 2014 Hanne Thoen and her colleagues showed that they are actually poor at telling similar colors apart. It seems they identify colors quickly by recognizing them, without comparing, which may speed up decisions.

The platypus looks like a collection of parts from different animals, with a duck's bill, a beaver's tail and an otter's feet. It's a mammal, since it has fur and feeds its young milk, but it lays eggs. It is one of only five living species of egg-laying mammal, called monotremes. The others are the echidnas. When the first specimen was sent to Britain in 1799, scientists suspected a hoax.
The platypus has other odd features. Its bill can sense the electrical fields produced by the muscles of its prey, so it can hunt with its eyes shut. The males have a venomous spur on their hind legs. In 2008 researchers sequenced its genome and found a mix of mammal, reptile and bird genes. It sits on an ancient branch of the mammal family tree.
An animal that regrows its limbs

The axolotl is a salamander that lives in a lake near Mexico City. It has a remarkable ability. If it loses a leg, it grows a new one that is perfect, with bones, muscles and nerves. It can regrow its tail, parts of its heart and spinal cord, and even parts of its brain, without scars.
When a limb is lost, cells at the wound form a clump called a blastema, which acts like a set of instructions for building a new limb. Scientists are working to understand how this happens, in the hope that human tissue could one day be coaxed to do the same. Humans can regrow only a few things, such as the liver and the tip of a child's finger. Wild axolotls are critically endangered, though many are kept in laboratories and as pets.
Bumblebees that learn from each other

In 2017 Olli Loukola and his colleagues taught bumblebees to do something they would never do in nature. A ball was placed at a distance from a platform with a reward, and the bees had to pull a string to move the ball to the reward. This is hard for a bee, and most untrained bees never solved it by themselves.
The researchers trained some of the bees, and then let other bees watch. The observers learned to do the task, and some even improved on the method. In later work, a skill taught to one bee spread through a colony as others watched. Insects were once seen as creatures of instinct. This result shows that a bee has a brain smaller than a sesame seed, and can still learn by watching, and can learn something new.

Irene Pepperberg bought an African gray parrot from a pet shop in 1977, and named him Alex. Over three decades, she trained him and tested what he understood. He didn't just repeat words. He could name dozens of objects, as well as colors and shapes, and answer questions about them.
Shown a tray of objects, Alex could be asked, "What color is the square one?" or "How many blue?" and give the right answer. He seemed to understand same and different, and could count small collections up to about six. He also asked for things, and once asked what color he was. It is debated how much of this reflects language as we know it. But the work showed that a bird's brain, which looks very different from ours, can do some of the same things.

Each bottlenose dolphin develops a signature whistle in its first year, a distinctive pattern that is like a name. Dolphins use it to identify themselves to others, and mothers and calves use it to find one another. In 2006 Vincent Janik and his colleagues tested what dolphins do when they hear another dolphin's whistle.
They played recordings of whistles to wild dolphins in Florida. A dolphin responded much more to the recording of the signature whistle of a close relative, or a long-term companion, than to that of a stranger. The recordings were made so that voice features were removed, which meant that the dolphins responded to the whistle pattern itself. Dolphins seem to use learned labels for individuals, which makes them one of the few animals other than humans known to do so.

The bowhead whale lives in the cold waters of the Arctic. It is a huge animal with a head that makes up about a third of its body, and it can break through ice that is several inches thick. In 1999 John George and his colleagues estimated the ages of bowheads by looking at chemical changes in the lens of the eye, which accumulate over a lifetime.
Some animals seemed to be more than a hundred years old, and a few over two hundred. Old stone harpoon points, of a kind that hunters stopped using long ago, have been found embedded in harvested whales. Bowheads seem to get cancer rarely, in spite of their size and their long lives, and scientists are studying why. Their genes suggest that the whales may be especially good at repairing damage to DNA.

Some things in conversation come in pairs. A question calls for an answer, a greeting for a greeting, an offer for an acceptance or a refusal. In the 1960s and 70s the sociologists Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson recorded ordinary talk and studied it line by line. They called these pairs adjacency pairs, and they showed that the first part sets up a strong expectation of the second.
You notice the expectation when it isn't met. If you say hello and get silence, it feels odd. If you ask a question and the other person doesn't reply, the silence itself is heard as a message. Other people can see that something is missing, and they interpret why. The pairs are a kind of hidden grammar of everyday talk, and we follow them without knowing that we do.
Why a "no" comes slower than a "yes"

When you invite someone to dinner, and they want to come, they usually say so right away. When they don't, the answer tends to come after a pause, and begins with a softener, such as "well" or "uh." In the 1980s Anita Pomerantz described this pattern as preference organization. Some responses are preferred, in the sense that they fit what the first speaker hoped for, and these come quickly and plainly.
In 2015 Kobin Kendrick and Francisco Torreira measured the gaps in a large set of recorded conversations in English. Responses that agreed with a request or an invitation came in sooner than those that turned it down, by a fraction of a second. We hear that small delay as a sign that a refusal is coming, and the speaker who delays is cushioning it. It's part of how people spare each other's feelings without saying so.
Who speaks when the phone rings?

When the phone rings, who speaks first? You probably say that it is the caller. In fact, it is the person who answers. In 1968 Emanuel Schegloff analyzed hundreds of recorded telephone calls. In nearly all of them, the person who picked up said hello first, and the caller replied. He argued that the ringing of the phone is a summons, like a call across the room, and that the answer is the response.
This leaves the caller to speak second, and to identify themselves, or to ask for someone. It's a small piece of order in something we don't think about. Schegloff found that the opening of a call has a clear structure, with a summons, an answer, an identification and a greeting. The structure varies from culture to culture, and from phone to phone, but the idea of a summons and an answer holds.

Ending a conversation is harder than it looks. We rarely just say goodbye and leave. We say, "Well," or "OK," and then there is a pause, and some more talk, and finally the goodbyes. In 1973 Emanuel Schegloff and Harvey Sacks studied how people close conversations. They found that the end has to be negotiated, because neither person wants to cut the other off.
A word like "well" or "so" signals a wish to end. It gives the other person a chance to bring up something else, or to agree. When both agree, they move to a closing, often with a recap of plans, such as "I'll talk to you soon." Only after this do they say goodbye. It's a collaboration, and it shows how much of talk is about managing the relationship.

In bilingual communities, people often slip between two languages in the same conversation, or even in the same sentence. It was once thought to be a sign of confusion, or of poor knowledge of both languages. In 1980 Shana Poplack studied Puerto Rican Spanish speakers in New York, who moved between Spanish and English as they talked. She found that the switching followed rules.
The speakers who switched the most were often the most fluent in both languages. They switched at points where the grammar of the two languages lines up, so the sentence stayed correct in each. Code-switching, as it's called, is a skill. It can also express identity, or add emphasis, or show that you belong to a particular community. It's a good example of how everyday speech can be more systematic than it seems.

In 1962 the linguist William Labov wanted to see whether the way New Yorkers pronounce the letter r reflects social class. He went to three department stores. One was expensive, one was medium priced, and one was cheap. He asked the salespeople where to find something that he knew was on the fourth floor, and, pretending that he hadn't heard, asked them to repeat it.
In the expensive store, the clerks were most likely to pronounce the r in "fourth floor." In the cheap store, they were least likely. In every store, they pronounced it more clearly the second time, when they spoke carefully. Labov concluded that pronouncing the r was seen as prestigious, and that speakers shifted toward it when they were conscious of being listened to. The study is a landmark for the way that it studied speech in real life.

On the island of Martha's Vineyard, off the coast of Massachusetts, the vowels in words such as "right" and "house" are pronounced in a distinctive way. In 1961 William Labov visited the island to study this. He found that the older, local pronunciation was becoming more common among some young islanders, and not less, though tourists and mainland influences were growing.
Those who used it most were the ones who wanted to stay on the island and who identified as islanders, often fishermen. Those who planned to leave for the mainland used it least. The way that people spoke signaled who they were and where they belonged. Labov showed that language changes are not just random drift. They can be a way of saying who you are, and of marking a group.
How a voice changes the way you are judged

In 1960 Wallace Lambert and his colleagues in Montreal invented a method to study attitudes toward languages. They recorded bilingual speakers reading the same passage once in English and once in French. Listeners heard the recordings, but didn't know that each speaker appeared twice. They were asked to rate the personality of each speaker, such as how intelligent, kind or ambitious they seemed.
English-speaking listeners rated the voices more favorably when they spoke English than when they spoke French, though they were the same people. Surprisingly, French-speaking listeners did the same, rating the English guises higher. The method, called the matched-guise technique, shows how stereotypes attach to languages and accents. People are judged by how they sound, in ways that have nothing to do with who they are.
Hearing an accent that isn't there

In 1992 Donald Rubin played American undergraduates a short lecture on a neutral topic. All of them heard the same recording, spoken by a native speaker of American English. For half of the students, a photograph of a white woman was shown, and they were told that she was the lecturer. For the others, a photograph of an Asian woman was shown.
Afterward, the students took a test on how much they remembered. Those who thought that the lecturer was Asian understood less, and many said that they could hear an accent. They did hear the same voice. Their expectation had changed how they listened. It's a clear example of how prejudice can make a listener work less hard, and then blame the speaker.
Accent is not the same as understanding

When we hear a foreign accent, it can feel as if the speech is hard to understand. In 1995 Murray Munro and Tracey Derwing tested this. They recorded speakers who were learning English, and asked native listeners to rate how strong the accent was. They also had the listeners write down what the speakers said, to see how much was understood.
The accent ratings and the understanding were related, but not closely. Many speakers with a strong accent were fully understood, and being understood depended on other things, such as the rhythm and the stress of the words. Intelligibility, the amount of speech that the listener gets, isn't the same as accent. It suggests that the aim of language teaching should be to be understood, and not to sound like a native.

Not all humor is the same. In 2003 Rod Martin and his colleagues developed a questionnaire that separates four styles. Affiliative humor is joking and teasing that brings people together. Self-enhancing humor is seeing the funny side of life's difficulties. Aggressive humor is ridicule that puts other people down. Self-defeating humor is making fun of oneself in order to be liked.
The first two styles were associated with better well-being, less depression and healthier relationships. The last two were not. Aggressive humor went with more hostility, and self-defeating humor went with more anxiety and lower self-esteem. It suggests that having a sense of humor is good for you, but only if you use it in a way that's kind to you and others.

Teasing is a mix of friendliness and aggression, and it is very common. In 2001 Dacher Keltner and his colleagues reviewed what is known about it. Teasing can be a way of bonding, showing affection through play. It can also be used to push away, to criticize or to enforce a norm.
What separates the two is the way it is done. Playful teasing is usually exaggerated, with a smile and a tone that signals that it's not meant seriously. It tends to be about things that the person can easily laugh at. Teasing about something sensitive, from someone who is not close, with no signs of play, is more likely to hurt. The same words can bond or wound, depending on the signals around them.

In the 1970s the linguist William O'Barr and his colleagues studied how witnesses talked in court. They noticed that some used what they called powerless speech, with hedges such as "sort of," hesitations such as "um," polite forms, and rising intonation at the end of statements. Others spoke in a more direct way.
In 1978 Bonnie Erickson and her colleagues tested the effect. Mock jurors listened to recordings of the same testimony in the two styles. The witnesses who spoke in the powerless style were seen as less convincing, less competent and less trustworthy. The pattern was linked to status and not to gender, since people of low status in court, men and women, were more likely to use it. It suggests that how we say things changes how our words are weighed.
How an interviewer's manner changes an applicant

In 1974 Carl Word, Mark Zanna and Joel Cooper ran a two-part study. In the first part, white college students interviewed job applicants who were actually part of the study, some of whom were Black and some white. The interviewers sat farther away from the Black applicants, made more speech errors, and cut the interviews shorter.
In the second part, trained interviewers treated white applicants in either of the two styles, the closer, warmer style or the more distant, less engaged one. The applicants who were treated in the distant way performed worse, and later said that they felt less comfortable. Our behavior can shape the behavior of others, in ways that confirm our expectations. This is one way that bias can create the very differences that it assumes.

Why is it so annoying to overhear someone talking on a phone? You can only hear one side. In 2010 Lauren Emberson and her colleagues tested whether this is more distracting than hearing both sides. People worked on tasks that needed attention while they heard either one side of a phone call, or a conversation between two people, or a monologue.
The half of a call was the most distracting. People did worse on their tasks, and they remembered more of the content of the overheard call. The researchers suggested that when we can only hear half of a conversation, we can't predict what will come next, and our minds work to fill in the gaps. This takes attention. The unpredictability is what makes it annoying.

In 2012 Casey Klofstad and his colleagues recorded men and women saying the words "I urge you to vote for me this November." They then changed the pitch of each recording, and made one version higher and one lower. They played the pairs to voters, and asked which candidate they would choose.
Voters preferred the lower-pitched voice, for both men and women. They saw it as stronger and more competent. In a later study of real elections, candidates with deeper voices were somewhat more likely to win. The effect is small, and it may reflect stereotypes about leadership more than any real difference in ability. But it is a case where a feature of the voice that has nothing to do with the message may influence what we think of the speaker.
Does a font change what we believe?

In 2012 the filmmaker Errol Morris ran a large online experiment with the New York Times. Readers took a quiz, which started with a short passage by a scientist about the chances that humans would survive for a long time. The passage was shown in one of six fonts. At the end, readers were asked whether they agreed that the writer was optimistic about the future of humanity.
The people who saw the passage in the font Baskerville were somewhat more likely to agree with it than those who saw it in the others, such as Comic Sans. The difference was small, and there are many reasons the fonts might differ. It is not a controlled study. But it fits with research showing that how easy something is to read affects whether we believe it. A clear typeface can add a little credibility.

Many people go into a negotiation assuming that whatever the other side gains, they lose. In the early 1980s Max Bazerman and Margaret Neale called this the fixed-pie bias. In 1990 Leigh Thompson and Reid Hastie tested it. Pairs of students negotiated over several issues, such as the price, the delivery time and the financing of a purchase. They were then asked what they thought the other side wanted.
Many of the students believed that their interests were directly opposed to the other's, when in fact the two sides valued the issues differently. One cared more about speed, and the other about price. Pairs that realized this could trade, giving up what mattered less to them for what mattered more, and both came out ahead. Asking questions about what the other side values is the key to making the pie bigger.
Why bids come at the last second

On eBay, auctions run for a set time, and many bidders wait until the last few seconds to place their bids. This is called sniping. In 2002 Alvin Roth and Axel Ockenfels compared eBay with Amazon, which at the time extended an auction if bids came in at the end. On eBay, a large share of bids came in the final minutes. On Amazon, that was much less common.
Sniping makes sense on eBay. If you bid early, you may start a bidding war with other people, or show that an item is valuable. If you bid at the last moment, others have no time to respond. The study shows how the rules of an auction shape the way people bid. A small difference in the way an auction ends changes the strategy completely.

In a normal sealed-bid auction, the highest bidder wins and pays what they bid. This gives people a reason to bid less than the item is worth to them, to make a profit. William Vickrey proposed a different rule in 1961. The highest bidder still wins, but pays only the amount of the second-highest bid.
Under this rule, the best strategy is to bid exactly what the item is worth to you. If you bid more, you risk winning at a price that is too high. If you bid less, you may lose an item that you could have had at a good price. Your own bid never sets the price you pay. Vickrey won the Nobel Prize in 1996 for this and related ideas. Versions of his auction are used today, for example in the way that online advertising space is sold.

The economist Martin Shubik invented a simple game in 1971. A dollar bill is auctioned off, and the highest bidder wins it. The twist is that the second-highest bidder also has to pay what they bid, and gets nothing. Any increase on a bid seems sensible, but the result is not.
When the bids reach a dollar, the second bidder, who has offered ninety-five cents, is about to lose ninety-five cents. By bidding a dollar and five cents, he will lose only a nickel, so he raises. Then the other bidder, who has offered a dollar, faces the same choice. People in classrooms often bid several dollars for a dollar bill. The game illustrates how escalation can trap people when they have already invested, and how hard it is to stop once you've started.

Why do people keep putting money into a project that is failing? In 1976 Barry Staw asked business students to play the role of a manager in a company. First, they chose where to invest funds in one of two divisions. Then they were told that the investment had done poorly, and they were asked to make a second round of investment.
The students who had made the first decision themselves invested significantly more in the failing division than students who were told that someone else had made it. Having committed to a course, they sought to justify it. This is called escalation of commitment. It's a pattern seen in business, in politics and in personal life. A useful question is whether you would make the same choice if you were starting afresh today.

In 2003 Fred Reichheld proposed that a company could track its health with a single question. How likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague, on a scale from zero to ten? The score, called the net promoter score, subtracts the share who answered zero to six from those who gave nine or ten. Reichheld claimed that it was the best predictor of growth.
The idea was adopted by thousands of companies. But when researchers tested it with other data, they found that it was no better at predicting growth than other measures of satisfaction. Keiningham and his colleagues published one such study in 2007. The score is easy to collect and to understand, and that may be why it's popular. As a single magic number, it has not held up well.

What makes customers loyal? Many companies try to delight them with extra service. In 2010 Matthew Dixon and his colleagues at a business research group surveyed tens of thousands of customers about their experiences with customer service. They found that going above and beyond made little difference to loyalty.
What seemed to matter more was how much effort the customer had to make. People who had to contact the company several times, repeat their story or switch channels were more likely to become disloyal. The authors proposed a measure called the customer effort score. The work comes from a consulting firm and is not a controlled experiment, so it should be taken with some care. But it fits a common sense idea. People value a problem solved with less hassle.
When asking costs more for women

Women are less likely to negotiate for higher pay than men. In 2007 Hannah Riley Bowles, Linda Babcock and Lei Lai studied one reason. They asked people to read about job candidates who either asked for a higher salary or accepted the first offer, and to say how much they would want to work with each one.
Male evaluators penalized women who asked, finding them less nice and more demanding, and did not penalize men for asking. Female evaluators penalized both women and men who asked. So the reluctance has a basis in how people react. The authors found that women did better when they gave a reason that fit with their relationships at work, such as that they were helping the company. The problem is the bias, and not the women.

In 2007 Wesley Schultz and his colleagues delivered cards to households in California that showed how much electricity each had used, compared with the average in the neighborhood. Households that used more than average cut back in the following weeks. But households that used less than average used more, and drifted up toward the norm.
It was a boomerang effect. Telling people what others do pulls them toward the average, in both directions. In a second version, the cards had a smiling face for households that used less than average, and a frowning face for those that used more. Now the low users stayed low. The smile told them that what they did was good, which kept them from sliding. A norm message works best when it also says what is approved.

After the work on social norms, a company called Opower began to send millions of households a report that compared their energy use with that of their neighbors. In 2011 the economist Hunt Allcott studied the results across several hundred thousand homes in many places. The households were randomly chosen, so the effect of the reports could be measured.
On average, the households that received the reports used about two percent less energy than the others. The effect is modest, but it's across many households, and it was achieved at low cost. It lasted for as long as the reports continued to arrive, and then faded slowly. It shows how a small nudge, applied widely, can have large effects, and it also shows that a nudge isn't a magic wand.

Most people say that they would like to save more for retirement, but few do. In 2004 Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi designed a plan that works with human nature. Employees are asked to commit now to saving a larger share of their pay in the future, with the increase tied to future pay raises. They can opt out at any time.
In the first company to use it, the employees who joined the plan raised their savings rate from about three and a half percent to over thirteen percent in three and a half years. The plan works because it avoids the pain of cutting take-home pay now, and it uses inertia to keep people in. It's one of the best-known examples of the use of behavioral economics in a real setting.

Many people have trouble saving, since cash is easy to spend. In 2006 Nava Ashraf, Dean Karlan and Wesley Yin offered a savings account with a twist to customers of a bank in the Philippines. In the account, they could not withdraw their money until they reached a goal they had set, or a date that they chose. The restrictions were voluntary.
About a quarter of those offered the account took it up. After a year, those who were offered it had saved substantially more than a comparison group. The people who chose to restrict themselves seemed to know that they would spend the money otherwise. It's an example of a commitment device. Tying your own hands may be a sign of wisdom, and it works best for people who know their weaknesses.

In 1990 Richard Thaler and Eric Johnson asked people to make a series of gambles. If they had won money earlier, they were more willing to take risks than if they had started from nothing. They seemed to feel that the money from the earlier win was not entirely theirs, and so it was less painful to lose.
The idea is called the house money effect, after the casino expression. It has been seen in lab studies and in real gambling. A gambler who is ahead may take riskier bets, and a person with a windfall may spend it more freely than they would earned income. Money is money, wherever it came from. But in our minds we put it in different accounts, and they have different rules.
Why we sell winners and keep losers

If you own two stocks, one that has gone up and another that has gone down, which are you more likely to sell? In 1998 Terrance Odean studied the trading records of ten thousand customers of a discount brokerage firm. He found that investors were much more likely to sell stocks that had gone up than stocks that had gone down.
This is called the disposition effect. Selling a winner lets us feel the pleasure of a gain, and selling a loser makes us admit a loss. But it's not good for returns. The stocks that investors sold went on to do better than the stocks that they kept. There's also a tax reason to do the opposite, since losses can offset gains. The pattern is a good example of how feelings about regret can lead us to a worse choice.
The more you trade, the less you make

In 2000 Brad Barber and Terrance Odean used records from a large brokerage firm to study how often individual investors trade, and how they did. They looked at tens of thousands of households over six years, and divided them by how often they bought and sold.
The households that traded the most earned the lowest returns, after costs. The most active group underperformed the market by several percentage points a year, while those who traded the least did best. The reasons were the costs of trading, and a tendency to be overconfident. The investors who traded most believed that they knew more than the market. The title of the paper summed it up. Trading is hazardous to your wealth.

In 1984 the educational psychologist Benjamin Bloom reported results from studies by his graduate students. Students who learned a subject with one-to-one tutoring, and with mastery methods, did far better than students in a normal class. The average tutored student scored about two standard deviations higher, which means better than ninety-eight percent of the students in the class. Bloom called the challenge of finding a way to give every student this benefit the two sigma problem.
Later reviews have found a smaller effect. In 2011 Kurt VanLehn looked at many studies of human tutoring and of computer tutors, and put the effect closer to three quarters of a standard deviation. That is still very large by the standards of education. Good tutors seem to give students quick feedback, ask them questions, and keep them working at the right level. It's a reason why a patient study partner or a good tutor is hard to beat.

For decades, teachers have argued about how much to tell students and how much to let them find out for themselves. One camp says that students learn best by discovering ideas through exploration. The other says that beginners need direct explanation, since the mind has a limited working memory. In 2011 Louis Alfieri and his colleagues combined the results of more than a hundred studies to see which was right.
The answer was neither. Unassisted discovery, where students are left to find things on their own, was generally worse than explicit teaching. But discovery with guidance did better. Students learned most when they were asked to explore, and also given feedback, examples or hints along the way. The best lessons mix the two. They let the learner struggle with a problem, and step in with help at the right time.
Feedback that says where to go next

Feedback is one of the strongest influences on learning, but it can also do nothing, or do harm. In 2007 John Hattie and Helen Timperley reviewed hundreds of studies of feedback. They found that its effects varied widely. The difference was in what the feedback said.
The most useful feedback answers three questions. Where am I going? How am I going? Where to next? Feedback that tells a student about the task and how to improve it was strong. Praise that was about the person, such as "you're so smart," added little. Feedback that comes too late is less useful, and so is feedback that is only a grade. The review suggests that when giving feedback, or asking for it, the next step is the most important part.

In 2009 John Hattie published a book that gathered over eight hundred reviews of research on education. He ranked influences on student achievement by their effect size, such as feedback, class size and homework. He proposed that an effect size of about 0.4 is a hinge point, and that anything above it is worth doing. The book became very influential with teachers and school leaders.
It has also been criticized. Statisticians pointed out that effect sizes from different kinds of studies can't be simply averaged and ranked, since they come from different designs and measures. Some of the figures contained errors, and a single number can hide large differences. The list is a useful source of ideas. But it's not a ranking that you should follow like a recipe.

Most of the research on practice testing was done in labs. In 2011 Henry Roediger and his colleagues tested it in a real middle school in Illinois. Students in sixth grade took short quizzes on parts of their social studies lessons. Other parts of the material were not quizzed, but were covered in the same way. All of it was part of the course.
On the unit tests, students did better on the material that had been quizzed, by about a letter grade. The advantage was still there on the final exam. The quizzes were low-stakes. They counted for little or nothing, and students had the chance to see the right answers afterward. The result shows that the benefits of retrieval practice carry over into everyday classrooms.

Many of us were taught the SQ3R method for reading. The letters stand for survey, question, read, recite and review. The method was devised by the psychologist Francis Robinson in the 1940s. First, you look over the headings. Then you turn them into questions, read to find the answers, recite what you have learned without looking, and finally review.
Its parts include good ideas, such as asking questions and retrieving. Those two have solid evidence. The method as a whole hasn't been tested directly very well, and the review by Dunlosky and his colleagues didn't find enough evidence to rate it. The parts that matter are probably the active ones, the questions and the recitation. Surveying and rereading do less. If you use SQ3R, put your effort into recalling what you have read.

Many teenagers don't get enough sleep, since their body clocks shift later in adolescence, and school starts early. In 2018 Gideon Dunster and his colleagues studied a natural experiment in Seattle. Two high schools moved their start time from 7:50 to 8:45 in the morning. The researchers asked students to wear sleep monitors before and after.
Students slept about thirty-four minutes more per night after the change. They went to bed at about the same time, but woke up later. Their grades went up, with the median grade rising by about four percent, and they were late and absent less often. Other studies of later start times have found benefits in test scores and in student well-being. Sleep is not a luxury for teenagers, and starting school later may be one of the simplest ways to help.
Do we really lose attention after ten minutes?

Many teachers have been told that students can pay attention for only ten or fifteen minutes in a lecture. The claim is repeated in books about teaching and on the internet. In 2016 Neil Bradbury traced the studies that were cited for it. He found that the evidence was thin, and that some of the citations led nowhere.
The studies that existed didn't show a steady drop in attention at a fixed time. Attention rose and fell through a lecture, depending on the content and on what the teacher was doing. The most reliable finding was that attention returns when the activity changes. There's no magic number of minutes. But the idea that varying the lesson, with a question, a problem or a story, can help is well supported.

How long do teachers wait after asking a question? In the early 1970s Mary Budd Rowe recorded hundreds of classrooms. On average, the teachers waited less than one second before calling on a student, or answering the question themselves. The silence was hard for them to bear.
When teachers were trained to wait three seconds or more, many things changed. The answers got longer and more thoughtful. More students took part, including those who rarely spoke. Students asked more questions, and the teachers asked deeper ones. The same applies to a conversation at home. Pausing after a question makes more room for a real answer, even though it feels long.
Math anxiety and the working mind

Some people feel tense or afraid when they have to do math. In 2001 Mark Ashcraft and Elizabeth Kirk tested what it does to thinking. They measured how anxious people were about math, and how well they did on tasks of working memory, such as keeping track of numbers while doing arithmetic.
People with high math anxiety did worse on the working memory tasks that involved numbers, especially when they were also asked to do a calculation. Worry takes up space in working memory, leaving less for the problem. This was an early explanation of why anxiety affects performance. It also suggests why people who understand the math can fail under pressure. Some of the cures are ones that reduce the worry, such as writing about it before a test.

Can a parent's worry about math pass to a child? In 2015 Erin Maloney and her colleagues studied about four hundred first and second graders and their parents. The parents filled out a questionnaire about how anxious they felt about math, and the children took a math test at the beginning and end of the school year.
On average, a parent's anxiety didn't harm the child's progress. But when math-anxious parents often helped their children with homework, the children learned less math during the year, and were more likely to become anxious themselves. The researchers suggested that the parents may have shown their worry, or taught less effective methods. It's not a reason to avoid helping. Parents who are anxious can use a book, a game or an app, and speak about math with ease.

How long do we remember a language that we learned? In 1993 Harry Bahrick and his family ran a study that lasted for years. Adults learned Spanish vocabulary with the same number of practice sessions. For some, the sessions were two weeks apart. For others, they were four weeks apart, or eight weeks apart. Then the researchers tested them one, two, three and five years later.
The people who had practiced with longer gaps between sessions remembered more, even after five years. The effect was large. Wide spacing gave better long-term memory than narrow spacing, even when it meant fewer sessions in the same period. It's some of the best evidence that the spacing effect lasts. If you want to keep what you learn for years, space out the practice over months.

The sandwich is named after John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, an English nobleman who lived in the eighteenth century. The most common story is that he was so absorbed in a card game that he asked for meat between two slices of bread, so that he could eat without leaving the table or getting his fingers greasy. Others at the table began to order what he was having.
The earl's own life was busy, as he was First Lord of the Admiralty, and some historians think that he ate at his desk. Either way, the name is well documented from the 1760s. The earl also gave his name to the Sandwich Islands, now Hawaii, which Captain Cook named in his honor. A man known for a snack and for the sea has two places that bear his title.

The cardigan is a knitted jacket that buttons down the front, and it's named after James Brudenell, the seventh Earl of Cardigan. He was a British cavalry officer who led the Charge of the Light Brigade in 1854, during the Crimean War. It was a doomed attack that became famous through a poem by Tennyson.
The knitted waistcoat came into fashion in the years after the war. According to the usual explanation, officers wore knitted garments like this one to keep out the cold, and it's said that the earl's example gave the garment its name. The exact route is hard to prove, but the dictionary records the word from the 1860s. Another garment, the raglan sleeve, comes from the name of another commander in the same war, Lord Raglan.

A silhouette is a dark outline, like a cut-paper portrait. The word comes from Étienne de Silhouette, who was the French finance minister in 1759. He tried to save the government money with harsh taxes and cuts, and he was widely mocked. Anything cheap or done on the cheap came to be called à la Silhouette.
Cut-paper portraits were an inexpensive alternative to painted ones, and they were popular in the years that followed. They became known by his name, probably in a sneering way. The word spread and widened to mean any dark shape against a light background. The minister was in office for less than a year, but he is remembered every time someone sees a shape against the sunset.

To be mesmerized is to be held spellbound. The word comes from Franz Anton Mesmer, an Austrian doctor who worked in Vienna and Paris in the late eighteenth century. He claimed to cure illness by moving magnets, and later his hands, over patients. He said that an invisible fluid, which he called animal magnetism, flowed through the body.
In 1784 a commission in France, which included Benjamin Franklin and the chemist Antoine Lavoisier, tested his claims. They found that the effects came from the patients' imagination and not from any fluid. The treatment was discredited, but it left a legacy. Mesmer's technique was an early form of what became hypnosis, and his name survives in the English language as a word for fascination.

The chemical in tobacco that causes addiction is named after Jean Nicot, a French diplomat. In the 1550s he was the French ambassador in Lisbon. There, he heard of the tobacco plant, which had come from the Americas, and he sent seeds and leaves to the French court. He promoted it as a medicine, and it was said to cure headaches and other ailments.
The plant was named Nicotiana in his honor, and when the active chemical was isolated in the early nineteenth century, it was called nicotine. Nicot was also the author of one of the first dictionaries of the French language. A man who compiled words gave his name to a plant, and a drug that killed millions.

A maverick is a person who doesn't go along with a group. The word comes from Samuel Maverick, a Texas lawyer and landowner in the nineteenth century. Maverick didn't brand his cattle, unlike his neighbors. One account says that he did it out of disinterest, and another that he did it deliberately to claim any unbranded cattle as his.
Neighbors started to call any unbranded calf a maverick, since it belonged to no one. Gradually, the word came to describe an unbranded animal that strayed from the herd, and from there, a person who is independent in thought. It has appeared in English since the 1860s. It's one of the few words to have begun as a rancher's habit.

The guillotine is named after Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, a French physician. He did not invent it, and he did not die by it, though many people think that he did. In 1789 Guillotin, who was a member of the National Assembly, proposed that executions should be quick and painless, and the same for all classes. At the time, nobles were beheaded, and commoners hanged or broken on the wheel.
A surgeon named Antoine Louis designed a machine for the purpose, and a German engineer built it. The public began to call it the guillotine, which upset Guillotin, whose family later petitioned to change the name. They couldn't, so they changed their own. He died in 1814 of natural causes. It's an odd fate to be attached to a machine that you only hoped would be kinder.

The word dollar goes back to a silver coin from a town in Bohemia, in what is now the Czech Republic. In the early sixteenth century, silver was mined in the valley of Joachimsthal, which means Joachim's valley. The mint there struck large silver coins called Joachimsthalers. People shortened it to thaler.
The coin was widely used across Europe, and the word traveled. In Dutch it was daler, and in English it became dollar. The Spanish silver coin, called the peso, was known as the Spanish dollar, and was used in the American colonies. When the United States chose a name for its currency in 1792, it took the familiar word. A mining town in Bohemia gave a name to the money of many countries.

A lunatic once meant someone whose mind was thought to be affected by the Moon. The word comes from the Latin luna, meaning moon. In ancient and medieval times, many people believed that the phases of the Moon caused madness, epilepsy and other disorders. The word has been in English since the thirteenth century.
The belief was so strong that it lasted for centuries. Studies of whether psychiatric admissions or crime rise at full moon have generally found no effect. The phrase lunatic fringe and the word loony, a shortened form of lunatic, came later. The word is now rarely used in medicine, since it's considered offensive. But it's a record of an old idea that the sky could control the mind.

The word vaccine comes from the Latin vacca, meaning cow. In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease, did not get smallpox. He tested the idea by taking material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid, and putting it into a scratch on a boy's arm. The boy later resisted smallpox.
Jenner called his method vaccination, from variolae vaccinae, the cow's pox. Later, Louis Pasteur extended the term to protection against other diseases, in honor of Jenner. The name has stuck for more than two hundred years. A word for a cow now stands for one of the most important medical advances in history. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.

The word gossip comes from the Old English godsibb, meaning a godparent, from god and sibb, a relative. It meant a person who is close, a sponsor at a baptism. Over time, it came to mean a close friend, usually a woman, and especially one who came to be with a woman at a birth.
By the sixteenth century, the word had taken on the meaning of someone who chatters idly about other people's affairs. It makes sense, since close friends are the ones who talk about everyone. Later, the word came to mean the talk itself, and not just the person who does it. The history of the word is also a history of the way that people who are close tend to share news about others.

In medieval times, a villain was a farm worker who was tied to a lord's estate. The word comes from the Latin villa, a country house or farm. A villein was a peasant, of a lower rank than a free man, and worked on the land of his lord. He was not necessarily wicked.
Because the nobles looked down on peasants, the word came to mean a person who was rude and low in behavior. By the sixteenth century, it meant a person who is wicked. The word shows how an insult can become a word for a crime, when a powerful group describes a weaker one. Words like churl and boor changed in similar ways, from a social rank to a flaw of character.

In chess, checkmate means that the king can't escape capture, and the game is over. The word comes from Persian, shāh māt, which is usually translated as the king is helpless, or the king is at a loss. Chess came to Europe from Persia, after reaching there from India, where the game began.
Some people say that the phrase meant the king is dead. It's a popular story, but the more likely meaning is that the king is defeated. The word came into Old French as eschec mat, and then into English. The word check, which gives a warning that the king is under attack, comes from the same Persian word for king. So the game's language has been traveling for over a thousand years.

The word algebra comes from Arabic, al-jabr, which means restoring or completion. It appears in the title of a book written by the mathematician al-Khwarizmi in Baghdad in about the year 820. The book is called Al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wa'l-muqabala, which means The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing.
Al-jabr referred to the operation of moving a negative term to the other side of an equation, to make it positive. The book set out rules for solving linear and quadratic equations, using words and geometry, and not symbols. The Latin translation of the book, in the twelfth century, introduced the word to Europe. It gave us both algebra and, from the author's name, the word algorithm.

Ketchup began as a fermented fish sauce. The word probably comes from the Hokkien Chinese kê-tsiap, a sauce made of fish brine. Sailors and traders brought it to Southeast Asia, and then to Britain in the seventeenth century. The British made their own versions, with mushrooms, walnuts and anchovies.
There was no tomato in ketchup until the late eighteenth century. Early American recipes, from about 1800, began to use tomatoes, and in the nineteenth century, the sweet tomato version became the standard. Sugar was added in large amounts when it became a commercial product. The sauce you put on fries began its life as the salty liquid of fermented fish, on the other side of the world.

The word salary comes from the Latin salarium, which is connected to sal, meaning salt. Many people say that Roman soldiers were paid in salt, which is why we speak of being worth our salt. That story is popular, but historians are not sure that it's right. Pliny the Elder wrote that the word came from salt, but the Romans paid soldiers in coins.
Another explanation is that the salarium was an allowance to buy salt, which was a basic necessity and an item of trade. Or it may have been the money for the soldiers to travel on the Via Salaria, the salt road, to Rome. The connection with salt is real, but the details are disputed. It's a good example of a word whose popular story is more certain than the evidence.

Socrates lived in Athens in the fifth century BC and wrote nothing. What we know of him comes from his students, above all Plato, and from the historian Xenophon. He spent his days in the marketplace asking people what they meant by words such as justice, courage and virtue. His questions showed that people who were sure that they knew often could not explain.
In 399 BC he was put on trial on charges of not honoring the city's gods and of corrupting the young. He was found guilty and sentenced to death by drinking hemlock. In Plato's account, he said that the unexamined life is not worth living. His method of patient questioning is still used in teaching, in law and in therapy.

Plato was a student of Socrates, and after his teacher's death, he traveled and then returned to Athens. Around 387 BC he founded the Academy, a school just outside the city. It lasted for centuries, and it's the origin of the word academic. His most famous student there was Aristotle.
Plato wrote dialogues, in which Socrates and others argue about big questions. In the Republic, he describes an ideal city, and the allegory of the cave. In it, prisoners who have only seen shadows on a wall mistake them for reality, until one is freed and sees the sun. Plato's point was that what we take for the real world may be only a shadow of something truer, and that education is a turning of the mind toward the light.

Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy for about twenty years, and later tutored the young Alexander the Great. In 335 BC he founded his own school in Athens, the Lyceum. He wrote on logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics and poetry, and what survives of his work fills many volumes.
He was a careful observer. He dissected animals and described hundreds of species, including the way a shark's embryo is attached by a kind of placenta, which was not confirmed for centuries. He was also wrong about many things, such as the idea that heavier objects fall faster, and that Earth is the center of the universe. His authority was so great that his errors held on for almost two thousand years. It is a lesson in how a great mind can be right and wrong at once.

Confucius was a teacher in China who lived from about 551 to 479 BC. He came from a modest family, and he tried to get a post as an adviser to the rulers of his time, but with little success.
