He spent his later years teaching a group of students. After his death, they recorded his sayings in a book called the Analects.
His teaching focused on how people should behave toward one another. He stressed respect for family, honesty, and learning as a lifelong task. He thought that a good ruler governs by example, and not by force. His ideas shaped Chinese education and government for over two thousand years, including the system of examinations for public office. He also gave the rule of not doing to others what you would not want done to yourself.

Epictetus was born a slave in the Roman Empire around the year 50 AD, in what is now Turkey. His owner allowed him to study philosophy, and after he was freed, he became a teacher in Rome and later in Greece. He wrote nothing himself. His student Arrian wrote down his lectures, which survive as the Discourses and a short handbook.
His central idea is that some things are up to us and others are not. Our opinions, desires and actions are in our power. The body, property, reputation and the actions of others are not. Peace comes from focusing on the first and accepting the second. The idea is the root of modern cognitive therapy. Several of its founders cited a line of his, that people are disturbed not by things, but by the views that they take of them.

Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome from 161 to 180 AD, in a time of war, plague and rebellion. He was also a Stoic philosopher. During his campaigns on the northern frontier, he wrote notes to himself in Greek, in the evenings. They were never meant to be published. They survive as the Meditations.
The notes are reminders. Take the long view, since all things pass. Do your duty, even when you'd prefer to stay in bed. Do not be angry at people who are acting out of ignorance. He wrote about the shortness of life and the need to act with fairness. The book has been read for almost two thousand years, and it is notable that it was written by the most powerful man of his time, who was working on his own character.

Hippocrates was a Greek physician who lived on the island of Kos in the fifth century BC. Little is known about his life. He's remembered because the collection of medical writings attributed to him, the Hippocratic Corpus, takes a new approach. It says that diseases have natural causes, and not divine ones.
The physicians in this tradition observed patients closely, kept records of the course of an illness, and valued rest, diet and fresh air. They wrote that the physician should help, or at least do no harm. The famous oath was probably not written by Hippocrates, and the writings are the work of many authors. But the idea that medicine should be based on observation, and on the patient's wellbeing, has lasted. The title father of medicine is a tribute to that change in thinking.

Galen was a Greek physician who was born in Pergamon in about 129 AD. He began as a doctor to gladiators, where he saw many wounds and learned anatomy. Later he went to Rome, where he treated emperors. He wrote hundreds of works, and he dissected animals, such as pigs and monkeys, since human dissection was forbidden.
His descriptions of the human body were therefore partly wrong, since he applied what he saw in animals to people. But his authority was enormous. For over one thousand years, in Europe and the Islamic world, his books were the standard text in medicine. It took the careful dissections of Andreas Vesalius in 1543 to show where Galen had been mistaken. His example shows how a good method with the wrong material can lead to lasting errors.

Ptolemy was a Greek astronomer who worked in Alexandria, in Egypt, in the second century AD. His great book, the Almagest, set out a mathematical model of the heavens, with the Earth at the center. The Sun, Moon and planets moved on circles within circles, called epicycles, which explained the odd loops that planets seem to make against the stars.
The model worked well. It could predict the positions of the planets with good accuracy, and so it was used for about fourteen hundred years, in Europe and the Islamic world. Ptolemy also wrote a book on geography, which gave the coordinates of thousands of places. When Copernicus proposed a Sun-centered model in 1543, he kept many of Ptolemy's methods. A wrong theory can still be a good tool for prediction.

Al-Razi, known in Europe as Rhazes, was a Persian physician who lived from about 865 to 925. He worked in Rayy, now near Tehran, and in Baghdad, where he led a hospital. He wrote more than a hundred books on medicine, philosophy and alchemy.
He is best known for his treatise on smallpox and measles, in which he was the first to describe the two diseases as separate. He wrote about how to tell them apart by the rash and the fever, and how to treat the patient. He also wrote a book of doubts about Galen, arguing that a physician should not accept authority without checking it against experience. He also wrote on the ethics of medicine, and on the need to treat the poor as carefully as the rich.

Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332. He worked as an adviser and judge to rulers across North Africa and Spain, and his life was full of political danger. In 1375 he withdrew to a fortress in Algeria to write. There, over a few months, he produced the introduction to a history of the world, called the Muqaddimah.
In it he tried to explain why states rise and fall. He argued that societies have laws that can be studied, like nature. A group with strong solidarity, which he called asabiyyah, conquers a settled civilization. But after a few generations, comfort and luxury weaken it, and a new group takes over. Many historians regard him as an early founder of sociology, and of economics. He saw history as something that can be understood by looking at causes.

Leonardo of Pisa, nicknamed Fibonacci, was born in about 1170 in Italy. As a boy, he traveled with his father, a merchant, to North Africa, where he learned the Hindu-Arabic system of numerals. He saw that it was much easier to calculate with than Roman numerals.
In 1202 he wrote a book, Liber Abaci, that explained the new system to Europe. It showed how to write the numbers from zero to nine, how to do arithmetic, and how to use them for business, for example in currency exchange and interest. The book included a puzzle about the breeding of rabbits, which gives a sequence of numbers now named after him. Its influence was slow but huge. Without the system that he introduced, modern mathematics and accounting would be much harder.

Michel de Montaigne was a French nobleman and lawyer who lived from 1533 to 1592. At thirty-eight, he retired to the tower of his family's château near Bordeaux, with a library, to think and write. He called his short pieces essais, meaning attempts or trials, and so he gave the essay its name.
The essays are about everything, such as friendship, death, cruelty, books, and the way that we are all different from one day to the next. Montaigne wrote honestly about himself, including his faults and his bad memory. His motto was Que sais-je? What do I know? He doubted that we can be certain about much. Writing in this way, from experience, with an open mind, was new, and it influenced writers from Shakespeare to modern essayists.

Francis Bacon was an English lawyer, statesman and philosopher who lived from 1561 to 1626. He argued that knowledge should be built by careful observation and experiment, and not by relying on ancient authorities. In his book Novum Organum, he set out a new way of going about science, collecting facts, and drawing general rules from them.
He also listed the errors that mislead the mind, which he called idols. The idols of the tribe are mistakes that are natural to all of us, such as seeing more order than there is. The idols of the cave come from our own upbringing. The idols of the marketplace come from careless words, and the idols of the theater from fashionable theories. It was an early list of cognitive biases, written almost four hundred years ago.

René Descartes was a French philosopher and mathematician who lived from 1596 to 1650. He wanted to find a basis for knowledge that could not be doubted. So he decided to doubt everything that he could. The senses can deceive us, and he might even be dreaming. But he could not doubt that he was doubting, and so thinking. This became the line, I think, therefore I am.
He also changed mathematics. By describing points on a plane with two numbers, he linked algebra and geometry, a system now known as Cartesian coordinates. He argued that mind and body are different kinds of thing, which led to a problem that still puzzles people, of how the two interact. Descartes lived in the Netherlands for much of his life, and died in Sweden, where he had been invited to tutor Queen Christina, in the cold of early mornings.

Blaise Pascal was born in France in 1623, and was a prodigy. As a teenager, he built one of the first mechanical calculators, to help his father, a tax official, with his sums. In 1654 he exchanged letters with Pierre de Fermat about a problem of dividing the stakes in an unfinished game of chance. The correspondence is regarded as the beginning of probability theory.
He also made discoveries in physics, showing that pressure in a fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. Later, he turned to religion, and wrote the Pensées, a collection of thoughts that includes his wager. It argues that believing in God is a good bet, since the possible gain is infinite and the cost small. Pascal was often ill, and died in 1662, aged thirty-nine.

David Hume was a Scottish philosopher who lived from 1711 to 1776. He wrote his first great work, A Treatise of Human Nature, in his twenties, and it was ignored. He said that it fell dead-born from the press. He rewrote it, and later became famous, mainly as a historian.
Hume argued that all our ideas come from experience. He noticed that we never see one event cause another. We only see that one follows the other, again and again, and we get used to expecting it. Our belief in causes, he said, is a habit of the mind. He also pointed out that you cannot derive what ought to be from what is. The problem of induction, as it is called, still troubles philosophers, and the is-ought gap is a staple of ethics.

Isaac Newton was born in England in 1642, in a farming family. He studied at Cambridge, and in the plague years of 1665 and 1666, when the university closed, he worked at home on mathematics, optics and gravity. In 1687 he published the Principia, which sets out the laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation.
The book showed that the same force that makes an apple fall also holds the Moon in orbit. It explained the tides and the paths of comets. Newton also invented calculus, and showed that white light is a mixture of colors. He was fierce in disputes, with Robert Hooke and with Gottfried Leibniz about calculus. In his later life, he ran the Royal Mint, and he spent a lot of time on alchemy and theology. He is buried in Westminster Abbey.

Gottfried Leibniz was a German mathematician and philosopher who lived from 1646 to 1716. He worked for noble families as a diplomat, a librarian and a lawyer, and he wrote on many subjects. In 1684 he published his version of calculus, independently of Newton, and the notation he used is the one that we use today, including the integral sign.
He also worked on the binary system of numbers, using only zero and one. He saw that it could be used to represent all numbers, and he built a calculating machine that could multiply and divide. A bitter quarrel over who had invented calculus first divided British and continental mathematicians for generations. Most historians now agree that each man found it on his own. Leibniz's binary idea waited about two and a half centuries to find its use in computers.

Leonhard Euler was a Swiss mathematician who lived from 1707 to 1783. He is regarded as one of the most productive mathematicians in history. His collected works fill dozens of large volumes, and cover number theory, geometry, calculus, physics and astronomy. He worked in Saint Petersburg and in Berlin.
He lost the sight of one eye in 1738, and was nearly blind by 1771. He kept working by dictating to assistants, and by doing the calculations in his head. Many of the symbols that we use were popularized by him, including the letter e for the base of natural logarithms, i for the square root of minus one, and the use of f(x) for a function. A story says that he could calculate faster than people could write down. His work in 1735 on the bridges of Königsberg was the start of graph theory.

Antoine Lavoisier was a French chemist who lived from 1743 to 1794. He used careful measurements with a balance, and not just observations, and changed chemistry into a quantitative science. He showed that when a substance burns, it combines with a part of the air, which he named oxygen. This replaced the earlier theory that burning released an element called phlogiston.
He also showed that matter is conserved in chemical reactions, and that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. He wrote the first modern textbook of chemistry, and helped to design the system of naming chemicals that we use. During the French Revolution, he was arrested because he had been a tax collector, and guillotined in 1794. The mathematician Lagrange is said to have remarked that it took a moment to cut off his head, and a century to grow another like it.

Charles Babbage was an English mathematician who lived from 1791 to 1871. He was annoyed by the mistakes in printed tables of numbers used for navigation, which were made by human calculators. In the 1820s he designed the Difference Engine, a mechanical device for calculating and printing tables, and received government money to build it.
The project stalled, in part because of disputes with his engineer. Meanwhile, Babbage had a bigger idea, the Analytical Engine, a machine that could be programmed using punched cards, with a store for numbers and a unit for calculating. It was never built in his lifetime. Ada Lovelace wrote notes about it that included what is considered an early program. In 1991 the Science Museum in London built a Difference Engine from his plans, and it worked.

Paul Erdős was a Hungarian mathematician who lived from 1913 to 1996. He had no home and no job in the usual sense. He traveled the world with two suitcases, staying with colleagues, and arriving with the words, my brain is open. He worked on problems with them, and moved on a few days later, leaving them with new ideas.
He wrote around fifteen hundred papers, more than almost any other mathematician, and with hundreds of different co-authors. Mathematicians define an Erdős number, which counts how many steps of co-authorship separate them from him. Someone who wrote a paper with Erdős has a number of one. He used a vocabulary of his own, calling children epsilons, and God the Supreme Fascist, who keeps the best proofs in a book.

William James was an American philosopher and psychologist who lived from 1842 to 1910. He trained as a doctor, but he suffered from depression and doubts about what to do with his life, and he found his way into teaching at Harvard. In 1890 he published The Principles of Psychology, after twelve years of work. It was a huge book, and it set the agenda for the field.
James described consciousness as a stream, always changing and continuous, and not a chain of separate ideas. He wrote about attention, habit, emotion and the self. He argued that habit is a flywheel of society, and that we should make our nervous system an ally. He also proposed that emotion follows the body's reaction, so that we are afraid because we run. He is the father of American psychology.

Wilhelm Wundt was a German physician and philosopher who lived from 1832 to 1920. In 1879 he set up a laboratory at the University of Leipzig, to study the mind by experiment. That year is usually given as the founding of psychology as a separate science.
His method was introspection, with trained observers reporting on their experiences when something was done to them, such as the sound of a metronome. He also measured reaction times. Students came from all over the world, and took his methods home, including many of the first American psychologists. Later psychologists criticized introspection as unreliable, and the field moved toward behavior. But Wundt's insistence that the mind could be studied scientifically was a turning point.

John Bowlby was a British psychiatrist who lived from 1907 to 1990. He worked in a clinic for troubled children, and noticed that many had suffered early separations from their mothers. During the Second World War, and after, he studied children who had been separated from their families, in hospitals and orphanages.
In 1951 the World Health Organization asked him to write a report on the mental health of homeless children. He argued that infants need a warm, continuous relationship with a caregiver. He drew on ethology, the study of animal behavior, and suggested that attachment is an evolved system for survival. His ideas were first rejected by psychoanalysts. Mary Ainsworth's work with infants then gave them an empirical base, and attachment theory is now a major influence.

Lev Vygotsky was a Russian psychologist who died of tuberculosis in 1934 at the age of thirty-seven. In a career of only about ten years, he wrote on language, play and learning. His work was banned for a time in the Soviet Union, and wasn't widely known in the West until it was translated in the 1960s and 70s.
He argued that thinking develops through social interaction. A child learns first with the help of other people, and then makes the skills their own. Language is a tool, first used to communicate with others, and then used silently, as inner speech, to guide thought. Children talk to themselves as they play, and he thought that this private speech helps them to plan. His idea of the zone of proximal development has had a deep influence on teaching.

Kurt Lewin was a German-American psychologist who lived from 1890 to 1947. He was Jewish, and left Germany in 1933 when the Nazis came to power, and eventually worked at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He is considered the founder of social psychology. He argued that behavior depends on the person and on the environment together.
In a famous study, he and his colleagues organized boys' clubs under adult leaders who were authoritarian, democratic or permissive. They found that the democratic groups were the most productive and happy, while the authoritarian leaders produced either aggression or apathy. He also started action research, in which people study problems in order to solve them. He is credited with the saying that there is nothing so practical as a good theory.

Carl Rogers was an American psychologist who lived from 1902 to 1987. He was dissatisfied with therapies in which the therapist told the client what was wrong. He developed the idea that the client has the capacity to grow, and that the therapist's job is to create the right conditions. He called it person-centered therapy.
The conditions, according to Rogers, are three. The therapist must be genuine, must accept the client without judgment, which he called unconditional positive regard, and must listen with empathy. He was also one of the first to record therapy sessions, and to study them scientifically. Research has found that the quality of the relationship between therapist and client predicts the outcome. His approach influenced counseling, education and the way that we think about good listening.

Viktor Frankl was an Austrian psychiatrist who lived from 1905 to 1997. In 1942 he and his family were sent to a Nazi ghetto, and then to concentration camps, including Auschwitz. His wife, his parents and his brother died. He survived, and in 1946 he wrote a book in nine days about what he had seen, called Man's Search for Meaning.
In it he argued that the main drive in humans is not pleasure or power, but meaning. He observed that prisoners who had a purpose, such as a person to see again or a task to finish, were more likely to endure. He developed a school of therapy, called logotherapy, that helps people find meaning. He often quoted Nietzsche, that he who has a why to live can bear almost any how. The book has sold millions of copies.

Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky met at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in the late 1960s. They were very different. Kahneman was an anxious, doubting man, and Tversky was a confident, quick-witted one. They became close friends, and for about a decade worked together almost every day, talking for hours, sometimes laughing so hard that people outside their office wondered what was going on.
Together they produced the research on heuristics and biases, and on prospect theory, that changed psychology and economics. They decided who would be listed first on each paper by turns. Tversky died of cancer in 1996, at fifty-nine. In 2002 Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in Economics, and said that Tversky would have shared it if he had lived, since the Nobel is not given after death.

Santiago Ramón y Cajal was a Spanish scientist who lived from 1852 to 1934. As a boy he wanted to be an artist, and his father, a doctor, pushed him toward medicine. He combined the two. Using a stain invented by the Italian Camillo Golgi, which colors a few nerve cells black, he looked at brain tissue under a microscope, and drew what he saw.
His drawings showed that the nervous system is made of separate cells, the neurons, which are not fused into a continuous net, as Golgi believed. This was the neuron doctrine. They shared the Nobel Prize in 1906, and made speeches that disagreed with each other. Cajal's drawings of neurons are so accurate and beautiful that they are still used in textbooks. He is regarded as the father of modern neuroscience.

Charles Sherrington was a British physiologist who lived from 1857 to 1952. He studied reflexes, such as the way a leg jerks when the knee is tapped. He found that nerve cells do not simply pass a signal along, but add up the messages that arrive, and so decide whether to fire.
In 1897 he coined the word synapse, from a Greek word meaning to clasp, for the junction where one nerve cell communicates with another. At the time, no one could see it. He deduced that it must exist from the speed and delay of the reflexes that he measured. Electron microscopes confirmed it decades later. He shared the Nobel Prize in 1932, and wrote a book, Man on His Nature, which asks how the brain relates to the mind.

Eric Kandel was born in Vienna in 1929. In 1938, when he was nine, the Nazis took over Austria, and his family had to flee, and eventually reached New York. He studied history and literature, and then medicine. He was interested in how memory works, and decided to look for it in an animal with a very simple nervous system, a large sea slug called Aplysia.
The slug has only about twenty thousand neurons, some of them large enough to see. Kandel showed that learning, such as becoming used to a touch, changes the strength of the connections between particular neurons. Short-term memory involves changes to existing proteins, and long-term memory requires new proteins to be made, and new connections to grow. He shared the Nobel Prize in 2000. His work showed that memory has a physical basis in the synapse.

Rita Levi-Montalcini was an Italian scientist who lived to be one hundred and three years old. She was born in 1909 in Turin. Her father didn't want her to go to university, but she persuaded him, and studied medicine. When the racial laws of Mussolini's government in 1938 barred Jewish people from academic jobs, she set up a small laboratory in her bedroom.
There, with a few simple tools, she studied the development of nerve fibers in chick embryos. After the war, she went to the United States, and in the early 1950s discovered nerve growth factor, a protein that helps nerve cells to grow and survive. It was the first of a family of growth factors. She shared the Nobel Prize in 1986. She continued to work in her laboratory into her nineties.

Oliver Sacks was a British neurologist who lived from 1933 to 2015, and who spent most of his career in New York. He was known for writing about his patients in a way that treated them as people with a story, and not just as cases. His books include Awakenings, about patients who had been frozen for decades by a sleeping sickness and were briefly roused by a drug.
His best-known book, The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat, collected case histories of people with unusual disorders of the brain. One was a musician who could no longer recognize faces, but could identify objects by their shape. Another was a man who lost his sense of the position of his own body. The stories made millions of readers curious about how the brain works, and how it can fail.

Noam Chomsky is an American linguist, born in 1928. In 1957 he published a short book, Syntactic Structures, that changed the study of language. He argued that the grammar of a language is a system of rules that can produce an unlimited number of sentences, and that a theory of language should explain how this is done.
In 1959 he wrote a famous review of B. F. Skinner's book on verbal behavior. He argued that children can't learn language by imitation and reward alone, because they produce sentences that they've never heard, and because the language that they hear is incomplete. He proposed that humans are born with a capacity for language. The review helped to end the dominance of behaviorism, and it shifted psychology toward the mind.

About forty-five hundred years ago, one of the world's first urban civilizations arose along the Indus River, in what is now Pakistan and northwest India. Its great cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, were carefully planned, with streets in a grid, and standard-sized bricks. Many houses had their own bathrooms and drains that emptied into covered sewers along the streets.
The people traded with Mesopotamia, and used a script that has never been deciphered. There are no known palaces, and no obvious temples or royal tombs, which makes the society hard to understand. The civilization declined from about 1900 BC, probably because of changes in climate and in the rivers. It was forgotten until the 1920s, when archaeologists dug up the ruins.

Cleopatra VII, the last active ruler of ancient Egypt, died in 30 BC. The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC, so it was already about two and a half thousand years old when she was born. She lived closer in time to the first Moon landing in 1969 than to the building of the pyramid. Counting from her death to 1969, it's about two thousand years.
It's a good way of feeling how long ancient Egypt lasted. Its history ran for about three thousand years before the Romans took it over. People in Cleopatra's time looked at the pyramids as ancient monuments, just as we look at Roman ruins. She was herself a Greek by descent, and a member of the Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals. She was reportedly the first of her family to learn the Egyptian language.
The collapse of the Bronze Age

Around 1200 BC, a number of rich civilizations in the eastern Mediterranean fell within a few decades. The palaces of the Mycenaean Greeks were burned and abandoned. The Hittite empire in Turkey broke up. Cities along the coast of Syria were destroyed, and Egypt was weakened. Writing was lost in parts of Greece, and a dark age followed.
For a long time, the explanation was invasion by mysterious Sea Peoples, whom the Egyptians recorded fighting. Modern historians, such as Eric Cline, think that no single cause was enough. Droughts, earthquakes, famine, rebellions and the breakdown of trade may have combined, each making the others worse. The societies were closely linked, and so a failure in one place spread to others. The story is often used as a warning about interconnected systems.

In 539 BC Cyrus the Great of Persia captured Babylon. Soon afterward, a clay cylinder was made, inscribed in Babylonian, which describes how the Babylonian god chose Cyrus, and how he entered the city peacefully. It also says that he allowed the people who had been moved to Babylon to return to their homelands, and restored their temples. It was found in 1879 and is in the British Museum.
The Cylinder has been called the first charter of human rights, and a copy is displayed at the United Nations. Many historians think that is too much. It is a royal proclamation, in the tradition of Mesopotamian kings, and it praises its ruler. But it does reflect a policy that was unusual. The Persians governed a vast, diverse empire in part by tolerating local customs and religions. The Bible also credits Cyrus with allowing the Jews to return from exile.

In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece with an enormous army. At a narrow pass called Thermopylae, a Greek force held it for three days. The famous part is the three hundred Spartans led by King Leonidas, but they were the royal guard, and they were joined by several thousand other Greeks, according to Herodotus.
On the third day, a local man showed the Persians a path around the pass, and the Greeks were outflanked. Leonidas sent most of the army away, and stayed with the Spartans and some others to hold the pass. They fought to the death. The delay allowed Athens to be evacuated, and gave the Greek fleet time to prepare. The Greeks won at the sea battle of Salamis a few weeks later. The story has been told for twenty-five centuries as an example of courage in a lost cause.

In 430 BC Athens was at war with Sparta, and had brought the people of the countryside inside its walls for protection. The city became crowded and hot. A plague struck, and killed a large part of the population, including the leader Pericles, who died in 429 BC. The historian Thucydides, who caught the disease and survived, described it.
His account is careful. He recorded the symptoms, such as fever, red eyes, a rash and terrible thirst, and noted that people who recovered did not catch it again. He also described how law and morality broke down, as people spent money quickly, since they expected to die. The cause of the disease is still unknown, and typhoid fever has been suggested. The plague weakened Athens, and contributed to its defeat in the war. Thucydides wrote so that readers could recognize it if it returned.

In 218 BC the Carthaginian general Hannibal set out to attack Rome during the Second Punic War. Rather than going by sea, which the Romans controlled, he marched a large army from Spain, through southern Gaul, and across the Alps, with war elephants, in the fall. It was a very hard march, and he lost many men and animals to the cold, to landslides and to attacks by mountain tribes.
He arrived in Italy and won several battles. The greatest was at Cannae in 216 BC, where he surrounded a larger Roman army and destroyed it, perhaps killing around fifty thousand men in a day. But he could not take Rome itself, and he was in a hostile country with no reinforcements. Eventually the Romans took the war to Africa. He was defeated at Zama in 202 BC. His tactics are still studied in military schools.

The Romans built with concrete, and much of it still stands. The Pantheon in Rome, completed in about 125 AD, has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Harbors made of concrete are still there, after two thousand years in the sea. Modern concrete often cracks after a few decades.
For years, scientists have wondered why the Roman version lasted so long. One answer was volcanic ash, which reacts with lime to form strong compounds, including in seawater. In 2023 Admir Masic and his colleagues found small white chunks of lime in samples of Roman concrete, and proposed that the Romans mixed the lime with the other ingredients while it was still hot. The chunks could then dissolve in water that seeped into cracks, and fill them again. It's an interesting idea, though the full story is still being studied.

The Maya civilization flourished in Mexico and Central America for over a thousand years, from about 250 to 900 AD in its classic period. The Maya built stone cities with pyramids, and developed a system of writing with glyphs. They also had a number system with a base of twenty, and a symbol for zero, which they used from at least the fourth century AD, independently of the Old World.
Their numbers were written with dots, standing for one, and bars, standing for five. They tracked time with several interlocking calendars. One had 260 days, and another 365 days, and they combined to repeat every 52 years. They also kept a long count of days from a starting date in the distant past. In calculating the cycles of Venus and eclipses, the Maya astronomers were remarkably accurate.

The Polynesians settled islands across the Pacific, an area larger than any other culture had explored. They crossed thousands of miles of open ocean in double-hulled canoes, and found tiny islands, from Hawaii to New Zealand to Easter Island. They had no compass, no charts and no metal tools.
Navigators memorized the positions of the stars as they rose and set, and used the swell of the waves, the flight of birds and the color of clouds to find land. In 1976 a replica canoe, the Hōkūle‘a, sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, about four thousand kilometers, guided by a Micronesian navigator, Mau Piailug, using traditional methods. The voyage showed that the settlement of the Pacific could have been done deliberately, and it revived pride in the old skills.

Marco Polo was a Venetian merchant who traveled to Asia with his father and uncle, and spent about twenty years there, from 1271 to 1295. He claimed to have served the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan. After he returned, he was captured in a war between Venice and Genoa, and in prison dictated an account of his travels to a writer named Rustichello.
The book was popular, and it is said to have inspired Columbus. But from the beginning, some people doubted that Polo had been to the places described. Some scholars note that he does not mention the Great Wall, tea or Chinese writing. Others answer that much of what he wrote is confirmed by Chinese sources, and that he may have used the accounts of others for parts. The debate is unsettled. Most historians believe that he did travel widely, but that his book mixes first-hand and second-hand stories.

In the early fifteenth century, the Ming emperors of China sent out huge fleets under an admiral named Zheng He, a Muslim eunuch from Yunnan. Between 1405 and 1433, there were seven voyages. They sailed through Southeast Asia, to India, Arabia and the east coast of Africa. The fleets included hundreds of ships and tens of thousands of men.
The largest ships, the treasure ships, were much bigger than any European ship of the time, though their exact size is debated. The voyages were meant to display the power of the Ming and to collect tribute. After the death of the emperor who had sponsored them, they ended. Officials who favored a focus on the land frontiers and on the cost won the argument, and many records were destroyed. Seventy years later, Portuguese ships arrived in the same waters.

The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built in Agra, India, as a tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal. She died in 1631 while giving birth to their fourteenth child. The work began in about 1632, and the main building was completed around 1643, with the grounds and other buildings finished in about 1653.
The tomb is made of white marble, brought from Rajasthan, and inlaid with semi-precious stones. It's built on a platform with four minarets, with a garden in front. Thousands of craftsmen and laborers worked on it, and the cost was enormous. The legend that the emperor cut off the hands of the workers is unsupported. Shah Jahan was later deposed by his own son, and held in a fort within view of the Taj, where he died in 1666. He was buried beside his wife.

From the fourteenth to the nineteenth centuries, Europe and some other parts of the world went through a cooler period known as the Little Ice Age. Winters were harder. Rivers such as the Thames froze, and frost fairs were held on the ice. Glaciers in the Alps advanced and swallowed farms. Harvests failed, and there were famines.
The causes are debated, and there was no single, uniform cooling. Possible causes include a reduced output from the Sun, in a period called the Maunder Minimum from about 1645 to 1715, and a series of large volcanic eruptions that put dust into the air. A decline in the population in the Americas after European contact may also have played a part, as forests regrew and took up carbon. The temperature change was small, perhaps a degree Celsius, but it had large effects.

In 1602 the Dutch government granted a charter to the United East India Company, called the VOC, a trading company with a monopoly on Dutch trade with Asia. Companies had existed before, but the VOC was unusual. It raised money by selling shares to the public, and the shares could be traded. Investors could put in money for the long term, without having to wait for each voyage to end.
A market for the shares grew up in Amsterdam, which is regarded as the first stock exchange. The company was the biggest in the world for a century, with a fleet of ships and its own armies. It also took part in a brutal colonial rule in Indonesia, and the slave trade. It was dissolved in 1799, after years of debt and corruption. The structure that it pioneered, a company owned by shareholders, became the model of modern business.

In 1692 in Salem Village, in colonial Massachusetts, several girls began to suffer from fits, and said they were being tormented by witches. Over the next months, more than two hundred people were accused. Nineteen were hanged, and one man, Giles Corey, was pressed to death with stones for refusing to enter a plea. Several others died in jail.
Many explanations have been offered. In 1976 a psychologist named Linnda Caporael proposed that the fits were caused by ergot, a fungus that grows on rye and can cause hallucinations and convulsions. Other researchers, such as Nicholas Spanos and Jack Gottlieb, replied that the symptoms don't fit ergot poisoning well. Historians tend to emphasize local quarrels, fear of attack by Native American tribes in the area, and religious belief. The trials ended in 1693, and the colony later apologized.

In 1845 a disease called potato blight struck the potato crop in Ireland. The potato was the main food of about a third of the population, especially the rural poor. The blight returned in the next years, and the harvests failed. Over the following years, about one million people died of hunger and disease, in a population of about eight million.
Another million or more emigrated, many to North America, in what were called coffin ships because of the deaths on board. During the famine, Ireland continued to export food, and the British government's response was widely seen as slow and inadequate, and shaped by the economic ideas of the day. The population of Ireland continued to decline for decades. It has still not returned to its level before the famine.
Counting the dead of the Civil War

For many years, the number of soldiers who died in the American Civil War was given as about 620,000, a figure that was worked out in the 1880s. It's an enormous number, bigger than the combined deaths of the United States in all its other wars up to Vietnam. In 2011 the historian J. David Hacker looked again at the census records, and used modern methods.
He estimated that the true toll was about 750,000, and that it might have been higher. The older count had missed deaths, particularly among Confederate soldiers and from disease, which killed more men than combat. A large share of them died from dysentery, typhoid and other illnesses in camp. As a share of the population, the war would be the equivalent of seven million deaths today.

In 1853 an American naval squadron under Commodore Matthew Perry arrived in Tokyo Bay, and demanded that Japan open itself to trade. For over two hundred years, the country had been ruled by the Tokugawa shogunate and had limited contact with the outside world. The arrival of the steam-powered warships showed the rulers how far behind Japan was in technology.
In 1868 a group of samurai and nobles overthrew the shogunate, and restored power to the emperor Meiji. They then set out on a rapid program of modernization. They created a conscript army, a national school system, banks and railways. They sent missions to Europe and America to study. Within about forty years, Japan had become an industrial power and defeated Russia in a war in 1905. It's one of history's most dramatic examples of a nation changing course.

On April 26, 1986, during a safety test at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union, a reactor exploded. A design flaw and mistakes by the operators led to a power surge. The explosion and fire released large amounts of radioactive material, which spread over much of Europe.
Two workers died in the explosion, and twenty-eight more firefighters and plant workers died within months from acute radiation sickness. Over a hundred thousand people were evacuated from the area, including the town of Pripyat, and an exclusion zone remains. Estimates of the eventual number of deaths from cancer vary widely, from a few thousand to many more, depending on the methods. The Soviet authorities were slow to disclose the accident. It has been called one of the factors in the loss of public trust in the government.

After the Second World War, Germany was divided into four zones, controlled by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. Berlin, which lay deep in the Soviet zone, was also divided. In June 1948 the Soviets blocked all road, rail and canal links to the western sectors of the city, hoping to force the Western powers out.
About two million people lived in West Berlin, and they needed food and coal. The United States and Britain began to supply them by air. At the peak, planes landed in Berlin every minute or so, around the clock, bringing in thousands of tons a day. In all, over fifteen months, about two and a third million tons of supplies were delivered. In May 1949 the Soviets ended the blockade. The airlift was a victory without a shot being fired.

After the Second World War, much of Europe was in ruins. Cities had been bombed, factories destroyed, and many people were hungry. In June 1947, the American Secretary of State, George Marshall, proposed that the United States should help Europe to rebuild. The plan was passed by Congress in 1948.
Over four years, the United States gave about thirteen billion dollars, a very large sum at the time, to sixteen European countries. The money bought food, fuel, machinery and raw materials. Production rose, and trade revived. The plan was motivated partly by generosity and partly by a fear that poverty would push countries toward communism. Historians debate how much it contributed to recovery. But it's remembered as an example of a victor helping its former enemies and allies alike.
Mandela and the end of apartheid

In 1948 the white minority government of South Africa began a system of racial separation called apartheid. It classified people by race, forced millions to live in separate areas, and denied the black majority the vote. Nelson Mandela, a lawyer, joined the African National Congress, which resisted the system. In 1964 he was sentenced to life imprisonment, and spent twenty-seven years in jail, most of them on Robben Island.
International pressure and unrest at home eventually forced the government to negotiate. Mandela was released in 1990. In 1994, in the first election in which all South Africans could vote, he was elected president. He chose not to seek revenge, and set up a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, in which people could confess to crimes in exchange for amnesty. He served one term and then stepped down.

In 1976 Muhammad Yunus, an economics professor in Bangladesh, visited a village and met women who made bamboo furniture. They had to borrow from moneylenders at very high interest, and were left with almost nothing. Yunus lent twenty-seven dollars of his own money to forty-two villagers. They repaid him.
He went on to found Grameen Bank, which makes small loans, mostly to poor women, without collateral. Borrowers are organized into groups, and the group members encourage one another to repay. Repayment rates were reported to be high. Yunus and the bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006. Later studies have found that the benefits of microcredit for lifting people out of poverty are more modest than first thought. But the idea that the poor are good credit risks was influential.
ENIAC and the women who programmed it

ENIAC, finished in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania, was one of the first large electronic computers. It filled a big room, and used about eighteen thousand vacuum tubes. It was built to calculate the paths of artillery shells. It could do in seconds what took people hours.
There was no software. To change the program, the operators had to rewire the machine by plugging cables, and setting thousands of switches. This job was given to six women, among them Kay McNulty, Betty Jean Jennings and Frances Bilas, who had been hired as human computers. They worked out how to program it from the wiring diagrams, with no manual. For many years, their role was not recognized in public. They are now regarded as among the first programmers.

In September 1947 a team working on the Harvard Mark II computer found that a relay was failing. When they looked, they found a moth trapped between its contacts. They removed it, and taped it into the logbook with the note: first actual case of bug being found. The page is now in the Smithsonian.
The word bug was used for faults in machines long before, and Thomas Edison used it in the 1870s. The joke in the logbook was that this time, the bug was a real one. Grace Hopper, who worked on the Mark II, often told the story, and helped to make it famous. The term debugging has since become the normal name for finding and fixing errors in code.

In 1969 at Bell Labs in New Jersey, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie began to write a small operating system on an old minicomputer that nobody was using. They called it Unix. Its ideas were simple. Programs should do one thing well, and could be linked together, so that the output of one became the input of the next.
Ritchie then created a programming language, C, to rewrite Unix so that it could be moved to other computers. That was unusual at the time, since operating systems were written for specific machines. C and Unix spread through universities. Their descendants include Linux, macOS, Android and iOS. The language C is the basis of many others, including C++ and Java. Two people in a lab built the foundation of much of modern computing.

In the 1970s, several networks existed, but they couldn't talk to one another, since each used its own rules. Vint Cerf and Robert Kahn designed a common set of rules for sending data between networks, which broke information into small packets, labeled them, and reassembled them at the other end. It was called TCP/IP.
The ARPANET, the American network that had begun in 1969, switched over on January 1, 1983. It was called flag day, and everyone had to change at once. Computers that didn't were cut off. Many people regard that date as the birth of the internet, since it was the start of a single network of networks. The design didn't need a central controller, and any network that followed the rules could join. It's a reason why the internet grew so fast.

In 1996 two graduate students at Stanford, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, began to work on a better way to rank pages in web search. At that time, search engines mostly counted the words on a page. The results were often poor, and easy to manipulate by repeating a word many times.
Page and Brin had an idea from academic papers. A paper is important if many other important papers cite it. In the same way, a web page is important if many important pages link to it. They called the method PageRank, partly after Page's name. A page's score depends on the scores of the pages that point to it. In 1998 they founded Google. The core idea was to treat the links that people make as votes.

On December 9, 1968, in San Francisco, Douglas Engelbart gave a ninety-minute presentation to about a thousand computer scientists. Sitting at a console on a stage, with his colleagues connected by video, he showed things that no one had seen. He used a mouse to move a pointer on the screen, and showed windows, hyperlinks, text editing, and video conferencing.
It later became known as the mother of all demos. Engelbart's aim was to use computers to extend human intelligence, and not just to calculate. Some of his team later moved to Xerox PARC, in Palo Alto, where in 1973 they built the Alto, a computer with a graphical interface. Steve Jobs saw it on a visit in 1979, and the ideas went into the Apple Macintosh. It was a long way from the idea to the product.
A disk the size of two refrigerators

In 1956 IBM released the 305 RAMAC, the first computer with a hard disk drive. The disk unit held fifty metal platters, each two feet across, spinning, and could store about five million characters, or about five megabytes. It was as large as two refrigerators, and was leased to businesses for thousands of dollars a month.
A modern smartphone can store millions of times more, in a chip the size of a fingernail. The idea of storing data on spinning magnetic disks lasted for decades, and is still used for cheap storage in data centers. The growth in capacity has been one of the most remarkable trends in technology, and helped to make possible everything from photographs to streaming music.

In 1975 Steven Sasson, a young engineer at Kodak, built the first digital camera. It was a clumsy box the size of a toaster, and weighed about eight pounds. It used a new kind of chip, a charge-coupled device, which converted light into electrical signals, and recorded the images on a cassette tape. The image was black and white, and was one hundredth of a megapixel.
It took about twenty-three seconds to record a picture, and a similar time to display it on a television. Kodak's management was unimpressed, and told Sasson that no one would want to look at photographs on a screen. The company made money from film, and was slow to move. Kodak went bankrupt in 2012. It's a famous case of a company that invented a new technology, and still failed to adapt.
The first call on a cell phone

On April 3, 1973, Martin Cooper, an engineer at Motorola, stood on a street in New York and made the first call on a handheld mobile phone. He called a rival at Bell Labs to tell him that he was calling from a portable cell phone. The prototype was nicknamed the brick. It weighed over two pounds, and had a battery that lasted about twenty minutes.
It took another decade before the phone was sold. The Motorola DynaTAC 8000X was released in 1983, and cost almost four thousand dollars. Mobile networks, with many small cells, were needed to make it work. By the 2000s, billions of people had mobile phones, and in many countries, people got one before they had a landline. Smartphones, from 2007, turned them into pocket computers.

A CAPTCHA is a puzzle, such as twisted letters, that humans can solve and software can't, used to prove that a user is not a robot. It was invented in the early 2000s by Luis von Ahn and his colleagues. Websites used it to stop programs from signing up for thousands of accounts.
Von Ahn realized that millions of people were spending a few seconds each solving them, and that the effort was wasted. In 2007 he created reCAPTCHA, which showed words that scanning software couldn't read, taken from old books and newspapers. When enough people agreed on a word, it was added to a digital copy. Over time, people typing in the words helped to digitize millions of books. Google bought the company in 2009.

In August 1991 a Finnish student, Linus Torvalds, posted a message to an online discussion group. He wrote that he was doing a free operating system, just a hobby, that wouldn't be big and professional like the others. He had written the core of a system, called a kernel, for the processors in personal computers.
He released the code under a license that let anyone use it and change it, as long as they shared their changes. Programmers around the world began to contribute. Linux now runs most of the world's web servers, all of the top supercomputers, and the Android phones that billions of people use. It is one of the greatest examples of collaborative building, and of the way that a small idea can grow when it is shared.

In 1972 an engineer named Allan Alcorn, working for a new company called Atari, built a simple video game as a training exercise. It was a game of table tennis, with two paddles and a ball that bounced between them. They called it Pong. Atari put a prototype in a bar in California. A few days later, the owner called to say that it had stopped working.
When the engineers opened the machine, they found that the coin box was jammed with quarters. Pong became the first big commercial success in video games. Home versions came in 1975. Soon, dozens of companies made games. Pong was based on a game made for another system, the Magnavox Odyssey, and the makers of that system sued. It was a simple idea that opened an industry.

Tetris was created in 1984 by a Russian software engineer, Alexey Pajitnov. Players rotate falling blocks to fit them together. It's a simple game, and it became one of the most popular of all time. It's also associated with the Tetris effect, in which people who play for a long time see the shapes in their mind's eye, or in dreams.
In 2009 Emily Holmes and her colleagues in Oxford tested an unusual use. People watched a disturbing film, and then, after a delay of half an hour, some played Tetris for ten minutes, while others did nothing. In the following week, the Tetris players had fewer intrusive memories of the film. The idea was that the game uses the same visual-spatial resources as the memory. It's a small, early study, and it has been followed by trials. It's not a treatment.

For many years, the advice was that passwords should be changed every few months, and should contain a mix of upper case letters, numbers and symbols. The man who wrote the original guidance for the US government in 2003, Bill Burr, later said that he regretted much of it. In 2017 the National Institute of Standards and Technology published new guidelines.
The new advice was that length matters more than complexity, that passwords should be checked against lists of those already known to be breached, and that people should not be forced to change them regularly unless there is a sign of a compromise. The old rules led people to choose predictable changes, such as adding a number at the end. A long phrase that you can remember is better than a short, complicated one. A password manager is better still.

The Enigma was a machine that the German forces used in the Second World War to encrypt messages. It looked like a typewriter, with rotors that scrambled each letter, and the settings changed every day. The number of possible settings was astronomical, and the Germans believed it was unbreakable.
It was first broken not by the British, but by three Polish mathematicians, Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski, in the 1930s. They gave their methods and a copy of the machine to the British and the French in 1939, just before the war began. At Bletchley Park in England, thousands of people, including Alan Turing, built on this work. They designed machines called bombes that searched for the settings. Historians have said that reading the messages shortened the war.

In 1967 Stanley Milgram posted packets to random people in Nebraska and Kansas, and asked them to get them to a stockbroker in Boston by passing them to someone whom they knew personally. Of the packets that arrived, the average chain had about six links. From that, the phrase six degrees of separation arose.
Milgram's study had problems, since most of the packets never arrived. In 2003 Peter Dodds and his colleagues repeated it using email, with sixty thousand people in a hundred and sixty-six countries trying to reach one of eighteen targets. The chains that were completed had a median length of about six to seven. The world is a small one, because even though most of our friends know each other, a few long-range links connect distant groups.

In 1956 Edsger Dijkstra, a young Dutch computer scientist, was shopping in Amsterdam with his fiancée. They stopped at a café, and he thought about a problem. How can you find the shortest route between two cities on a map? In about twenty minutes, he said later, he came up with an algorithm, without a pen or paper.
Dijkstra's algorithm works from the starting point, always extending the shortest path found so far, until it reaches the goal. He published it in 1959, in a paper of three pages. It is used in map software, in computer networks that route data, and in many other settings. He said that the lack of pencil and paper had pushed him toward a simple, elegant solution. He received the Turing Award in 1972.
The perceptron and the first AI winter

In 1958 Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist at Cornell, unveiled the perceptron, a machine that could learn to recognize patterns by adjusting the weights of its connections. It was a simple model of a neuron. The New York Times reported that the Navy expected it to be able to walk, talk and be conscious of its existence.
In 1969 Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published a book that analyzed the limits of the simplest perceptrons. They showed that a single layer couldn't solve certain problems, such as the exclusive or. It was widely taken to mean that neural networks were a dead end, though they had said that more layers might help. Funding dried up. It was one of the periods called AI winters. The ideas came back in the 1980s, and in the 2010s led to deep learning.

Every year from 2010, researchers competed in a contest called ImageNet. Their programs had to name the objects in a million photographs, drawn from a thousand categories, such as cats, cars and mushrooms. The best programs made mistakes on about a quarter of the images.
In 2012 a team from the University of Toronto, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, entered a deep neural network called AlexNet. It was trained on graphics processors, which were designed for video games. It cut the error rate to about fifteen percent, far better than the next entry. It was a turning point. Within a few years, nearly everyone in the field was using deep networks, and the technique spread to speech, translation and many other tasks.
The robot cars in the desert

In 2004 the US Defense Department's research agency offered a million dollars to the team whose driverless vehicle could finish a course of about a hundred and fifty miles across the Mojave Desert. Fifteen vehicles started. None finished. The best went about seven miles, and then got stuck.
A year later, in 2005, the contest was held again. This time, five vehicles finished the course. The winner was a modified Volkswagen named Stanley, built by a team from Stanford led by Sebastian Thrun, which finished in just under seven hours. In the year between, the teams had made huge progress in sensors and software. Many of the people involved went on to lead the self-driving car projects of the following decade.

In 1979 Dan Bricklin, a student at Harvard Business School, was tired of the way that financial models were done on paper. If you changed one number, you had to recalculate everything by hand. He imagined a grid on a screen, where each cell could hold a number or a formula, and where a change would flow through to all the others.
With a programmer, Bob Frankston, he created VisiCalc, the first spreadsheet program, for the Apple II computer. It sold for about a hundred dollars. Businesses bought Apple IIs just to run it, and it's often called the first killer app. It helped to turn the personal computer from a hobbyist's toy into a tool for business. Bricklin never patented it, and later said that he did not regret it.

In 1901 sponge divers found a shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera. Among the treasures was a corroded lump of bronze, which turned out to contain dozens of gears. It was dated to about the second or first century BC. For decades, no one knew what it was.
X-ray scans in the 2000s revealed the details. The device had at least thirty meshing gears, and dials. Turning a handle showed the positions of the Sun and Moon, the phases of the Moon, and when eclipses were likely. It also seems to have shown the dates of the ancient Olympic Games. It is the most complex machine known from the ancient world. Nothing of similar sophistication appears again for over a thousand years, when astronomical clocks were built in medieval Europe.

For centuries, sailors could find their latitude by the Sun or stars, but not their longitude. To know it, they needed to know the time at a reference point, such as their home port, and compare it with local time. A pendulum clock wouldn't work on a heaving ship. Ships were lost on rocks because of errors, and in 1707, four warships were wrecked off the Isles of Scilly, with the loss of about two thousand men.
In 1714 the British government offered a large prize for a method that worked. John Harrison, a self-taught clockmaker from Yorkshire, spent decades building a series of marine timekeepers. His fourth, H4, looked like a large pocket watch, and in 1761 it lost only a few seconds on a voyage to Jamaica. The board was slow to award the prize, and he was not fully paid until 1773. His clocks made the sea much safer.

How many people do you need in a room before there's a better than even chance that two of them share a birthday? Most people guess at around a hundred and eighty, half the number of days in a year. The answer is twenty-three. With twenty-three people, the chance is about fifty-one percent. With fifty-seven people, it's about ninety-nine percent.
The surprise comes from counting pairs, and not people. In a group of twenty-three, there are two hundred and fifty-three different pairs of people, and each pair has a small chance of matching. Those chances add up fast. The idea matters outside parties. It explains why random codes and identifiers can collide much sooner than expected, a fact used in the design of computer security systems.

If your money grows at a steady percentage each year, how long will it take to double? There's a shortcut. Divide seventy-two by the percentage rate, and the answer is roughly the number of years. At six percent, it takes about twelve years. At nine percent, about eight years. At two percent, thirty-six years.
The rule works because of the mathematics of compound growth, and it's accurate for rates from about two to ten percent. It appeared in print in 1494, in a book by the Italian mathematician Luca Pacioli, though it may be older. It works in reverse for anything that grows or shrinks by a steady rate, such as the price of goods with inflation, or a population. At three percent inflation, prices double in about twenty-four years.

Take a sheet of paper that is a tenth of a millimeter thick. Fold it in half, and it's twice as thick. Fold it again, and four times. After seven folds, it's about as thick as a notebook. After ten, it is about a hand's width. After twenty-three folds, it's about as tall as a tall building. After forty-two folds, it would reach the Moon.
In practice, no one can fold paper more than about eleven or twelve times, as Britney Gallivan showed in 2002. She was a high school student who worked out the formula for how much paper you need, and folded a very long sheet twelve times. But the arithmetic of doubling is what matters. It shows how fast exponential growth takes off, and why we tend to underestimate it.

If you put eleven pigeons in ten holes, at least one hole must contain two pigeons. It's obvious, and it's also a powerful tool. It was named by the German mathematician Peter Dirichlet in the 1830s, who used it to prove results in number theory.
It can be used for some surprising conclusions. In any city with more people than there are possible numbers of hairs on a human head, at least two people must have exactly the same number of hairs. The number of hairs on a head is under a million, so in New York City, with millions of people, many must match. The principle doesn't tell you who they are. It proves they exist, which is the power of a simple counting argument.

Start with a single one at the top. Then write rows below it, in which each number is the sum of the two numbers above it. The result is a triangle of numbers, one, one one, one two one, one three three one, and so on. It's named after Blaise Pascal, who wrote a treatise on it in 1654, but it was known earlier in China, India and Persia. In China it was called Yang Hui's triangle.
The numbers in each row are the coefficients that you get when you expand a binomial, such as the square of a plus b. They also count the number of ways to choose items from a set, and they appear in probability. If you shade the odd numbers, a fractal pattern called the Sierpinski triangle appears. The sums of the rows are the powers of two. A simple rule hides many patterns.

A perfect number is a number that equals the sum of its proper divisors, the numbers that divide into it, not counting itself. Six is perfect, since one plus two plus three makes six. Twenty-eight is perfect too, since one, two, four, seven and fourteen add up to twenty-eight. The next are 496 and 8128. The ancient Greeks knew these four.
Euclid showed that whenever a certain kind of prime, called a Mersenne prime, exists, it gives a perfect number. In the eighteenth century, Euler proved that every even perfect number has this form. No one knows whether there are any odd perfect numbers, or whether the list goes on forever. It's one of the oldest unsolved problems in mathematics, and it has been open for over two thousand years.

In August 1900 the German mathematician David Hilbert gave a lecture at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris. He described twenty-three problems that he thought would be important in the century to come. They ranged from the foundations of mathematics to number theory and geometry.
The list became a guide for research. Some problems have been solved, such as the tenth, about whether there's a general method of solving certain equations, which was shown to be impossible in 1970. Gödel's theorems, in 1931, answered a part of the second problem, about whether mathematics can be proved to be consistent. Others remain open, such as the Riemann hypothesis, the eighth. Hilbert ended his talk by saying that in mathematics there is no ignorabimus, no we shall not know.

Does 0.999 with an endless string of nines equal one? Many people feel that it falls a little short. It's a famous puzzle, and the answer is that they are exactly equal. There are several ways to see this. One is that one third is 0.333 repeating, and three times one third is one, but also three times 0.333 repeating is 0.999 repeating.
Another way is to call x the number 0.999 repeating. Then ten times x is 9.999 repeating, and subtracting x gives nine times x equals nine, so x is one. A third way uses the idea of a limit. The number is defined as the limit of the sequence 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, and that limit is one. The feeling that something is missing comes from thinking of the nines as a process that never finishes, not as a number.

Here is a game. A fair coin is tossed until it lands heads. If heads comes up on the first toss, you win two dollars. If it takes two tosses, you win four dollars, then eight, sixteen and so on, doubling each time. How much would you pay to play?
The expected value is infinite, since each possible outcome adds one dollar to the average, and there are infinitely many. Yet most people would pay only a few dollars. In 1738 Daniel Bernoulli proposed a solution. The value of money to a person is not the same as its amount. An extra dollar matters less to a rich person than to a poor one. This idea of diminishing utility became a foundation of economics, and of the study of how people choose under risk.

Thomas Bayes was an English minister and mathematician who lived from 1701 to 1761. He published little in his life. After he died, his friend Richard Price found a paper among his things, and sent it to the Royal Society, which printed it in 1763. In it, Bayes showed how to work out the probability of a cause, given an effect.
The rule says that you should start with a prior belief, and then update it by how well the new evidence fits each possibility. If a test is positive, the chance that you really have the condition depends on how common the condition is, and on how accurate the test is. The idea was neglected for a long time, and then revived in the twentieth century. It is now central to statistics, to machine learning, and to the way that we think about evidence.

In 1927 two Scottish scientists, William Kermack and Anderson McKendrick, published a model of how an infectious disease spreads. People are divided into three groups, susceptible, infected and recovered. The model uses simple equations to show how many people move from one group to the next. It is called the SIR model.
A key number in the model is the basic reproduction number, called R-naught. It's the average number of people that one infected person infects in a population with no immunity. If it's greater than one, the disease spreads. If it's less than one, it dies out. The model also shows that an epidemic ends before everyone has been infected, because the number of susceptible people falls. Versions of it were used to guide decisions in the COVID-19 pandemic.

In 1976 the biologist Robert May published a short paper on a very simple equation. It describes how a population changes from one year to the next, with growth limited by a lack of resources. The next population equals a growth rate times the current population times one minus the current population. A child could use it with a calculator.
May found that the behavior depends on the growth rate. At low rates, the population settles at a steady level. At higher rates, it bounces between two values, then four, then eight, and at still higher rates it becomes chaotic, with no pattern at all. A simple rule, with nothing random, can produce behavior that looks random. His paper helped to spread the study of chaos, and it showed that unpredictability doesn't need complexity.

In 1970 the mathematician John Conway invented a game with no players. It is played on a grid of squares, each of which is alive or dead. At each step, a few rules decide what happens. A live cell with two or three live neighbors survives. A dead cell with exactly three live neighbors comes to life. All others die or stay dead.
From these rules, complex patterns emerge. Some patterns stay still. Some oscillate, and some, called gliders, move across the grid. People have built patterns that act like computers, and which can calculate anything that a computer can. Martin Gardner described the game in Scientific American, and it became a craze. It's often used as an example of how complexity and life-like behavior can come from simple rules.

Take a solid with flat faces, such as a cube. It has eight corners, twelve edges and six faces. Count the corners minus the edges plus the faces, and you get eight minus twelve plus six, which is two. Try a pyramid with a square base. It has five corners, eight edges and five faces, and five minus eight plus five is again two.
Leonhard Euler noticed in 1750 that this works for any solid without holes, so that the corners minus the edges plus the faces is always two. It was one of the first results in topology, the study of shapes that stay the same when stretched. For a donut shape, which has a hole, the number is zero. The count gives you a way of telling shapes apart without measuring anything.

There are exactly five solids whose faces are identical regular polygons, with the same number meeting at each corner. They are the tetrahedron, with four triangles, the cube, with six squares, the octahedron, with eight triangles, the dodecahedron, with twelve pentagons, and the icosahedron, with twenty triangles. They are called the Platonic solids.
The Greeks knew them well. Plato linked four of them to the elements, fire, earth, air and water, and the fifth to the heavens. In the last book of the Elements, Euclid proved that there can be no others. The reason is that at each corner, the angles must add up to less than a full circle. Kepler, in 1596, tried to explain the orbits of the planets by nesting the five solids inside one another. It was a wrong idea, but a beautiful one.

If you want to stack oranges as tightly as possible, how should you do it? Grocers know the answer. You arrange them in layers, with each orange sitting in the hollow between three below. It fills about seventy-four percent of the space. In 1611 Johannes Kepler stated that no arrangement of equal spheres could do better. It is called the Kepler conjecture.
No one could prove it for almost four hundred years. In 1998 Thomas Hales announced a proof that used a lot of computer calculations. The referees of the journal spent years on it, and said that they were ninety-nine percent sure it was right, but couldn't check it all. In 2014 a team led by Hales completed a formal proof, checked by software. It's a story of how the nature of proof has changed.

A googol is the number one followed by a hundred zeros. The word was made up in 1920 by Milton Sirotta, who was nine years old. He was the nephew of the American mathematician Edward Kasner, who asked him for a name for a very big number. Kasner used it in a book in 1940.
Kasner also proposed a bigger number, the googolplex, which is one followed by a googol of zeros. It's so large that you couldn't write it down, even if you used every atom in the observable universe for a digit. The search engine Google took its name from the word, with a different spelling, in 1998, to suggest the vast amount of information on the web. A googol is bigger than the number of atoms in the observable universe, which is about ten to the eightieth power.

In October 2024 a retired engineer named Luke Durant announced the discovery of the largest known prime number. It's two raised to the power 136,279,841, minus one. It has more than forty-one million digits. Printed in a normal size, it would fill many thousands of pages. It's a Mersenne prime, a prime of the form two to a power minus one.
Durant found it using graphics processors rented in cloud data centers around the world. Previous records were mostly found by volunteers using their own computers, through the Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search. There is a prize from the Electronic Frontier Foundation for the first prime with over a hundred million digits. The primes are infinite, as Euclid showed, so there will always be a larger one.

When we are upset, many of us try to hide it. In 1993 James Gross and Robert Levenson showed people a disturbing film while instructing some of them to keep their faces still, so that no one watching would know how they felt. The people who suppressed their expressions felt just as disgusted as those who didn't. But their bodies reacted more, with greater activity in the sympathetic nervous system.
In 2003 Gross and Oliver John looked at what happens in everyday life. People who often suppress their emotions tend to feel less satisfied with life, to have less close relationships, and to be less well liked. Suppression takes effort, and it doesn't make the feeling go away. It also keeps other people from knowing how you feel, which makes it harder for them to support you.

There's another way of handling an emotion, which is to change the way that you think about the situation. This is called reappraisal. A person facing a stressful event might tell themselves that it's a chance to learn, or that a medical scene in a film is a doctor doing her job. In 1998 James Gross tested this with a disgusting film. People who were asked to watch with the detachment of a medical professional felt less disgust, and showed a smaller bodily reaction.
In 2002 Kevin Ochsner and his colleagues scanned the brains of people doing the same task. When they reappraised a sad picture, activity rose in the prefrontal cortex and fell in the amygdala. Thinking differently about something changes the response of the emotional brain. Reappraisal is one of the skills at the heart of cognitive therapy, and the evidence suggests that, unlike suppression, it works.
Why a sad mood remembers sad things

When we feel down, memories of sad times come to mind, and when we feel cheerful, happy ones do. In the 1980s Gordon Bower tested this in the lab. He put people in a happy or sad mood with hypnosis, and then asked them to recall events, or to read a story about two characters, one happy and one sad.
People in a sad mood recalled more sad events from their lives, and identified with the sad character in the story. People in a happy mood did the opposite. It's called mood-congruent memory. It helps to explain why depression can feel so bleak. A low mood makes bad memories more available, and they make the mood worse. It also suggests a way out. Doing something that lifts your mood a little can make other memories easier to reach.

Is a hot temper bad for the heart? In 2009 Yoichi Chida and Andrew Steptoe combined the results of dozens of studies that followed people for years. They looked at anger and hostility, and at heart disease. In people who were healthy at the start, those who were angry or hostile were more likely to develop coronary heart disease later.
Among people who already had heart disease, anger and hostility were linked to worse outcomes. The link was stronger in men than in women. The effect is modest, and it is not easy to separate from other factors, such as smoking and diet, which are more common in angry people. But the connection has been seen repeatedly. A possible reason is that repeated surges of stress hormones put a strain on the cardiovascular system.

In the early 1990s Sheldon Cohen and his colleagues carried out an unusual experiment in Sheffield, England. They gave about four hundred volunteers a questionnaire about the stress in their lives. Then they dropped a cold virus into each person's nose. The volunteers stayed in quarantine for several days, and doctors checked who got ill.
The more stress a person had reported, the more likely they were to develop a cold, and the effect rose steadily with the level of stress. It was seen even after the researchers accounted for age, smoking and other factors. Stress didn't change whether people were infected, but it changed whether they got sick.
