The study was among the first to show, under controlled conditions, that stress can affect the immune system.

Do social connections protect against illness? In 1997 Sheldon Cohen and his colleagues asked volunteers about their social ties, including whether they were married, had friends and family, belonged to groups and attended religious services. Then they exposed them to a cold virus, and watched who got sick.
The people with the most varied social ties were much less likely to come down with a cold than those who had few. The difference was large. It was not explained by health habits, or by the amount of virus in the body. The researchers thought that social support might protect by helping people cope with stress. The result fits a body of work that links relationships with good health. It's one more reason to nurture friendships.

If you sleep badly, do you catch more colds? In 2009 Sheldon Cohen and his colleagues followed one hundred and fifty-three healthy adults. For two weeks, they kept track of how much people slept. Then the volunteers were given drops of a cold virus in the nose, and were watched for a week.
People who had slept less than seven hours a night were nearly three times as likely to develop a cold as those who slept eight hours or more. The link remained after the researchers accounted for age, stress and other factors. Sleep seems to help the immune system to do its work. It's one more reason to protect your sleep when you've been exposed to an illness.

Hugs are a form of social support, which is known to protect against stress. In 2015 Sheldon Cohen and his colleagues asked whether hugging could help to protect against illness. Four hundred volunteers were interviewed by telephone on fourteen evenings, and asked about their conflicts and hugs. Then they were given a cold virus.
Those who had more social support were less likely to get ill. The people who had been hugged more often, among those who had had arguments with others, had less severe symptoms. The researchers suggested that hugging works as a sign of support, which in turn eases the effects of stress. It was an observational study, and it can't prove cause. But it's an easy and pleasant thing to try.

In 2014 Christina Draganich and Kristi Erdal ran a clever experiment on what people believe about their sleep. Students slept in the lab, and in the morning they were attached to a machine, and were told that it had measured their sleep. Some were told that they had had above-average sleep, and others below average. The information was made up.
The students told that they had slept well did better on tests of attention and thinking than those told that they had slept poorly. Their beliefs about their sleep changed their performance. The effect was found only in a small study, and later results have been mixed. But it may help to explain why worry about sleep can make you perform worse. It's a reminder not to catastrophize about a bad night.

Why do so many people fear snakes and spiders, and so few fear cars, guns or electrical outlets, which are much more dangerous today? In 1971 Martin Seligman proposed that humans are prepared to learn some fears easily. These are the ones that threatened our ancestors.
In lab experiments, Arne Öhman and his colleagues paired pictures with a mild shock. People learned to fear pictures of snakes and spiders faster, and the fear was harder to extinguish, than when the pictures were of flowers or mushrooms, or even of guns. In 2001 Öhman and Susan Mineka proposed a fear module in the brain, which acts quickly and is built around the amygdala. It's a reason why some fears are easy to acquire and hard to lose.
Learning to fear a snake by watching

In the 1980s Susan Mineka studied monkeys raised in a lab, which showed no fear of snakes. She had them watch a video of wild-reared monkeys that showed a strong fear when they were shown a snake. After a short time, the lab-raised monkeys also acted afraid of snakes, and the fear lasted for months.
The researchers then edited the video so that the monkeys seemed to be afraid of a flower instead. The watching monkeys did not develop a fear of flowers. So the monkeys had learned from others, but only when the object was one that they were ready to fear. The study shows how fears can spread socially. It's a reason why children can pick up a phobia from a parent, and why a calm model can help them to lose it.
A single afternoon for a phobia

Phobias are among the most treatable of mental health problems. In the 1980s the Swedish psychologist Lars-Göran Öst developed a method that works in a single long session. A person with a spider phobia, for example, is guided in stages to face the feared thing, with a therapist who models the behavior, from looking at a spider in a jar to touching it with a hand.
In his studies, most patients were greatly improved after about three hours, and the benefits lasted for years. A review in 2008 by Kristin Zlomke and Thompson Davis confirmed that one-session treatments work well for many kinds of specific phobias, and for children and adults. The key is that the person stays with the fear until it falls, and finds that nothing bad happens. It's a fast and effective treatment.

Why do people eat hot chili peppers, take cold plunges or watch films that make them cry? In 2013 Paul Rozin and his colleagues studied what they called benign masochism. In a series of surveys, people listed activities where they enjoy something that the body sees as a threat, including very hot baths, spicy food, scary rides and sad music.
The researchers suggested that the pleasure comes from enjoying a negative feeling in a safe setting. The body reacts as if there is danger, while the mind knows that there is none. This lets us feel a thrill, and a sense of mastery over our own reactions. It's a special human trait, since animals don't seem to take pleasure in chili. It reminds us that emotions can be mixed, and that it's possible to enjoy being a little afraid.

Imagine a man in a closed room who doesn't know any Chinese. He has a big book of rules, written in English, that tells him which Chinese symbols to send out in reply to the symbols that are passed in through a slot. People outside, who read Chinese, find that the answers make sense. They think that the person in the room understands Chinese. But he doesn't. He is only following rules.
The philosopher John Searle put this forward in 1980 as an argument against the idea that a computer running a program could understand anything. A program is about manipulating symbols according to rules, which is syntax. Understanding involves meaning, which is something else. Many replies have been offered, for example that the whole system, the room together with the man and the book, understands. The argument is still debated, and is raised again whenever a program holds a convincing conversation.

Mary is a scientist who has spent her whole life in a black-and-white room. She has never seen color. But she knows everything that could be known about the physics and biology of color vision, including how light of different wavelengths affects the eye and brain. One day, she leaves the room and sees a red tomato. Does she learn something new?
The philosopher Frank Jackson argued in 1982 that she does. She learns what red looks like. If so, there are facts about experience that are not captured by the physical facts, and physicalism, the view that everything is physical, is incomplete. Others reply that she gains an ability, not a fact, or that she learns an old fact in a new way. Jackson himself later changed his mind. The thought experiment remains a standard way to bring out the puzzle of consciousness.
What is it like to be a bat?

Bats find their way in the dark by echolocation. They experience the world through sound, in a way that is very unlike ours. We could study their brains in the greatest detail. In 1974 the philosopher Thomas Nagel asked whether that would ever tell us what it is like to be a bat. He argued that a creature has conscious experience if there is something that it is like to be that creature, from its own point of view.
Imagining that we hang upside down and eat insects doesn't help. We would only be imagining what it would be like for us to behave like a bat. Nagel's point was that a theory of the mind that leaves out the subjective view is incomplete. The essay is one of the most cited in the philosophy of mind, and it set the agenda for debates about consciousness in animals and machines.

Imagine a being that looks and acts just like you, with the same brain, the same behavior and the same words. It says that it is in pain when it's hurt, and that it loves the taste of chocolate. But inside, there is nothing. It has no experience at all. Philosophers call this a zombie, but not the kind in films.
David Chalmers used the idea in the 1990s to argue that consciousness is more than physical processes. If a zombie is even conceivable, he said, then the physical facts don't settle whether there is experience. He called the question of why there is any experience at all the hard problem. Critics reply that a zombie is not really conceivable, or that conceiving something doesn't show that it's possible. The problem is still unsettled.

Suppose that you could plug into a machine that gave you any experiences that you liked. You would think that you were writing a great novel, or making friends, or falling in love, and it would all seem completely real. Your body would float in a tank, with electrodes in your brain. Would you plug in for life?
Robert Nozick asked this in 1974, and he thought that most people would say no. He argued that we care about more than how things feel. We want to actually do things, and to be a certain kind of person, and to be in touch with reality. If this is right, then pleasure isn't the only thing of value. Studies of what people say when asked suggest that many decline the machine, though the answers change if the question is worded differently.

Suppose that you are a brain in a vat of nutrients, connected to a computer that gives you the experience of a normal life. How could you know that you're not? The idea is a modern version of Descartes's demon, and it's the basis of films such as The Matrix. The philosopher Hilary Putnam gave it a twist in 1981.
He argued that a brain in a vat could not even think the thought that I am a brain in a vat. Its words would refer to things in the computer's simulation, not to real vats. So if you are saying the sentence, and it is true that you are in a vat, then the sentence is false. His argument is clever, and it has been much debated. Some think that it only shows something about language, and does not remove the doubt.

You step into a machine on Earth. It scans every atom of your body, destroying it in the process, and sends the information to Mars. There a machine builds an exact copy of you from new atoms. The copy remembers your life and has your character. Have you survived the trip, or have you died, and been replaced by a copy?
The philosopher Derek Parfit used this puzzle in 1984 to question our ideas about identity. He suggested that what matters is not whether the same person continues, but the connections of memory and character. If the copy has these, he thought, it is about as good as survival. Many people find this hard to accept. Parfit also said that it freed him from a fear of death, since his own life was just a part of a stream of experiences.

You are walking past a shallow pond and see a child drowning. You can wade in and save the child, but your clothes will be ruined. Should you do it? Almost everyone says yes. The cost is small, and the life is at stake. In 1972 the philosopher Peter Singer used this case to argue for a very demanding conclusion.
He said that distance doesn't change the moral situation. A child dying of poverty far away is as much in need as the one in the pond. If we can prevent something very bad, at little cost to ourselves, we ought to do so. Most of us could give much more than we do to charity. The argument has been highly influential, and gave rise to the effective altruism movement. It has also been criticized as too demanding.
Bentham, Mill and the greatest happiness

Jeremy Bentham, an English philosopher who lived from 1748 to 1832, argued that the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number. He proposed to count pleasure and pain as the measure of value. For him, a game of pushpin was as good as poetry, if it gave as much pleasure.
His follower John Stuart Mill refined the idea in 1861. He said that some pleasures are higher than others, and that it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. This view is called utilitarianism. It has been very influential in law, economics and public policy. The main objection is that it may allow terrible acts if they make the total happiness larger, which has led to many arguments over rights and fairness.

How does science change? The usual story was that it grows steadily, as facts accumulate. In 1962 the physicist and historian Thomas Kuhn offered a different picture. In normal science, he said, researchers work within a framework of shared assumptions, which he called a paradigm. They solve puzzles that the framework defines.
Over time, anomalies pile up, results that the paradigm cannot explain. At first, they are ignored. Eventually there is a crisis, and a new paradigm arrives, such as the move from Newton's physics to Einstein's. Scientists then see the world in a new way. Kuhn argued that the two paradigms can't be compared easily, since they use different standards. The phrase paradigm shift, which he made popular, is now used well outside of science.

For centuries, philosophers said that knowledge is justified true belief. To know something, you have to believe it, it has to be true, and you must have good reasons. In 1963 Edmund Gettier published a three-page paper that raised a problem with this.
Here is a case in the spirit of his. You look at a clock that says two o'clock, and you believe that it is two. You have good reason, because the clock has always been reliable. And it is two. But the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago. Your belief is justified and true, but you were right by luck. Do you know the time? Most people say no. The paper set off decades of attempts to repair the definition, and no fix has been fully accepted.

A single grain of sand is not a heap. Two grains are not a heap either. Adding one grain to something that is not a heap never makes a heap. Yet if you keep adding grains one at a time, you will end up with a heap. Where did it start? This puzzle is attributed to a Greek philosopher, Eubulides, in the fourth century BC. It's called the sorites paradox, from the Greek word for heap.
The puzzle applies to any vague word. When does a man become bald as hairs fall out? When does a color shift from red to orange? There is no sharp line, and yet the ends are clearly different. Philosophers have proposed several solutions, including a hidden sharp boundary that we can't know, and logics where truth comes in degrees. The problem matters for the law, where vague terms such as reasonable must be applied to cases.

Consider the sentence: this sentence is false. If it's true, then what it says is correct, so it is false. If it's false, then what it says is wrong, so it is true. It seems to be both. This is the liar paradox, which has been known since ancient Greece. It has often been attributed to Eubulides, and also to Epimenides, a Cretan who is said to have remarked that all Cretans are liars.
In the 1930s the logician Alfred Tarski showed that the paradox causes trouble for any language that can talk about its own truth. His solution was to separate levels. A statement about the truth of sentences in a language must be made in a different, higher language. The paradox is close to the ones that Kurt Gödel used in 1931 to prove his incompleteness theorems, in which a sentence says that it cannot be proved.

In 1902 the British philosopher Bertrand Russell wrote to the German logician Gottlob Frege, who had just finished the second volume of his life's work, an attempt to base arithmetic on logic. Russell pointed out a flaw. Consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. Does this set contain itself? If it does, then it doesn't. If it doesn't, then it does.
Frege replied that arithmetic totters. The paradox showed that the natural idea that any property defines a set leads to a contradiction. Russell and others spent years building new foundations. The standard solution is a set theory with axioms, devised by Ernst Zermelo and others, that restricts how sets can be formed. A popular version of the paradox is the barber who shaves all those, and only those, who do not shave themselves.

A superintelligent being has put two boxes in front of you. Box A is clear and holds a thousand dollars. Box B is opaque, and holds either a million dollars or nothing. You may take both boxes, or only box B. Here is the catch. The being has predicted what you will do. If it predicted that you would take only box B, it put a million dollars in it. If it predicted that you would take both, it left it empty. It has been right many times before.
One argument says to take only B, since people who do so seem to leave with a million. Another says to take both, since the contents are already fixed, and you can't change them by choosing, so you may as well take the extra thousand. William Newcomb devised the problem, and Robert Nozick described it in 1969. Philosophers are split almost evenly on the right answer.

Two drivers are each a little drunk, and both drive home. One of them gets there safely. The other, by bad luck, hits a child who runs into the road. Is the second driver more blameworthy than the first? Most of us feel that he is. And yet, what separates them is chance, which neither of them controlled.
In 1976 the philosophers Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel raised this puzzle, which they called moral luck. We usually say that people should be judged only by what is in their control. But in practice, our judgments depend on outcomes, on how people were brought up, and on the circumstances they happened to face. The problem suggests that our idea of responsibility may be less coherent than we think. It's relevant to law, where the same act is punished differently depending on the result.

Suppose that you want to maximize the total amount of happiness in the world. Consider a world with ten billion people, each with a very good life. Compare it with a world with many more people, whose lives are barely worth living. If the numbers are big enough, the total in the second world can be larger, because many small pieces of happiness add up. So the second might seem better.
Derek Parfit called this the repugnant conclusion, and he found it impossible to accept. Yet it follows from some attractive ideas about how to add up well-being. He spent years trying to find a way out, and never fully succeeded. The problem is central to the study of population ethics, which asks how we should weigh the interests of future people, including questions about the size of the population.

In a short dialogue by Plato, Socrates meets a man named Euthyphro near a court in Athens. Euthyphro is going to prosecute his own father for a killing, and is confident that it is the pious thing to do. Socrates asks him what piety is. Euthyphro says that it's what all the gods love. Then Socrates asks: is something pious because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is pious?
The question applies to morality in general. If something is good only because a god commands it, then goodness seems arbitrary, as the god could have commanded the opposite. If the gods love it because it is good, then goodness exists independently of the gods, and they are not its source. Philosophers and theologians have argued over this for over two thousand years. The dialogue ends without an answer, as many of Plato's early ones do.

Should a tolerant society tolerate intolerance? In 1945 the philosopher Karl Popper wrote a note on the question, which he called the paradox of tolerance. He argued that unlimited tolerance leads to the disappearance of tolerance. If a society is tolerant without limit toward those who are intolerant, and who would destroy it, the tolerant will be destroyed.
His conclusion was that a society has a right to protect itself. He said that we should claim the right to suppress intolerant philosophies if they won't engage in rational argument, and respond with force. But he added that, as long as such views can be countered by argument, they should be allowed. People still disagree about where to draw the line. It was written just after the Second World War, and shaped by the rise of Nazism.

Ludwig Wittgenstein was an Austrian philosopher who lived from 1889 to 1951. He thought that he had solved the main problems of philosophy in his first book. Later, he changed his mind. His second book, the Philosophical Investigations, was published after his death in 1953, and it argued against his own early view.
He proposed that the meaning of a word is its use in a language, and not an object that it stands for. Think of the word game. There is no one feature shared by all games, only family resemblances, as in a family where no one trait is common to all. Language is a set of language games, tied to activities. He also wrote that if a lion could speak, we could not understand him, because our forms of life would be so different.

About 2,300 years ago, Aristotle wrote a book on how speakers persuade people. He said that there are three means of persuasion. Ethos is the character of the speaker, whether they seem trustworthy, knowledgeable and well-meaning. Pathos is the emotion that the speech arouses in the audience. Logos is the argument itself, with its reasons and evidence.
A good speech uses all three. A speaker with sound arguments, but who seems untrustworthy, may not convince. A speaker with ethos and emotion but no real reasons may sway people, and mislead them. Modern research on persuasion has confirmed that credibility, feeling and argument quality each matter. The three terms are still used to analyze speeches, advertising and political messages. It's a short list that has lasted for twenty-three centuries.
The man with pebbles in his mouth

Demosthenes was an Athenian orator of the fourth century BC, and is often named as the greatest speaker of ancient Greece. According to the biographer Plutarch, writing about four hundred years later, he started out with a weak voice, a stammer and an awkward way of speaking. His first speeches in the assembly were mocked.
Plutarch says that he trained himself by practicing with pebbles in his mouth, and by reciting verses as he ran uphill, or spoke against the roar of the sea. He is also said to have shaved half of his head so that he would be ashamed to go out, and would stay at home to study. How much of this is true is unknown. But the story has stuck as an image of how practice can overcome a handicap.

In the winter of 431 BC, at the end of the first year of the war with Sparta, Athens held a public funeral for those who had died. Pericles, its leading statesman, gave the speech. The version that survives was written by the historian Thucydides, who said he had given the general sense of what was said.
In it, Pericles praises Athens, and not just the dead. He says that the constitution is called a democracy because power is in the hands of the many, and not of a few. Everyone is equal before the law, and advancement is by merit. He speaks of freedom in daily life, and of the courage of citizens. The speech has been read as one of the great statements of democratic ideals. It was given at a moment when the city was about to face the plague.

On November 19, 1863, a cemetery was dedicated at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, four months after the battle in which tens of thousands of soldiers were killed or wounded. The main speaker was Edward Everett, a famous orator, who spoke for about two hours. President Abraham Lincoln was asked to follow with a few remarks.
He spoke for about two minutes, in roughly 270 words. He began with four score and seven years ago, and said that the nation was conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal. He closed with the hope that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth. Everett wrote to Lincoln the next day that he wished he could have come as near to the central idea in two hours as Lincoln did in two minutes.
We shall fight on the beaches

On June 4, 1940, Winston Churchill spoke in the House of Commons about the evacuation of Dunkirk. In a few weeks, more than three hundred thousand British and French soldiers had been taken off the beaches by an array of ships. He warned that wars are not won by evacuations. Then he said that Britain would go on to the end, that we shall fight on the beaches, on the landing grounds, in the fields and in the streets, and that we shall never surrender.
The speech was not broadcast live. It was given in the Commons, and the news that night told the public what he had said. A BBC announcer read out extracts. Churchill didn't make a recording of the speech until 1949. Many people remember hearing him say it on the radio, but what they remember was probably his later broadcasts. The words became famous because they were printed and repeated.

On August 28, 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. spoke to a crowd of about a quarter of a million people at the March on Washington. He had prepared a text. As he came to the end, according to those near him, the gospel singer Mahalia Jackson called out from behind him, tell them about the dream, Martin. He put aside his script, and began to speak of his dream.
The lines about his four little children, and about a day when they would be judged by the content of their character, were not in the prepared text. He had used the dream theme in earlier speeches, and now he drew on it. The speech has been called one of the greatest of the twentieth century. It shows how an orator can respond to an audience, and how a speech grows from a text, with a cadence that comes from the preaching tradition.

In 1863 the German novelist and critic Gustav Freytag wrote a book on the technique of drama. Studying ancient Greek tragedies and the plays of Shakespeare, he saw that most of them follow a five-part pattern. It's usually drawn as a pyramid, rising and then falling.
It starts with an introduction, which sets the scene. Then comes a rising action, in which tension builds. At the peak is the climax, a turning point. After it comes the falling action, as consequences unfold. The final part is the resolution, or catastrophe in a tragedy. The scheme doesn't fit every story, and it was based on a limited set of plays. But it's still widely taught, and it's a useful way of seeing how stories are shaped to hold attention.

Kurt Vonnegut once gave a lecture in which he drew the shapes of stories on a blackboard, as lines that rise and fall with the fortunes of the hero. In 2016 Andrew Reagan and his colleagues tested the idea with data. They analyzed the words in about 1,300 works of fiction from Project Gutenberg, tracking how happy or sad the language was as the story went on.
They found six basic arcs. Rags to riches is a steady rise. Riches to rags is a fall. There are also a fall then a rise, a rise then a fall, a rise then a fall then a rise, and a fall then a rise then a fall. The arcs with more twists, such as Cinderella, which rises, falls and rises again, and Oedipus, which falls, rises and falls, were downloaded more than the simple rise or fall. The study is a nice example of using computers to find patterns in the way that stories are told.

In 1946 George Orwell wrote an essay arguing that bad writing can make clear thinking harder, and that it helps political lies to sound respectable. He ended with six rules. Never use a metaphor, simile or figure of speech that you are used to seeing in print. Never use a long word where a short one will do. If it's possible to cut a word out, always cut it out.
Never use the passive where you can use the active. Never use a foreign phrase, a scientific word or a jargon word if you can think of an everyday English equivalent. And break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous. His argument was that vague, stale language lets us avoid thinking. The essay is still widely read, and the rules are a good checklist for anyone who writes.

William Shakespeare is often credited with having invented about seventeen hundred English words, such as lonely, bedroom, eyeball, swagger and assassination. The claim is based on the Oxford English Dictionary, which lists his plays as the earliest known use of many words. It's repeated in books and on websites.
The truth is more complicated. The dictionary's editors, over a century ago, relied on what they could read, and Shakespeare was widely studied, so he was cited more than other writers. As more early texts have been searched, many of his words have turned up in earlier works. He certainly used new words, and combined old ones in new ways, but he was probably not the sole inventor of most. He also made words popular, which is a form of influence.
OMG is a hundred years old

OMG seems like a product of the age of text messages, but it's older. The Oxford English Dictionary's earliest known use is in a letter of 1917 from Admiral John Fisher, a retired British naval officer, to Winston Churchill. Fisher wrote that he had heard of a new order of chivalry that was being planned, and he added O.M.G., Oh! My God!, urging that its honors be showered on the Admiralty.
So the abbreviation is more than a century old. Telegrams and notes used many such shortenings, and slang often arises where people write quickly. The phrase became widespread in the 1990s with online chats, and entered the dictionary in 2011. It's a reminder that new communication tools often revive old habits, and that what seems new may have a longer history.

There are about seven thousand languages in the world. Many of them have very few speakers. Almost half of the world's languages are classed as endangered, and a small number of languages, such as Mandarin, Spanish and English, are spoken by hundreds of millions or even billions of people. Many languages have only a few hundred speakers, and some only a handful of elderly ones.
A language is endangered when children stop learning it. This often happens when a community moves to cities, or when a dominant language is the language of schools, work and media. Linguists fear that a large share of today's languages may fall silent within this century. When a language disappears, so does a store of knowledge about plants, animals, stories and ways of seeing the world. Some communities, such as the Māori in New Zealand, have worked to revive their languages.

For about eighteen hundred years, Hebrew was not a spoken language in daily life. It was used for prayer, and for writing, but people spoke the languages of the countries where they lived. In the late nineteenth century, Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, who emigrated to Jerusalem in 1881, set out to make it a living language again. He insisted on speaking only Hebrew at home.
His son Ittamar, born in 1882, is often called the first native speaker of modern Hebrew. Ben-Yehuda compiled a large dictionary, and helped to invent words for modern things, such as the words for newspaper and bicycle. Others took up the cause, with schools that taught in Hebrew. Today, Hebrew is the national language of Israel, and is spoken by millions. It's the only case of a dead language being revived as the everyday speech of a nation.

In 1887 Ludwik Zamenhof, a Polish-Jewish eye doctor, published a book that introduced a constructed language. He had grown up in a city, Białystok, where Poles, Russians, Germans and Jews spoke different languages and often fought. He thought that a neutral, easy language could help people to understand one another. He published it under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, meaning the one who hopes.
The language has simple rules, a small number of roots, and regular grammar. There are no exceptions to learn. It has attracted speakers around the world, though estimates of their numbers vary widely, from tens of thousands to a couple of million. It has not become a global language, since English has filled that role. Still, it is the most successful of the constructed languages, and has a literature and annual world congresses.

Until the middle of the twentieth century, many people believed that sign languages were just gestures, or a simple code for spoken language. In 1960 William Stokoe, a professor at Gallaudet University, a school for the deaf in Washington, published an analysis of American Sign Language. He showed that signs are made of smaller parts that are combined.
Each sign has a handshape, a location and a movement, which are like the sounds of a spoken language. Changing just one of these changes the meaning, as changing a sound does in a word. Later research showed that sign languages have complex grammar, and they are learned by children in the same stages as spoken languages are. The brain processes them in the same areas that process speech. It's now accepted that sign languages are full languages in their own right.

On La Gomera, one of the Canary Islands, shepherds and farmers used to talk across deep ravines by whistling. The whistled language, called Silbo Gomero, is a way of speaking Spanish. Each word is whistled, using a limited set of tones and breaks that stand for the vowels and consonants. A whistle can be heard up to a few kilometers away, far more than a shout.
Brain scans of whistlers show that they use the language areas of the brain, and not just the areas for sound. Similar whistled languages are used in Turkey, Greece, Mexico and elsewhere in places with steep valleys or dense forests. The practice declined in the twentieth century with roads and phones. In the 1990s, Silbo was introduced into the island's schools, and UNESCO added it to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2009.

Almost every language in Europe belongs to one of a few large families. Basque does not. It's spoken in the mountains along the border between Spain and France, by about three-quarters of a million people. It's called a language isolate, since no relationship with any other living language has been proved.
Many theories have been proposed, linking it to Caucasian languages, Berber, or others, but none has been accepted. The best guess is that it descends from a language spoken in the region before the arrival of Indo-European languages, perhaps for thousands of years. It was suppressed under Franco in Spain, and was nearly lost. It has since been revived, taught in schools and used on television. Its grammar and vocabulary are very different from its neighbors'.

Most languages take new words for new things from other languages. Icelandic often does the opposite. It creates new words from old roots. The word for computer, tölva, was invented in 1965 by a professor, Sigurður Nordal. It combines tala, meaning number, and völva, an old word for a seeress or prophetess. So it means a number prophetess.
The word for telephone is sími, an old word for thread. Television is sjónvarp, a vision-caster. A committee and many volunteers coin the terms. Icelanders can still read the medieval sagas, written eight hundred years ago, with little difficulty, because the language has changed little. This careful protection of the language is possible partly because of the small number of speakers, about three hundred and fifty thousand, and the isolation of the island.

Before the fifteenth century, Koreans wrote with Chinese characters, which took years to learn, and were used mainly by the educated elite. King Sejong the Great, who ruled from 1418 to 1450, wanted a system that ordinary people could learn easily. A group of scholars, probably with the king's own contribution, created an alphabet. It was introduced in 1443, and published in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum, the correct sounds for the instruction of the people.
Hangul is unusual in that the shapes of the consonants are based on the position of the mouth and tongue when making them. The letters are grouped into blocks that make up syllables. The alphabet has only twenty-four basic letters, and it's regarded as one of the most scientific writing systems. Literacy rates in South Korea are among the highest in the world. Hangul Day is a national day of celebration.

Sequoyah was a Cherokee silversmith, who could not read English. He was impressed that white people could send messages on paper, and he wanted to do the same for his own language. Around 1809, he began to work on a writing system. At first he tried a symbol for each word, and found that there were too many. Then he decided to use a symbol for each syllable.
In 1821 he finished a set of eighty-five characters, each standing for a syllable of Cherokee. It was so well suited to the language that people could learn to read it in a few days. Within a few years, many Cherokees were literate, and in 1828 the tribe began to print a newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix. Sequoyah is one of the few people in history who is known to have created a writing system, on his own, from nothing.
Entropy and the arrow of time

If you watch a film of an egg breaking, and then a film of it running backward, you know which is real. Most laws of physics don't distinguish between forward and backward in time. A collision between two billiard balls looks fine in reverse. What gives time a direction is the second law of thermodynamics, which says that entropy, a measure of disorder, tends to increase in a closed system.
In the 1860s Rudolf Clausius coined the word entropy, and in the 1870s Ludwig Boltzmann explained it statistically. There are far more ways for things to be mixed up than ordered, so the system drifts toward mixed-up states, simply by probability. A cup of hot coffee cools down, and never heats up by itself. The reason why entropy was low in the beginning, in the early universe, is still an open question.
Why you can't build a perpetual motion machine

For centuries, inventors tried to build machines that run forever without fuel. In 1824 a young French engineer, Sadi Carnot, studied steam engines. He wanted to know the limits of their efficiency. He showed that any engine that produces work from heat must also give off waste heat to a colder place. There's a maximum fraction of the heat that can be turned into work, which depends only on the temperatures of the hot and cold sides.
His result became the basis of the second law of thermodynamics. No engine can be perfectly efficient, and none can run forever. Carnot died of cholera at thirty-six, and much of his work was lost, since his papers were burned along with his belongings. Some patent offices, including the American one, refuse applications for perpetual motion machines unless a working model is provided.

Cosmic rays striking the upper atmosphere create a radioactive form of carbon, carbon-14. It mixes into carbon dioxide, and is taken up by plants, and by the animals that eat them. A living thing has a steady proportion of carbon-14 to ordinary carbon. When it dies, it stops taking in carbon, and the carbon-14 decays, with a half-life of about 5,730 years. Half of it is gone after that time, and half of what remains after the next.
In 1949 the chemist Willard Libby realized that measuring what's left could date organic remains. It was tested on objects of known age, such as wood from an Egyptian tomb. He won the Nobel Prize in 1960. The method works for things up to about fifty thousand years old, and it has been calibrated using tree rings, which show that the amount of carbon-14 in the air has varied over time.

In 1964 several physicists, among them Peter Higgs, proposed a mechanism to explain why some particles have mass. An invisible field fills all of space. Particles that interact with it strongly are heavier, and those that don't, such as the particle of light, have no mass. The field should have a particle of its own, a boson.
On July 4, 2012, two teams of thousands of scientists at CERN, near Geneva, announced that they had found a particle that fits. It took the Large Hadron Collider, a ring seventeen miles around, which smashes protons together at nearly the speed of light. Higgs and François Englert won the Nobel Prize in 2013. The nickname God particle, which came from a book title, is disliked by many physicists.

Neutrinos are particles with almost no mass and no electric charge. They interact so weakly that most pass straight through the Earth. About sixty-five billion of them from the Sun pass through every square centimeter of your body each second, and you don't feel a thing. Wolfgang Pauli predicted them in 1930, to save the law of conservation of energy in radioactive decay, and he said that he had done a terrible thing, since he'd proposed a particle that could not be detected.
In 1956 Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines detected them from a nuclear reactor. In 1998 an experiment in Japan showed that neutrinos change from one type to another as they travel, which means that they have mass, though a tiny amount. Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald shared the Nobel Prize in 2015. Neutrinos from distant supernovas have been used to study stars.

In 1928 the physicist Paul Dirac wrote an equation that described the electron with relativity. It had a strange feature. It predicted a particle just like the electron, with the opposite electric charge. Dirac was at first reluctant to say that it was real. In 1932 Carl Anderson, studying cosmic rays in a cloud chamber at Caltech, saw a track that curved the wrong way. It was the positron, the antielectron.
Every kind of particle has an antiparticle. When matter and antimatter meet, they annihilate in a burst of energy. This is used in medicine. In a PET scan, a patient is given a tracer that emits positrons, which annihilate with electrons in the body, and detectors pick up the flashes. A mystery remains. The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, but the universe is almost all matter.

A laser makes a beam of light in which all of the waves are in step, with the same color and direction. The idea came from Albert Einstein, who in 1917 described stimulated emission. An atom that has been excited can be triggered by passing light to emit a second particle of light, identical to the first. If many atoms are excited, a chain reaction of light builds up.
In 1960 Theodore Maiman, a physicist at Hughes Research Laboratories in California, built the first working laser, using a ruby crystal and a flash lamp. Some people called it a solution looking for a problem. It's now in barcode scanners, in surgery, in the fiber-optic cables that carry the internet, and in the gravitational wave detectors that measure changes smaller than an atom.

In 1911 the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury to a temperature of about four degrees above absolute zero, and found that its electrical resistance suddenly dropped to zero. A current in a loop of superconducting wire can flow without loss, and, in experiments, for years. He had also been the first to liquefy helium, which made the cold temperatures possible.
Superconductors also push out magnetic fields, so that a magnet floats above one. This is the Meissner effect. Superconducting magnets are used in MRI scanners and in particle accelerators. For decades, the materials had to be kept very cold. In 1986 Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller found a ceramic that worked at a higher temperature, and the record at normal pressure is now about minus one hundred and forty degrees Celsius. A material that superconducts at room temperature and normal pressure would transform the electric grid, and has not been found.

Fusion is the reaction that powers the Sun. When light atoms such as hydrogen are forced together at very high temperature and pressure, they merge into helium and release a great deal of energy. If it could be done on Earth, it would give a clean power source with fuel from seawater. But the conditions are extreme, and for seventy years, the experiments used more energy than they gave out.
On December 5, 2022, the National Ignition Facility in California fired 192 lasers at a pellet of hydrogen fuel the size of a peppercorn. It produced about three megajoules of fusion energy, from about two megajoules of laser light that reached the target. It was the first time that a fusion experiment got more energy out than was put in, counting the laser energy at the target. The lasers themselves used far more power from the grid, so a power plant is still a long way off.

For thousands of years, astronomers did not know how far away the stars are. If the Earth goes around the Sun, nearby stars should seem to shift very slightly against the background of more distant stars as we move, an effect known as parallax. Astronomers looked for it for centuries, and found none. The stars were too far away, and the shifts too small to measure.
In 1838 the German astronomer Friedrich Bessel measured the parallax of a faint star, 61 Cygni. He found that it was about ten light-years away. That's about sixty trillion miles. It was the first distance to a star ever measured, and it confirmed that the Earth moves around the Sun. It also showed how large the universe is. Even the nearest stars are so far away that their light takes years to reach us.
The first picture of a black hole

A black hole gives off no light, so how do you photograph it? In April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration released an image of a glowing ring around a dark center. It was the shadow of a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy called M87, some fifty-five million light-years away. The black hole has a mass of about six and a half billion Suns.
To make the picture, radio telescopes in several places on Earth were linked, so that together they acted as a single telescope as large as the planet. The data from the observations filled so many hard drives that they were flown to a central lab. In 2022 the team released an image of Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the center of our own galaxy. The images match the predictions of Einstein's general relativity.

When cosmic rays hit the upper atmosphere, they create particles called muons. A muon is unstable, and lives for about two millionths of a second before it decays. Even at nearly the speed of light, that is only long enough to travel about six hundred meters. Yet the muons are created about fifteen kilometers up, and plenty of them reach the ground.
The explanation is time dilation, one of the predictions of Einstein's theory of special relativity. To an observer on Earth, a muon moving at high speed experiences time more slowly, so it lasts longer than it would at rest. In 1941 Bruno Rossi and David Hall measured the decay of muons on a mountain top and at sea level, and the results agreed with relativity. It's one of the clearest everyday tests of the theory.
The failed experiment that changed physics

In the nineteenth century, physicists believed that light is a wave, and that waves need a medium. They imagined an invisible substance called the ether, which filled the universe. The Earth, moving through it, should feel an ether wind, and light should travel at different speeds in different directions.
In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley built a very sensitive device in Cleveland, in which two beams of light were sent at right angles, and compared. They floated it on a pool of mercury so that it could be rotated smoothly. They found no difference. The result puzzled physicists for almost two decades. It was one of the clues that led Einstein to special relativity in 1905, in which there's no ether, and the speed of light is the same for all observers.
Graphene and a roll of tape

Graphite is the material in a pencil. It's made of sheets of carbon atoms, in a honeycomb pattern, stacked loosely together. A single sheet is called graphene, and for a long time, it was thought that such a thin material could not exist on its own. In 2004 Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, at the University of Manchester, isolated it. They used a piece of sticky tape.
They pressed the tape onto a lump of graphite, and peeled it off, again and again, until they had flakes just one atom thick. Graphene is the thinnest material known. It's about two hundred times stronger than steel by weight, and conducts electricity and heat very well. Geim and Novoselov won the Nobel Prize in 2010. Many applications are being developed, though making it cheaply in large quantities has been a challenge.

You might think that the ocean is blue because it reflects the sky. The sky does play a small part, but the main reason is that water itself absorbs light. Pure water takes up red, orange and yellow light much more strongly than blue light. The longer wavelengths are absorbed within a few meters. The blue light travels farthest, and is scattered back to our eyes.
It's why deep water looks darker blue, and why divers lose the colors, red first, as they descend. In coastal seas, algae and sediment can change the color to green or brown. Chlorophyll in the algae absorbs blue and red. A swimming pool looks light blue for the same reason, though the effect is less strong in a thin layer. The color of the sea is the color of the light that water does not absorb.
Why stars twinkle and planets don't

On a clear night, the stars seem to twinkle, shimmering and changing color slightly. Planets shine with a steadier light. The reason has nothing to do with the stars themselves. It comes from the Earth's air. The atmosphere is full of pockets of air at different temperatures and densities, which bend light a little differently, and move around in the wind.
A star is so far away that it looks like a single point of light, and so the bending of that point makes it dance. A planet is much closer, and appears as a tiny disk, made up of many points. The twinkling of the different points averages out. Astronomers call it scintillation, or seeing. It's the reason that telescopes are placed on high mountains, and why the Hubble Space Telescope, above the atmosphere, can take sharper pictures.

On the morning of September 1, 1859, an English amateur astronomer named Richard Carrington was drawing sunspots, when he saw a patch of intense white light flare up in the spots. It lasted a few minutes. About eighteen hours later, the biggest geomagnetic storm on record hit the Earth. Auroras were seen as far south as the Caribbean, and in Hawaii.
Telegraph systems failed across Europe and North America. Operators reported sparks, and shocks, and paper catching fire. Some were able to send messages for a time without a battery, using only the current induced by the storm. A solar storm of this size today could damage satellites and power grids over a wide area. A smaller one in 1989 knocked out the power in Quebec for nine hours.

About seven hundred million years ago, according to one hypothesis, the Earth was frozen from the poles to the equator. Ice sheets covered the land, and perhaps the seas too, a state called Snowball Earth. It would have lasted millions of years, until volcanoes released enough carbon dioxide to warm the planet and melt the ice.
The idea was put forward by Joseph Kirschvink in 1992, and developed by Paul Hoffman and others. The evidence is rocks that were laid down by glaciers near the equator, as shown by their magnetism, and layers of rock that formed just after the ice. Some scientists think that the oceans were never fully frozen, and that a slushy belt stayed open near the equator. The question is still debated. Soon after the thaw, complex animals first appear in the fossil record.

For most of the history of life, organisms were small and simple. Then, about 540 million years ago, in a geological moment of perhaps ten to twenty million years, the fossil record shows a burst of new kinds of animals. Most of the major groups that exist today appear, with hard shells, eyes, legs and jaws. This is the Cambrian explosion.
The best fossils come from the Burgess Shale in the Canadian Rockies, found in 1909 by Charles Walcott. It preserved soft-bodied animals, some of them very strange, such as Opabinia, which has five eyes. What caused the explosion is debated. Possible factors include a rise in oxygen, the evolution of predators that set off an arms race, and the development of genes for body plans. Some life existed before, but the Cambrian was when animals took off.
The rats that pressed the lever

In 1953 James Olds and Peter Milner at McGill University were implanting electrodes in the brains of rats. One electrode ended up in the wrong place, in a region near the base of the brain. When the rat was given a mild electrical pulse there, it came back to the same corner of its cage, as if it wanted more.
The researchers put the animals in a box with a lever that delivered the pulse. The rats pressed it again and again, thousands of times an hour, for many hours. Some ignored food, even when they were starving. It seemed to be a pleasure center. We now know that the system is more about wanting than enjoying, and that dopamine is central to it. But the experiment was the beginning of the study of the brain's reward circuits, and the biology of addiction.

It was long said that addictive drugs are so strong that any animal that tastes them will keep taking them. The evidence came from experiments in which rats, kept alone in small cages, would drink water laced with morphine until they were dependent. In the 1970s the psychologist Bruce Alexander in Canada asked whether the cage had something to do with it.
He built Rat Park, a large enclosure with room to roam, tunnels, toys and other rats. In his experiments, rats in the park drank much less of the morphine water than rats in isolation. He argued that addiction depends on environment, and not just on the drug. Later attempts to repeat the work had mixed results, and the original study was criticized for its design. But the idea that isolation and stress make addiction more likely is supported by much research.

When you learn to do something, such as driving a route or tying a shoe, it starts out as a series of steps that you think about. With practice, it becomes automatic. In the 1990s Ann Graybiel and her team at MIT recorded from neurons in the basal ganglia of rats learning to run a maze. They had to turn left or right at a signal.
At first, many neurons fired throughout the run. As the rats learned, the pattern changed. Neurons fired mainly at the start and at the end of the sequence. The brain had bundled the steps into a single unit, or chunk, with a beginning and an end. It's why a habit can run by itself once it's triggered, and why it's so hard to stop in the middle. Habits are stored in a different system from the one used for deliberate choices.

Pain is unpleasant, but it protects us. A few people are born unable to feel it. In 2006 James Cox and his colleagues studied three families in northern Pakistan in which some children could not feel pain. One boy had worked as a street performer, putting knives through his arms and walking on hot coals. He died at the age of fourteen after jumping off a roof.
The researchers found that the people had mutations in a gene called SCN9A, which makes a channel in nerve cells that carries pain signals. Without it, the nerves can't send the message. People with this condition can badly injure themselves without knowing, and often have broken bones and burns. The discovery has led drug companies to look for painkillers that block the channel, without the side effects of opioids.
The artist who remembers a city

Stephen Wiltshire was born in London in 1974. He was diagnosed with autism, and did not speak until he was five. At school, he was drawn to art, and he began to draw buildings. He has become known for an ability to draw detailed landscapes of cities from memory, after a short look.
In one famous feat, he took a helicopter ride over Rome, lasting about forty-five minutes. Over the next several days, he drew a panorama of the city on a sheet that was more than ten feet long, with its buildings in accurate detail. He has done the same for Tokyo, New York and other cities. He is called an autistic savant, a person with a disability who has an extraordinary skill. How he does it is not fully understood, though it seems to depend on very detailed visual memory.

In 2000 a woman in California wrote to the memory researcher James McGaugh to say that she could remember almost every day of her life since about the age of fourteen. She could give the date, the day of the week, what she did and what was on the news. The scientists tested her, and checked her claims against diaries and records. She was correct.
The condition is now called highly superior autobiographical memory. About a hundred people have been identified. They are not better at memorizing lists or numbers, and their memory for the events of their own lives is exceptional. Some people say that it is a burden, since they cannot stop reliving painful moments. Studies have found some differences in the brain, in areas related to memory, though the cause is unknown.

Close your eyes and imagine a red apple on a table. Most people can see it, more or less clearly, in the mind's eye. Some people see it vividly, and others only vaguely. For a few people, there's nothing. The apple doesn't appear at all. They know what an apple looks like, and can describe it, but they cannot form the picture.
In 2015 Adam Zeman and his colleagues named this condition aphantasia, from the Greek for imagination. It affects a few percent of people. Many don't know that others can see images until they find out in adulthood. People with aphantasia can do well in school and in their careers, and many are good at math and writing. They also tend to have fewer vivid dreams. It's an example of how people can differ in ways that they have never noticed.

Many people assume that everyone thinks in words, with an inner voice. In fact, people differ. The psychologist Russell Hurlburt has spent decades studying the inner experience of people, by giving them a beeper that sounds at random times. When it beeps, they note exactly what they were experiencing at that moment, and then they're interviewed about it.
He found that some people have an inner voice much of the time, and others rarely. Some think mostly in images, or in feelings, or have no particular awareness of their thoughts at all, only an idea that they know. In one set of samples, inner speech was present in about a quarter of the moments, with huge differences between people. The method has been criticized, because people's reports can be inaccurate. But the main finding, that inner experience varies, is widely accepted.
The patient who denies her paralysis

After some strokes, a patient may be paralyzed on one side of the body, and yet insist that nothing is wrong. Asked to move the left arm, they might say that they have done it, though the arm hasn't moved. Shown the arm lying still, they may say that it belongs to someone else, or explain that they don't feel like moving it. In 1914 the neurologist Joseph Babinski called this anosognosia, meaning lack of knowledge of illness.
It isn't a simple matter of denial. It usually follows damage to the right side of the brain, in regions that are involved in monitoring the body, and the person seems truly unaware. Ramachandran described patients who invented elaborate excuses. The condition shows that awareness of our own state depends on brain systems that can fail, without our knowing that they've failed.

A person with Capgras syndrome believes that someone close to them, such as a spouse or a parent, has been replaced by an identical impostor. The patient sees the face and recognizes it, but feels that it isn't the real person. It was first described in 1923 by the French psychiatrist Joseph Capgras.
One explanation, popularized by V. S. Ramachandran, is that the pathway that links the visual recognition of a face to the emotional response is damaged. The patient sees the right face, but doesn't feel the familiar warmth. The brain tries to make sense of the mismatch, and comes up with the idea of an impostor. Patients often recognize the voice on the phone, since the auditory pathway to emotion is intact. It's a striking case of how recognition has both a thinking part and a feeling part.
The belief that you are dead

In 1880 the French neurologist Jules Cotard described a patient who said that she had no brain, no nerves, no chest and no intestines, and that she was only a decomposing body. He called the condition the delusion of negation. It's now known as Cotard syndrome, or walking corpse syndrome.
People with it may believe that they are dead, or that they don't exist, or that their organs have rotted away. It's most often seen in severe depression, and sometimes after brain injury. Some patients stop eating, since they think there is no point. Treatment can involve antidepressants, antipsychotic drugs and electroconvulsive therapy, and it's often effective. The syndrome is rare, and it shows how deeply our sense of being alive depends on how the brain makes us feel.
The hand with a will of its own

In alien hand syndrome, a person's hand behaves as if it belongs to someone else. It may reach out and grab an object, or unbutton a shirt that the person has just buttoned, or in some cases, even grab the person's own throat. The person is aware that the movement is happening, but says that they are not controlling it.
It was first described in 1908, in a woman whose left hand acted on its own. It's often associated with damage to the corpus callosum, the bundle of fibers that connects the two halves of the brain, or to the frontal lobes. In the film Dr. Strangelove, a character struggles with a hand that makes a Nazi salute. The syndrome suggests that the feeling of controlling our actions is separate from the actions themselves.
The woman who couldn't see motion

In the early 1980s a woman, called L.M. in the medical report, suffered a stroke that damaged a part of the brain at the back and side. After this, she lost the ability to see movement. The world, for her, was a series of still pictures. She could not pour tea, because the liquid seemed to be frozen like a glacier, and she could not tell when to stop pouring, as the cup overflowed.
Crossing a street was dangerous. A car would seem to be far away, and then suddenly close, without having appeared to move. She found it hard to follow conversations, since she couldn't see lips moving. The condition is called akinetopsia. It was important evidence that the brain has a specialized area, now known as MT or V5, which processes motion, separately from the other parts of vision.
The diving bell and the butterfly

In December 1995 Jean-Dominique Bauby, the editor of the French magazine Elle, had a stroke at the age of forty-three. When he woke up, he was almost completely paralyzed. He could not speak or move, apart from his left eyelid. His mind was unaffected. It's called locked-in syndrome.
With the help of a speech therapist, he was able to communicate by blinking, using a system in which a helper recited the alphabet, ordered by how often letters are used, and he blinked at the right letter. In this way, he dictated a book about his experience, The Diving Bell and the Butterfly. It's said to have taken some two hundred thousand blinks. The book was published in March 1997, and he died just three days later.

After a severe brain injury, some patients are in a vegetative state. They open their eyes and cycle through sleep and waking, but seem to show no sign of awareness. In 2006 Adrian Owen and his colleagues tested a twenty-three-year-old woman who had been in this state for five months after a car accident.
Inside a brain scanner, they asked her to imagine playing tennis, and then to imagine walking through the rooms of her house. Her brain lit up in the same areas, in the same way, as in healthy volunteers doing the same tasks. Though she could not move or speak, she appeared to understand and to follow the instructions. The study showed that some patients may be conscious, and has led to new ways of testing for awareness.
Moving a cursor with a thought

In 2004 a man named Matthew Nagle, who had been paralyzed from the neck down after being stabbed, took part in a pioneering experiment. Surgeons put a small array of ninety-six electrodes, about the size of a baby aspirin, into the part of his motor cortex that controls the hand. Wires connected it to a computer.
After training, Nagle could move a cursor on a screen just by thinking about moving his hand. He could open email, play a simple video game, and control a robotic arm. John Donoghue led the team. Since then, people with similar implants have controlled robotic limbs and typed on a screen. In 2023 teams reported that implants had enabled people who could not speak to communicate at speeds approaching natural conversation.

In 1987 the French neurosurgeon Alim-Louis Benabid was operating on a patient with a severe tremor. To find the right spot in the brain, he stimulated it with a small electrical current. To his surprise, the tremor stopped. He realized that continuous stimulation at a high frequency could do the work of destroying the tissue.
He began to implant electrodes connected to a pacemaker-like device under the skin of the chest. The method is called deep brain stimulation. It was approved in the United States for the tremor of Parkinson's disease in 1997 and for the disease itself in 2002. More than a hundred thousand people have received the implants. It's also being tested for depression, obsessive compulsive disorder and epilepsy. How it works is not fully understood.

In 1946 Solomon Asch read people a list of traits describing an imaginary person: intelligent, skillful, industrious, warm, determined, practical, cautious. Then he asked them to say what the person was like. A second group heard the same list, with one word changed. The word warm was replaced by cold.
The impressions were quite different. The warm person was seen as generous, happy and good-natured. The cold person was seen as unsympathetic and ungenerous. Changing only one word altered the meaning of all the others. Asch called warm and cold central traits. In 1950 Harold Kelley showed that the effect works with real people. Students who were told that a guest lecturer was warm took part more and liked him more than those who were told he was cold, though the lecture was the same.
Why my mistake is the situation's fault

If someone cuts in front of you in traffic, you may think that they're a rude person. If you cut in front of someone yourself, you probably think that you were in a hurry, or didn't see them. In 1971 Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett noted this pattern, and called it the actor-observer difference. When we explain our own behavior, we tend to look at the situation. When we explain the behavior of others, we tend to look at the person.
The reason may be that we are aware of the pressures that we face, and that we see only other people's actions. We know our own history of good intentions. The bias works in both directions. It causes people to be too harsh on others and too easy on themselves. A useful habit is to give other people the same explanation that you would give yourself, when you've made the same mistake.

In 1978 Steven Berglas and Edward Jones invited students to take a test of intellectual ability. After the first part, some of the students were told that they'd done very well, but on questions that had no right answer, so that they could not understand why. Then they were offered a choice of two drugs before the second part, one said to improve performance, and the other said to impair it.
The students who had been given unexplained success, and were afraid that they couldn't repeat it, often chose the drug that would impair performance. If they failed, they could blame the drug. This is self-handicapping. We do it by not studying before a test, or by staying up late, so that a poor result has an excuse. It protects the ego in the short term, and costs performance in the long term.

In 1976 Robert Cialdini and his colleagues counted the number of students at seven American universities who wore school colors or insignia on the Mondays after football games. They found more people wearing them after a win than after a loss. They also asked students about the results of the games. After a win, they said we won. After a loss, they said they lost.
The researchers called it basking in reflected glory. We like to be connected with success, and to put distance between ourselves and failure, even when we have had nothing to do with the result. It's not limited to sport. People mention famous people they know, or the success of their schools. The pattern shows how much of our self-image depends on the groups we belong to.
The big fish in the little pond

Suppose that a student goes from an ordinary school to one that selects only the highest achievers. You would expect their confidence to rise, since they are now with brilliant people. In fact, the opposite is more likely. In the 1980s the psychologist Herbert Marsh described the big-fish-little-pond effect. Students with the same ability have a lower academic self-concept in a school of high achievers than in one of average achievers.
In 2003 Marsh and Kit-Tai Hau studied about a hundred thousand students from twenty-six countries. The effect appeared in every one. Students compare themselves with their classmates, and not with the world. It suggests that going to a more selective school may harm confidence, even while it helps the education. It's a reminder that how we feel about our abilities depends on who we compare ourselves with.

How do people judge groups? In 2002 Susan Fiske and her colleagues proposed that we judge on two dimensions. One is warmth, whether the group has good or bad intentions. The other is competence, whether it has the ability to carry them out. They tested it with surveys in several countries.
The results sorted groups into four types. Groups that are seen as warm and competent, such as one's own group, and close allies, get admiration. Groups seen as warm but not competent, such as elderly people, get pity. Cold but competent groups, such as rich people or some immigrant groups, get envy. Cold and incompetent ones, such as homeless people, get contempt. The model shows that prejudice is not a single feeling, and that different stereotypes lead to different emotions and actions.

Do people everywhere think of themselves in the same way? In 1991 Hazel Markus and Shinobu Kitayama argued that they don't. In many Western countries, people tend to see themselves as independent. The self is a separate individual, with its own traits, abilities and goals, and a good person is true to themselves and stands out.
In many East Asian countries, and in many other cultures, people tend to see themselves as interdependent. The self is defined by relationships, roles and duties to others, and a good person fits in and adjusts. It's a matter of degree, and people in every culture have both. The difference affects what makes people happy, how they handle conflict, and how they explain events. It also shows that much of what we call human nature depends on where we grew up.

In 2001 Takahiko Masuda and Richard Nisbett showed Japanese and American students short animated underwater scenes. Each had a large fish in the foreground, and other fish, plants and rocks. They were asked to describe what they had seen.
The Americans started by describing the large fish, and its features. The Japanese were more likely to start with the setting, saying something like there was a pond. They also mentioned more of the background and the relationships between objects. In later tests, the Japanese were better at remembering the background, and their memory of the main object was affected by a change of background. It suggests that culture may shape what people notice, with Westerners focusing on objects, and East Asians on context.

Farming rice and farming wheat are very different. Rice paddies need a lot of work, and an irrigation system shared among neighbors. People must cooperate, and share the water and the labor. Wheat is grown on dry land, with much less work, and farmers can work more independently.
In 2014 Thomas Talhelm and his colleagues tested people in six regions of China, in provinces that grow rice and ones that grow wheat. In the rice provinces, people were more likely to show interdependent thinking. They tended to draw themselves about the same size as their friends, and to see objects in terms of relationships. People in wheat provinces were more individualist. Divorce was also higher in wheat areas. The results suggest that culture can be shaped over centuries by the way that people make a living.

In 2010 Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan pointed out a problem. Most psychological research is done on people from Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic societies. They gave this the acronym WEIRD. Many studies are done on college students in the United States, who are not typical of the world.
They reviewed cross-cultural studies and found that WEIRD people are often outliers. In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two lines of equal length look different because of the arrowheads at the ends. Americans are strongly fooled, while some groups, such as the San people of the Kalahari, are hardly fooled at all. The same is true for fairness, moral reasoning and thinking style. It means that findings about human nature may only be about a small part of humanity.

Do people everywhere read emotions in the same way from faces? In 2012 Rachael Jack and her colleagues at the University of Glasgow tested Western Caucasian and East Asian volunteers. The volunteers watched computer-generated faces whose muscles moved randomly, and said which emotion they saw in them. The researchers then worked out what pattern of movement each person associated with each emotion.
The two groups had different mental pictures of the emotions. Westerners used the mouth and the eyebrows. East Asians put more emphasis on the eyes, particularly the way that they look. The authors suggested that the universal six expressions are not as universal as supposed. Others have argued that the basic emotions are recognized well across cultures, and that the differences are about the details. The debate continues.

How honest are people? In 2019 Alain Cohn and his colleagues ran an experiment in forty countries. They handed in more than seventeen thousand wallets to people working in places such as banks, hotels and post offices, saying that someone had left it behind. Each wallet had a business card, so that it could be returned. Some wallets held no money, and others held the equivalent of about thirteen dollars.
In most countries, the wallets with money were returned more often than those without. In the countries overall, around forty percent of wallets with no money were reported, and over half of the ones with money. It's the opposite of what economists would predict, since keeping more money is more tempting. The researchers suggested that people care about not being thieves, and that taking more makes them feel more like one. Honesty is often driven by self-image.

Popular books say that men and women are very different in the way that they think and behave. In 2005 Janet Hyde reviewed forty-six reviews of research that had compared the sexes on a range of traits, including math ability, language, aggression, self-esteem and many others. She looked at the size of the differences.
She found that most of the differences were small or close to zero. About three-quarters were in this range. A few were larger, such as throwing distance and some aspects of sexuality, and some were moderate, such as aggression. She called it the gender similarities hypothesis. The two sexes overlap greatly on most psychological traits. A difference between averages tells little about any one person, and it is not a reason to expect a person to be a certain way.
Koch and the germ of tuberculosis

In the nineteenth century, tuberculosis was one of the leading causes of death in Europe. It was thought to be hereditary, or caused by bad air. On March 24, 1882, the German physician Robert Koch announced to a meeting in Berlin that he had found the cause. It was a rod-shaped bacterium that he had seen under the microscope, by staining tissue from diseased lungs, and grown in pure culture.
Koch developed a set of rules for proving that a germ causes a disease. The microbe should be found in every case, grown in pure culture, cause the disease when given to a healthy animal, and then be found again in the sick animal. They're known as Koch's postulates. They guided the identification of the causes of many diseases. He won the Nobel Prize in 1905. March 24 is now World Tuberculosis Day.

Before the 1840s, surgery was performed on fully conscious patients, held down by assistants. Surgeons prized speed, and an amputation might be finished in less than a minute. On October 16, 1846, in an operating theater at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, a dentist named William Morton demonstrated ether, a vapor that he had his patient breathe.
The surgeon John Collins Warren removed a tumor from the neck of a printer named Gilbert Abbott. The patient felt no pain. Warren is said to have turned to the audience and said, gentlemen, this is no humbug. The news spread across the world within weeks. The room is now a museum called the Ether Dome. Surgery changed from a desperate last resort to something that could be done slowly and carefully.

In November 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen, a physics professor in Würzburg, Germany, was experimenting with a glass tube from which the air had been removed, and through which electricity passed. He noticed that a screen coated with a chemical glowed, though the tube was covered with black cardboard and the screen was across the room. Something invisible was passing through.
He called the rays X, for unknown. They passed through flesh but not through bone. On December 22 he made a photograph of his wife's hand, which showed her bones and her wedding ring. Within weeks, doctors across Europe and America were using X-rays to find broken bones and bullets. Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901, and refused to patent his discovery, so that it could be used freely.

Before 1922, a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes was a death sentence. The only treatment was a starvation diet, which prolonged life by a few months. In 1921 a young surgeon, Frederick Banting, and a student assistant, Charles Best, at the University of Toronto, extracted a substance from the pancreas of dogs. It lowered the blood sugar of diabetic dogs.
