In January 1922 they gave a purified extract to Leonard Thompson, a fourteen-year-old who was dying in a hospital in Toronto. His blood sugar fell, and he improved. Soon, hospitals were filled with children who were revived, in what was called a resurrection. Banting and the chemist James Collip agreed to sell the patent to the university for one dollar. Banting and John Macleod received the Nobel Prize in 1923, and Banting shared his prize money with Best.

In the early 1900s, the German scientist Paul Ehrlich had a dream. He wanted to find a chemical that would kill the microbes that cause a disease, without harming the patient. He called it a magic bullet. He tested hundreds of compounds made from arsenic against the microbe that causes syphilis, a feared disease at the time with no effective treatment.
In 1909 Ehrlich and his collaborator, Sahachiro Hata, found that the six hundred and sixth compound that they tried was effective. It was marketed in 1910 as Salvarsan. It was the first modern drug designed to attack an infectious organism. It had serious side effects, and was replaced by penicillin in the 1940s. But it started the age of chemotherapy, and the idea that a disease could be targeted by a designed molecule.

The Human Genome Project began in 1990. Its aim was to read the complete sequence of the three billion letters of human DNA. It was an international effort, led in the United States by the National Institutes of Health, with groups in Britain, Japan, France, Germany and China. A private company, Celera, led by Craig Venter, competed with it, and in 2000 the two sides jointly announced a first draft.
The project was declared complete in 2003, at a cost of about three billion dollars. It had left some gaps in regions that were hard to sequence. In 2022 a team called the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium filled them, and published the first truly complete human genome. Sequencing a genome now costs a few hundred dollars and takes a day. The project made it possible to find the genes behind many diseases.
Henrietta Lacks and the immortal cells

In January 1951 Henrietta Lacks, a thirty-year-old African American mother of five from Baltimore, went to Johns Hopkins Hospital with a tumor in her cervix. Doctors took a sample of the tumor, as they did with many patients, without telling her. She died in October of that year. The sample, though, gave scientists something that they had been trying to get for decades. Her cells grew in the laboratory and kept dividing, and didn't die.
They were called HeLa cells, and they became the first human cell line. They were used to develop the polio vaccine, and in research on cancer, viruses and genes, and have been sent into space. Her family was not told for decades. In 2013 they reached an agreement with the National Institutes of Health on access to her genome data. The story is central to the debate about consent in research.

Imagine that you have a single molecule of DNA, from a crime scene or an ancient bone, and you need billions of copies to study it. In 1983 Kary Mullis, a chemist working for a biotech company in California, had an idea while driving along a highway at night. He realized that a repeated cycle of heating and cooling, with the right ingredients, could double the amount of DNA each time.
The method is called the polymerase chain reaction, or PCR. After thirty cycles, one molecule becomes about a billion. An enzyme that withstood the heat was needed, and it was found in a bacterium that lives in the hot springs of Yellowstone. Mullis received the Nobel Prize in 1993. PCR is used in forensic science, in diagnosing infections, and in tests for the coronavirus.

Cholera and other diarrheal diseases kill by dehydration. For a long time, the only treatment was a drip of fluid into a vein, which required equipment and trained staff that were not available in poor places. In the 1960s researchers, including David Nalin and Richard Cash working in Dhaka and Calcutta, found that a solution of salt and glucose, taken by mouth, was absorbed by the gut even in a person with cholera.
This oral rehydration therapy can be made at home from clean water, sugar and salt. In 1978 the British medical journal The Lancet said that it was potentially the most important medical advance of the century. It's estimated to have saved many millions of lives, mostly of children. It's a case of an advance that came not from a new drug, but from understanding a simple mechanism.

Archie Cochrane was a Scottish doctor who was held as a prisoner of war during the Second World War. In a camp, he ran a trial of yeast for a group of prisoners suffering from swelling, and he saw how powerful a controlled test could be. After the war, he was struck by how many medical treatments were used with no evidence.
In 1972 he published a short book, Effectiveness and Efficiency, arguing that all treatments should be tested in randomized controlled trials, and that the results should be gathered in one place and made available. He once gave a wooden spoon to the specialty that, in his view, had the least solid evidence, obstetrics. The Cochrane Collaboration, founded in 1993 and named in his honor, now produces reviews of the evidence on health care. His message was that good intentions are not enough.

In 1948 doctors in Framingham, Massachusetts, a town about twenty miles west of Boston, invited residents to take part in a study of heart disease. They recruited more than five thousand healthy adults, and examined them every two years, measuring blood pressure, cholesterol, weight and habits, and watched who got sick.
The study has continued for more than seventy years, and now includes their children and grandchildren. In 1961 it reported that high blood pressure, high cholesterol and smoking increased the chance of heart disease, and the term risk factor was coined. Later work added diabetes, obesity and physical inactivity. Before Framingham, heart disease was often thought to be an inevitable part of aging. The study showed that much of it can be prevented.

In the first half of the twentieth century, lung cancer was becoming more common, and smoking was very widespread. In 1950 two British researchers, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill, compared the habits of patients with lung cancer and those without, and found that the cancer patients were much more likely to have smoked. Many experts were skeptical, and thought that something else might be the cause.
In 1951 they began following more than thirty-four thousand British doctors, and in 1954 they reported that smokers died of lung cancer far more often than non-smokers. The doctors' study went on for fifty years. In 2004 the results showed that long-term smokers lost about ten years of life on average, and that stopping, even in middle age, regained much of it. It was a landmark in showing how epidemiology can identify a cause.

Almost all living things have an internal clock that runs on a cycle of about twenty-four hours. In 1971 Ronald Konopka and Seymour Benzer at Caltech looked for the cause. They treated fruit flies with chemicals that caused mutations, and found flies with clocks that were too fast, too slow, or absent. The mutations were in a single gene, which they called period.
In the 1980s and 1990s Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young cloned the gene, and showed how it works. The cell makes a protein that builds up at night, and then switches off its own gene. As the protein breaks down, the cycle starts again. They received the Nobel Prize in 2017. The clock genes are found in humans too, and help to explain jet lag, shift work and why some people are early birds.

Each of our chromosomes has a protective cap at both ends, like the plastic tip of a shoelace. These caps are called telomeres. Every time that a cell divides, a little of the telomere is lost. When it becomes too short, the cell stops dividing or dies. In this way, telomeres act as a kind of counter for the number of divisions a cell has made.
Elizabeth Blackburn and Jack Szostak discovered how telomeres are protected, and in 1984 Blackburn and her student Carol Greider found an enzyme, telomerase, that builds them up again. Cancer cells use telomerase to divide without limit. The three shared the Nobel Prize in 2009. Telomere length has been linked to aging and stress, but the claims of products that promise to lengthen telomeres are not well supported.

Cells have a system for breaking down and recycling their own parts. Damaged proteins and worn-out structures are wrapped in a membrane, and delivered to a compartment that digests them. The process is called autophagy, from Greek words for self-eating. It was observed in the 1960s, but no one knew how it worked.
In the early 1990s Yoshinori Ohsumi, a Japanese biologist, studied it in yeast. He starved the cells, which forced them to recycle, and looked for the genes that were needed. He found about fifteen of them. Similar genes exist in humans. Faults in autophagy are linked to cancer, to Parkinson's disease and to diabetes. Ohsumi received the Nobel Prize in 2016. Cells, like households, need to take out the trash as well as to bring things in.
How mRNA vaccines came to be

Messenger RNA carries the instructions from a gene to the machinery that builds a protein. The idea of using it as a medicine, by giving cells the instructions to make a protein that trains the immune system, is old. The problem was that the body treated the injected RNA as an invader, and attacked it, causing a strong inflammatory reaction.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman worked on the problem for years at the University of Pennsylvania. Karikó struggled to get grants, and was at one point demoted. In 2005 they reported that changing one of the building blocks of the RNA hid it from the immune system, and allowed it to make more protein. This discovery was used in the vaccines against COVID-19, which were developed and used in 2020 and 2021. They received the Nobel Prize in 2023.

In 1924 John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach, two psychologists at Cornell University, ran a small but famous experiment. Two students learned lists of nonsense syllables, such as ZOF and LUB. Then, after intervals of one, two, four or eight hours, they tried to recall them. Sometimes they had gone to sleep after learning, and sometimes they had stayed awake and gone about their normal day.
After sleeping, they remembered much more than after the same time awake. The difference was clearest after a few hours. During waking, new experiences seemed to interfere with the old ones. During sleep, the memories were left alone, and perhaps strengthened. The study was small, but it started a long line of research that now shows how sleep helps the brain to consolidate learning. If you've just learned something, a nap or a night's sleep is a good way of keeping it.

Look at this list, and then try to recall it: table, chair, bed, lamp, banana, sofa, desk. Most people remember banana. In 1933 the German psychologist Hedwig von Restorff showed that an item that is different from the others in a list is remembered better. It can be different in color, size, meaning or shape. This is called the isolation effect, or the von Restorff effect.
The reason is that the unusual item gets extra attention. The brain notices what is different, and spends more effort on it. The effect is used by designers and advertisers, who make something stand out on a page. For studying, it means that if you want to remember a key point, highlight it sparingly. If everything is marked, nothing stands out. It also suggests that attaching a strange image to a fact can help you to remember it.

How good is human memory? In 1973 Lionel Standing at Bishop's University in Canada ran an experiment with an extreme number of items. He showed people up to ten thousand photographs, one at a time, for a few seconds each. Afterward he showed them pairs of pictures, one old and one new, and asked which they had seen.
They picked the right one about eighty-three percent of the time, even when they had seen ten thousand. It was much better than their performance with words, which was lower. Pictures seem to be remembered in a different, richer way, which is called the picture superiority effect. The result is one reason why teachers and speakers use images, and why turning an idea into a mental picture may help you to remember it.
Letting a gadget hold your memory

When you set a reminder on your phone, or write a note on your hand, you are using the world to carry some of the load of your thinking. In 2016 Evan Risko and Sam Gilbert called this cognitive offloading. It's a sensible strategy. We have limited mental capacity, and tools can extend it.
Offloading has benefits and costs. Writing down a task frees your mind, and may help you to attend to something else. But in experiments, people who offloaded information remembered less of it later, and when the tool was taken away, they did worse. When people trust a device to remember, they tend to put less effort into encoding. A good rule is to offload what you only need to keep for a while, such as appointments, and to work to remember what you want to know and use.
Does a GPS weaken your sense of direction?

Drivers who use a GPS may worry that they are losing their own sense of direction. In 2020 Louisa Dahmani and Véronique Bohbot, at McGill University, studied this. They asked fifty people about their use of GPS, and then tested their ability to find their way and to form a mental map of places they knew. In a second part, they followed participants for three years.
People who relied more on GPS did worse at forming mental maps, and the decline continued over the three years in those who used it most. The study was not a controlled experiment, so it's possible that people with a poor sense of direction use GPS more. But the authors suggest that when we follow turn by turn directions, we use habit-based parts of the brain, and not the hippocampus, which makes maps. Using a map, or trying to navigate yourself sometimes, may keep that skill in practice.

Are memory champions born, or made? In 2017 Martin Dresler and his colleagues in the Netherlands and Germany tested whether ordinary people can learn the methods of memory athletes. They took people with average memory, and trained a group for six weeks, for thirty minutes a day, in the method of loci. This is the technique of placing the items to be remembered along a familiar route, in imagination.
After training, the group's recall of a list of words more than doubled. Brain scans showed that their pattern of connections had changed, and had become more like that of the champions. Four months later, much of the improvement was still there. The people had not become smarter in general. They had learned a trick. It shows that the skills of a memory athlete can be learned by anyone, with practice.

Some children start school knowing a lot about numbers, and some know little. In 2008 Robert Siegler and Geetha Ramani gave preschoolers from low-income families a simple game, played for about one hour in total over two weeks. It was a board game with squares in a row, numbered from one to ten. The children took turns moving a token, and said the numbers aloud as they moved.
After playing, the children were better at telling which of two numbers is bigger, at estimating the position of a number on a line, and at counting. The benefits lasted for nine weeks. Children in a control group, who played a similar game with colors, did not improve. The game gives children a sense of numbers as positions along a line. It's a cheap and effective way of preparing children for school.

For decades, teachers argued about how to teach children to read. One side favored phonics, teaching the connections between letters and sounds. The other favored whole language, in which children learn to read by exposure to meaningful text and guessing words from the context. In 1997 the United States Congress asked a panel of experts, the National Reading Panel, to review the evidence.
In 2000 it reported that systematic phonics instruction was more effective than instruction without phonics, particularly for young children and for those who were at risk of reading failure. It also said that other skills matter, including the ability to hear sounds in words, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension. The findings were debated, but later research has supported the importance of explicit teaching of the sound system. The best programs combine phonics with rich language and reading for meaning.

How many words per minute can a person read? Teachers and speed-reading courses often give very high figures. In 2019 Marc Brysbaert reviewed almost two hundred studies of silent reading by adults, covering many languages. He worked out an average, taking account of the kind of text.
For non-fiction, the average adult reads about two hundred and thirty-eight words a minute, with a comprehension of about seventy-five percent. For fiction, it's about two hundred and sixty. Reading aloud is slower, at about one hundred and fifty. Skilled readers can reach more than three hundred words a minute, and a few reach four hundred, with a small loss in understanding. The claims of speed readers of a thousand words or more are not borne out by tests.
Do hard-to-read fonts help you learn?

In 2011 Connor Diemand-Yauman, Daniel Oppenheimer and Erikka Vaughan reported a surprising result. Students who studied material printed in a hard-to-read font, such as Monotype Corsiva or Comic Sans Italicized, remembered it better than those who studied it in a plain font. The idea was that the difficulty makes people think more deeply. They also tested it in a high school, where students whose classroom materials were in the odd fonts did slightly better.
It was widely reported, and some teachers began to change the fonts of their worksheets. But other labs tried to repeat the finding, and mostly failed. A review of many studies by Xie and colleagues in 2018 found no benefit overall. It seems that making text harder to read doesn't help, unless the difficulty is the right kind. Desirable difficulties, such as spacing and self-testing, work. Ugly fonts don't.

Tycho Brahe was a Danish nobleman, born in 1546. When he was twenty, he fought a duel with another student over a point of mathematics, and lost part of his nose. He wore a replacement made of metal for the rest of his life. He became an astronomer, after seeing a new star in the sky in 1572, and the king of Denmark gave him an island, Hven, where he built a large observatory.
With no telescope, since it hadn't been invented, he used large instruments of his own design to measure the positions of the stars and planets more accurately than anyone before. His records covered decades. In 1600 he hired a young mathematician, Johannes Kepler. When Tycho died in 1601, Kepler used the data to discover that the planets move in ellipses. Good observations were the key.

William Herschel was born in Germany in 1738, and moved to England as a young musician. He earned his living as an organist and teacher, and astronomy was his hobby. Unable to buy a good telescope, he made his own, grinding the mirrors by hand. On the night of March 13, 1781, in the garden of his house in Bath, he saw a faint object that didn't look like a star.
At first, he thought that it was a comet. It was a new planet, the first discovered since ancient times, now called Uranus. He wanted to name it Georgium Sidus, George's Star, after King George III, who gave him a pension. The name didn't last. Herschel went on to discover moons of Saturn and Uranus, and in 1800 he found infrared radiation, by measuring the temperature beyond the red end of a spectrum.

Caroline Herschel was the younger sister of William. Born in Germany in 1750, she had smallpox as a child, which left her scarred, and her growth was stunted. Her family expected her to be a servant. In 1772 she moved to England to live with her brother, and became his assistant, helping with his telescopes, and recording his observations at night.
She began her own search of the sky, using a small telescope. Between 1786 and 1797 she discovered eight comets. In 1787 the king gave her a salary of fifty pounds a year for her work. It's often said that she was the first woman in England to be paid for science. She also made a catalog of stars. In 1828 the Royal Astronomical Society awarded her its gold medal, and she lived to be ninety-seven.

Maria Mitchell grew up on Nantucket, Massachusetts, in a Quaker family that valued education for girls. Her father, a teacher and amateur astronomer, taught her to use a telescope. She worked as a librarian, and spent her evenings watching the sky from the roof of the bank where her family lived.
On October 1, 1847, she saw a faint comet that no one had seen before. The King of Denmark had offered a gold medal for the discovery of a comet by telescope, and it was awarded to her. She became the first woman elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 1865 she became professor of astronomy at the new Vassar College. She taught her students to observe for themselves, and she was paid less than her male colleagues, which she protested.

Annie Jump Cannon was born in Delaware in 1863. As a young woman, she lost most of her hearing, probably from an illness, and threw herself into her work. She studied physics at Wellesley College, and in 1896 went to work at the Harvard College Observatory, where a group of women analyzed photographic plates of the sky. They were called computers.
Cannon sorted stars by their spectra, the patterns of colors in their light. She could classify three stars a minute by eye. The system that she devised, with the letters O, B, A, F, G, K and M, in order of temperature, is still used. She classified about a third of a million stars in her life. A well-known memory aid for the order is Oh, Be A Fine Girl, Kiss Me. In 1938 she was given an official post at Harvard, when she was seventy-five.

In 1930 a nineteen-year-old Indian physics student, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, sailed from India to England to study at Cambridge. On the voyage, he worked out what happens to a white dwarf, the dense remains of a star like the Sun, when it has used up its fuel. He combined quantum mechanics and relativity, and found that there is an upper limit to the mass of such a star, about one and a half times the mass of the Sun.
A heavier star could not support itself against gravity, and would collapse. This is now called the Chandrasekhar limit. The famous astronomer Arthur Eddington ridiculed the idea in public, and Chandrasekhar was discouraged. He moved to the United States, and kept working. His work was later seen as the prediction of neutron stars and black holes. He received the Nobel Prize in 1983, fifty-three years after the voyage.

Enrico Fermi was born in Rome in 1901, and was a rare physicist who was brilliant at both theory and experiment. He won the Nobel Prize in 1938, for work on radioactivity caused by neutrons. He used the trip to Stockholm to receive it to leave Fascist Italy with his Jewish wife, and he went to the United States.
On December 2, 1942, in a squash court under the stands of a stadium at the University of Chicago, he led the team that started the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. The device, called Chicago Pile-1, was a stack of graphite blocks and uranium. It ran for about four and a half minutes. Fermi also had a gift for quick estimates, and he asked a famous question about extraterrestrial life: where is everybody? He died in 1954, at fifty-three.

Humphry Davy was an English chemist who lived from 1778 to 1829. He was a showman as well as a scientist, and his public lectures at the Royal Institution in London were enormously popular. He used electricity to split compounds apart. By doing so, in 1807 and 1808, he discovered sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, barium and strontium.
He also experimented on himself with nitrous oxide, laughing gas, and noted that it might be used to relieve pain. In 1815 he invented a safety lamp for miners, in which the flame was surrounded by a wire gauze, that reduced the risk of igniting explosive gas. In 1813 he hired a young bookbinder's apprentice, Michael Faraday, as an assistant. Davy is said to have remarked, late in life, that his greatest discovery was Faraday.

Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist and engineer, born in 1833. In 1867 he patented dynamite, a safer way of handling the unstable explosive nitroglycerin. It was used in mining and construction, and also in war. He became very rich, with factories in many countries, and held more than three hundred patents.
In 1888 his brother Ludvig died, and a French newspaper mistakenly published an obituary for Alfred, with the headline that the merchant of death is dead. The story is that he was shocked by it, and wanted to be remembered differently. In his will, signed in 1895, he left most of his fortune for prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. The first prizes were given in 1901, five years after his death. The economics prize was added in 1968, by the Swedish central bank.

Dorothy Hodgkin was a British chemist, born in 1910 in Egypt. She became fascinated by crystals as a girl. She used X-rays to find the structure of molecules. When X-rays pass through a crystal, they are scattered in a pattern, and from the pattern, one can work out where the atoms are. Her subjects were molecules of huge complexity.
In 1945 she worked out the structure of penicillin. In 1956 she found that of vitamin B12, which has more than a hundred and eighty atoms, with the help of an early computer. She began to work on insulin in 1934, and published the structure in 1969, after thirty-five years. She won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964. Arthritis crippled her hands, but she kept working. One of her students at Oxford was Margaret Thatcher, who studied chemistry.

Linus Pauling was an American chemist who lived from 1901 to 1994. His work on the nature of the chemical bond, in the 1930s, showed how quantum mechanics explains how atoms join to form molecules. He also showed that sickle cell anemia is a molecular disease, the first time that a disease had been traced to a change in a single molecule. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954.
He campaigned against nuclear weapons testing, and in 1962 he received the Nobel Peace Prize. He's the only person to have won two unshared Nobel Prizes. He also made mistakes. He proposed a wrong structure for DNA, a triple helix, a few months before Watson and Crick. And in later life he promoted large doses of vitamin C as a way of preventing colds and treating cancer, claims that have not been supported by trials.

Lynn Margulis was an American biologist who lived from 1938 to 2011. In the 1960s she became interested in an old idea, that some parts of cells arose from bacteria that were swallowed by larger cells, and went on living inside them. She argued that mitochondria, the power plants of cells, and chloroplasts, which carry out photosynthesis in plants, are descended from free-living bacteria. This is called endosymbiosis.
She wrote a paper in 1966 that was rejected by about fifteen journals, before it was published in 1967. Many biologists were hostile. But the evidence grew. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA, which looks like that of bacteria, and they divide on their own. By the 1980s, the theory was accepted, and it's now in the textbooks. She also supported the controversial Gaia hypothesis, with James Lovelock.

In the 1840s, no medical school in the United States would accept women. Elizabeth Blackwell, born in England in 1821 and raised in the United States, applied to more than a dozen schools, and was turned down by all of them. Geneva Medical College in New York accepted her, in part because of a prank. The faculty put her application to the students for a vote, and the students, thinking it was a joke, voted yes.
She was not treated as a joke once she arrived. She studied hard, and graduated first in her class in 1849, the first woman to receive a medical degree in the United States. She later opened a hospital and a medical college for women in New York, and helped to start a school in England. Her sister Emily also became a doctor. She spent her life encouraging women to enter medicine.

Virginia Apgar was an American doctor who lived from 1909 to 1974. She wanted to be a surgeon, but was discouraged, and became an anesthesiologist, one of the first women to lead a hospital department in the field. At Columbia University, she worked in obstetrics, and noticed that newborn babies were not always carefully assessed in the first minutes of life.
In 1952 she devised a quick test that could be given to every baby, one minute after birth, and again at five minutes. It scored five signs on a scale of zero to two: skin color, pulse, reflexes, muscle tone and breathing. The sum is the Apgar score. It helped staff to see quickly which babies needed help, and it's used in hospitals all over the world. Her last name was later made into a memory aid for the five signs.

Maryam Mirzakhani was born in Tehran in 1977. As a girl, she was more interested in reading novels than in mathematics, but a teacher inspired her. At high school she won gold medals at the International Mathematical Olympiad. She went to Harvard for her doctorate, and later became a professor at Stanford.
She worked on the geometry of curved surfaces, and on how they can be deformed. She liked to think about problems by drawing on large sheets of paper, and her daughter said that her mother was painting. In 2014 she was awarded the Fields Medal, the highest honor in mathematics, the first woman to receive it in the prize's eighty-year history. She died of breast cancer in 2017, at forty. Her birthday, May 12, is now celebrated as a day for women in mathematics.

In 2002 and 2003 a Russian mathematician, Grigori Perelman, posted three papers on the internet, which gave a proof of the Poincaré conjecture. It's a question about the shape of three-dimensional space that had been open for a hundred years, and was one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems with a reward of a million dollars. He did not send the papers to a journal.
Mathematicians spent years checking the proof, and found it to be correct. In 2006 he was offered the Fields Medal, and he turned it down. In 2010 the Clay Institute awarded him its million-dollar prize, and he declined that as well. He said he wasn't interested in money or fame, and he had left the field. He lives quietly in Saint Petersburg. It's the only Millennium Problem solved so far.

Thomas Edison was born in Ohio in 1847. He was partly deaf from childhood, and had only a few months of formal schooling. He became a telegraph operator, and then an inventor. In 1876 he set up a laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey. He called it an invention factory. It had a team of machinists and scientists, and aimed to turn out a minor invention every ten days and a big one every six months.
He held over one thousand patents in the United States, for things such as the phonograph, an improved light bulb and a motion picture camera. His method was trial and error on a huge scale. For the light bulb, his team tested thousands of materials for the filament, such as carbon and bamboo. He also built the first power station in New York, in 1882. His real talent was in organizing invention.

Alexander Graham Bell was born in Scotland in 1847, and moved to Canada, and then to Boston. He was a teacher of the deaf, and his mother and wife were both deaf. His father had developed a system of symbols for the sounds of speech, that he used. He was trying to improve the telegraph, when he realized that a telephone might be possible.
On March 10, 1876, in his laboratory in Boston, he spoke into the device to his assistant, Thomas Watson, in another room: Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you. Watson heard it. Bell's patent had been granted three days earlier. It had been filed on the same day that another inventor, Elisha Gray, filed a notice of a similar idea. The dispute went on for years, and Bell won. He devoted much of his later life to teaching the deaf.

James Watt was a Scottish instrument maker, who was born in 1736. In 1763 he was asked to repair a model of an engine invented by Thomas Newcomen, which was used to pump water out of mines. He saw that it wasted a great deal of heat, since the cylinder was heated and then cooled on each stroke. In 1765, according to his own account, he had the idea of a separate condenser.
With the help of the manufacturer Matthew Boulton, in Birmingham, he built engines that used much less coal. He invented ways of making them turn a wheel, so that they could drive machines, and not just pumps. To sell them, he compared their power with that of horses, which led to the term horsepower. The unit of power, the watt, is named for him. His engines helped to power the Industrial Revolution.

Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1304. In 1325, when he was twenty-one, he set out on a pilgrimage to Mecca. He planned to be away for a year or two. He did not come home for almost thirty years. During this time, he visited most of the Muslim world, and more. He traveled to Egypt, Syria, Persia, East Africa, Anatolia, India, the Maldives, Southeast Asia and China.
He covered about seventy-five thousand miles, more than Marco Polo, and he worked as a judge in places such as Delhi. He was robbed, shipwrecked and caught up in wars. He survived the plague. After his return, the Sultan of Morocco asked him to dictate an account of his journeys. It's called the Rihla, and it's an important source on the societies of the fourteenth century.

In the summer of 1816, eighteen-year-old Mary Godwin, who later became Mary Shelley, was staying near Geneva, Switzerland, with her future husband, the poet Percy Shelley, and with Lord Byron. It was the year without a summer. The eruption of the volcano Tambora in Indonesia in the previous year had filled the air with dust, and there was cold and rain across Europe. The group stayed indoors.
Byron proposed that each of them should write a ghost story. Mary struggled, and then, after a conversation about the nature of life, and the new experiments with electricity, she had a waking dream about a scientist who brought a creature to life. This became Frankenstein, published when she was twenty. It's often called the first science fiction novel. It asks what responsibility a creator has for what it makes, a question that still matters.

John Maynard Keynes was a British economist who lived from 1883 to 1946. He worked in the government, and was an adviser at the peace conference after the First World War. He resigned, and wrote a book arguing that the harsh terms imposed on Germany would cause disaster. He was also a collector of art, and a successful investor, and a leading member of the Bloomsbury group of writers and artists.
In the Great Depression, he argued that governments should spend more, even if it meant a deficit, to raise demand, and to create jobs. His book of 1936 changed the study of economics. He said that markets are driven by animal spirits, the waves of confidence and fear. He is also remembered for the remark that in the long run we are all dead, made in 1923. At the Bretton Woods conference in 1944, he helped to plan the postwar financial system.

Elinor Ostrom was an American political scientist who lived from 1933 to 2012. She grew up poor in Los Angeles, and was told that girls shouldn't study mathematics. She became a professor at Indiana University. In 1990 she published a book that challenged a very influential idea, the tragedy of the commons, which holds that shared resources will be overused and ruined, unless they are privatized or controlled by a government.
She studied real communities that had managed commons for centuries, such as Swiss alpine meadows, Japanese forests and irrigation systems in Spain and the Philippines. She found that people often cooperate successfully. She identified features of the successful ones, such as clear boundaries, rules that fit local conditions, monitoring, and graduated penalties. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics.

Amartya Sen was born in India in 1933. As a boy of nine, he saw the Bengal famine of 1943, in which about three million people died. He remembered the sight of starving people at his family's door. Later, as an economist, he asked what causes famines. The common idea was that they occur when there's not enough food.
In his book Poverty and Famines, in 1981, he showed that famines often occur even when the food supply is adequate. People starve because they have lost the means of buying food, owing to a fall in wages or a rise in prices. He also observed that no famine has taken place in a functioning democracy with a free press, since governments face pressure to act. He won the Nobel Prize in 1998. His work shifted the focus of development to people's real freedoms.

Herbert Simon was an American scientist who lived from 1916 to 2001. He worked in economics, psychology, political science and computer science, at Carnegie Mellon University. In economics, he argued against the idea that people are perfectly rational. He proposed bounded rationality. People have limited time and ability, and so they don't find the best option. They look for one that is good enough, a strategy that he called satisficing.
With Allen Newell, in 1956, he wrote the Logic Theorist, a program that proved theorems from the mathematics textbook Principia Mathematica. It's often called the first artificial intelligence program. Simon claimed that it solved the mind-body problem. He won the Turing Award in 1975, and the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1978. He was a curious man, who learned several languages, and played chess and piano.

Hans Rosling was a Swedish physician and statistician, who lived from 1948 to 2017. He worked on public health in Africa, and became known for lively talks about world statistics, using animated graphs. He co-founded the Gapminder Foundation. In the talks, he asked the audience questions about the state of the world, such as how many of the world's children have been vaccinated, and what share of people live in extreme poverty.
Each question had three answers. If you picked at random, you would be right a third of the time. Even a chimpanzee, he said, picking from bananas, would get one in three. In his surveys of people in many countries, including students, doctors and leaders, the average score was below that, often only a couple of correct answers out of twelve. People held outdated, gloomy pictures of the world. Rosling's message was that the facts are generally better than we think.

Vera Rubin was an American astronomer who lived from 1928 to 2016. As a girl, she built a telescope. At Vassar College she was the only astronomy major in her year, and when she applied to Princeton for graduate study, she was not allowed to apply, because it did not accept women in astronomy. She studied at Georgetown, and became an astronomer at the Carnegie Institution in Washington.
In the 1970s she and Kent Ford measured how fast stars at different distances from the center of a galaxy move. According to Newton's laws, those at the edge should move more slowly. They didn't. They moved just as fast, as if the galaxy was held together by much more mass than could be seen. It was strong evidence for dark matter. She never received a Nobel Prize, though many thought that she deserved one. Dark matter is now thought to make up most of the matter in the universe.
The ad that called its own product a lemon

In the 1950s, American car ads were loud and glossy, and promised bigger and better everything. In 1959 the agency Doyle Dane Bernbach launched a campaign for the Volkswagen Beetle, a small, odd-looking German car. The ad had a photograph of the car, with a large amount of blank space, and a headline of two words: Think small. It went against everything that was being done.
Another ad in the campaign, called Lemon, showed a picture of a Beetle, and explained that a car had been rejected because of a small blemish on the glove compartment, which an inspector had spotted. The idea was that VW was so careful that it threw out a car for a trivial flaw. The ads were funny and honest, and respectful of readers. In 1999 Advertising Age named the Volkswagen campaign the best of the century.

In the 1920s it was considered improper for women to smoke in public, and cigarette companies were missing half the market. The American Tobacco Company hired Edward Bernays, a pioneer of public relations, and a nephew of Sigmund Freud. In March 1929 he arranged for a group of young women to march in the Easter Parade on Fifth Avenue in New York, and to light cigarettes together at a signal.
He had tipped off the press that the women would be lighting torches of freedom, as a protest for the equality of the sexes. The photographs appeared in newspapers across the country. Bernays understood that people respond to a story, and not to a sales pitch, and that a product can be tied to a cause. Smoking rates among women rose in the following years. It's often seen as the birth of modern public relations, and as a cautionary tale.

In 1957 a market researcher named James Vicary announced that he had flashed the messages Eat Popcorn and Drink Coca-Cola on a movie screen for a fraction of a second, too fast for viewers to notice. He claimed that sales of popcorn rose by almost sixty percent, and sales of Coke by eighteen percent. The story created a panic about mind control, and it led to proposals for laws against subliminal advertising.
In 1962 Vicary admitted that he had made it up, since he had not had enough data. No one had been able to reproduce his results. Later research has shown that very brief messages can have small effects in the lab, but there's no evidence that they can make you do something that you don't want to do. The hoax shows how readily people believe in the power of hidden persuasion.
A hidden brand, for the thirsty

Can a hidden message ever influence a choice? In 2006 Johan Karremans and his colleagues in the Netherlands tested it. Students did a computer task, in which the brand name Lipton Ice was flashed on screen for a few hundredths of a second, too fast to read. For others, a meaningless string of letters was flashed instead. Afterward, they were asked which drink they would prefer.
The students who had been primed with the brand were more likely to choose Lipton Ice, but only if they were thirsty. It suggests that a brief message may tip a choice that someone already wants to make, but doesn't create a new desire. Other labs have had mixed results, and the effects are small. It's an answer to the question of whether Vicary's hoax had any truth. It's a little, in narrow conditions.

In 1971 Phil Knight, who ran a small company that sold running shoes, needed a logo. He asked Carolyn Davidson, a graphic design student at Portland State University, who had done some work for him. She came up with several designs. Knight reportedly said that he didn't love it, but that he thought it would grow on him. She was paid thirty-five dollars for her time.
The design was the swoosh, which became one of the best-known logos in the world. The company named itself Nike, after the Greek goddess of victory. In 1983, when Nike had become hugely successful, Knight gave Davidson a gold ring with a swoosh set in diamonds, and an envelope with shares of the company. A logo that cost thirty-five dollars is now worth far more than that.
Coca-Cola did not invent Santa's red suit

It's often said that Coca-Cola invented the modern Santa Claus, with his red suit and white beard. The truth is a little different. Santa was shown in red as early as the 1800s. The cartoonist Thomas Nast drew a plump, jolly Santa in a red suit for Harper's Weekly in the 1860s, and many other images of Santa in red appeared before the 1930s, in stores, magazines and advertisements.
What Coca-Cola did, from 1931, was to commission the artist Haddon Sundblom to paint Santa for its Christmas ads, and the ads ran for more than thirty years. They showed a warm, human, friendly Santa, drinking a Coke. It made the image more widespread, and more consistent. It's a case of a company taking an existing idea, and by repeating it, making it its own.

Advertisers have long used a simple model of how a sale works. First, you get the customer's attention. Then you arouse their interest. Then you create a desire for the product. Finally, you move them to action, such as buying. The four steps are known by their initial letters, AIDA. The model is usually credited to an American advertising pioneer, E. St. Elmo Lewis, who proposed it around 1898.
The scheme has been criticized as too simple, since people don't always move through the steps in order, and some buy without much desire. But it's a useful checklist for a message. Does it catch attention? Does it hold interest? Does it make the person want it? Does it make it easy to act? It's still taught in business schools more than a hundred years later.
When people see through the pitch

How do we deal with attempts to persuade us? In 1994 Marian Friestad and Peter Wright proposed that all of us develop what they called persuasion knowledge. Over the years, we learn how advertisers and salespeople work. We learn to recognize their tricks, such as a fake sale, a flattering remark or an appeal to fear, and we learn to guess their motives.
When people notice a persuasion attempt, they tend to resist. They become more skeptical, and may react against the message. The knowledge develops with age, and children before the age of seven or eight often don't see that an ad is trying to sell. It's why marketers try to hide the ad, as in sponsored content or product placement. Being aware of the techniques is our main defense.

Early in the history of the web, researchers noticed something odd. People looking for information on a web page often failed to see things that were in plain view, if they looked like advertisements. In 1998 Jan Panero Benway and David Lane tested this. They designed a page in which the important information was in a large, brightly colored banner at the top.
Many of the users, who were searching for the information, didn't notice it. They had learned to ignore the area at the top, and anything that looked like an ad. It's called banner blindness. Later eye-tracking studies confirmed that people tend to look at the content, and skip over the places where ads usually are. Advertisers responded by making ads look more like content, which is why some of them are hard to tell apart.

On October 27, 1994, the online magazine HotWired put an advertisement on its web page. It was a rectangular banner, and it was paid for by AT&T. It said, Have you ever clicked your mouse right here? YOU WILL. An arrow pointed at the words. It was one of the first ads to be displayed on the web.
It reportedly drew a response from a large share of those who saw it. Figures of forty-four percent are often given, though the web had few users, and the ad was a novelty. Today the average rate of clicking on a banner is a small fraction of a percent. The first banner shows how a new medium can make a message stand out, and how the effect fades as people get used to it.

In 2007 the presidential campaign of Barack Obama used a website to collect the email addresses of supporters. A young engineer named Dan Siroker, who was working with the campaign, suggested that they test different versions of the page. They tried several different buttons, with words such as Sign Up, Learn More and Join Us Now. They also tried different images and videos.
The best combination, a family photograph and the button Learn More, produced about forty percent more sign-ups than the original. Over the course of the campaign, the team estimated that the improvement brought in millions of extra email addresses, and tens of millions of dollars in donations. Siroker later started a company, Optimizely, that offered such tests to others. It showed that small details can have big effects, and that guesses about what works are often wrong.

Almost everyone knows the experience of having a tune play over and over in the mind, without wanting it to. It's called an earworm, a word borrowed from German, Ohrwurm. In surveys, around nine in ten people say that they experience it at least once a week. Most say that it's not very bothersome.
Research has found some patterns. Earworms tend to be songs that were heard recently, and often. They are usually simple, with a fast tempo and a repeating melody. A trigger might be a memory, a word or a mood. Some people try to get rid of a song by chewing gum, which interferes with the inner voice, and a study found that it helped. Listening to the whole song may also work, or solving a puzzle. Advertisers use catchy jingles on purpose.

Mindfulness meditation has become very popular, and many claims are made for it. In 2014 Madhav Goyal and his colleagues at Johns Hopkins reviewed the evidence from trials. They found forty-seven trials, with about thirty-five hundred participants, that compared meditation programs with a control, such as a waiting list or education. They looked at what was reported in terms of anxiety, depression, pain and stress.
There was moderate evidence that the programs improved anxiety, depression and pain. The size of the effects was modest, about the same as that seen with antidepressants in some trials. The evidence for stress and quality of life was weaker, and there was little evidence of effects on mood, attention or sleep. Mindfulness was no better than other active treatments, such as exercise or medicine. It's a useful tool, and not a cure for everything.
A walk in nature and the ruminating mind

Rumination is the habit of going over and over negative thoughts, and it's linked to depression. In 2015 Gregory Bratman and his colleagues at Stanford asked people to take a ninety-minute walk, either in a grassy area with oaks near the university, or along a busy road in Palo Alto. Before and after, they were asked about rumination, and their brains were scanned.
After the nature walk, people reported less rumination. Their brain scans showed less activity in the subgenual prefrontal cortex, a region that is overactive when people brood. The walk on the busy road produced no such change. The study was small, but it fits other research on the benefits of green spaces. A short walk in a park may not cure depression, but it's an easy way to get some distance from a thought loop.
How many sessions does therapy need?

How long does it take for psychotherapy to help? In 1986 Kenneth Howard and his colleagues combined the data from fifteen studies, with over two thousand patients. They plotted how the percentage of patients who had improved rose with the number of sessions.
About half of the patients had improved after eight weekly sessions, and about three quarters after twenty-six. Most of the improvement came early, and then the gains became smaller, which is called a diminishing returns curve. Later studies have found a similar pattern, though people with more severe or long-standing problems often need more. The research is a reason to expect some benefit within a couple of months, and to review progress if there is none.

Many people turn to self-help books for depression and anxiety. Do they work? In 1997 Pim Cuijpers combined the results of studies of bibliotherapy, in which people with depression read a book based on cognitive behavioral therapy. The people who read the books improved more than those who were put on a waiting list. The effect was large.
A later review in 2010, by Pim Cuijpers and his colleagues, looked at studies of guided self-help, in which a person gets some support from a therapist, and found that it worked about as well as face-to-face therapy for depression and anxiety. The books that work are based on techniques that have been tested, such as behavioral activation and thought records. It's a reasonable first step, for mild to moderate problems, and also a supplement to therapy.
Writing about your best possible self

In 2001 Laura King asked students to write for twenty minutes a day, for four days. One group wrote about their best possible future selves, imagining that everything had gone as well as it could. A second group wrote about a traumatic event. A third wrote about their plans for the day. Months later, those who wrote about their best selves were happier, and had fewer visits to the health center.
In 2006 Kennon Sheldon and Sonja Lyubomirsky used it again, and found that it gave a short-term boost in mood, particularly when people kept doing it, and found it meaningful. Later studies show a small but consistent effect on optimism and well-being. It may work because it helps people to set goals, and think about what matters to them. It's a simple exercise, and it costs nothing to try.
Cutting social media for three weeks

In 2018 Melissa Hunt and her colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania asked a hundred and forty-three undergraduates to use their phones in one of two ways for three weeks. One group continued as usual. The other group limited its use of Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat to ten minutes a day on each. The students sent in screenshots to show how much they were using.
At the end of the three weeks, the group with limits reported less loneliness and less depression than the control group. Both groups improved on other measures, such as anxiety, perhaps because they were paying more attention to their use. Other studies of giving up social media have had mixed results, and effects depend on how people use it. But the findings suggest that there may be benefits to cutting back, particularly for those who feel worse after scrolling.

Loneliness is painful, and it's linked to poor health. What can be done about it? In 2011 Christopher Masi and his colleagues combined the results of fifty studies of attempts to reduce loneliness. They compared four approaches. These were improving social skills, enhancing social support, increasing opportunities for contact, and addressing maladaptive social thinking.
The most effective approach was the last. Lonely people often expect rejection, and notice signs of it, and pull back, which makes more loneliness. Programs that helped them to question those expectations did better than those that only gave them more chances to meet people. It doesn't mean that contact doesn't matter. But it suggests that how we think about others is a key part of the problem, and of the solution.

Obsessive compulsive disorder involves unwanted thoughts, and rituals that people feel driven to perform to reduce their anxiety, such as washing hands or checking a lock many times. The most effective psychological treatment is exposure and response prevention. The person is gradually exposed to the thing that triggers the fear, and prevented from doing the ritual. They learn that the anxiety falls on its own.
In 2005 Edna Foa and her colleagues compared this therapy with the antidepressant clomipramine, and with a placebo, in over a hundred adults. The therapy worked better than the drug, and the combination was not better than the therapy alone. Many patients had a major reduction in symptoms. The treatment is hard, since it asks people to face their fears. But it's a good example of the principle that facing a fear lets it fade.
How much of happiness is in the genes?

In 1996 David Lykken and Auke Tellegen studied thousands of pairs of twins in Minnesota. They asked them how happy they were, and compared identical twins, who share all their genes, with fraternal twins, who share half. They found that identical twins were much more alike in happiness. They concluded that about half of the differences between people's well-being, at a given time, could be due to genes.
The authors said that happiness is largely a matter of a stable personality, with a set point, and that people return to it after good or bad events. The idea has been used to say that we can't become happier. But heritability describes differences between people, in a group, and not what is fixed in a person. Studies also show that people's well-being can change a lot over years, and that it's affected by circumstances and by choices.
The scar of losing a job

People adapt to many life changes, but not to all. In 2008 Andrew Clark and his colleagues used the German Socio-Economic Panel, a survey that followed thousands of people for up to twenty years. They looked at how life satisfaction changed before and after events such as marriage, divorce, widowhood and unemployment.
Marriage gave a short boost in satisfaction, which faded within a couple of years. Unemployment was different. Satisfaction fell sharply, and even years later, it had not recovered, even if the person had found a new job. The effect was not just due to a loss of income. Losing work seems to hit our sense of identity and purpose, and it leaves a scar. It's a good reason to take the emotional side of job loss seriously.

Economists would expect people to choose a long commute only if they get something in return, such as a bigger house or a better salary. In 2008 Alois Stutzer and Bruno Frey analyzed a German survey, and found that people with longer commutes reported lower satisfaction with life. The extra pay or housing didn't seem to make up for the cost.
They called it the commuting paradox. People seem to underestimate how much a long daily journey will bother them, and overestimate the pleasure of the benefits, which we get used to. Commuting is stressful, since it's unpredictable and cannot be controlled. People who commute by walking or cycling are happier than those who drive. If you are weighing a house or a job, count the daily journey with care.

In 2004 Daniel Kahneman and his colleagues developed a method for studying how people feel through the day, called the day reconstruction method. About nine hundred working women in Texas listed what they had done on the previous day, in short episodes, and rated how they felt in each one. The researchers added up the time spent, and the mood.
The most pleasant activities were intimate relations, socializing after work, and relaxing. The least pleasant were the morning commute, work, and the evening commute. Child care ranked lower than many expected, though it's often rated as meaningful. The study highlights the difference between how we feel moment by moment and how we judge our lives overall. It suggests that we might improve our days by arranging more time for the activities we enjoy.
The opera house that cost fourteen times too much

In 1957 a Danish architect, Jørn Utzon, won a competition to design an opera house for the harbor of Sydney, Australia. His design had a set of white sail-shaped shells, and it's now one of the most recognizable buildings in the world. The government estimated that it would cost about seven million Australian dollars, and be finished in 1963.
It opened in 1973, ten years late, and the final cost was about a hundred and two million dollars, more than fourteen times the estimate. The shells were difficult to build, and the engineers had to find a way of constructing them. Utzon resigned in 1966, after a dispute with the government, and never returned to Australia to see his building. The overrun was extreme, but not unusual. The planning fallacy applies to large public projects, as well as to our own tasks.

In 1988 the University of Iowa started a small online market in which people could bet real money on the outcome of elections. In the Iowa Electronic Markets, a share in a candidate pays one dollar if that candidate wins the popular vote. The price of the share is the market's guess of the chance of winning, and traders profit if they are right.
Over several decades, the prices were closer to the actual results than polls, in most cases, especially when the election was weeks away. The reason is that the market gathers the knowledge of many people, who have a reason to be right, and it responds quickly to news. It's an example of the wisdom of crowds. Prediction markets have been used for forecasting many other things, though they can be distorted by a few traders with a lot of money, and by thin trading.

The psychologist Gary Klein wanted to study how experienced people make decisions under pressure. In the 1980s he interviewed fire commanders about their hardest calls. He expected that they would say that they compared options, weighing the pros and cons. They said that they didn't. In most cases, they said that they never made decisions at all, and just did what was obvious.
Klein found that the commanders recognized the situation as one of a type that they had seen before, and a course of action came to mind. They checked it by imagining how it would play out. If it seemed to work, they did it. If not, they changed it. He called it recognition-primed decision-making. It means that expert intuition is based on pattern recognition built from years of experience, and that it works best where the situation is familiar, and feedback is quick.
The regret of the neighbor's lottery

In the Netherlands, a lottery draws a postal code, and everyone who lives there and has a ticket wins a prize. In 2004 Marcel Zeelenberg and Rik Pieters studied what happens when a person who doesn't have a ticket sees their neighbors win. The sight triggers a strong feeling of regret, since they would have won, if they had taken part.
The researchers found that the feeling of regret was greater than that of a person who plays and loses, and that it motivated people to take part. Regret is felt more strongly when the outcome of the option that we didn't choose is known, and when it was easy to choose. It's a force that marketers use, and that we use in our own choices. People often buy insurance, or tickets, to avoid the pain of regret.
The cost of being able to change your mind

In 2002 Daniel Gilbert and Jane Ebert ran an experiment in a photography course at Harvard. Students took photographs, and then picked their two favorites to print. They were asked to choose one to keep, and the other would be kept by the researchers. For some students, the choice was final. Others were told that they could change their minds within five days, and swap.
When asked later how they felt about their photographs, the students who could not change their minds liked their pictures more than those who could. Yet, when asked beforehand, most people said that they would prefer to have the option of changing. The ability to switch kept the students from fully accepting their choice. The finding suggests that we like our choices better when we have no way out, and that keeping options open has a hidden cost.

Why are people more afraid of some risks than others? In the 1970s and 80s Paul Slovic and his colleagues asked people to rate dozens of hazards, such as nuclear power, motor vehicles, pesticides and swimming. The ratings were compared with the statistics of deaths. Experts ranked the risks according to the number of deaths. Ordinary people ranked them differently.
Slovic found two main factors. One was dread, how much a risk is feared, as for something uncontrollable, catastrophic and fatal. The other was how unknown the risk is, to the people exposed, and to science. Nuclear power scored high on both, and was ranked as very risky by laypeople, while experts put it far lower. Risks like driving, with many deaths spread over time, caused less fear. It suggests that fear tracks the character of a risk, and not just its size.

You are looking at apartments, or job candidates. You see them one at a time, and you must decide on the spot whether to take one. If you refuse, you can't go back. How many should you look at before you choose? This is called the secretary problem, and it has a surprising answer.
The best strategy is to look at the first thirty-seven percent of the options without choosing any, just noting the best so far. Then take the first one that is better than all of those. This gives about a thirty-seven percent chance of getting the very best. The number is one divided by e, the base of natural logarithms. In experiments, people tend to stop earlier than the optimal point. The rule assumes that you can only compare options, and that you can't go back, so it's a rough guide.

Can small changes in a cafeteria make people eat more healthily? In 2012 Anne Thorndike and her colleagues tried it at the cafeteria of Massachusetts General Hospital, which serves thousands of employees and visitors. They labeled food and drinks with colored dots. Green meant healthy, yellow meant less healthy and red meant unhealthy.
Three months later, they rearranged the display, putting the green items, such as bottled water, at eye level and in the most visible places. Sales of red items fell, and sales of green items rose. The effect continued for the following two years. There were no bans, and no change in prices. People could still choose anything. It's an example of choice architecture, and it suggests that an environment can steer us without removing our freedom.

In 2000 William Chaplin and his colleagues studied handshakes. Students were trained to rate the way that people shook hands, on grip strength, vigor, duration and eye contact, and they shook hands with more than a hundred people. The same people took personality tests. A firm handshake with good eye contact was linked to being extraverted and open to experience, and less shy and anxious. It also made a better first impression.
In 2019 Juliana Schroeder and her colleagues tested what a handshake does at the start of a negotiation. Pairs who shook hands before beginning were more likely to cooperate, and to reach deals. The effect was found in both lab and real settings. The handshake works as a signal of cooperative intent. It seems that a small ritual of touch can change how two strangers see each other.

In 1970 Richard Warren played people a recording of a sentence, in which a single speech sound had been cut out, and replaced with a cough. The sentence was, the state governors met with their respective legislatures convening in the capital city. The "s" in legislatures had been removed, and a cough was put in its place.
The listeners did not notice that a sound was missing. Most of them said that they heard the whole word, with the cough in the background. Even when told that a sound was missing, they could not say where it had been. This is called phonemic restoration. The brain uses the context to fill in missing parts of speech, and we hear what we expect to hear. It helps us to understand speech in noisy places, and it's also one reason why we mishear things.

Vocal fry is a low, creaky sound at the end of a phrase, produced when the vocal cords vibrate slowly. It has become common among young American women, and it has been criticized in the press. In 2014 Rindy Anderson and her colleagues tested its effect. They recorded young men and women saying a phrase, either in a normal voice or with fry, and played it to hundreds of listeners.
The listeners rated the voices with vocal fry as less competent, less educated, less trustworthy and less attractive, and said that they would be less likely to hire them. The effect was stronger for women than for men. Other studies have had mixed results, and some have found that vocal fry is a normal feature of speech, in both men and women. The bias may be a matter of habit. It shows how the sound of a voice can sway a judgment that should be based on the content.

Singing in a group is found in all cultures. Why? In 2015 Eiluned Pearce, Jacques Launay and the anthropologist Robin Dunbar studied people who joined adult education classes. Some were in singing classes, which met weekly for seven months, and others were in creative writing or crafts classes. They asked the members how close they felt to the group at several points in time.
In the early weeks, the feelings of closeness grew faster in the singing groups than in the others. After a few months, the groups were equally close. Singing seems to be a quick way of forming bonds, and it works even with large groups. Dunbar suggested that it may have played a part in human evolution, since it allows many people to feel connected at once, as grooming does for primates. It's a good reason to join a choir.

When two friends talk about their problems, going over them again and again, and dwelling on them, it's called co-rumination. In 2002 Amanda Rose surveyed children and teenagers about their friendships, and asked how much they spoke with their friends about problems, and how they felt.
The ones who co-ruminated had closer friendships. They also had more depression and anxiety, and over time, their symptoms grew. It was more common among girls than boys. Talking about problems is good when it leads to solutions, or to feeling understood. But when it consists of going over the same ground, it can make people feel worse. It's a good question to ask, in a conversation with a friend. Are we working on a problem, or just feeding it?

Sometimes people help us in ways that we don't see, and this may be the best kind. In 2000 Niall Bolger and his colleagues studied couples in which one partner was preparing for the bar exam, a time of great stress. Each day, over thirty-five days, both partners recorded the stress and the support that was given.
The support came in two forms. In visible support, the person noticed that they were being helped, and recorded it. In invisible support, the partner said that they'd given help, but the person didn't notice. The people who received visible support were not less anxious. In fact, those who got invisible support were less upset. Noticing help may remind us of our own needs, and make us feel less capable. The best help may be offered in a way that doesn't call attention to itself.
The mother tongue and the feelings

If you speak two languages, you've probably noticed that some things feel different in each. In 2006 Catherine Harris and her colleagues at Boston University measured people's skin conductance, a sign of emotional arousal, while they heard words in their first and their second languages. The participants were Turkish speakers who had learned English as adults.
Their bodies reacted more strongly to words like taboo words, and to reprimands, in Turkish than in English. Even when they were fluent in English, the first language had a stronger emotional pull. It's one reason why people say I love you in their mother tongue, and why swearing seems weaker in a second language. Some immigrants find it easier to talk about painful things in the second language, because it feels more distant. It's a useful thing to know in therapy and conversation.

In the 1960s the anthropologist Edward Hall studied the use of space in conversation. He called it proxemics. He observed that people, without realizing it, keep different distances from others, depending on the relationship. He described four zones, based on his observations of middle-class Americans.
The intimate zone is closer than about eighteen inches, which is for close relationships. The personal zone is up to about four feet, for friends and family. The social zone is up to about twelve feet, for acquaintances and business. The public zone is beyond that, for speakers and audiences. The distances differ between cultures. People from Latin America and the Middle East often stand closer, and those from Northern Europe and East Asia farther. Discomfort arises when one person's norm is broken.

How can you tell when someone is lying? In 2006 a team of researchers asked people in seventy-five countries what they believed. They asked, how can you tell when a person is lying? Across all the countries, the most common answer was that liars avoid looking you in the eye. It was the same in rich and poor countries, and in every culture.
But research shows that gaze aversion is not a reliable sign. Liars and truth-tellers look at others to about the same degree. Some liars even look people in the eye more, to appear honest. The belief is so widespread that it may be one reason why we are so bad at spotting lies. The accuracy of most people is little better than chance. It's wise not to rely on a feeling that someone looks shifty.

A coral reef looks like a rock garden, but it's alive. Each coral is a colony of tiny animals, called polyps, which build a skeleton of limestone. Inside the tissue of the polyps live microscopic algae, called zooxanthellae. The algae use sunlight to make sugars, and pass most of them to the coral, which gives them shelter and nutrients in return. The algae give corals their colors.
When the water becomes too warm, the algae are expelled, and the coral turns white. It's called bleaching. A bleached coral isn't dead, but it's starving, and if the heat lasts, it dies. Mass bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef has occurred several times, in 1998, 2002, 2016, 2017 and later. Reefs cover a small part of the ocean floor, but support a large share of marine species. How much they can adapt to warmer seas is a critical question.

Many of the foods that we eat depend on animals that carry pollen between flowers. In 2007 Alexandra-Maria Klein and her colleagues reviewed data on the crops of the world. Of the leading food crops, about three quarters depend on animal pollinators, at least in part. They include fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds, such as apples, almonds and coffee.
However, by volume, most of the world's calories come from crops such as wheat, rice and corn, which are wind-pollinated or self-pollinated. The pollinated crops account for about a third of production. They are crucial for nutrition, since they provide many of the vitamins and minerals in our diets. Bees, flies, butterflies and bats all play a part. Declines in wild bees and other insects are a concern for food security.
A vault for the world's seeds

In the mountainside on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, about six hundred miles from the North Pole, there's a tunnel that leads to a vault. Opened in 2008, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a safety deposit box for the world's crops. Seed banks from many countries send duplicates of their collections, and the vault stores them at a temperature of about minus eighteen degrees Celsius.
It now holds more than a million samples, representing thousands of varieties of food plants. If a collection is lost in a war, a natural disaster or a failure of equipment, seeds can be taken back. This happened in 2015, when a seed bank in Aleppo, Syria, was unable to use its collection because of the war, and it asked for its seeds to be returned. The permafrost helps to keep the vault cold, even without power.

In 1935 the Australian government brought a hundred and two cane toads from Hawaii to Queensland. The aim was to control beetles that were damaging sugar cane. The toads did not eat the beetles. They did, however, thrive, and breed. They are poisonous, and they have no natural predators in Australia, so they have spread across the north of the country.
The toad population is now in the many millions, and it has moved west into the Northern Territory and Western Australia. Native animals that eat the toads, such as quolls, goannas and snakes, have been poisoned, and some have declined. The case is a classic example of an invasive species, and of how introducing an animal to control a pest can make things worse. Scientists are now working on methods to protect native animals, such as training them to avoid the toads.

In 1859 a wealthy landowner in Victoria, Australia, named Thomas Austin, wrote to a relative in England and asked for some rabbits to be sent over, so that he could hunt them for sport. The twenty-four rabbits he received bred rapidly. There was plenty of food, and no natural enemies. Within a few decades, rabbits had spread across much of the continent, in one of the fastest spreads of a mammal ever recorded.
They ate vegetation, caused erosion, and competed with native animals and with sheep. Fences, poisons and shooting made little difference. In 1950 the authorities released a virus, myxomatosis, which killed a huge number of rabbits. But the survivors became resistant, and the population recovered. Rabbit numbers are still a problem. It's often given as a lesson in how fragile an ecosystem can be.

The passenger pigeon was once the most numerous bird in North America, and perhaps in the world. Flocks of millions darkened the sky for hours or days. Estimates of the population run to several billion. The naturalist John James Audubon described a flock in 1813 that took three days to pass overhead.
The birds were hunted on an industrial scale for food, shipped by railroad to the cities, and their forest habitat was cleared. By the 1890s, they were almost gone from the wild. The last one, a female called Martha, died in the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. Her body was frozen in a block of ice, and sent to the Smithsonian. The loss of a species of such numbers within a few decades showed that abundance is no protection.
To the bottom of the sea

The deepest known place in the ocean is the Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific. It is about eleven kilometers down, nearly seven miles. It's deeper than Mount Everest is high, and at the bottom, the pressure is more than a thousand times that at the surface. In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Lieutenant Don Walsh of the United States Navy reached it in a submersible called the Trieste. They spent about twenty minutes there.
They saw a flat fish, which they took to be a sole, but it's now doubted that fish could live at that depth. In 2012 the film director James Cameron made the first solo descent, in a submersible that he helped to design. Since then, other crewed and unmanned vehicles have visited. Animals live even there, among them amphipods and sea cucumbers. And sadly, plastic waste has been found at the bottom.

In 1977 scientists diving in the submersible Alvin, near the Galápagos Islands, found something that no one had expected. On the ocean floor, over two kilometers deep, hot water was gushing out of cracks in the rock, forming chimneys. Around them, in the dark and cold, there was a thriving community of animals, including giant tube worms, clams and crabs.
It was thought that all life depended on sunlight, which supports the plants at the base of the food chain. But here, bacteria were making food from chemicals in the hot water, such as hydrogen sulfide, in a process called chemosynthesis. The tube worms, which have no mouth or gut, housed the bacteria in their bodies. The discovery changed our ideas about where life can live, and suggested that it might exist on other worlds, such as the oceans of icy moons.

Most of the ocean is dark, and many creatures there make their own light. In 2017 Séverine Martini and Steven Haddock studied the animals in the water column off Monterey Bay in California. They went down in robotic submersibles, and counted the animals that they saw, looking for those that were known to glow.
