They found that about three quarters of the animals that they saw, from the surface to a depth of about four kilometers, could produce light. This is called bioluminescence. The animals use it for many things, including attracting prey, evading predators, and finding mates. Jellyfish, squid, shrimp and fish all do it. It's the most common form of communication on Earth, by the volume of living space that it covers.

On the morning of November 1, 1755, which was All Saints' Day, an earthquake struck Lisbon, the capital of Portugal. The churches were full. The quake was followed by fires, and then, about forty minutes later, by a tsunami that rushed into the harbor. Tens of thousands of people died, estimates run from thirty thousand to fifty thousand, and most of the city was destroyed.
The disaster shocked Europe, and it caused a crisis of thought. If the world was governed by a benevolent God, how could such a thing happen, and on a holy day? Voltaire wrote a poem on the disaster, and made it a theme in his novel Candide. The philosopher Immanuel Kant wrote about natural causes of earthquakes. Some historians see it as a turning point in the Enlightenment, and in the beginning of seismology.

On December 26, 2004, a huge earthquake occurred under the sea off the coast of Sumatra, Indonesia. It had a magnitude of about 9.1, one of the strongest ever recorded. It displaced a large section of the seafloor, and generated a series of giant waves that crossed the Indian Ocean, reaching coasts as far away as East Africa.
About two hundred and thirty thousand people died, in fourteen countries, and many more lost their homes. Most of the dead were in Indonesia. There was no warning system in the Indian Ocean, as there was in the Pacific, and many people did not know to run away from the sea. Afterward, an international tsunami warning system was set up for the region. A warning that gives people even minutes can save many lives.

On November 24, 1974, the American paleoanthropologist Donald Johanson and a student, Tom Gray, were looking for fossils in the Afar region of Ethiopia. They spotted a piece of an arm bone, and then other bones nearby. Over the next days, the team found about forty percent of a skeleton. It was a small, adult female. She was about three feet seven inches tall.
The fossil was dated to about 3.2 million years ago. It was named Lucy, after the Beatles song Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds, which was playing in the camp. She belonged to a species, Australopithecus afarensis. Her pelvis and leg bones showed that she walked upright, while her skull was small, with a brain not much bigger than a chimpanzee's. She showed that our ancestors walked upright before their brains grew large.

On April 13, 1970, two days into the Apollo 13 mission to the Moon, an oxygen tank exploded in the service module. The astronauts, Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise, were about two hundred thousand miles from Earth. The explosion crippled the electrical system, and the crew had to use the lunar module, designed for two men for two days, as a lifeboat for three people for four days.
The air in the lunar module started to fill with carbon dioxide, since the filters were the wrong shape for the command module's equipment. Engineers on the ground, working against the clock, designed an adapter using only the items that were on board, such as plastic bags, cardboard and duct tape. The crew built it by following instructions read out over the radio. They splashed down safely on April 17. The mission is often called a successful failure.
The ice water and the O-rings

On January 28, 1986, the space shuttle Challenger broke apart seventy-three seconds after launch, killing all seven crew. The weather had been unusually cold. A presidential commission was set up to find the cause. One of its members was the physicist Richard Feynman.
Feynman learned from engineers that the rubber O-rings that seal the joints in the solid rocket boosters might lose their flexibility in the cold. At a televised hearing on February 11, he clamped a piece of the rubber in a small clamp, dropped it in a glass of ice water, and then pulled it out. It didn't spring back. The commission concluded that the O-ring failure was the immediate cause, and that managers had ignored warnings. Feynman wrote that nature cannot be fooled.

The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in April 1990 after years of delays, and at a cost of about a billion and a half dollars. When the first images came back, scientists saw that something was wrong. The pictures were blurry. The main mirror, which is eight feet across, had been ground to the wrong shape. It was too flat at the edge by about one fiftieth the width of a human hair.
The error had been caused by a flaw in a test instrument that had been assembled incorrectly. In December 1993 astronauts on the space shuttle Endeavour, over five days, installed a set of corrective mirrors, in effect, glasses for the telescope. After that, Hubble produced sharp pictures, and went on to make some of the greatest discoveries in astronomy. It has been serviced several times, and was still in use more than thirty years after launch.

In 1919 a New York hotel owner, Raymond Orteig, offered a prize of twenty-five thousand dollars to the first pilot to fly nonstop between New York and Paris. Several teams tried and failed, and some died in the attempt. In 1927 a twenty-five-year-old airmail pilot named Charles Lindbergh decided to try it alone, in a single-engine plane built for the purpose, the Spirit of St. Louis.
He took off from Long Island on the morning of May 20, 1927. He had no radio, and no parachute, and he stayed awake for the whole flight, using a periscope to see forward, as the tank blocked the view from the cockpit. After thirty-three and a half hours, he landed at Le Bourget airfield outside Paris, where about a hundred and fifty thousand people were waiting. He became an international hero overnight.

In the early twentieth century, farmers plowed up millions of acres of the grasslands of the American Great Plains to grow wheat. The deep-rooted native grass had held the soil in place. In the 1930s a severe drought set in, and the crops failed. With nothing to hold it, the dry topsoil blew away.
On April 14, 1935, which came to be known as Black Sunday, a huge dust storm swept across Oklahoma, Texas and Kansas, turning the afternoon to night. Dust drifted like snow, and it caused a lung disease called dust pneumonia. Hundreds of thousands of people left the region, many of them to California. In response, the government set up the Soil Conservation Service, and encouraged farmers to plant trees and to plow in ways that protected the soil. It's one of the great examples of an environmental disaster that was caused by human practices.

The Suez Canal in Egypt, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. It saved ships about four thousand miles on a voyage from Britain to India, since they no longer had to sail around Africa. It was built by a French company led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, and it took ten years, using the labor of many thousands of Egyptians.
De Lesseps then tried to build a canal across Panama, and failed. The French effort began in 1881, and was ruined by disease, mostly yellow fever and malaria, and by landslides. More than twenty thousand workers died. The Americans took over in 1904. Doctor William Gorgas led a campaign to eliminate the mosquitoes that spread the diseases, which was the key to success. The Panama Canal opened in 1914. It cut the trip from New York to San Francisco by about eight thousand miles.

Before 1869, crossing the United States took months by wagon, or weeks by ship around South America. In the 1860s two companies built a railroad to link the East and West. The Central Pacific started in Sacramento, California, and built eastward, over the Sierra Nevada mountains. The Union Pacific started in Omaha, Nebraska, and built westward, across the plains.
Much of the labor was done by Chinese immigrants on the Central Pacific, and Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans on the Union Pacific. The two lines met on May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit, Utah. A golden spike was driven into the final tie. The news was telegraphed across the country. A journey that took months could now be made in about a week. The railroad changed the nation's economy and opened the West to settlement, at a terrible cost to Native Americans.

Until the middle of the nineteenth century, news from Europe took about ten days to reach America, carried by ship. In 1858 an American businessman, Cyrus Field, led the effort to lay a telegraph cable on the floor of the Atlantic Ocean. It took several attempts, and two ships had to meet in mid-ocean to splice two halves of the cable.
On August 16, 1858, Queen Victoria sent a message of ninety-eight words to President James Buchanan. It took sixteen hours to send, as the signal was weak. There were celebrations in New York, with fireworks, which set the city hall on fire. A few weeks later, the cable failed, probably because a technician had used too high a voltage. A durable cable was laid in 1866, and it worked. Messages now crossed the ocean in minutes.

In 1085, at Christmas, William the Conqueror, who had conquered England in 1066, decided to carry out a survey. He sent officials to every part of the kingdom, with the aim of finding out who owned what, how much land and how many animals and people there were, and how much tax should be due. The work was done in about a year.
The results were written in a book that was called Domesday, since there was no appeal from its judgments, as with the Last Judgment. It records about thirteen thousand places. It's a snapshot of eleventh-century England, and it's the earliest public record that survives. The Domesday Book is held at the National Archives in Kew. A survey on such a scale was very rare in medieval Europe. It suggests how thoroughly the Normans took over the country.

In 1947 a young Bedouin shepherd, probably Muhammed edh-Dhib, was looking for a lost goat near the Dead Sea. He threw a stone into a cave, and heard the sound of breaking pottery. Inside were clay jars that contained ancient scrolls wrapped in linen. Over the next ten years, scrolls were found in eleven caves near the site of Qumran, in what is now the West Bank.
There were about nine hundred manuscripts, most of them in fragments. They include the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible, a thousand years older than any other. They date from about the third century BC to the first century AD. Some of the scrolls are on the rules and beliefs of a Jewish community, possibly the Essenes, who lived at Qumran. It was one of the great manuscript discoveries of the twentieth century.

In March 1974 some farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an in China hit something hard. It was a clay head. Archaeologists came, and found the tomb complex of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China, who died in 210 BC. He had ordered an army of clay soldiers to be made, to protect him in the afterlife.
Excavations have revealed thousands of life-size warriors, in battle formation, with horses and chariots. It's estimated that there are about eight thousand soldiers. Each of them has a different face, and they were originally painted in bright colors, which have flaked off. The emperor's own burial chamber has not been opened. Ancient historians wrote that it contains rivers of mercury, and soil tests have found high levels of the metal.

On November 4, 1922, the English archaeologist Howard Carter, who had spent years searching the Valley of the Kings in Egypt, uncovered a step cut into the rock. It led to a doorway sealed with plaster. When it was opened, a few weeks later, in the presence of his sponsor, Lord Carnarvon, Carter peered in with a candle. Asked if he could see anything, he said, yes, wonderful things.
It was the tomb of Tutankhamun, a young king who died in about 1323 BC, at about eighteen or nineteen. It was almost untouched, and held thousands of objects, including a gold funeral mask, a throne and chariots. A story spread that a curse killed those who opened it, after Carnarvon died of an infection in 1923. But most of the people involved lived for many years. Carter himself lived until 1939.

Easter Island, or Rapa Nui, is a small island in the Pacific, more than two thousand miles from South America. It's famous for its nearly nine hundred huge stone statues, the moai. A popular story, told by Jared Diamond among others, is that the islanders cut down all of the island's trees to move the statues, destroyed their own environment, and collapsed into war and famine.
Archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo have proposed a different account. They say that rats, brought by the first Polynesian settlers, ate the seeds of the palm trees and stopped them from regrowing. They also find that the islanders were skillful, and that they could walk the statues upright, with ropes, rather than dragging them on logs. And the population collapse may have been caused largely by diseases and slave raids brought by Europeans. The debate is still going on.
The whole is more than the parts

In the early twentieth century, a group of German psychologists, including Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka, argued that we don't see the world as a collection of separate dots and lines. We see organized wholes. They called their school Gestalt psychology, from the German word for form. Their motto was that the whole is something other than the sum of its parts.
In 1923 Wertheimer listed the principles by which we group things. Items that are close together are seen as a group, which is proximity. Items that look alike are grouped, which is similarity. We fill in gaps to see a complete shape, which is closure. We prefer smooth, continuous lines. These rules work so automatically that we don't notice them. They are used by every graphic designer.

Two lights are placed a short distance apart. If one is switched on and then off, and then the other is switched on, at the right interval, you don't see two lights flashing. You see one light moving from the first position to the second. In 1912 Max Wertheimer studied this illusion on a train, and with a device in a hotel room in Frankfurt. He called it the phi phenomenon.
The phi phenomenon is the basis of apparent motion, in film and animation. A film is made of still pictures, shown at about twenty-four frames a second, and the brain turns them into smooth movement. It showed that perception is not just a record of what hits the eye. The brain builds motion between the pictures, and that was an important piece of evidence for the Gestalt view.

You might know the picture. It's of a white vase in the middle, and, if you look at the dark areas on each side instead, two faces looking at each other. It was designed by the Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915. You can see either the vase or the faces, but not both at once. The picture flips back and forth.
Rubin used it to study figure and ground. When we look at a scene, we divide it into the object that we focus on, the figure, and the background. The figure seems to be in front, and to have a shape, while the ground seems to extend behind it. The same lines can be seen in two ways, which shows that perception is an act of interpretation. The picture is still used to teach this idea.

In 1832 the Swiss crystallographer Louis Necker was looking at drawings of crystals under a microscope. He noticed that a drawing of a transparent cube, made of lines, would sometimes appear to change its orientation. The face that seemed to be at the front turned to the back, without any change on the page. The cube is now called the Necker cube.
The drawing is ambiguous, because a flat picture of a cube can be seen in two three-dimensional ways. The brain picks one, and holds it for a few seconds, and then switches to the other. The changes happen on their own, even when you try to hold one view. It's an example of bistable perception. It shows that what we see is the brain's best guess, and that when the evidence is equal, the guess can flip.

Look at the cross in the middle of a page, and keep your eyes still. After a few seconds, a faint colored blur in the corner of your vision will disappear, even though it's still there. It's called Troxler fading. It was described in 1804 by the Swiss physician Ignaz Troxler. The effect is strongest in peripheral vision.
The explanation is that the brain tunes out things that don't change. Neurons in the visual system respond to change, and if an image stays fixed on the retina, their response weakens. Normally our eyes make tiny movements all the time, which refresh the image. When you hold your gaze steady, the periphery fades. It's a good demonstration of the principle that the senses are built to detect differences, not constant stimulation.

Stare at a picture of a green, black and yellow flag for half a minute, and then look at a white wall. You will see a red, white and blue flag. This is a negative afterimage. The cells in your retina that respond to green get tired, and when you look away, the cells for the opposite color, red, dominate.
The effect fits the opponent process theory, proposed by the German physiologist Ewald Hering in 1878. He argued that color vision is organized in opposing pairs, red against green, blue against yellow, and black against white. This explains why we never see a reddish green or a yellowish blue. In 1957 Leo Hurvich and Dorothea Jameson gave it a quantitative form. Later work showed that the opponent system is built into the nerve cells that receive the signals from the cones.
The room that changes your size

In 1946 the American scientist Adelbert Ames built a strange room. Seen through a peephole, it looks like an ordinary rectangular room. But it is actually a trapezoid. One corner is much farther away than the other, and the ceiling and floor slope. When two people stand in the corners, the person in the far corner looks like a tiny person, and the one in the near corner looks like a giant. A person walking from one corner to the other seems to grow or shrink.
The illusion works because our brains assume that rooms are rectangular, and that the walls meet at right angles. Given that assumption, the only way to explain the images is to change the sizes of people. The room is used in films, such as the Lord of the Rings, to make actors seem to be different sizes. It's evidence of how strongly our assumptions shape what we see.

The Moon looks much bigger when it's near the horizon than when it's high in the sky. But it's the same size. A photograph taken at both times shows no difference, and you can check by holding a small coin at arm's length. This moon illusion has been noted since ancient times, by Aristotle and Ptolemy.
There's no agreed explanation. One popular theory is that the sky looks like a flattened dome, so the horizon seems farther away than the zenith, and the brain scales the size accordingly. But experiments have found problems with this. Other ideas involve the cues that we use to judge size and distance, and the way the eyes are positioned. Looking at the Moon upside down, between your legs, makes the illusion smaller. It's an old puzzle that has not been fully solved.
The grill that burns without heat

In 1896 the Swedish physician Torsten Thunberg discovered a strange effect. If he placed a person's hand on a set of metal rods, with every other rod warm, and the ones in between cool, the person felt a burning pain. Yet each rod, on its own, would be harmless. It is called the thermal grill illusion.
In 1994 A. D. Craig and Catherine Bushnell studied it in the laboratory. They found that the burning sensation arose from a clash between the signals in the pathways that carry warmth, cold and pain. When both warm and cold nerve fibers are active, the brain's circuits for pain are fooled. It suggests that pain is not just a direct report of damage. It's a construct that comes from combining several signals, and can be created when they conflict.

Some people find broccoli and black coffee intensely bitter, and others find them mild. In the 1990s Linda Bartoshuk, a psychologist at Yale, found that about a quarter of people are supertasters. They have more taste buds on the tongue than average, and they find bitter tastes, such as of a chemical called PROP, much stronger. About a quarter are nontasters, who find it nearly tasteless, and half are in between.
Supertasters often dislike bitter vegetables, and tend to find spicy food, fat and alcohol more intense. Some studies link it to eating fewer vegetables. It is partly genetic, and is more common in women. Children are often more sensitive than adults. If you hate Brussels sprouts, it may be that your tongue is more sensitive. It's a reminder that we may not experience the same food in the same way.
Why cilantro tastes like soap to some people

Many people love the fresh herb cilantro, also called coriander. Some people say that it tastes like soap, or like bugs. It's one of the most divisive foods. In 2012 Nicholas Eriksson and his colleagues at the genetic testing company 23andMe asked thousands of people about their reactions, and compared them with their DNA.
They found a variation near a gene called OR6A2, which codes for a receptor in the nose that is sensitive to aldehydes, chemicals that are found in cilantro and in some soaps. People with a certain version were more likely to say that it tasted like soap. The link is not very strong, and it's likely that other genes and experiences matter too. For some, repeated exposure makes the taste more tolerable. The effect varies between populations.
The fruit that makes lemons sweet

A small red berry from West Africa, called the miracle fruit, has a very unusual effect. If you chew it, and then eat something sour, like a lemon or vinegar, it tastes sweet. The effect lasts for half an hour or so. The people of West Africa have long used it to sweeten sour foods and drinks.
In the late 1960s Kenzo Kurihara and Lloyd Beidler found that the active substance is a protein, now called miraculin. It sticks to the sweet receptors on the tongue. In a neutral mouth, it does nothing. But when acid is present, it changes shape, and activates the receptors, so the acid is tasted as sweet. The berries have been used to help people undergoing chemotherapy, whose sense of taste is altered. It's a good case of how taste depends on the receptors and on chemistry.
A thousand kinds of smell receptor

For a long time, no one knew how the nose detects smells. In 1991 Linda Buck and Richard Axel, working at Columbia University, found a large family of genes that code for odor receptors. In mice, there are about a thousand of them, and it's the largest gene family in the mammal genome. Each receptor is found on a different type of nerve cell in the nose.
A single odor molecule can activate several receptors, and each receptor responds to several odors. The brain recognizes a smell by the pattern of activation, like a chord on a piano. Humans have about four hundred working receptor genes. Buck and Axel shared the Nobel Prize in 2004. The discovery explained how we can tell apart thousands of different smells, with a limited number of receptors, and why some people cannot smell certain things.
Does smell guide choice of a mate?

In 1995 the Swiss biologist Claus Wedekind asked men to wear the same cotton T-shirt for two nights, without using any scented products. Then he asked women to smell the shirts, and rate them for pleasantness. The women also had their genes tested. They were particularly interested in the genes for the immune system, the major histocompatibility complex.
The women tended to prefer the smell of shirts worn by men whose immune genes differed from their own. It was suggested that smell helps us to choose partners whose children would have a wider range of immune defenses. The study was small, and later work has been mixed, with some studies finding the same, and others not. The effect, if it exists, appears to be weak. The idea that humans have a hidden chemical sense of compatibility remains unproven.

Some people have woken up and found that they can't move, or speak. They are conscious, and feel a pressure on the chest. They may see or hear something frightening, such as a shadowy figure in the room. It lasts a few seconds, or a few minutes, and then ends. This is sleep paralysis, and it's far more common than most people think. About one in twelve people has had it.
During dream sleep, the brain keeps the muscles from moving, so that we don't act out our dreams. In sleep paralysis, the person wakes up while this paralysis is still in effect. The hallucinations are dreams intruding on waking. It's linked to irregular sleep, stress, and sleeping on the back. In folklore around the world, it has been blamed on demons, witches, and a visiting Old Hag. Knowing that it's harmless can make it less frightening.

A lucid dream is a dream in which you know you're dreaming, and may be able to control it. For years, scientists doubted that they happened. In 1981 Stephen LaBerge at Stanford found a way to prove it. He knew that in dream sleep, the eyes move, while the rest of the body is paralyzed. So he asked lucid dreamers to move their eyes in a pattern, left, right, left, right, as a signal when they realized that they were dreaming.
In the sleep lab, the researchers saw the signals on the recording of the eye movements, while the person was in dream sleep. The dreamers confirmed later that they had been lucid. The experiment showed that a sleeper could send a message from inside a dream. People can learn to have lucid dreams through techniques such as checking whether they are dreaming during the day. It's used for research on dreams, and to treat nightmares.

A newborn can tell the sounds of any language in the world apart. In 1984 Janet Werker and Richard Tees tested babies from English-speaking families. They played them speech sounds from Hindi and from a Native American language, Nlaka'pamux, that English speakers find hard to distinguish. The six-month-old babies could hear the difference.
By the age of ten to twelve months, the babies had lost the ability. They had become attuned to the sounds of their own language, and tuned out the ones that don't matter. Babies raised in Hindi-speaking homes kept the ability. The brain prunes what it doesn't use. It's the reason that adults find it so hard to hear and say some sounds of a foreign language, and why early exposure helps.

In 2003 Patricia Kuhl and her colleagues tested whether babies can learn a foreign language just by hearing it. American babies of nine months were given twelve sessions of play with a native speaker of Mandarin Chinese, who read to them and talked to them. Another group heard the same material, but from a recording, or in a video. A third group had no Mandarin.
The babies who played with the live speaker learned to tell apart Mandarin sounds, as well as babies in Taiwan. The babies who saw or heard the recording learned nothing, as if they had never heard it. A person's presence, and the give and take of interaction, seem to be necessary. It's a reminder that language is learned in social situations, and not just by listening. A baby learns from people.
A song of joy, in any culture

Does music convey the same emotions to everyone? In 2009 Thomas Fritz and his colleagues went to Cameroon, to visit the Mafa, a people who live in the mountains in the north of the country, and who had no exposure to Western music, radio or television. They played the Mafa piano music, which was written to sound happy, sad or scary, and asked them to point to a face that matched.
The Mafa picked the right emotion more often than chance, for all three. The fast, major-key pieces sounded happy, and the slow, low pieces sounded sad. Western listeners did the same for Mafa music. It suggests that some emotional cues in music, such as tempo and loudness, are universal. Others, such as the idea that minor keys are sad, may be learned. Music is partly universal and partly cultural.

Do we learn rhythm, or are we born with it? In 2009 István Winkler and his colleagues in Hungary and the Netherlands tested newborn babies, who were two or three days old. They played them a rock drum pattern, with a bass drum on the downbeat, and other drums in between. Sometimes, the downbeat was left out. They recorded electrical activity from the babies' brains.
When the beat was missing, the babies' brains showed a response, a sign of surprise. They seemed to expect the beat. It suggests that the ability to sense a regular pulse is present at birth, and doesn't need to be learned. Rhythm is basic to music and dance, and to speech. The study also gives a hint of why babies like to be rocked and sung to.

Western listeners generally find some combinations of notes pleasant, such as a major chord, and others harsh, such as notes a semitone apart. It's often said that this preference is built into the brain, because the sounds of the pleasant chords have a simple mathematical relationship. In 2016 Josh McDermott and his colleagues tested the idea with the Tsimane', an Amazonian people who live in villages in Bolivia, with little exposure to Western music.
The Tsimane' showed no preference for consonant chords over dissonant ones. They rated them about the same. They did, however, show a preference for sounds that were not rough, as Westerners do. It suggests that the liking of consonance is learned, through exposure to music in which it's common, and not purely biological. It's a case where a feature that seemed universal turned out to be cultural.

In 1980 Michael Posner published a simple experiment that changed the study of attention. People looked at a dot in the center of a screen, and pressed a key as soon as a light appeared on the left or the right. Before each light, an arrow gave a hint about where it would appear. Most of the time, the arrow was right.
When the hint was correct, people responded faster. When it was wrong, they were slower. Their eyes stayed fixed on the dot, so it wasn't a matter of looking. Attention can be moved to a place without moving the eyes. Posner compared it to a spotlight, which illuminates one area and leaves the rest in the dark. The task is still widely used. It's the basis for much of what we know about how attention works in the brain.

The feedback sandwich is a popular way of giving criticism. You start with something positive, then give the criticism, and end on another positive note. The idea is that praise softens the blow. It has been taught in management courses for decades, and is common in schools and medical training.
The evidence for it is thin. In 2013 Jenny Parkes and her colleagues tested it with students. The sandwich changed how the feedback felt, but not how well the students performed. People may learn to expect a criticism after praise, so the praise loses its value. The main message can also be lost in the padding. Studies suggest that feedback works best when it is specific, timely, focused on the work and not on the person, and when it's clear what to do next. A sandwich is fine, but clarity matters more.

Some leaders inspire their followers, and others only manage them. In the 1980s the political scientist James MacGregor Burns and the psychologist Bernard Bass described transformational leadership. These leaders articulate a vision, set an example, encourage new ways of thinking, and pay attention to the needs of each individual. Transactional leaders, in contrast, rely on rewards and punishments.
In 2004 Timothy Judge and Ronald Piccolo combined the results of dozens of studies. They found that transformational leadership was linked to better follower satisfaction, motivation and performance, more than transactional methods. The link was found across many types of organization. But most studies were surveys, in which the same people rated both the leader and the outcome, so the results may be inflated. It's still some of the best evidence that how a leader communicates matters.

We often picture a leader as someone confident, bold and sure of themselves. But in 2012 Bradley Owens and David Hekman interviewed leaders and followers in many types of organization, and asked what humility looked like. Leaders said that it meant admitting mistakes, spotlighting the strengths of others, and being open to feedback and new ideas.
A follow-up study in 2013 found that when leaders behaved in this way, followers were more engaged, and more likely to stay in their jobs. They also learned more, and teams performed better. A humble leader sets an example that makes it safe to say I don't know, or I was wrong. The finding goes against the stereotype of the heroic leader. Admitting a limit seems to make people trust you more, not less.

Do tall people earn more? In 2004 Timothy Judge and Daniel Cable analyzed data from four large studies that had followed thousands of people through their working lives. They looked at the relationship between height and income, while taking account of age, sex and weight.
Each additional inch of height was linked to about eight hundred dollars more in annual earnings. For someone six feet tall, compared with someone five feet five, that amounted to thousands of dollars a year. The effect held for men and women. The researchers suggested that taller people may be seen as more leaderlike, and gain confidence. It's a striking example of bias in the workplace, working in ways that most of us don't notice.

In 1994 the economists Daniel Hamermesh and Jeff Biddle asked a simple question. Do better-looking people earn more? They analyzed surveys in which interviewers had rated the physical attractiveness of workers on a scale. They then compared pay, while accounting for education, experience and other factors.
People who were rated as below average in looks earned several percent less than those of average looks. Those who were above average earned a few percent more. The penalty for plainness was bigger than the premium for good looks. The effect was found for both men and women, though it was a little stronger for men. It occurs in occupations in which looks should not matter. The gap was found in many later studies, and it's a form of discrimination that is rarely discussed.

Open-plan offices are supposed to encourage collaboration, by removing walls. In 2018 Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban studied two companies that moved from traditional offices to open plans. The employees wore sensors that tracked who talked with whom, and the researchers also collected email records.
The result was the opposite of what was expected. Face-to-face interaction fell by about seventy percent. Email use increased. People seemed to withdraw, wearing headphones and avoiding the discomfort of being seen and heard. The researchers suggested that the lack of privacy made people less willing to talk. Open offices may bring benefits, such as cost savings. But if the aim is to get people to talk, the evidence suggests that taking down the walls may not work.

In 2010 Nicholas Bloom and his colleagues ran an experiment at Ctrip, a large travel agency in China, with a call center of thousands of employees. Employees who volunteered were randomly assigned to work from home for nine months, or to stay in the office. Their performance was tracked by the number of calls they handled.
The people who worked at home were thirteen percent more productive. About nine percent of that came from working more minutes per shift, with fewer breaks and sick days, and the rest from taking more calls per minute, in a quieter environment. They were also happier, and the rate of quitting fell by half. Some of them later chose to return to the office, because of loneliness. Home working was good for routine tasks, but promotions fell for those who stayed away.

Does saying thank you make people work harder? In 2010 Adam Grant and Francesca Gino ran an experiment with university fundraisers who called alumni to ask for donations. Their work was often met with rejection. One day, the director of fundraising visited some of them, and said, I am very grateful for your hard work. We sincerely appreciate your contributions. Others were not visited.
In the week after, the callers who had been thanked made about fifty percent more calls than those who had not. They felt more valued. In follow-up experiments, people helped a stranger more often after being thanked. The thanks wasn't a reward in money. It made people feel that their efforts mattered, and so they wanted to do more. It's a cheap and effective way of encouraging people, and few of us do it as often as we could.

At a call center at a university, workers phoned alumni to ask for money for scholarships. It was a difficult job, and many found it boring. In a study in 2007, Adam Grant and his colleagues arranged for a student who had benefited from a scholarship to visit the call center. He spent five minutes telling the callers how the scholarships had changed his life.
A month later, the callers who had met the student were spending more time on the phone, and the amount of money that they raised was far higher, more than doubled, than that of the others. The callers themselves said that they had not noticed any change. Knowing the effect of what you do on a real person seems to make work more meaningful. It's a lesson for managers, and for anyone who wants to stay motivated.

In 1791 the French Academy of Sciences proposed a new unit of length, to be the same for all people and all time. It would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian through Paris. Two astronomers, Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain, spent seven years surveying the distance from Dunkirk to Barcelona to work it out.
The meter was later defined by a platinum bar, and then by the wavelength of light from krypton. Since 1983 it has been defined by the speed of light. A meter is the distance that light travels in a vacuum in one 299,792,458th of a second. The unit began with the size of the Earth, and now rests on a constant of nature. Méchain, who found a small error in his data, was troubled by it until he died.
The kilogram without a lump of metal

For 130 years, the kilogram was defined by a lump of platinum and iridium, kept in a vault near Paris, known as Le Grand K. Copies were sent to other countries. Over time, the copies and the original drifted apart by about fifty micrograms, roughly the weight of a grain of sand. Since the definition was an object, no one could say which had changed.
On May 20, 2019, the kilogram was redefined in terms of the Planck constant, a fixed number from quantum physics. It's measured using a machine called a Kibble balance, which compares mechanical power with electrical power. Now every unit in the metric system is defined in terms of nature, and not an artifact. A scientist in any laboratory can, in principle, make a kilogram, and the old cylinder is just a historical object.

For most of history, the second was defined as a fraction of a day. It was one eighty-six-thousand-four-hundredth part. But the Earth's rotation is not constant. It slows slightly because of tides, and varies unpredictably. In the 1950s, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the National Physical Laboratory in Britain built the first accurate atomic clock, using the vibrations of cesium atoms.
In 1967 the second was redefined as 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation from a cesium-133 atom. Modern atomic clocks are so precise that they would not lose a second in hundreds of millions of years. Newer clocks, which use light, may do better still. Occasionally, a leap second is added to the calendar to keep our clocks in step with the Earth's slowing spin. The accuracy of clocks is used in GPS and in the internet.

In 1724 the German instrument maker Daniel Fahrenheit built mercury thermometers that were more accurate than earlier ones. He set zero as the temperature of a mixture of ice, water and salt, which was the coldest he could reach. He put the freezing point of plain water at thirty-two, and set his scale so that human body temperature came to about ninety-six.
In 1742 the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius proposed a scale with one hundred degrees between the freezing and boiling points of water. Oddly, he put zero at the boiling point and a hundred at the freezing point. It was reversed after his death. In 1848 William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed a scale starting at absolute zero, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. The kelvin has no negative values, and is used in science.

Sound is measured in decibels, a unit named for Alexander Graham Bell, who made the first telephone. It was invented in the 1920s by engineers at Bell Telephone Laboratories, to measure the loss of signal in telephone cables. The scale is logarithmic, which means that each increase of ten decibels means ten times as much sound energy.
It's a good match for the way we hear. We don't notice absolute changes in loudness, but ratios. A rise of ten decibels sounds about twice as loud. A whisper is about thirty decibels, normal conversation about sixty, and a rock concert more than a hundred. Sound above eighty-five decibels over a long time can damage hearing, and a jet engine nearby reaches a level that causes pain. The scale shows how the senses respond to ratios.

In 1935 the seismologist Charles Richter, working at Caltech, devised a scale to compare earthquakes. It was based on the size of the waves recorded by a seismograph. The scale is logarithmic. For each whole number, the size of the ground motion is ten times larger. A magnitude seven earthquake shakes the ground ten times as much as a magnitude six.
The energy released rises even faster, by about thirty-two times for each step. So a magnitude eight earthquake releases about a thousand times the energy of a magnitude six. Today seismologists use the moment magnitude scale, devised in 1979 by Thomas Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori, which works better for large quakes. The numbers are reported on the same scale. The largest recorded earthquake was in Chile, in 1960, at magnitude 9.5.

The Julian calendar, introduced by Julius Caesar in 45 BC, had a year of 365.25 days, with a leap year every four years. But the true length of the year is about 365.2422 days. The difference of about eleven minutes a year added up, and by the sixteenth century, the calendar was ten days out of line with the seasons. Easter was drifting away from spring.
In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII decreed a new calendar. Ten days were dropped. In Catholic countries, the day after October 4 was October 15. The new rule was that century years are leap years only if divisible by four hundred. Protestant countries were slow to adopt it. Britain and its colonies changed in 1752, when eleven days were dropped, and there were reportedly protests. Russia changed only in 1918.

Before the nineteenth century, each town kept its own time, set by the Sun, and noon was a little different in every place. It didn't matter when travel was slow. But with the railroads, the confusion became a problem. A traveler in the United States might have to deal with dozens of local times, and timetables were a mess.
The Canadian engineer Sandford Fleming, who was angry after missing a train in Ireland in 1876, because the timetable said p.m. rather than a.m., campaigned for a worldwide system. In 1883 the American railroads adopted standard time zones. In 1884 an international conference in Washington chose the meridian through Greenwich in England as the starting point, from which time zones were measured. Governments were slower to adopt the system.

In 1784 Benjamin Franklin, who was then the American ambassador in Paris, wrote a humorous letter to a newspaper. He had been surprised to learn that the Sun rises early, and that Parisians slept through the morning light and then burned candles at night. He suggested a tax on shutters and a rule that church bells should ring at sunrise. He meant it as a joke, but it's often cited as the first mention of the idea.
The first country to adopt daylight saving time was Germany, in 1916, during the First World War, to save coal. Other countries followed. It has been introduced and dropped many times since. Whether it saves energy is disputed, and studies have linked the change in the spring to a rise in heart attacks and accidents. Many places have debated ending it. It's one of the more argued-over inventions in the calendar.

The French Revolution did more than change the government. The new regime wanted to remake everything on rational lines, including time. In 1793 it introduced the French Republican calendar, with months of three ten-day weeks, and with names such as Brumaire, for fog, and Thermidor, for heat. It took a year of twelve months of thirty days, and five or six extra days at the end.
The revolutionaries also introduced decimal time. The day was divided into ten hours, each of a hundred minutes, each of a hundred seconds. Some watches were made with two dials. It was unpopular, since people had no wish to change the way they lived, and the ten-day week gave workers one rest day in ten, instead of one in seven. Decimal time was suspended in 1795. The calendar lasted until 1806, when Napoleon abolished it.
Paper sizes and a square root

If you fold a sheet of A4 paper in half, you get two sheets of A5, which have the same shape as the original. Fold again, and you have A6. The shape stays the same at every size. This works only if the ratio of the long side to the short side is the square root of two, about 1.414. The German scientist Georg Lichtenberg noticed this property in 1786.
The system was used in Germany from 1922, and it was adopted as the international standard in 1975. A0 is a sheet with an area of one square meter, and each size down is half the area. A4 is the size used throughout the world, except in North America, which uses letter size. A neat feature is that you can enlarge or reduce a document by a standard factor, and it will fit on the next size of paper.
A dozen and the finger joints

Why do we have a dozen eggs and twelve inches in a foot, when we count in tens? One theory is that it's based on the hand. If you use your thumb to count the segments of the other four fingers, there are three on each finger, which gives twelve. With the other hand, you can keep count of the dozens, up to five, and so reach sixty. This is a system that is still used in some parts of Asia.
It may be the origin of the Babylonian sixty-based number system, and of the twelve hours of the day and night, and the twelve months. Twelve has many divisors, two, three, four and six, which makes it handy for sharing things. A ten has only two. Some mathematicians have argued that a base of twelve would have been better than ten. The Dozenal Society still campaigns for it.

The word mile comes from the Latin mille passus, a thousand paces. A Roman pace was two steps, from the point where one foot leaves the ground to the point where that same foot lands again, so a mile was about a thousand double steps, or about fifteen hundred meters. Roman soldiers marched in this way, and milestones were set up along the roads.
The modern mile is about sixteen hundred and nine meters, a little longer, as it was changed to fit other measures. In England in 1593, a statute fixed it at eight furlongs, and a furlong was originally the length of a furrow in a plowed field, a furrow-long. An acre was said to be the area that a team of oxen could plow in a day. Many of our units have their origins in human work.

A nautical mile is a little longer than an ordinary mile, at 1,852 meters. It has a logical basis. It's the length of one minute of latitude, one sixtieth of a degree, on the surface of the Earth. This makes it handy for navigators, who work with charts. If you travel one nautical mile north, your latitude changes by one minute.
A knot is one nautical mile per hour. The name comes from the way that sailors once measured speed. They threw a piece of wood on a rope, which had knots at regular distances, off the stern of a ship, and counted how many knots ran out in a set time. The nautical mile was set at its present length by an international conference in 1929. Airplanes also use nautical miles and knots.

The word pandemonium now means wild noise and confusion, but it was invented as the name of a place. In 1667 the English poet John Milton published his epic poem Paradise Lost. In it, the fallen angels build a capital for hell, a great palace, and he called it Pandæmonium. He made the name from two Greek words, pan, meaning all, and daimon, meaning spirit or demon. It was the place of all the demons.
The poem was very popular, and the word took on a life of its own. By the eighteenth century, people were using it for any wild, noisy place, and later for any uproar. Milton invented hundreds of words, and it's one of the most successful. It's a case of a word that began as one man's coinage and became ordinary speech.

In 1516 the English lawyer and writer Thomas More published a short book about an imaginary island, which he called Utopia. In it, a traveler describes a land where there is no private property, everyone works six hours a day, and religion is tolerated. It's a satire as well as a vision, and More used it to criticize the faults of his own society.
The word is made from two Greek words. It could be ou-topos, meaning no place, or eu-topos, meaning good place. More probably intended the pun. The word is now used for any ideal society, and gave rise to dystopia, an imagined society of misery. More was later beheaded by Henry VIII for refusing to accept the king as head of the Church. He is now regarded as a saint by the Catholic Church.

Don Quixote is the title character of a novel by the Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615. He is an elderly gentleman who has read so many tales of chivalry that he loses his mind. He sets out on a horse, called Rocinante, in rusty armor, with a squire, Sancho Panza, to right wrongs and to win glory.
In the most famous scene, he mistakes windmills for giants, and charges at them. From his name, the adjective quixotic means idealistic in a foolish, impractical way. The word has been in English since the early 1700s. The novel is often called the first modern novel. It's also one of the most translated books, and has been in print for over four hundred years.

In the play The Rivals, written by Richard Brinsley Sheridan in 1775, a character called Mrs. Malaprop tries to sound educated, but keeps using the wrong word. She says that someone is the very pineapple of politeness, when she means pinnacle. She speaks of an allegory on the banks of the Nile, when she means alligator. Her name comes from the French mal à propos, meaning inappropriate.
The word malapropism now means the mistaken use of a word that sounds like another, with a comic effect. It differs from a simple mistake, in that the word is a real one, but not the one meant. Many of Mrs. Malaprop's errors have a kind of logic. Famous people have made them, too, and they can turn up in everyday talk, when we reach for a word that we don't know well.

A spoonerism is a slip in which the sounds of two words are swapped, such as saying a blushing crow, instead of a crushing blow. The word is named after the Reverend William Archibald Spooner, who was warden of New College, Oxford, from 1903 to 1924. He was known for making slips of the tongue of this kind.
Many of the stories told about him, such as that he said you have hissed all my mystery lectures, are probably invented by students. He himself said that he could recall only one, in which he had announced the hymn, Kinquering Congs Their Titles Take. But the name stuck, and the word is in the dictionary from 1900. Such slips happen to all of us, and are studied by linguists because they show how the brain plans speech.

A Hobson's choice is a choice that is no choice at all, take it or leave it. It's named after Thomas Hobson, who kept a livery stable in Cambridge, England, in the seventeenth century. He rented out horses to students at the university. To keep his best horses from being overworked, so the story goes, he insisted that each customer take the horse that was nearest the door.
A customer could take that horse, or none. Hobson died in 1631, and John Milton, who was a student in Cambridge then, wrote two humorous poems about him. The phrase Hobson's choice is recorded by the 1640s. It's often confused with a dilemma, in which there are two choices that are both bad. In a true Hobson's choice there is only one option, offered as if it were a choice.

In 1812 the governor of Massachusetts, Elbridge Gerry, signed a bill that redrew the electoral districts of the state. The new boundaries were designed to favor his party, the Democratic-Republicans. One of the districts, north of Boston, had an odd, twisting shape. A newspaper, the Boston Gazette, published a cartoon of the district, with wings and claws added. They said it looked like a salamander.
Someone called it a Gerry-mander, and the name stuck. To gerrymander is to draw the boundaries of an electoral district in order to benefit one party or group. The practice has been used by both parties for more than two hundred years, and with the help of computers today, it can be done very precisely. Courts and reformers continue to debate how to limit it. Gerry himself was not the author of the plan. He is said to have disliked it.

The word sideburns is a backward form. It comes from the name of General Ambrose Burnside, a Union general in the American Civil War. He was famous for his whiskers, which grew in front of his ears, and joined a thick mustache, though the chin was clean-shaven. People called them burnsides.
Over time, the two parts of his name were reversed, to side-burns, perhaps because the whiskers grew at the side of the face. The word sideburns has been in use since the 1880s. Burnside's military record was mixed. He led the Union forces in the disastrous Battle of Fredericksburg in December 1862. He later became governor of Rhode Island and a senator. He is remembered for his whiskers more than for his battles.

In November 1902 President Theodore Roosevelt went on a hunting trip in Mississippi. After several days, he had not found a bear. His guides caught a black bear, tied it to a tree, and invited him to shoot it. Roosevelt refused, saying that it would be unsportsmanlike. The incident was reported in the press, and the cartoonist Clifford Berryman drew it in the Washington Post, showing a small, cute bear.
A shop owner in Brooklyn, Morris Michtom, saw the cartoon. He and his wife made a stuffed bear, and put it in the window, with a note saying that it was Teddy's bear, after receiving permission from the president. It was a great success. In Germany, the toy company Steiff was making plush bears at the same time. The name teddy bear has been in use ever since. Roosevelt's nickname, Teddy, which he disliked, became a toy.

Many units of measurement are named after scientists. The volt is named for the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta, who invented the battery. The ampere, the unit of current, honors the French physicist André-Marie Ampère. The ohm, the unit of resistance, is named for the German physicist Georg Ohm. Watt, for the Scottish engineer James Watt, is the unit of power, and the joule, for James Joule, a brewer's son in England, is the unit of energy.
The newton, the unit of force, honors Isaac Newton, and the hertz, a unit of frequency, honors Heinrich Hertz, who discovered radio waves. The pascal, for pressure, honors Blaise Pascal, and the tesla, for magnetic fields, honors Nikola Tesla. By convention, the name of the unit is written in lower case, even though it comes from a name, but the symbol is a capital letter. Each is a way of keeping a scientist's name alive.

The word nightmare has nothing to do with a horse. The second part, mare, is an old English word for a kind of evil spirit. In Anglo-Saxon folklore, a mare was a female demon that sat on a sleeper's chest, causing a feeling of suffocation and terror. The belief may be linked to the experience of sleep paralysis.
By the Middle Ages, the word nightmare meant the spirit, and then the bad dream itself. The idea of a horse came later, perhaps because of the sound of the word. In German, the word for nightmare is Albtraum, an elf's dream, and in French, cauchemar, which includes the same root. In many cultures, a spirit was blamed for a frightening dream. The word is a fossil of an ancient belief.

A soldier was originally someone who was paid. The word comes from the Latin solidus, which was a gold coin of the later Roman Empire, introduced by the emperor Constantine in the fourth century. The coin was used to pay troops. The Latin word gave the Old French soudier, a man who fights for pay, and then the English word soldier, in the thirteenth century.
The same coin gave other words. The Italian soldo, the French sou and the Spanish sueldo, meaning salary, come from it. The English word solid, from the same root, means whole, as in a coin of full value. In English, an old abbreviation of pounds, shillings and pence used the letter s for solidus. A soldier was a man who earned his solidi.

A cappuccino is named after a religious order. The Capuchin friars, founded in Italy in the sixteenth century, wore a brown habit with a pointed hood. The Italian word for hood is cappuccio. The friars were called Cappuccini, the little hooded ones, and the order's name came into English as Capuchin.
By the 1700s, the color of the coffee, brown with milk, in Vienna and Italy was said to match the color of the friars' robes. A drink was named kapuziner in Vienna. The modern cappuccino, made with espresso and foamed milk, developed after the espresso machine was invented in the early twentieth century. A type of monkey, the capuchin, was also named for the hood-like crown of hair on its head.

On July 1, 1946, the United States military exploded an atomic bomb at Bikini Atoll, a ring of coral islands in the Pacific. It was part of a series of tests, and the people who lived there had been moved off. Four days later, on July 5, a French designer, Louis Réard, presented a tiny two-piece swimsuit at a fashion show in Paris.
He called it the bikini, hoping that it would cause an explosive reaction, like the bomb. Models were reluctant to wear it, and he had to hire a nude dancer. It was banned in some countries and on some beaches. It became popular in the 1960s. The name of the atoll in the Marshallese language is thought to mean the place of coconuts. The islanders were never able to return to live there in safety.

Two clothing words come from French cities. Jeans comes from Gênes, the French name for Genoa, in Italy. In the sixteenth century, sailors from Genoa wore a sturdy cotton or wool-cotton cloth. The cloth was called jean in English. The word for a pair of trousers made of it became jeans.
Denim comes from de Nîmes, meaning from Nîmes, a town in southern France where a tough cloth, serge de Nîmes, was made. In the 1870s Levi Strauss, a merchant in San Francisco, and a tailor, Jacob Davis, patented the use of metal rivets to strengthen the pockets of work trousers. Jeans have since become the world's most popular clothing. Two words that began as place names are on millions of people.

A tuxedo is a man's formal dinner jacket, usually black. The name comes from a place, Tuxedo Park, a private community for the rich in New York State, about forty miles from New York City. It was founded in 1885 by Pierre Lorillard IV, a tobacco heir. The name of the area itself came from a Native American word, probably from the Lenape language.
The story goes that in 1886, at the park's fall ball, a young man appeared in a short dinner jacket, without tails, which was an English style. Others copied it, and the jacket was named for the place. It became standard formal wear in the United States. In Britain, it's called a dinner jacket. The Lenape name probably means place of the bear, or crooked river, in some accounts.

Mayday is the international call for help in an emergency, by radio. It was created in 1923 by Frederick Stanley Mockford, a senior radio officer at Croydon Airport near London. He was asked to find a word that would be understood by pilots and ground staff in both English and French. Much of the traffic was between London and Paris.
He proposed mayday, from the French m'aider, an abbreviation of venez m'aider, meaning come and help me. The word is spoken three times in a row, to avoid mistakes. It was adopted by international agreement in 1927. It has nothing to do with the spring festival. The distress signal in Morse code, SOS, is a pattern of three dots, three dashes and three dots, and doesn't stand for any words, though some people say it means save our ship.

Both karaoke and karate begin with the Japanese word kara, meaning empty. Karate is made of kara and te, hand, and it means empty hand, a style of fighting that uses no weapons. The name was adopted in Okinawa in the early twentieth century. Before that, the art was known by another word, which meant China hand, because of its origins.
Karaoke is made of kara and oke, a shortening of the Japanese word for orchestra, okesutora. It means empty orchestra, a recording of music without a singer. It is usually said that karaoke was invented in Japan in the early 1970s, by a musician named Daisuke Inoue, who made a machine that played recorded accompaniment for people to sing along. He never patented it. Karaoke has become popular all over the world.

The word tsunami is Japanese. It's made up of tsu, meaning harbor, and nami, meaning wave. A harbor wave. Fishermen coming back from the sea would find their harbor destroyed, though they had not noticed any large wave on the open ocean. The reason is that a tsunami, in deep water, is long and low, a swell perhaps a few feet high, but moving as fast as a jet plane. As it reaches shallow water, it slows, and rises.
In English, such waves used to be called tidal waves, though they have nothing to do with the tides. The word tsunami was adopted by scientists, and became widely known after the Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004. It's now the standard word. Japan has the longest written record of these waves, which goes back more than a thousand years.

When Christopher Columbus landed in the Caribbean in 1492, the people he first met were the Taíno, who spoke an Arawakan language. It was the first language of the New World that Europeans met, and a number of its words entered Spanish and then English. The list includes hurricane, from huracán, the name of a god of storms. It includes canoe, hammock, barbecue and tobacco.
The word barbecue comes from barbacoa, a wooden frame that was used for cooking, and for sleeping. Potato may come from batata, the Taíno name for the sweet potato. Savannah, maybe, and iguana, are also thought to be Taíno. The Taíno population declined catastrophically within decades of the arrival of the Spaniards, from disease and violence. The words they gave are among the few things of their language that survive.

Nahuatl was the language of the Aztecs, and it's still spoken by about a million and a half people in Mexico. When the Spanish arrived in the sixteenth century, they took many words from it, and some of them traveled into English. Tomato comes from the Nahuatl tomatl. Chocolate is thought to come from xocolatl, which may mean bitter water, though its origin is debated. Avocado comes from ahuacatl.
The word ahuacatl also meant testicle, probably because of the shape of the fruit, and the pairs that hang together on a tree. The Spanish changed it to aguacate, and the English changed it to avocado, which sounded like the word for lawyer, abogado. Other Nahuatl words are chili, coyote, tamale and guacamole, which is made of the words for avocado and sauce. The foods came to the world with their names.

The word safari is Swahili, and it means a journey. It comes from the Arabic safar, which also means travel. In East Africa, it was used for the long caravans of traders who traveled from the coast to the interior. The word came into English in the late nineteenth century, through accounts of hunting trips by British explorers, such as Richard Burton.
Hunting safaris were popular with wealthy Europeans and Americans, among them Theodore Roosevelt, who went to Africa in 1909, with his son, and shot about five hundred animals. Today, most safaris use cameras instead of guns. Safari has also come to mean any kind of long trip to see wild animals, and in computing, the name of a web browser. A word for a trade journey became a word for tourism.

The British ruled much of India for about two centuries, and as a result, English has borrowed many words from Hindi and other languages of the subcontinent. Shampoo comes from the Hindi chāmpo, from a verb meaning to press or knead, a kind of massage with oils. Bungalow comes from bangla, meaning of Bengal, a type of low house. Pajamas comes from a Persian-Hindi word meaning leg garment.
Jungle comes from jangal, meaning wild or uncultivated land. Loot comes from lūṭ, meaning plunder. Thug is from thag, a swindler, or a member of a gang of robbers. Many other words, such as veranda, cot, dungarees and juggernaut, have also come into the language. A famous dictionary of such words, Hobson-Jobson, published in 1886, is named for an English version of the cry of Muslim mourners, Ya Hasan, Ya Husain.

The International Space Station is the largest object ever put into space. Its first module was launched in 1998, and since November 2000, it has been continuously occupied, with astronauts from many countries taking turns. It's about the size of a football field, and orbits about four hundred kilometers above the Earth, at around twenty-eight thousand kilometers an hour.
At that speed, it circles the planet about sixteen times a day. The astronauts see sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets every twenty-four hours. They live in free fall, so they float, and they must exercise for about two hours a day to keep their muscles and bones from weakening. The station was built by five space agencies, from the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. It's often cited as an example of international cooperation.

The first wheeled vehicle to drive on Mars was Sojourner, a rover about the size of a microwave oven, which landed in 1997. It traveled about a hundred meters. In 2004 two bigger rovers, Spirit and Opportunity, landed on opposite sides of the planet. They were designed to last ninety days. Opportunity kept going for nearly fourteen years, until a dust storm silenced it in 2018.
Curiosity, a rover the size of a car, landed in 2012, and found that Mars once had conditions that could have supported microbes. Perseverance arrived in 2021 with a small helicopter, Ingenuity. On April 19, 2021, Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet, lasting about forty seconds. It went on to make dozens more. The rovers have shown that Mars was once warmer and wetter.

Venus is nearly the same size as Earth, and for a time, people imagined that it might be a tropical world. The truth is closer to hell. Its thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, and the surface is hot enough to melt lead, about four hundred and sixty-five degrees Celsius. The air pressure is about ninety times that on Earth. The clouds are made of sulfuric acid.
On December 15, 1970, the Soviet probe Venera 7 became the first spacecraft to land on another planet and send back data. It survived on the surface for about twenty-three minutes. Later Venera landers took photographs of the rocky ground. None lasted for more than about two hours. Venus is a warning of what can happen to a planet's climate. It's also being studied for clues to the fate of Earth.

On November 3, 1957, a month after Sputnik, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2. It carried a dog, a small stray from the streets of Moscow, named Laika, which means barker. She was the first animal to orbit the Earth. The aim was to show that a living creature could survive in space, before sending a human.
The Soviets said at first that she had lived for several days. In 2002, it was revealed that she died within hours, from overheating and stress. There was no plan for her return. The mission raised protests from animal lovers around the world. Later animal passengers, such as dogs Belka and Strelka in 1960, did return safely. A monument to Laika was put up in Moscow in 2008.

Valentina Tereshkova was born in 1937 in a village in Russia. She worked in a textile factory, and was a keen amateur parachutist. In 1962 she was selected, with four other women, from several hundred applicants to train as a cosmonaut. Her parachuting skill was valued, since cosmonauts landed by ejecting from their capsule and parachuting down.
On June 16, 1963, she launched in Vostok 6, and spent almost three days in space, orbiting the Earth forty-eight times. She became the first woman in space. The next woman did not fly until 1982, nearly twenty years later. The first American woman, Sally Ride, flew in 1983. Tereshkova later entered politics, and she remains a national figure in Russia. She has said that she would still like to fly to Mars.

On March 18, 1965, the Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov left his spacecraft, Voskhod 2, and floated into space on a tether. It was the first spacewalk in history. For about twelve minutes, he drifted over the Earth, and he was amazed by the view. Then he found he had a problem. In the vacuum, his spacesuit had inflated like a balloon, and he couldn't bend his arms and legs to get back into the airlock.
He had to open a valve and let out some of the air in the suit, which was dangerous, since it might lead to a condition like the bends. He finally got in, head first, instead of feet first as planned. Then the spacecraft landed far off course, in a snowy forest in the Urals. The crew spent a night there, among wolves, before being rescued. Details were kept secret for years.

In December 1968 Apollo 8 became the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth orbit, and the first to go around the Moon. Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and Bill Anders were looking at the gray, barren lunar surface, when, on their fourth orbit, the Earth rose above the horizon. Anders grabbed a camera and took a photograph in color.
The picture, known as Earthrise, shows a blue and white globe, small and fragile, above a stark landscape. It's one of the most famous photographs ever taken. The nature photographer Galen Rowell called it the most influential environmental photograph. It helped to inspire the first Earth Day in 1970. On Christmas Eve, the astronauts read from the Book of Genesis in a broadcast watched by perhaps a billion people.

Many astronauts have described a deep change in perspective, on seeing the Earth from space. The Earth looks tiny, without borders, and very fragile. The atmosphere, which seems so vast from the ground, is a thin blue line. Many have said that they felt a sense of awe, and a greater connection to all humanity. The astronaut Edgar Mitchell, of Apollo 14, called it an instant global consciousness.
In 1987 the writer Frank White gave this experience a name, the overview effect, after interviewing astronauts. Studies of astronauts' accounts suggest that many have come back with a stronger concern for the environment. Some researchers are looking for ways of producing something like it on Earth, using virtual reality, or the experience of awe. It's a reminder of how our view of the world depends on where we stand.

In December 1995 the astronomer Robert Williams, who was then the director of the Space Telescope Science Institute, made an unusual decision. He used a part of his own time on the Hubble Space Telescope for a risky experiment. He pointed the telescope at a tiny, dark and apparently empty patch of sky, near the Big Dipper. It was about the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length.
For ten days, the telescope took hundreds of exposures of this patch. When they were combined, the image revealed about three thousand galaxies, of many shapes and sizes, some of them among the most distant ever seen. In what looked like nothing, there was a universe. A later Hubble Ultra Deep Field showed about ten thousand. They imply that there are hundreds of billions of galaxies in the observable universe.

New Horizons was launched in January 2006. It was the fastest spacecraft ever launched at that time, and it took more than nine years to reach Pluto, which is about three billion miles from the Sun. On July 14, 2015, it flew past Pluto at about thirty thousand miles an hour, and took the first close-up pictures. The signals took four and a half hours to reach Earth.
Pluto turned out to be a surprising world. It has mountains of water ice as high as the Rocky Mountains, and a large, smooth, heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice, named Tombaugh Regio, after the discoverer of Pluto. There are signs of glaciers, and a haze of blue in the thin atmosphere. A world that was thought to be a dead ball of ice was geologically active. New Horizons has since continued out into the Kuiper Belt.

Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, is the only moon in the solar system with a thick atmosphere. It's hidden by an orange haze, and for centuries, no one knew what lay below. In 1997 the Cassini spacecraft was launched toward Saturn, carrying a small probe, Huygens, built by the European Space Agency. After a seven-year journey, Huygens separated, and on January 14, 2005, it parachuted into Titan's atmosphere.
It took about two and a half hours to fall, and then it landed on a surface of damp, sandy ground, with pebbles of ice. It sent data for about ninety minutes. The pictures showed channels cut by liquid, and a shoreline. Titan has lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane, with a rainfall of methane. It is the only place other than Earth with liquid on its surface. It's the farthest landing ever made.

In 2004 the European Space Agency launched Rosetta, a spacecraft that was to catch up with a comet. It took ten years, and four flybys of planets, to get to Comet 67P, also called Churyumov-Gerasimenko, which is about four kilometers across and shaped like a rubber duck. In November 2014, Rosetta released a small lander, Philae, to the surface.
The landing didn't go as planned. Harpoons that were supposed to anchor the lander failed, and it bounced twice, and came to rest on its side in the shadow of a cliff, where its solar panels got little light. It worked for about sixty hours on battery power, and sent back data, including the first sniff of organic molecules on a comet. In 2015 it woke up briefly. Rosetta was deliberately crashed onto the comet in 2016.
Seven worlds around a small star

In February 2017 astronomers announced that a small, cool star, TRAPPIST-1, about forty light-years away, has seven planets about the size of Earth. The star is much smaller and dimmer than the Sun, about the size of Jupiter. The planets orbit it very closely, all closer than Mercury is to the Sun. The year on the nearest takes only a day and a half.
Three of the planets lie in the habitable zone, where water could be liquid. They are so close together that, from the surface of one, the others would look as big as the Moon does to us. It's not known whether any has an atmosphere, or water. The James Webb Space Telescope is being used to look for them. TRAPPIST-1 is an example of how common small planets are around the commonest kind of star.
A message on a golden record

When the two Voyager spacecraft were launched in 1977, each carried a gold-plated copper disk, designed to be played like a record. A committee headed by Carl Sagan chose its contents. It was meant to give a picture of life on Earth to any extraterrestrial finder. The disk holds one hundred and fifteen images, greetings in fifty-five languages, sounds of nature, and ninety minutes of music.
The sounds include the songs of whales, thunder, a kiss and the sound of a mother's first words to her baby. The music includes Bach, Beethoven, a Peruvian panpipe song, and Chuck Berry's Johnny B. Goode. The record also had instructions for how to play it, and a map showing the position of the Sun, using pulsars. It may last for a billion years. Sagan said that it was a bottle in the cosmic ocean.

On November 16, 1974, the astronomers Frank Drake and Carl Sagan used the huge radio telescope at Arecibo, in Puerto Rico, to send a message into space. It lasted less than three minutes. It was a string of 1,679 binary digits, zeros and ones, which can be arranged in a grid of 73 rows by 23 columns, to make a picture.
The picture showed the numbers one to ten, the atomic numbers of the elements that make up DNA, a diagram of a human figure, the Solar System, and the telescope itself. It was aimed at a cluster of stars, called M13, about twenty-five thousand light-years away. It will take that long to arrive, so we can expect no reply for fifty thousand years. It was mainly a demonstration of the telescope's power. Some scientists have worried about the wisdom of announcing ourselves.

On August 15, 1977, a radio telescope at Ohio State University, called Big Ear, was scanning the sky for signals from intelligent life. A volunteer, Jerry Ehman, was looking over the printouts of the data a few days later. He saw a series of letters and numbers, 6EQUJ5, which showed a signal that was far stronger than the background. He circled it, and wrote Wow! in the margin.
The signal lasted for seventy-two seconds, the time it took for the telescope to scan across that spot in the sky, and it came from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. It was at a frequency of the hydrogen line, which some had suggested for communication. It was never heard again, despite many searches. Its origin is unknown. Possible explanations include a comet, or a natural source. It's the best candidate that we have for a message from space, and no one can say what it was.

Since Sputnik in 1957, thousands of satellites have been launched. Many are no longer working. They've joined spent rocket stages and fragments from explosions and collisions, in orbit around the Earth. Tens of thousands of objects larger than a softball are tracked by radar, and there are millions of smaller pieces, such as flecks of paint. At orbital speed, even a speck can damage a spacecraft.
In 1978 Donald Kessler, a NASA scientist, warned of a danger. If there are enough objects in orbit, collisions will produce more debris, which would cause more collisions, in a chain reaction. This is called the Kessler syndrome. A collision between two satellites in 2009 created thousands of fragments. The International Space Station has made emergency maneuvers to avoid debris. Cleaning up is hard, and is being studied.

Large asteroids have hit the Earth before, and will again. The question is whether we can do anything about it. In September 2022 NASA tested one method.
