The Double Asteroid Redirection Test, DART, sent a spacecraft the size of a vending machine to crash into a small asteroid called Dimorphos. Dimorphos is a moonlet, about the size of a stadium, that orbits a larger asteroid, Didymos. Neither poses a threat to Earth.
The impact was on September 26, 2022, at about fourteen thousand miles an hour. It was watched by telescopes on Earth. Afterward, astronomers found that Dimorphos's orbit around its partner had been shortened by about thirty-two minutes, much more than the minimum for success. It was the first time that humans had changed the motion of a celestial body. It showed that, with enough warning, we could nudge an asteroid away.

In 1948 B. F. Skinner put hungry pigeons in a box. A feeder dropped a little food every fifteen seconds, regardless of what the birds did. There was nothing that the pigeons could do to get the food. Skinner expected them to ignore it. Instead, most of the birds developed a habit of their own. One turned counterclockwise in the cage. Another thrust its head into a corner. A third swung its head back and forth like a pendulum.
Skinner's explanation was that whatever the bird happened to be doing when the food arrived was accidentally rewarded, so it did it more, and so was more likely to be doing it when the next food came. He called it superstition. People have similar habits, such as wearing lucky socks. Later researchers offered other explanations, but the experiment is a vivid example of how we may see a link between our action and an outcome that isn't there.
The sickness that taught a rat

In the 1950s John Garcia noticed that rats exposed to radiation, which made them sick, later avoided the plastic water bottles that they had used in the chamber. It seemed to contradict the standard theory of conditioning, which said that learning needed the cause and the effect to come close together in time. The nausea came hours after the drinking.
In 1966 Garcia and Robert Koelling tested it. Rats drank flavored water, or water with lights and clicks. Then some were given a shock to the feet, and others were made sick. The rats that were made sick learned to avoid the taste, but not the lights and clicks. The rats that were shocked learned to avoid the lights and clicks, but not the taste. Animals are prepared to link nausea with food. It's why one bad meal can put you off a food for life.
The chimpanzee who saw the answer

During the First World War, the German psychologist Wolfgang Köhler was stuck on the island of Tenerife, in the Canary Islands, where he ran a research station for apes. He gave problems to chimpanzees. A banana was hung from the ceiling, out of reach, and boxes were scattered about the room. A chimpanzee named Sultan, after trying to jump, sat for a while, and then suddenly got up, stacked the boxes and climbed up to get the fruit.
Köhler said that the animal had insight. He didn't solve the problem by trial and error, but by seeing the relationship between the objects, and the goal, all at once. Sultan also joined two sticks together to make a pole long enough to reach a banana outside the cage. The work challenged the view that animals learn only through blind trial and error. The word aha has been used for such moments of insight ever since.
The cat in the puzzle box

In 1898 the American psychologist Edward Thorndike, then a graduate student, put hungry cats in boxes with a latch. To get out, and to reach a piece of fish outside, the cat had to pull a string or press a lever. At first, they scratched and clawed, and by accident, hit the right device. Each time, he timed how long it took them to escape.
Over repeated trials, the times fell, slowly and gradually, without any sudden jump. Thorndike concluded that the cats were not reasoning. They were learning to repeat the behavior that led to a good result. He called it the law of effect. Actions that are followed by satisfying consequences become more likely, and ones followed by discomfort become less likely. The idea was the basis of Skinner's later work on operant conditioning.
The goslings that followed a man

In the 1930s the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz divided a clutch of goose eggs. One half hatched with their mother. The other half were put in an incubator, and he was the first thing they saw when they hatched. The goslings followed him around, as they would have followed their mother, and they ignored real geese. They would line up behind him, and even swim after him.
Lorenz called this imprinting. It occurs in a short sensitive period soon after birth, and seems to be irreversible. The young animal learns who is its parent, and also, later, what species to mate with. He shared the Nobel Prize in 1973. Later work showed that imprinting is more flexible than he thought. The research has influenced the study of human attachment, though human babies are far less rigid.

In the 1950s Donald Broadbent, a British psychologist, was working on a practical problem. Air traffic controllers and pilots had to listen to several messages at once, and he wanted to understand why they missed things. He tested people by playing different digits to each ear at the same time, and asking them what they heard.
People could repeat all the digits from one ear and then the other, but not mix them. Broadbent proposed that attention works like a filter. Many sensory signals reach the brain, but only one channel is let through for deeper processing, chosen by physical features such as the ear it comes from. The others are blocked. The model was soon found to be too simple, but it opened the study of attention.

Broadbent had proposed that unattended messages are blocked. In 1960 Anne Treisman tested it by a method called shadowing. People wore headphones, and heard a different message in each ear. They were told to repeat aloud the message in one ear, and ignore the other. In one experiment, a story switched ears in the middle of a sentence.
Some people followed the meaning of the story to the wrong ear, for a word or two, though they were meant to ignore it. So the unattended message was not completely blocked. Treisman proposed that the filter works like a volume control. It turns down the unattended channel, but doesn't switch it off. Important words, such as your own name, can get through. It's a model that explains the cocktail party effect.
The memory that vanishes in a second

In 1960 George Sperling, a graduate student, flashed a grid of twelve letters, in three rows of four, on a screen for a twentieth of a second. When he asked people to recall as many as they could, they could say only about four or five. Yet they insisted that they had seen all of them, and that the letters faded as they tried to name them.
He then used a trick. After the grid disappeared, he played a tone, high, middle or low, to signal which row to report. People could then report nearly all four letters in the row, whichever was asked. So they must have had all twelve letters available in memory, for a moment. The memory faded within about a second. Sperling called it iconic memory. It's a brief visual store that precedes attention.

In 1959 Lloyd Peterson and Margaret Peterson, at Indiana University, tested how long a small amount of information stays in memory without being repeated. People were given a three-letter nonsense syllable, such as CHJ. Then they were asked to count backward by threes from a number, to stop them rehearsing it. After a delay, they were asked to recall the syllable.
After three seconds, they remembered about eighty percent. After eighteen seconds, they remembered only about ten percent. It seemed that information in short-term memory is lost in about twenty seconds, if it isn't rehearsed. Later work suggested that it was not simply decay but interference from the counting. The study led to the idea of short-term memory as a limited store, and showed why we have to repeat a phone number to ourselves.

In 1978 Richard Anderson and James Pichert had students read a story about two boys who skip school and go to the home of one of them. The house is described in detail, with its features, such as a fireplace, a new color television, a leaky roof and a damp basement. Some of the students were told to read it as a prospective home buyer, and others as a burglar.
Later, they were asked to recall the story. The ones who read as home buyers remembered the details that would matter to a buyer, such as the leaky roof. The burglars remembered details such as the television. Then, the researchers asked each of them to switch to the other viewpoint, and recall again. They came up with new details that they hadn't mentioned before. What we remember depends on the perspective we took when we read.
The paragraph that made no sense

In 1972 John Bransford and Marcia Johnson gave people a short passage that described a procedure in dull, general terms. It said that you should first arrange things into different groups, that one pile might be enough if there isn't much to do, and that you may have to go somewhere else if you lack the facilities. It never said what the things were. They asked people to recall it later.
People did poorly, and rated it as hard to understand. But another group was told that the title was Washing Clothes. These people understood it, and remembered about twice as much. Once you know the context, every sentence makes sense. The study showed that comprehension depends on having a framework. It's also a good reason to give the big picture before details, when you teach.
The words that changed a drawing

In 1932 Leonard Carmichael and his colleagues showed people ambiguous line drawings, and read a word to describe each one. One group heard one label, and another group heard a different label for the same figure. For example, a shape like two circles joined by a line was called eyeglasses by one group, and dumbbells by the other. Afterward, they were asked to redraw them from memory.
Their drawings tended to be distorted toward the label. The ones who heard eyeglasses drew something more like glasses, and the ones who heard dumbbells drew something more like weights. The experiment suggests that memory is altered by the words that we use. It was an early demonstration of how language can shape what we recall. Later work has found that the effect is real, though it may be smaller than the original suggested.

In 1981 William Brewer and Janet Treyens asked students to wait for about thirty-five seconds in a room that they were told was the experimenter's office, before the experiment began. It was a normal graduate student's office, with a desk, a typewriter, a coffee pot and shelves. But it had no books. Then they were taken to another room, and asked to write down everything that they could remember.
Almost a third of them recalled books, though there were none. They remembered the desk and the chair, which fit with their idea of an office. They were less likely to recall odd items, such as a skull, or a piece of wood. The mind seems to fill gaps with what it expects to see. It's an example of a schema, a mental framework that guides perception and memory, and sometimes leads to errors.

In 1962 Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer injected volunteers with adrenaline, which raises the heart rate and makes the hands tremble. Some were told what to expect. Others were told nothing. Then each was placed in a room with a confederate, who behaved either in a joyful, silly manner or in an angry one. The researchers observed how the volunteers acted, and asked how they felt.
Those who didn't know why their bodies were aroused were more influenced by the confederate, and tended to take on the mood. The authors concluded that emotion has two parts, a physical arousal and a mental label based on the situation. It was one of the best-known studies in psychology. But it has been criticized, and attempts to repeat it have failed to find the pattern. The theory is probably too simple. But the idea that context shapes how we read our own feelings has held up.

In April 1938 a young chemist at DuPont, Roy Plunkett, was working on refrigerants. He had a cylinder of a gas, tetrafluoroethylene, and when he opened the valve, nothing came out. The cylinder was not empty. It weighed as much as before. Puzzled, he cut the cylinder open, and found a white, waxy powder inside. The gas had polymerized on its own.
The powder was extremely slippery, and it was not harmed by acids, heat or solvents. It was named Teflon. Its first big use was in the Manhattan Project, where it lined pipes that carried corrosive gases. Only later, in the 1950s, was it used for frying pans, after a French engineer, Marc Grégoire, applied it to his fishing tackle, and his wife suggested using it on her pans. A failure in the lab gave us the nonstick pan.
The candy bar and the microwave

Percy Spencer was an engineer at the American company Raytheon, working on magnetrons, the tubes that produce microwaves for radar. He had only a primary school education, but became one of the best engineers of his time. One day around 1945, as he stood near a magnetron, he noticed that a candy bar in his pocket had melted.
He was curious. He tried popcorn kernels, which popped, and then an egg, which exploded in the face of a colleague. Raytheon patented a microwave cooking device, and in 1947 sold the first Radarange. It was nearly six feet tall, weighed about seven hundred pounds, and cost thousands of dollars. Smaller ones, for homes, came out in the late 1960s. Today, more than ninety percent of American homes have one.

In 1941 a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral went for a walk in the Alps with his dog. When he got home, he found that the dog's fur, and his own trousers, were covered with burrs, the seed pods of the burdock plant. He was curious about how they stuck so firmly, and looked at one under a microscope.
He saw that each burr was covered in tiny hooks, which caught on loops in the fabric. It took him almost fifteen years to develop a way of making a fastener that used the same principle, with one strip of tiny hooks, and one of tiny loops. He patented it in 1955, and called it Velcro, from the French velours, velvet, and crochet, hook. It was used in space suits, in shoes and in many other places. It's a famous example of nature giving an idea to engineers.
A weak glue and a hymnbook

In 1968 Spencer Silver, a chemist at 3M, was trying to make a very strong adhesive. He failed. He made a glue that was weak. It stuck to things, but could be peeled off without leaving a mark, and be used again. He thought it was interesting, but no one could think of a use for it. He promoted it inside the company for years.
In 1974 another 3M employee, Art Fry, who sang in a church choir, was annoyed that the slips of paper that he used as bookmarks in his hymnbook kept falling out. He remembered Silver's glue, and put a little on the paper. The notes stayed put, and could be removed without damage. They were launched as Post-it Notes in 1980. Silver's glue had been a solution in search of a problem, until Fry found one.

In 1903 a French chemist, Édouard Bénédictus, was in his laboratory, when he knocked a glass flask off a shelf. It fell to the floor and cracked, but didn't shatter. It stayed in the shape of a flask, with the pieces held together. He asked his assistant what had been in it. It had held a solution of cellulose nitrate, a plastic, which had dried to form a thin coating on the inside.
Bénédictus thought of the injuries from broken windshields, and he realized that this could be used to make safety glass. He patented a laminated glass, with a layer of plastic between two sheets of glass, in 1909. It was first used in gas masks in the First World War. It was adopted in cars in the 1920s, and is now required in windshields. A clumsy moment helped to save many lives.

Natural rubber was a disappointment. In heat, it became soft and sticky, and in cold, it grew brittle. Many people tried to make it more useful. Charles Goodyear, an American inventor who was repeatedly in debt, and went to jail more than once for unpaid bills, devoted years to experiments.
In 1839, according to his own account, he accidentally dropped a mixture of rubber and sulfur on a hot stove. It charred, like leather, but stayed flexible. He found the right temperature and time for heating, a process that is now called vulcanization, after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire. It made rubber durable and elastic. It led to tires, hoses, belts and shoe soles. Goodyear never became rich. He died deep in debt in 1860.
The sweet taste on his hands

In 1879 Constantin Fahlberg, a Russian chemist who worked in the laboratory of Ira Remsen at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, was studying coal tar compounds. One evening, he sat down to dinner and noticed that the bread tasted unusually sweet. He realized that it was his hands. He had not washed them properly after the day's work.
He went back to the laboratory, and tasted what was in his beakers, which was not wise, and found the sweet one. It was saccharin, the first artificial sweetener, about three hundred times sweeter than sugar. Fahlberg patented it, and made a fortune, without giving credit to Remsen, which angered him. It came into wide use during sugar shortages in the First World War. Questions about its safety were raised for years, and it's now regarded as safe.

In 1943 Richard James, a naval engineer in Philadelphia, was working on a spring for ships, to keep sensitive instruments steady in rough seas. One of the springs fell off a shelf, and rather than lying where it landed, it flipped over end after end, and walked down to the floor. He took it home to show his wife, Betty, who said that children would like it.
She found a name in the dictionary, Slinky, meaning sleek and graceful. They borrowed about five hundred dollars to make four hundred. In November 1945, at a department store in Philadelphia, Gimbels, the display was a slope with a Slinky walking down it. They sold all the Slinkies in ninety minutes. It has since sold hundreds of millions. It's a toy that was invented by chance, and with the price kept low for many years.

Play-Doh began as a product for cleaning coal soot from wallpaper. In the 1930s the Cincinnati company Kutol Products made a soft, putty-like compound that was rolled over the walls. It worked well when homes were heated by coal. But after the Second World War, when oil and gas replaced coal, sales fell.
In the early 1950s a nursery school teacher, who was the sister-in-law of the company's owner, found that children liked to model with the wallpaper cleaner. A nontoxic version was developed, with colors added. It was marketed in 1956, as Play-Doh. Within a few years, it was a huge success, and it's sold billions of cans. The product is a case of finding a new use for something that no longer worked in its old one.

In the late nineteenth century, a bakery in Bridgeport, Connecticut, the Frisbie Pie Company, sold pies in round metal tins, stamped with the name Frisbie. College students in New England had a habit of throwing the empty tins to each other, shouting frisbie as a warning. After the Second World War, a Californian, Walter Frederick Morrison, made a plastic version, based on a flying disc that he and his future wife had tossed on a beach.
He sold the disc under the name Pluto Platter, after the interest in flying saucers. In 1957 the toy company Wham-O bought the rights, and changed the name to Frisbee, which alluded to the tins. It has sold in the hundreds of millions, and gave rise to sports such as ultimate and disc golf. The name came from a pie.

The earliest surviving photograph was taken by a French inventor, Nicéphore Niépce, in about 1826 or 1827, from an upstairs window of his estate at Le Gras. He used a pewter plate coated with bitumen, a type of asphalt, which hardens in light, and exposed it in a camera for many hours, perhaps eight or more. The image, called View from the Window at Le Gras, shows rooftops, in a blurry way.
Niépce teamed up with Louis Daguerre, a painter and showman. Niépce died in 1833, and Daguerre developed a faster, clearer process, using a silvered copper plate. He announced the daguerreotype in 1839, and the French government bought the rights, and gave them to the world. Exposure times fell to a few minutes. The first photo of a person, probably by accident, shows a man having his boots shined on a Paris street, in 1838.

Spectacles were probably invented in Italy around 1286. Nobody knows who the inventor was. A monk in Pisa wrote in 1306 that they had been invented about twenty years before, and that he'd met the man who invented them. They were convex lenses, to help old people to read, and they spread quickly across Europe.
The telescope came more than three hundred years later. In 1608 a Dutch spectacle maker, Hans Lipperhey, applied for a patent on a device that made distant objects seem near. The authorities refused, because other people claimed the same idea. Galileo heard of it in 1609, built his own, and turned it on the sky. He saw the mountains of the Moon, the moons of Jupiter, and the phases of Venus. A device meant for ships and soldiers changed astronomy.

Before 1937, shoppers carried baskets. In that year, Sylvan Goldman, who owned a chain of grocery stores in Oklahoma City, noticed that customers stopped buying when their baskets got heavy. He looked at a folding chair, and had an idea. He asked a mechanic to attach wheels to the legs and a wire basket to the seat. The first carts were made.
Shoppers didn't want to use them. Men thought them unmanly, and women thought them like a baby carriage. Goldman hired people, models, to push the carts around the store, to demonstrate that it was normal. It worked. Sales rose, since people bought more. Carts spread, and Goldman became a millionaire. In the 1940s, a design that nested was introduced, so that carts could be stored in a smaller space.
The pen that won the war

László Bíró was a Hungarian journalist. He was annoyed by fountain pens, which leaked, and smudged. At a newspaper printing plant, he saw that the ink used for printing dried quickly. He thought it might work in a pen, but it was too thick to flow. His brother, a chemist, helped him to make a pen with a small ball at the tip, which picked up thick ink from a reservoir and rolled it onto the paper. They patented it in 1938.
Bíró fled the Nazis, and moved to Argentina in 1940. The British Royal Air Force bought thousands of his pens during the war, since they worked at high altitudes where fountain pens leaked. Later the French Baron Bich simplified the manufacture. His company, Bic, sold the pen at a very low price. The ballpoint is still the best-selling pen. Bíró's birthday, September 29, is the Day of the Inventor in Argentina.

Philo Farnsworth was a farm boy from Idaho. At the age of fourteen, plowing a field, he realized that an image could be captured in horizontal lines, like the rows of a plowed field, and be sent as an electronic signal. He explained it to his chemistry teacher, who kept his sketch. At twenty-one, in a laboratory in San Francisco, he succeeded. On September 7, 1927, he sent an electronic image of a straight line.
A struggle over patents followed with a large company, RCA. The teacher's sketch, which he produced, helped Farnsworth to win. By the time that television became popular after the Second World War, his patents had nearly run out, and he gained little. In his later years, he turned to nuclear fusion. He appeared once on television, on a game show, in 1957. The mechanical television of John Logie Baird, in Britain, came first, in 1926, but the electronic form won.
Was QWERTY made to slow typists?

The keyboard layout used on most computers, called QWERTY after the first six letters on the top row, is awkward. Common letters are placed far from the strongest fingers. A popular story says that it was designed on purpose to slow down typists, so that the mechanical typewriter wouldn't jam. The story was widely repeated, and used as an example of how a poor standard can lock itself in.
Historians now doubt it. The typewriter was invented by Christopher Latham Sholes, in Milwaukee, in the 1860s. The layout evolved over several years, and there's evidence that it was shaped by the needs of telegraph operators, who transcribed messages. It was sold by Remington in 1873. Rival layouts, such as Dvorak, have not been shown to be much faster. The truth is still debated, but the neat story may be too neat.

The idea that a person should sleep for eight hours in a row may be recent. In 2001 the historian Roger Ekirch published a study of hundreds of references, in diaries, court records and literature, from the Middle Ages up to the early modern period. They mention first sleep and second sleep. People went to bed soon after dusk, slept for a few hours, woke around midnight, and stayed awake for an hour or two, before sleeping again until dawn.
In the interval, they might pray, talk, make love, or visit neighbors. In 1992 the psychiatrist Thomas Wehr tested whether this is natural. He kept volunteers in darkness for fourteen hours a night, for a month. After a few weeks, their sleep settled into two parts, with a quiet, wakeful period in between. It suggests that waking in the night may not always be a disorder. Many people worry about it more than is needed.

Parents of teenagers often complain that they won't go to bed, and then can't get up. It's not just laziness. In the 1990s Mary Carskadon at Brown University found that the body clocks of adolescents shift later at puberty. Their brains release melatonin, the hormone that signals night, later than those of younger children. They feel sleepy later, and wake later.
At the same time, they still need about eight to ten hours of sleep. Early school start times, such as seven thirty, clash with the biology. A teenager who wakes at six may be, in biological terms, in the middle of the night. Studies of schools that moved the start time later found that students slept more, were less depressed, and had fewer car accidents. The pattern is found in many mammals. It reverses in the early twenties.

Some people are at their best in the morning, and others in the evening. In the 1970s the psychologists Jim Horne and Olov Östberg created a questionnaire to measure it. The tendency is called chronotype. People are sometimes called larks, if they like the morning, and owls, if they like the night. In 2007 Till Roenneberg and his colleagues collected data on the sleep habits of more than fifty thousand people in Europe.
They found that chronotypes are spread across a continuous range, not in two groups. Most people are somewhere in the middle. Genes explain a part of the difference, and so does age. It also varies with light exposure. Those who live in cities, with artificial light, tend to be later. A mismatch between a person's body clock and the working day is called social jet lag, and it's associated with poorer health. Forcing an owl to act like a lark is difficult.
What a short sleeper's gene does

A very few people get along with only four to six hours of sleep, without feeling tired, and without any apparent harm. They are called natural short sleepers. In 2009 Ying-Hui Fu and Louis Ptáček, at the University of California, San Francisco, studied a family in which a mother and daughter slept about six hours a night, much less than the usual eight. They found a mutation in a gene called DEC2.
When the researchers put the mutation into mice, the mice also slept less. In 2019 the same team found a mutation in another gene, ADRB1, in another family of short sleepers. People with such mutations are rare. It is not possible to train yourself to be a short sleeper. Most people who say they can manage on five hours are probably running a sleep debt, and don't notice the effects.

Do all animals sleep? In 2000 Paul Shaw and his colleagues showed that fruit flies do. They watched flies in tubes, and found that they had long periods of rest each night, in which they were less responsive to stimuli, and had a typical posture. If the flies were prevented from resting, by shaking the tubes, they rested more afterward, as if they had a sleep debt.
The flies were also affected by caffeine, which kept them awake, and by sleeping pills. The discovery meant that the genes that control sleep could be studied in an animal that is easy to breed and manipulate. Many of the genes that control sleep in flies, such as the clock gene period, also play a role in humans. Sleep is found in animals from jellyfish to humans, which suggests an ancient and essential function.
Dolphins that sleep with half a brain

A dolphin must come to the surface to breathe, and so it can't fall into a deep sleep, as a human can. In the 1970s Lev Mukhametov, a Soviet scientist, recorded the brain waves of bottlenose dolphins. He found that they sleep with one half of the brain at a time. While one hemisphere shows the slow waves of sleep, the other is awake, and the dolphin swims slowly, with one eye open.
This is called unihemispheric sleep. After a while, the two halves switch. Some birds do it too. In 1999 Niels Rattenborg and his colleagues showed that ducks at the edge of a group keep the eye that faces outward open, and the hemisphere of the brain opposite is awake, keeping watch for predators. It's a way of staying alert while resting. Humans have a mild form. In a new place, the left half of the brain sleeps more lightly on the first night.

Many people sleep badly on the first night in a hotel or a new bed. In 2016 Masako Tamaki and her colleagues at Brown University tested why. They monitored the brains of volunteers who spent two nights in the sleep laboratory. On the first night, there was a difference between the two halves of the brain. The left half had more activity in a network of regions, when the deep sleep was at its deepest.
The left hemisphere seemed to stay on watch, and was more responsive to sounds. On the second night, the difference had gone. In another experiment, odd sounds were played to one ear. They woke people more easily on the first night, when played to the right ear, which sends signals to the left half of the brain. It seems that the brain is on guard in a strange place. A familiar pillow, or a second night, helps.

In 2013 Maiken Nedergaard and her colleagues at the University of Rochester published a study that made headlines. They injected a dye into the brains of mice, and watched how it spread. When the mice were awake, the dye moved slowly. When they were asleep, or anesthetized, the dye flowed through the brain much faster. The spaces between the brain cells expanded by about sixty percent during sleep.
The flow allows cerebrospinal fluid to wash through the brain and clear away waste, including a protein called beta-amyloid, which builds up in Alzheimer's disease. Nedergaard called it the glymphatic system, because it depends on glial cells. The idea suggests a reason why we need sleep, and why poor sleep may be linked to dementia. It's still being tested, and some scientists have questioned how strong the effect is in humans.

Many people feel sleepy in the early afternoon, even if they have had a good night's sleep and a light lunch. It's partly a dip in the body clock, which has a small trough in alertness at about two or three in the afternoon, as well as a major one in the middle of the night. It occurs even in people who don't eat lunch. In many cultures, a nap in the afternoon is common, such as the Spanish siesta.
In 2003 Sara Mednick and her colleagues at Harvard tested naps. People learned a visual task in the morning, and then were tested in the afternoon and evening. Those who took a nap of an hour or so, which contained both slow-wave and dream sleep, improved a lot, while those who stayed awake got worse. Short naps of about ten to twenty minutes can boost alertness without grogginess. Long naps can leave you groggy.
The cost of lost sleep for the heart

Sleeping too little is linked to many health problems. In 2011 Francesco Cappuccio and his colleagues combined the results of fifteen studies of sleep and cardiovascular disease, covering more than four hundred thousand people. They found that those who slept less than about six hours a night had a higher risk of heart disease and stroke than those who slept seven or eight.
Those who slept for a very long time, more than nine hours, had a higher risk as well, which may be because illness itself makes people sleep longer. The studies were observational. It's hard to be sure that sleep loss is the cause, and other factors, such as stress and depression, could play a part. But experiments have also shown that cutting sleep raises blood pressure, and increases inflammation. A natural experiment suggests an effect. In the spring, when the clocks go forward, there is a rise in heart attacks.

Yawning is common to almost all vertebrates, and we begin to do it in the womb. Yet no one is sure of its function. The old idea was that it takes in more oxygen, and removes carbon dioxide. But in a famous experiment, Robert Provine found that breathing air that was rich in oxygen, or in carbon dioxide, did not change how much people yawned.
Another idea was proposed by Andrew Gallup and Gordon Gallup in 2007. It's that yawning cools the brain. In their studies, people yawned less when they held a cold pack to the forehead, and more in warm conditions. A yawn draws in cool air, and increases blood flow to the head. The idea is plausible, and it's supported by some animal studies, though others have not repeated the result. It could explain why we yawn when tired, since the brain is warmer. The question is not yet settled.

Smoking is hard to give up, and many programs have low success rates. In 2009 Kevin Volpp and his colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania tried a simple idea, to pay people. They recruited about nine hundred employees of a large company who smoked. All were offered information on quitting, and access to counseling and medicine. Half of them were also offered financial rewards for staying off cigarettes.
Those in the reward group could earn up to seven hundred and fifty dollars, for completing a cessation program, and for being confirmed as non-smokers by a test at six months, and again at nine to twelve months. Six months after the payments ended, about ten percent of them were still not smoking, compared with about four percent of the others. The rate was still low, but more than double. It's often called contingency management, and it's among the most effective ways of helping people to stop.

In 2021 a team of economists in Sweden tested whether a small payment could persuade more people to be vaccinated against COVID-19. They randomly assigned about eight thousand people, who had not yet been vaccinated, to groups. One group was offered about twenty-four dollars, and the others were offered nothing. The payment was offered by letter, and the vaccination was recorded in the national register.
The payment of two hundred Swedish kronor raised the rate of vaccination by about four percentage points. It was a small effect, but cheap, and it worked at a time when others were pushing hard. The researchers argued that incentives could be one tool among others. The study also found that the money did not make people think badly of vaccination, as some had feared. It's a good example of the use of a randomized trial to answer a policy question.

In May 2021 the state of Ohio launched a lottery for people who had been vaccinated against COVID-19. It was called Vax-a-Million, and offered five prizes of a million dollars. Other states copied it, with prizes of cash, scholarships and even a hunting rifle. The idea was that a chance to win a big prize would motivate people who were hesitant.
Researchers tried to find out if it worked. One study, by Allan Walkey and his colleagues, compared Ohio with other states, and found no increase in vaccinations. Another, by Neil Sehgal, found a rise in Ohio. Later work on many states was also mixed, with some showing small effects and some none. Part of the problem is that it's hard to separate the lottery from other trends. The evidence suggests that lotteries are not as effective as hoped.

Cigarette packs in many countries carry warnings. Some use only words, and some also have a photograph, such as of a diseased lung or a rotting tooth. Canada was the first country to require picture warnings, in 2000. Does the picture make a difference? In 2016 Seth Noar and his colleagues combined the results of dozens of studies from many countries.
They found that pictorial warnings were more effective than text-only ones, at attracting attention, at making people think about the risks, and at making smokers say they intended to quit. The strongest warnings were those that were graphic and aroused strong feelings, such as fear. There is less evidence on the effect on actual smoking, but studies from countries that adopted them show small declines. Emotion draws attention in a way that statistics do not.

In January 2014 Mexico introduced a tax of one peso per liter on sugary drinks, about ten percent of the price. Mexico had one of the highest rates of obesity and diabetes in the world, and it was also one of the biggest consumers of soda per person. In 2016 Arantxa Colchero and her colleagues analyzed the purchases of thousands of households before and after the tax.
In the first year, the purchases of taxed drinks fell by about six percent, on average. The decline was greater for poorer households, about nine percent. Purchases of untaxed drinks, such as water, rose slightly. Later studies found that the effect continued. Similar taxes have since been introduced in many places, including cities in the United States and the United Kingdom. They reduce the amount of sugar consumed, and raise money for health programs.
Telling people about their neighbors' taxes

Governments lose a lot of money to people who do not pay their taxes on time. In 2011 the British government's Behavioral Insights Team, sometimes called the Nudge Unit, ran an experiment with the tax authority. People who were late in paying their tax received a letter. Some of the letters were the normal reminder. Others added a sentence that was based on the facts, such as that nine out of ten people in the country pay their tax on time.
The letters that stressed the social norm increased the share of people who paid in the following weeks, by a few percentage points. It was most effective when the norm was local, such as saying that most people in your town have paid. The effect was small per person, but with millions of letters, it was worth millions of pounds. Telling people what others do is a cheap and powerful tool, as long as it's true.

In November 1660, after a lecture at Gresham College in London by the young architect and astronomer Christopher Wren, a group of men met to form a society for the promotion of experimental knowledge. It became the Royal Society, chartered by King Charles II in 1662. Its early members included Robert Boyle, Robert Hooke and, later, Isaac Newton.
The society's motto, adopted early on, is Nullius in verba, which means take nobody's word for it. It was a declaration that claims should be settled by evidence and experiment, and not by the authority of an ancient writer or a famous person. Members were expected to show their results before witnesses. In 1665 the society began to publish Philosophical Transactions, which is the oldest scientific journal still in print. The spirit of the motto is the center of science.

Peer review, in which unnamed experts evaluate a paper before it is published, was not a routine practice until the second half of the twentieth century. In 1936 Albert Einstein, who was then living in Princeton, sent a paper to the American journal Physical Review. He and a colleague, Nathan Rosen, argued that gravitational waves could not exist.
The editor sent it to a reviewer, who found a mistake, and wrote a long critical report. Einstein was furious. He wrote to the editor that he had not authorized him to show the paper to anyone before it was printed, and that he saw no reason to address the comments of an anonymous expert. He withdrew the paper, and is said never to have sent anything to that journal again. Later, with the help of a colleague, he found that the reviewer was right. Gravitational waves were detected in 2015.

In 1747 the French writer Denis Diderot was asked to translate an English encyclopedia. He turned it into something much larger. With the mathematician Jean le Rond d'Alembert, he set out to gather all human knowledge in one work, and to make it accessible. The Encyclopédie took twenty-five years. It filled twenty-eight volumes, with about seventy-two thousand articles, and thousands of illustrations of trades and machines.
Hundreds of people wrote for it, including Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu. Its articles promoted reason, science and tolerance, and criticized superstition and absolute power. The Church and the government opposed it, and it was banned more than once. Diderot worked on it in secret at times. Many historians see it as the most important project of the Enlightenment. It showed that knowledge could be organized and spread widely.
Flying a kite in a storm

Benjamin Franklin suspected that lightning was electrical. In the spring of 1752, he proposed an experiment using a tall metal rod on a building, or a sentry box. A French team tried it first, in May, near Paris, and saw sparks from the rod. In June 1752, according to his own account, Franklin flew a kite in a thunderstorm in Philadelphia, with a key at the end of the string, and was able to draw sparks from the key.
The experiment was dangerous. In 1753 a Russian physicist, Georg Richmann, was killed in St. Petersburg when he tried a similar experiment, and was hit by a ball of lightning. Franklin used what he had learned to invent the lightning rod, which protects buildings by providing a safe path for the current. It was one of the first practical results of research into electricity.

In 1783 two paper manufacturers in the French town of Annonay, Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier, noticed that smoke rose. They made a large balloon of paper and cloth, and filled it with hot air from a fire. It rose in front of a crowd. In September of that year, they sent up a balloon from the palace of Versailles, in front of the king, with a sheep, a duck and a rooster in a basket. The animals landed safely.
On November 21, 1783, in Paris, two men, Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes, made the first free flight by humans. They rose in a Montgolfier balloon, and flew for about twenty-five minutes, crossing part of the city, and landed about five miles away. Crowds watched. Ten days later, a hydrogen balloon, built by the physicist Jacques Charles, carried people too. The era of flight had begun.

In the years 1811 to 1816, bands of workers in the textile towns of the English Midlands and North broke into factories and smashed machines. They claimed to be led by a mythical figure, General Ned Ludd, and they called themselves Luddites. They were mainly skilled weavers and knitters, who were losing their income because of new machines that allowed unskilled workers, women and children, to do the job at a lower wage.
The government responded with force. It sent in thousands of troops, and made frame-breaking a crime that was punishable by death. Several men were hanged, and others were transported. Today, the word Luddite is often used for someone who dislikes technology. But the Luddites were not against machines as such. They were fighting for decent wages and conditions, at a time of hardship.

In December 1831 the British Navy ship HMS Beagle left Plymouth on a survey voyage around the world. On board as a companion to the captain, Robert FitzRoy, was a twenty-two-year-old man who had abandoned a medical degree, and was training for the clergy, Charles Darwin. The voyage was meant to last two years. It took nearly five.
Darwin collected specimens, kept notes, and read Charles Lyell's new book on geology, which said that the Earth was very old. He saw fossils of giant extinct animals in South America, and the different birds on the Galápagos Islands. He came home in 1836 with ideas that took him more than twenty years to develop. When On the Origin of Species was published in November 1859, the whole first printing of twelve hundred and fifty copies sold on the first day.

In 1851 Britain held the Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations, in Hyde Park, London. It was Prince Albert's idea, and it was meant to display the achievements of the Industrial Revolution, and to show British superiority. The building was as remarkable as the exhibits. Designed by Joseph Paxton, a gardener, it was a huge hall of glass and cast iron, nearly two thousand feet long, called the Crystal Palace.
It was built in about nine months, from prefabricated parts. More than six million people visited it in five months. They saw steam engines, textile machines, a huge diamond, the first public toilets, and inventions from many countries. The profits were used to found museums in South Kensington, such as the Victoria and Albert Museum. The building was moved to south London, where it burned down in 1936.

In the nineteenth century, London was growing rapidly, and its sewage flowed into the River Thames, the source of much of the city's drinking water. Cholera outbreaks killed thousands. At the time, most doctors believed that disease was caused by bad air, miasma, and not by germs in water. In the hot summer of 1858 the smell from the river became unbearable, and Parliament, which stands on the bank, had to hang curtains soaked in chloride of lime over its windows.
The Great Stink, as it was called, gave politicians a reason to act. Within weeks, they passed a bill to build a new sewer system, designed by the engineer Joseph Bazalgette. It took about sixteen years, and included about eighty miles of large intercepting sewers, which carried waste to the east, away from the center. The system is still in use. It's often credited with ending cholera epidemics in London.

In 1905 Albert Einstein was twenty-six years old, and working as a clerk in the patent office in Bern, Switzerland. He had failed to get a university post. In that one year, in his spare time, he published four papers in the journal Annalen der Physik, each of which changed physics. He called them revolutionary in a letter to a friend.
The first explained the photoelectric effect, by suggesting that light comes in packets, now called photons, which helped to found quantum theory. It earned him the Nobel Prize. The second explained Brownian motion, the jiggling of particles in a fluid, as the effect of molecules, and so gave strong evidence for atoms. The third was the special theory of relativity. The fourth, a short follow-up, gave the equation E equals mc squared. The year is called his annus mirabilis.

In October 1927 the fifth Solvay Conference was held in Brussels. It had been organized by the Belgian industrialist Ernest Solvay, and its subject was electrons and photons. Twenty-nine of the world's top physicists attended, and seventeen of them won, or were later to win, a Nobel Prize. They included Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Planck, Curie and Dirac.
The conference is known for the debates between Niels Bohr and Albert Einstein about the meaning of quantum mechanics. Einstein disliked the idea that nature is governed by chance, saying that God does not play dice. Bohr is said to have replied that Einstein should stop telling God what to do. Each morning, Einstein would propose a thought experiment to show a flaw, and by evening, Bohr would have found the answer. The photograph of the group is one of the most famous in science.

In the 1890s two psychologists at Indiana University, William Lowe Bryan and Noble Harter, studied how telegraph operators learned to send and receive Morse code. They collected records of the speed of learners over many weeks. The curve of progress did not rise smoothly. It rose quickly at first, and then flattened for a while, before rising again. The flat stretch is called a plateau.
The researchers suggested that the plateau occurs when a learner has mastered the individual letters, and has to start to learn whole words and phrases. The brain has to reorganize its skills at a higher level, and that takes time, without visible progress. It's a good thing to know when you are learning a skill, such as a language or an instrument. A plateau is not a sign of failure. It's often a stage before a new level.

How quickly do we improve with practice? In 1959 Edward Crossman studied cigar makers in a factory in Cuba. He had records of how many cigars each worker made per hour, over years. They improved rapidly in the first weeks, and then more slowly, but they kept improving for years. It was a smooth curve, with each doubling of practice producing a similar proportional gain in speed.
In 1981 Allen Newell and Paul Rosenbloom showed that the same pattern fits many skills, from typing to reading mirror writing to solving problems. It's called the power law of practice. The early gains are big, and later gains are small but continue. It tells us that to keep making progress at an advanced level, much more practice is needed. And it suggests that a beginner shouldn't be discouraged. The first few hours bring the biggest returns.

In 1978 Robert Kerr and Bernard Booth tested a simple idea about practice. Children of eight and twelve years old learned to throw a beanbag at a target on the floor. All of them practiced the same number of throws. One group threw from a distance of three feet. The other group threw from two feet and four feet, but never from three.
After twelve weeks, they were tested at three feet. The children who had practiced at two other distances did better than those who had practiced at three, the one in the test. They were also better when they were given a new task. The variety seems to teach the learner a general rule, and not just a single response. When practicing a skill, such as a tennis serve or a speech, it helps to vary the conditions.

In 1979 John Shea and Robyn Morgan had people learn three different arm movements, each of which involved knocking down a set of wooden barriers as fast as possible. One group practiced in blocks, with one movement repeated many times, and then another. The other group practiced in a random order, with a different movement each time.
During practice, the blocked group did better and improved faster. The random group seemed to be doing worse. But in a test ten days later, the results were reversed. The random group performed better, and especially in a new situation. This is called contextual interference. Switching tasks makes practice harder, which forces the learner to retrieve the plan each time, and that builds a stronger memory. It's the same principle as interleaving in study.

You would think that a learner should get feedback after every attempt. In 1990 Carolee Winstein and Richard Schmidt tested this. People learned to move a lever in a particular pattern, and were told after each trial how close they were. One group got feedback after every trial. Another group got it on only half of the trials, chosen at random.
During practice, the group with constant feedback did a little better. But in a test the next day, without any feedback, the group that had been given feedback half of the time did better. When feedback is given every time, the learner may come to depend on it, and not learn to judge their own performance. Self-assessment is part of the skill. A coach who talks less may be better than one who comments on everything.
Think about the effect, not the body

When a golfer is learning to swing, should they think about the movement of their arms, or about where they want the ball to go? Gabriele Wulf, a researcher in motor learning, has studied this question for over twenty years. She has found that people perform better and learn faster when their attention is directed to the effect of the movement on the environment, such as the path of a club, than when it's directed to their own body.
The instruction to think about the arms is called an internal focus. The instruction to think about the club, or the target, is an external focus. In dozens of studies, from basketball to balance to singing, the external focus has helped. A meta-analysis in 2021 confirmed the effect. The reason may be that thinking about the body interferes with automatic control. It's a practical tip for any skill that is physical.

Chess is often promoted as a way of improving children's thinking, and it has been introduced in schools in many countries. In 2016 Giovanni Sala and Fernand Gobet combined the results of twenty-four studies of chess instruction in schools. They looked at whether it improved math, reading and general thinking skills.
They found modest effects on math, reading and thinking skills, but the effects were smaller in studies that used a good control group, in which the children in the comparison group had other activities of equal interest. The authors concluded that there is some benefit, but that it is probably due to the extra attention or the motivation, and not to a special effect of chess. It's another example of a failure of far transfer.

The idea that anyone can become an expert with enough practice has been popular. In 2014 Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald combined the results of eighty-eight studies of the relationship between deliberate practice and performance, in music, games, sports, education and professions.
They found that practice mattered a lot, but not as much as often claimed. It accounted for about a quarter of the differences in performance in games like chess, about a fifth in music, and about a fifth in sports. In education, it explained only about four percent, and in professions less than one percent. Much of the variation was due to other factors, such as when people began, their abilities, and their situations. Practice is necessary, but it's not the whole story.

Pianists differ in how well they can play a piece of music at first sight. It's a skill that depends on practice, and on other things. In 2010 Elizabeth Meinz and David Hambrick tested a group of pianists, ranging from beginners to advanced. They measured how much they had practiced, how well they sight-read, and their working memory, the capacity to hold information in mind.
Practice was a strong predictor, and accounted for about half of the differences in sight-reading. But working memory made an independent contribution, of about seven percent. Among people with the same amount of practice, those with a bigger working memory did better, even at the highest levels of practice. The study suggests that talent has a role, and that even in a skill that depends on practice, individual abilities matter.

The ten thousand hours rule says that it takes about ten thousand hours of practice to become an expert. In 2007 Fernand Gobet and Guillermo Campitelli tested the rule with chess players. They surveyed the hours of serious practice that players had put in before they reached master level, in Argentina and in Britain.
The average was around eleven thousand hours, but the variation was huge. Some of the players reached master level in about three thousand hours, and others had practiced for more than twenty-three thousand hours and had still not got there. Some players never reached the level, despite many years of practice. There's no magic number. Practice matters a great deal, but people differ in how quickly they improve.

The cheetah is the fastest land animal. It can accelerate from a standstill to sixty miles an hour in about three seconds, faster than most sports cars. Speeds of about sixty miles an hour or more have been recorded, though it can't keep them up for more than a few hundred meters. In 2013 Alan Wilson and his colleagues at the Royal Veterinary College fitted wild cheetahs in Botswana with collars that had GPS and motion sensors.
They found that the cheetahs rarely ran at top speed in hunts. They used their agility, and the ability to slow down and turn sharply, more than their top speed. A cheetah has a long, flexible spine, large nostrils, and claws that act like cleats. But it's not an endurance runner. After a chase, it needs to rest, and often loses its kill to lions or hyenas.

The fastest animal on Earth is not a runner. It's the peregrine falcon, which dives on its prey in a steep plunge called a stoop. Its speed in a dive has been measured at more than two hundred miles an hour. In 1998 Vance Tucker trained a falcon to dive from a height, with a small recorder on its back, and he measured speeds of about two hundred miles an hour.
The falcon has features that allow it to survive the dive. Small cones in its nostrils help it to breathe at high speeds, by controlling the flow of air. It has a third eyelid, a membrane, that clears its eyes. It strikes the prey, usually a bird, with its feet, and often kills it on contact. Peregrines were nearly wiped out in the mid-twentieth century by the pesticide DDT. They have since recovered.

A giraffe's neck can be about six feet long, and it has just seven vertebrae, the same number as in the neck of a human. Almost all mammals have seven neck vertebrae, from the mouse to the blue whale. The exceptions are the sloths, which have between six and ten, and the manatees, which have six. Each of the giraffe's vertebrae is greatly elongated, and may be ten inches long.
Why so constant? One idea is that a change in the number of vertebrae could disrupt the genes that control the development of the nerves and the diaphragm. Mutations that cause an extra rib in the neck are linked to a higher risk of cancer in children, and such changes are often lethal. Evolution has been conservative. The giraffe has made a long neck out of the same parts that we have.
The squid axon that explained the nerve

In the 1930s the British biologist John Zachary Young found that squids have a very large nerve fiber, called a giant axon, which is up to a millimeter across, a hundred times wider than a human one. It controls the squid's escape response. It was large enough that an electrode could be placed inside it.
In the late 1940s Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley, at Cambridge, used it to study how nerves send signals. They worked out the electrical changes, and found that the signal, the action potential, is caused by the flow of sodium and potassium ions through the nerve membrane. They wrote equations to describe it in 1952. These explained the basis of all nerve signaling, in the human brain as well as in squids. They shared the Nobel Prize in 1963.
The shrimp that snaps like a gun

The pistol shrimp is a small animal, only a few centimeters long, which lives in shallow seas. It has one claw that is much bigger than the other. It can snap it shut so quickly that it shoots out a jet of water at nearly a hundred kilometers an hour. The jet makes a bubble, which collapses with a bang. It can stun or kill small fish.
In 2000 Michel Versluis and his colleagues studied the effect. The collapsing bubble produces a sound of about two hundred decibels, louder than a gunshot, and a flash of light, and the gas inside briefly reaches a temperature of thousands of degrees. This is called cavitation. A group of pistol shrimp snapping can be so loud that it interferes with sonar. Naval submarines have used the noise as cover.
The beetle that sprays boiling liquid

The bombardier beetle defends itself with a chemical weapon. When threatened, it squirts a jet of a hot, caustic liquid from the tip of its abdomen, and it can aim it, over a wide angle. The liquid is boiling, at about one hundred degrees Celsius. It can kill a small insect, and it irritates the mouth of a predator.
The beetle makes it with two chemicals, hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide, which it stores separately in a reservoir. When it's attacked, it squeezes them into a chamber with enzymes, where they react explosively. It pulses the spray, up to about five hundred times a second. In 2015 researchers used high speed X-ray imaging to look inside living beetles as they sprayed.

The electric eel, which lives in the rivers of South America, is not an eel but a kind of knifefish. It can produce shocks of up to about six hundred volts, strong enough to stun a horse. About eighty percent of its body is made up of electric organs, which consist of thousands of cells stacked like the cells in a battery. It uses weak pulses to sense its surroundings, like radar.
In 2014 Kenneth Catania at Vanderbilt University found something surprising. When an eel attacks a fish that is out of the water, it leaps up, and presses its chin on the prey, and sends the current through the air, along the body of the prey, and back into the water. The shock goes through the prey, as if it were a wire. It's an unusual use of electricity, and it's an example of how clever predators can be.

Dung beetles roll balls of dung away from the pile in a straight line, so that they will not be robbed by others. They can do this at night. In 2013 Marie Dacke and her colleagues in South Africa and Sweden wondered how they find their way when there's no Sun and no Moon. They put little cardboard hats on some of the beetles, so that they couldn't see the sky.
The beetles with hats wandered in circles. Those without them went straight. The beetles seemed to be using the stars. When the researchers took the beetles to a planetarium, and showed them a sky with only the Milky Way, they still rolled their balls in a straight line. It was the first evidence that an insect uses the Milky Way for navigation. It's a feat that is done by a brain no bigger than a grain of rice.

The northern elephant seal spends most of its life at sea, and much of it underwater. Researchers fitted tags on seals from California to track their dives. The seals dived to depths of about five hundred meters on average, and the deepest dives went to more than fifteen hundred meters, nearly a mile. A dive lasted for twenty minutes or more, with just a few minutes at the surface between dives.
Some of the dives lasted for over an hour. The seal can do this because its blood holds a large amount of oxygen, and its muscles are full of a protein, myoglobin, which stores oxygen. Its heart slows down, and blood is sent mainly to the brain and heart. During a trip of several months, the seals spend ninety percent of the time underwater. They even seem to sleep while diving, drifting down in a spiral.
The penguins who endure the winter

The emperor penguin is the only animal that breeds during the Antarctic winter. In March, the penguins walk up to sixty miles inland, to a place far from the sea. The female lays a single egg, and passes it to the male, who balances it on his feet under a fold of skin. She then walks back to the sea to feed.
The males stand in the dark, with temperatures down to minus forty degrees Celsius and winds of a hundred miles an hour. They go without food for about two months, and lose up to half of their body weight. To survive, they huddle together in a large group, and take turns moving from the cold edge to the warm center. When the females return, with food, the chicks hatch, and the males go to the sea to feed.
The bird that circles the world

The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any bird, up to eleven feet. It spends most of its life at sea, and comes to land only to breed. It travels huge distances. In 1990 Pierre Jouventin and Henri Weimerskirch began to track albatrosses with satellite tags, and later work with GPS tags has shown that they can circle the Southern Ocean in a few weeks, in one case in about forty-six days.
The albatross uses almost no energy to stay in the air. It uses a technique called dynamic soaring, in which it takes advantage of the difference in wind speed between the surface of the sea and the air a few meters above. It glides on stiff wings, and can go for hours without a wingbeat. Its heart rate when flying is only slightly above the rate at rest. Many albatrosses mate for life, and some live for over sixty years.

When a snake flicks its tongue, it's not tasting the air, as is often thought. It's collecting chemical particles from the air, or from the ground. The tongue is forked, and when the snake pulls it back into its mouth, it presses the tips into two small pits in the roof of its mouth. They are the openings of the vomeronasal organ, also called Jacobson's organ, which analyzes the chemicals.
The fork has a purpose. In 1994 Kurt Schwenk argued that, like having two ears, having two tips allows the snake to sample two places at once. It can tell which side the scent is stronger on, and follow a trail, such as that of a mouse, by turning toward the stronger side. Snakes can also track a trail left by a mate. It's a form of stereo smell. Lizards, such as monitors, have forked tongues too.

In the 1980s the biologist Katy Payne was at the Portland zoo, where she noticed a throbbing feeling in the air near the elephants. She thought of the low sounds that whales make, which travel for long distances. She went back with recording equipment, and detected sounds that were below the range of human hearing, called infrasound. The elephants were communicating at frequencies of fourteen to thirty-five hertz.
Low sounds travel a long way. In studies in Africa, Payne and others found that elephants can hear each other's calls from several miles away. They may also sense vibrations through their feet, which are transmitted through the ground. Calls can be used to find mates, and warn of danger. The elephants were talking to each other all the time, and people had never heard them.
The songs that cross the ocean

Male humpback whales sing long and complex songs, which can last for twenty minutes, and be repeated for hours. All the whales in a population sing the same song at a given time, and it changes gradually over the season. In 2011 Ellen Garland and her colleagues studied the songs of whales in the South Pacific, over eleven years.
They found that a new song would appear among the whales off eastern Australia, and then spread, within a year or two, to the whales in the next population to the east, and then on again, as far as French Polynesia, some six thousand kilometers away. The whales seem to learn the new song from one another. It's one of the best-known cases of cultural transmission in animals. The songs change as they pass, like a hit song that spreads from one country to the next.

Termites in Africa build great towers of mud, up to ten feet tall or more, which house colonies of millions. The mounds were long said to work as natural air-conditioners. The idea was that hot air from the nest rises through channels in the chimney, and fresh air is drawn in at the bottom, keeping the temperature steady at about thirty degrees, as the termites need.
The ideas inspired some architecture. A shopping complex in Zimbabwe, called Eastgate, was designed in 1996 with a cooling system said to be modeled on the mounds. Recent studies, however, have questioned the details. In 2015 researchers found that the mounds work more like a lung, with air moving in and out in a daily cycle, driven by the day-night changes in temperature. The mound is a remarkable structure. But how it works is still under debate.
The feet that stick without glue

A gecko can run up a smooth glass wall, and hang from the ceiling by one toe. It uses no glue, and its feet are not sticky. For centuries, scientists wondered how it did this. In 2000 a team of biologists and engineers, led from Lewis & Clark College in Oregon, showed that the answer lay in the tiny hairs on its toes. A gecko's foot has about half a million microscopic hairs, called setae, and each has hundreds of tips, called spatulae, only about two hundred nanometers wide.
The tips get so close to the surface that weak attractive forces between molecules, called van der Waals forces, hold them. Each tip's pull is tiny, but with billions of them, the total is enough to support the animal's weight many times over. The gecko releases its grip by changing the angle of the toe. Engineers have used the idea to make adhesive tapes and robots that climb walls.

Sharks are very old. The first creatures that look like sharks appeared in the oceans more than four hundred million years ago, in the Silurian or Devonian periods. The earliest known trees, such as Archaeopteris, did not appear on land until about three hundred and eighty-five million years ago. So sharks are older than trees, and older than the dinosaurs, by a long way.
Sharks have survived five mass extinctions. Their skeletons are made of cartilage, which does not fossilize well, so most of what we know about early sharks comes from their teeth. Modern sharks vary widely, from the dwarf lanternshark, which is about eight inches long, to the whale shark, at more than forty feet. Many species are now threatened by overfishing. Some are killed for their fins, or caught by accident, in numbers of tens of millions a year.
The blue blood that saves lives

The horseshoe crab, a creature that has existed for about four hundred and fifty million years, has blue blood. It's blue because it uses a copper-based molecule, hemocyanin, to carry oxygen, and not the iron-based hemoglobin that makes our blood red. The blood has another feature. It clots when it comes into contact with bacterial toxins.
In the 1960s Frederik Bang and Jack Levin found that a substance in the crab's blood cells could detect even tiny amounts of bacterial endotoxin. It was developed into a test, called the LAL test. It's used to make sure that vaccines, injectable drugs and medical devices are free from contamination. Every year, many thousands of crabs are caught, bled, and returned to the sea, though some die. Synthetic alternatives, which do not need the crabs, are now being adopted.

Do animals plan for the future? Humans are thought to be special in this, and in the past, evidence from animals was disputed. In 2017 Can Kabadayi and Mathias Osvath, at Lund University in Sweden, tested ravens. They taught the birds to use a tool, a stone, to open a box with a reward. Then they removed the box, and gave the ravens a choice of objects. One was a tool, among others that were useless.
Some time later, the ravens were given access to the box, in another room. The birds that had picked the tool carried it, and used it. When a raven was offered a choice of the tool or a smaller treat, it often chose the tool. The ravens seemed to understand that they would need the tool later, in a different place. Similar planning was found in apes. It shows that the ability to plan for the future is not unique to humans.

New Caledonian crows live on a Pacific island, and they are known for using tools. They make hooks from twigs, and use them to pull grubs from holes. In 2002 Alex Weir and his colleagues at Oxford were studying a captive female, called Betty. She had been given a choice of a straight piece of wire and a hooked one, to fish a small bucket of food out of a tube.
The male crow took the hooked wire, leaving Betty with the straight one. Without having been trained, she picked up the straight wire, wedged one end in a crack, and bent it with her beak to make a hook. She then lifted the bucket. She repeated it in nine out of ten trials, and bent it in different ways. It was striking evidence of a bird's ability to manufacture a tool for a purpose.

Killer whales, or orcas, are among the few animals, besides humans, in which females live long after they stop reproducing. A female orca may stop having calves at about forty, and live to be eighty or ninety. Why? In 2015 Lauren Brent and her colleagues studied a population of orcas in the Pacific Northwest, which had been followed for over forty years.
They found that older females, the grandmothers, were the leaders of the groups when the whales were hunting for salmon. They tended to lead the group more as they grew older, particularly when the food was scarce. They seemed to hold knowledge about where to find the fish. The calves of mothers who had a living grandmother also had a better chance of surviving. It supports the grandmother hypothesis, that older females can help their families.

How can you measure public opinion without asking people? In the 1960s Stanley Milgram and his colleagues developed the lost-letter technique. He placed hundreds of stamped, addressed envelopes in public places, such as on the sidewalk, as though they had been dropped. Each was addressed to an organization. Some went to a group such as Friends of the Nazi Party, some to a Friends of the Communist Party, and others to a medical research society, or to a private individual.
How many letters were mailed by passersby depended on where they were addressed. Many more of the letters to the medical society were posted than those to the Nazi or Communist groups. And the rates differed by neighborhood, matching the way people in those places voted. It was a way of testing attitudes by what people did, and not by what they said. It has been used in many places since.

Vampire bats feed on blood, and a bat that fails to find a meal for two or three nights can starve. In 1984 Gerald Wilkinson studied a colony in Costa Rica. He noticed that bats that had fed would sometimes regurgitate blood into the mouth of a hungry roost mate. Was it just kin looking after kin?
He found that many of the donors and receivers were not relatives. The bats were more likely to share with those who had shared with them before, and who they had roosted with for a long time. They kept track of favors. It's an example of reciprocal altruism, in which a cost today is repaid by a benefit later. It requires a good memory for individuals, and the ability to punish cheats. It's one of the best-known cases of cooperation among nonrelatives.

Why would an animal help others, at a cost to itself? In 1964 the British biologist William Hamilton offered an answer. A gene can spread not only by helping the individual that carries it to reproduce, but also by helping relatives, who have copies of the same gene. He wrote a simple rule, now called Hamilton's rule. A gene for helping will spread if the benefit to the relative, multiplied by the degree of relatedness, is greater than the cost to the helper.
The geneticist J. B. S. Haldane is said to have joked, in a pub, that he would lay down his life for two brothers or eight cousins. A brother shares half of your genes, and a cousin one eighth. The idea explains the sterile workers of social insects, who help their mother to raise sisters. It's called kin selection. It has become one of the foundations of modern evolutionary biology.

In 1995 Joyce Berg, John Dickhaut and Kevin McCabe devised a game to measure trust. A person, the sender, is given ten dollars, and can send any part of it to an anonymous partner, the receiver. The amount that is sent is tripled by the experimenter. The receiver can then send back any share of the larger amount, or keep it all. The players never meet.
A purely selfish receiver would keep everything, and a selfish sender, expecting that, would send nothing. But in the experiment, most senders sent about half, and receivers sent back about as much as the senders had sent. Trust and trustworthiness were common, even between strangers. The game has been played in dozens of countries, and by many groups. It's used to study how much people trust one another, and what affects it.

In the 1990s economists wanted to test whether people share when they don't have to. In a game used by Robert Forsythe and his colleagues in 1994, one student is given a sum of money, such as ten dollars, and is told to divide it between themselves and another student, whom they will never meet. The other student has no say. It's called the dictator game. Under the theory that people are selfish, the dictator would keep it all.
Many of the dictators did keep it all. But a large share gave something, and some split it equally. On average, the gifts were around a fifth of the money, though it varied widely between experiments. People don't give away all that they could, but many give something. The result suggests that fairness matters to people, even when no one is watching. Later studies found that giving drops if the dictator can hide the choice.

In the ultimatum game, one player offers to split a sum of money, and the other can accept, or reject it, in which case both get nothing. In industrial societies, the typical offer is nearly half, and low offers are often rejected. It was thought to show a universal sense of fairness. In the late 1990s Joseph Henrich and a team of anthropologists played it in fifteen small societies around the world, among foragers, herders and farmers.
The results varied widely. The Machiguenga, in the Peruvian Amazon, made offers of about a quarter, and nearly always accepted. The Lamalera, whale hunters in Indonesia, offered more than half, since they share their catch. The way that people played matched how much they depended on cooperation in daily life, and on markets. It suggests that ideas of fairness are shaped by culture.

If you see someone cheat another person, and it doesn't affect you, would you pay to punish them? In 2004 Ernst Fehr and Urs Fischbacher tested this. In one experiment, a person was given a sum of money, and could share it with another player, who had nothing. A third person watched, and could pay a price to reduce the first player's pay.
Many of the observers were willing to pay, and punished those who shared too little, in proportion to the degree of unfairness. They didn't gain anything themselves. It's called third-party punishment. It has been found in many cultures, though its strength varies. Some scholars see it as a basis for social norms. It may help to explain why people form groups that enforce rules, without a police force.

Does being generous encourage others to be generous? In 2010 James Fowler and Nicholas Christakis tested this in a series of public goods games. Players were put into groups of four, and each was given money, which they could contribute to a pot, which was multiplied and shared equally. The groups were changed after every round, so that no one played with the same people twice.
Despite this, people who had received generosity in one round gave more in the next, to new people. A donation made in the first round could lead to an additional contribution of about three times the original, as it spread through the network of people. They called it a cascade of cooperation. The effect shows that behavior is contagious, and that a single act can ripple through a community.
Watched by a picture of eyes

In a university department in Newcastle, England, staff kept a shelf of coffee and tea supplies, with an honesty box for people to pay what they owed. The price list was displayed.
