In 2006 Melissa Bateson and her colleagues did an experiment. Each week, they put a new image above the price list. It was either a picture of flowers, or a pair of eyes looking at the viewer. They alternated the two for ten weeks.
In the weeks with the eyes, people paid almost three times as much for their drinks as in the weeks with flowers. No one noticed the pattern. It's an example of how the feeling of being watched, even by a picture, makes people behave better. The effect has been found in other studies, though a few have not found it. It suggests that reputation is a strong force.
Does a white coat change your thinking?

In 2012 Hajo Adam and Adam Galinsky proposed the idea of enclothed cognition, that the clothes we wear can influence the way we think. In one experiment, people put on a white coat, and did an attention task, in which they were asked to spot differences in pictures. Those who were told that it was a doctor's coat did better than those who were told that it was a painter's coat, or who just saw a doctor's coat.
The authors said that it was both the symbolic meaning of the coat, and the act of wearing it, that mattered. The finding was widely reported. Later attempts to repeat the studies have been mixed, and some large studies found no effect. It's one of many results from social priming that are now regarded with caution. Clothes may well affect how we feel, though, and how others see us.

Does heat make people more aggressive? In 2011 Richard Larrick and his colleagues examined data on almost sixty thousand Major League Baseball games over several decades. They looked at when pitchers hit batters with the ball, and in particular whether the pitchers did so in retaliation after one of their own batters had been hit.
When the temperature was higher, a pitcher was more likely to hit an opposing batter after a teammate had been hit, and the effect grew with each degree. Without a previous incident, heat made no difference to the rate of hit batters, so it was not that the ball was harder to control. It was that heat increased the urge to retaliate. The study fits with others, which link hot weather to violent crime.

In 2012 a Swiss physician, Franz Messerli, published a short article in a leading medical journal. He plotted the chocolate consumption per person in twenty-two countries against the number of Nobel Prize winners per ten million people. The line was striking. Countries that ate more chocolate had more Nobel laureates, and the correlation was about 0.8, very strong.
Messerli did not claim that chocolate makes people win Nobel Prizes, though he joked that it might improve cognition. The article was partly a satire, to show how a correlation can appear without a cause. A rich country, with a good education system, may well eat more chocolate and produce more scientists. Switzerland was the top of the chart on both. It's a good example to keep in mind when reading a headline about a link between a food and a health outcome.

Ronald Fisher was one of the greatest statisticians of the twentieth century. He invented much of modern experimental design. He was also a heavy pipe smoker. In the 1950s, as the evidence mounted that smoking caused lung cancer, he argued against it. He said that the data showed only a correlation. It was possible that something else, such as a gene, caused both a desire to smoke and a tendency to get cancer.
He was also paid as a consultant by the tobacco industry. Whether that colored his views is debated. His argument was logical, but was not borne out. Studies of twins, of people who quit, and of smokers' doses, as well as experiments in animals, built the case for causation. The episode illustrates the difficulty of proving cause without an experiment, and also how even brilliant people can be led by their habits.

In 1965 the British statistician Austin Bradford Hill gave a talk in which he proposed a set of considerations for deciding whether an association is likely to be a cause. He had worked on the smoking and lung cancer studies. He called them nine viewpoints, but they are often called the Bradford Hill criteria.
They include the strength of the association, whether it's consistent in different studies and places, and whether the cause comes before the effect. Also important are a dose-response relationship, in which more exposure leads to more disease, a plausible mechanism, and whether stopping the exposure reduces the risk. Hill stressed that none of these is a hard rule, and that they are aids to judgment. They're still used in medicine and public health.

In 1947 streptomycin, a new antibiotic, was available in Britain in tiny amounts. There was not enough to treat all the patients with tuberculosis. The Medical Research Council, with Austin Bradford Hill as its statistician, decided to use the shortage to do a proper trial. One group of patients was given streptomycin and bed rest, and another was given bed rest only.
The patients were assigned by random numbers, from sealed envelopes, so that the doctors could not choose who got the drug. The X-rays were read by experts who did not know which group a patient was in. After six months, many more of the patients on the drug had improved, and fewer had died. It's regarded as the first properly randomized clinical trial. The method has since been used to test almost every medical treatment.

In many sciences, a result is said to be significant if the probability of getting it by chance is less than five percent, which is a p-value of 0.05. Where did the number come from? In 1925 the statistician Ronald Fisher wrote a handbook for researchers, which suggested that it was convenient to take a probability of one in twenty as a limit for judging whether a deviation is significant.
It was a rule of thumb, meant to be flexible, and not a law of nature. Fisher said later that a scientist should look at the whole body of results, and not rely on a single threshold. But the number became a fixed rule, and a large part of the literature has been shaped by it. Many researchers now argue that a lower threshold should be used for new findings, or that p-values should be replaced by other measures.
Why most findings may be false

In 2005 John Ioannidis, a physician and scientist at Stanford, published an essay with a startling title, Why Most Published Research Findings Are False. He used a simple argument based on probabilities. If many of the hypotheses that are tested are false, or if studies are small, or if there are many ways of analyzing the data, then a large share of the positive results will be false alarms.
The essay became one of the most downloaded in the history of the journal. Its claim has been debated. Some statisticians argue that his assumptions were too pessimistic, and that the rate of false findings differs between fields. But later large efforts to repeat studies in psychology, and in cancer biology, found that many results did not hold. The paper helped to start the movement for open and reliable science.

Suppose that you run an experiment, look at the data, and find an interesting pattern. Then you write the paper as if you had predicted it from the start. In 1998 the psychologist Norbert Kerr gave this practice a name, HARKing, which stands for Hypothesizing After the Results are Known. He pointed out that it is common, and that it may seem harmless.
But it makes the evidence look stronger than it is. A pattern that is found by looking is often due to chance, since with enough comparisons, something will always look significant. A hypothesis that predicted it in advance deserves more trust. The remedy is pre-registration, in which researchers state their plan and predictions before seeing the data, and register it in a public place.

In 2018 a group of researchers led by Raphael Silberzahn and Eric Uhlmann posed a question. Do soccer referees give more red cards to players with darker skin? They gave the same large dataset to twenty-nine research teams, with sixty-one analysts, and asked each to analyze it independently.
The teams chose different methods, and reached different conclusions. About two thirds found that dark-skinned players were more likely to get a red card, by a statistically significant margin, and a third found no significant effect. The estimates ranged from a slightly lower chance to nearly three times the chance. The study shows that results depend on the choices of the analyst, and not only on the data. It suggests that conclusions should be checked by more than one team.

In 1854 a severe outbreak of cholera hit the Soho district of London. In ten days, more than five hundred people died, in a few streets. At the time, most doctors believed that cholera was caused by bad air. A local physician, John Snow, thought it was spread in water. He talked to residents, and marked each death on a map of the area.
The deaths clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. Snow found that people who lived farther away, but who had drunk from the pump, also got sick, while workers at a nearby brewery, who drank beer, did not. He persuaded the local officials to remove the pump handle. The outbreak was already waning, but his map was a landmark of epidemiology. A decade later, the evidence for germ theory made his view the standard.

Snow's study of the Broad Street pump is better known, but he considered another, larger study to be his best. In 1854, in the south of London, two water companies supplied houses on the same streets, in a mixed pattern. The Lambeth company drew its water from the Thames upstream of the city, where it was cleaner. The Southwark and Vauxhall company drew its water from below the city's sewage outflows.
Snow counted the cholera deaths in the houses supplied by each. The households that got water from Southwark and Vauxhall were about eight or nine times more likely to die of cholera than those supplied by Lambeth. Since the customers were similar, and the houses were mixed on the same streets, it was like an experiment that nature had set up. He called it a grand experiment. It's an early example of a natural experiment, a method that economists and epidemiologists still use.

For decades, the height of Mount Everest was given as 8,848 meters, or 29,029 feet, based on a survey made in 1955. In December 2020 China and Nepal jointly announced a new figure, after separate surveys by each country. The summit was found to be 8,848.86 meters, or about 29,031.7 feet, nearly a meter higher than the old figure.
The mountain is not fixed. The collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates is pushing the Himalayas up, by about four millimeters a year, according to some measures. The great earthquake in Nepal in 2015 may have lowered it by a little. And the height depends on what counts as the top, the rock or the snow on top. Everest is the highest point above sea level, but not the tallest mountain from base to peak.

If you measure a mountain from its base to its summit, Everest is not the tallest. That title goes to Mauna Kea, a volcano on the island of Hawaii. Its peak is only about 4,200 meters above sea level. But its base is on the ocean floor, about six thousand meters below the surface. From base to summit, it's over ten thousand meters, more than a kilometer taller than Everest.
Most of it is underwater. The Hawaiian Islands are the tops of a chain of volcanoes that were formed by a hot spot in the Earth's mantle, as the Pacific Plate moved over it. The mass of the island is so great that it pushes the crust of the Earth down. Because the air is clear and dry at its summit, Mauna Kea hosts some of the world's largest telescopes.

The shore of the Dead Sea, on the border between Israel, Jordan and the West Bank, is the lowest place on dry land. It lies about four hundred and thirty meters below sea level, and it's sinking further. The sea is a lake, with no outlet, and the water in it is about nine and a half times as salty as the ocean. A swimmer floats, since the water is so dense.
The Dead Sea has been shrinking, at the rate of about a meter a year. Much of the water that used to flow into it from the River Jordan has been taken for use in farms and cities. Sinkholes have opened up on its shores, and it has lost about a third of its surface area in fifty years. Plans have been discussed to bring in water from the Red Sea.

Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world, at 1,642 meters, or just over a mile. It's also the oldest, at about twenty-five million years. It holds about twenty percent of the world's fresh surface water, more than all the North American Great Lakes put together. It's about four hundred miles long, but only about fifty miles wide.
The water is very clear, and cold, and rich in oxygen even in the deep. Most of the animal species in it are found nowhere else. They include the Baikal seal, one of the few freshwater seals in the world, and a small fish, the golomyanka, that bears live young. In winter, the lake is covered with ice that is more than a meter thick, which can carry trucks.

A desert is defined by how little precipitation falls, not by the temperature. By that definition, the largest desert in the world is not the Sahara but Antarctica, with an area of about fourteen million square kilometers. Large parts of the interior get less than fifty millimeters of precipitation a year, in the form of snow.
Antarctica also holds about seventy percent of the world's fresh water, in an ice sheet that is up to nearly five kilometers thick, in places. If it all melted, sea levels would rise by about sixty meters. In the McMurdo Dry Valleys, there are areas that have been free of ice and snow for millions of years, because of strong winds. The continent has no permanent residents, though several thousand scientists live there in summer.
The Sahara, as big as the United States

The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world. It covers about nine million square kilometers, an area close to that of the United States, or of China. It stretches across North Africa from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, and runs through eleven countries. It's not all sand dunes. Only about a fifth is covered by sand. The rest is stony plain, bare rock and mountains.
The Sahara hasn't always been dry. About eleven thousand to five thousand years ago, in a period called the African Humid Period, it was a green land with lakes, grass and animals. Rock paintings in the middle of the desert show hippos, giraffes and cattle. The change from green to desert, probably caused by a shift in the Earth's orbit, took a few centuries. Dust from the Sahara blows across the Atlantic, and fertilizes the Amazon.

The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is the driest nonpolar place on Earth. Some of its weather stations have never recorded rain. In parts of it, there have been no rainfall events for several years at a time, and a few places, according to some records, have not had a shower for decades. It lies between the Andes and the Pacific, in a double rain shadow.
The desert is so dry and so unlike other places that NASA has used it to test equipment for Mars. In some parts, the soil has hardly any microbes. Yet life does hang on. Some bacteria live inside salt rocks, and absorb moisture from the air. Fog from the ocean, called camanchaca, gives enough water for some plants. After rare rains, the desert can bloom with flowers.

Mawsynram, a village in the hills of northeastern India, is often given as the wettest place on Earth. It gets, on average, about eleven meters, or thirty-six feet, of rain a year, though it varies from source to source and from year to year. The rain falls mainly in the summer monsoon, from June to September.
The cause is the shape of the land. Moist air from the Bay of Bengal travels northward over the plains of Bangladesh, and meets the Khasi Hills, which force it to rise and cool. The water in the air condenses and falls. People there wear a woven shield of bamboo and leaves, called a knup, on their backs, as they work in the rain. The people of the Khasi Hills also grow living bridges from the roots of rubber fig trees.

About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, and much of the rest is at risk of flooding. The country's name means low lands. Over a thousand years, the Dutch have built dikes, drained lakes and reclaimed land from the sea, in large areas called polders. A saying goes that God made the world, but the Dutch made the Netherlands.
Windmills were used to pump water out of the polders. Today, the work is done by electric pumps. After a great flood in 1953, which killed more than eighteen hundred people, the Dutch built a huge system of dams and barriers, called the Delta Works. It took more than forty years. It's regarded as one of the great engineering projects. The country is a world leader in water management.

Greenland is the largest island in the world, with an area of about 2.2 million square kilometers. It belongs to Denmark, but governs itself. It has only about fifty-six thousand people, most of whom live on the southwest coast. About eighty percent of the island is covered by an ice sheet, which is up to three kilometers thick.
The ice sheet holds enough water to raise the level of the world's oceans by about seven meters if it all melted. It has been losing mass at an increasing rate, in recent decades, by hundreds of billions of tons a year. Much of the ice is more than a hundred thousand years old, and cores drilled from it give a record of past climates. The name, Greenland, was given by Erik the Red, to attract settlers.

Indonesia is made up of more than seventeen thousand islands, about six thousand of which are inhabited. It's the largest archipelago in the world. It stretches for about five thousand kilometers from east to west, a distance as great as that from London to Baghdad. The country has hundreds of languages and the fourth largest population in the world.
Japan has even more islands than most people think. In 2023 the country counted 14,125, after a recount that used better methods. Earlier, the figure was 6,852. The four main islands hold almost all of the population. Both countries lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where many volcanoes and earthquakes occur. The difference between the two counts of Japan's islands shows that a definition of an island is needed for a count.

Russia is the largest country in the world, and spans eleven time zones. When it's morning in Kaliningrad, it's already evening in Kamchatka, at the other end of the country. It would be natural to think that it has the most time zones of any country. In fact, France does, if you count its overseas territories.
France has twelve, or thirteen if you include a claim in Antarctica, because of islands and territories, such as French Polynesia, Réunion and French Guiana, spread across the world's oceans. The United States has eleven, if you include its territories. China, which is about as big as the United States, uses only one, set to Beijing time, which means that the Sun rises at about ten in the morning in the far west.

Africa is the second-largest continent, and has fifty-four countries recognized by the United Nations, more than any other. Most of them became independent in the twentieth century, mainly between the 1950s and the 1970s. The borders were drawn by European powers, notably at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, which divided up the continent without consulting its people.
Africa has about one and a half billion people, about eighteen percent of the world's population, and is the youngest continent, with a median age of around nineteen. More than two thousand languages are spoken. Nigeria is the most populous country, and Algeria the largest by area. The smallest country is the Seychelles, an island nation. The continent is growing fast, and by 2050, may have a quarter of the world's people.

Vatican City is the smallest country in the world, with an area of about forty-four hectares, or a bit over a hundred acres. It's smaller than most golf courses. It lies inside the city of Rome, and has a population of around eight hundred. It's the seat of the Catholic Church, and is ruled by the Pope. It became independent under a treaty with Italy in 1929.
It has its own post office, radio station, newspaper, bank, pharmacy and a small army, the Swiss Guard, whose members have been recruited from Switzerland since 1506. The country has no income tax, and has more than a thousand visitors for every resident. Monaco, the next smallest, is a little more than four times larger. The Vatican Museums hold one of the greatest collections of art in the world, including the Sistine Chapel.

The Nile and the Amazon are the two candidates for the longest river in the world. The Nile is usually given as about 6,650 kilometers, and the Amazon as about 6,400. But the figures are disputed. The answer depends on where you say a river begins, and how you measure its winding course. The source of a river can be hard to define. There are many headwaters, and the lengths change with the seasons.
In 2007 a Brazilian team claimed that the Amazon was longer, at about 6,990 kilometers, by taking a different source in the Peruvian Andes. Other studies disagree. The Amazon is by far the largest by volume. It discharges about a fifth of all the fresh water that rivers deliver to the oceans, more than the next seven rivers together.
The roof of the navigable world

Lake Titicaca lies on the border between Peru and Bolivia, in the Andes, at an altitude of about 3,800 meters, or over twelve thousand feet. It's the highest large lake in the world that can be navigated by commercial ships. It's also the largest lake in South America by volume, and covers about eight thousand square kilometers.
The Inca believed that the Sun was born on one of its islands. The Uros people live on floating islands that they make from the totora reeds that grow in the lake. They renew the top layer constantly, as the bottom rots. The lake is home to a giant frog, the Titicaca water frog, which has a lot of loose skin that allows it to breathe underwater, in the thin air.

On many world maps, Greenland looks about as big as Africa. In reality, Africa is about fourteen times larger. The difference is a result of the map projection. In 1569 the Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator created a map that was designed for sailors. On it, a straight line of constant compass direction is a straight line. This was very useful for navigation.
To achieve it, the map has to stretch the areas toward the poles, and the stretching gets larger the farther they are from the equator. So Greenland, Canada and Russia look huge, and Africa and South America look small. There's no way to show a sphere on a flat map without distortion. Many alternative maps, such as the Gall-Peters, have been proposed, but all of them distort something.
Where the sun rises over the Pacific

Panama is a country of surprises. Most people picture it as a thin strip of land between the Atlantic on the east, and the Pacific on the west. But because the isthmus twists, running east and west instead of north and south, the Atlantic entrance of the canal is farther west than the Pacific entrance. A ship traveling through the canal from the Atlantic to the Pacific goes southeast.
It's often said that Panama is a place where you can see the Sun rise over the Pacific, and set over the Atlantic. At the Pacific end of the canal, the bridge, the Bridge of the Americas, is about forty-three kilometers east of the Atlantic end, at Colón. The canal is about eighty kilometers long. A passage takes about eight to ten hours, with locks that lift ships twenty-six meters.

On November 15, 2022, the United Nations declared that the world's population had reached eight billion. The figure is an estimate. It had taken twelve years to rise from seven billion, in 2011. In 1800 there were about a billion people. It took more than a century to double, and the population then grew very fast in the twentieth century, due to advances in health, and falling death rates, especially among children.
The rate of growth is now slowing. Families are smaller in most places, and the UN expects that the population will peak at about ten billion, around the 2080s, and then begin to fall. In 2023, India passed China as the most populous country. Half of the world's people live in just seven countries. The fastest growth is in Africa, and many countries in Europe and East Asia are shrinking.
We think we're clearer than we are

When we say something, we know what we mean, and so it seems clear. In 2002 Boaz Keysar and Anne Henly tested how well speakers judge their own clarity. Speakers were given ambiguous sentences, such as "the man chased the woman on the bicycle," and a picture to show which meaning they intended. They read the sentences aloud to a partner, who had to pick the meaning.
The speakers estimated that their partners understood them correctly about seventy-two percent of the time. In fact, the partners picked the right meaning only about sixty-one percent of the time, not much better than a coin toss. The speakers couldn't help hearing the sentence in the way they meant. It's called the curse of knowledge. When you want to be understood, it's best to check, and not to assume that you were clear.
How well do we read each other's minds?

In 1990 William Ickes and his colleagues asked pairs of strangers to sit together for six minutes in a room, and chat while they were filmed. Afterward, each person watched the tape alone, and wrote down what they had been thinking and feeling at certain points. Then each watched again, and tried to guess what their partner had been thinking at those moments.
Strangers were right about one fifth of the time, in their guesses about thoughts and feelings. Close friends did a little better, about a third. And the accuracy rose only slightly with the length of the friendship. Ickes called it empathic accuracy. It's a task at which most of us are mediocre, even with those we are close to.

Jerry Harvey, a professor of management, told a story about his own family. One hot afternoon in Texas, in a town called Coleman, the family was playing dominoes on the porch. His father-in-law suggested that they drive to Abilene, fifty-three miles away, to have dinner at a cafeteria. Harvey thought it was a crazy idea, but said that it sounded fine. The others agreed.
The trip was in a car without air conditioning, in a dust storm, with a temperature of a hundred and four degrees, and the food was bad. Back at home, they discovered that none of them had wanted to go. Each had gone along, because they thought the others wanted to. Harvey called it the Abilene paradox, the situation in which a group does something that no member wants, since each is afraid to speak up. It is a failure of communication, and not of decision.

When someone answers a question, we judge how sure they are, not just from the words, but from the way they speak. In 1993 Vicki Smith and Herbert Clark asked people trivia questions, such as, who was the first man on the Moon. They noted the answers, and how they were said, and then asked the people how sure they were.
People who were unsure took longer to answer, used fillers such as um and uh, and ended with a rising tone, as if asking. In 1995 Susan Brennan and Maurice Williams played recordings of the answers to other listeners, who were asked to judge how likely it was that the speaker knew the answer. They used the same cues. A listener can tell what a speaker's own memory is saying. It's a case in which metacognition is visible in speech.

We usually assume that a confident speaker is more convincing. In 2010 Uma Karmarkar and Zakary Tormala tested what happens when a speaker says that they are uncertain. People read reviews of a product. Some were written by an expert, and some by a nonexpert. In some, the reviewer said that they were certain, and in others, that they were not sure.
When the reviewer was a nonexpert, certainty was more persuasive. But when the reviewer was an expert, and showed uncertainty, readers paid more attention, and were more persuaded than when the expert was certain. They seemed to think that if an expert is unsure, it must be a hard question, and they worked harder to understand the reasons. Admitting doubt can be a strength, if you are known to know.

If you have to decide whom to believe, who do you pick? In 2004 Paul Price and Eric Stone ran a series of experiments in which people received advice from several sources. In one, students were asked to estimate the answers to factual questions, and each advisor gave a range.
The students picked the advisors who gave the narrowest ranges, which signaled the greatest confidence, even when they were told that the advisors were no more accurate. It's called the confidence heuristic. We take confidence as a sign of knowledge. In real life, it's often a reasonable rule, but it makes us vulnerable to people who sound sure and are wrong. It's a reason to ask what a person's track record is, and not just how they sound.

When someone says thank you in a flat voice, or says it's fine with an irritated tone, which do you pay attention to, the meaning of the words, or the sound? In 2003 Keiko Ishii, José Reyes and Shinobu Kitayama tested Americans and Japanese. Participants heard words with a pleasant or unpleasant meaning, such as congratulations or disgusting, spoken in a pleasant or unpleasant tone. They had to say whether the word's meaning, or the tone, was pleasant.
The Americans found it easier to attend to the words, and to ignore the tone. The Japanese found it easier to attend to the tone, and were slowed down by it when it conflicted with the words. The researchers suggested that in cultures that depend more on context, people have learned to listen to how things are said. It's a reminder that misunderstandings can arise from a difference in what people attend to.
Screen time in the toddler years

How does the amount of time that young children spend in front of screens affect their development? In 2019 Sheri Madigan and her colleagues in Canada followed about twenty-five hundred children in Calgary. Their mothers reported how many hours a day the children watched television and used other screens at the ages of two, three and five. The children were assessed on communication, motor skills, problem solving and social skills at each age.
Children who had more screen time at two and three did worse on the tests at three and five. The link held after accounting for family income and parenting. It does not prove that screens caused the delays, since a child who is developing more slowly may get more screen time. But the pattern was consistent, and it fits the advice of pediatricians that young children need talk, play and interaction more than screens.

In the 1980s the Harvard psychologist Jerome Kagan studied four-month-old babies. He showed them new things, such as mobiles, voices and smells. About one baby in five reacted strongly, with vigorous movements, arching of the back and crying. About two in five were calm. He called the first group high-reactive and the second low-reactive.
He followed the children for years. Many of the high-reactive infants became shy and cautious toddlers, and some were anxious as teenagers. Many of the low-reactive children were bold and outgoing. The link was far from perfect, and experiences changed the course for many children. High-reactive children raised by warm and encouraging parents were often less shy. Still, it was strong evidence that people differ in temperament from the first months of life.
Do parents matter less than peers?

In 1998 the writer Judith Rich Harris published a book that made a provocative claim. Her argument was that parents have much less effect on how their children turn out than most people think. She pointed to studies of twins and adopted children, which show that genes explain a large share of personality, and that the shared home environment explains very little. She argued that the other big influence is peers.
Children, she said, learn how to behave from the groups they belong to, and not from their parents. They may behave one way at home and another way at school. The book was a bestseller, and was criticized strongly. Critics said that parents matter for many things, such as values, health habits and a child's sense of security, and that parents influence which peers a child has. Most psychologists now accept a part of her argument, but not the strong version.

In 2010 Mariah Evans and her colleagues analyzed surveys from twenty-seven countries, with more than seventy thousand people. Each respondent was asked about how many books there had been in their home when they were sixteen, and how much education they had attained. They compared the results, while accounting for the education of the parents, and the family's wealth.
The more books there were at home, the more years of schooling the person went on to complete. Growing up in a home with five hundred books or more was associated with about three years more education than growing up with very few. Even a small library, of twenty books, made a difference. The study can't prove that books were the cause, since homes with books differ in many ways. But it's a reminder of how reading at home may support learning.

Do toddlers learn more words if their parents talk to them more? In 2013 Adriana Weisleder and Anne Fernald studied twenty-nine Spanish-speaking families with low incomes in California. They recorded entire days in the homes of the children, at the age of nineteen months, using a small recorder in a vest, and counted the words that were spoken to the children.
The amount of speech that was directed at the child varied very widely from one family to another. At twenty-four months, the children who heard more speech from caregivers knew more words, and were quicker at recognizing them. Speech that was just overheard in the room was not related to learning. What counted was talk that was directed at the child. It supports the advice to chat with babies and toddlers.

In 2013 Elizabeth Gunderson, Susan Levine and their colleagues at the University of Chicago studied how parents praise their young children. They made video recordings of fifty-three parents and children, at home, on three occasions, when the children were between fourteen and thirty-eight months old. They counted the praise that focused on the child's effort or strategy, such as you worked hard, and the praise that focused on the child's traits, such as you're so smart.
When the children were seven or eight, they were asked questions about their beliefs. Those whose parents had given more praise for effort, when they were toddlers, were more likely to believe that intelligence can grow with effort. The link was stronger than for any other aspect of the parents' style that they measured. It shows that the habits of praise may start to shape a child's mindset very early.
Does more time with mother help?

Many parents worry that they don't spend enough time with their children. In 2015 Melissa Milkie, Kei Nomaguchi and Kathleen Denny analyzed data from a large American study, which followed more than a thousand families from 1997 to 2014. They looked at the hours that mothers spent with their children, and at how the children fared, in behavior, emotions and test scores.
For children aged three to eleven, the amount of time that mothers spent with them made almost no difference to the outcomes. What mattered more was the quality of the time, and the mother's stress. A stressed, tired mother seemed to do harm. For adolescents, time spent together was related to fewer delinquent behaviors, though not to other measures. The findings suggest that the quality of time, and the parents' well-being, matter more than the number of hours.

Almost all children lie at some time, and it starts early. In 2002 Victoria Talwar and Kang Lee tested the honesty of young children with a peeking game. A child was left alone in a room with a toy hidden behind them, and told not to peek. A researcher returned and asked whether the child had peeked. Many of the three-year-olds lied, about a third. By the age of seven, most did.
The older children also lied more skillfully. They could keep their stories consistent, and faked a surprised reaction. In 2011 the researchers found that children in a school with harsh punishments lied more than those in a school with a gentler approach. Lying is a sign of developing thinking. It requires a child to understand that others have beliefs which can be changed. Punishment makes it more likely, and not less.
When does the window for grammar close?

It's often said that children learn languages better than adults. But when exactly does the ability fall, and how fast? In 2018 Joshua Hartshorne, Joshua Tenenbaum and Steven Pinker put a grammar quiz online. It was taken by about two-thirds of a million people, from many countries, who had begun learning English at all kinds of ages. Because the quiz went viral, the sample was far larger than any lab could recruit.
The ability to pick up grammar stayed high until about the age of seventeen, and only then began to decline. That is much later than most researchers had expected. Reaching a fully native-like level still seemed to need an early start, but people who began later could reach a high level. The authors suggested that the decline may reflect changes in life, such as leaving school and having less time for immersion, as well as biology. Starting early helps, but starting late is not hopeless.
No sudden end to the learning years

Is there a sudden end to the best years for learning a language, as the critical period idea says, or does the ability fade slowly? In 2003 Kenji Hakuta, Ellen Bialystok and Edward Wiley used the 1990 United States census, which asked immigrants how well they spoke English. They looked at about 2.3 million people from Spanish and Chinese speaking backgrounds, and at the age at which each person had arrived.
If a critical period existed, they argued, there should be a sharp break in the results at some age. They tested for a break at fifteen and at twenty, and found none. English skill fell steadily as the age of arrival rose, with no sudden jump. A critic challenged how the data were analyzed, and the authors replied that further tests gave the same answer. The debate over the critical period is not settled, but this study made the case for a gradual decline.

Many people learn a language by watching films with subtitles. Does it help? In 2009 Holger Mitterer and James McQueen tested Dutch students who found Scottish and Australian English hard to understand. The students watched short videos with Dutch subtitles, with English subtitles that matched what was said, or with no subtitles. Afterward, they had to repeat what they heard in audio clips.
English subtitles gave the best results, both for clips the students had seen and for new clips in the same accents. Dutch subtitles helped with the clips they had already seen, but made them worse at understanding new ones. The researchers suggested that the viewers used the meaning given in their own language to decode the speech, and so did not learn how the accent sounded. If you want to learn from a film, use subtitles in the language of the film.
How many words do you need?

How many words must a learner know to read a book or follow a conversation? In 2006 the linguist Paul Nation analyzed large collections of written and spoken English, and counted how much of each text is covered by the most common words. He counted word families, such as help, helps, helped and helpful, as a single item.
The most common few thousand families cover most of the words in everyday English, but the last few percent are hard to get. To know about ninety-eight percent of the words, which is roughly what is needed to read without help, takes eight to nine thousand families for written text, and six to seven thousand for speech. So the first words are the most valuable, and each later word brings less. It makes sense to learn the most common words first.

Can you learn a language in your sleep? Earlier studies found that people do not learn new material that is played to them while they are asleep. In 2015 Thomas Schreiner and Björn Rasch tried something more modest, which was to use sleep to strengthen words that had already been learned. German speakers studied Dutch words with their German translations in the evening, and then slept in a lab. During deep sleep, some of the Dutch words were quietly played again, without the translations.
The next morning, the sleepers remembered the translations of the replayed words better than those of the words that were not replayed. The words that were not replayed were remembered about as well as in a group that heard nothing. Replaying the words while people were awake did not help. The cue seems to reactivate a memory that is already there, so the words had to be studied first. It is a lab finding, and not a shortcut to learning.

Does learning a second language leave a mark on the brain? In 2004 Andrea Mechelli and her colleagues at University College London scanned the brains of eighty-three people. Twenty-five spoke only one language. The others spoke English and Italian, twenty-five of whom had learned their second language early in life, and thirty-three later. The scans measured the density of gray matter, the tissue that contains the cell bodies of neurons.
The bilingual people had denser gray matter in the left inferior parietal cortex, a region involved in language, than the others. The difference was larger in those who had learned their second language early, and it was related to how well they spoke it. That fits the idea that the brain changes with experience. But a scan is a snapshot, so it cannot show which came first, and later studies that followed people as they learned were needed to test the idea.

In 1947 almost every eleven-year-old in Scotland took an intelligence test. In 2008 to 2010, Thomas Bak and his colleagues at the University of Edinburgh tracked down 853 of the people born in 1936 who had taken it, and tested them again at about seventy-three. Of these, 262 said that they spoke at least one language besides English. The researchers asked whether the later test results were better or worse than the scores at eleven would predict.
The bilingual people did better than predicted, especially in general intelligence and reading. The benefit appeared even in those who had learned their second language as adults. The effect was small, and the study was observational, so it cannot show that language learning caused the difference. Other studies of bilingualism and aging have had mixed results. It is a promising hint, but not a proof.

Language apps have millions of users, but do they teach? In 2012 Roumen Vesselinov, of Queens College, and John Grego, of the University of South Carolina, studied the best known of them, Duolingo. The company paid for the study, and the researchers say that they did the analysis independently. Volunteers who answered an ad took a Spanish test, used the app for about eight weeks, and took a test again.
The report estimated that about thirty-four hours of use equaled a semester of college Spanish. Critics pointed out that the volunteers answered an ad, and that the study did not show that the app was better than other ways of learning. Independent research on language apps is limited. They may help with vocabulary and with building a daily habit, but it is good to add real conversation as well.
Why English is hard to learn to read

Why does learning to read English take children so long? In 2003 Philip Seymour, Mikko Aro and Jane Erskine tested young children in thirteen European writing systems, including English. They checked how well children in their first year of school knew their letters, read familiar words, and sounded out simple made-up words.
Most European children became accurate and fluent by the end of the first year. The exceptions were children learning French, Portuguese, Danish and, above all, English. English reading developed more than twice as slowly as in the languages with the most regular spelling, such as Finnish and Italian. The gap was not explained by when the children started school or by how well they knew their letters. It was the spelling system itself, in which one letter can stand for many sounds, that made the first steps slower.

Dyslexia is a difficulty with reading, and it is found in every country. But does it look the same in every language? In 2001 Eraldo Paulesu and an international team studied dyslexic adults in Italy, France and Britain, and compared them with ordinary readers in each country. They tested reading and sound skills, and used PET scans to look at brain activity during reading.
The Italian dyslexic readers did better at reading than the French and British ones, since Italian spelling is regular and easier to sound out. But compared with the ordinary readers in their own country, all three groups were equally impaired, and all showed reduced activity in the same region of the left temporal lobe. The researchers concluded that dyslexia has a common biological basis, and that the language decides how much it shows. A later study of Chinese readers suggested that the brain differences may depend on the writing system.

Is it easier to remember foreign phrases if you sing them? In a study published in 2014, Karen Ludke and her colleagues taught Hungarian phrases to sixty adults who did not know the language. They were assigned at random to learn by speaking the phrases, by speaking them in rhythm, or by singing them to a simple tune. Each group had fifteen minutes.
Afterward, all of them were tested. The singing group did better overall than the other two, and it was best at remembering the phrases word for word. Because one group spoke in rhythm, the benefit was not due to rhythm alone. A tune may link the words together, so that each one cues the next. It was a short test with phrases, and not a whole language, but it suggests that a song is a good way to hold a phrase in mind.

Do hand gestures help us remember new words? In 2011 Manuela Macedonia and her colleagues at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig taught adults new words from an artificial language. Some of the words were paired with gestures that acted out the meaning, and others with gestures that had nothing to do with it.
The words that were learned with meaningful gestures were remembered better over time. When the learners later recognized the words inside a brain scanner, the movement areas of their cortex were active for those words, as if the memory included the action. The effect is not guaranteed, since some later studies found that gestures can sometimes get in the way of learning words. Still, if you are learning vocabulary, it is worth trying to act the words out.

Do we make different decisions in a foreign language? In 2012 Boaz Keysar, Sayuri Hayakawa and Sun Gyu An tested students who had learned a foreign language in class. In one test, people read a problem about a disease outbreak, in which the same outcome was described either as lives saved or as lives lost. In their own language, people usually chose differently depending on the wording.
In the foreign language, that effect mostly disappeared. In other experiments, people were more willing to accept bets with a good expected payoff, so they seemed less afraid of losing. The researchers suggested that a foreign language creates distance, and moves us from gut feelings toward slower, more deliberate thinking. Others have suggested that it simply carries less emotion. The effect has been found with many languages, but how it works is still debated.
The baboon troop that turned peaceful

In the 1980s the neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky was studying a troop of wild olive baboons in Kenya, which he called the Forest Troop. Baboon troops are usually harsh places, where males fight for rank and take out their stress on those below them. Then the most aggressive males in this troop died, after eating food from a garbage dump. The females and the less aggressive males, who had not gone to the dump, were left.
Over the next years the troop became unusually relaxed. The remaining males groomed the females more, the hierarchy was less harsh, and their stress hormone levels were lower than in neighboring troops. Even more striking, males who joined later from other troops took up the same relaxed habits. The authors described it as a culture that was passed on. It was one troop, so it is a case and not a rule, but it shows how much a social setting can shape what a primate does.

In 2005 the psychologist Barbara Fredrickson and Marcial Losada reported a number that sounded like a rule for a good life. People who had at least 2.9013 positive feelings for each negative one, they said, flourished, and below that they languished. The number was said to come from a mathematical model borrowed from the study of fluid flow, called the Lorenz equations, and it spread through books, talks and corporate training.
In 2013 Nicholas Brown, Alan Sokal and Harris Friedman examined the mathematics, and found no reason to use equations about fluids to describe emotions. Fredrickson and Losada withdrew the modeling part of their paper. Fredrickson still holds that positive emotions matter, and points to other studies. But the exact ratio has no basis. The episode is a lesson that a precise number can sound more scientific than the evidence behind it.
Does the body know before you do?

In the Iowa Gambling Task, a player picks cards from four decks, and wins or loses money. Two of the decks give big wins but even bigger losses, and two give small wins and smaller losses, so the first pair is a bad bet. In 1997 Antoine Bechara, Antonio Damasio and their colleagues tested healthy volunteers, and patients with damage to the front of the brain who had made poor decisions in real life. They also measured the sweat on the players' skin.
Healthy players began to prefer the good decks before they could say which were good, and showed a sweat response just before reaching for a bad deck. The patients never developed that response, and kept choosing the bad decks even after they knew the better strategy. It suggested that the body gives hunches before conscious knowledge does. Later, Maia and McClelland argued that people knew more than the early tests showed, and the debate continues.
Does a correction make a false belief stronger?

Some people fear that correcting a false belief only makes it stronger. In 2010 Brendan Nyhan and Jason Reifler gave people news stories that contained a false claim, followed by a correction, such as the claim that weapons of mass destruction had been found in Iraq. For some people whose politics favored the claim, the correction seemed to make them believe it more. It was called the backfire effect, and it was widely repeated.
In 2019 Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter tested 52 issues, in five studies with more than ten thousand people. They did not find a correction that caused backfire, even on divisive issues. People who saw the facts moved toward them, even when they disliked them. Backfire may happen in some cases, but it does not look like the rule. It seems to be worth correcting a false claim.

Most people think that they are less likely than average to suffer a divorce, a disease or a theft. In 2011 Tali Sharot and her colleagues set out to see how that belief survives the facts. They asked people to estimate their own chances of eighty bad events, such as getting cancer or having a car stolen. Then they showed them the true average risk, and asked again, while a scanner recorded their brains.
People changed their estimates more when the truth was better than they had feared than when it was worse. Parts of the prefrontal cortex tracked the surprises about good news well. The most optimistic people tracked the surprises about bad news less. Later work found that disrupting a region of the right frontal cortex with magnetic stimulation reduced the difference. So optimism is not only a feeling. It is partly a way of updating.
The same film, a different soundtrack

How much stress a scene causes depends on more than the scene. In the early 1960s Richard Lazarus and his colleagues showed volunteers a disturbing film, called Subincision, about a crude surgical ritual among Aboriginal Australians. The picture was always the same, but the sound was changed. One version had a soundtrack that dwelt on the pain and the danger. Another denied the pain, and said that the people were happy. A third gave a calm anthropological commentary.
The viewers' heart rates and skin responses were measured, and they also rated how they felt. The soundtrack that stressed the trauma produced the most stress, while the denial and the detached commentary produced less. Lazarus later built a theory on this, that stress depends on how we appraise an event, and not only on the event. It suggests that the story we tell ourselves about something can change how the body reacts.

In 1967 Stanley Milgram gave packages to people in the American Midwest, and asked them to get each one to a stranger near Boston by passing it only to someone they knew on a first-name basis. Some chains reached the target, which led to the idea of six degrees of separation. In 2003 Peter Dodds, Roby Muhamad and Duncan Watts repeated the experiment with email, on a global scale. More than sixty thousand people tried to reach one of eighteen targets, in thirteen countries.
Most of the chains broke, since people did not pass the message on, so the researchers corrected for the dropouts. They estimated that it takes a median of five to seven steps to reach a stranger anywhere in the world. The chains that succeeded went mostly through weaker ties, such as work contacts, and not through close friends. Your acquaintances matter because they know different people than you do.

When you recall a photograph, how much of the scene do you think was in it? In 1989 Helene Intraub and Michael Richardson showed people pictures of scenes, and some time later asked them to judge whether new pictures were the same as the ones they had seen, or closer, or wider. Some of the pictures were close-ups, and others were wider views.
People tended to remember the close-up views as wider than they had been. When they were shown the same close-up again, they said that it looked too close, as if it had been cropped. The mind seems to fill in the space just beyond the edge of what we see, based on what we expect. The effect has been called boundary extension. It is a small example of how a memory is partly built from expectation, and is not only a recording.

Where were you when you heard about the attacks of September 11? Many people feel that their memory of that day is as clear as a photograph. In 2003 Jennifer Talarico and David Rubin tested that feeling. The day after the attacks, students at Duke University wrote down how they had heard the news. They also wrote down a recent everyday event. Later, groups of them were tested again, after one, six or thirty-two weeks.
The students' accuracy fell at the same rate for the news of September 11 and for the everyday events. But their confidence did not fall in the same way. They stayed as sure of the vivid memory as they had been, while their belief in the ordinary memories declined. So memories of big events are not special in being right, but in feeling right. The more emotion people felt at the time, the more sure they were later, but not the more accurate.
A touch and a bigger tip

Can a very small gesture change how much people pay? In 1984 April Crusco and Christopher Wetzel arranged for waitresses in a restaurant to touch some of the customers briefly, when they returned the change. For some customers the touch was on the hand, for others on the shoulder, and for the rest there was no touch. The researchers recorded the tips.
Customers who were touched left larger tips than those who were not, and it made little difference whether the touch was on the hand or the shoulder, or whether the customer was a man or a woman. The touch did not change how the customers rated the waitress or the restaurant, so it worked without changing what they said they felt. Small signs of warmth can change behavior, but this was one early field experiment in a single setting.

Suppose that you must meet a stranger in New York City tomorrow, and neither of you can communicate with the other beforehand. Where, and when, do you go? In his 1960 book The Strategy of Conflict, the economist Thomas Schelling put the question to his students. The most common answer was the information booth at Grand Central Terminal, at noon. They had no way of agreeing, but they landed on the same spot.
Schelling called such a spot a focal point. It is a choice that stands out, so each person expects the other to pick it. People use focal points when they choose heads over tails, or a round number. Schelling shared the Nobel Prize in economics in 2005 for his work on conflict and cooperation. In a negotiation, a clear landmark, such as a round number or a past precedent, can help two sides to settle.
The man who lived in the present

In March of 1985 the British musician Clive Wearing, a leading expert on early music who worked for BBC Radio 3, caught a viral infection of the brain, called herpes encephalitis. He survived, but the infection damaged parts of the brain which are needed to form new memories. He could remember for only a few seconds, between seven and thirty by different estimates. After that, each moment felt to him as if he had just woken up.
His diary shows the effect. Again and again he wrote that he was awake for the first time, and he recorded it with relief. Yet he kept his musical skill, and his love for his wife, Deborah, which she said never faded. His case shows that there are different kinds of memory, and that the memory for skills and for feelings can survive when the memory for events is lost.
Why a hard initiation makes a group seem better

Do people value something more if they had to suffer to get it? In 1959 Elliot Aronson and Judson Mills invited female volunteers to join a discussion group about the psychology of sex. To get in, some had to read a list of obscene words, and a vivid passage, aloud to a man. For others, the words were mild, and others went through no test. Then all of them listened to a recording of the group's discussion, which had been made to be dull.
The women who had gone through the severe test rated the group and its discussion as more interesting than the others did. The authors explained it by cognitive dissonance, since it is hard to believe that you went through something awful for nothing. Critics noted that contrast might explain the result, and later replications gave mixed results. It still helps to explain why hazing may raise loyalty, and why we should be wary of the things that we paid for dearly.

When you picture a map in your head, can you travel across it? In 1978 Stephen Kosslyn, Thomas Ball and Brian Reiser asked volunteers to memorize a map of an imaginary island, with landmarks such as a hut, a well and a tree. Then the map was taken away. The volunteers were asked to picture it, and to imagine a small dot moving from one landmark to another.
The longer the real distance between two landmarks, the longer the scan took, and the time grew in step with the distance. The mind's picture seemed to behave like a real map. Critics, such as Zenon Pylyshyn, argued that the volunteers may have known what was expected of them, and simply took longer for the farther places. The debate over mental images, and what they are made of, went on for years.
A survey of a hundred thousand IBM workers

In the late 1960s and early 1970s the Dutch researcher Geert Hofstede analyzed attitude surveys of employees of IBM in dozens of countries. There were more than a hundred thousand questionnaires. Because the people worked for one company, in similar jobs, he reasoned that differences in their answers came from national culture. He found that countries differed along a few dimensions, such as power distance, which measures how far people accept that power is unequal.
Another dimension was individualism, which is the degree to which people see themselves as individuals more than as members of groups. The ideas have been used widely, in business and in the study of communication across cultures. Critics point out that IBM employees are not typical of their countries, that the surveys were not made to study culture, and that cultures change. It is a useful starting point for talking about differences, but it should not be used to predict a single person.

In the mid-1930s Hans Selye, a young researcher at McGill University in Montreal, injected rats with an extract from the ovary, hoping to discover a new hormone. The rats showed three changes. The outer part of the adrenal glands grew larger, the thymus gland shrank, and the stomach and intestine developed ulcers. At first he believed that he had found a hormone. Then he found that the same changes followed other irritating substances, and also cold, injury or exhaustion.
In a short letter to Nature in 1936 he described a common reaction of the body to many kinds of harm. He later called it the general adaptation syndrome, and he became famous for bringing the word stress into the study of health. Many details of his picture have been revised since. But the idea that very different kinds of strain can trigger a shared response in the body remains central.
The powerful forget the other side

Draw the letter E on your own forehead, as fast as you can. Some people draw it so that it reads correctly to themselves, and others draw it so that it reads correctly to someone facing them. In 2006 Adam Galinsky, Joe Magee, Marlone Inesi and Deborah Gruenfeld first made volunteers feel powerful or powerless, by asking them to recall a time when they had power over others, or when others had power over them. Then they asked them to draw the E.
People who had been made to feel powerful were almost three times as likely to draw the E so that it faced themselves, and would look backward to anyone looking at them. In other experiments the powerful were less likely to allow that other people did not share their knowledge, and less accurate at reading the emotions on faces. The effects arose from a brief feeling of power. Studies of priming have been hard to repeat, so this is suggestive, but it is a good reason for anyone in charge to ask how things look from the other side.
Can an angry woman get ahead?

Is anger judged in the same way in a man and in a woman? In 2008 Victoria Brescoll and Eric Uhlmann asked people to evaluate men and women who showed anger or sadness at work. The raters were asked how much status each person deserved. They also looked at whether it mattered if the person was described as a trainee or as a chief executive.
Angry men were given more status than sad men. Angry women were given less status than angry men, and even a woman who was a chief executive was given less status if she showed anger than if she did not. People tended to explain a woman's anger by her character, as if she were out of control, and a man's anger by the situation. When a clear outside reason for the anger was given, the difference mostly went away. The study is about how others judge, and not about how anyone should feel.

Do people who have power talk more? In 2011 Victoria Brescoll measured how long each United States senator spoke on the Senate floor, during the sessions of 2005 and 2007. She compared the time with a score for each senator's power, which was given by a non-partisan firm. She also ran an experiment in which people read about a chief executive who spoke more than others.
For men, more power meant more talking. For women, it did not, since powerful women did not talk more than less powerful ones. In the experiment, a female executive who talked a lot was rated as less competent and less suitable for leadership than a male one who talked as much. The author suggested that powerful women hold back because they expect a penalty, and that they are right to expect it. It is a case in which a rule about speaking up applies differently to different people.
Women who succeed at men's jobs

When a woman succeeds in a job that is seen as a man's job, she is often liked less. In 2007 Madeline Heilman and Tyler Okimoto set out to find out why. In three experiments, people read about a manager who had succeeded in a job of that kind. Some read about a man, and some about a woman. Then they rated how likable and how hostile the manager seemed.
Their idea was that success in such a job suggests a lack of warmth and concern for others, which they called an implied communality deficit. When the evaluators were also given information that showed that the woman was caring, such as that she was a mother, or when she acted in a communal way, the penalty was reduced. It suggests that the dislike came from broken expectations, and not from the success itself. It is still true that expectations like that are unfair.
What an unfair offer does to the brain

In the ultimatum game, one player proposes how to split a sum of money, and another can accept, or reject, in which case both get nothing. A purely selfish responder would accept anything, since something is better than nothing. But people often reject offers that they see as unfair. In 2003 Alan Sanfey, James Rilling and their colleagues scanned the brains of responders as they received offers from other people, and from computers.
Unfair offers made the anterior insula active, a region that is linked with negative feelings, and the activity was stronger as the offer got less fair. It was especially strong before the responder rejected an offer. A region of the prefrontal cortex, which is tied to goals and reasoning, responded as well. The authors concluded that emotion plays a real part in economic choices. Later work has asked whether the insula signal means arousal, or the sense that a social rule was broken.
When a stereotype is named out loud

Do stereotypes change how people negotiate? In 2001 Laura Kray, Leigh Thompson and Adam Galinsky paired men and women in a negotiation exercise. Before it, some were told that the task was a very good measure of negotiating ability, which brings to mind the stereotype that men negotiate better. For others, the stereotype was not raised.
When the stereotype was raised in a subtle way, women did worse than men. But when the men were told outright that men tend to do better than women, the women did better than the men. The authors called this reactance, which is the urge to prove a stereotype wrong. Later work found that the effect depends on how the stereotype is raised, and on what it says. It suggests that the way a task is framed can change how people perform, in either direction.
When control is lost, patterns appear

Do we see patterns more when we feel that things are out of our control? In 2008 Jennifer Whitson and Adam Galinsky asked some people to recall a time when they had no control over what happened, and others to recall a time when they were in control. Then they gave them tasks. In one, they showed grainy pictures that were mostly visual noise, some of which hid a faint object.
People who had recalled losing control were more likely to see shapes in the noise. They were also more likely to see links in made-up stock market data, to believe in conspiracies and to hold superstitions. When they were first given a chance to think about their core values, the effect shrank. The samples in each study were small, but the idea is useful. When we feel helpless, the mind looks harder for order, even when there is none.

In 2014 a large group of researchers, led by Richard Klein, tested thirteen well-known findings in psychology, each in many places. The project, called Many Labs, used thirty-six samples, in laboratories and online, with a total of 6,344 people. They used the same procedures and materials for each one, and shared the data publicly.
Ten of the thirteen effects held up. One, in which imagining contact reduces prejudice, had weak support. Two did not replicate. In one of them, seeing the American flag was supposed to make people more conservative, and in the other, seeing money was supposed to make people defend the system more. The place and the type of sample made little difference. What mattered most was the effect itself. It shows that some findings are sturdy and some are not, and that you can find out by repeating them.
The honesty pledge and the invented data

In 2012 a team of five researchers reported a neat trick for making people more honest. When people signed a statement of honesty at the top of a form, before filling it in, they cheated less than when they signed at the bottom. One of the studies was a field test with a car insurance company, in which more than thirteen thousand customers reported the mileage of their cars. The paper appeared in a leading journal, and it was widely cited.
In 2020 the authors reported that they could not repeat the laboratory experiments. In 2021 other researchers, who run a blog called Data Colada, analyzed the posted data and showed that the insurance data had been fabricated, and the journal retracted the paper. Who altered the data has not been established. The episode is a reminder that a striking result with a simple cure needs to be checked more than once, and that checking is a job for the whole field.

On La Gomera, one of the Canary Islands, shepherds have long talked across deep valleys by whistling. The whistled speech is called Silbo Gomero, and it is a version of Spanish. The whistler turns the sounds of the words into pitch and rhythm, and a skilled listener can understand a message from far across a ravine. In 2005 Manuel Carreiras and his colleagues put five whistlers and five Spanish speakers who did not know Silbo into a brain scanner.
Both groups showed similar activity when they heard ordinary Spanish. When they heard whistled sentences, only the whistlers used the regions of the left temporal lobe that handle speech. The others used areas that are not tied to language. The brain treated the whistles as words, when the person knew how. One of the researchers pointed out that Silbo is not a full language of its own, since children are not born whistling it. It is a way of carrying Spanish on a different sound.

Do people talk like their class, or like their friends? In the early 1980s the linguist Penelope Eckert spent two years at a high school in the suburbs of Detroit, which she called Belten High, and shorter periods at four other schools. She found that the students were divided into two main groups. The jocks were centered on the school and its activities. The burnouts were centered on the local area and the city.
She measured the vowels that the students used, which in the Detroit area were changing in a pattern known as the Northern Cities Shift. The pronunciations tended to follow the social group, and not only the parents' income. The burnouts used the newest forms more than the jocks did. A way of speaking can be a badge, which shows who you spend time with and what you stand for. Language change often moves through groups like these, and not through whole towns at once.

Most linguists have long held that the sound of a word has nothing to do with its meaning. The word dog does not sound like a dog, and other languages use other sounds. In 2016 Damián Blasi and his colleagues checked this with word lists that covered nearly two thirds of the world's languages. They looked at a hundred basic words, such as nose, tongue, small and full, and asked whether certain sounds were used for them more often than chance would predict.
Some were. Words for nose tend to have an n sound, words for tongue an l, words for small an i, and words for full a p or b. The patterns recurred in different continents and language families, and they seemed to have arisen independently. Some researchers point out that earlier work had also found links between sound and meaning. It does not mean that the sounds are fixed, only that the link between sound and meaning is not always arbitrary.

In the sentence Clover ate a mouse, the subject comes first, then the verb, then the object. English does it that way, and so do Spanish, Russian and Mandarin. But in the World Atlas of Language Structures, which surveys 1,377 languages, the most common order is a different one. The subject comes first, then the object, and the verb comes last. About 565 languages, or 41 percent, do it that way, including Japanese, Korean, Turkish and Hindi.
The order that English uses comes second, with 488 languages, or 35 percent. Languages in which the verb comes first, such as Welsh, make up about 7 percent, and the other orders are rare. A few languages put the object first, and the invented language Klingon was designed to put the object before the verb and the subject last. The speakers of each language find their own order natural, but it is only one of the ways in which the same idea can be built.
A judge in Calcutta notices a pattern

In 1786 William Jones, a British judge who worked in Calcutta and who had learned Sanskrit, gave a talk to the Asiatic Society that he had founded. He said that Sanskrit, however old it was, had a structure that was wonderful, and that it was more perfect than Greek and richer than Latin. Then he made a larger point. It had a stronger likeness to both of them, in the roots of the verbs and in the forms of the grammar, than could have been produced by accident.
He suggested that the three had sprung from a common source which perhaps no longer existed. He also thought that Gothic, Celtic and Persian might belong to the same family. It was not the first time the resemblance had been noticed, but his clear statement is often seen as the start of the study of Indo-European languages. From that idea came the search for the reconstructed ancestor, which is now called Proto-Indo-European, and for the people who spoke it.

The Indo-European languages, from English and Hindi to Russian and Persian, share an ancestor, but where and when it was spoken is disputed. One view puts it on the steppe north of the Black Sea, about 6,000 years ago. Another puts it in Anatolia, in what is now Turkey, with farmers who spread out about 8,000 years ago. In 2012 Remco Bouckaert and his colleagues took basic vocabulary from 103 ancient and modern languages and used statistical methods developed to trace the spread of viruses.
They found strong support for Anatolia, with a date between about 7,800 and 9,800 years ago. Critics were not convinced. They questioned the statistical methods, and pointed to words for wheeled vehicles, which seem to have been shared at a later time and which fit the steppe story. Later studies of ancient DNA have mostly favored the steppe story, though the question is still discussed. It is an example of a question where different kinds of evidence can pull in different directions.

Ethnologue, a catalog of the world's languages, counts about 7,160 that are in use today. The number changes from year to year, because it is hard to decide where one language ends and a dialect begins. They are not spread evenly. Papua New Guinea alone has more than eight hundred, and many of them are spoken by only a few thousand people.
About 40 percent of all languages are classed as endangered, which is more than three thousand of them, and many have fewer than a thousand speakers left. A language is usually lost not in one stroke, but when children stop learning it, because the parents think that another language will give them better chances. When the last fluent speaker dies, the stories, names and ways of describing the world that were carried in the language go with it. Some communities are working to revive theirs, with classes and recordings.
Time that runs from east to west

In English, we speak of the future as ahead, and we lay out time from left to right, as on a calendar. In Kuuk Thaayorre, a language spoken in the community of Pormpuraaw in northern Australia, there are few words for left and right. People use compass directions for everything, even small distances, and they greet each other by asking where they are going, in terms such as north-northeast.
In 2010 Lera Boroditsky and Alice Gaby gave sets of picture cards to fourteen people from Pormpuraaw and fourteen students at Stanford. Each set showed a progression, such as a person growing older, and was shuffled. The participants were asked to lay out the cards in the order of time. The students put them from left to right. The Kuuk Thaayorre speakers put them from east to west, no matter which way they were facing. Their language, it seems, taught them to keep track of direction at all times.

When adults speak to babies they change their voices. The pitch rises, the pace slows and the vowels are drawn out. It is often called baby talk, or parentese. In 1997 Patricia Kuhl and her colleagues recorded thirty mothers who spoke English, Russian and Swedish, first to another adult and then to their baby. They analyzed more than two thousand words.
In all three languages, the mothers stretched their vowels more when they spoke to the baby. The vowels were pushed farther apart from one another, so that they were easier to tell apart. Kuhl suggested that it helps infants to learn the sounds of their language. Some later work found that the vowels in baby talk overlap more than this suggests, and the benefit is debated. But it is a striking fact that parents on different continents do the same thing, without being taught.

We say that someone attacked a weak point in an argument, that a claim was defended, that a position was indefensible, and that a debate was won or lost. In 1980 George Lakoff and Mark Johnson pointed out how much of everyday talk about arguments uses the language of war. They said that this was not decoration. It showed that we think about arguments as a kind of fight, and so we act in that way.
They gave other examples. We spend, waste and save time, as if it were money. We speak of ideas as being on a path, and of life as a journey. Their book argued that abstract thought is built on metaphors drawn from bodily and physical experience. The evidence in it was mostly from the patterns of language, and not from experiments, and some linguists disagree. Later experiments have shown that a metaphor can change how people reason.

When people who have no common language have to work together, they invent a simple way to talk, which is called a pidgin. A pidgin has a small vocabulary and little grammar. It happened on sugar plantations in Hawaii, where workers came from China, Japan, Portugal and the Philippines, and their children grew up hearing it. The linguist Derek Bickerton studied what happened next.
The children did not just copy the pidgin. They made a fuller language of it, with a consistent grammar, which is called a creole. Bickerton argued that children are born with a built-in ability to make grammar, and that this explains how creoles arise so quickly.
