Other linguists think that the change was more gradual, and that other languages had an influence. Tok Pisin, which began as a pidgin and is now an official language of Papua New Guinea, shows how a language like that can grow.

Many people mean to save for retirement and never get around to signing up. In 2001 Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea studied a large American company that changed how it enrolled new employees in its retirement plan. Before, employees had to choose to join. Afterward, they were joined automatically, at a set contribution rate, and could opt out if they wished.
Participation among new employees roughly doubled. But many of them stayed with the default amounts, which were low, at 3 percent of pay in a very safe fund, and which they might never have chosen on their own. The default seemed to serve as a signal of what the company thought was right, and as a path of least effort. The finding helped to inspire rules that made automatic enrollment easier for employers, and a debate on how high the default should be.

In 2008 New York City began to enforce a rule that chain restaurants must post the calories of their items. Bryan Bollinger, Phillip Leslie and Alan Sorensen obtained the records of every purchase at the Starbucks stores in New York, Boston and Philadelphia, from January 2008 to February 2009. Boston and Philadelphia had no such rule, so they could serve as a comparison.
In New York the average calories per purchase fell by about 6 percent, from 247 to 232. Almost all of the drop came from food, as people bought fewer items or lower-calorie ones, and not from drinks. The effect was larger among the customers who usually bought the most, who cut about a quarter. The authors cautioned that a drop of 6 percent is too small to make a big difference to the nation's health on its own.

When people have a little spare money, they usually buy things. In 2017 Ashley Whillans, Elizabeth Dunn and their colleagues asked whether it is better to buy time, by paying someone to do the chores that we dislike. They surveyed more than six thousand adults in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands about how they spent their money, and how satisfied they were with life.
People who spent money to save time, for example on cleaning or delivery, reported greater satisfaction, and this was so at different income levels. In an experiment with sixty working adults in Vancouver, each person was given forty dollars on two weekends, to spend on a time-saving purchase on one weekend and on a material purchase on the other. They felt happier after the time purchase. The effects were modest, but they suggest that for many people a chore is worth paying to avoid.
The white wine that was dyed red

How much does the color of a drink change the way it smells? In 2001 Gil Morrot, Frédérique Brochet and Denis Dubourdieu, from Bordeaux, a center of wine research, asked wine tasters to describe the aromas of a white wine. Later they asked them to describe the same wine, after it had been colored red with an odorless dye.
The tasters described the dyed wine with the words that they usually use for red wines, such as cherry and prune, though it was the same white wine. They were fooled by the color. A later study, by Ballester and colleagues in 2009, found a similar result, but also noted problems with the method of the first. The study suggests that smell is not a clean channel, and that what we see changes what we perceive.

Does the sound of food change how it tastes? In 2004 Massimiliano Zampini and Charles Spence asked people to bite into potato chips with their front teeth, and to rate how crisp and how fresh each one was. The people wore headphones. The sound of their own biting was picked up by a microphone, altered, and played back to them as they bit.
When the sound was louder, or when the high frequencies were boosted, the chips seemed crisper and fresher, even though they were the same chips. Only the sound had been changed. The study won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2008. It suggests that the makers of snacks have a reason to care about how their products sound, as well as how they look and taste.

Do people who prefer a brand of beer know it by its taste? In 1964 Ralph Allison and Kenneth Uhl asked beer drinkers to taste several beers, first with the labels hidden, and then with the brand names shown. The beers were the major brands. They asked the drinkers to rate the beers on taste, with measures such as strength and bitterness, and to give an overall rating.
With the labels hidden, the drinkers could not tell the brands apart, and could not pick out their usual brand. When they could see the labels, their ratings changed to fit what they believed about each brand. The taste that people reported was partly the reputation of the beer. It was an early demonstration that the brand, and not only the product, shapes the experience.

Imagine that you bought an apartment for a high price, and now the market has fallen. Should that change what you ask for it? Economists say that the price you paid is gone, and only the current market should matter. In 2001 David Genesove and Christopher Mayer looked at sales of condominiums in downtown Boston in the 1990s, and compared the owners who would sell at a loss with those who would not.
Owners who faced a loss on paper set higher asking prices. The markup was about a quarter to a third of the gap between what the unit was probably worth and what they had paid. They also tended to hold on longer, and got somewhat higher prices, but not as high as they asked. It is loss aversion at work, since people dislike locking in a loss. It helps to explain why housing sales slow down when prices fall.

We talk about brands as if they were people. One is honest, another is daring, another is stuffy. In 1997 Jennifer Aaker asked whether people agree about this. She had people rate well-known brands on a long list of human traits, and then analyzed which traits go together, as is done in studies of human personality.
She found five groups of traits. They were sincerity, as in down-to-earth and honest, excitement, as in daring and spirited, competence, as in reliable and successful, sophistication, as in upper class and charming, and ruggedness, as in outdoorsy and tough. Later studies found that these five do not hold up in every country. But the idea that a brand has a personality that people can describe is now used widely in marketing.
Do drivers of fancy cars give way?

In 2012 Paul Piff, Dacher Keltner and their colleagues asked whether people with more money behave less ethically. Observers watched drivers at a busy intersection in the San Francisco Bay Area, and rated how expensive each car was. Then they watched the drivers at a crosswalk, where a person was waiting to cross.
Drivers of more expensive cars were more likely to cut off other cars, and less likely to stop for the person waiting to cross. In a laboratory study, students who said that they came from a higher social class were more likely to take candy that was meant for children. The authors suggested that having more resources makes people more focused on themselves. Other researchers have not always found the same, and the question is still debated.

Do shops sell more if they smell good? In 1996 Eric Spangenberg, Ayn Crowley and Pamela Henderson tested the idea in a simulated store, in which they spread a pleasant scent in the air in some conditions, and used no scent in others. Mostly students were asked to evaluate the store and its products, and to say what they meant to do.
In the scented store, people rated the store and its products more highly, and said that they were more likely to visit and to buy. They also thought that they had spent less time there than they really had. The study was done in a laboratory with students, and later work suggests that the effect depends on the scent and the setting. Smell is a quiet part of how a place feels.
The tax that the tags revealed

In most American stores, the price on the shelf does not include the sales tax, which is added at the register. Do shoppers take it into account? In 2009 Raj Chetty, Adam Looney and Kory Kroft tested it in a grocery store. For three weeks they posted tags that showed the price with the tax included, for about 750 items in three categories, which were cosmetics, hair care accessories and deodorants.
Using scanner data, they compared the sales of those items with those of similar items, and with other stores. Demand for the tagged items fell by about 8 percent, which is about what a price rise of the size of the tax would do. So most shoppers had not been counting the tax. In a survey, nearly all of them ignored it when estimating the total of a basket, but when the tags were shown, most computed it correctly.

When you pay a toll with cash, you feel it. When a device in your car pays it for you, you hardly notice. In 2009 the economist Amy Finkelstein studied the roads, bridges and tunnels in the United States that adopted electronic toll collection, such as E-ZPass. She compared their toll rates before and after.
After a toll road adopted electronic collection, its toll rates rose. She estimated that in the long run they were 20 to 40 percent higher than they would have been. Drivers became less sensitive to the price, and the officials who set the rates were less affected by the election calendar. The payment had become less visible, so it was easier to raise. It shows how a method of payment can change the price.
When a prize makes you slower

You are given a candle, a box of tacks and a book of matches, and you must fix the candle to a wall so that the wax does not drip on the floor. This is the candle problem, which the psychologist Karl Duncker devised. The solution is to tack the box to the wall and stand the candle in it. Most people are slow to see this, because they think of the box as a container for the tacks, and not as a shelf. It is called functional fixedness.
In 1962 Sam Glucksberg tried the problem with and without cash prizes for speed. In some versions the tacks were inside the box, which made it harder to see the box as a shelf. In those versions the people who were offered prizes did worse than those who were not. Wanting hard to succeed can make us cling to the obvious use of a thing. When the answer needs a new view, a calmer mind may help more than a bigger motive.

A patient has a tumor that cannot be removed by surgery. Rays strong enough to destroy it would also destroy the healthy tissue around it, and weak rays would do nothing to the tumor. What can the doctor do? Duncker posed this puzzle too. The answer is to aim several weak rays at the tumor from different directions, so that they add up only at the tumor.
In 1980 Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak had people read a story first. In it, a general wanted to capture a fortress at the center of a country, but the roads were mined so that a large force could not pass. He divided his army and sent small groups along different roads, so that they met at the fortress. When people were told that the story could help, about three quarters of them solved the tumor problem. Without the hint, far fewer did. We often hold the right idea in memory and fail to see that it applies.

Two cords hang from the ceiling of a room, too far apart for a person to hold one while reaching the other. The task is to tie them together, and there are tools on a table, such as a pair of pliers. In 1931 Norman Maier gave this problem to people. The solution is to tie the pliers to one cord and swing it, then catch it while holding the other cord. Many people were stuck for a long time.
Maier's hint was that the experimenter walked across the room and, in passing, set one of the cords swinging. After that, many solved the problem within a minute. Some said afterward that the idea had come to them all at once, and did not mention the cord. Other researchers argued that the hint was not the only thing that helped, and the details are debated. But it is a good example of how a solution can arrive without our seeing where it came from.

In sports like basketball, golf and shooting, what do the best performers look at, and for how long? In 1996 Joan Vickers tracked the eye movements of basketball players as they shot free throws. The experts fixed their gaze on the target, at the front of the rim, for about a second before they began to shoot, and held it there as the shot began. Players who were good but not elite looked for less than half as long.
Vickers called it the quiet eye. Longer fixations went with more accurate shots, in both groups, and when players missed they had often looked for a shorter time. Later studies tried to train it. Golfers who were taught to hold a steady gaze putted better, and held up better when they were made anxious. The training studies are smaller than the first findings, but the idea is simple. Calm, steady attention at the right moment is a skill that can be learned.
Why a lesson looks easier than it is

When you study a pair of items, such as a word and its meaning, the answer is in front of you. It seems obvious, and you feel that you know it. But at the test, the answer will not be there. In 2005 Asher Koriat and Robert Bjork used word pairs to study this trap, which they called foresight bias. They varied how strongly the first word of a pair brought the second to mind.
Students did not take the strength of the link into account when they predicted how well they would remember. Their predictions were much less sensitive to it than their actual recall was. They were fooled by seeing the answer. The remedy that the authors suggested is to test yourself later, with the answer covered. If you cannot produce the answer, the feeling of knowing it was an illusion, and you know what to study.
Waiting before you judge your reading

After reading a chapter, how well do you know it? People are often poor at judging this. In studies that tested their understanding of texts, their predictions of how well they would do on a test were only weakly related to how they really did. Keith Thiede, John Dunlosky and their colleagues asked whether a small task could make the judgments better.
The task was to write down a few keywords that capture the text. When people did it right after reading, it made no difference. When they did it after a delay, their predictions improved a good deal. The delay seems to matter, because it lets the feeling of having just read fade, and makes you rely on what you can recall. The practical advice is to wait a little, and then check what you can say about what you read, before deciding that you are done.
When searching makes you feel smarter

If you look something up on the Internet, do you know it better, or does it only feel that way? In 2015 Matthew Fisher, Mariel Goddu and Frank Keil asked people to search the Internet for explanations to everyday questions. Then they asked them to rate how well they could explain quite different topics, which they had not searched for. A comparison group did not search.
People who had searched rated themselves as more able to explain the other topics than those who had not. The effect did not appear for people who were shown the same text without searching. It appeared even when the searches failed to find an answer. The authors suggested that we do not keep apart what we know and what we can reach. The risk is that we feel expert, and then find that the connection is down.
What students do when they study alone

Self-testing is among the best ways to learn, but do students use it? In 2009 Jeffrey Karpicke, Andrew Butler and Henry Roediger asked 177 college students how they study. They asked them to list the strategies that they used, and then to rank them.
The most common answer, given by about 84 percent, was to read notes or the textbook again. Fewer students said that they tested themselves, and those who did often spent little time on it. More than half rated rereading as the most important of their strategies. Rereading gives a feeling of fluency, which feels like learning. The authors argued that students choose it because of that illusion, and so they miss the better method.

In the 1970s a group of researchers hired an actor, and introduced him as Dr. Myron Fox, an expert on a topic of mathematics and education. They gave him a lecture to deliver, which was written to be full of double talk and made-up terms. He was charming and he spoke with enthusiasm. His audiences were educators and professionals, and most of them rated the lecture highly. Some said that it was stimulating.
The study was small, and it was not designed like a modern experiment. A later study in 1975 by John Ware and Reed Williams tested the idea with 207 students, who saw six lectures that differed in content and in how seductive the presentation was. Students gave higher ratings to the seductive lectures, and the ratings did not track the content when the style was seductive. A lecturer's charm can be mistaken for how much was taught, and ratings alone do not tell us how much was learned.

Can a short course in mindfulness improve attention and thinking? In 2013 Michael Mrazek and his colleagues at the University of California, Santa Barbara, assigned 48 undergraduates by chance to a two-week class in mindfulness, or to a class on nutrition. Before and after, they tested all of them on a reading section from the Graduate Record Examination, on a working memory task, and on how often their minds wandered.
The students who took the mindfulness class improved on the reading test and on working memory, and they mind-wandered less while they were tested. The students in the nutrition class did not change. The authors found that the better scores came with reduced mind wandering, among students who were prone to wander. The study was small and used students, and a single experiment is not proof. But it fits the idea that attention is a skill, which can be practiced.
The experiment that came in a dream

For a long time scientists argued about how a nerve passes its signal on to the next cell, or to a muscle. Some thought that it was an electrical spark, and others that it was a chemical. By his own account, in 1921 the Austrian pharmacologist Otto Loewi woke in the night with an idea for an experiment that could decide it, scribbled a few notes, and fell asleep again. In the morning he could not read them, and the idea was gone. The next night he dreamed it again, and this time he went straight to his laboratory.
He took two frog hearts, and kept the nerve on one of them. When he stimulated the nerve, the heart slowed. He then took the fluid that had bathed that heart and poured it over the second heart, which also slowed. Something chemical had passed from one to the other. He called it vagus substance, and it was later identified as acetylcholine. In 1936 Loewi shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Henry Dale.
A Nobel Prize for the lobotomy

In 1935 the Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz began to cut the connections between the front of the brain and the rest, to treat severe mental illness. He called it leucotomy. In 1936 the American doctors Walter Freeman and James Watts did the first such operation in the United States, and called it a lobotomy. In 1949 Moniz shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The committee cited the value of the operation in certain psychoses.
In 1946 Freeman began to use a quicker method, which went through the eye socket, and which he took around the country. About 50,000 people had lobotomies in the United States, most in the late 1940s and early 1950s. Some patients calmed. Many were left dull, passive or disabled, such as Rosemary Kennedy, who was operated on in 1941. The practice faded in the 1950s, as drugs for psychosis arrived. It is a warning about a treatment that was widely praised, without proper trials.

Where in the brain is a memory stored? In the 1920s and 1930s the psychologist Karl Lashley trained rats to run mazes, and then cut out different parts of their cortex. The more cortex he removed, the worse the rats did, but it did not seem to matter which part. He concluded that memories are spread across the cortex, and spent years looking for the engram, which is the physical trace of a memory, without finding it.
In 2012 Xu Liu, Steve Ramirez and Susumu Tonegawa tried a new tool. In mice, they marked the cells in a part of the hippocampus that were active while the mice learned to fear a box, and made those cells sensitive to light. Later, in a different box, they switched on the marked cells with a beam of light. The mice froze, as if they were afraid. A small, specific set of cells could bring back a memory. It is now thought that memories are stored by groups of cells that can be located.
The brain map that redrew itself

The surface of the brain has a map of the body. Each patch of the sensory cortex receives touch from one part of the skin, and for the hand, the fingers are laid out in order. For a long time it was thought that this map was fixed in adults. In the early 1980s Michael Merzenich and his colleagues tested that in monkeys. They cut a nerve that brings touch from part of the hand, and later recorded from the cortex.
The patch of cortex that had belonged to the cut nerve did not go silent. Within weeks and months it was taken over by touch from the neighboring skin, and the new map was still orderly. When they removed a finger, the neighboring fingers spread into the empty territory in a similar way. The adult brain can redraw its maps after an injury. The finding opened the study of how experience and damage change the brain, and of recovery after strokes.
The disease of the funeral feast

In the 1950s a fatal disease was killing many of the Fore people, in the highlands of Papua New Guinea. Its name was kuru, which means shaking. Victims lost control of their movements, and died within a year. Many thought that it was inherited. The American doctor Carleton Gajdusek went to the region and, with local people, studied it. He found that it spread through funeral rites, in which relatives handled the bodies of the dead and, in some cases, ate them.
Gajdusek showed in the 1960s that kuru could be passed to chimpanzees, by injecting them with brain tissue, and that it was caused by something that took years to act. He shared the Nobel Prize in 1976. Later Stanley Prusiner proposed that such diseases are caused by a misfolded protein, which he called a prion, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1997. Kuru faded after the rites were given up. It belongs to a family of diseases that includes scrapie in sheep and mad cow disease.
Seeing things that aren't there, in a clear mind

Some people who lose their sight begin to see things that are not there. They may see faces, patterns, people in old-fashioned clothes, or animals. They are not confused, and they know that the pictures are not real. The condition is called Charles Bonnet syndrome, after a Swiss naturalist who wrote in the 1700s about his grandfather, who lost his sight and saw such visions. Many patients keep quiet about it, because they fear that others will think that they are mad.
Estimates of how common it is vary widely, from under one percent to about a third of people with low vision, depending on the study. One analysis of the studies found that about one in five people over forty with low vision had it. The leading idea is that the visual part of the brain, deprived of input, begins to make images of its own. It helps people a great deal to be told what the condition is, and that it is not a sign of madness. It shows that what we see is partly something that the brain builds.
The woman who could not forget

In 2006 the neuroscientists Elizabeth Parker, Larry Cahill and James McGaugh reported a case of a woman whom they called AJ. She could recall an extraordinary number of the days of her life, with the date, the weather and what she had done. The memories came without effort, and she could not turn them off. They were, she said, nonstop, uncontrollable and automatic. She did not use any tricks to remember, as memory champions do.
The scientists named it hyperthymestic syndrome, and it is now called highly superior autobiographical memory. In 2012 Aurora LePort and her colleagues studied eleven people with the ability. They tested them on their memories of their own lives, and on standard tests, and scanned their brains. It is very rare. It shows that the memory for a life can be separate from other kinds of memory, and that remembering everything may be a burden.

Can a single nerve cell be said to represent the number three? In 2002 Andreas Nieder, David Freedman and Earl Miller trained monkeys to judge whether two successive displays had the same number of dots. The numbers ran from one to five. They changed the size and position of the dots from trial to trial, so that the monkeys could not rely on those cues. Then they recorded the activity of 352 neurons in the prefrontal cortex.
Many neurons had a favorite number. A neuron that liked three fired most for three dots, a little less for two or four, and still less for one or five. The tuning was sharper for small numbers than for large ones, which fits the way people and animals find it easier to tell two from three than eight from nine. The finding suggests that a sense of number is built into the brain. It is part of the basis from which human arithmetic grew.

In the early 1900s, the German anatomist Korbinian Brodmann looked at slices of human and animal brains under the microscope. He stained them to show the cells, and noticed that the cortex was not uniform. In some places the layers of cells were thick, and in others thin, and the types of cells differed. He drew lines around the regions that looked alike.
In 1909 he published a map with 52 areas of the human cortex, each with a number. The numbers are still used. Area 17 is the primary visual cortex, area 4 is the primary motor cortex, and areas 44 and 45 are a part of Broca's area. He did not know what each region did, since he had only looked at the cells. Later work with injuries and scans showed that many of his regions do have distinct jobs. His map shows that structure points to function.
The dye that stopped at the brain

In the 1880s the German scientist Paul Ehrlich injected a dye into the blood of animals. The dye stained every organ, except one. The brain stayed pale. Ehrlich thought that the brain simply did not take up the dye. Some years later his student Edwin Goldmann tried the opposite. He injected the dye into the fluid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord. Now the brain was stained, but the rest of the body was not.
The two results together showed that there is a barrier between the blood and the brain. We now know that it is made of tightly joined cells in the walls of the brain's blood vessels. It keeps out many germs and toxins, and it controls what enters. It also makes it hard to get drugs into the brain, which is a difficulty for treating many diseases of the brain. Much of the work in designing such drugs is about finding a way across.
The small word that shows who is in charge

Who is the boss in a conversation? Look at the pronouns. In 2014 Ewa Kacewicz, James Pennebaker and their colleagues reported five studies of how rank shows in the use of small words, such as I, we and you, by people in small groups. They compared people with higher and lower status, whether it was given by their role or arose in the group.
The people with higher status used fewer first-person singular pronouns, such as I, me and my, and more of the others, such as we and you. Pennebaker suggested that people of lower status are more focused on themselves, and those higher up look outward. It is a case in which little words that we hardly notice carry information. It is a tendency in groups, and not a way to judge the rank of one person from a sentence.
Words that give away a lie

Can a computer tell a lie from the words alone? In 2003 Matthew Newman, James Pennebaker and their colleagues asked people to tell the truth and to lie on several topics, in writing and out loud. They used a text program, called LIWC, to count the kinds of words in what they said.
Liars used fewer first-person singular pronouns, such as I and me, fewer words that mark exceptions and distinctions, such as but and except, and more words for negative emotions and for movement. The idea was that a liar keeps a distance from the story, and finds it hard to build complex detail. Later reviews found that these signs are weak, and that they vary with the situation. No list of words works as a lie detector for one person.

Complaining that you are tired of being asked for identification because you look so young is a humblebrag, which is a boast hidden behind a complaint or an act of modesty. In 2018 Ovul Sezer, Francesca Gino and Michael Norton ran nine studies of how it goes over, including a week-long diary study and an experiment in the field.
Humblebraggers were rated as less likable than people who bragged outright, or who simply complained. They were also seen as less competent, and people were less willing to do what they asked. The authors found that observers thought they were insincere. A plain boast at least gets some credit for honesty. If you want people to know about an achievement, it is better to say it simply, or to let someone else say it.

Why do people swear when they hurt themselves? In 2009 Richard Stephens, John Atkins and Andrew Kingston asked 67 students to hold a hand in ice water for as long as they could. On one trial they repeated a swear word of their choice, and on the other a neutral word. Then they compared how long each person lasted, how much it hurt, and their heart rates.
Swearing let people keep their hand in the cold water longer, by about 40 seconds on average, and they rated the pain as lower. Their heart rates went up. The effect was not found in men who tended to think the worst about pain. The authors thought that swearing might trigger a stress response, though they later said they had not shown that. It won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2010, and it is a small study, but it is a rare one that backs a common habit.
Is public speaking feared more than death?

It is a famous joke that people fear speaking in public more than death. It comes from a 1973 survey by a company called Bruskin, in which people picked their fears from a list. In 2012 Kathleen Dwyer and Marlina Davidson repeated the survey with 815 college students. They asked them in two ways.
When students were asked to check all of their fears from a list, public speaking was the one that they checked most often, and death came further down. But when they were asked to rank their top fears, death came first, and public speaking second, though not by much. The answer depends on how you ask. Fear of speaking is very common, and a lot of people also dread being judged. It is not that they would rather die.
The five parts of a speech

About two thousand years ago, a Roman teacher wrote a handbook for speakers. We do not know his name. The book is called Rhetorica ad Herennium, and for centuries it was believed to be by Cicero. It lists five tasks of a speaker. They are invention, which is finding what to say, arrangement, which is putting it in order, and style, which is choosing the words. The other two are memory, and delivery, which covers the voice and gestures.
The list was taken up by Cicero and later teachers, and it is still a good checklist. Most poor talks fail at one of the five. A talk with good content may be hard to follow because it is not arranged, or flat because it is read aloud in a monotone. The handbook also gives the earliest surviving description of the memory method of placing images of what you want to say in familiar places.

Around AD 95 the Roman teacher Quintilian completed the Institutio Oratoria, a work in twelve books on how to educate an orator, from childhood on. His ideal, which he took from an older saying of Cato, was a good man skilled in speaking. He argued that skill without character is dangerous, because a speaker who is persuasive and dishonest does harm.
He also gave practical advice. He thought that teachers should be kind, that children learn through play, and that they should not be beaten. He wrote that a speaker should read widely, and write a lot, since writing is the best way to improve speaking. His book was lost for a time, and was found again in 1416, in a monastery in Switzerland, by an Italian scholar, Poggio Bracciolini. It then shaped the schools of the Renaissance.

In 1958 the philosopher Stephen Toulmin argued that everyday arguments do not look like the neat syllogisms of logic textbooks, and he gave a pattern for the parts of a good one. The claim is what you want people to accept. The grounds are the facts that you offer for it. The warrant is the rule that links the grounds to the claim.
The other parts are the backing, which supports the rule, the qualifier, which says how strong the claim is, and the rebuttal, which names the conditions under which it would fail. His example was Harry, who was born in Bermuda, and so is presumably a British subject, unless both of his parents were aliens. It is useful to ask of any argument what the warrant is. It is usually the part that is left unsaid, and it is often where the argument is weak.
Fifty years of advice about the passive

Many people were taught that the passive voice is weak and should be avoided. The advice goes back at least to The Elements of Style, by William Strunk and E. B. White, which tells writers to use the active voice. In 2009 the linguist Geoffrey Pullum wrote a sharp essay, arguing that the authors did not understand what a passive is. He noted that most of the examples that they gave of the passive in their rule were not passives.
Strunk and White did not ask that the passive be banned. They wrote that it is frequently convenient and sometimes necessary. Pullum's critics said that he was too harsh, and that the real aim of the advice was to avoid limp writing. The lesson is that a rule of thumb about writing should be tested against real sentences. The passive is useful, for example, when you want the object of an action to come first.
Stress and the speed of healing

Can an argument slow the healing of a cut? In 2005 Janice Kiecolt-Glaser and her colleagues at Ohio State University invited married couples to the laboratory, where a small blister was raised on each person's arm. Then the couples spent time talking, once about a topic that caused conflict and once about a way in which they supported each other. The researchers checked the blisters each day, and measured chemical signals of inflammation in the blood.
The wounds healed more slowly after the conflict than after the support talk. The effect was greatest in the couples who were most hostile in their talk. Their wounds healed at about 60 percent of the rate of the others, and they had higher levels of a signal of inflammation called IL-6. A study in 1995 found that women caring for a relative with dementia took about 24 percent longer to heal a standard wound. The samples were small, but they show that stress and conflict can reach the body.
The five stages that were not a map

In 1969 the psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross wrote that people who are dying pass through five stages. They are denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. The idea was soon applied to people who are grieving, and it became one of the best known ideas in psychology. Many people have been told that they should expect to pass through the stages, in order, and have worried when their own grief did not fit.
The model rested on limited evidence, which was a series of interviews. Kübler-Ross herself later said that the stages are not a linear or predictable progression. George Bonanno followed people from before they were bereaved, and found that the most common pattern was resilience, in which people grieved but kept functioning. Longer and more severe grief affected a minority, perhaps one in ten. Grief does not come in a fixed order, and there is no single right way to do it.

What makes people satisfied at work, and what makes them unhappy? In the 1950s the psychologist Frederick Herzberg and his colleagues interviewed 203 engineers and accountants in Pittsburgh. They asked each person to recall a time when they felt exceptionally good about their job, and a time when they felt exceptionally bad, and to say what had caused it.
The good times were linked to achievement, recognition, interesting work and responsibility, which he called motivators. The bad times were linked to things like company policy, supervision, pay and working conditions, which he called hygiene factors. His point was that removing a cause of unhappiness does not create satisfaction. Critics noted that people tend to credit themselves for good events and blame their surroundings for bad ones, and later studies using other methods did not find the clean split. Still, the idea has shaped how managers think.

In 1960 the management professor Douglas McGregor described two sets of beliefs that managers hold about their workers. He called them Theory X and Theory Y. A manager who holds Theory X believes that people dislike work, avoid responsibility, and have to be controlled, directed and threatened. A manager who holds Theory Y believes that people find work natural, will direct themselves toward goals that they accept, and will seek responsibility.
His main argument was that a manager's beliefs shape what happens. A manager who assumes the worst will supervise closely, and workers will do just what they are told, which seems to prove the belief. A manager who assumes the best will give people freedom, and most will repay it. McGregor offered it as a way of thinking, and not as a result of experiments, and it has been criticized as too simple. But it is a useful question to ask about oneself.

Why do people put effort into some tasks, and not others? In 1964 the psychologist Victor Vroom proposed that a person asks three questions, usually without being aware of it. Can I do it, if I try, which is expectancy. If I do it, will I get a reward, which is instrumentality. And do I care about the reward, which is valence. The motivation is the product of the three, so if any one of them is zero, the motivation is zero.
It explains why a bonus does not work if people think they cannot reach it, or if they do not trust that it will be paid, or if they do not value it. Studies have found that the three parts do predict effort, though not very strongly. It is a useful checklist for anyone who wants to understand why a person is not trying. Often the answer is that one of the three questions has a no for an answer.
Three styles of leading a club

In 1938 the psychologist Kurt Lewin and his students at the University of Iowa set up after-school clubs for ten-year-old boys, who made masks and did other crafts. Each club had an adult leader who had been trained to lead in one of three ways. The authoritarian leader gave orders and decided everything. The democratic leader let the group discuss and choose. The laissez-faire leader gave almost no direction.
The boys under the authoritarian leader were either passive and obedient, or hostile to one another, and work tended to stop when the leader left the room. The boys in the democratic club were friendlier, and kept working when the leader was away. The clubs were few and small, and the study is better known than it is rigorous. But it was among the first experiments to show that the style of a leader changes how a group behaves.
Why some people go along, and some agree

When people change their behavior because of someone else, are they changing their minds? In 1958 the psychologist Herbert Kelman said that there are three different processes, and that they have different effects. The first is compliance, in which a person goes along to gain a reward or avoid a punishment. They show it in public, but they do not believe it, and they stop when no one is watching.
The second is identification, in which a person adopts a view in order to be like someone they admire, or to keep a relationship. It lasts as long as the relationship does. The third is internalization, in which the person accepts the view because it fits their own values, and it lasts without any outside support. It matters because if you want a lasting change in someone, pressure and charm are weaker than reasons that they can make their own.
Six parts of a good life

Is a good life the same as a happy one? In 1989 the psychologist Carol Ryff argued that well-being has more parts than a feeling of pleasure. She went through writings of philosophers and psychologists, and from them she drew six dimensions. They are self-acceptance, positive relations with others, autonomy, mastery of one's surroundings, purpose in life, and personal growth.
She built a questionnaire for them, which has been used with thousands of people in many countries. People can score high on one dimension and low on another, so they do not always go together. Her findings include that purpose and personal growth tend to drop in older age, while mastery of one's surroundings and autonomy rise. The scale gives us a way to ask more questions than how happy a person feels.
What the policemen did at Józefów

On the morning of July 13, 1942, in the Polish village of Józefów, the men of Reserve Police Battalion 101 were told by their commander, Major Wilhelm Trapp, that they were to round up the Jews of the village. The men were mostly middle-aged, from Hamburg, and not trained soldiers. Trapp, who was visibly distressed, then did something unusual. He offered that any older man who did not feel up to the task could step out.
Only a small number stepped out. Most of the others took part in the killing of some 1,500 people that day. The historian Christopher Browning, in his book Ordinary Men, argued that the men were not fanatics, and that the forces at work included conformity, pressure from comrades, deference to authority and ambition. Other historians, such as Daniel Goldhagen, argued that antisemitism was the main cause. It remains one of the most studied cases of how ordinary people do terrible things.
